### THE POSSESSED

->A N D<-
## NIGHTLY TERRORS:

->THAT IS, THREE BOOKS, IN WHICH THE KINDS AND CONDITIONS<-
->*of spirits who besiege and infest humans are explained, as well as the troubles they bring,*<-

->*it is possible to be freed from those same troubles.*<-

->BY THE AUTHOR PETER THYRÆUS OF NEUSS,<- <note>original: "Petro Thyræo Novesiano." Neuss (Novesia) was his birthplace in the Rhineland.</note>

<meta>This page serves as the formal dedication for a combined edition of two works on demonology by Petrus Thyraeus. It follows the title page and addresses the high-ranking ecclesiastical figures of the region, establishing the religious and political authority behind the publication.</meta>

# TO THE MOST REVEREND
# FATHER IN CHRIST, THE MOST
# ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE AND LORD,
## LORD JULIUS, BISHOP OF WÜRZBURG,
<note>original: "Herbipolensi". Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn (1545–1617) was a dominant figure of the Counter-Reformation in Germany.</note> Duke of East Franconia, <term>Maecenas</term><note>A reference to Gaius Maecenas, the Roman patron of the arts; here it signifies a generous financial supporter of scholarship.</note> and Patron of Studies.

# LIKEWISE TO THE MOST RELIGIOUS AND
## VERY REVEREND MEN,
### HIERONYMUS IN EBRACH,
### MICHAEL IN BILDHAUSEN,
### WIGAND IN BRONNBACH,
Abbots and Prelates of the monasteries of the same East Franconia, of the noble <term>Order of Saint Bernard of Cîteaux</term><note>The Cistercian Order.</note>, lords to be most highly respected.
->F. P. & O. B.<-
<note>These initials likely represent a formal dedicatory formula, such as "Fidelitatem precatur & obsequium beadum" (Prays for faithfulness and blessed obedience).</note>

<image-desc>A decorative historiated drop cap 'Q' featuring a seated cleric or saint figure, possibly in a monastic setting, holding a staff.</image-desc>

Those books titled *On the Possessed* and *On Haunted Places*, which first saw the light of day under your august names, most Reverend Prince and most religious Fathers, now look toward a second and, as it were, a new light, supported by that same protection. For they come now, not separated as before, but in a slightly different form, both joined into a single volume. I have done this, not out of fear that the protection I felt sufficiently from the authority of each of you in the first edition would be lacking, but led both by the similarity of the subject matter and for the convenience of the reader. 

The subject of both works was nearly the same, dealing chiefly with the deep-rooted malice of demons by which they plague humans; they are harmful sometimes by slipping into bodies <note>Referring to demonic possession.</note>, and sometimes by entering into our houses and dwellings <note>Referring to hauntings or infestations.</note>. They do both for no other end than to attack and harass wretched mortals, whom they bitterly hate. This double wickedness required a double remedy: or rather, a "kinship" of wickedness, so to speak, required a remedy either single or joined together. Indeed, the reader has demanded this union above all: because if they found anything lacking in one work, they did not wish—nor indeed should they have had to—look for it anywhere more quickly or conveniently than from its companion, just as from a [neighbor...]
<note>The text cuts off here as the catchword "pro." indicates the next page begins with "propinquo" (neighbor/relative).</note>

<summary>This page contains a formal dedication by the author to Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn, Bishop of Würzburg, and three Cistercian abbots, explaining that his two previously separate treatises on possession and haunted houses are now being published as a single combined volume.</summary>
<keywords>Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn, Würzburg, Cistercians, demonology, possession, haunted houses, patronage, Counter-Reformation</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the formal dedication begun on the previous page, where Peter Thyraeus explains his decision to combine his two major works on demonology—one on possession and one on haunted houses—into a single volume. This page includes his signature and a celebratory poem by a contemporary praising the book’s power to dispel the "shadows" of error and superstition.</meta>

...to bring forth from a nearby storehouse; especially since one provides mutual aid to the other in such a way that, with joined forces, it supplies from both sides the evidence to expose the enemy and the arguments to refute them. Therefore, for the sake of this purpose, I pray again and again that those works which now return to the public joined together may be recommended by your combined and, as it were, doubled favor.

At Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipoli"</note>, from the College of the Society of Jesus <note>The Jesuits</note>, on the eve of the Kalends of January <note>December 31st</note> in the year 1601.

Peter Thyraeus, of the Society of Jesus.

# POEM
## ON THIS THIRD EDITION CONCERNING THE POSSESSED AND HAUNTED PLACES.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'T' with floral scrolling patterns begins the poem.</image-desc>

*Thyraeus shines forth for the third time,*
*For the third time he puts to flight the oncoming darkness:*
*Whether that which ignorant Error casts in our way,*
*Or that which presses upon harmful hearts—*
*The nurse of sacrilege and parent of [false] worship,*
*Perverse Religion* <note>In the context of the Counter-Reformation, Thyraeus is likely referring to Protestantism or folk superstitions as "perverse religion."</note>; *or Fear, that executioner*
*Brooding over the mind, who, terrified by the flashing torch*
*Of Learning, sucks back those shadows*
*Which Tartarus* <note>A classical term for the underworld or Hell.</note> *was just now vomiting forth.*
*From this light flee the household spirits* <note>original: "Lares"</note>, *the Furies* <note>original: "Erinnes"</note>,
*The face of Panic, the little familiar spirits* <note>original: "Paredri homulli"; these were minor demons or spirits believed to serve a person.</note>,
*Those seeds of terror:*
*Suddenly, everything belonging to them everywhere vanishes,*
*While you, Thyraeus, raise your torches again,*
*While you again put to flight the impious darkness.*

H.A.V.V.

# TABLE OF CONTENTS OR INDEX OF THE BOOKS CONCERNING THE POSSESSED, HAUNTED PLACES, AND NIGHTLY TERRORS:

->With brief summaries.<-

---

## THE FIRST BOOK CONCERNING THE POSSESSED,
consists of four parts: in the first of which, the nature of the possessing demons, their operations, their power over the possessed, and likewise the ways in which they afflict humans, etc., are explained.

---

### Chapter one of the first part.
That demons truly enter 
human beings and possess 
them, which is taught by:
*Sensory experience.*
*The history of past times.*
*The opinion of the Jews.*
*The judgment of Christ, in many ways.*
*The example of the Apostles.*

---

### Chapter two.
That for the possession of humans 
by demons, two things are 
necessary; namely, that 
*The demons be within the humans themselves:*
*and then that they have power over them.*
*They are within, indeed:*
*not as accidents in subjects.* <note>In the Aristotelian philosophy used by the author, an "accident" is a quality (like "redness") that cannot exist without a "subject" (like an apple). Thyraeus is arguing that a demon is a distinct entity, not just a quality of the person.</note>
*not as parts in their wholes.*
*not as nature in its own individual substances.* <note>original: "suppositis"</note>
*but, as movers in things moved.*

<column-break/>

*Their power consists*
*in the torture and distress which they bring.*

---

### Chapter three.
That demons are not within 
humans in an external and 
visible form, although they 
may sometimes be seen in 
an external form.
*That it is always possible, however:*
*it is taught that they sometimes are,*
*and the reasoning regarding the flies and spiders* <note>Early modern accounts of exorcism frequently describe the possessed vomiting or seeing insects, which were believed to be physical manifestations of the demonic presence.</note> *which are sometimes noted during possession.*

---

### Chapter four.
What demons are able to do 
to bodies and to souls while 
they possess humans.
*Bodies*
*they afflict in wondrous ways.*
*Souls*

# INDEX

*They cannot transform into the forms of beasts:*
*they cannot deprive humans of their innate faculties:*
*they cannot strip away their habits:* <note>original: "habitibus." In the Scholastic philosophy used by Thyraeus, a "habit" is a stable quality or disposition of the soul, such as a virtue or a skill, rather than just a repetitive behavior.</note>
*they cannot force those who resist to act.*
*But they can hinder the exercise of virtues:*
*they can incline the will:*
*they can deprive humans of sensory comforts:*
*they can weaken the strength of habits.*

### Chapter five.

->How great the power of Demons is over the bodies of the Possessed. The answer is given:<-

*that it is finite, and they cannot do as much as they wish;*
*and that this finite power is granted by God for just causes, namely:*
*so that God’s goodness toward humans may be evident:*
*so that the Possessed do not lose heart;*
*so that the wicked Spirits themselves may be confounded;*
*and so that it may be understood that sin is voluntary.*

---

### Chapter six.

->Sixfold evils are brought upon Possessed humans by Demons, namely:<-

*internal torments:*
*deprivation of the senses:*
*transformation of the natural form:*
*corruption of the imagination:* <note>original: "phantasiae." In early modern psychology, the "phantasy" or imagination was considered a physical faculty of the brain that processed and stored sensory images.</note>
*extreme distress of the soul:*

<column-break/>

*death of the body.*

---

### Chapter seven.

->That Demons bring trouble to the bodies of the Possessed in roughly five ways: namely,<-

*by the bewitching of the senses and the imagination:*
*by the weakening of human strength:*
*by the corruption of the organs:*
*by the distortion of the limbs:*
*by the physical driving of the body.*

---

### Chapter eight.

->That Demons neither always trouble the Possessed, nor are they always present with them: but nevertheless,<-

*the former happens more frequently:*
*the latter happens more rarely:*
*both are also within their own power:*
*and the former occurs through God’s providence, human weakness, and the demons’ wickedness.*
*The latter occurs mostly by the will of the Demons.*

---

### Chapter nine.

->Through which part do the wicked Spirits enter humans? It is taught that<-

*they sometimes enter through the mouth:*
*they enter through other passages as well:*
*they even penetrate the bodies themselves.*

---

## Chapter eleven.
That demons sometimes reveal their entry into humans by certain signs:
*such as, primarily,*
*the display of a horrific form:*
*the stirring up of disturbances:*
*the infliction of trouble:*
*wondrous visions in sleep:*
*And by these and similar signs they reveal their entry,*
*in emulation of God:* <note>original: "aemulatione Dei." The idea that the devil mimics God's actions—such as divine manifestations—to deceive people or mock the divine.</note>
*in imitation of the Angels:*
*by the command of God:*
*due to the condition of humans:*
*yet they have no need for these signs:*
*often, indeed, no signs at all intervene.*

## Chapter twelve.
Of which Orders the demons who possess humans belong to, and how this may be known.
*For an order among them is required by*
*their own natural condition:*
*divine wisdom:*

<column-break/>

*their own zeal for doing harm. But*
*those who are troublesome*
*are of the lowest order:*
*nevertheless, not these alone.*
*There are also those of the highest order:*
*and sometimes the highest of the highest order.* <note>original: "in supremo summus." Thyraeus refers to the "Orders" or hierarchies of angels (like Seraphim or Cherubim). He argues that even the highest-ranking fallen angels can possess a person.</note>
*Yet you would say with difficulty what kind*
*occupy the person. It is likely they may be detected*
->those who<-
*are of the superior orders*
*from the severity of the evils that are brought:*
*from their difficult departure from the humans:*
*from confession extorted by exorcists.*

---

## Chapter thirteen.
That several demons are sometimes in a human. This is established:
*by the example of Scripture:* <note>Likely referring to the biblical account of "Legion," the man possessed by many spirits at once (Mark 5:9).</note>
*by natural reason:*
*and that most often there are several in the Possessed.*
*Demons also delight in this fellowship.*
*it is difficult to say whether there are several, and how many there are.*

---

Whether several Spirits torment more: and whether individuals bring the same torments to the Possessed; it is taught:
*that many torment more:*
*that all who are in the human torment him:*
*that the same evils are sometimes brought by several:*

### Chapter fifteen.
Concerning the ends—or purposes—which are set for demons in the possession of humans. It is taught:
*that demons are not freed from their own punishments by doing this;* <note>original: "non per hoc à suis pænis liberari." Medieval and Early Modern theologians argued that even while possessing a human on Earth, demons still suffer the fires of Hell.</note>
*that they enter in order to cause trouble and torment;*
*that the cause of this is hatred toward humans, which arises:*
*from a hatred of God;*
*from envy of human happiness;*
*from envy of the salvation of those same humans;*
*that they also enter out of pride, and to seek divine honors.* <note>original: "diuinosque honores aucupandos." This refers to the belief that demons desire to be worshiped as gods, as they were in pagan antiquity.</note>

---

### Chapter sixteen.
Whether, and who, can send demons into humans. It is taught:
*that God can send them;*
*that the Devil can send them;*
*that holy men can send them;*
*that evil men can send them;*
*but nevertheless, in different ways.* <note>The author distinguishes between God's "permissive" or "just" will and the "malicious" intent of a sorcerer or the Devil.</note>

---

### Chapter seventeen.
Concerning the various operations of demons in the possessed, and to whom they should be attributed.
*Some operations belong properly to the demons, arising from their own*

<column-break/>

*intellect and will;*
*also those operations by which they bring torment to the possessed;*
*those which exceed human strength;* <note>original: "humanas vires superant." Manifestations of superhuman strength were a primary diagnostic sign used by the Church to distinguish true possession from natural illness.</note>
*very often also the speech of the possessed, about which more will be said.*

### Chapter eighteen.
Whether Catechumens <note>People receiving instruction in Christianity but not yet baptized.</note> and those not yet baptized may be possessed by a demon.
*that demons have some power over them,*
*both in life and in death;* <note>original: "in vita & in morte." The OCR text "invita" is a common error for "in vita."</note>
*yet they are not truly "possessed" in the strict sense;*
*nonetheless, exorcism is rightly applied to them.*

---

### Chapter nineteen.
Whether witches and sorcerers are possessed by demons. It is taught:
*that not all of them are possessed;*
*that their condition is worse than that of the possessed;* <note>The "possessed" were often seen as innocent victims, whereas "witches" (sagæ) were seen as voluntary collaborators with the Devil.</note>
*that nothing can be concluded from the trial of cold water, etc.* <note>original: "probatione Aquæ frigidæ." This refers to the 'swimming test' where an accused person was thrown into water; if they floated, they were deemed guilty. Thyraeus is skeptical of this folk practice.</note>

## Chapter twenty-seven.

### Chapter twenty-six.
Whether, and what form distinguishes human Spirits from appearing Demons.
*Human form does not distinguish between the two: because it is common to both: even to Demons for many reasons.*
*The form of beasts and monsters distinguishes them: because it is specific to Demons: and this for just causes.*
*It is also likely that the human form distinguishes them—specifically that which has no flaw—by reason of some part, or color, or clothing <note>original: "habitus"; this can refer to a person's physical bearing or the garments they appear to be wearing.</note>, or size, because it betrays Demons if it has a flaw.*

---

### Chapter twenty-seven.
Whether and which noises distinguish human spirits from the Spirits of Demons.
*Those do not distinguish which are characteristic of the living and are bare sounds: either articulate or inarticulate: which are indicators of concepts:*

<column-break/>

*or high-pitched and low-pitched: or violent and light: or obscure and clear.*
But these do distinguish: those which recall monsters and beasts: and those which occur with great tumult; these almost always prove the presence of Demons.
Those also distinguish which are certain signs of a sad soul: these generally belong to humans.

---

### Chapter twenty-eight.
Whether, and what speech distinguishes human and Demonic Spirits.
*Openly evil speech does not distinguish these Spirits: because it is common to both.*
*Speech encouraging good does not distinguish: because that too is common to both.*
*Speech full of vanity does not distinguish: for the same reason.*
*Speech that reveals hidden things <note>original: "occultorum revelatrix"; the ability to know secrets or future events was often considered a "tell" for a demonic entity rather than a human soul.</note> distinguishes them: because it belongs to Demons alone.*

---

### Chapter twenty-nine.
Whether from the troubles and evils which are inflicted by Spirits, it can be discerned whether they are spirits of men or of Demons.
The following strongly indicate Demons:
*death brought about by the Spirit,*
*wounds inflicted,*
*severe beatings,*
*great damage done to property and resources <note>original: "facultatibus"; referring to a person's wealth, livestock, or physical possessions.</note>.*
*If there are any others, they do not distinguish them in the same way.*

# THE FIRST PART

A 2

<meta>catchword: Iudæo-</meta>

# OF THE DISPUTATION, IN WHICH
## THE CONDITION, OPERATIONS, AND
### power of possessing demons over the possessed; likewise the ways in which they afflict men, and similar matters, are explained.

## CHAPTER I.

->*That demons truly enter certain men and possess them.*<-

<margin>9.</margin>
The first Chapter, which is to be treated in this part of the Disputation, supplies a very great and rich amount of material. For it is asked, whether demons truly <term>possess</term> <note>original: "obsideant," the root of the word "obsession." In the 16th and 17th centuries, "obsession" often referred to the demon's presence within the body, which we now usually call "possession."</note> men: and what that state might be. It is asked, how they possess them; and what they effect and work within the possessed men. It is asked, by what part they enter; and having already entered, where they hide. Furthermore, from which <term>Orders</term> <note>This refers to the "Celestial Hierarchy," the idea that angels and demons are organized into different ranks or classes, such as Thrones, Dominions, or Powers.</note> they come who are occupied in this kind of work; likewise, how many enter one man, and by whose command. Finally, for what purposes they possess and torture wretched mortals.

**10.** That evil spirits enter and possess men cannot be denied by anyone who does not think their own senses are untrustworthy, nor believes that all history of past times should be denied, and that the contents of the Sacred Scriptures should be called into doubt.

**11.** We see quite often certain people tormented by demons, presenting an image of human misery and a clear example of diabolical cruelty. We see these same people liberated from the demons by the power of Christ. We see the inhabitation of the Devil in men, and his departure from men, confirmed by such evidence that a wise person could not ask for anything greater.

**12.** How many past centuries supply examples here? We recount none: because we do not know which ones ought to be preferred over others. There is scarcely any Saint famous for the performance of divine miracles who does not provide proof of this, either by the extraction of demons from bodies, or through written books, or by some other means.

**13.** But the Sacred Scriptures confirm this matter excellently. They show that this was a very widely accepted opinion among the Jews, so that they believed men could be possessed by demons. They teach that Christ the Lord thought no differently, and that He provided great arguments in favor of this. They demonstrate that in later times the Devil would use this power against men. Finally, they prove that the Apostles were a terror to the demons in possessed men, and commanded their departure.

# PART I. OF THE DISPUTATION.

14. The opinion of the Jews is revealed by their own speech, in which they reproach Christ the Lord with the highest insult, claiming that he has a demon. They say, "Do we not say well that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?" <note>original: "Nonne bene dicimus nos, quia Samaritanus es tu, & dæmonium habes?" (John 8:48). To be called a Samaritan was a grave ethnic and religious insult to a Jew of that era.</note> From this perspective comes that other claim of theirs: "He casts out demons by the prince of demons" <note>original: "In principe dæmoniorum eijcit dæmonia."</note>; and also: "Why do you listen to him? He has a demon." And so spoke the enemies of Christ—men who were otherwise not ignorant. Those who brought <term>demoniacs</term> <note>People believed to be inhabited or possessed by evil spirits.</note> to Christ to be cured shared this same understanding.

<margin>Matt. 17.</margin>
15. Christ’s own judgment is first declared by the rule or method which he wished to be observed in casting out certain demons, which is: that fasting be joined with prayer. He says, "This kind of demon is not cast out except by fasting and prayer." <note>original: "Hoc genus dæmoniorum non eijcitur nisi in ieiunio & oratione." (Matthew 17:21).</note> It is further declared by his calm response to the aforementioned slanders and accusations. For he does not deny that it is possible for devils to enter men (by which response he could have easily pushed away every insult); rather, he admits that it can happen. He only denies that he himself is possessed or occupied by them; he denies that he casts out demons by <term>Beelzebub</term>, the Prince of demons.

<margin>Matt. 12. 15. 17.</margin>
<margin>MARK 1. 3. 5. 7. 9.</margin>
16. A greater argument than these is that he drove many demons out of human bodies while he lived his common life with us on earth. He did this not in one place, but in many; in various ways, and not by a single method for everyone. The demons themselves also cried out and testified that force was being used against them and that they were being driven from their dwellings and seats <note>The "dwellings" here refer to the human bodies the demons had inhabited.</note>.

<margin>Luke 4. 8. 9. 11.</margin>
<margin>MARK 3.</margin>
<margin>Matt. 7.</margin>
<margin>Mark 16.</margin>
17. He also announced that in later and following times, demons would have this power over human bodies. When was this? While he was sending the Apostles into the whole world with the power to conquer demons; while he taught that those would come on the last day who would want the way to heaven open to them because they had cast out demons; and while he asserted that his doctrine would be confirmed throughout the entire world by the expulsion of demons from possessed bodies. He said: "These signs will follow those who believe: In my name they will cast out demons, they will speak with new tongues, etc." <note>Original: "Signa eos, qui crediderint, hæc sequentur: In nomine meo dæmonia eijcient, linguis loquentur nouis, &c." (Mark 16:17).</note>

<margin>Luke 10.</margin>
18. To this consensus of the Jews, and to the deeds, judgment, and promises of Christ, is added the example of the Apostles. The power of casting out demons was given to them by the Lord. And that demons were indeed cast out by them is declared by their own speech: "Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name." <note>original: "Domine, etiam in nomine tuo subijciuntur nobis dæmonia." (Luke 10:17).</note>

19. No one desires more arguments for this matter. Perhaps so many have been brought by us, especially in such a clear matter, that they are troublesome. Nevertheless, they should not be troublesome, both because they are from the Sacred Scriptures, whose authority is greatest...

# ON DEMONIACS.

<meta>Handwritten "23" in top right corner; catchword "iuis" (the start of "iuxta" or "iuisset" on the next page) at bottom right.</meta>
A 3

19. ...arguments are of the greatest importance; they are sought out because they are perhaps necessary to address those who believe men suffer from "natural diseases"—of what sort I do not know—when they are actually being possessed and tormented by demons. Among these people, Levinus Lemnius <note>Levinus Lemnius (1505–1568) was a famous Dutch physician. In his work *The Secret Miracles of Nature*, he often tried to find medical explanations for behavior that others attributed to the devil.</note> holds a prominent place in Book 2 of *On the Secret Wonders of Nature*, chapter 2.

20. The rashness of these people can be refuted by the arguments already stated. One might also ask them: since they believe these are merely diseases, how can they explain people who predict the future; who report distant things as if they were present; or who speak in foreign tongues? <note>These three abilities—clairvoyance, remote viewing, and xenoglossy (speaking unknown languages)—were traditionally considered the "signs" of true possession as opposed to mental illness.</note> Are these the effects of natural diseases? By no means. They are the works of demons who lie hidden within humans. But there is no need for more words on this. It is established that demons are able to enter human bodies and possess men. Now let us pursue the remaining points.

## CHAPTER II.

->*That two things are necessary for the possession of humans by demons.*<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a decorative floral and foliage design.</image-desc>
21. As happens in other matters—where we may know that things exist, yet remain largely ignorant of what they actually are—the same occurs for many with this subject. They know, of course, that demons possess certain men, yet they do not know what that possession actually is, or in what way the logic of "possession" consists. These things, therefore, must be investigated.

22. I would say that two things are generally necessary. One is that the demons must be *inside* the humans themselves. The other is that they must have received a certain *power* over those same people. If either of these is missing, we cannot rightly say that the men are possessed by demons.

<margin>Matthew 13, 15, 17, and 1.</margin>
23. Both of these conditions can be gathered from those who are described as "possessed" in the Holy Scriptures. The first is proved by the fact that demons are said to have "entered" men and to have been "cast out" of them. The second is proved by the fact that they tormented them: they made them mute, blind, and deaf; they threw them now into the water, now into the fire; and they drove them through fields and mountains. These things are not properly described if the demons were not *inside* the men, and these actions fully confirm that the demons held some *power* over the possessed.

24. Furthermore, regarding that first condition, it is not enough for demons to be "in" humans in the same way that things are said to be "somewhere" when only their influence is present or they are merely working from a distance. Demons are present and "inside" many things in that way, yet no one would call those things "possessed." It is required that they be present and inside truly and <term>in their own person</term> <note>original Greek: αυτοπροςώπως (*autoproposopos*), meaning physically or personally present, rather than just acting through an effect.</note>.

52. However, because the ways in which some things are "inside" others vary—for some things are inside as qualities of their subjects, and some as parts—

<summary>The author refutes the idea that possession is merely a natural disease, citing supernatural signs like speaking in tongues. He defines true possession as requiring both the physical presence of the demon within the body and the demon's exercise of power over the person.</summary>

### PART I. DISPUTATION.
<meta>catchword: defi- (likely leading to the word "defining" or "definition" on the next page)</meta>

...within their wholes; some as complete and absolute things placed under something else; and some as **movers** within the things they move) in what way should we believe demons are within possessed humans?

26. They are not present as **accidents** <note>In traditional philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that cannot exist by itself, such as a color or a feeling. The author is arguing that a demon is an independent "substance," not just a temporary state of the person.</note> within their subjects. For these Spirits are not accidents; they are true and complete substances, and are thus more perfect than all these lower, earthly things.

27. They are not present as parts within their wholes and composites. Shall we say a possessing demon is some part of a human? Which part, I ask? The body or the soul? For a human consists of these many parts, and no more. No one would say it takes the place of the body; it is impossible for it to take the place of the soul unless we say the soul first departs the body—and thus the human himself ceases to be—before the demon arrives. Even then, you could not truly call the demon a "part" of the human.

21. <note>Likely a typographical error for 28 in the original printing sequence.</note> It should also not be believed that two complete natures come together here and are received into a single **hypostasis** <note>original: "hypostasi." In theology, this refers to the fundamental reality or "personhood" that supports a nature. The author is arguing that the demon and human do not merge into a single "person."</note>. In Christ the Lord alone does one hypostasis receive two natures, the human and the divine. This He claims as His own by divine arrangement. Furthermore, which hypostasis would support which nature besides its own here? Would the human's support the demon? Or the demon's support the human? But before the demons enter the human, the demon has its own hypostasis and the human has his own; and just as a human will never abandon his own, neither will the demons ever abandon theirs.

29. Therefore, in the humans they possess, demons are present like **movers** within the bodies they move. They act in such a way that they impart no quality to the human body, give it no new "being," and do not—strictly speaking—form a single entity with the possessed human.

<margin>Chapters 5, 6</margin>
30. This is one of the two things we said are necessary for humans to be called "possessed" by demons. However, this is not enough; it is further required that they have received some power over those in whom they reside, so that they can afflict, torture, or affect them with some other trouble. But since more must be said about this power elsewhere, we conclude this present Chapter here, after adding two points as a corollary.

<margin>Job 1; Athanasius in *The Life of Anthony*</margin>
31. The first is that it follows from what has been said that not everyone who suffers grave persecutions from demons should be called "possessed"—I do not mean only in the soul or in external goods, but even in the body itself. How much did the most holy Job suffer in his body from demons? How much did Saint Anthony? How much did many other Saints? Shall we say they were possessed by demons for that reason? Since the first of the things we called necessary here...

...is lacking; that is, because in those cases the demons did not take up their seats within them, but being placed outside them, caused these evils to flow in, they should by no means be called Possessed.

32. The second point is that many should not be called Possessed, even those into whom the devil himself has entered. After receiving the morsel <note>original: "buccellam." This refers to the biblical account of the Last Supper where Satan entered Judas Iscariot after he took a piece of bread.</note>, the devil entered into Judas, as sacred history attests; yet we would not easily say that Judas was Possessed. Why is this? Because it is not enough for a demon to have entered a man for him to be called Possessed; it is required, furthermore, that it has obtained from God the power of acting or raging within him.

## CHAPTER III.

->*Demons do not exist within humans under an external and visible form, although they are sometimes seen under the appearance of spiders and flies.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' containing a miniature scene of a figure seated in a landscape with a tree.</image-desc>
We have said that two things are required for humans to be called possessed by demons: first, that the demons themselves are within the humans; second, that they have received a certain power over the humans. But since both can happen in various ways, a question arises regarding each. In the first case, it is asked whether they are within humans under a visible form and bodily appearance; in the second, what and how much power they receive over humans.

34. For although (to settle that first point first) demons are spirits and do not have bodies, because they are nevertheless able to take on bodies, and are sometimes seen in the mouths of the possessed in the form of flies and spiders—and sometimes they even cause a certain swelling <term>tuber: a physical lump or growth</term> in other parts of the human body—some people believe they possess humans under a bodily form.

35. Truly, demons do not necessarily take on a body here. For what reason would they? Let them enter so that they may afflict and trouble humans: what need is there for an assumed body? Is it perhaps that they cannot cause trouble except in an assumed body? A body does not help them here at all. Whatever they are able to do and actually do, they accomplish by the power implanted in them, without the aid of a body.

36. Meanwhile, although it is not necessary for them to take on bodies, they can do so if they wish. They can hide within humans under the appearance of a spider or a fly; the smallness of the body they might assume is no hindrance here. Just as they can hide under the form of a human, so can they hide under that of a fly or a spider, or under the appearance of any animal whatever, even one smaller than a fly or a spider.

37. Therefore, demons are capable of these things. However, whether they have always taken on the body of a fly or a spider when these little creatures are seen in the mouths of the possessed can hardly be determined. Suppose they themselves made these animals,

...they have done and continue to do, it is nevertheless not necessary that they always remain hidden within those creatures; they are able to assist them and, being positioned outside of them, drive them wherever they please.

38. And, to speak my mind, I would think that these flies and these spiders are neither created by demons of their own free will, nor do the demons often assist or dwell in them except against their will and under compulsion. Rather, they are forced by God's command both to form such little creatures <note>original: "animalcula"</note> and either to hide within them or to testify to their presence through them.

39. I would say there is no slight argument for this: that they reveal their presence almost exclusively during Exorcisms, and testify to their departure from humans by the withdrawal of these creatures. But what of this? Should they not be thought to desire to remain hidden then, if ever, most of all? Or perhaps they desire to leave humans, and so wish to manifest their departure in this way? If ever they desire to hide, it is then most of all. They labor vehemently lest they be driven from their seats, or appear to be expelled. Therefore, as for the spiders or flies we notice, let us believe they are present by God's command, though through the work of demons.

40. I would believe it happens by the same command of God that they take up and exhibit these filthy little creatures, loathed by the human race. God does this to confound those spirits. He does it to instruct humans. Those spirits understand that it is because of their sin that they are compared to the filthiest animals; these humans understand how miserable it is to be under the command of those who can be bothersome only with flies, or infuse lethal poison with spiders.

41. Furthermore, if ever they dwell in the aforementioned little creatures, it must not be believed that they cannot then be troublesome in any other part of the possessed person’s body than where those animals are seen. Although, for example, a fly may keep itself above or below the tongue, the demon hiding in the fly can move, agitate, and afflict not only the tongue but also other members of the body. This is proved in the Possessed <note>original: "Obsessis," those beset or occupied by a demon.</note> now by the massive shouts they stir up; now by the twisting of the eyes in various directions; now by the throwing of the arms; now by the most violent and disordered movements of the whole body. Theologians say: the sphere of activity of demons is greater than their substantial presence. <note>original: "sphæra actiuitatis Dæmonum, quàm præsentia substantialis." This means a demon's "field of influence" can extend far beyond the specific point where its "substance" or essence is currently located.</note>

### CHAPTER IV.

->*Demons, while they possess humans, have and exercise power primarily over their bodies.*<-

<margin>42</margin>
We must now inquire into what the power of demons over possessed humans is, and how great it is. In this part, it is asked to what part of a human their power extends; here, whether as much as they are powerful...

-># ON THE POSSESSED<-

...are able to trouble the possessed, or how they might do so. The first point is answered in this Chapter, and the second in the following one.

43. It has been demonstrated above that demons have power over the possessed. However, because humans consist of two parts, soul and body, the question is raised whether this power extends only to the soul, or also to the body, or to both.

44. Let it first be established here that the ways demons harm the Soul can be understood in four ways: namely, in the substance of the soul itself; in its faculties; in the habits <note>In this context, "habits" refers to acquired qualities or dispositions of the soul, such as virtues or knowledge.</note> with which souls are equipped; and finally, in its operations. Regarding the substance of the soul, this would be if they were to transmute it into that of a brute or some beast; in its faculties, if they were to take them away; in its habits, if they were to strip the soul of them; and in its functions, if they were to either force a person to do something against their will or impede them in their own proper duties.

45. Let it secondly be established that harming the Body <note>Original: "Copori," likely a typo for "Corpori"</note> can also be understood in many ways. Indeed, the body can be killed; it can be deprived of the use of its limbs; it can be stripped of the senses that reside within it; it can be deformed; it can be afflicted by diseases; or it can be tortured in many and various ways. Let these points be established.

46. Now, then, which part do Demons harm in the wretched siege <term>obsessio</term> <note>The author uses the term "obssessio" (siege) to describe possession, suggesting an external force surrounding and attacking the person.</note> of mortals? What evils do they bring? We answer briefly, as the matter stands: That power is given to them chiefly over bodies; over souls they can do nothing or very little; yet they do bring certain harms to souls. Let us explain these three points.

<margin>Matthew 12, 15, 17. Luke 4, 8, 9. etc.</margin>
47. That the capability over bodies is given to demons is manifest from the examples of those who are read to have been possessed at various times. How few are those to whom some physical harm has not been brought? Let us consult the Holy Scriptures; they teach that some were deprived of their senses, others were cast now into water, now into fire; others were so tortured that, having abandoned cities and human society, they wandered in the mountains and desert places like wild beasts.

<margin>1 Corinthians 5.</margin>
48. The Apostle Paul teaches no differently. For when someone in Corinth had committed fornication—and of such a kind as is scarcely found even among the Gentiles—the Apostle handed him over to Satan for the destruction, as he says, of the Flesh, so that the Spirit might be saved.

49. Furthermore, it is clear that demons do not properly harm the souls of possessed men by the introduction of those things which pertain to souls.

<margin>On prodigies and the Apparitions of the living.</margin>
50. They never transmute the souls <note>original: "animos"</note> of the humans they possess into the forms of brutes. Why is this? Because they do not even have the power to transmute them. Since this has been demonstrated elsewhere, it is not necessary to pursue it further here.

->### PART I. DISPUTATION<-

15. <note>The number 15 appears here in the original, though it follows section 50 from the previous page; it is likely a printer's error for 51.</note> I can never deprive these same souls of those powers and faculties that are innate and inborn to them. These have taken such deep and firm roots in the souls that it is almost as difficult to remove them as it is to reduce the souls themselves to nothing.

<margin>Gregory of Valencia on the first part of Saint Thomas [Aquinas], disputation 8, question 6.</margin>
52. Thus, they cannot take away the **habits** <note>In this context, "habits" (habitus) refers to stable dispositions or qualities of the soul, such as virtues or ingrained knowledge.</note> which reside in the aforementioned faculties. They cannot deprive souls of those divine gifts of **faith, hope, and charity**. They cannot strip away the remaining virtues, whether those seats of virtue are held in the **will** or the **intellect**. Such is the condition of human souls, of their faculties, and of the habits within them, that they admit only the pure and absolute command of God; He alone holds supreme right here.

53. Nor can demons compel the resisting powers of souls to act. Everyone knows this, and it is clear and manifest from the fact that, were it otherwise, these wicked spirits would drive mortals to sin even against their will.

54. Nevertheless (this was the third point to be proven), while the Demons rage against the body, certain harms also reach the soul. For just as when the body is healthy, no small benefits flow to the soul, so too when the body is afflicted and ill-affected, the soul feels its own losses.

55. Among these, the first is that during the time when malignant spirits rage against the body, it becomes necessary for souls to cease from the pursuit of virtues; for most virtues cannot be exercised except with the assistance of the body's service, or at least without being hindered by the body's troubles.

56. Next, although they cannot drive human **wills** by themselves, they can nevertheless incline them greatly, and add a kind of "weight," as it were, so that they follow evil. They do this sometimes by exciting certain movements in the body to which the will easily accommodates itself, and sometimes by proposing objects that entice both the internal and external senses.

<margin>Luke 11.</margin>
57. A third point is added: when the demon deprives someone of the use of their senses (which happens quite often), they also deprive them of all the benefits obtained through the service of those senses. Truly, how many and how great are these at times? The one deaf man in the Gospel <note>A reference to the healing of the deaf-mute in the Gospels, illustrating the spiritual isolation caused by physical sensory loss.</note> can teach this by his great misfortune.

58. The fourth point is that even if they do not remove the habits of virtues, they frequently weaken them so much that they have little or no function in humans. This is most evident in those habits we call **Intellectual**; for although these have their seat in the soul's faculties, they nevertheless need the service of phantasms <term>phantasmata</term> <note>In the philosophy of the time, "phantasms" were mental images or sensory impressions required by the mind to form abstract thoughts.</note> if they are to exercise their acts. But those who occupy humans have great power over these phantasms,

### CHAPTER V.

->*That a limited and definite power is given to demons over the bodies of the possessed, and this for just causes.*<-

Those even moderately practiced in the Holy Scriptures know that the power of demons is great. In one place it is said: *There is no power upon earth that can be compared with him who was made to fear no one. He beholds every high thing; he is king over all the children of pride.* <note>The author is quoting Job 41:24–25 from the Latin Vulgate (Job 41:33-34 in modern Bibles), describing Leviathan, who was traditionally interpreted by theologians as a symbol for the Devil.</note>

60. However, they are not always permitted to exercise this power against those they enter. Unless a bridle were placed upon these torturers, no possessed person would escape their tyranny with their life intact. For they lack neither the will nor the desire to inflict the ultimate harms upon mortals, nor do they lack the power or strength. Why then do they not bring about the ultimate evils? Because they are not permitted to do so; their hands are bound.

61. And truly this is well-ordered. For they cannot enter mortals according to their own whim; they must wait for God’s judgment and will. Therefore, just as they do not enter bodies unless they have obtained God's permission; so too are they unable to trouble the people they have entered any more than is permitted and prescribed by God the Best and Greatest. <note>original: "Deo Opt. Max." (Deo Optimo Maximo), a title borrowed from Roman descriptions of Jupiter and adopted by Christians to describe the supreme majesty of God.</note>

<margin>Matthew 15.</margin>
<margin>Luke 11.</margin>
62. Hence there is such a great difference among possessed people. Some suffer the most grievous torments, like the daughter of the Canaanite woman; others suffer less severely, such as those we read about who were deprived of their sense of hearing or the ability to speak by demons. There are those who keep themselves in one place; others cannot be confined to any location. Thus, some are cruel toward themselves, while others are cruel toward others.

<margin>Job 1.</margin>
63. The demon who envied the happiness of the most holy Job could do no more than what was permitted by God. At first, he raged against Job's fortunes, but he did not dare to touch the holy man's body. Then, with God's permission, he raged against the body; but he was prohibited from bringing any harm to the soul.

64. The very affliction brought upon men teaches us that certain laws are prescribed for demons. Since here [on earth] punishment is usually taken for sin, it is fitting that—because this punishment is exacted by God's authority according to the nature of the offense—the person suffers not as much as the demons would desire, but as much as justice demands.

65. Therefore, the power of demons over possessed people is limited; it is bound by certain laws. They can do only as much as God permits them. But how much is this? The demons who do the torturing know this. He knows, by whom they [are commanded...]

PART I. DISPUTATION.

This is especially true when Spirits <note>In this context, "Spirits" refers to fallen angels or demons.</note> rage against those who brought this evil upon themselves through their own vice. 68. Thirdly, it declares the wretched condition of the demons. Even though they are capable of causing great harm and intensely desire to do so, they are nonetheless not permitted. Instead, they depend entirely on the will and permission of the one they hate most.

69. Finally, one can understand from this that the complaint of those who claim they are circumvented by the cunning and power of demons and brought to sin against their will is unjust. Most merciful God does not permit demons to rage against bodies to the full extent of their power; would He then permit them to circumvent the innocent and lead them to sin against their will? Sin is so voluntary that unless it is voluntary, it is not sin. <note>This is a foundational concept in moral theology: for an act to be a "sin," the person must have the free will to choose it.</note>

### CHAPTER VI.

->*Six types of evils that can be brought upon possessed persons through demons.*<-

<margin>70.</margin>
<margin>Chap. 4.</margin>
No one doubts that various inconveniences and evils are brought upon human bodies through the effort and work of demons. We have noted six kinds of these above. For they either bring death, deprive one of the use of limbs, procure another form quite unsuitable to a human <note>Likely referring to physical deformities or the appearance of transformation.</note>, spoil the senses, afflict with diseases, or torture through hidden means and ways.

71. They accomplish these things partly while they possess people, and partly while they are outside of people; and sometimes by themselves, and sometimes through those who hire out their services to them. <note>original: "qui ipsis operas suas locant." This refers to the belief that witches or sorcerers could contract demons to harm others.</note>

72. Nevertheless, they perform certain actions more frequently while hidden inside people, and others more frequently when positioned outside of them; although they are capable of performing all things whether inside people or outside them, both by themselves and through others.

# CONCERNING THE POSSESSED.

B 3

73. <margin>*In the life of Hilarion*</margin> Let us now list the evils that demons bring upon the possessed. Here the first and most frequent is that they torture and torment them through certain hidden means for which no remedy can be brought by the medical art. Thus one of them afflicted a Virgin, whom the Blessed Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a priest and theologian best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note> mentions. So too are those whose horrendous cries we hear daily and whose extreme anguishes and difficulties we witness.

74. <margin>*Luke 11*</margin> The second is that they deprive people of their senses. Sacred Scripture provides an illustrious example of this in the "mute and deaf demon" which the Lord is recorded to have cast out. For it is not to be believed that the demon itself was mute and deaf; rather, the possessed person was mute and deaf, and indeed by the work of the demon, which is therefore called "mute and deaf."

75. <margin>*Luke 13*</margin> The third is that they sometimes destroy the natural form of men and induce a strange appearance, one not at all suited to human functions. Sacred Scripture supplies an example of this in the woman who for eighteen years walked so bent over that she was utterly unable to look upward.

76. <margin>*Mark 5*</margin> The fourth is that they corrupt the human imagination <note>In the psychological language of the time, the "imagination" was the faculty that processed sensory data; its corruption led to madness or hallucinations.</note> and drive people to a kind of madness, making them very similar to cruel beasts. Thus it is not rarely necessary to apply chains and shackles to the wretched ones so that they do not harm themselves or others. In this way the demon afflicted those whom the Evangelist reports to have hidden in tombs; seized by fury, they raged sometimes against passersby, and sometimes against themselves.

77. <margin>*Mark 9*</margin> The fifth is that they sometimes reduce mortals to such a state that they feel they must altogether commit suicide; nor do they attempt this rarely. A man was vexed by a similar Spirit, whom Saint Mark reports was dashed to the ground, foaming foully, grinding his teeth, and wasting away; he was also frequently cast into fire and water.

68. <note>The number 68 is a printer's error for 78.</note> <margin>*In the Chronicles*</margin> To these I would add a sixth evil: death itself, which they sometimes bring. What else was the demon striving for in the case Mark mentions, cited above? Sigebert <note>Sigebert of Gembloux (c. 1030–1112), a medieval monk and influential chronicler.</note> testifies that a demon brought about the same for Gunderic, King of the Vandals; after he had captured Seville <note>original: "Hispalis"</note> and entered God's temple intending to profane it, the demon invaded him. Soon indeed, by the just judgment of God, it miserably slaughtered the King.

79. These are the principal evils which demons bring upon the bodies of the possessed. If there are any others, they are easily traced back to these.

## CHAPTER VII.

->That there are roughly five ways in which Demons bring distress to the bodies of the possessed.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'Q' featuring foliage and scrollwork inside a square frame.</image-desc>
Just as demons are accustomed to afflict the human race with various evils, so too they have various methods and ways by which they cause suffering. Because we are disputing only those spirits that "besiege" (or possess), we will only investigate those methods by which they harm the people they inhabit.

81. Therefore, they cause trouble to these people either by themselves without the help of any other created thing, or through the work or ministry of other creatures, which they freely use in order to afflict the person even more severely.

82. They seem to have caused trouble by themselves in those cases mentioned in the Sacred Scriptures. However, they also work through physical objects; in our own times, after demons were cast out of people, they have left behind pins, hair, nails, or shards of glass as evidence of their cruelty. Those who had been possessed vomited these things up <note>The phenomenon of "allotriophagy"—the vomiting of strange objects—was a standard diagnostic sign of possession in early modern demonology.</note> as soon as the demon was expelled.

83. This latter method—using physical objects—is rarer among the possessed; it is more common among those whose services the demons use. I speak here of Mages and Sorcerers <note>original: "Magos & Maleficos"</note>. But the former method [acting directly] is more frequent in the cases we are discussing. Indeed, evil spirits enter human beings for this reason: to harm by their own power, to torment by their own power, and to bring ruin to human bodies by their own power.

84. Indeed, whatever evils they bring, they seem to accomplish them in five ways: by the fascination of the imagination <term>phantasiæ fascinatione; in the science of the time, "imagination" was a physical faculty of the brain that could be "bewitched" to see things that weren't there</term>, by the weakening of a person's vital strength, by the corruption of the organs, by the pulling or displacement of the limbs, and finally by the collapse or violent impulse of the body.

85. In the first way, they bring it about that mortals persuade themselves that they see their enemies; that they see bloody beasts or demons who wish to bring death or other horrors. They may even judge themselves to have been turned into beasts <note>This refers to lycanthropy or "zoanthropy," where a person believes they are a wolf or other animal.</note> and, for that reason, rage most cruelly against others as if they were wild animals.

86. The weakening of strength often destroys and dissolves the human form. For just as a person's individual limbs stay in their proper places and perform their duties when their strength is intact, so too if that strength is weakened, the beautiful constitution of man is dissolved, and the limbs are rendered unfit for performing their natural duties.

87. The corruption of the organs either removes or dulls the senses located within those organs. Since the nature of the senses is such that they cannot perform their functions except through physical bodily organs, it is no wonder that when demons destroy those organs, the senses are lost.

88. We would not be wrong to say that the cause of the pains—which the possessed sometimes experience with great intensity—is the contraction and distraction [pulling apart] of certain limbs, which the Spirit effects in specific parts of the body. For the greatest...

## CHAPTER VIII.

->*That demons neither always harass the possessed, nor are they always present within them.*<-

<margin>91</margin>
A question seems very closely connected to what has just been said: Whether demons are always troublesome and tormenting while they "besiege" (or possess) bodies, and whether they always remain and reside within the bodies of those they possess. The diversity of <term>efficient causes</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "efficient cause" is the primary source of change or rest; here, it refers to the demons as the active force behind the possession.</note> and agents provides the occasion for this question.

92. For there are two kinds of agents: some act with reason and freely, while others act without reason and out of necessity. The latter are determined to a single course of action; the former can act in contrary ways. Because those that act out of necessity cannot do otherwise, they must act; whereas the former, since they act freely, can act at one moment and interrupt their actions at another.

93. If demons belonged to the latter class of agents <note>those acting by blind necessity</note>, the answer to the proposed question would be easy. But because they belong to the first order—acting freely—the answer is not so simple, especially if the question concerns what actually happens in practice. For if we are speaking only of the power of the spirits, there is no great difficulty.

94. And to say this in passing regarding the power <note>original: "potestate"</note> of demons: there is no doubt that they are able and desire to be troublesome at all times when they are in a person. They do not lack the lust for harming, nor do they lack strength. Those faculties in us humans which are fatigued or broken down by constant exercise and frequent use—preventing us from continuous action—by no means grow faint or cease in demons.

95. Likewise, there is no doubt that they can leave the bodies they inhabit for a period of time. Their union with the body is not as substantial as the union of the human soul with its own body. Within bodies, they act only as "movers" <note>An external force that animates or moves an object without becoming part of its biological essence.</note>; therefore, it is as easy for them to enter a body as it is to leave it.

96. But as we have said, the present question is not about their power; it is asked whether they actually do what they are capable of doing, and whether in the midst of the torment...

On the day that Martin Luther departed from this life, the possessed people—of whom there were very many at Geel <note>original: "Gheola," a town in modern-day Belgium famous for the shrine of St. Dymphna</note> (a town in Brabant) and who were expecting liberation through the patronage of Saint Dymphna (which many had experienced over many years)—were all liberated from their demons. However, not long after, they were again occupied by the same spirits. This matter is not obscure. Indeed, on the following day, when the cruel spirits again tortured those miserable men, they were asked where they had hidden the day before. They replied that, by the command of their Prince <note>Referring to Satan or a high-ranking demon.</note>, they had been summoned to the funeral of the "new Prophet" and faithful coworker Luther, and had been present there. This matter was confirmed by Luther's servant, who was present at his miserable death; when he looked through the window to catch a breeze, he saw, not without great terror, many foul spirits dancing and performing dances nearby. <margin>Caesarius, Book 12, Chapter 10</margin> This is further confirmed by the crows which accompanied Luther's body with great clamor as it was carried from Eisleben to Wittenberg. See Bredenbach, *Collationes*, Book 7, Chapter 39. We read a similar thing about Bruno, the Cupbearer of the Count of Berg <note>original: "Monte"</note>. For the demons, who had left the possessed for a time, are said to have been present at his funeral as well.

...linger and have their seats <note>Demonologists often used the term "seat" to describe the specific location within the body where a demon resided.</note>. For the laws of nature do not allow two bodies to penetrate one another; these same laws also require that all things occupy a certain and defined place.

**101.** There are those who attribute no physical bodies to them (which is the more probable opinion of the <term>Doctors</term> <note>Referring to the Doctors of the Church, the authoritative theologians of Catholic tradition.</note>). Although these thinkers are not bound by the same physical laws as the previous group, they nevertheless establish that demons exist within humans—demons who were not always there. Therefore, they must also explain by what path the spirits entered, and in what corner they hide once they have come inside. For it does not seem possible for the human mind to grasp how Spirits could be said to have entered into men if there were no path through which they entered, nor how they could be said to be inside men if no specific place can be assigned for where they dwell.

**102.** Let us first examine the entry. There are those who believe that they enter human bodies through the mouth. They are perhaps persuaded of this because we read not infrequently in notable authors that spirits were swallowed along with food or drink in which they lay hidden, and soon afterward gave great examples of their tyranny over those miserable people.

**103.** Nor are there lacking those who wish to justify the custom among Catholics that, whenever they <term>yawn</term> <note>original: "oscitent"</note>, they fortify the mouth with the sign of the cross; it is as if by this <term>signing of the cross</term> <note>original: "crucifignatione"</note> the entry of demons into the body is prohibited.

**104.** This is confirmed by the fact that in <term>Exorcisms</term>, when demons are cast out of bodies, they often exit the mouth in the form of a fly or a spider. For they thus indicate that this same door must stand open for both entering and exiting.

**105.** Although these reasons do not have great strength, they are nonetheless not entirely void. It is certain that demons have sometimes entered humans through the mouth; it is also certain that the custom of "cross-signing," accepted by Catholics for many years, should not be rebuked; finally, it is certain that they have often exited through the mouth. Therefore, those who believe that they enter humans through the mouth should not be said to hold an entirely bad opinion.

**106.** But yet, one must not believe that no other way is open to spirits. Just as they enter through the mouth, so they can enter—and do enter not infrequently—through any passage <note>original: "meatum"</note> whatsoever, and even through the thinnest and barely perceptible pores of the human body.

**107.** What if they do not even need pores for entry? What if their approach is not blocked even by solid bodies placed in their way? What if nothing can be so massive and firm that they cannot penetrate it without difficulty or trouble? This is the condition of Spirits (the order of beings to which demons belong): neither their power, nor their presence, nor their operation can be delayed or hindered by physical objects.

### CHAPTER X.

->*In which part of the possessed person the Demons hide, and have their seats.*<-

<margin>108.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' featuring foliage and a small central floral motif.</image-desc> Through which path the evil Spirits enter the possessed has been established; now it must be investigated where they hide once they have entered. Here, after we have first explained what is possible, we will then reveal what we think most commonly happens.

109. It is possible for demons to occupy the entire human body, in such a way, clearly, that they are in no part of the body which they occupy that they are not also in every other part: let them be in the head, the arms, the belly, the legs, and so on. This is not surprising; just as the human soul is, so demons conduct themselves in the body; although meanwhile the demons have one set of operations, and the soul another, the soul being even more tightly joined with the body than demons are.

110. It is also possible that they are in some single limb of the person—namely the head, the arms, the leg, or the chest. And in this they differ from the very soul by which the body lives. Because the soul gives life to all parts of the body, it must be joined to all of them; Demons, since they do not bestow life upon bodies, but only movement, can have their seats in one particular part of the bodies.

111. But they do not even need limbs in which to reside. They can hide under any part of a person, even the smallest and thus hardly perceptible; and indeed those spirits who once possessed the largest and most vast bodies. Nor is this new. Is it not the same human soul which now hides in the smallest body, when a person first receives life, and now animates a vast one, and is diffused, so to speak, through all parts of the largest body?

112. All these things are possible. Furthermore, what actually happens? In which part of the possessed person do the demons hide? That is difficult to assert. If it could be detected from anything, it would surely be from the operations <note>original: "operationibus", referring here to the physical manifestations or symptoms produced by the demon</note> which they carry out in people: Nevertheless, a certain argument cannot be taken from this. Why? Because it is not necessary that where they work, the spirits themselves are present in person <note>original: "αὐτοπροσώπως" (autoprosōpōs) — meaning in their own person or direct presence</note>; they can exist in this place and work in another. The sphere of a Demon's activity is one thing, the sphere of its presence another.

113. Therefore, if they cause a swelling in some part of the person; if they thrust out the tongue of the possessed; if they afflict this or that limb with distress, it is not immediately necessary to say the spirit is there. All these things can be done by the power of demons, which extends to more things than their presence itself does.

114. Similarly, while spiders or flies <note>In early modern accounts, the appearance of small animals or insects in the mouth was often cited as a physical sign of a demonic presence or a swallowed charm.</note> are seen in the mouths of the possessed...

## CHAPTER XI.

->*Demons sometimes reveal their entry into human bodies by certain signs—and those of four types—and this for just causes.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring foliate and floral vine motifs.</image-desc>
Some signs exist by which demons prove their entry into humans; others by which they demonstrate that they are hiding within humans and inhabiting them. Concerning the latter, we will deal with them in Chapter 22 and those following; the former we investigate in this place.

<margin>124.</margin> Two things are asked here. One is: do the Spirits always declare by some signs that they are entering humans? The other is: what are those signs most especially?

<margin>125.</margin> Regarding the first, there is no doubt that they most often reveal their entry into humans. This can be shown by the examples of many who were at one time possessed. Some of them, before they were possessed, asserted that they saw the spirit in the form of a dog or a black Ethiopian <note>original: "nigri Aethiopis." In the demonological literature of this period, demons were frequently described as appearing in the guise of animals or people of different races—figures the contemporary audience found "other" or frightening.</note>; some were struck by a certain noise and commotion; some had certain heavy and troublesome imaginations <note>In this context, "imaginations" refers to vivid, disturbing mental images or hallucinations experienced while sleeping or waking.</note> in their sleep.

<margin>126.</margin> It is clear both that these things have happened and that they still happen daily; however, the reasons for them are not so clear. Just as there are many other things for which reasons can scarcely be assigned, so a certain reason can hardly be given as to why some demons do not enter human bodies except after some signs.

<margin>127.</margin> Perhaps one reason is that the Spirits may seem able to imitate God in this matter: just as He testifies and indicates His coming into or to men by certain external and great proofs, so also the spirits wish to make their own arrival known, lest they seem inferior to God in this regard.

<margin>128.</margin> Perhaps also by this logic they wish to imitate the good Angels. For they, too, for the most part, revealed their presence by external signs. This can be taught by many clear passages of Holy Scripture.

<margin>129.</margin> Perhaps the logic of divine providence demands the same. For it is not rare for those to be possessed by demons who are involved in grave sins, and who open, as it were, a door for them to enter. For their greater (yet most just) punishment, God permits that their executioners...

143. Thus it follows that one cannot know for certain from which ranks <note>original: "ordinibus." In medieval theology, both angels and demons were classified into nine hierarchical "orders" or ranks, such as Thrones, Powers, or Principalities.</note> those who possess humans come.

144. Meanwhile, from what has been said, we seem to correctly gather two points. The first is that there is no doubt that those who are from the lowest rank enter and trouble humans. For it is not beneath them to descend to private and specific matters; the condition of their nature requires this. Nor is it foreign to their will to be burdensome and to torment: they are driven to this by an almost total and deep-rooted desire to do harm.

145. The second point is that even those who are of the higher ranks employ their efforts here and trouble people through the bodies they possess. For although their nature might require weightier and higher concerns, their zeal for doing harm is so great that they willingly lower themselves even to the most menial tasks.

<margin>Mark 9.</margin>

<margin>Luke 11.</margin>
147. Perhaps the silence of Christ proves the same opinion. In one place, the Scribes of the Law objected that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons; what did the Lord say to this? Instead, he denied that he himself possessed the prince of demons or cast out demons in his name.

<margin>Luke 10.</margin>

<margin>Ephesians 6.</margin>

Did he not mark the spirits of the higher ranks with the very words "Principalities" and "Powers"? By asserting that we struggle against them, he certainly implies that they also enter bodies and bring great suffering to those they possess.

150. Therefore, demons from all ranks enter human bodies. There is none in any rank who would refuse to enter mortals if God so permits. But as to which rank those who hide within humans belong, it is not so easily said.

151. For if we use any specific rule to determine whether a person is obsessed <note>original: "obsessi." In this period, "obsession" and "possession" were often used interchangeably in general writing, though technically obsession referred to an external spiritual attack and possession to an internal one.</note>, and we wish to use that same rule for this specific matter [identifying their rank], we would wander far from the truth. 
<margin>Thomas Aquinas, Part 1, Question 51, Article 2.</margin> 
Why is this? It is because we detect possession through actions that are entirely unsuited to a human being; however, these actions do not distinguish the ranks <note>original: "ordines." This refers to the celestial hierarchy—such as Seraphim or Powers—which the fallen angels belonged to before their exile from heaven.</note> of demons. One will hardly notice any actions in the possessed that even the lowest of demons could not perform, provided he wished to do so and was not prevented by the power of a superior.

152. However, I would not say that those who believe spirits of the higher orders can be detected by two specific signs are entirely mistaken: First, from the magnitude and severity of the evils they inflict upon the possessed; and second, from the difficulty that Exorcists experience in driving them out of human bodies. The higher-ranking spirits seem to inflict greater damage and are cast out of human bodies with much more difficulty.

153. A more certain proof than either of these is a confession extorted from them by force through the Exorcists. For although one should not believe them when they assert many things of their own accord—since they frequently lie and deceive humans—it must be believed that just as they are compelled by the power of exorcisms to confess other truths, they are also compelled to betray their own orders and classes.

**156.** Just as nothing prevents many demons from besieging the same man, so there is almost nothing that fully persuades us that there are *always* many who besiege one person. ### CHAPTER XIV.

->Whether many spirits cause more torture, and whether each brings the same or different torments.<-

<margin>165.</margin>

166. There is no doubt that the evil of possessed men is increased by a multitude of occupying demons. For if it is an evil to be possessed by one, how is it not a greater evil to be possessed by many?

171. In the first case, they execute commands given with authority like servants; in the second, because of the pacts they have with the wretched, they merely simulate servitude.

<margin>Book 5, chapter 26.</margin>
**203.** And thus let the matter of human command over demons be settled. We add one thing before we conclude this chapter, namely that by another means it sometimes happens that one human is the cause of this diabolic tyranny for another human. By what means? By the evil curse <note>original: *imprecatione*—the act of calling down evil or a curse upon someone</note> of a superior. For it is nothing new that those who have been cursed to the demons by others are soon occupied by them. We could produce recent examples of this argument, but we will be content with one or two from Caesarius <note>Caesarius of Heisterbach (c. 1180–1240), a Cistercian monk famous for his "Dialogue on Miracles," a collection of stories used for moral instruction.</note>. He relates that an angry father cursed his five-year-old daughter, while she was eating milk, wishing that she would swallow the devil along with the milk. Scarcely has he uttered the word, and the girl is occupied by the devil, and she endures a wretched servitude until she reaches maturity. The same Caesarius has two similar stories in chapters 11 and 12 of the same book, one concerning a wife whose husband cursed her, and another concerning a son whose father had cursed a demon upon him.

### CHAPTER XVII.

->*On the various operations of demons in possessed bodies, and which of them can be attributed to humans.*<-

<margin>204.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial O with floral patterns and scrolling foliage.</image-desc>The operations which demons exercise in possessed bodies are twofold: some they exercise in the possessed bodies, but not through the possessed bodies; some both in and through the possessed bodies.
