# PART I. DISPUTATION

...demons, although they act within human bodies, there is no doubt that they differ greatly from human actions. These primary actions of the will and intellect differ in this way: it is not necessary for those wishing to understand to pay attention to the mental images <note>original: *phantasmata*—in medieval psychology, these are sensory images stored in the imagination that the human mind requires to think</note> which are in the human imagination. The reason for this is readily available: because spirits do not inhabit bodies in the same way that a soul exists within a body.

**207.** Thus, the bodies do not hinder the spirits in these operations, nor do they help them to understand more things or to understand more easily. Whatever things they can perceive, and however many things they are able to perceive while they are free from human bodies, they can perceive those same things—all of them, in fact—while lurking within bodies.

**208.** The reasoning behind the secondary operations was explained above and should not be repeated here. I would only add that they should in no way be called "human" actions, because humans do not appear to contribute to them, but behave merely as passive subjects <note>original: *patientium tantum modum*—meaning the human is a victim or a vessel rather than an active participant</note>.

<margin>Chapter 8</margin>
**209.** Regarding the tertiary operations, there is no doubt that those which human strength is unequal to performing must be attributed to demons. However, there is a question concerning the speech and prayer which the possessed <note>original: *obsessi*—those "beset" or possessed by a spirit</note> utter: whether they belong to the demons or to the humans. Our judgment is this: although the possessed may say many things on their own to which the spirit contributes nothing, it very often happens that the entire speech belongs to the demons. This is most evident when they produce terrifying roars and disordered shouts, when they predict future events that cannot be known by men, or when they reveal things that escape the knowledge of the possessed person.

**210.** Whenever these things happen, the voices that are heard are not truly human voices, just as those voices which spirits form in assumed bodies <note>original: *assumptis corporibus*—referring to instances where a spirit manifests a physical form out of thin air</note> are not true voices. This remains true even though in the case of possession they use the living organs of a person, whereas in the other case they use organs that are not living, but are instead condensed from the air or taken from elsewhere.

**211.** Furthermore, the possessed do not even know what is being said. Just as the sounds being formed are the work of demons, so too the things represented by those sounds are not the thoughts or concepts of the possessed humans, but of the possessing demons.

**212.** From this it follows that there is no sin on the part of the possessed if they should commit perjury, blaspheme, or reveal secrets against justice and Christian charity. Just as there is no sin in the sword which a thief uses to slaughter men, so there is no sin here in the possessed. The demons are the ones committing the offense here, just as the thief is in the other case.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>213.</margin> Just as there were many matters concerning the demons who "besiege" <note>original: *obsidentibus*—the author uses the metaphor of a siege to describe possession</note> which presented great difficulty, so too there are quite a few things debated and brought into controversy regarding the possessed themselves. <margin>214.</margin> All these matters seem capable of being reduced to four main Chapters. In the first, we discuss certain specific types of people and whether they are truly possessed. In the second, we investigate the signs that betray the presence of the possessed. In the third, the miserable and unhappy condition of the possessed is explained. In the fourth, we investigate the causes for which spirits exercise this tyranny over mortals.

<margin>215.</margin> In the first Chapter, the primary dispute concerns four classes of people. First are infants and all those who have not yet been initiated by the sacrament of Baptism. ### CONCERNING THE POSSESSED.

**223.** Nevertheless, although demons have this power over infants and all those not yet reborn, they are not, however, said to <term>besiege<note>original: *obsidere*. In this context, it refers to an external spiritual occupation or harassment.</note></term> or <term>possess<note>original: *possidere*. This refers to internal control of the body.</note></term> them. For demons are not said to "besiege" people simply because they have some power over them, but because they hide within the bodies themselves and have received permission from God to be a nuisance within those people.

**224.** But no one is so foolish as to count either infants or the unbaptized among the number of the possessed. How great, good God, would the number of the possessed be? How many chains would be needed to bind them all? How many shackles? Especially if the demons wished to exercise their full power?

**225.** Add to this that one might say all sinners whatsoever are "besieged" by demons. Why so? Because the power of demons over sinners is no less (if not greater) than their power over the unbaptized. But who, even in a dream, would think to regard all sinners as possessed?

**226.** It is customary to detect by certain signs that an evil spirit is hiding within people. These are: if they predict the future; if they reveal secrets; if they speak in different languages; if they endure labors superior to human strength, and so on. Are these signs found in infants? As long as we do not detect these signs in infants, in infidels, or in any sinners, we shall by no means call them "possessed," even though, on account of sin, demons have the greatest power over them.

<margin>Book 4, chapters 19, 24.</margin>
**227.** To what purpose, then, are Exorcisms? Why is the devil commanded to go out from infants? Why is he told to depart and give place to Christ? John Calvin <note>A primary leader of the Protestant Reformation who rejected many traditional Catholic rituals as superstitious.</note> mocks this custom of exorcising demons—which has been accepted in the Church since the times of the Apostles—as he does most other practices of the Christian Religion; he wishes it to be entirely vain and fictitious. But this is no small insult to the most Holy Fathers, whose testimonies in favor of this rite are very weighty. Let us hear one or two from among many. Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Greek Father known for his preaching.</note> speaks thus:
> When they come to the sacrament of rebirth, they do not enter the fountain of life before the unclean spirit is driven away from them by the Exorcisms and <term>insufflations<note>original: *exsufflationibus*. A ritual act of breathing or blowing on a person to symbolize driving out the devil and breathing in the Holy Spirit.</note></term> of the Clergy, and they are thereafter rescued from being his vessels.

<margin>Sermon on Adam and Eve. Catechesis 2.</margin>
Cyril, Bishop of Jerusalem <note>A 4th-century theologian known for his "Catechetical Lectures" for those preparing for baptism.</note>, speaks to the same effect:
> The breathings of the Saints and the invocation of the divine name, like a most powerful flame, burn the demons and turn them to flight.

These are the Greek Fathers. Let us add three from the Latin:
<margin>Book 4 against Parmenianus.</margin>
The first is Optatus of Milevis <note>A 4th-century North African bishop who wrote against the Donatist heresy.</note>, who has it thus:
> No man who is born is without a spirit [the evil one]; he cannot be clean, and it is necessary that this spirit be excluded before the saving washing [baptism].

Rabanus Maurus <note>A 9th-century Benedictine monk and scholar.</note> says the same:
> The devil is exorcised so that, acknowledging his own wickedness and fearing the just Judge above him, he may depart from the man and no longer strive to subvert him with his craft, lest the man attain baptism.

<header>PART II. DISPUTATION.</header>

<margin>
Book on the Instruction of the Clergy.
</margin>
...speaks in Book 1 *On the Creed*, chapter 1: "As you know, dearest brothers, infants are <term>blown upon<note>original: *exsufflantur*. This refers to the ritual of "exsufflation," where a priest breathes or blows on the person being baptized to symbolize the driving away of the devil.</note></term> and exorcised, so that the hostile power of the devil may be driven from them—he who deceived man so that he might possess men. Therefore, it is not the creature in the infants that is exorcised or blown upon, but rather he under whose power those who are born in sin remain." So say the Fathers.

<margin>
Thesis: 227.
</margin>
**228.** Let us also ask of <term>Calvin<note>John Calvin (1509–1564), a central figure in the Protestant Reformation who was skeptical of certain traditional exorcism rituals.</note></term>, what exactly he thinks is to be condemned here? Is it that we believe the devil has some power over the <term>Energumeni<note>A Greek-derived term for "the possessed" or those being "worked upon" by an external spirit.</note></term> and unbaptized children, or is it that we command him to leave them? First, he cannot rightly condemn the belief itself. The Doctors of the Church, St. Paul, and Christ Himself affirm it. If he condemns the second—the command—he must then admit that there is no power over demons within the Church of Christ.

**229.** But perhaps he thinks it is ridiculous for a demon to be told to "go out" from a person if he was not <term>personally present<note>original Greek: *autoprosōpōs* (αὐτοπροσώπως), meaning "in one's own person" or "physically inhabiting."</note></term> within that person? This is not ridiculous. The demon is not commanded to depart from a body he inhabits; rather, he is commanded not to use the power he holds over the person. That is: he who is not "personally present" outside the person is commanded to "go out" in terms of his effect and operation; he is commanded to resign his claim which he has over the person and hand it over to Christ, who redeemed the person through His own blood.

**230.** This form of speaking is neither new nor unusual. Is it not said that Moses "went out" from Pharaoh? Did Peter not ask the Lord to "depart" from him? Was Moses therefore inside Pharaoh, or the Lord <margin>Exodus: 11. Luke [5].</margin> inside Peter? In these cases, things are said to "be" where they hold command and exercise power; they are said to "go out" from where they are deprived of that command and power. But let us move to the second points.

### CHAPTER XIX.
#### Whether Witches and Sorcerers are Besieged by Demons.

<margin>
231.
</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'D' decorated with scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
THERE is also a question regarding <term>Witches<note>original: *Sagis*. Derived from *saga*, a term for a wise woman or sorceress, often associated with divination.</note></term> and <term>Sorcerers<note>original: *Maleficis*. Literally "evildoers," specifically those who use "maleficium" or harmful magic.</note></term>. Some have entirely convinced themselves that these people are possessed by demons. They take their argument from the <term>trial by cold water<note>original: *purgatione aquæ frigidæ*. A form of ordeal where a suspect was thrown into water; if they floated, they were considered guilty; if they sank, they were innocent. It was based on the idea that the "pure" water would reject the "impure" sinner.</note></term>. For they believe that if women suspected of witchcraft are cast into the water and float, they are guilty of the crime; if they sink, they are innocent. Thus they wish to detect a witch or an innocent person. However, they think this floating happens because they have demons within their bodies by whom they are possessed; since the demon is of a "fiery" or "airy" nature (as they say), he causes the bodies of the witches not to sink at all, but to float upon the waters. So a certain person recently argued in a published book.

**232.** In truth, there are many and great errors in this opinion. The first is that he tries to prove it by the trial of cold water. That practice is in no way permitted.

**233.** The second error is that they believe demons are of an airy or fiery nature, and for that reason are light and float upon the waters. ## CHAPTER XXII.

->*On the twelve signs which are not certain and indubitable proofs of demons hiding within men.*<-

From the number of the Possessed we have excluded <term>Energumens<note>From the Greek 'energoumenos', referring to those physically or mentally agitated by an indwelling spirit, though sometimes used as a general term for the possessed.</note></term>, <term>Sorcerers<note>original: "Maleficos"</note></term>, Witches, Diviners, and Heretics; concerning whom there could have been a greater suspicion than of others. ### ON THE POSSESSED.

...sed [they are called possessed] because they have their speech through a demon. And perhaps someone might call them "possessed" for the reason that <margin>Matthew 12</margin> it is said elsewhere: *Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.* But nevertheless, although demons are not far from such people (as Saint Gregory <note>Likely referring to Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD), whose "Dialogues" contain many accounts of the supernatural.</note> teaches in an excellent example elsewhere), it is still not necessary to call them "Possessed." Not all who act wickedly are possessed by demons.

270. Similarly, those who—having abandoned the true God—consecrate themselves entirely, body and soul, to demons and obey his commands in all things (even the most foul and cruel), are not "possessed" by demons. These are the duties of <margin>Chapter 19</margin> Witches and <term>Sorcerers<note>original: "Maleficorum"; specifically those believed to use "maleficium" or harmful magic.</note></term>, and it was demonstrated above that they are not to be numbered among the Possessed.

271. There are those found who are safe in no place. Everywhere they experience spirits bothering them, and sometimes even cruelly venting their rage upon their bodies: should these perhaps be called "possessed"? They are not. Even if they suffer troubles no less grave—indeed, sometimes even more grave—than the Possessed, those troubles are not brought about by spirits inhabiting them, but by <term>attending spirits<note>original: "assistentibus spiritibus"; a theological distinction where spirits harass a person from the outside (obsession) rather than the inside (possession).</note></term>.

272. And those who, weary of this present life, lay cruel hands upon themselves and deprive themselves of the enjoyment of this life, do not necessarily belong to the rank of the Possessed. If they did belong, that very death which they bring upon themselves would not be turned into a vice for them: they would not pay heavy penalties in the name of that death in the future life; the death would be attributed to the demons, and there would be no fault of their own in this. But in truth, the death is attributed to them, and they deservedly endure the most grievous torments in the future life. <note>The author argues that because suicide is a punishable sin, the person must have been acting of their own free will, whereas a truly possessed person would not be held morally responsible for the demon's actions.</note>

273. Or, do those who long for the presence of the demons they have summoned, and pray that they may be snatched away by them, and are soon after snatched away, become "possessed" by those who carry them off? Without a doubt, the devil *could* possess such people; however, he does not possess them. There is no need: why should he enter their bodies if he must transport them elsewhere? Indeed, one should not believe that he desires to enter those whom he must soon leave behind.

274. Is <term>fury<note>original: "Furia"; here meaning a state of violent, manic madness.</note></term> perhaps an argument for a demon hiding within a person? Sometimes it is: but not always. Fury is not stirred up by demons alone; it sometimes has natural causes within a person. Sometimes it is even procured by the work of abandoned men with the help of devils; finally, it can also happen through the power of certain herbs.

275. What about the forgetting of known things? This is sometimes brought about by the work of demons, but even spirits existing *outside* of men can be the authors of this. Furthermore, this can also have natural causes.

276. What of the fact that even the revelation of secrets does not provide a sufficiently great argument here? <margin>Chapter 20</margin> Diviners reveal secrets, but nevertheless, not all are possessed by demons. But more on this elsewhere.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

->*In what way and what kind of revelation of hidden things betrays the demons lurking within men.*<-

<margin>278.</margin> <image-desc>Decorative initial 'P' with floral scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>Following this, the true signs must be assigned, by which it is detected whether men are possessed by demons. These appear to be of two kinds: for some are those by which the Spirits appear to act, while others are those by which they are made to suffer something. The former are signs of either the intellect or the body; the latter are, for the most part, extorted by sacred things. Signs of the intellect are the revelation of secrets and the knowledge of languages; signs of the body are great strength, heavy torments, and things similar to these. Sacred things [used for testing] are the Gospel of Saint John, the Relics of the Saints, Exorcisms, and so on. Let us discuss each one individually.

<margin>279.</margin> The first place is held by the revelation of hidden things <note>original: "occultorum reuelatio"</note> which are beyond the knowledge of the people who reveal them. For since it is necessary that such information be suggested by a mind or spirit, if it does not come from the person's own spirit, and if God or a good Angel are not the cause of it (as is sometimes the case), it is absolutely necessary that it proceeds from an evil spirit.

<margin>280.</margin> These secrets are of two kinds. Some are indeed hidden from those who reveal them, yet they are not of such a nature that they could never be known by them; others are those which it is impossible for human wit and strength to achieve.

<margin>281.</margin> The former are categorized by three differences of time. For they are either past, such as historical deeds; or present, which men nevertheless cannot know because of the distance of the locations; or future, which have all the being they possess within their own causes <note>In Aristotelian and Scholastic philosophy, "causes" refer to the conditions that make an event inevitable; demons were thought to predict the future by observing these natural patterns.</note>. The latter kind of secrets are those which depend on the human will and <term>free choice<note>original: "libero arbitrio"; the theological concept that human decisions are not pre-determined and thus are theoretically hidden from all but God.</note></term>.

<margin>282.</margin> In all these matters, the Demons know many things very well which either men do not know or cannot know. They know deeds done since the creation of the world. They know what is currently being done in regions most remote from us, even though they are present here with us. They know what will happen after many ages.

284. 285. Yet it is not always necessary for these things to be performed by evil spirits, or even by those who have their seats within the humans through whom these things are revealed. Whatever the evil can do, the good can do; and the evil, just like the good, are not bound to any single law by which they do these things.

Inspired by the Holy Spirit, the holy men of God spoke.

### CHAPTER XXIV.

->*Concerning the knowledge of languages, and whether that alone reveals demons inhabiting humans.*<-

<margin>291.</margin>
The knowledge of foreign idioms <term>idioms<note>original: "idiomatum"; in this context, it refers to specific languages or regional dialects.</note></term> and the understanding of languages also reveal spirits hiding within humans. And rightly so. The matter will be clear if three points are established: first, that it is naturally impossible for someone to use a language or idiom which they do not know. Second: that there is no idiom which demons do not know, or cannot soon master. Third: that every action observed in humans has some cause from which it arises.

<margin>2 Cor. 12.</margin>
<margin>292.</margin>
Regarding the first point, there is no controversy. This is the common sense and consensus of all. This is confirmed by the great labor we undertake in learning languages—to say nothing of the fact that the gift of tongues <note>The ability to speak languages one has never studied, famously attributed to the Apostles at Pentecost.</note> is numbered among the benefits once conferred on the Apostles by the singular gift of God.

<margin>293.</margin>
Likewise, there is no doubt that demons know all idioms. Humans learn them by the custom of those with whom they live; why, then, would demons not learn them, who are always present among men? Do they not observe what they speak? Do they not note what they do?

<margin>294.</margin>
It is also most certain that every action detected in humans has some cause. For since an action is the effect and work of an agent, and the agent is ranked among the causes, it is impossible for any action to exist for which no cause can be given.

<margin>295.</margin>
Therefore, foreign speech in the humans who sound it comes from someone. But from whom? Entirely from a spirit or a mind. Why so? Because all speech is the messenger of that which lies hidden in the mind or spirit; wherefore it is absolutely necessary that, just as smoke reveals fire, so speech reveals the mind and spirit.

<margin>296.</margin>
From what spirit, then, will it be? Surely not from a human one. It is not the human who forms the foreign speech. What they have not learned, they do not speak...

## CHAPTER XXVII.

*Concerning the wretched condition of possessed men, on account of the evils which demons bring partly to their bodies and partly to their souls.*

<margin>326.</margin>
There is no doubt that men who are besieged by wicked spirits <note>original: *Spiritibus nequam*</note> are wretched; we must inquire from whence this misery comes, or how it happens. For in the former point, all agree who either know what it is for men to be possessed, or have at some time seen the possessed. Who was there ever who did not feel for the possessed, or did not pity them?

327. Truly, misery is always derived from one of two things: from the evils which are inflicted upon men, or from the goods of which they are deprived. Where either no evil is inflicted, or no loss of any good occurs, although they may seem wretched to themselves, in truth they are not wretched.

328. Now, since demoniacs are indeed wretched, it must be seen whether they suffer evils, or suffer the loss of goods, or sustain adversities and evils together with the loss of goods.

329. Is there need for many words? It is certain that evils are brought upon the Possessed; it is certain they are deprived of goods; therefore, they are wretched on two counts.

<margin>Chapter 8, section 2.</margin>
330. But, because evil is manifold and there are various kinds of goods, we must ask: of how many and of what goods do demons deprive wretched men? Also, how many and what are the evils which they bring? Let us discuss this second point first, and afterward we shall pursue the other.

331. Evils, therefore, are either of the bodies or of the souls. What and how great the evils are that demons bring upon bodies has been shown above; let us speak, therefore, of what things they trouble the souls with, or what evils they inflict upon them.

<margin>Chapter 4.</margin>

333. So, perhaps, some might say. But yet, demons do not bring both of these evils upon the possessed. Granting that they may be the cause of the pain and sadness of which men perceive no small amount from such great misery; but yet, divine offense...

...do not reconcile to men <note>The text continues from the previous page, likely arguing that these actions do not make the person guilty before God.</note>. This is because they are not the cause for men to sin, nor can sin be attributed to men in any way, because it is the demons residing in them who are working.

334. We do not deny at this point that many sins are committed through the possessed. Do we not hear blasphemies? Slanders? Insults? False accusations? Do we not see death sometimes brought to some, or wounds inflicted? Are these perhaps not sins? Certainly they are. These also provoke divine wrath: but although they are committed *through* the possessed, they are not committed *by* the possessed.

<margin>Chapter 23, etc.</margin>
335. All these are the works of demons. Therefore, they are not to be attributed to the wretched possessed, but to the unhappy demons, just as we otherwise attribute to them the revelation of secrets, unknown speech, foreign languages, the trembling of limbs, and similar things.

336. There is one thing we can say belongs to the Possessed: namely, that the wicked spirits use their limbs and bodies—the tongue to form the voice, the mouth to vomit up blasphemies, the hand to bring death and wounds, and so on.

337. But yet, even then they do not use the limbs of men in the same way that men use them themselves. When men use their own limbs, the actions can truly be attributed to the limbs; they themselves move them to act, and the limbs truly act. But when the spirits use them in the possessed, the operations cannot properly be attributed to the limbs, nor is it truly the limbs themselves that act, but rather they are acted upon and driven by the inhabiting demons <note>original: *aguntur potius, & impelluntur*. The author distinguishes between the person as an "actor" and the person as a "tool" being moved by another.</note>.

338. This is the reason why whatever is committed here is not the sin of the men; nor should it be turned into a vice or disgrace for the men, no matter what kind of outrage they commit, just as a hatchet is not blamed for the fact that a robber uses it to slaughter men.

339. This is the reason why the possessed are not held to repair the damages, if any have been caused by them. Just as it is not they themselves who sin, so it is not they themselves who bring damage to bodies or fortunes. But if anyone is held to the restitution of damages caused by the possessed, those are held to whom the care of the possessed pertains in any way, and by whose negligence—which they could and should have avoided—the damages were brought about.

340. Finally, this is the reason why punishments <term>supplicia: refers here to legal penalties or executions</term> should not be taken from the Possessed, even though the greatest outrages are committed through them. For are punishments just in a case where there are no crimes? If the quantity of punishment ought to be according to the quantity of the crimes, there shall be no punishments where there are no crimes—which is the case here.

## ON THE POSSESSED.
<sig>G 3</sig>

**341.** Furthermore, although we may free those who are **Possessed** from the guilt of certain sins, we do not free them from all of them. There are some sins which they commit themselves, for which they are no more to be excused than those who are not possessed. These are the things which are done both through them and by them, and are carried out by their own proper will.

**342.** For demons are not always harassing the possessed; sometimes the individuals are left to themselves and suffer no disturbances. At such times, just as they are capable of earning merit before God, so too can they provoke divine wrath through their own sins.

**343.** Therefore, sins must be distinguished according to the **author** of the acts, separating the sins of the demons from those of the **Possessed** humans. If the demons are the authors, the sins belong to the demons and not the humans. But the sins belong to the humans, and not the demons, in cases where the humans themselves are the cause.

**344.** Thus, many are greatly mistaken who, whenever they witness outrages committed by the **Possessed**, immediately attribute those acts to the victims themselves, and by this standard they measure the wretchedness of the **Possessed**. How miserable their condition would be if everything done through the **Possessed** were their own fault! <margin>Chapter 32.</margin> How then shall we excuse God from sin—He who, for most just causes, often subjects mortals to this misery of being occupied by demons? We even find certain holy men, most dear to God, who actually requested from God the "butchery" of demons <note>original: "daemonum carnicifiam"—a vivid term for physical or spiritual torment used as a form of extreme asceticism or purification</note> as a way to atone for their sins. Did they perhaps also request that they might offend God with sins? And was this trial and vexation granted to them for the expiation of their sins—something that would be impossible to endure without the gravest offense against God? <margin>Thesis 433.</margin>

**345.** They are also mistaken who attribute everything done by the **Possessed** to the occupying demons, and believe that pardon should be granted for every act. Not everything is to be attributed to the demons, and pardon is not to be granted for everything. Many things must be atoned for through the sign of a contrite heart, through <term>sacramental confession</term> <note>The Catholic ritual of confessing sins to a priest to receive absolution</note>, and through the worthy fruits of penance.

**346.** They err, too, who divide the guilt itself, thinking it should be attributed partly to the demons and partly to the **Possessed**. Although perhaps this division might have a place in some instances, it does not apply to all. Some acts are to be attributed entirely to the demons, and some entirely to the **Possessed**.

**347.** To what has been said, it must be added that although demons are not the cause of sins in the **Possessed**, nor do they of themselves rub off any guilt <note>original: "affricent"—meaning the demon's inherent sinfulness does not automatically "rub off" on the human soul</note> onto them, they can nevertheless greatly push and drive them toward sin. This is not surprising. If they can influence those whom they do not occupy, why should they not be able to influence those whom they do?

**348.** Indeed, how many do they drive toward sin from among those they do not possess? The prayer of Christ teaches this more than enough when He calls them the **princes of this world** <note>original: "principes huius mundi"—a reference to John 12:31</note>; and the teaching of the Blessed Paul also calls them the **princes of the power of the air** <note>original: "principes potestatis aeris"—a reference to Ephesians 2:2</note>, and...

<summary>This page argues that being possessed does not grant a person total moral immunity; they remain responsible for sins committed by their own will during periods of demonic inactivity. The author clarifies that while demons can tempt and drive the possessed toward sin, the "authorship" of the act determines whether the human or the demon is at fault.</summary>

...he says [the devil] works in the sons of disobedience. The most holy <term>Augustine<note>A foundational Christian theologian (354–430 AD) whose writings on the nature of evil and the human will were central to late-Renaissance thought.</note></term> teaches this, calling them the **Princes of Desires**, through whom everything that is fleeting is lusted after. 

And toward how many and how diverse sins do they drive us? In some, they stir up brotherly hatred, for as the Apostle says: *he who hates his brother is a murderer*, and the devil was a murderer from the beginning. In others, they stir up a passion for lying; hence the devil is called a liar by the Lord, and the father of lies. In others, they incite lust: for which reason he is called an <term>Unclean Spirit<note>original: "Spiritus immundus" — a common theological term for a demon, emphasizing its role in promoting moral impurity.</note></term> by that same Lord. In others, they incite pride: hence the demon is called the **King over all the children of pride**. In others, they stir up greed, which is why it is said of the greedy Judas: *one of you is a devil*. In others, they incite wrath: so that the Apostle most excellently warned that we must take care that the sun does not go down on our anger, lest a place be given to the devil. In others, they provoke trickery and deception, as the Apostle indicates when he calls **Elymas the Magician** a son of the devil.

**350.** These spirits are capable of such things in those who are *not* possessed; will they not be able to do the same in the wretched <term>Possessed<note>original: "Obsessos" — those whose bodies are physically occupied by a demonic presence.</note></term>? Their power over these victims is no less, as we have said, than it is over those not possessed; indeed, why should it not seem that they can do even more in these cases? This is both because they are able to block the possessed from many and greater goods which they have seized for themselves, and also because they can make greater impressions upon those faculties which the <term>will<note>In this context, the "will" is the human capacity for choice, which theologians argued remained free even under demonic harassment.</note></term> follows when it falls into sin.

**351.** For there is no doubt that a "spur" is added to sin in both ways. In the first way, because they hinder the duties of the virtues in no small measure; therefore, while men are hindered in these, they are, as it were, incited toward vice. In the latter way, because it is arduous and difficult for the will to enter a path other than the one to which it is invited by the appearance of a **perceived good**, or by the impulse of the <term>appetites<note>original: "appetitus" — the sensory drives or physical desires that influence human behavior.</note></term> and emotions.

**352.** Now, for the reasons stated, demons are very powerful against the **Possessed**. They can hinder them in the pursuit of virtues: they can make great attacks upon those faculties to which the will accommodates itself. The former point will be demonstrated in the following chapter; the latter is understood by anyone who remembers that these are the powers of demons: that they can delude the faculties we call <term>Cognitive<note>original: "Cognoscitiuæ" — the mental powers of perception, reason, and imagination.</note></term> with the appearance of a false good, and stir up wondrous movements in the body and the appetitive faculties.

**353.** Therefore, demons will drive the **Possessed** toward sins in three ways: one indirectly, and two directly. **Indirectly**, while they either distract them from or hinder them in good things. **Directly**, first, while they invite them with the appearance of a deceptive good; secondly, while they seize the lower appetitive powers and the wicked impulses within the human as an aid, in order to incline the will toward sinning.

**354.** But nevertheless, they promote it in such a way that they never [take away] the will's own freedom...

## CHAPTER XXVIII.

->*On the miserable condition of the obsessed, regarding the goods of which they are deprived by demons.*<-

Although there are many kinds of goods, the inquiry of the present chapter can be reduced to two primary types. For some belong to the future life, and some to the present. To the future life belong the joys of the kingdom of heaven; to this present life belong whatever things lead toward that future life.

358. These latter goods are of a triple order. First are the <term>Theological habits<note>Refers to the "Theological Virtues" (Faith, Hope, and Charity) which were considered divinely infused habits of the soul.</note></term>, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and especially faith. Second are the exercises of the virtues, which we call "good works." Third is the use of the sacraments, and especially the <term>most holy Eucharist<note>The sacrament of Holy Communion. The author is addressing a contemporary debate about whether a possessed person's body is too "unclean" to receive the host.</note></term>.

359. Regarding these, the question is: Are obsessed men deprived of all these things by spirits? Specifically, is the entrance to eternal life closed to them? Are they bereaved of the Christian faith? Are they unable to do anything good that might lead them to eternal life? Should they also be barred from the most holy sacrament of the Eucharist and other mysteries of the Christian religion? We define the matter briefly.

360. Demons do not deprive the possessed of the hope of eternal life. Simply because someone is obsessed, they are not excluded from the kingdom of heaven. This assertion is easily believed by those who know the laws of that kingdom: that it repels no one, except him whom the conscience of some <term>lethal sin<note>original: "peccati lethalis" — commonly known as mortal sin, a grave sin that "kills" the life of grace in the soul.</note></term> weighs down. Since those whom demons inhabit can be free from such sin, it is altogether to be believed that the entrance to heaven is not closed to them.

Because it has been demonstrated thus far both that they are not deprived of any of the three types of goods we have established, and furthermore, that the condition of the Possessed is much better than that of certain others whom we nevertheless judge to be entirely unhappy.

375 Granted, there are others unhappier than the Possessed, but that does not mean the Possessed suffer no misery. Even if it is lesser, some misery remains. Even if the demons do not deprive the Possessed of those spiritual goods we mentioned, they nevertheless deprive them of many other goods, and in manifold ways.

# PART I. THE DISPUTATION.
<page-num>58</page-num>
<header>PART I. THE DISPUTATION.</header>

376. In the preceding chapter, we distinguished between two types of evils: those of the Body and those of the Soul. We now distinguish between two types of goods, for there are certain goods of the Body and certain goods of the Soul. If demons do not deprive the <term>possessed<note>Latin: *obsessi*. Those physically besieged or occupied by a demonic presence.</note></term> of the goods of the soul, they certainly deprive them of the goods of the Body. This matter is made clear by the examples of those whom we have accepted as being possessed.

377. But even in the goods of the Soul, these miserable people suffer losses—specifically regarding those very matters about which the inquiry was established at the beginning of this chapter. We demonstrate the reason for this in the following sections.

378. The hope of eternal life is not taken away from the possessed by demons; this was stated above in Thesis 159. Nevertheless, those who have brought this <term>demonic torture<note>original: "dæmonum carnificinam" — literally "the demon's butchery" or "shambles," emphasizing the brutal physical and mental toll of possession.</note></term> upon themselves because of grave crimes, and who are left by the just judgment of God to these spirits, find themselves in the most immediate danger of their salvation if they do not have a period of time free from harassment to return to themselves and perform penance for the sins they committed.

379. The demons themselves do not deprive the possessed of Faith; this was stated in Thesis 361. However, they do hinder some so that they do not apply their minds to faith. Others, who have already been instructed in the faith, they hold back so that they do not <term>elicit<note>To "elicit" an act of faith means to consciously and willfully put one's faith into practice or prayer.</note></term> acts of faith for their own spiritual benefit.

380. The logic regarding Faith is the same for other <term>habits<note>In scholastic philosophy, a "habit" (habitus) is a stable disposition of the soul, such as a virtue, that allows a person to perform certain actions easily and consistently.</note></term>. For those whom the demons hinder from embracing the Christian faith, they also hinder from obtaining the remaining habits—whether those that follow faith or those joined with it. And just as they hold some back from exercising acts of faith, they do the same regarding the acts of the other virtues, whatever they may be. Therefore, when we said in Thesis 364 that the condition of the possessed and the non-possessed in the exercise of virtues was the same, it was said for this reason: so that it would not be believed that the duties of virtue are forbidden to men simply because they are possessed. Not everyone who is possessed is excluded from the "school of virtues," even though they often suffer great losses.

381. Is it not true that the principal loss of goods suffered by the <term>demoniacs<note>Latin: *dæmoniaci*. A term used interchangeably with "the possessed."</note></term> is found in the duties of the virtues? Those who are well-instructed in the Catholic religion know that no small gain for souls comes from the study of virtues. They know that a great harvest is brought into the granaries of souls through the duties of Christian Justice. When, therefore, the demons call the demoniacs away from these duties—when they hinder or retard them in these things—it cannot be denied that mortals are deprived of great goods by the malice of the Demons.

382. But perhaps the Spirits do not have the power to hinder the study of virtues? Why would they not have the power? They are perfectly capable of it, and they are capable not in one way, but in many. For, in the first place, there are many things which cannot be exercised except through the ministry of our bodies.

<summary>This page discusses how demonic possession deprives individuals of both physical and spiritual "goods." While demons cannot technically remove internal virtues like faith or hope, they can hinder a person's ability to act upon them, especially actions requiring bodily cooperation, thereby creating a "loss" of spiritual merit.</summary>

...these things, since the Demons have bodies in their power, it is beyond all controversy that their works can be hindered—and are frequently hindered. *Second*, these same [virtuous acts] demand a present mind and require that they be performed with reason and judgment. But since the mind, in its operations, must have recourse to <term>mental images<note>original: *phantasmata*. In the psychology of the time, these were sensory images or "snapshots" stored in the brain that the mind requires to think or process information.</note></term> (over which the Spirits have no small power), the mind will be as easily disturbed and hindered as it is easy for the Spirits to disturb a person's imagination. *Third*, they require the work of the will, without which nothing at all is rightly performed in a person. But the Demons can do nothing against the will itself; yet, because the will exists in the body, it is aided by the body's benefits and slowed by its harms. Therefore, by the same logic that the Spirits disadvantage bodies, they hinder the will.

Those under the influence or physical control of a demon.</note></term> can suffer in the third kind of goods, namely, the use of the *Sacraments*. Since these are, for the most part, either acts of virtue or joined with virtues, the possessed will suffer the same losses in the use of the Sacraments as they experience in the duties of the virtues themselves. These are the goods of which the <term>Besieged<note>Latin: *Obsessi*. Another term for the possessed, implying someone being "sat upon" or "occupied" by an external force.</note></term> are deprived.

### CHAPTER XXIX.

->*Whether the Possessed are always the cause of their own misery and the tyranny they suffer from Demons.*<-

<margin>384.</margin>
Regarding the cause for which people are besieged by Demons, there is a question; and it is called into controversy *whether they themselves are the authors of their own evils*, although strictly speaking, the question is not so much this, as *whether they are always the authors*; and if not always themselves, to what causes their misery should be attributed.

It is established that the Possessed are sometimes the cause of their own evils. It is asked whether they also sometimes suffer these things without any merit of their own. Although it does not reveal the cause for which she was <term>Possessed<note>original: *Obsessa*. And when he comes, he finds it swept clean and decorated. Then he goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there.* <note>Matthew 12:43-45.</note>

Why does the Spirit return to the house from which it departed? Because the rest it did not find in arid places, it found in that house. For its greatest rest is in the hearts of the ungodly; there, therefore, it will fix its seat; there it will choose its dwelling.

Who truly can doubt that this evil happened to him because of his sins? If the advice of Daniel, urging him to give alms, does not prove it, then surely the speech that rang in his ears does: 
> *To you it is said, King Nebuchadnezzar: the kingdom shall pass from you, and they shall drive you from men, and your dwelling shall be with the wild beasts: you shall eat grass like an ox, and seven times shall change over you, until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, and gives it to whomever He wishes.*

Was he not possessed through his own fault? For why is he so often rebuked? Why is it said that he lost through pride the kingdom he obtained through humility?

...in several places; in this disputation, it serves to use the words of Jerome himself:
> In a town near the port of Gaza, *he says*, a young neighbor was desperately in love with a Virgin of God. When he had gained nothing through frequent touch, jests, nods, whistling, and other such things—which are usually the beginnings of a virginity about to perish—he set out for Memphis, so that having confessed his wound, he might return to the Virgin armed with <term>Magic Arts<note>The text refers to the use of occult or "forbidden" knowledge, often associated in this period with ancient Egyptian or pagan rituals.</note></term>. Therefore, after a year, having been instructed by the Priests of Asclepius <note>original: *AEsculapij Vatibus*. Asclepius was the Greek god of medicine, but here his priests are associated with dark magic or sorcery.</note>, he buried certain "tormented words" and monstrous figures engraved on a plate of Cyprian copper beneath the threshold of the girl's house. Immediately, the Virgin began to go mad; throwing off her head-covering, she would whirl her hair, gnash her teeth, and cry out the name of the youth. Indeed, the magnitude of her love had turned into a frenzy. Led by her parents to the Monastery, she was handed over to the Elder (Hilarion). The demon immediately began howling and confessing: "I have suffered violence; I was brought here against my will! How well I used to delude men in Memphis with dreams! O what crosses, O what torments I suffer! You compel me to go out, yet I am held bound beneath the threshold. I will not leave, unless the Youth who holds me lets me go." Then the Elder said: "Great is your strength indeed, you who are held tight by a piece of thread and a copper plate! Tell me, why did you dare to enter a girl of God?" "To preserve her," *he said*, "as a virgin." [Hilarion replied:] "You would preserve her, you betrayer of chastity? Why did you not rather enter into him who sent you?" "For what purpose," he replied, "should I enter into him, who already possessed my colleague, the demon of love?" However, the Saint did not wish to order that the signs <note>The physical charms or "incantations" buried under the door.</note> be searched for, lest it should seem either that the demon had departed only because the incantations were destroyed, or that he himself had placed any faith in the demon's words; for he asserted that demons are deceptive and skillful at pretending. Once her health was restored, however, he severely rebuked the Virgin, asking why she had done such things through which a demon could have entered. Thus writes the Blessed Jerome.

393. These examples confirm our hypothesis remarkably well, but reason does so no less. What wonder is it if God, in this present life, should avenge sins through demons—the very same sins He is to avenge through demons in the life to come?

394. What wonder is it if He sends wicked spirits into men to exact penalties for a life badly lived, when not infrequently He has stirred up spirits (though positioned outside of men rather than within them) to bring extreme evils and even death upon the unfortunate? It was excellently said by the Psalmist <note>original: *Psalmographo*. Refers to the author of the Book of Psalms.</note> that He sends the "indignation of His wrath through evil angels." <note>A reference to Psalm 78:49.</note>

395. God does not have only one way of avenging sins; He has many. Sometimes the elements and the heavens fight for Him; sometimes He arms savage beasts. He also uses spirits, sometimes good and sometimes evil. And why not? For is not the entire world destined to fight on His side?

396. Hence, Blessed Augustine says well in *The City of God*, Book 4, Chapter 34: *Demons,* he says, *cannot possess anyone except those whom they have deceived by trickery.* And again: *The enemy power conquers or subjugates no one, except through a fellowship of sin.* <note>original: *societate peccati*. This suggests that the demon gains a "legal" or spiritual foothold through the victim's own moral failings.</note>

### CHAPTER XXX.

->On account of which faults of their own the Possessed suffer the tyranny of Demons.<-

<margin>397.</margin> Some faults are Mortal <note>original: *Lethales*, meaning "deadly." In Catholic theology, these are serious sins that "kill" the life of grace in the soul.</note>, others are Venial <note>Lesser sins that do not break one's relationship with God but weaken it.</note>. The former provoke divine vengeance and are called Mortal because they bring death to the soul; the latter take their name from the pardon <note>Latin: *venia*.</note> which they easily obtain. Each kind is varied and manifold, just as it happens that God is offended in many and various ways.

398. **Regarding these, it is asked: which are they that open the door for demons to enter men? Is it only Mortal sins, or also Venial ones? And if either or both, do all sins of that kind provide this entry, or rather are there certain and determined ones in each category?** The matter, because it does not present a very great difficulty, is to be settled briefly.

399. **It is certain that men are possessed by demons on account of Mortal sins.** Almost all the examples from the previous Chapter teach this: both those supplied by Sacred Scripture and those from secular History; therefore, there is no need for a longer proof.

400. **It is also certain that Venial faults have provided the opportunity for demons to enter men.** "We have known even holy men," says Cassian <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435), a monk and theologian whose *Conferences* (Collationes) were foundational for Western monasticism.</note> in *Conference* 7, chapter 25, "to be handed over bodily to Satan for even the slightest offenses, or to be afflicted with great infirmities." Perhaps the example of the girl proves this, which we cited in the preceding chapter from Saint Jerome. Perhaps also another example mentioned by Prosper of Aquitaine <note>A 5th-century Christian writer and disciple of St. Augustine.</note>: a woman who, when she had looked too immodestly at a certain statue of Venus in a bath and had mimicked its pose, was soon possessed by the devil; she was so tormented that the Wicked Spirit blocked her throat, taking away her ability to take food and drink for seventy days.

401. But if there is doubt about whether the faults of these women were Venial, there is certainly no doubt regarding the Abbot Moses and a certain nun. The former, as Cassian testifies, confessed he was possessed because of impatience and a harshly spoken word; the latter because of a slight gluttony, as Saint Gregory the Great <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604), whose *Dialogues* contain many accounts of miracles and possessions.</note> records in *Dialogues*, Book 1, Chapter 4. But let us record the examples not in our own words, but in theirs. Regarding Moses, therefore, thus says Cassian in *Conference* 7, Chapter 27:

And although Venial sins are light—and, as we said, take their name from the "pardon" they easily obtain—no injury is done to men when they are handed over to the <term>demon’s torture-chamber<note>The Latin *carnificina* refers specifically to a place of execution or the work of a hangman; the author views possession as a form of divine corrective punishment.</note></term> even because of these. For those sins which are light in comparison to Mortal sins are great when compared with any worldly punishments, and leave them far behind.

### ON THE POSSESSED

...even, without any merit of their own, some may undergo the same. But since this argument requires more space, it must be explained in the following chapter.

<margin>404.</margin> Now, since we have said that there are manifold faults, both *Venial* <note>Lesser sins that do not fully sever the soul's relationship with God.</note> and *Mortal* <note>Grave sins that "kill" the life of grace in the soul.</note>; *let us inquire whether there are certain specific kinds of sins that more justly suffer the vengeance of demons and more easily open an entrance to them. What, then, are they?*

<margin>405.</margin> To the point, we say briefly: nothing can be established as certain here. Just as *Venial* and *Mortal faults* open an entrance for demons to enter men, so whatever they may be—if God so permits and wills—they can open the way.

<margin>406.</margin> Nevertheless, I would not deny that there are some sins which provide an entrance more easily: either those which God seems to punish more justly by this means, or those on account of which the demons themselves are more able to strive for and desire an entry into men. *And which are they?*

<margin>407.</margin> The first is infidelity, or *the Assaulting and Denying of the Known Truth*. Thus Stapleton <note>Thomas Stapleton (1535–1598), a prominent English Catholic theologian and controversialist.</note> teaches from Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an early Christian bishop and martyr.</note>, in his sermon for the *Second Sunday of Lent*, that many were formerly possessed by demons for the reason that they had fallen away from the faith. And is it not fitting that the Father of Lies <note>original: *Pater mendacij*; a traditional title for the Devil based on John 8:44.</note> should have power over those who reject the Master of Truth? Should they not be possessed by the powers of darkness who refuse to let the light of truth shine in their hearts?

<margin>408.</margin> The second is the *Abuse of the Most Holy Eucharist*. In the same place, Cyprian brings forward examples for this, reporting that both men and women were possessed by evil spirits because they had approached the Lord's table without Confession and Penance for their sins. Perhaps certain of the Corinthians are to be grouped with these, whom the Apostle <note>St. Paul, in 1 Corinthians 11:30.</note> recounts as being weakened and subject to diseases for the reason that they communicated in the Sacraments of the altar without being tested.

<margin>409.</margin> The third is *Blasphemy*. This opened the door to the demons who entered Alexander and Hymenaeus <note>Biblical figures mentioned in 1 Timothy 1:20 who were "handed over to Satan" to be taught not to blaspheme.</note>. Certainly, blasphemers are worthy to be occupied by the Spirits of Blasphemy.

<margin>410.</margin> The fourth is the sin of *Pride*. Is it not appropriate that he who is King *over all the children of Pride* <note>A reference to Job 41:34, traditionally interpreted as describing Leviathan or the Devil.</note> should have a seat among the proud and exercise power over them? Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: *Nabuchodonosor*.</note>, the most proud King of the Assyrians, teaches to his own great misfortune how fitting this is—to say nothing of countless others.

<margin>411.</margin> The fifth is *Lust* <note>original: *Luxuria*, which in a theological context refers specifically to sexual immorality or lechery.</note>. Because of this, the Corinthian was delivered to Satan by the Apostle. Perhaps because of the same, Mary Magdalene suffered the tyranny of seven demons. Because of the same, if not possessed, certainly seven men were slain who sought Sarah <note>A reference to the Book of Tobit, where the demon Asmodeus kills the seven husbands of Sarah on their wedding nights.</note>. Moreover, a certain girl, because she looked too immodestly upon an image of Venus and conformed herself to it, was possessed by a demon, as noted by *Prosper of Aquitaine* <note>A 5th-century Christian writer and disciple of St. Augustine.</note>.

**418.** Those who devote themselves to demons and pray to be carried off by them may also come to fear those same demons. And not without reason. Is it not just for a person to be subjected to the butchery of the one they demanded as their own executioner? <note>Original: "carnificem efflagitat." **419.** Closely related to these are the Magicians and Diviners who, even if they have not formally devoted themselves to demons, certainly have great and sacrilegious pacts and alliances with them. There is no doubt that demons have occasionally brought a miserable death upon these people. History, citing Blessed Jerome elsewhere, proves that such people have also been possessed by demons at times. But whatever the case may be with them, if it is just that a person be punished by the very thing through which they sinned, we shall say that no injury is done to them if they experience the tortures of those whose pretended services they once enjoyed.

**420.** To what has been said, I add the contempt or neglect of the Sacrament of Confirmation. <note>In the Catholic tradition, Confirmation is the sacrament that "strengthens" the believer with the Holy Spirit to resist evil.</note> We know not just one, but many people who suffered grave harassments and persecutions from the devil before they were initiated into the Sacrament of Confirmation; they were liberated as soon as they received the sacrament. Why indeed would the devil not enter, or demand to enter, those whom he otherwise finds easy to harass?

**421.** Many more could be added to the sins we have already reviewed; but since we consider these the principal ones, and the rest can be reduced to them, we shall make an end here. Let us now inquire whether humans might also be possessed by demons through no fault of their own.

### CHAPTER XXXI.

->*Humans are sometimes subjected to the tyranny of Demons not because of their own faults, but because of the faults of others.*<-

Such invisible matters must be left to the inscrutable judgment of the Most High God. So says Blessed Jerome.

**423.** Saint John Chrysostom <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquent preaching; "Chrysostom" means "golden-mouthed."</note> agrees with Blessed Jerome on this matter. In the books he wrote concerning Divine Providence, Chrysostom recognizes God's wisdom even in the fact that holy men are sometimes possessed by demons. He notes that while these men lived in sin and indulged in vices, no such adversity troubled them. He used this same reasoning to comfort a man named Theodorus, who was possessed by demons.

**424.** This matter is not in doubt, as shown first by the example of children. It is impossible for them to sin due to their lack of age, yet daily examples prove they are sometimes possessed by demons. Blessed Jerome even confirms this occurs in three-year-olds, two-year-olds, and infants still nursing at their mothers' breasts.

<margin>John 9.</margin>
**425.** Furthermore, logic supports this view. The afflictions brought by spirits are no different from the other types of "evils of punishment" <note>In traditional theology, a distinction is made between the "evil of fault" (sin) and the "evil of punishment" (suffering or natural disasters).</note> that we encounter; yet it is not necessary that these be inflicted because of one’s own merits or failings. *Neither has this man sinned, nor his parents,* <note>original: "Neque hic peccauit, neque parentes eius"</note> the Lord said concerning a certain man who suffered the heavy punishment of blindness.

<margin>Sulpicius in the Life of Martin, Dialogue 1.</margin>
**426.** To this we may add the judgment of a certain Hermit. It is said that he asked and obtained from God that his body be afflicted for several months by an inhabiting demon. He did this because he feared the danger of the sin of pride. This pious man certainly understood that the torture of demons is not always granted because of past sins already committed, but is sometimes permitted so that men do not fall into future sins and offend God.

<margin>Job 1.</margin>
**427.** Consider how many evils the devil brought upon the most holy Job, not only in his fortune, but even in his very body. Was it perhaps all his own fault? Scripture teaches that he was holy and upright. If a demon, positioned outside of Job’s body, was able to do these things, why could it not do the same while inhabiting him—even without any fault on the holy man's part?

<margin>Thes. 396.</margin>
**438.** <note>The original page numbering skips from 427 to 438.</note> We know that Blessed Augustine said that demons do not possess men unless they have deceived them through trickery. He also said: *The enemy subjugates no one except through a partnership with sin.* <note>original: "Inimicum neminem subiugare, nisi societate peccati"</note> However, the Most Holy Father Augustine was attending not to what *must* happen by necessity, but to what *usually* happens in most cases.

**429.** Meanwhile, although the possessed do not always suffer the tyranny of demons because of their own personal fault, they do not always suffer it without *any* fault being involved. Just as the sin of some can be the cause of punishment for others, so too can the sins of others summon the tyranny and butchery of demons upon a person.

**430.** What we are saying does not violate the laws of justice. Can a person not be justly punished through the goods they possess? And are not some men...

### ON THE POSSESSED.

**435.** And this is exactly how the matter stands. It happens quite often that, without any personal demerit of the individuals, people suffer not only this demonic butchery <note>original: "carnificinam." This evocative term literally refers to the work of a executioner or butcher, suggesting the extreme physical and mental torture of possession.</note> we are discussing, but also whatever other evils might trouble their bodies or their fortunes. In certain evils, we can find hardly any other cause than divine providence.

**436.** And indeed, divine providence can have many reasons for permitting or even commanding this butchery by demons, even when there is no fault on the part of the people. Specifically, the purpose here is either to instruct humanity, to deter them from vices and incite them toward the pursuit of virtues, to establish an example of patience, or to make them fit and capable of receiving greater rewards in the life to come.

**437.** It instructs in two ways. First, from this they understand that, besides physical bodies, there are certain Spirits entirely devoid of material substance <note>original: "omnis concretionis expertes." This refers to the theological concept that spirits are not "composed" of matter.</note>—something the Sadducees <note>A Jewish sect at the time of Jesus known for denying the resurrection of the dead and the existence of spirits or angels.</note> used to deny. Second, they conclude that it is not surprising if they possess a soul <margin>Acts 19.</margin> that is separate from the body; a soul which, like an immortal spirit, is eternal and will enter another way of living after this life.

**438.** Furthermore, here, as if in an image, those ultimate tortures and torments that await the wicked after this life are placed before one's eyes. Through consideration of these, mortals may flee from the sins by which they would deserve the dominion and butchery of demons in the future life.

**439.** They also recognize how great the hatred of unclean spirits <note>original: "spirituum immundorum." A common scriptural term for demons.</note> is toward the human race, since they rage with such barbarity against wretched men, and even against the innocent. This meditation has the benefit of turning the minds of mortals (unless perhaps their salvation is beyond hope) away from spirits, and it dissolves all society and communion with them.

**440.** From this, people can also learn what demons work within the souls of those who have committed deadly sins <term>Lethalia peccata: Mortal or "deadly" sins, which in Catholic theology are grave actions that destroy the relationship with God.</term>. # CHAPTER XXXIII.

## *That there is some power and virtue by which demons may be cast out of human bodies.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap initial 'T' with floral patterns.</image-desc>
The third part of the Disputation <note>original: "Disputationis." A formal academic or theological debate common in the Renaissance and Early Modern periods.</note> focuses on the method and the reasons for driving out the wicked spirit from human bodies. In this section, generally speaking, four main questions are investigated. First, is there any power by which demons can be driven out of men? Second, in whose hands does this power reside? Third, upon what things does this power chiefly rely? Fourth, what are the causes why these spirits leave humans with such great difficulty?

444. This first chapter, like the others, contains several parts. For it must not only be demonstrated that such a power exists; but it must also be defined whether that power is a single kind or manifold; and if it is manifold, whether the condition of all these powers is the same, or what the distinction is between them.

445. And indeed, that there is nevertheless some power, no one ought to doubt who is even moderately well-versed in the Sacred Scriptures. For those writings both demonstrate by whom this power was granted, and to whom it was granted, and for what reason it was granted; and furthermore, they suggest with no small arguments how it was not granted in vain.

446. They [the Scriptures] teach that it was conferred by Christ the Lord. For those whom He sent into the whole world to bring a new light into the world and to teach heavenly doctrine, He willed to be armed and equipped with this power, so that, whenever they judged it appropriate, they might cast out demons from human bodies.

447. They teach that this was communicated to all the faithful, but nevertheless especially to the Apostles and the Disciples of Christ. "I have given" (He speaks to His... <note>The text cuts off here at the bottom of the page.</note>)

Moreover, wishing to satisfy and prove to those present that he possessed this power, Eleazar would place before them either a cup or a basin full of water, and he would command the demon, as it departed from the man, to overturn it, and thus provide a sign to the onlookers that it had left the man. ...purification, like physicians who treat the body, they made a profession of it and collected money.

460. Regarding this fourth method, there was no doubt among the Jewish Scribes and Pharisees. Hence, they sought to devalue the miracles of Christ and his expulsion of demons by saying: "By the prince of demons, Beelzebub, he casts out demons." <note>A reference to Matthew 12:24. Beelzebub was a name used for a high-ranking demon or the devil himself.</note> But this should not be seen as something new; for it is well established that the powers of all demons are not equal, but some are more powerful than others, and for this reason, it easily happens that the superior ones drive the inferior ones from their seats.

461. And although the Lord appears in some places to prove that it is impossible for demons to cast out demons—lest they wish their own kingdom to be destroyed—he did not necessarily intend to deny that demons possess this power. Rather, he indicated that this objection could be raised against the argument he himself put forward. This can be gathered from the fact that he, not content with that argument as being sufficiently firm, wished to bring forward others that would not have such an easy objection. Nevertheless, it can also be said that the Lord wished to signify that unwilling devils are never driven out by their fellows. For when they yield to the command of their associates, they are not so much "expelled" as they depart of their own accord.

462. From what has been said, it follows that a fourfold power of driving out demons can be distinguished. One may be called the power of Christ; the second, of God; the third, of Solomon; and the fourth, Diabolical. Indeed, this distinction is taken from the authors of the acts themselves. Thus, we shall say that one is divine and the other is natural. The natural power is that by which demons are driven out by the force of other demons; the divine is that which occurs by the gift and favor of God, as happened in the cases of God, Christ, and Solomon.

## CHAPTER XXXV.

->*On the multiple differences between the fourfold power of expelling Demons.*<-

<margin>473.</margin>
Many are the differences between the methods by which we said in the previous chapter that demons are expelled; some are derived from their authors, some from their form, some from the subjects, some from their ends, and others from different causes and circumstances.

464. The first three methods, which we said rely on divine authority, have God as their author—if, at least, we wish to consider from where they first originated. There is no doubt about the power which Christ shared with his followers, since we all profess Christ to be the true God. It is also clear regarding the power by which demons are driven out through the invocation of the name of the <term>Tetragrammaton</term> <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, considered holy and powerful in exorcism.</note>. Nor can we doubt the power of Solomon, since <insert>the historian</insert> Josephus testifies that it was communicated by divine gift, and indeed every power by which demons are expelled, provided it is lawful, is divine. But the Diabolical power differs from these...

It argues that while demons can leave by "natural" agreement with superior demons, true "divine" expulsion comes from God.</summary>

...differs. For just as this method takes its name from the demon, so too it acknowledges a demon as its author.

465. The form in all of these is different from one another. The **Divine** form consisted of the invocation of the *Tetragrammaton* <note>The sacred four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, often considered too holy to pronounce.</note>; the **Solomonic** required a ring having beneath its seal a root shown by Solomon, which also had to be brought to the nostrils of the one who was possessed; the **Christological** formerly had especially the invocation of his name, or such things that served to establish his divinity or confirm his doctrine. The **Diabolical** method had none of these.

466. They also differ in their subjects or ministers: the **Diabolical** seems to have been practiced not by just anyone, but by those who had vowed themselves to demons. The **Divine** was among those to whom it was permitted in the name of the *Tetragrammaton*, as Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), a prominent bishop and writer who chronicled various religious practices and heresies.</note> suggests. The **Solomonic** had specific exorcists. But that of **Christ**, although granted especially to the Apostles, was in the beginning shared with all the faithful without exception.

467. No one doubts that there were different ends in these diverse methods. For the same end is never proposed to God and to demons. Therefore, in the power which is from God, the glory and increase of the divine name is sought, along with the safety and salvation of men, and freedom from misery; in the **Diabolical**, if perhaps this last benefit <note>i.e., relief from the misery of possession</note> is granted, the former goals are certainly expected in vain.

468. But if we investigate the origins and principles of these powers, we may also perceive some distinction from this. The last of all is that which the Lord conferred upon his Church; others are earlier than this. Among these, if an order is to be established, the power of **God** can be placed first. For it is not likely that the **Solomonic** preceded it, since there is no doubt that mortals were possessed by demons before Solomon; and it should be believed that they did not lack means by which they might be helped. We seem to be able to assert, however, that the **Diabolical** is later than the **Divine**, for the demon is called the "ape of God," <note>original: *dæmon Dei ſimia*. A common theological concept that the Devil can only mimic or distort God's true creations rather than create anything truly new.</note> who imitates and fashions the works of God in all things.

469. The power of **Christ** seems to surpass all others in efficacy. We gather this not only from the fact that the Lord exercised it in his own person and, with no effort and using the simplest of means, expelled a nearly innumerable multitude of demons; but also from the fact that he promised to his own a greater virtue and power than even he himself had in performing miracles.
<margin>Thesis 583.</margin>
Do not the belts of St. Paul and the shadows of Peter prove what we are saying? <note>References to the New Testament (Acts 19:12 and 5:15) where objects touched by Paul or the mere shadow of Peter were said to heal the sick and drive out spirits.</note> And also the demons driven out by those who, although they did not believe in Christ, nevertheless used the invocation of Christ's name in the ejection of demons.

# ON THOSE POSSESSED BY DEMONS.

470. They also differ in duration. That method of Christ for putting demons to flight is far more constant. He abolished the power that used to drive out spirits through the invocation of the *Tetragrammaton* <note>original: "tetragrammaton inuocationem"; the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, used in ancient Jewish exorcisms.</note>; that power of Solomon has lost its strength; but Christ’s power will endure as long as His Church remains on earth. If diabolical power remains, it does not remain by its own strength, but by the permission of God.

471. One may seek another distinction here: what is it? That the former methods—that is, the divine ones—are absolute, while the diabolical is not. However great the strength of the higher demons may be, and however ready the lower demons are to execute the commands of the higher ones, they cannot drive them out of human bodies through sorcerers <note>original: "Magos"</note> unless God so permits; just as neither group—that is, the lower nor the higher—can enter and possess men except by God’s permission.

472. We add a final difference to what has been said, by which the diabolical method is distinguished from the rest. Those three methods which have divine authority ought not to be condemned; but the diabolical method can be approved by no reasoning. No matter what good may be proposed here, or what evil might be avoided, it must not be permitted for anyone to use the works of demons in driving out demons.

---

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

->*For what purpose the Lord conferred upon His Church the power of casting out demons from the bodies of men.*<-

<margin>473.</margin>
The question here is not so much why the Lord, when about to send the Apostles to preach the Gospel, granted them the faculty of casting out demons, but rather for what cause He willed this power to remain in His Church for all time. There are perhaps fewer reasons for the former, and more for the latter; because these latter reasons encompass the former in their scope, they are the only ones to be reported in this place.

474. These reasons can be sought from the conditions of Him who conferred this power on the Church; or of those who exercise the power; or of those who are being freed from demons; or even of the demons themselves who are cast out from the possessed.

475. Christ's primary purpose at the beginning of the nascent Church was to persuade the world of His Gospel. Since there was need of the greatest "engines" <note>A metaphor for powerful tools or arguments.</note> for this task, the ejection of demons, which everyone regards as a great miracle, could not be omitted.

476. And although it was for other reasons as well, yet it was primarily for the demons...

476. Therefore, it should not seem strange that the Lord occupied Himself more with this type of miracle, and used several methods here. Which ones? For since the power of demons is supreme, and there is none which can be compared with theirs, certainly, when they are routed at Christ’s command, He is proved to be superior to all demons.

479. # CONCERNING THE POSSESSED.

...women were gathered to him, all of whom were cured by the same man. **So says Jerome.** <note>original: "Haec Hieronymus." Referring to St. Jerome, a 4th-century Church Father known for his Bible translations and commentaries.</note>

481. Another reason related to this is that the Lord wishes this power to be effective for the honor of Holy men. Are we unaware that it is God’s purpose, even in this mortal life, to bestow honors upon those who serve Him and promptly carry out His will? Indeed, how much honor returns to the Saints from this; when now, by their command while they were alive, demons were routed; and now, after they have departed from this life, those demons cannot even endure their dust <note>A reference to the power of relics (remains of saints) in Catholic tradition.</note>?
