482. God also wished to provide for possessed men through this power. For although He is primarily the physician of souls and seeks the salvation of souls above all things, He does not entirely abandon the care of bodies. He removes even those things which are harmful to them (such as the distress brought by spirits) out of His humanity and benevolence toward the human race; and all the more was help to be expected from Him here, because He alone was able to help.

483. The dignity of man can also be perceived from this, as well as God's supreme love and benevolence toward him. How so? At the beginning of the world's creation, He had subjected the entire physical creation to Man. In the restoration and renewal of the world, He also confers upon man power over the spiritual creation: the power, I say, of treading upon serpents, scorpions, and demons. Is this not a great dignity for man?

<margin>Ephesians 5.</margin>
484. Furthermore, this power shared with the Church—which Christ loved most greatly—contributes to the Church's splendor and beauty. In this way, He allows it to lack no kind of love. He did not only want it to be equipped with those spiritual safeguards by which the gains and benefits of souls are maintained—I speak of the <term>Sacraments</term> <note>The formal rites of the Church, such as Baptism or the Eucharist, believed to confer divine grace.</note>—but He also wanted it to be adorned with the power by which it would be able to drive out demons from human bodies.

<margin>1 Peter 5.</margin>
485. From this, mortals can also understand that whenever they sin, the blame for the fault of sin is not to be attributed to demons, but to themselves. Granted, the demons may prowl about like lions and place their nets everywhere, and set snares everywhere; yet man is superior to them. A great proof of this is that man can drive them from their seats even against their will.

486. Finally, this power serves to shame the spirits. How heavy is the disgrace if a most powerful leader is defeated by a filthy and ragged man? If he is driven from his own fortress and home? If he is deprived of his possession and goods? How great, indeed, is the power of demons! But nevertheless, any Christian soldier...

->*In whose hands lies the power of casting out demons, which Christ the Lord left to His Church.*<-

<margin>487.</margin>
It follows that we should define in whose hands the demonic power of casting out demons lies. While we do this, we must simultaneously discuss what is required in those who wish to use this power lawfully and fruitfully.

<margin>488.</margin>
However, our discussion concerns only the power of Christ, which He left for the benefit of the human race in His Church. For if we were to speak of the whole category of such power, there is no doubt that it is held by God, by the Angels, and even by some of these very same wicked spirits.

<margin>489.</margin>
Regarding God, the matter is clear. In His hand are all the ends of the earth: all things are placed under His jurisdiction. All things obey His command. He who was created so as to fear no one, fears God. Just as God created all things from nothing, so He can reduce all things to nothing; so He can move them from their place, and so He can drive them out from their seats.

This is especially seen in the writings of Ignatius, a disciple of the Apostles, who lists Exorcists among the other ecclesiastical ranks and offices. And Pope Cornelius, writing to Fabius of Antioch, says that in the Roman Church fifty-two Exorcists and Readers, together with Porters, were established. Furthermore, the Councils of Rome (under Sylvester), Laodicea, and Carthage II, III, and II <note>likely a reference to several councils in Carthage</note> number Exorcists among the clergy, as does Saint Jerome writing in his Letter to Titus, chapter 3. Moreover, in the aforementioned Council of Laodicea, it was decreed that those who are not ordained by Bishops should not presume to exorcise either in churches or in homes. Indeed, lest any superstition should creep into the exorcisms, it was provided that the Exorcist to be ordained should receive a booklet <note>original: "libellum"</note> from the hand of the Bishop in which the exorcisms were written, with the Bishop saying to him: "Receive this, and commit it to memory; and have the power of laying hands upon the <term>Energumen<gloss>From the Greek 'energoumenos,' referring to a person 'worked upon' by an external force, specifically one possessed by a demon.</gloss></term>, whether baptized or a <term>catechumen<gloss>A person receiving basic instruction in the principles of the Christian religion with a view to baptism.</gloss></term>," as is clear from the ancient ritual books of the Church and the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 7.

# CONCERNING THE POSSESSED.

**504.** Therefore, just as many things are necessary for accomplishing all difficult tasks, so not a few things are required from those who attempt to free human bodies from demons. What, truly, are these things? What machines <note>The author uses "machines" metaphorically here, referring to spiritual tools or methods.</note> are needed here? What defenses?

**505.** If cities or citadels were to be stormed, siege engines <note>original: "tormenta bellica"</note> could be employed; if some tyrant were to be driven from a kingdom, a wealth of soldiers would be needed. But truly, since here it is not citadels to be stormed, nor tyrants who come into view, but a war undertaken against most powerful Spirits; other machines must be employed, other engines, than those by which walls are shaken or tyrants driven out.

**506.** Yet these "Machines" used to rout demons must have this in common with those of war: that they are adverse and contrary to the enemy; he himself hates them and cannot endure them. Here, too, the saying holds: *Opposites are driven out by opposites.* <note>original: "Contraria contrarijs pelluntur," a common philosophical and medical principle suggesting that a condition is cured by its opposite.</note>

**507.** From this, we understand that the conditions required of exorcists, whenever they enter this contest, are most just. It is required that they cleanse their conscience by the confession of sins <note>original: "exomologesi peccatorum," using the Greek term for formal confession</note>, that they persist in prayer, that they afflict the body with fasting, that they bring a great submission of soul to this work, that they burn with the love of God, and hope well for divine aid.

**508.** These conditions are most just. For they are hated by demons, and it can be proven—both by examples and by logic, as well as by the most weighty authority of Christ—that these conditions have great power to break the strength of demons and dissolve their works.

**509.** Confession of sins produces a clean conscience and brings holiness of life. What is more hated than these by unclean Spirits? Do not the examples of those people prove this, in whose presence [demons] now fell silent within idols, now confessed they were being tortured, and even left the idols they had inhabited for many years?

## CHAPTER 40.

->*Whether a heretical exorcist, or one who professes a religion other than the Catholic one, is able to cast out demons?*<-

<margin>529.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 24.</margin>
One who pays attention to the words of the Lord will easily believe it possible for a heretic <note>In this context, a "heretic" refers to someone whose theological beliefs deviate from the official Catholic doctrine of the time.</note> to cast out demons from human bodies. For in a certain place, He speaks thus: **"False Christs and false prophets shall arise, and shall show great signs and wonders, so as to lead into error, if it were possible, even the elect."** <note>original: "Surgent pseudochristi, & pseudoprophetae..."</note>

530. But someone who considers the purpose God intended in performing miracles will judge the opposite. Since the purpose of a miracle is the confirmation of truth, and heretics are enemies of truth, God should not be said to cooperate in the expulsion of demons (which is classified as a miracle) for any reason; therefore, heretics will never cast out demons.

531. And here is how the matter stands: Heretics will never drive demons from the bodies of men whenever or as often as they attempt it in order to confirm the doctrine they profess. In addition to the argument already presented, there are four points that seem to prove this.

<margin>Mark, last chapter.</margin>
532. The first is the discourse of Christ, which implies that the casting out of demons is a sign belonging to the faithful. He says: "These signs shall follow those who believe: In my name they shall cast out demons," etc. <note>original: "Signa, inquit, eos qui crediderint, haec sequentur..." — referring to Mark 16:17.</note> However, heretics are not counted among the number of the faithful. Therefore, they will not be able to drive out demons using power communicated to them by Christ.

### CHAPTER XLI.

->*On five different ways in which, in Christianity, or among Catholics, demons are cast out from human bodies.*<-

<margin>538.</margin> No one is unaware that people have been freed from unclean spirits in various ways. For indeed, the same method was not maintained by those who cast out demons of old under the Old Law, and those who performed the same under the New Law. This is clear from Chapter 42 and those following in this present Disputation.

539. But in the Old Law, those who were instructed by Solomon <note>King Solomon was traditionally credited with the authorship of many incantations and methods for binding demons, such as those found in the "Testament of Solomon."</note> kept one method; those who used the Tetragrammaton <note>original: "Tetragrammaton" — the sacred four-letter Hebrew name of God (YHVH), used in Jewish and early Christian exorcism traditions.</note> name used another. And in the New Law, one single method does not seem to have been used by everyone. Christ used one, the Apostles another, and the successors of the Apostles used yet another—though the successors of the Apostles did not always use methods different from the Apostles, nor was there always one and the same method for all the Apostles.

540. Even Christ the Lord did not always follow the same way. Sometimes he expelled demons with a word, and sometimes he applied certain rites, as it were, of Exorcism. For when he was about to heal a certain demoniac who was deaf and mute, first of all he took him aside, then led him away from the crowd; soon he puts his fingers into his ears, then spat and touched the tongue of the possessed man; finally, looking up to heaven, he said: *Be opened* <note>original: "Epheta" — an Aramaic word (Ephphatha) meaning "be opened," used by Jesus in Mark 7:34.</note>. <margin>Mark 9.</margin> <note>The margin incorrectly cites Mark 9; this event is found in Mark 7:31-37.</note>

541. It is not necessary to pursue those methods of the Old Testament. They have been antiquated and abolished by age, if for no other reason. Nor will we discuss the method which Christ used. The remaining methods must be vindicated from slanders, because they suffer great attacks from certain people in our age and are misrepresented beyond all reason—but first we shall define what those methods are by which demons were expelled of old and are expelled in our own times.

542. The first method, therefore, is through the invocation of the name of our Lord JESUS Christ. Regarding this, Justin <note>Justin Martyr, a 2nd-century Christian apologist.</note> speaks in this manner: "By the name," he says, "of the very Son of God, and the firstborn of every creature, every demon adjured is conquered and reduced to submission." <margin>Disputation with Trypho.</margin> And a little before:

## CHAPTER XLII.

### *The first method is examined, by which demons are cast out from human bodies through the Invocation of the name of Jesus.*

<margin>§48. Mark 16; Luke 10; Acts 16; Book 2, chapter 27; Luke 9; Acts chapter 19.</margin>
The manner and reason for casting out demons through the name of our Lord seems to have been prescribed by the Lord himself, observed by the Apostles, and employed by holy men. The Lord prescribed it when he said: *In my name they shall cast out devils.* The Apostles congratulate themselves that demons were subjected to them in Christ's own name. Saint Paul, in the name of Jesus, commands a demon to go out of a girl. Justin and Prudentius, cited above, provide testimony for the early Christians, to whom Lactantius <note>Lactantius Firmianus (c. 250–325 AD), an early Christian author and advisor to Constantine the Great.</note> is added. Finally, Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius of Alexandria, who wrote the "Life of Saint Anthony."</note> testifies in his *Life of Saint Anthony* that Anthony cast out spirits by the invocation of that same name. Furthermore, even those who did not profess the doctrine of Christ used the same! John says: *We saw a certain man casting out demons, who does not follow with us.* To this I will add those whom Luke mentions in the history of the Apostles <note>The Acts of the Apostles.</note>, who traveled around Judea and invoked the name of the Lord over those who had evil spirits; likewise the Josephus mentioned by Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), a bishop known for his "Panarion" which cataloged and refuted various heresies.</note>.

§49. Truly, in this method of casting out demons, there are four things that seem to come into question. First: what it means for demons to be cast out "in the name of Christ." Second: why their departure is commanded in the name of Christ rather than in the name of the Father or the Holy Spirit. Third: which name of Christ specifically—for he has many—is adopted here. Fourth and last: whether the bare utterance of the name of Christ possesses some inherent power in itself to drive spirits out of men.

551. Having established this, we say that although it can be said that demons are cast out by Christ’s command, by Christ’s merits, and by Christ’s authority when they are driven out at the invocation of His Name; yet, properly speaking, we understand it to be His power. Thus, to command the host of demons "in the name of Christ" is the same as doing so by the power of Christ.

552. Anyone who considers what kind of work the ejection of demons is will easily prove what we are saying. It is an entirely divine task, far surpassing human strength; it therefore requires divine power. To demonstrate that demons are expelled, we invoke the name of Christ—that is, the power which is divine.

553. Therefore, in this method of casting out demons, two things seem to concur: the first is the use of Christ’s name; the second is the power and authority of that same name. The former is expressed by the voice; the latter is conceived in the mind and instilled through the word. And thus, let this be the answer to the first question.

554. The second question is more difficult: but we shall say briefly that for many great reasons, demons are driven out in the name of the Son rather than in the name of either the Father or the Holy Spirit, or even simply "God." For although the power of all the <term>Persons</term> <note>Referring to the three Persons of the Holy Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note> is equal, yet because the divinity of the Son had to be asserted and His doctrine confirmed, it was altogether fitting that demons should be driven out by the invocation of the Son’s name, as this act served both purposes excellently.

555. In ages past, the first Person of the divinity [the Father] had become known to the world; the Son had not. Just as the Father had proven Himself by many means, so the second Person, the Son of God, had to prove His divinity through signs and wonders.

556. Someone might say that this same reasoning also applies to the Person of the Holy Spirit. We are not ignorant of this. But other reasons were not lacking to Him by which He asserted His divinity—

...required by the men to whom that doctrine was to be handed down. It was also required by those through whom it was to be handed down. The doctrine of Christ (as it has now been accepted) could never have been persuaded to the world, unless these engines <note>original: "machinae" — the author uses the metaphor of siege engines or complex mechanisms to describe the persuasive power of miracles.</note> of wonders and the driving out of demons <note>original: "daemonum profligationes"</note> had been employed to introduce this faith and to uproot its opposite.

558. This doctrine surpassed all powers of the human mind. It was contrary to the desires of the flesh; it despised those things which the world held in the highest honor. This doctrine had to be handed down to those who were powerful in the sharpness of their intellect, and who judged as a paradox whatever they could not grasp by reason. It had to be handed down to those who believed that no other goods existed beyond the delights of the flesh and of this present life. And by whom was it to be handed down? Not by the Wise, nor by the Masters of Nature <note>original: "Naturae magistri" — likely referring to natural philosophers or scientists of the era.</note> who had been practiced for many years in academic assemblies; not by the powerful or those equipped with a multitude of soldiers; but by fishermen—men who seemed hardly fit to be admitted into the sight of honorable men. Therefore, how great an effort was needed here—and with what kind of engines—if anything was to be accomplished successfully?

559. Granted, other engines could have been employed here; perhaps they were indeed employed, and not in vain. Nevertheless, it was fitting that demons also be routed in the name of Christ—those very spirits, that is, who already held dominion <note>original: "principatum"</note> in the world: who had mocked men in many ways for very many years; for the dissolving of whose kingdom, the plundering of whose spoils, and the seizing of whose fortresses Christ had chiefly come into the world.

560. Hence it is that among the noble deeds performed by Christ, nothing is so proclaimed as the ejection of demons from men. Nor is there any work in which He seems more frequently occupied; almost none that men so marveled at; and none that His enemies and adversaries more greatly slandered.

561. But a third question calls us to itself, by which it is asked: Why did both the Apostles and the successors of the Apostles use the name of Christ above all others in the routing of demons? And at this point, to state what I believe, I think it is beyond controversy that the power <term>virtus</term> <note>referring here to inherent miraculous efficacy rather than moral virtue.</note> of all the names of Christ is great; and that what is done by the use of one can be done by all the others. This is demonstrated—to say nothing of other evidence—by the Rite of Exorcism now used (not fruitlessly) for the possessed, in which are found almost all the names attributed to Christ.

562. Nevertheless, although the power of all His names is great, we seem best able to affirm that they used the name of **Jesus**, and that more protection could be found in it, for the following reasons. First, because although many names were attributed to the Lord, one was nevertheless His own proper name. It was called

565. To this is added the consensus of all the faithful who exist now (and without doubt, those of earlier times) and a custom which cannot be condemned (except perhaps by the enemies of Christ). By this custom, they call upon this name more frequently than any other whenever they are terrified or falling; they cry this out especially when dying; they depict it more than others; and they exhibit a greater reverence for it than for others, sometimes by bowing or uncovering the head, and sometimes by kneeling.

566. Moreover, reason itself fights remarkably in favor of this opinion. The goal intended in the casting out of demons required this name rather than any other. Why so? Because since the purpose here was to make the glory and divinity of Christ known, and for him to be received and held as the true God, was it not necessary to take up that name which was most properly Christ's? The name by which he was called by everyone everywhere? And that this is the sweetest name of Jesus, the "Triumphal Title" <note>original: "Titulus Triumphalis" — the inscription (INRI) placed upon the Cross of Christ during the crucifixion.</note> as we call it, declares more than enough.

567. Furthermore, these things said in response to the third question do not a little toward the solution of the fourth. For they suggest quite clearly that the "naked" name of Jesus was itself troublesome and heavy to the demons, and that it made a great impression in driving them out from human dwellings. This also seems to be confirmed by the example of those who, although they did not follow Christ and did not yet believe—and perhaps were even his enemies and adversaries—nevertheless drove out demons by invoking the name of Jesus.

We know that both the demons and the present crowd have suddenly vanished if the name of Jesus happened to slip from one of the companions, even unintentionally.

§ 70. Julian <note>Julian the Apostate, the Roman Emperor who attempted to revive paganism</note>, the deserter and persecutor of the Christian Religion, once consulted demons. But when they appeared to him in a form so terrible that he could not endure it, out of the habit he still held from when he was a Christian, he protected himself with the sign of the cross, though he was an enemy of the cross. They immediately vanished, proving that the name of Jesus itself is a horror to demons.

§ 71. These are no small arguments. But to conclude this chapter, we state four points: first, the power of this name is great if it is spoken with reverence and piety. Second, it is also very effective even if those who use it have no pious feeling, provided they use it for the purpose of obtaining something through Christ’s power. Third, it has no power at all if it is considered merely as a bare voice uttered into the air. Fourth, if it is used as a sign, it can be a terror to demons even if pious affection is absent and nothing is expected by the person who utters it.

<margin>Mark, final chapter</margin>
§ 72. That first point is proven by the demons cast out by the Apostles, the handling of serpents, the drinking of poison without harm, the curing of the sick, and similar things—to say nothing of the fact that a pious soul, with any means at all (and why not with the invocation of the divine name?), can achieve a great deal.

§ 73. The second point is beyond doubt. Those very people whom we have already often cited are witnesses to this: those, I say, who were reported to Christ by the disciples for casting out demons in his name though they did not follow him. Here, men ought to understand that Christ's power is great, since even those who did not approve of his teaching in all things could cast out demons in his name.

<margin>Evidence: 1 Kings, chapter 16, question 40 <note>This likely refers to David soothing Saul’s "evil spirit" with music</note></margin>
§ 74. The third point, if I am not mistaken, everyone admits. For since a voice uttered into the air is nothing other than struck air, it would accomplish nothing that struck air does not perform. If a magpie or a parrot were taught to utter the name of Jesus, it would have no more power than any other name uttered.

§ 75. Regarding what we proposed in the fourth place—that the name of Christ has certain powers when used as a sign—one will easily believe it if they notice that demons are terrified and tortured not only by things, but also by signs. This is clear regarding the sign of the Cross; wherever they see it, and however it is formed, these imposters hate and detest it, just as thieves hate the wheel and the gallows <note>original: *rotas & patibula*; instruments of public execution and torture used to punish criminals</note>.

<header>PART III. DISPUTATION.
CHAPTER XLIII.</header>

### *The second method is examined, by which demons are cast out of human bodies through the use of the Relics of the Saints.*

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial A featuring scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
The second method of casting out demons is through the use of the Relics of the Saints. In support of this, we previously brought forward the opinion of Blessed Chrysostom. To Chrysostom, we add the aprons and handkerchiefs of the Apostle Paul, concerning which St. Luke says: God did extraordinary miracles <note>original Latin: "virtutes... non quaslibet," literally "not just any virtues/powers"</note> by the hand of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs and aprons were carried from his body to the sick; and the diseases left them, and the wicked spirits went out of them. We also add the shadow of Peter, by which it is not obscurely suggested in the fifth chapter of the History of the Apostles <note>The Acts of the Apostles</note> that force was brought against demons.

The arguments already mentioned could be sufficient for this point; however, since this method of exorcising has many great adversaries <note>This likely refers to Protestant Reformers who, during the 16th and 17th centuries, were highly skeptical of the miraculous power of physical relics</note>, it seems necessary to illustrate and explain it with more examples and reasons.

We begin with examples. Blessed Jerome relates to Eustochium concerning the life of Paula that demons were accustomed to roar at the tombs of Elisha, John the Baptist, and Obadiah. Blessed Ambrose testifies, with the attestation of the entire people of Milan, that the same happened at the tombs of Protasius and Gervasius <note>Gervasius and Protasius were early Christian martyrs whose remains Ambrose famously "discovered" in Milan in 386 AD</note>, in his work *On Protasius and Gervasius*.

The memorial of these same saints, Protasius and Gervasius, was in the Victoriana villa near Hippo Regius <note>Modern-day Annaba, Algeria</note>, less than thirty miles away. A certain youth was brought there who, while washing his horse in the middle of summer, encountered a demon in the whirlpool of the river. There he lay, either near death or very much like a corpse, until finally he was freed when the demon took flight. So writes Blessed Augustine in *The City of God*, Book 22, Chapter 8.

Nazianzenus <note>Gregory of Nazianzus, a 4th-century Church Father</note>, in his 19th Oration, leaves it as a matter manifest to all that demons were cast out at the tomb of the Martyr Cyprian.

Histories also teach and testify that many demons were cast out through the chain of St. Peter. In the year of salvation 900, it happened that a certain Count, a close associate of Emperor Otto, was possessed by an unclean spirit and mangled himself with his teeth. By the Emperor's command, he was led to Pope John, and as soon as he touched the sacred chain, the wicked spirit broke out and left the man free. Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais, a medieval encyclopedist</note> records this in Book 24, Chapter 88, as does the *Chronicle of Saxony*.

Those to whom Belgium is known are not unaware that at Geel in Brabant, at the most holy relics of St. Dymphna <note>St. Dymphna is the patron saint of the mentally ill; the town of Geel remains famous today for its unique model of community care for psychiatric patients</note>, those possessed by demons are liberated to this very day by the singular favor of God the Best and Greatest, says Breidenbach in his work on Cologne, Chapter 37.

<meta>This page continues the catalogue of historical and hagiographical evidence for the power of relics over demons, moving from the accounts of Jerome and Ambrose on the previous page to more "recent" examples from the medieval period and the 16th century.</meta>

->## ON THE POSSESSED.<-

Thus, in the year 1541 in Sicily, in the temple of Saint Philip—who was a disciple of Saint Peter—nearly two hundred women were liberated; and every year on the feast of Saint Philip himself, many are delivered, as Thomas Fazellus <note>Tommaso Fazello (1498–1570) was a Sicilian Dominican friar and historian, often called the "father of Sicilian history."</note> relates in a certain passage.

Gregory, the Bishop of Langres, used to cure <term>Energumenos: a term derived from Greek used to describe those troubled or "worked upon" by unclean spirits; the possessed</term> brought to him with the sign of the cross and the spoken word. But even in his absence, many drove out demons from the possessed using the staff <note>original Latin: "virga"</note> that he was accustomed to carry, as Gregory of Tours records in his *Life*. The same Gregory, in Book 2 of the *Miracles*, chapter 44, teaches that at the relics <note>original Latin: "pignora," literally "pledges" or "tokens," a common term for holy relics</note> of Saint Julian, a possessed man cast out both blood and a demon through vomiting.

Similarly, demons cried out that they were being tortured by a "double fire" when Saint Genevieve visited the relics of Saint Martin; this was because they could endure neither the relics of the holy man nor the presence of the holy Virgin. Reference: Surius, Volume 1 <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578) was a German Carthusian hagiographer known for his massive collection of lives of the saints.</note>.

Pepin, the father of Charlemagne, recognized this power of relics. When he desired his cleric (named Brunco) to be freed from the tyranny of a demon, he sent him to the relics of the saints. His hope did not fail him: for as soon as he reached the threshold of the Church of Saint Maximinus, Bishop of Trier, Brunco was cured, as witnessed by Lupus in the *Life of Saint Maximinus*, found in Surius, Volume 3.

The same Lupus adds that on one and the same day, thirty-seven people were liberated from demons by the benefit of those same relics at the shrine of Saint Maximinus. Among their number was a woman whom the spirit left after forty-seven years of satanic butchery, filling the temple with a sulfurous stench <note>In historical accounts of exorcism, a foul smell like sulfur was frequently cited as physical proof of a demon's departure</note> upon its departure. Likewise, in the following year, on the same feast day of Saint Maximinus, twenty-two were cured; in the third year, thirteen were cured.

Concerning the relics of Saint Liborius, Bishop of Le Mans, it is written that when his body was raised from the tomb in the year 836 to be transferred to Paderborn, a deacon whom the devil had tormented for many years was liberated. During the journey, when a possessed woman was brought to the saint's holy relics, the demon began to bellow, hiss, and make the sounds of wild beasts in a horrific manner; but soon it was forced to depart as soon as she touched the bier. This is found in Surius, Volume 4, folio 338.

Regarding the dust into which was poured the water used to wash the bones of Blessed Oswald, Bede relates in Book 3 of the *History of the English*, chapter 11, that it healed a possessed man upon whom exorcisms had previously had no effect.

In the same way, nothing was being achieved in the monastery of Belval by all the exorcisms employed by the religious men of said monastery; however, when the stole <note>A liturgical vestment worn by priests, here treated as a secondary relic because it was used by a saint</note> which Saint Bernard was accustomed to use was placed upon the possessed man...

PART III. DISPUTATION.

...to him, and when the relics were brought near, the Abbot suddenly drove out the Spirit, as witnessed by William of Saint-Thierry in the *Life of Bernard*, Book 4, Chapter 1.

Gregory of Nyssa writes concerning Gregory Thaumaturgus <note>Gregory "the Wonderworker" (c. 213–270 AD) was a transformational bishop in Asia Minor known for his numerous miracles.</note> in his *Life* (found in Surius, Volume 4), that he breathed upon a veil with the breath of his mouth; by placing this veil upon a possessed man, he expelled the demon.

Sigebert, who wrote his *Life* (found in Surius, Volume 6), testifies concerning Bishop Maltonius that when he was asked to cure the daughter of a certain nobleman whom a demon was miserably tormenting, he threw his own small handkerchief <note>original Latin: "strophiolum"</note> around the neck of the possessed girl. Immediately, the Spirit broke out into insults and, after she drank blessed water, it departed.

In the same way, Terentianus, a prefect of the praetorian cohort, was invaded by unclean spirits—the avengers of the crime he had committed—along with his son, because of the death of the Roman citizens John and Paul, which he had overseen by the order of Julian the Apostate. However, he was liberated from them as soon as he was led to the tombs of the Martyrs. This is recorded in the *Life of John and Paul* written by Terentianus, as witnessed by Baronius in the *Martyrology* for July 16th.

<margin>4.</margin>
The account related by Bernard of Bonneval, the Abbot, concerning Saint Bernard also belongs here. While Bernard was about to celebrate the liturgy in the Church of Saint Ambrose in Milan, they brought to him a girl possessed by a demon, imploring his help. What did the Saint do? He ordered water to be poured over his hands; when he had given this to the girl to drink, she was soon restored to her former health. Also relevant is the account Blessed Augustine provides in *The City of God*, Book 22, Chapter 8: he says he saw a house in Milan that was being vexed by a demon, which was liberated from the demon's infestation when holy earth <note>This refers to earth brought from the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.</note> was hung up in that part of the house. From this, Blessed Jerome spoke most excellently to the demon who was talking through the mouth of Vigilantius <note>Vigilantius was a 4th-century priest who opposed the veneration of relics, prompting a famous and vitriolic rebuttal from St. Jerome.</note>, who despised relics: *“By this most worthless dust, you are often entirely tormented.”* <note>original Latin: "Tu hoc vilissimo totus es sæpe puluere."</note>

<margin>5.</margin>
Nor is it a wonder that demons are either put to flight or tortured by relics, since we know that even greater, or certainly equal, things have been accomplished by the touch and power of relics. For through these, sight has been restored to some; to others, the use of their feet was returned; to others, life was given; others were freed from incurable diseases. Thus, it was well said by the Fathers of the Second Council of Nicaea <note>Held in 787 AD, this Council restored the veneration of icons and relics after the first phase of Byzantine Iconoclasm.</note> that the relics of the Saints are "health-giving springs" from which God grants many benefits to mankind. Nor are examples lacking here. A certain woman had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years. She had spent all her resources on every physician. Catching sight of Christ in the midst of the crowd, she thought that if she could but touch even the hem of His garment, she would be healed. Why say more? Her desire for health overcame her shame; she approached the Lord secretly, touched the hem, and was soon restored to health.

The corpse of a certain man was cast into the tomb of the Prophet Elisha...

-># ON THE POSSESSED.<-

...of a certain deceased man; suddenly, when he touched the bones of Elisha, the man rose up alive,
<margin>4 Kings 13 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 13:21. The passage describes a dead man coming back to life after his body touched the bones of the prophet Elisha.</note></margin>

Saint Epiphanius writes in his *Life of the Prophets* that the tombs of Ezekiel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah were frequently visited by many people because of the numerous blessings that God conferred in those places due to the merits of those same men.

Basil, in his *Oration on Saint Mamas*, says that the miracles are known to everyone—how the Martyr restored health to some and life to others. In the same way, in his *Oration on Saint Julitta*, he records that when the relics of Saint Julitta were brought to a certain place suffering from a lack of water, a spring of the sweetest water erupted from the earth; it seemed as if that holy woman, acting as a common mother and nurse, wished to nourish that entire region with her own "milk" <note>Saint Basil uses the metaphor of "milk" to describe the life-giving water provided by the saint’s intercession.</note>.

Saint Gregory Nazianzen <note>One of the "Cappadocian Fathers," a 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople known for his influential theology.</note>, in his *Oration on Saint Cyprian*, says: "The dust of Cyprian can do all things with faith, as those know who have experienced it themselves and have passed the miracle down to us."

Ambrose, in his *Sermon on Saints Gervasius and Protasius* and in his *Letter to his Sister* regarding them, reports—among other deeds—that even a blind man named Severus, a butcher <note>original Latin: "Lanionem"</note> by trade and very well known to everyone, was cured upon touching the bier <note>A frame or stand on which a corpse or coffin is placed.</note> on which the Relics were being carried.

Blessed Augustine, in Book 22 of *The City of God*, Chapter 8, asserts that so many miracles were performed in a very short time at the Relics of Saint Stephen that many books would have to be written if they were all to be recorded. Sulpicius, in his *Life of Saint Martin*, says that a woman was cured of a flow of blood simply by touching his garment. One should also read Jacobus Rabus regarding miracles, written against Morbachius.

<margin>6.</margin>
The things we have said are great. But this proves the power of Relics even more: that our ancestors even used handkerchiefs or veils (which were called <term>Sanctuaria</term> or <term>Brandea</term> <note>These were pieces of cloth that were lowered into a saint's tomb or touched to their relics. It was believed they absorbed the holy power of the saint and could then be used for healing or protection.</note>) when the opportunity to touch the relics themselves was not granted. Afterward, they used these as sacred objects to accomplish great things. So that we are not too long-winded, one should consult Caesar Baronius in the *Martyrology* for June 15th. Moreover, Blessed Pope Gregory is a wealthy witness to how much power veils of this kind drew when moved near the tombs of the Saints, as he writes to Constantia Augusta in Book 3, Chapter 30; as are Gregory of Tours in *The Glory of the Martyrs*, Chapter 28, and the Deacon in the *Life of Gregory*.

<margin>7.</margin>
What of the fact that not only veils and small cloths were placed near the Relics, but even the clothes of the sick and the dead were placed upon the sacred altars where the Relics of the Saints were kept? In this way, they contracted a certain divine power, so that when they were later applied to the infirm or the dead, they brought an immediate remedy. The most holy Augustine supports this, who—to prove the impiety of the Gentiles <note>Non-Christians, specifically those following traditional Roman or local religions.</note>—compiled a catalog of several miracles performed in Africa in his own time...

-># PART III. DISPUTATION.<-

...wove a long account; he shows with many examples that the same grace was customarily imparted to flowers which were moved to the same shrines <note>original: "loculis," literally small compartments or caskets for relics.</note> of the sacred Relics. See Book 22 of *The City of God*, chapter 8.

To these great things we add even greater: even the **Dust** and the grime <note>original: "situs," referring to the dust or mold that accumulates in ancient, holy places.</note> found around the tombs of the Martyrs was endowed with the greatest power on account of the Martyrs. Almost all the Fathers attest to the integrity of this faith, but especially Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century theologian and mystic from Cappadocia, known for his defense of the Nicene Creed.</note> in his *Oration on Saint Theodore*, who says this regarding the custom of collecting the aforementioned **Dust**: "If anyone is permitted to take away the Dust which covers the tomb where the body of the Martyr rests, the dust is received as a gift and gathered like a thing of great price to be stored away."

Furthermore, how many and how great were the miracles that God was accustomed to work through the collected Dust lying around the tombs of the Saints, the Blessed Pope Gregory <note>Gregory the Great, a 6th-century Pope and influential writer.</note> is a truthful witness in Book 3 of his *Dialogues*, chapter 17. He reports with faithful testimony that, by means of collected Dust from the pedestal of an altar, a dead man was recalled to life. Gregory of Tours <note>A 6th-century bishop and historian known for documenting the miracles of the Merovingian era.</note> records many things of this kind concerning those who, like himself, experienced many things, in his *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, Book 2, chapter 1; Book 3, chapter 12; and Book 4, chapter 32 and following. Likewise in his first book, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 62; and Book 2, chapters 33, 42, and 45.

<margin>9</margin>
We have not yet made an end. We add this also: that even things separated from the shrines of the Saints—provided they are employed in their honor—attained the same capacity for producing miracles. This is manifest regarding the **oil**, which, according to the custom observed in the Church since antiquity, is usually lit in lamps around the tombs of the Saints. For with this oil the corpse of the son of Irenaeus <note>A significant early Christian theologian and Bishop of Lugdunum (modern Lyon).</note> was anointed and soon returned to life, as recorded by the Blessed Augustine in *The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8. In the same way, Theodoret <note>A 5th-century bishop and influential theologian of the Church of Antioch.</note> reports in his *History of the Holy Fathers* that great miracles were produced by the **Oil** from the lamps at the burials of the Martyrs. Concerning a particle of **Wax** brought from the temple of Saint Martin, Gregory of Tours commemorates that, when cast into a fire, it extinguished the entire conflagration in which a house was burning; by a new miracle, the Wax, which usually nourishes fire, suppressed the violence of the flames.

<margin>10</margin>
We add one more thing for the glory of the Relics and the confirmation of our argument: that even the very instruments of punishment <note>original: "pœnarum instrumenta," referring to the tools of torture used during martyrdom.</note> with which the Martyrs were tortured drew great power and force from the limbs of the Saints. This is testified by the **Stone** with which the arm of the Blessed Stephen the Protomartyr <note>The first martyr of the Christian Church, as recorded in the Book of Acts.</note> was struck; concerning this, Saint Augustine says in his *Sermons on Various Subjects*, 31 and 32, that many miracles were performed by it at Ancona, where it was religiously preserved.

The **Chains** of Saint Peter <note>original: "D. Petri Catenæ," referring to the chains that bound the Apostle Peter in prison.</note> testify to this as well; concerning them, the same Augustine says in his *Sermon on the Saints*, 29: "Rightly," he says, "throughout all the Churches of Christ, [they are held] dearer than precious gold—"

->## ON THE POSSESSED.<-

...is considered that Iron of the penal bonds <note>original: "poenalium vinculorum," referring to the chains used to imprison or torture martyrs.</note>. If the mere shadow of the visitor <note>A reference to Acts 5:15, where the shadow of the Apostle Peter healed the sick.</note> was so healing, how much more so were the Chains of the one bound? If a fleeting form or empty image (a shadow) could contain within itself the power of salvation, how much more did the Bonds of the passion—the iron weight of which was impressed upon sacred limbs—deserve to draw forth healing from the body?

The Griddle of Saint Lawrence <note>Saint Lawrence was a 3rd-century deacon in Rome who, according to tradition, was martyred by being roasted on a gridiron.</note> bears witness to this, the miracles of which are recorded by the Blessed Pope Gregory in Book 2, Letter 33 of his *Register*. On this point, Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" known for his influential theology.</note> speaks most excellently in his first *Oration against Julian*: "The bodies of the Martyrs possess the same power as their souls, whether they are touched by hands or honored; even their drops of blood alone, and the small signs of their passion, have the same power as their bodies."

<margin>11.</margin>
Our ancestors, without doubt, understood this Virtue of Relics. We can perceive this from *four* primary points. The first is that they undertook long and difficult Pilgrimages to the Relics of the Saints. *Because (as Saint Chrysostom says) miracles are performed by the martyrs, a great multitude flows to them in abundance.*

The second point is that they sought these relics out with zeal, acquired them with great diligence, and once acquired, held them in no other place than as the greatest of treasures. Hence Theodoret <note>A 5th-century bishop and historian from Syria.</note>, writing to the Greeks concerning the Martyrs, says:
> *The souls of the triumphant Martyrs now lead their lives in the heavenly fatherland, placed among the choirs of Angels; their bodies, however, are not buried individually in single monuments. Instead, cities, towns, and village assemblies have divided these remains among themselves by lot, and they never cease to acknowledge them as healthy remedies for troubled souls and sick bodies.*

The third point is that they judged these same relics should be held in the highest honor. Gennadius <note>A 5th-century priest from Marseilles known for his biographies of ecclesiastical writers.</note> expresses this beautifully in his work *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*:
> *We believe that the bodies of the Saints, and especially the Relics of the blessed Martyrs, are to be most sincerely honored as if they were the very limbs of Christ; and we believe the basilicas named after them should be approached with the most pious affection and faithful devotion as holy places dedicated to divine worship. If anyone goes against this sentiment, they are believed to be not a Christian, but a follower of Eunomius or Vigilantius <note>Eunomius and Vigilantius were historical figures declared heretics for, among other things, opposing the veneration of relics.</note>.*

The fourth point is that they considered it a great blessing if they could have their own graves in those places where the Relics of the Saints were preserved.
> *In Constantinople (says Saint Chrysostom in his homily "That Christ is God"), our Kings think it a great favor, not if they are buried near the Apostles, but if their bodies are buried even outside the vestibules of the Apostles; thus Kings become the Gatekeepers of the Fishermen.*

<margin>12.</margin>
What we have said, unless we are mistaken, confirms our argument remarkably...

It highlights that the physical remains of saints were treated as treasures capable of healing and that even emperors sought burial near them to act as spiritual "gatekeepers."</summary>

# PART III OF THE DISPUTATION

...they confirm. There is no need for more; we bring this to an end if we teach in a few words for what reason God willed demons to be expelled through the use of Relics, and simultaneously explain whether any power <note>original: "virtus," referring here to a spiritual or physical efficacy.</note> truly resides in Relics which demons cannot endure.

<margin>13.</margin> Regarding the first point, we may correctly say there are two causes. One is the confirmation of the divinity of Christ and the divine power; the other is the declaration of the holiness of the person at whose Relics the demons are routed. Sometimes these two causes occur together; at other times, only one of them has a place.

<margin>14.</margin> Formerly, when miracles were performed even at the invocation of the Name of the Lord, the glory of Christ was the primary goal. For this reason, people did not marvel so much at those individuals whose presence and touch drove out demons, but rather at the power by which they were expelled. Thus, they were not so much stirred to praise the Apostles and Disciples of Christ as they were urged to embrace the Christian Religion.

<margin>15.</margin> In subsequent times and in our own, now that the Christian Religion is established, the miracles performed at Relics are almost entirely arguments for holiness. God wishes those who serve Him to be honored. Since miracles and the ejection of demons do much to achieve this end, He wills these things to occur at the Relics and Dust <note>original: "Pulueres," referring to the cremated remains or decayed dust of a saint's body.</note> of the Saints. In this way, men certainly conceive a greater opinion of the holiness of the Saints. Thus they pay them greater honor; they more fervently implore their patronage <note>original: "patrocinia," the protective intercession of a saint.</note>; and they trust more securely in their merits—though even in these things, the glory of Christ is the ultimate goal.

<margin>16.</margin> Nevertheless (as was to be explained in the second place), *it must be said that no natural power by which demons are routed resides either in the Relics themselves or in those things joined with the Relics.* For what other power shall we say exists in physical objects except a physical one? Yet the power by which demons are driven away must not be physical. Physical things contribute nothing to the routing of demons; they contribute nothing to matters that surpass the forces of nature.

<margin>17.</margin> It is, therefore, a divine power by which demons are cast out. The Apostle Peter demonstrates this excellently in a similar case. For when he had once healed a man lame from birth <note>original: "ex vtero," literally "from the womb."</note>, and because of this everyone had turned their eyes and faces toward him, he redirected the miracle performed from himself toward God with this speech:

> "Men of Israel," he said, "why do you wonder at this, or why do you look at us as if by our own power or authority we made this man walk? The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, has glorified His Son Jesus. In faith in His name, His name has strengthened this man whom you now see and know; and the faith which is through Him has given complete heal-" <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with "ing" on the next page; the Latin catchword is "tatem," completing the word "sanitatem" or health/healing.</note>

<summary>This page explores why God performs miracles through relics, identifying two main reasons: to confirm Christ's divinity and to demonstrate the holiness of saints. It clarifies that relics have no inherent "natural" power over demons, but serve as physical conduits for divine power.</summary>

# CONCERNING THE DEMON-POSSESSED

...this <term>holiness</term> <note>original: "tatem istam," likely concluding a word like "sanctitatem" (holiness) from the previous page.</note> in the sight of all of you. So says Peter.

<margin>18.</margin>
Meanwhile, the banishment of demons and other wonders are also attributed to Relics. Although they have God as their first and highest author, they can nevertheless have other causes as well. The Lord was not unaware that demons are cast out by "the finger of God"; yet, He confirms that men also truly cast out demons by this reasoning: *In my name they shall cast out demons.*

<margin>19.</margin>
But what kind of cause do Relics serve in this business? I suspect they are <term>instrumental</term> <note>In scholastic philosophy, an instrumental cause is a tool used by a primary agent (God) to achieve an effect.</note>. Through Relics, God drives out demons as if through certain instruments, just as He torments and punishes them through fire as instruments of justice. But these matters require another place for discussion. Let us pursue our own topic.

---

### CHAPTER XLIV.

->*The third method is examined, by which demons are cast out of human bodies through the use of the Sign of the Cross.*<-

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop cap 'C' begins the chapter text, featuring intricate foliage and scrollwork patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

<margin>1.</margin>
There are various reasons and ways to consider the Cross. We understand one thing by the "Cross of Christ" and another by the "Sign of the Cross." By the **Cross**, we mean that very wood upon which the Lord worked our salvation; by the **Sign of the Cross**, we mean whatever presents that image to the senses. The question here concerns the *sign*. For the Cross itself belongs to the preceding chapter regarding Relics.

<margin>2.</margin>
Indeed, the Sign of the Cross can be distinguished in two ways. One is *permanent*, the other is *transient*. The **permanent** sign is made either from wood or another solid material, or is depicted in color on a flat surface. The **transient** sign ceases to exist as soon as it is formed. The former is categorized with **Images**; the latter we established above among the methods by which demons are put to flight.

<margin>3.</margin>
There is a twofold use of this **transient** sign. One type people impress upon themselves (as when, out of a desire for piety, they fortify their forehead, breast, or mouth with a Cross). The other type is applied to others, as occurs in the administration of the <term>Sacraments</term>, most especially in **Baptism**, **Confirmation**, and **Extreme Unction** <note>Now commonly referred to as the Anointing of the Sick.</note>; and when the faithful people in the Church are blessed by Bishops and Priests.

<margin>4.</margin>
Both methods are very ancient and have been frequently used with no small benefit to the faithful. This can be observed in many other matters, as well as in the ejection and routing of demons; for it is nothing new that they are cast out of human bodies by the power of the Cross, as a most serious witness...

<summary>This page explains that relics act as "instruments" of God's power to expel demons and introduces the Sign of the Cross as a distinct spiritual tool. It categorizes the Sign of the Cross into permanent objects (like crucifixes) and transient gestures used in personal piety and the Sacraments.</summary>

<keywords>instrumental cause, relics, Sign of the Cross, exorcism, Sacraments, permanent vs transient signs, spiritual warfare</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of historical testimonies regarding the efficacy of the Sign of the Cross in exorcising demons, moving from early Church Fathers to medieval saints.</meta>

PART III. DISPUTATION.

Lactantius Firmianus, whom we produced as a witness above, is one such authority. Nor are examples lacking here. From many, we offer a few. Gregory, Bishop of Langres, when those possessed by spirits (<term>energumenis</term> <note>A term derived from Greek for those "worked upon" or driven by an external force, specifically a demon.</note>) were brought to him, would command the demons to depart by making the Sign of the Cross alone, as Gregory of Tours writes in *The Life of the Fathers*, chapter 7. By that same Sign, Albinus, Bishop of Angers, drove out demons from a certain woman, as Vincent <note>Likely Vincent of Beauvais, a prolific medieval encyclopedist.</note> testifies in Book 23, chapter 243.

<margin>6.</margin> Epiphanius writes in *Against Heresies*, book 30, that a certain man named Joseph, while not yet a Christian, cast out demons with the Cross of Christ; later, having become a Christian, he destroyed the incantations of the Jews with that same Sign.

By that same Cross, St. Catherine of Siena was seen driving out a demon; as it exited, it caused horrendous swellings in the throat of the possessed person, as Raymond <note>Raymond of Capua, her biographer and confessor.</note> teaches in her *Life*, found in Surius, Volume 4.

Theodore the Archimandrite <note>A title for a head of a monastery or group of monasteries in the Eastern tradition.</note> used the same Sign; first, in curing the daughter of a prince who had endured grave torments from a hidden spirit for twenty-eight years; then, in a woman whom a demon, emerging from a certain hill, had attacked and miserably tormented; and thirdly, in his doorkeeper Eutychius, into whose body the spirit could not enter beyond the arm, as the holy man opposed its efforts with the Cross. These things were recorded by Gregory the priest, his disciple, in the *Life of Theodore*.

Blessed Germain, Bishop of Paris, used the same Sign while casting out a certain hidden demon from a girl. Indeed, immediately after the Cross was pressed upon the girl, the spirit exited through her nostrils in the form of a fly. See Venantius Fortunatus, Bishop of Poitiers, in the *Life of Germain*, chapter 27.

St. Bridget the widow used the same in the curing of a certain woman, as the writer of her *Life* testifies in Surius, Volume 4, folio 350.

Arnulph, Bishop of Soissons, did the same when a possessed youth was brought to him, who was suffering grave torture from an entire legion of demons. Although he could scarcely be restrained by any chains, as soon as he saw the Cross, he became as quiet as a lamb and adored the holy man. Lisiard, Bishop of the Church of Soissons, writes this in his *Life*, chapter 24.

St. Bernard used the same: while performing the Sacrifice of the Mass, whenever he signed the Sacred Host with the Cross, he also pressed the Cross upon the possessed woman. See chapter 46 of this Disputation. He also used it when he cast out a spirit from a boy, which was particularly troublesome and stubborn, especially when the boy entered a church, was sprinkled with holy water, was compelled to hear the Gospel, or was present for the divine sacraments. See the *Life of Bernard*, chapter 3, book 2.

It highlights the Cross as a physical and ritual tool that compels demons to flee, sometimes in visible forms like a fly.</summary>

# ON THE POSSESSED.

The same Maurice, Bishop of Angers <note>original: "Mauritius Episcopus Andegauensis." He was a 6th-century bishop known for his piety.</note>, in freeing a possessed woman <note>original: "daemoniaca"</note> whom it had been necessary to bind with chains because of a raging spirit, as Fortunatus <note>Venantius Fortunatus, a Latin poet and hagiographer of the 6th century.</note> testifies in his *Life*.

St. Laurence, Archbishop of Dublin, also pressed the Cross to the breast of a possessed woman, just as he poured holy water into her mouth; and after both [actions] he turned to prayer and cast out the demon. So it is recorded in chapter 28 of his *Life*, Volume 6, in the works of Surius <note>Laurentius Surius, a Carthusian monk who compiled a famous collection of the lives of saints.</note>.

Likewise Patroclus, a dweller in the wilderness, is read to have cured very many possessed persons; but by the Sign of the Cross, according to Gregory of Tours in chapter 9 of his *Life*. This same Gregory of Tours, in the *Life of Nicetius, Bishop of Trier*, reports that beneath his garment (wishing to avoid arrogance <note>The Bishop hid the Cross to perform the miracle humbly, without drawing attention to his own power.</note>) he held a Cross against a possessed person, and thus freed the wretch from the demon's torment. We gave the story at length above in the final Thesis, chapter 32.

<margin>6.</margin>
It is truly no wonder that demons are driven from the bodies of men by the Sign of the Cross. Even when situated outside of human bodies, they were unable to bear its power whenever Christians of old took this up and attacked them. Gregory of Neocaesarea <note>Known as Gregory "the Wonderworker" (c. 213–270 AD).</note> experienced the power of the Cross; Gregory of Nyssa testifies in his *Life* that he often fought against demons with these weapons.

The soldier Gregory experienced it; he shattered the idol of Apollo with these [weapons] when he was led to the temple to sacrifice to Apollo by order of Diocletian: as testified by Metaphrastes <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a celebrated Byzantine hagiographer.</note> in his *Life*.

St. Margaret experienced it, who put to flight a demon approaching her in the form of a dragon with the Cross; as the same Metaphrastes writes on July 27th.

The most holy Anthony experienced it, who, with this type of weapon, was terrifying to all wicked spirits: just as the Blessed Jerome teaches in the *Life of Paul*.

Gregory of Nyssa also relates, in the *Life of [Gregory] of Neocaesarea*, that a Deacon of Gregory of Neocaesarea, protected by the Sign of the Cross, went out at night unharmed from the baths amidst innumerable specters; from which no one who had entered at night had ever come out alive.

Lactantius relates, in Book 4, chapter 24, that in the presence of a Christian who had signed his forehead with the Cross, the Devil did not dare to give an answer to the Emperor <note>Referring to the silencing of pagan oracles in the presence of the Cross.</note>.

<margin>7.</margin>

### PART III: DISPUTATION

<meta>catchword: mor</meta>

[he makes] the sign, and puts to flight the demons he had summoned, as Gregory of Nazianzus <note>original: "Nazianz." Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD) was a highly influential Archbishop of Constantinople and theologian.</note> testifies in his *Oration against Julian*.

In the same way, Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a famous Roman satirist known for his wit and skepticism toward religion.</note>, although he was an Epicurean and a mocker of any religion, records that Eucrates—a man worthy of trust—once he had received an iron ring made from a certain Cross, was rendered safe against wicked demons. Therefore, says Caesar Baronius <note>A 16th-century Cardinal and historian (1538–1607) who wrote the *Annales Ecclesiastici* to defend the history of the Catholic Church.</note>, in the year of Christ 60: just as the Jewish exorcists, though they did not believe in Jesus Christ, nevertheless used the name of Jesus to drive demons out of possessed men because they knew that demons were expelled by Paul and other Christians in that name; so too the magicians [Magi], seeing that it was successfully practiced by Christians—namely, that they commanded demons by the power of the Cross—themselves wished to use the sign of the Cross to restrain the attacks of demons when necessary.

Here the excellent opinions of the Church Fathers find their place. St. Basil <note>Basil the Great (330–379 AD), one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" who shaped early Christian doctrine.</note>, in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, calls the Cross the most wholesome remedy for driving away demons. Ephrem <note>St. Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373 AD), a prominent theologian and hymnographer from Mesopotamia.</note>, in chapter 3 of *On Penitence*, asserts it is the invincible armor of Christians. The same author, in chapter 2 of his book *On Spiritual Armor*, says: "In place of a shield, fortify yourself with the sign of the Cross; for it is the strongest armor." Origen <note>An early Christian scholar and theologian (c. 184–253 AD) from Alexandria.</note> speaks to the same effect in Homily 6 on chapter 5 of *Exodus*: "Fear and trembling," he says, "fall upon the demons when they see the sign of the Cross faithfully fixed upon you." The same author in Homily 8 *To Various People* says: "Let us carry the immortal <term>labarum</term> <note>A military standard or banner used by the Roman Empire, later adapted as a Christian symbol. The text here specifically identifies it with the Cross.</note> (the Cross) on our foreheads. When the demons see this, they will tremble—those who do not fear even the gilded Capitols <note>The "Capitolia" refers to the grand Roman temples, like the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitoline Hill, suggesting that demons are more afraid of a humble cross than of magnificent pagan structures.</note>." St. Augustine, in his address *To the Catechumens* <note>People receiving instruction in the Christian faith before baptism.</note>, teaches that they are signed with the Cross for this very reason: so that they may be a source of terror to demons. St. Anthony <note>Anthony the Great, a 4th-century "Desert Father" and a pioneer of Christian monasticism.</note>, as Athanasius testifies in his *Life of Anthony*, commanded his monks to be secure against all terrors by the sign of the Cross alone. Paulinus <note>Paulinus of Nola (c. 354–431 AD), a Roman senator who gave up his wealth to become a bishop and poet.</note> sang thus in favor of the Cross, in his 8th *Birthday Poem for St. Felix*:

> The sign and confession of the unconquered Cross protects us,
> And armed in spirit by God, we do not seek the weapons
> Of the body; and though we may seem defenseless in our limbs,
> We nevertheless carry weapons with which, even in serene peace,
> We contend with our minds against incorporeal enemies.

Therefore, this exhortation of Cyril <note>Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313–386 AD), a bishop and Doctor of the Church.</note> is not in vain: "Let it not shame you," he says, "to confess Christ crucified; but let the sign of the Cross be confidently impressed with the fingers on the forehead: and let the Cross be made in all other things: in the bread we eat, and the cups we drink, and in going out, and in coming in; before lying down for sleep, and upon rising; in traveling and in resting. This is a great safeguard: which is given for free for the sake of the poor; without labor for the sake of the infirm; since this grace and hon[or] <note>The Latin text cuts off at "ti-", likely continuing "titulus" (honor/title) or "timor" (fear) on the next page.</note> is from God—"

# CONCERNING THOSE POSSESSED BY DEMONS #

[...the] fear <note>original: "mor," likely the conclusion of "timor," meaning fear</note> of demons. For He triumphed over him [the devil] by this sign. Display it to him boldly; for when they see the Cross, they remember the Crucified One; for they fear Him who crushed the heads of the Dragon <note>A reference to Psalm 74:13, often interpreted as Christ's victory over Satan.</note>. Thus says *Cyril of Jerusalem* <note>St. Cyril (c. 313–386 AD) was the Bishop of Jerusalem; his "Catechetical Lectures" provided essential instruction for early converts.</note> in his *Catechesis 9*.

<margin>9.</margin>
And indeed, I would hardly doubt that this is the primary reason—or certainly among the primary reasons—why there has been such a great *Use* of the Cross among Christians at all times; so that (as *Tertullian* <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD) known as the "Father of Latin Theology."</note> says in *On the Military Crown*, chapter 3) they wore down their foreheads with the *sign* of the Cross at every step and movement, at every entry and exit, when putting on clothes or shoes, at the baths, at the tables, when lighting lamps, in their bedrooms, and at their seats; in short, in whatever activity life occupied them. Thus it is no wonder what *Theodoret* <note>A 5th-century influential theologian and historian from Syria.</note> records: that a certain soldier was recognized as a *Christian* by the fact that he made the sign over his cup at every drink. <margin>See book 3, chapter 16 of Theodoret.</margin>

<margin>10.</margin>
But if we review the histories of the ancients and more carefully weigh the things God wished to accomplish—and indeed did accomplish—through the sign of the Cross, we will neither wonder that the demons were unable to bear the sign of the Cross, nor that our ancestors used it most religiously. The arguments for this are almost incredible and infinite. *Palladius* <note>Author of the "Lausiac History," a 5th-century collection of stories about the desert monks.</note> relates in the *History of Lausus*, chapter 2, that a certain old man, when he saw an asp in a well, protected the well with the *sign of the Cross*; he then drew water without fear and drank what he had drawn without any harm. There was another likewise (found in *chapter 54*) who, protected by the *sign of the Cross*, remained in the midst of flames for a long time. He also writes that he read in the book of *Hippolytus*, *Concerning the Virgin*, that when she refused the *Judge* access to her body, she was thrust into a brothel <note>original: "postibulum," a place of prostitution. Such stories were common in early martyr accounts to show divine protection of chastity.</note>, but was set free by the *sign of the cross*. See chapter 149.

<margin>11.</margin>
*Theodoret* testifies that through the martyrs *Julian and Marcian*, giant dragons were killed by the *sign of the cross*. Likewise, the Saints *Aphraates, Macedonius, Peter*, and others cured various diseases by the same sign, as recorded *in their Lives*.

Bishop *Eugenius* restored the light of sight to a *blind man* with the cross, as *Victor of Vita* <note>A 5th-century bishop who wrote a history of the persecution of Christians by the Vandals in North Africa.</note> records in *On the Vandal Persecution*, and as the martyr *Lawrence* did, as noted by *Ado of Trier* <note>Likely referring to the 9th-century Archbishop Ado of Vienne, whose Martyrology was a standard historical text.</note>.

*Tiburtius* had been ordered by the prefects of the Emperor *Diocletian* either to sacrifice to idols or to walk over glowing coals. The martyr chose the latter; but protecting himself with the *sign of the cross*, he suffered no harm, as *Metaphrastes* <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine author who compiled the "Lives of the Saints."</note> relates.

A certain archdeacon, as *St. Gregory* <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD).</note> writes, had offered poison to *Bishop Sabinus*; the bishop, having made the sign of the cross, drank the poison and felt no ill effect.

### PART III. DISPUTATION. ###

After the death of Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (r. 361–363 AD), the last pagan Roman Emperor who attempted to revive polytheism.</note>, the sea overflowed its boundaries, threatening a new deluge; struck by the novelty of the event, the locals in the city of Epidaurus in Dalmatia brought forth St. Hilarion <note>St. Hilarion (291–371 AD) was an anchorite who is credited with bringing the monastic life to Palestine.</note>, and placing him on the shore, begged him to turn away the sea and the wrath of God with his prayers. What did Hilarion do? Having made three Crosses in the sand, he raised his hands against the waves: and behold, suddenly they rose up in the manner of a wall, and as if feeling a force exerted upon them, they gradually receded. *Jerome* records this in the *Life of Hilarion*.

During the time when Maurice <note>Byzantine Emperor Maurice (r. 582–602 AD).</note> held power, certain Turks <note>The author likely refers to Central Asian peoples or Gokturks who interacted with the Persians and Byzantines.</note> came to Constantinople, sent by King Khosrow <note>Khosrow II, the last great Sasanian King of Persia.</note>; when asked by the Emperor why they bore the sign of the Cross on their foreheads (for everyone’s forehead was marked with a Cross), even though they thought no honor should be given to the Cross, they replied that this Sign was a symbol of a great benefit: they had once been liberated by it from a raging plague, after they had been taught by Christians to mark their foreheads with such a sign. Thus says *Nicephorus* <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos (c. 1256–1335), a Greek historian known for his "Ecclesiastical History."</note>.

These were the words of St. Martin to Julian: "I," he said, "protected by the sign of the Cross, and not by shield or helmet, shall penetrate the enemy ranks in safety." *Sulpicius* <note>Sulpicius Severus, the 4th-century biographer of St. Martin of Tours.</note> says this in his *Life*. Prudentius <note>Aurelius Prudentius Clemens (c. 348–413 AD), a Roman Christian poet.</note> sang of this matter in a hymn before sleep:

> Make it so, when sleep calls, &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Cross drives away every crime,
> And you seek your chaste bed, &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The darkness flees from the Cross;
> That the figure of the Cross &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Dedicated to such a sign,
> Signs your forehead and heart. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The mind knows not how to waver.

To these we add one more from Augustine, and indeed in Augustine’s own words, from *The City of God*, book 22, chapter 8. "In Carthage," he says, "Innocentia, a most religious woman and one of the leading figures of that city, had cancer in her breast; a matter which, as doctors say, is curable by no medicines. She had heard this from a skilled physician and a close friend of her house, and she had turned herself to God alone in prayer. She was admonished in a dream, as Easter was approaching, that she should watch at the baptistery on the women's side, and whichever woman first met her after being baptized, she should mark the spot with the sign of Christ’s Cross. She did so, and health followed immediately." Thus says Augustine.

<margin>11.</margin> Since these things are so, it is a wonder that in our times men are found who wish there to be no power of the Cross against demons; they even attribute it to the cunning of the same demons if they ever depart at this sign—as if the Wicked One intended to foster and promote the superstition of men by this flight, which they claim he feigns.

<margin>12.</margin> If they recognize no power of the Cross in the flight of demons, what will they say to so many, so great, and so certain wonders which have been perfected by the sign of the cross alone? To the routing of diseases? To the restoration of health? To the drinking of poison without harm or loss of safety? To the removal of massive dragons? Or the breaking and repelling of the waves of the sea? To the prostration of enemies?

# ON THE POSSESSED. #

...thrown down? toward the cast down and shattered idols? toward countless other things which could not have been achieved by the demon's craft?

<margin>13.</margin>
It is a wonder that this power can be attributed to demons, when all antiquity attributed it not to demons, but to the Sign of the Cross. It is a wonder that it can be said these are proofs of superstition, when they were adopted by the holiest men—who were the most sworn enemies of demons—as firm defenses of the Christian religion to drive away all adversity. It is a wonder that it can be said they conspired with demons; for the wicked spirits could not endure the presence of those men while they lived, nor even their ashes after they had died.

<margin>14.</margin>
Here we understand not the craftiness of demons, but their weakness, when they depart at the sign of the Cross. Just as in all other things that we have set out, so in the casting out of demons do we recognize the power of the Cross. We believe and profess, with Basil <note>St. Basil the Great (c. 330–379 AD), an influential theologian who wrote extensively on the liturgy and the Holy Spirit.</note>, that the Cross is a most healthy remedy for driving away spirits. "Let him come," we say with Athanasius <note>St. Athanasius (c. 296–373 AD), the Bishop of Alexandria famous for his defense of orthodoxy.</note> (in his book *On the Incarnation and the Saving Advent of the Lord*), "let him come, I say, who wishes to take a test of these words: in the very deceits of the demons, the impostures of oracles, and the miracles of magic, let him use the Sign of the Cross which they deride. Let him invoke the name of Christ, and he will see how the demons flee out of fear of that thing, the oracles fall silent, and magic and sorceries lie defeated." Thus says Athanasius.

<margin>15.</margin>
*But what is the cause, someone will ask, for the demons to flee at the sign of the Cross?* This question, though it may seem curious <note>In this context, "curious" implies a deep or speculative inquiry into the mechanics of faith.</note>, nevertheless offers a useful debate. For it is asked: is there some power in the Cross that tortures the demons, or is it rather that their hatred of the Cross itself is so great that they would rather retreat in disgrace than endure the Cross with distress?

<margin>16.</margin>
Indeed, power can be understood to reside in this Sign in two ways. The first is that, just as power is "impressed" upon other things by which they act <note>Like heat is a property "impressed" upon fire.</note>, so it is also impressed upon the sign of the Cross. The second is that power is not actually impressed upon the sign itself, but it is taken up as an instrument of God, which God—by His own power and <term>ex opere operato</term> <note>original: "ex opere operato"; a Latin theological term meaning "from the work performed." It suggests the action is effective by the very fact of being carried out, rather than being dependent on the piety of the person doing it.</note>, as we say in the schools—wills to be effective for putting demons to flight.

<margin>17.</margin>
It can in no way be said that power resides in a Cross formed in the air or pressed upon the forehead in the same way that power is said to reside in natural things. If we consider what it possesses by the forces of nature, this signing of the Cross made in the air will have no more power than any other shape formed in the air by a person's finger or hand.

<margin>18.</margin>
That God wills for demons to be put to flight by the Cross as an instrument and, as we said, <term>through the work performed</term>, is quite probable: and indeed

### PART III. DISPUTATION ###

...indeed, if from nowhere else, this is certainly clear from the fact that Jewish and Pagan men, even without true faith or devotion, have often been helped by the sign of the cross. Nazianzen <note>St. Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 329–390 AD), a prominent theologian and orator of the early church. Original: "Nazianzenus, *Orat. in Iulian.*"</note> testifies to this regarding Julian the Apostate, as does Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403 AD), known for his "Panarion" against heresies.
