Original: "quæstione 79. qq. 83."</note>: "It is no wonder," he says, "that these Signs are effective when they are employed by good Christians; for they are effective even when they are used by outsiders who have not given their names to this military service at all <note>Augustine is using a military metaphor; "outsiders" refers to those who have not been baptized into the "militia of Christ."</note>, because of the honor of the most excellent Emperor. However, when the Powers <note>Refers to demonic principalities or spiritual powers.</note> do not yield to these Signs, God himself prohibits it in hidden ways when he judges it just and useful. For in no way do any Spirits dare to despise these Signs; they tremble at them wherever they catch sight of them." Thus says Saint Augustine.

<margin>19.
1 Timothy 4.</margin>
Human piety—as the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> testifies regarding all other things—is also useful and effective here. For when people take up this Sign out of a desire for piety, they ask for and invoke the merits of Christ, which are, as it were, expressed through the sign of the cross. Therefore, to oppose demons with the sign of the cross is to oppose them with Christ's passion and to call upon God through Christ's merits. Are these not of the greatest value?

<margin>20.</margin>
But the hatred of demons is most powerful here. It is incredible how great their hatred is toward the cross of Christ. Therefore, just as you flee things that are invisible and hateful to you, so they detest and flee the cross.

<margin>21.
Colossians 2.</margin>
There are, if I am not mistaken, two causes for this hatred. The primary one is that by this Sign, their strengths were broken and their kingdom dissolved. For Christ (as the Apostle says) <note>A translation of Colossians 2:14-15. Original: "Christus enim (inquit Apostolus) chirographum decreti, quod erat contrarium nobis tulit de medio, affigens illud Cruci, expolians Principatus & Potestates, traduxit palam confidenter, triumphans illos in semetipso."</note> took away the legal document of the decree that was against us from our midst, pinning it to the Cross; and stripping the Principalities and Powers, he led them away openly and confidently, triumphing over them in himself. Therefore, just as a dog detests the stick with which it was struck, so the devil detests the cross.

<margin>22.</margin>
The second cause of hatred arises from the "fruit" <note>The spiritual benefits or graces.</note> which the faithful can gather from this Sign. For this is no small thing. And even if I do not mention that the memory of Christ's passion is refreshed by this Sign—which brings the greatest benefit—this same Sign explains, first, the whole of Christian perfection. The *depth* of the cross suggests faith; the *height* suggests hope; the *breadth* suggests charity; the *length* suggests perseverance: if these are found in a Christian, they constitute perfection. Next, it explains the effect of Christ's Passion: which is the opening of heaven (suggested by the *summit* of the cross); the vastness and emptiness of hell (suggested by the extension of the sign down to the *breast*); and the redemption and salvation of the whole world (suggested by the movement of the *hand from the left to the right side*). So much for the third way.

ON THE POSSESSED.

# CHAPTER XLV.

## *The fourth method is examined, by which demons are expelled from human bodies through the use of Consecrated Things.*

<margin>1.</margin>
The fourth method for casting out demons is, as we have said, through the *Use of Consecrated Things*. This seems to differ from the previous three methods in this regard: whatever power it has over demons, it receives through Prayer and the Word of God; whereas the former methods derive their force not from the prayer of the Church, but from elsewhere. <note>The author distinguishes between the inherent power of Christ's name or the Sign of the Cross and objects that must be specifically "charged" by the Church's ritual prayers.</note>

<margin>2.</margin>
This method is not simple, just as the types of things that are consecrated and blessed are not of one kind alone. *Water* is blessed; *salt* is blessed; *herbs* are blessed; and *wax images* are blessed, which we call "Agnus Dei" <note>Latin for "Lamb of God." These were small discs of wax, usually from the previous year's Paschal candle, impressed with the figure of a lamb and blessed by the Pope.</note> from the likeness of the lamb impressed upon the wax. Indeed, these things are blessed not merely for the purpose of being free from demonic infestations themselves (in the way certain other things are blessed), but so that we may use them *against* the infestations and harassments of demons.

<margin>3.</margin>
We can gather what we are saying from the formulas which the Church employs in the blessing of these items. In the blessing of *Salt*, she prays as follows:

> We humbly implore your immense mercy, Almighty Eternal God, that you might deign to bless and sanctify this creature <note>In historical liturgical Latin, "creatura" (creature) refers to any created element of nature, such as salt, water, or oil, before it is sanctified for religious use.</note> of Salt, which you have granted for the use of the human race; so that it may be health of soul and body to all who take it; and that whatever has been touched or sprinkled by it may be free from all impurity, and from every attack of spiritual wickedness. Through our Lord. <note>original: "Immensam clementiam tuam... Per Domin."</note>

In the consecration of Water, she uses this form:

> O God, who for the salvation of the human race established the greatest <term>Sacraments: here referring to "sacramentals" or sacred signs that mimic the sacraments</term> in the substance of waters: be mercifully present to our invocations; and pour into this element, prepared by manifold purifications, the power of your blessing; so that your creature, serving your mysteries, may receive the effect of divine grace for driving away demons and dispelling diseases, etc. <note>original: "Deus, qui ad salutem... morbosque pellendos diuinæ gratiæ sumat effectum, &c."</note>

Likewise, when the priest blesses Herbs and Branches, he asks that whoever receives them may receive protection for mind and body, etc. When blessing the Wax Images, he prays among other things as follows:

> We beseech you, Lord, that you might deign to bless, sanctify, and consecrate these Lambs, which we have formed from virgin wax in your honor, and which have been bathed in the sacred and eternal wave and the balsam of holy Chrism <note>A mixture of olive oil and balsam consecrated by a bishop, used in various Christian rites.</note>: so that, having been blessed by you, they may receive power against all diabolical temptations: and all who carry them may be safe amidst both adversity and prosperity, so that having received your consolation, they may fear no danger, and dread no shadow: no diabolical cruelty, or [cunning...] <note>The text ends mid-sentence. The original Latin catchword "sutia" indicates the next page begins with "versutia," meaning cunning or craftiness.</note>

### PART III. DISPUTATION.
<page-num>112</page-num>

...that human craftiness may not harm them; but strengthened by the power of your virtue, they may glory in your consolation; you who are truly called the <term>Paraclete</term> <note>From the Greek *parakletos*, meaning "advocate" or "comforter," a title for the Holy Spirit.</note>, etc.

<margin>4.</margin>
These are the prayers of the Church. What do we judge their effect to be? If, as the Lord said: *Whatever we ask the Father in his name, we have obtained*, shall we be frustrated in our desire here? And when we pray that He wills his <term>creatures</term> <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to any created thing in the physical world, such as water, salt, or oil, rather than specifically animals.</note> to be effective in routing demons, will He reject our vows?

<margin>5.</margin>
Perhaps these things are not asked of the Father in His (Christ’s) name: But the conclusion of every prayer—in which we ask for it to be granted <note>original: "Per Dominum nostrum"</note> *Through our Lord*, etc.—proves that they are. Perhaps what we confess in words, we deny in deeds; while we ask for something superstitious and contrary to divine laws. And what would that be? That we want creatures to be blessed? That we want things already blessed to be effective for performing prodigious things? That we ask for power to be granted to rout demons? But these things are not superstitious. The blessing of creatures is not opposed to divine laws. Nor is the opinion that blessed things should be effective for prodigious things. Nor the opinion that they are effective for the ejection of demons from human bodies. We teach these three things.

<margin>6.</margin>
First of all, *to bless creatures is not superstitious*, nor contrary to divine laws. What is superstitious is superstitious for everyone: What is repugnant to divine laws, God himself does not want permitted even to himself. What then follows? That the blessing of creatures is free from superstition and does not conflict with divine laws. Why is this? Because that God blessed His creatures is as certain as the most certain thing.

<margin>7.</margin>
Perhaps because creatures were already blessed by God <note>referring to the creation in Genesis</note>, we should take care lest they be blessed a second time. Why, I ask? Is it because what has been well done once cannot be done a second time? Where is the law that prohibits an act from being repeated? Moreover, we do not bless creatures in the same way, or for the same reason, that God did. By our blessing, we ask that they be effective in driving away diseases and casting out demons. This was not the purpose in the first condition of things when God originally blessed them.

<margin>8.</margin>
Add to this, that the Savior himself would not be without fault if this were true: for He did not use this kind of blessing only once. He used it before He departed from this life; and after He rose glorious from death. He used it in the desert, and in <term>Emmaus</term> <note>Referring to the "Supper at Emmaus" (Luke 24:30), where Jesus took bread, blessed it, and broke it.</note>. Or perhaps the blessing that God bestowed on all things at the beginning of the created world did not pertain to the loaves of bread which the Lord blessed?

<margin>9.</margin>
Those things which we can curse, we can also bless. No one would deny this. But we can curse creatures: Therefore, we will be able...

<margin>
Mark 11.
Assumption.

...[we are able] therefore also to bless. The assumption <note>original: "Assumptio"; referring to the logical premise of the argument.</note> is certain, since even in the New Law the Lord cursed the fig tree <note>original: "maledixit Dominus ficum"; see Mark 11:12-21.</note>: and in the Old Law, if ever a hidden crime of adultery had to be revealed, God willed it to be done through waters cursed by the priest <note>A reference to the "Ordeal of the Bitter Water" described in Numbers 5:11–31.</note>.

<margin>
10.
Mark 7.
</margin>
The **blessing of created things** is not a new thing in Christ's Church. It holds great authority from venerable antiquity. The *oil* with which the Apostles cured the sick possessed this power through a mystical blessing. It was blessed oil that Tertullian writes was customarily administered through the "Christian Cup" <note>Tertullian was an early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD). The "Christian Cup" likely refers to a vessel for blessed oil used in healing.</note> in his work *To Scapula*, chapter 4. St. Basil, in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, teaches that it is an Apostolic tradition that we bless *water*. But antiquity is proved most especially by the *Prayer* found among the *Constitutions* written by Clement <note>The *Apostolic Constitutions*, a 4th-century collection of ecclesiastical law once attributed to Clement of Rome.</note>. There it is said:

> Lord of <term>Sabaoth</term> <note>A Hebrew title for God meaning "Lord of Hosts" or "Lord of Armies."</note>, God of virtues, Creator of waters, and giver of oil, merciful and kind, who gave water for drinking and cleanliness, and oil for gladdening the face in the exultation of joy; may you yourself now also sanctify the water and this oil, in the name of those who brought them; and grant the power of producing health, of expelling sickness, and of putting demons to flight, being an adversary to all snares, through Christ, who is our hope, with whom to you be glory and honor and worship, with the Holy Spirit. Amen.

<margin>
11.
</margin>
Furthermore, just as it is not new, neither has the blessing of created things been rare in the Church of Christ. First, regarding *water*, this is clear by the testimony of many. Dionysius, in *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, says that *water* is consecrated by sacred invocations. Cyril, in *Catechesis 3*, teaches that simple *water* becomes holy by the invocation of God. Cyprian says in Book 1, Epistle 3: *It is necessary that the waters first be cleansed and sanctified by the Priest.* Ambrose, in Book 1 of *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, chapter 3, teaches that water has no use in the Church unless it is first hallowed by the sign of the cross. Finally, blessed *water* is mentioned by Epiphanius in *Against Heresies*, 40; by Theodoret in Book 5, chapter 21; and by Augustine in his 27th Homily (out of 50), in Sermon 19 *On the Saints*, and in Book 6 *Against Julian*, chapter 8.

<margin>
12.
</margin>
Similar testimonies exist for the consecration and blessing of other things. Clement, Dionysius, and Tertullian mention the blessing of *oil* in the places cited above, as does Augustine in his 118th tractate on John. St. Augustine mentions the blessing of *bread* outside of the Eucharist in the second book of *On the Merits of Sinners*, chapter 26, as does Paulinus in his letters to Alypius and Romanianus (which are numbers 35 and 36 among the letters of St. Augustine). Strabo mentions the blessing of the *Paschal Candle* in chapter 30, as do the Fathers in the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 8. Blessed Maximinus—whose homilies inscribed for Ash Wednesday still exist—mentions the blessing of *Palms* and *Ashes*.

...[Ash Wed]nesday, and Palm Sunday, etc. This concludes the first Chapter.

<margin>13.</margin> It follows that we should teach (which was our second point) *that it is done without sin when created things are employed for marvelous effects that surpass nature.* For this argument, the records of the Holy Scriptures fight excellently on our behalf—not only from the books of the Old Testament, but also from the New. Naaman the Syrian, suffering from an incurable disease, came to the prophet Elisha to seek health from him: and behold, after he had, as commanded, *washed himself seven times in the Jordan*, he was soon *restored to his former health* by the benefit of the waters. <note>See 2 Kings 5. Naaman was a commander of the Syrian army suffering from leprosy.</note> How marvelous is that which is read in Numbers 5? That upon taking the water into which the Priest had gathered curses, *the thigh of the adulteress should rot, and her swelling womb should burst?* <note>The "Ordeal of the Bitter Water" used to determine a wife's fidelity.</note> These examples are from the Old Testament. From the New is that which the Evangelist reports: *that the Apostles used oil in the expulsion of all kinds of infirmities*; and what is said of the *Sheep Pool <note>original: "aqua probatica"; the Pool of Bethesda in Jerusalem.</note> moved by an Angel*, which brought the most immediate health to the first person to enter it.

<margin>14.</margin> Furthermore, examples are not lacking in those matters which are currently under dispute. We show this first in the case of **Holy Water**. Theodoret, in his *Life*, relates that the Blessed Aphrates <note>A 4th-century Syrian monk.</note> put to flight a great force of locusts that were consuming everything using this water. This same *water*, poured out in four directions, once drove the same pests from a garden, according to Theodore, the <term>Archimandrite</term> <note>A title for an abbot or head of a monastery in Eastern Christianity.</note> of Sykeon, as Metaphrastes <note>Simeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer (writer of saints' lives).</note> records in his life; just as, by the same witness, he elsewhere freed the beasts of burden of the people of Ancyra from a raging plague.

St. Germanus shattered the swelling and strengthening waves of the sea with this water—waves which a demon, wishing to hinder the holy man's arrival in England, had stirred up—as Bede records in the *History of the English*, Book 1, Chapter 17.

Quintianus, Bishop of Auvergne, sprinkled this water in the house of a certain Hortensius where fever had seized everyone, and health followed immediately, according to Gregory of Tours in his *Life*.

With this water, the Blessed Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> freed and restored to health the son of Evelia, an Antiochian woman, who was close to death; witnessed by Metaphrastes on the 13th of November. Likewise, Gilbert, Bishop of Ireland, cured the servant of a certain English Count who was already dead in the extremities of his body, as the Venerable Bede records in his life.

St. Brigid healed a paralytic with this water (according to Surius <note>Laurentius Surius, a 16th-century German monk and hagiographer.</note> in her *Life*), as well as a leper and a blind man. St. Theodore, whom we mentioned above, cured those suffering from fever and the difficulties of childbirth, as did St. Bernard, as Bernard of Bonneval writes in his *Life*, Book 2, Chapter 3.

Furthermore, a certain Goth, falling from his horse while on a journey, had broken his hip, as the Blessed Gregory writes in the *Dialogues*, Book 1, Chapter 16; he immediately petitioned Fortunatus...

...[For]tunatus, the Bishop of Todi, for his health. He sprinkled the soldier’s hip with holy water, and so on, and behold: the entire fracture was so thoroughly mended that he rose from his bed and, having mounted his horse, completed the journey he had begun. <note>Fortunatus was a 6th-century bishop known for his healing miracles recorded by Gregory the Great.</note>

Blessed Marcellus, the Bishop of Apamea, completely overcame the efforts of the Devil—who was struggling to prevent the famous temple of Jupiter of Apamea from being burned—by using water blessed with the sign of the cross. Theodoret describes this event more extensively in Book 5, Chapter 21. <note>Theodoret of Cyrus was a 5th-century Christian historian; this story describes a temple to a Roman god that could not be burned until holy water broke the pagan "spell."</note>

Henry, the Count of Ratzeburg, held certain Parisians captive, raging against them with many tortures. Evernoldus, the Bishop of Ratzeburg, interceded for them, but it achieved nothing. It was the solemn day of Easter when the captives stood in chains under guard in the Church. As the Bishop went around sprinkling the faithful with holy water, he also sprinkled the chains of the captives, saying: *The Lord sets the prisoners free.* <note>original: "Dominus soluit compeditos"; a quotation from Psalm 146:7.</note> What happened then? Immediately, the chains shattered, and they departed freely. The chains are preserved as a testimony to the deed. Albert Krantz records this in Book 5 of *Wandalia*. <note>Krantz was a 15th-century historian; *Wandalia* is his history of the Slavic peoples and Northern Germany.</note>

<margin>15.</margin>
We have been quite extensive in examples for the sake of confirming the power of Holy Water. No doubt our speech would bring boredom if we were to produce a similar forest of examples for the remaining items. Therefore, a limit must be placed on our discourse. It will suffice to produce one or two examples for the others. Thus, Hilarion cured many people with blessed Oil, as Blessed Jerome testifies in his *Life of Hilarion*. Sozomen writes in his history (Book 6, Chapters 21 and 29), and Rufinus before him (Book 2, Chapter 4), that the monks of Egypt used the same oil to impart health. Theodore the Archimandrite <note>A title for an abbot or head of a monastery.</note> used the same to drive out an evil spirit <note>original: "Cacodaemonem"; a term derived from Greek meaning a malevolent demon.</note> which was bringing a strange torment and trembling to the limbs of a possessed sailor; the priest George writes of this in the *Life of Theodore*. And we read concerning Vrismarus in the work of Ratherius, Bishop of Verona, in the *Life of Vrismarus*, that a nun—from whom he had cast out a demon—anointed her mouth, eyes, and nostrils with blessed oil.

<margin>16.</margin>
Gregory of Tours mentions blessed salt in the *Life of Saint Monegundis*, who lived in the year of our Lord 560. Because she, being dead, could not heal the sick as she had done while living, she was asked to bless oil and salt so they might be administered to the sick who were begging for a blessing. She complied with their wishes, and indeed with benefit to many; for, as the same Gregory says, many sick people experienced the benefits of health from the mentioned blessing after her passing.

<margin>17.</margin>
Concerning the wax Image, which is called the *Agnus Dei* <note>original: "Lamb of God"; these were small wax discs blessed by the Pope, often made from the previous year's Paschal candle.</note>, Molanus writes as follows concerning the year 1568, when the Prince of Orange attempted to break into Brabant with a numerous army: in the territory of Jülich, near Maastricht <note>original: "Traiectum ad Mosam"; the Latin name for the city on the Meuse River.</note>, he had a certain Spanish captive, whom he had condemned to death...

...soldiers attempted to kill a man tied to a tree with muskets or cannons. But they discharged their bronze engines of war against him in vain. Indeed, so far were they from being able to pierce him with their guns while he was thus tied to the tree, that even with the most frequent volleys, they could not harm him. Seeing this and being struck with amazement, they began to strip him of his clothes, thinking the man was protected by some hidden armor that the force of the engines could not penetrate. However, no protection was found on him except for an amulet of the **Agnus Dei** <note>A sacramental wax disc blessed by the Pope, usually bearing the image of the Lamb of God.</note> hanging from his neck. Once this was taken from him, he was killed and fell dead at the first shot of the musket. The Decretals are collections of Church law and precedents.</note> Our own age has observed many things of this kind, and they can be confirmed by the testimony of those still living who have experienced the power of this Image. Thus, we judge that the one who sang of this matter did not err:

> *By this sign, the temptation of the Devil’s art is driven away,*
> *And piety rises in the soul, while fear departs.*
> *By this, poisons flee, and the sudden dangers of death,*
> *And with this protector, you shall be safe from ambushes.*
> *Lest lightning strike, or cruel thunders harm,*
> *Lest a wicked storm overwhelm you, hold this fast.*
> *It repels the peril of the waves and of fire alike,*
> *And it prevails so that no enemy force may cause harm.*
> *With this granting an easy birth, the woman in labor*
> *Shall bring forth her child safely to the world and to God.*

A certain author has encompassed these points more clearly and briefly in the following lines:

*It wards off lightning,*

*It bestows many*

*Benefits the wicked*
*As much as the greatest.*

<margin>18.</margin>
**Can these things which we have said happen through Consecrated Things not also (which is our third Chapter) be used to drive demons out of human bodies?** If we examine the causes of why these wonders we have just recounted were performed through the benefit of Consecrated Things, we shall find no other reason than that they obtained this power through the prayer and consecration of the Church. But just as God was asked that He might wish these created things to be effective in putting diseases to flight and averting storms, etc., so too was He asked that He might wish them to be effective in putting demons to flight. Or is it perhaps to be thought that here He has withdrawn His hand and denied His help?

<margin>91.</margin>
Perhaps demons are not driven away by sensible and physical things; nor do these things possess the power to expel them? In fact, even by these things they are driven away; even these things possess that power. Nor are examples lacking here. Did not the demon leave King Saul when David played the lyre? <margin>1 Samuel 16</margin> And the gall, which Tobias removed from the fish at the command of the Angel—did it not have the power to put demons to flight? <margin>Tobit 6</margin> What of the fact that Solomon wished to use herbs in the casting out of demons? See Josephus, Book 8, Chapter 2. <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century historian, describes Solomon’s legendary expertise in exorcism and botany in his *Antiquities of the Jews*.</note>

<margin>20.</margin>
Sensible things <note>In this context, "sensible" (sensibiles) refers to things that can be perceived by the five senses, as opposed to "intelligible" or purely spiritual beings.</note> are those that are formed in the air, such as voices when we invoke the name of Christ; sensible things are the crosses we form with our fingers; sensible things are the Relics of the Saints. Nevertheless, by the benefit of these things, the power of invisible and incorporeal spirits is broken. In the presence of these things, the wicked spirits were unable to remain, as was demonstrated in Chapter 24 and those following.

<margin>21.</margin>
It is possible, therefore, for demons to be put to flight by these things. But let us not only teach what *can* happen; let us also show that it *has* happened. First, the holy man **Macarius** presents himself here: Palladius, in the book titled *The Paradise of Heraclides*, Chapter 6, teaches that he healed a possessed boy with **Holy Water**. <note>original: *Aqua benedicta*. Saint Macarius the Egyptian (c. 300–391) was a prominent Desert Father; Palladius was his contemporary and biographer.</note>

Second, **Saint Eligius**, the holy Bishop of Noyon, presents himself. He was attempting to remove certain impious superstitions in a certain village not far from the town of Noyon. However, when he gained nothing from many sermons and was even treated with injury and insult by his listeners, following the example of the Apostle, *he handed them over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved.* <note>Quoting 1 Corinthians 5:5; this refers to a form of spiritual discipline or excommunication where the body is afflicted to prompt repentance.</note> Because of this, the friends of the possessed ran to the holy man, seeking help with great desire; but Eligius did not promise this except after a year of penance. Then, once they were brought to him (there were more than fifty of them), he liberated them from the spirits by the sprinkling of **Holy Water**. Audoenus, Bishop of Rouen, records these things in his *Life of Eligius*, Book 2, Chapter 20. <note>Saint Eligius (also known as Eloi, d. 660) was a renowned goldsmith and advisor to Frankish kings before becoming a bishop.</note>

Third, there is a certain boy offered by his parents to **Saint Eucharius**, to be instructed with others in the monastery according to the Rule. When he once drank water offered by a demon (appearing in the form of a man) before he had signed it with the cross, he was possessed by that same demon. Soon he was led to the altar of Saint Eucharius. Prayers were made for him, water was hallowed and offered for him to drink; once it was swallowed, the demon was suddenly driven out. So says Surius in the *History of the Discovery of Saint Celsus*, Chapter 11, Volume 7. <note>Laurentius Surius was a 16th-century German hagiographer who compiled lives of the saints.</note>

To these sayings we add a fourth. **Arnold**, Bishop of Soissons, was about to arrange peace between certain parties. While a certain man resisted him and fled, lest he be forced into peace by the prayer of the holy man, he was [seized] by a De- <note>The page ends mid-word: "Dæmone" (Demon).</note>

# DISPUTATION: PART II #

...the demon is driven to flight. What then? Others pray for the health of the possessed man; and they obtain it, having given a pledge of the peace to be received; but by the benefit of <term>Holy Water</term> <note>original: "Aquæ benedictæ"</note>, which the holy man sprinkled upon the demoniac. Lisiard, Bishop of Soissons, records this in his *Life*, chapter 24.

To St. Bernard (this is the fifth example) a boy is brought, who for three years had been most severely tortured by an occupying demon, in the hope of gaining freedom. Bernard orders, among other things, that <term>consecrated water</term> <note>original: "aquam consecratam"</note> be poured into the mouth of the possessed; but the demon began to struggle against it, pressing the lips together and grinding his teeth. Finally, leaving behind a most foul vomit, he departed. From the *Life of Bernard*, Book 2, chapter 3.

St. Laurence, Archbishop of Dublin, and Bishop Maltonius (whose life Sigebert describes) also serve our purpose here. Both thought that <term>Holy Water</term> <note>original: "Aquam benedictam"</note> should be used in the healing of <term>Energumeni</term> <note>A term derived from Greek, used in the early Church to refer to those "worked upon" or possessed by an evil spirit.</note>. Indeed, its remarkable power was observed: for as soon as it was drunk, the spirits were put to flight, as is clear in the *Lives* of both, found in Surius, Volume 6.

And in the *Life of Saint Elizabeth*, Queen of Hungary, James of Speyer writes in chapter 30 that a girl was brought to her sarcophagus <note>The stone coffin or tomb of the saint.</note>, who was suffering the torture of a demon due to an evil curse from her parents; she was restored to her former health as soon as she consumed a little <term>blessed bread</term> <note>original: "benedicti panis"</note> and <term>sacred water</term> <note>original: "sacræ undæ"</note>.

<margin>22.</margin>
Similar to these, or rather confirming them, are the following accounts. Metaphrastes says that a certain house was greatly vexed by demons. When the household members were eating lunch or dinner, stones were thrown upon the tables; the women’s looms were broken; so great a multitude of mice and serpents occupied the house that no one dared enter for fear. However, Theodore, the Archimandrite <note>An administrative title for the head of a monastery in the Eastern Church; this refers to St. Theodore of Sykeon.</note> of the Sykeotes, entered at the request of others; and, after prayer, he sprinkled everything with <term>Water</term> <note>original: "Aqua"</note> which he had blessed, and freed it from the unclean spirits. Thus Metaphrastes writes in his *Life*.

There was also a demon who for three years, in the village of Gaumon <note>original: "Camonte," likely modern Gaulsheim</note>, not far from Bingen, afflicted the city of Mainz and its neighbors with its illusions; finally, the priests drove it away with Litanies and <term>Holy Water</term> <note>original: "Aqua benedicta"</note>, as Sigebert testifies under the year 858. Bernard Crucius writes in the *Life of Emperor Louis II* that a house in Mainz was liberated in the same way. Therefore, we believe it is most truly said:

->*By this water, the hidden acts*<-
->*of the demon are driven away.*<-

## CHAPTER XLVI.

### *An examination of the fifth method, by which demons are cast out from the bodies of men through Exorcisms.*

<margin>1.</margin> By the name of <term>Exorcism</term> <note>Derived from the Greek *exorkismos*, meaning "binding by an oath." In this context, it refers to the formal command given to a demon in the name of God.</note>, in this place, we understand that method by which wicked spirits are adjured through God; they are compelled to depart from human bodies, to restore to God His creature whom they possess, and to cease their torment.

That this practice is ancient is clear from the testimony of <term>Cyprian the Martyr</term> <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage and an important early Christian writer.</note> and the Christian poet Prudentius. To both of these we add <term>Tertullian</term> <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD) known as the "father of Latin theology."</note>, so that "by the mouth of three witnesses every word may be established." In one passage (*On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 40), he inveighs against certain "little women" who presumed to exorcise, with these words: *How bold are these heretical women? Who would dare to teach? To act as exorcists?* etc. <note>original: "Ipsæ mulieres Hæreticæ; quam procaces? Quæ audeant docere? exorcistas agere?"</note>

<margin>2.</margin> That the power of this method is not small is proven by the cries, groans, and wailing which demons have very often given forth from within possessed men. Regarding these, Cyprian writes in *On the Vanity of Idols*: *When adjured by us through the true God,* he says, *they immediately yield and confess; they are forced to exit the possessed bodies. You might see them, by our voice and the operation of hidden Majesty, lashed as if by whips and scorched by fire, stretched out as their punishment increases, wailing, groaning, and begging; confessing from whence they come and when they depart.* Thus says Cyprian.

<margin>3.</margin> The power of exorcism is also proven by the Abbots <term>Hilarion</term> <note>Saint Hilarion (291–371 AD), an anchorite who brought the monastic lifestyle to Palestine.</note> and Bernard. Hilarion showed its force in the case of Marsita; Bernard in the case of a woman of Milan. Marsita was a very strong young man from the territory of Jerusalem, so powerful in strength that he could carry fifteen <term>modii</term> <note>A Roman dry measure; fifteen modii would weigh roughly 300 pounds.</note> of grain for a long time and over a great distance; he held the prize for strength as if he could outdo donkeys. This man, afflicted by a most evil demon, could not be restrained by chains, shackles, or even the heavy bars of doors. He had bitten off the noses and ears of many; he had broken the feet of some and the throats of others. He had struck such terror into everyone that he had to be dragged to the monastery of Hilarion the Hermit like a ferocious bull, weighed down with chains and ropes by men pulling in different directions. When the brothers saw him (for he was of a wondrous size), they were terrified and informed the Father. Hilarion, just as he was sitting there, ordered the man to be dragged to him and released. Once the youth was unbound, Hilarion said: *Bow your head and come.* <note>original: "Inclina, ait, caput, & veni."</note> The man began to tremble and bow his neck, not daring to look back; all his ferocity having been set aside, he began to lick the feet of the seated saint. Thus the demon who had possessed the youth, being adjured and tormented, departed on the seventh day. Jerome records these things in the *Life of Hilarion*.

<margin>4.</margin> In Milan, Bernard truly [assisted] a certain woman, whom a <term>Wicked Spirit</term> <note>original: "Spiritus Nequam"</note>

The wicked spirit was tormenting her; he placed the <term>host</term> <note>The consecrated bread used in the Eucharist, believed by Catholics to be the literal body of Christ.</note> which had been placed upon a plate, over her, with these words: "Behold," he said, "the Spirit is present; your judge is here, the supreme power. Now resist, if you can. He is present who, about to suffer for our salvation, said: *Now the Prince of this world shall be cast out.* <note>original: "Nunc Princeps huius mundi eijcietur foras." A reference to John 12:31.</note> In His power, therefore, I command you to depart from this His handmaid." What then? The spirit was compelled to give way. These things are found in the *Life of Bernard*, Book 2, Chapter 4.

<margin>5.</margin> I think its excellence may also be gathered from another matter (unless perhaps this is a testimony to the sanctity of the man). We read of <term>Abbot Eugenius</term> <note>Likely referring to a local or monastic saint recorded in hagiographies like those of Surius.</note> that when asked to liberate a girl from an unclean spirit, he first poured out much prayer to God; then he wrote a brief Exorcism, sealed it, and ordered it to be tied around the girl's neck. Indeed, the demon departed before the Exorcism had even been brought to the girl. See <term>Surius</term> <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a German monk and hagiographer famous for his multi-volume collection of the lives of the saints.</note>, Volume 1, in January. Something similar is held regarding <term>St. Bernard</term> <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a major French abbot and mystic.</note> in his *Life*, Chapter 4, Book 2. He had expelled a certain wicked spirit from a possessed woman for the second time. Because he feared that it would enter the poor woman again after his departure, he fastened this Exorcism to her neck:
> *In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I command you, Demon: do not enter this woman.*

<margin>6.</margin> Furthermore, there has not always been one and the same form of this Method for casting out demons. In the past, it seems to have consisted of fewer things; now, sometimes more are employed, because it seems that bodies are not as easily liberated from demons now as they were in the past.

<margin>7.</margin> Hence, I would believe it to be the case that we read of demons being cast out by different people in different ways. <term>St. Lawrence Justinian</term> <note>The first Patriarch of Venice (1381–1455), known for his asceticism and administrative reforms.</note> is said to have first rebuked the spirit, and then immediately commanded and ordered its exit. <term>Bernard Justinian</term> <note>An orator and historian, nephew of Lawrence Justinian.</note>, the Venetian Ambassador, teaches this in Chapter 8 of the *Life of Lawrence*. In exactly the same way, <term>Bertulph</term>, Abbot of Bobbio, liberated an infant, as witnessed by Jonas, who describes his deeds in Surius. <term>Parthenius</term>, according to <term>Metaphrastes</term> <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer known for his standard collection of the lives of saints.</note> on February 7th, commanded only the departure from a certain person, and thus restored the possessed man to his former health. The same is read to have been performed by <term>St. Remigius</term> <note>The "Apostle of the Franks" (c. 437–533) who famously baptized King Clovis I.</note> for a demoniac whom <term>St. Benedict</term> <note>The father of Western monasticism (c. 480–547) and author of the Rule of St. Benedict.</note> sent to him, as <term>Hincmar</term> <note>The Archbishop of Reims (806–882), who wrote an influential biography of Remigius.</note> teaches in the *Life of Remigius*.

<term>Anatolia</term> <note>A 3rd-century Roman martyr.</note>, a most holy virgin, first breathed upon the demoniac; then turning to the demon, she said: "Go out from the man, and let the wretch congratulate you on his health." <note>original: "Exi, inquit, ab homine & de sanitate tibi gratulatur miser."</note> Thus it is in her *Life*, in Surius, Volume 4.
<term>St. Columbanus</term> <note>An Irish missionary (c. 540–615) who founded several monasteries across Europe, including Bobbio.</note>, when he was entering the city of Paris to visit King <term>Clotarius</term> <note>Chlothar II, King of the Franks.</note>, encountered a possessed person attacking him with many insults. The man of God commanded the spirit to depart; but it finally went out only after he had put his fingers into the man's mouth and handled his tongue for some time. The form which St. Bernard used was indicated above in Thesis 4.

<sig>Q</sig>

<term>Gregory of Langres</term> <note>Gregory (d. 539 AD) was the Bishop of Langres and the great-grandfather of the historian Gregory of Tours.</note> joined a command with the sign of the Cross, as <term>Gregory of Tours</term> <note>A Gallo-Roman historian and bishop (c. 538–594 AD) whose writings are the primary source for Merovingian history.</note> testifies in his *Life of Gregory of Langres*, chapter 6. <term>Abbot Eugenius</term>, as has been said, wrote a brief Exorcism; he commanded the same to be tied around the neck of the possessed person, and so Satan fled. See <term>Surius</term>, Volume 1.

<margin>8.</margin>
From this, I would also say it follows that the <term>Heretics</term> <note>A common term used by Catholic authors of this period to refer to Protestant Reformers, who often rejected many of the physical rituals and "sacramentals" of the Catholic Church.</note>, who bring almost all the pious practices of Catholics under scrutiny, now also have more things to carp at and condemn in our rite of Exorcism than in that which was received in those earlier times.

<margin>9.</margin>
Nevertheless, their censure is unjust. Their judgment is rash and false. What we say will finally be made clear once we have demonstrated that everything occurring in the Exorcism is *entirely justified and free from all superstition*. Come then, let us fulfill this task.

<margin>10.</margin>
There are, however, various elements found in an Exorcism. Nevertheless, they can be reduced to two main types: *actions and words*. The *words* are directed partly to God; partly to the Saints, the friends of God; and partly to the possessing Demons. They are directed to God through Prayer and the Sacrifice of the Mass; to the Saints through the Litany; and to the Demons through <term>Adjuration</term> <note>The formal act of commanding a spirit in the name of God.</note>. In Prayer, one can observe either what is being asked for, or the manner—that is, through whom the request is made. In the Litanies, the focus is primarily the invocation of the Saints. In Adjuration, one considers the manner of speaking; the adjuration itself; and what specifically is commanded of the demons.

<margin>11.</margin>
Forgiveness of sins is asked from God. It is requested that He deign to assist His ministers in such a burning and difficult matter; that He also deign to have mercy on the possessed man and rescue him from the power of the Demons. These things are asked through the merits of Christ and the Saints. The Saints are invoked so that they may pray for us and for the <term>energumen</term> <note>original: "Energumeno." A technical term for a person possessed by a demon.</note>. The demons are rebuked with harsher words; they are sometimes commanded to reveal themselves, to state their names, to reveal their associates, and to explain the reasons why they entered the humans. They are ordered to depart from the humans, to head for hell, and to declare their departure with some sign.

<margin>12.</margin>
The *actions* <note>original: "Res" (literally "things" or "realities"). Here referring to the physical/material components of the rite.</note> in Exorcism are similarly varied and manifold. Some are sacred; some are signs of sacred things. The various elements include the Most Holy Body of Christ, which is offered under visible forms; the Relics of the Saints, which are sometimes employed; and Holy Water, with which the possessed are sprinkled. The signs of sacred things are primarily the Cross, which is pressed now to the forehead, now to the chest, now to other limbs of the possessed. To these I add the Place where the Exorcism is performed, which is usually a church; likewise the sacred vestments with which the Exorcist is clothed; the Stole, which is sometimes placed upon the possessed; the <term>Laying on of Hands</term> by the priests; burning candles; for which sometimes whips are used; and the insertion of the Exorcist's fingers into the mouth of the possessed.

<summary>This page defends the Catholic rite of exorcism against Protestant criticism by categorizing its elements into "words" (prayers, litanies, and commands) and "actions" (relics, holy water, and physical gestures).</summary>

### PART III. DISPUTATION.
->22.<-

These are generally the elements found within an Exorcism. However, just as not everything is strictly necessary, so too are they not always employed; sometimes more are used, sometimes fewer. Yet, whether they are included or omitted, *all of them are free from superstition* <note>original: "superstitione vacant omnia"</note>; we shall now demonstrate this very briefly in the following sections, so that the authority of Exorcism may remain firm.

<margin>14.</margin>
*Prayer, when it is employed, must not be condemned.* Those who have at any time cast out unclean spirits have believed that prayer is the greatest defense against them. <term>Saint Gregory</term> <note>Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD), a Pope and influential writer whose "Dialogues" contain many accounts of miracles.</note> writes in the first book of his *Dialogues*, chapter 10, that <term>Fortunatus</term>, Bishop of the Church of Todi, freed men from demons by this means. Similarly, <term>Saint Bernard</term> <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153 AD), a major Cistercian abbot and mystic.</note> expelled a demon in Cremona through a whole night of prayer—a demon which had wickedly feigned that it had been cast out by him in Pavia; <term>Bernard of Bonneval</term> is the source for this in the second book of his *Life*, chapter 4. <term>Saint Jerome</term>, in his *Life of Hilarion*, teaches that <term>Blessed Hilarion</term> freed nearly two hundred men and women through prayer on the island of Cyprus, where he had hoped to remain hidden.

A boy was once brought to <term>Saint Macarius</term> <note>Likely Macarius of Egypt (c. 300–391 AD), a desert father known for his spiritual wisdom.</note>; a demon was vexing him in a strange manner. The holy man cured him through Prayer, after he had placed one of his hands on the boy’s head and moved the other to his chest: so says <term>Palladius</term> in his *Life*.

And <term>Genevieve</term>, the holy virgin, cured those <term>Energumens</term> <note>original: "Energumenos," a technical term from the early Church referring to people possessed by spirits and undergoing exorcism.</note> whom she healed at Tours; she cured them through Prayer offered to God, as is known from her *Life* found in <term>Surius</term> <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a Carthusian monk who compiled a massive, multi-volume collection of the lives of the saints.</note>, Volume 1.

The same Prayer was used by <term>Parthenius</term>, of whom <term>Metaphrastes</term> <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer.</note> writes on February 7th; <term>Abbot Eugenius</term>, about whom Surius writes in Volume 1; <term>Arnulphus</term>, Bishop of Metz, in Surius Volume 4; <term>Herbert</term>, Archbishop of Cologne, according to <term>Rupert of Deutz</term> in his *Life*; likewise <term>Patroclus</term>, a dweller of the wilderness, of whom <term>Gregory of Tours</term> writes in chapter 9 of his *Life*; <term>Lawrence</term>, Archbishop of Dublin, in Surius Volume 6; and <term>Marcianus</term>, as recorded by <term>Theodoret</term>, Section 3.

Some of these men called upon others to pray with them, as did Arnulphus and Bernard on occasion; others were content with private prayer, though they used it sometimes with great fervor and sometimes for a very long duration. For it is read that Lawrence of Dublin prayed to God while prostrate on the ground, and Patroclus indeed employed a three-day prayer. No more examples are needed. The Lord himself teaches that there is a certain kind of demon which is not driven out except by *Prayer*.

<margin>15.</margin>

The most holy <term>Augustine</term> <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential theologians in Western Christianity.</note> mentions the Sacrifice of the Mass being offered for the purification of a house that was greatly infested by demons; he teaches that after the sacrifice was performed, the house was liberated.

And <term>Saint Bernard</term> <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153 AD), a Cistercian abbot known for his mystical writings and influence on the Church.</note> believed that no small amount of protection was placed in the Mass. For he employed that very <term>Exorcism</term> <note>original: "Exorcismum"</note> which we mentioned in Thesis 4 of this Chapter during the Most Holy Office of the Mass; he believed this was effective for routing a spirit so insolent and cruel as the one with whom he was then at war. Indeed, this spirit had possessed a woman for many years: it had deprived her of sight, hearing, and the ability to speak; it had so altered the face of the possessed woman that she resembled not a human, but a monster; sometimes she even thrust out her tongue in the manner of an elephant’s trunk. When she was brought to the holy man, she even kicked him. Therefore, the holy man requested the prayers of the people present for the possessed woman and took up the Sacrifice of the Mass as a support. Whenever, while performing the Sacrifice, he made the sign of the cross over the <term>host</term> <note>The bread used in the Eucharist, which Catholics believe becomes the body of Christ.</note>, he turned toward the woman and signed her with that same host. The demon always grew more and more ferocious in the possessed woman, until finally, having applied the aforementioned Exorcism after the <term>Lord’s Prayer</term> <note>The "Our Father" (Paternoster).</note> was recited during the Sacrifice, he routed the spirit.

<margin>16.</margin> This point is entirely supported by what <term>Blessed Chrysostom</term> <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople, famed for his eloquent preaching.</note> teaches in his 4th Homily against the <term>Armenians</term> <note>original: "Armenos"; likely referring to his homilies against the Anomoeans, though the text states Armenians.</note>, stating that it was once the custom and practice for demoniacs to be brought to the Sacrifice itself during the time of the Divine Offices. These are his words: "I will explain the reason why the Deacon commands men agitated by a demon, and summoned by that foulest fury, to be brought forward at that time and to bow their heads. For what reason is this done? I will say what I think. The agitation of demons consists of very small but heavy chains—chains stronger than iron. Therefore, just as at the approaching hour when a Judge is accustomed to come forth and sit upon the tribunal, the guards lead all the prisoners whom they hold in chains out of the prison and place them—squalid, filthy, covered in dirt, and wretchedly draped in rags—before the gates and enclosures of the court: so the <term>Fathers</term> <note>The early leaders and teachers of the Christian Church.</note> had established that when Christ was soon to sit as if upon a tribunal and appear in the Sacraments themselves, men agitated by a demon should be brought there as if held by certain chains. This was not so they might undergo an examination of the things they had committed, in the manner of those who are in chains; nor so they might pay the penalty and be afflicted with punishment; but so that, with the people and the entire city present, common supplications might be made for them, and that everyone might pray with constant harmony to the common Lord for them, and strive with a great cry that He might have mercy." So says Chrysostom.

# PART III. DISPUTATION.

...prayers are employed, let nothing be sought that would be unworthy for us to ask, or unbecoming for God to grant. We seek that which we were instructed by the Lord to seek: namely, that our transgressions be forgiven us, and that we be delivered from evil, both of the body and of the soul. What is superstitious here?

<margin>18.</margin>
Nor can the *Method* by which we seek those things from God be condemned: namely, that we seek them through the merits of Christ and the Saints. What are the merits of Christ not capable of? What can the Father deny to those who pray through the wounds and blood of his Son? The Son is here for us: *If,* he said, *you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you.* <note>John 16:23</note>

Perhaps the merits of the Saints are condemned. But wrongly. How many and how great were the benefits God conferred upon the people of the Jews because of the merits of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob? The merits of the Patriarchs please God; shall the merits of the Apostles Peter and Paul not please Him? And those of the other Saints, who, as the Apostle says, *experienced mockings and floggings, and even chains and imprisonment; they were stoned, they were sawn asunder, they were tempted, they were killed by the edge of the sword; they went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, distressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy?* <note>original: "ludibria & verbera experti..." quoting Hebrews 11:36-38</note> Here also the example of Pontius, Abbot of Bellevaux, serves us: when he had seen many things employed in vain by his companions to free a certain possessed man from the tyranny of a demon, he applied to the possessed man the <term>Stole</term> <note>A long, narrow strip of cloth worn by Christian deacons, priests, and bishops as a symbol of their office.</note> which <term>Saint Bernard</term> was accustomed to use during the offering of the most holy <term>Host</term> <note>The bread used in the Eucharist or Mass.</note>; and by the power of Christ, through the *Merit* of the holy man whose stole he held, he successfully commanded the demon's departure. See William, Abbot of Saint-Thierry, in the *Life of Bernard*, Book 4, Chapter 11.

<margin>19.</margin>
There is no reason for anyone to quibble that the merits of Christ are *obscured* by this reasoning; the merits of the Saints actually illustrate the merits of Christ. They amplify the glory of Christ, for from this we understand that His merits were so powerful that the fruit of His passion conferred great virtue upon the merits of His servants as well.

<margin>20.</margin>
*Litanies are not employed in Exorcism in vain.* They have often brought many benefits to Christianity, as has been said elsewhere. But also, through Litanies, most successful exorcisms of demons from human bodies have been completed, as Isengringius, Gervase of Tournai, and Jacob Rabus teach. To this is added that, at the urging of <term>Gregory the Great</term> <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604 AD), known for his liturgical reforms and writings.</note>, a formidable specter of a demon—appearing as if horned—which was so troublesome to a certain place that no one could stay there, was finally driven off and expelled by Litanies, just as we have taught concerning another instance above, in the fields and city of <term>Mainz</term> <note>original: "Moguntinensi"</note>. See Chapter 1 concerning infested places for both accounts. Furthermore, if the spirits cannot bear the ashes of the Saints, will they bear their Names, which are recited in the Litanies? That demons fled at the mere name of <term>Saint Anthony</term> <note>Saint Anthony the Great (c. 251–356 AD), a Desert Father famous for his battles with demonic temptations.</note> is attested by a most reliable witness, Saint Athanasius, in his *Life*.

->### ON THE POSSESSED.<-

<margin>21.</margin>
The *Adjuration* <note>original: "Adiuratio" — a formal, authoritative command used in exorcism to compel a spirit to obey</note> itself (we now proceed to the Prayer addressed to the Spirits) is not an evil thing. The examples of the most holy Fathers, who were the first leaders of the Christian flock, confirm its use. "Demons," says Justin <note>Justin Martyr, a 2nd-century Christian philosopher</note>, "obey us when they are adjured." And Cyprian <note>St. Cyprian, a 3rd-century Bishop of Carthage</note> states: "Demons, when adjured by us, are tortured and cast out." See chapter 41; let us now examine the manner of this Adjuration.

<margin>22.</margin>
*This manner requires that the speech be harsh, vehement, and not friendly.* In this, we follow the example of Christ and the Apostles, who are recorded to have rebuked demons. Of Christ, it is said in Matthew 17: *And Jesus rebuked* him (the Demon). And in Mark 9:
> *He threatened the unclean spirit, saying: You deaf and unclean spirit, I command you, come out of him.*

Regarding the Apostles, especially Paul, it is read in Acts 16 that, having turned, he said to the spirit:
> *I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of him.*

So it is related of St. Lawrence Giustiniani, the Patriarch of Venice, that he more harshly rebuked a spirit foaming at the mouth and gnashing its teeth; he threw it back as a reproach that the spirit had entered a weak little woman. Thus writes Bernardo Giustiniani, the Venetian Orator, in his *Life of Lawrence*. And with enemies—indeed, the most sworn of enemies—who can speak in a friendly manner? Perhaps just as lashes are a scourge to the body, so harsh speech is troublesome to the Spirits.

<margin>23.</margin>
Do those things imposed upon Demons during an adjuration savor of superstition? They do not. It is permitted to command the demons to reveal themselves. Theodore the Archimandrite <note>An "Archimandrite" is a title for a superior abbot in the Eastern Christian tradition</note> (according to his disciple, the priest George, in his *Life*) commanded the spirit that had tortured a certain girl for 28 years in strange and hidden ways to reveal itself. It is permitted to demand *that they reveal their name.* Christ’s own example stands before us in this. It is permitted to urge *that they identify their associates*, so it may be known which enemies the war is being waged against. Let the Exorcists be aware of this. It is permitted to ask *the reason for their entry into humans*; so that, if this cause can be removed, the power of the Spirits over humans may be lessened, and they can be more easily driven out. It is permitted to *demand a sign of departure*, so that the victory won for us over the enemies may be confirmed. It is permitted to *send them away to hell*: because this place, by Christ's own testimony, is prepared for them.

<margin>24.</margin>
In the Words, therefore, there is no superstition. *In the objects used, there is even less danger.* Why so? Because most of them have already been vindicated from all suspicion of superstition above: namely, the Relics of the Saints, Holy Water, and the Sign of the Holy Cross. The power of these remaining things is confirmed not only by logic, but also by the weightiest examples which nearly every age provides.

<margin>25.</margin>
Is it displeasing *that the most holy body of Christ in the Sacrament of the Eucharist is employed*? But here to support us is that most holy man, Bernard <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic and doctor of the Church</note>, who applied the same to a woman of Milan and routed the Demons.

There was a very wide and most pleasant plain, hedged in on all sides by very high trees and surrounded by terrifying rocks. One could also hear all sorts of harmonies, flowing with every sweetness; finally, everything was present that could hold the minds of men with the most delightful charms. ...having drawn it out, he placed it in that woman's lap. A marvelous thing. Everything immediately vanished. Thus far the Count of Mirandola <note>Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, author of "Strix" (The Witch), a famous work on demonology</note>, regarding the power of the Eucharist against demons.

<margin>26.</margin>
That Exorcisms are mostly performed in a *Church* <note>original: "Templo"</note> should not be condemned. We teach by this reasoning whose power we implore here: on whose power we rely; namely, God's, whose house the Church is. Furthermore, the most ready weapons are here at hand, which weaken the demons not a little. The faithful people are present here, whose prayers greatly assist the Exorcists. Finally, the Place itself is for many reasons quite hateful to demons; an argument for this is that (as Sigebert <note>Sigebert of Gembloux, a medieval chronicler</note> reports) on the night before St. Peter’s Church in Cologne was consecrated, the voices of malignant Spirits were heard, complaining loudly because they were being driven from their seats. And so also St. Bernard, when he once had a very difficult Spirit to deal with, chose the Church as the place of battle; and he asked the Christians present to assist with their prayers, as was said above.

With the Church, I join the Sacrarium <note>A sanctuary or holy room within a church for sacred objects</note>, which Blessed Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre <note>original: "Antisiodorensis"</note>, used. For when he was in Italy and was asked to cure those possessed by demons, he cured all who were brought to him in the Sacrarium, as witnessed by Constantinus the Priest, in his *Life*, book 2, chapter 10, found in Surius, Volume 4. In confirmation of both places [the Church and the holy room], there were three possessed persons brought at one and the same time to St. Theodore the Archimandrite <note>A title for a superior of a monastery</note>, who cried out that the Cell of the Holy man in which they were confined was a grave torment to them. The Holy man confirmed the same. For when he was called away by St. Cyriacus the Patriarch while busy with their cure, he freed two from the demon; but to the third, whose cure was more difficult, he commanded that he should endure the torture of that same place until his return; so says the Priest George in his *Life*.

*Sometimes Exorcists are clothed in Sacred Vestments. What is the sin in this?* We are not so foolish as to be ignorant that these garments contribute little to the ejection of demons [by their own power]; yet we say they are not used without reason. By this *Vestment*, Exorcists demonstrate that they do not rely on their own virtue or merits, but on the power divinely communicated to them: likewise, that they perform the office of their Order, which relies on Christ's authority, not human merits. ### PART III. DISPUTATION.

Is it perhaps unworthy for one to wear the insignia of his own art and office?

***The Stole is also placed upon the Energumens <note>original: "Energumenis" — a term for those "worked upon" or possessed by an unclean spirit</note> and the possessed:*** But this follows the example of the Elders. By this means, a certain Priest—whom St. Gregory mentions somewhere in the first book of the *Dialogues*, according to Jean Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and writer on demonology</note> in *On the Demon-mania of Witches*, book 3, chapter 6—drove a demon out of a woman. And a certain Pontius, Abbot of the Monastery of Bellevaux, expelled demons using that same stole which St. Bernard once used, as recorded in the *Life of Bernard*, book 7. I will say nothing of the fact that the Stole is numbered among those signs which demons cannot endure; for, as Alcuin <note>Alcuin of York (c. 735–804), a leading scholar and advisor to Charlemagne</note> notes, he who is clothed in it is warned to be mindful that he is under the yoke of Christ. Furthermore, as Bonaventure <note>St. Bonaventure (1221–1274), a major scholastic theologian</note> says in his exposition of the Mass, when it is crossed over the breast in the manner of a Cross, it signifies first that the passion of Christ must be carried in both mind and body; and second, that the Jewish people pass from the right to the left, while the Gentiles pass from the left to the right. Add to this that it signifies the obedience of Christ, as Rupert of Deutz <note>Rupert of Deutz (c. 1075–1129), a Benedictine abbot and theologian</note> wishes in *On Divine Offices*, which He, though Lord of all, exhibited for our salvation when He assumed the form of a servant. See the same author in book 1, chapter 21.

***Exorcists also lay their hands upon the Possessed.*** There is nothing new in this. St. Martin once laid his hand upon a servant of Tetradius at Trier, as Sulpitius <note>Sulpitius Severus, biographer of St. Martin of Tours</note> witnesses in his *Life*; and just as Martin did not do so in vain (for he both drove out the demon and moved Tetradius to the faith of Christ), so too the Priests do not do so in vain. Similarly, a boy was freed from a most savage spirit, as Palladius witnesses in the *Life of Macarius*, after he had placed one hand upon his head and the other upon his breast, and directed a prayer to God, from whom all good comes.

Theodore the Archimandrite also employed the Laying on of Hands in the healing of the daughter of a certain Prince, whom a demon had already grievously tortured for twenty-eight years. Gregory the Presbyter, a disciple of Theodore who is frequently cited, records this. Likewise, Metaphrastes <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer</note> testifies concerning Gregory, Bishop of Agrigento, in his *Life*, that he restored the son of a jailer—who was bound to a column because of a spirit raging within him—to his former health as soon as he laid his Hand upon the head of the Possessed man. Gregory of Tours <note>A 6th-century historian and bishop</note> reports the same of Hospitius, a man of great self-restraint, in the sixth book of his *History of the Franks*. Indeed, why should they not follow the example of the Apostles here, *who laid hands upon the sick, and they recovered?*

<margin>30.</margin>
***The Light of Wax Candles*** is not employed so that the Spirits might be seen; rather, it either possesses the same reasoning and efficacy as other sacred objects, or it is used so that Satan, as he departs from a man, might testify to his departure by the extinguishing of the light.

<margin>31.</margin>
***Scourges*** <note>original: "Flagella" — whips or cords used for symbolic or physical discipline</note> are used more rarely, yet they are used nonetheless. I suspect this is for two reasons. One is that they remarkably confound the Demons when they realize these are used as evidence of contempt for them. The other is that

### ON THE POSSESSED.

...which seem to be effective for their ejection; for while the conditions they demand in human bodies are dissolved by these means, they find their dwellings less suitable. Gerard of Nazareth <note>Gerard of Nazareth (12th century), Bishop of Laodicea</note> reports in Chapter 20 of *On the Conversation of the Servants of God* that a Devil was driven out from a man by means of whips [flagella], who—after many other remedies, even sacred ones, had been applied—had refused to leave.

With whips we join *slaps* <note>original: "Alapas" — sharp blows with the open hand</note>, by which both the Blessed Benedict and St. Hubert freed the possessed. Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a German monk and hagiographer known for his multi-volume collection of saints' lives</note> testifies to this regarding the latter on November 3rd in his *Life*; Blessed Gregory records the former in Book 2 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 30; and Krantz <note>Albert Krantz (1448–1517), a German historian</note> mentions a third case in the final chapter of the fifth book of his *Vandal History*. To these we add a fourth: a monk who was possessed by a demon on account of disobedience, and was helped through the prayers of the brothers after his Abbot Poppo <note>St. Poppo of Stavelot (977–1048), a prominent monastic reformer</note> struck him with a *slap*. Everhelm, Abbot of Hautmont, recounts this history in chapter 18 of the *Life of Poppo*, found in Volume 1 of Surius. And a fifth case: a man whom a demon entered because of a habit of debauchery. Leontius, Bishop of Neapolis in Cyprus, mentions him in the *Life of Abbot Simeon*. The Abbot expelled the demon by delivering a *slap*, saying: *Commit adultery no more, and the demon shall by no means approach you.* <note>original: "Noli amplius moechari: & daemon ad te minimè accedet"</note>

We also link with the use of whips the force applied by Theodore the Archimandrite <note>Theodore of Sykeon (d. 613), a Byzantine saint famous for his miracles</note> to a certain possessed woman. It is read that he seized her by the hair, and finally, having made the sign of the Cross, he drove out the spirit. Another deed of the same Theodore serves this argument. When he was still a boy, someone moved by the holiness of his life brought a possessed son to him, praying fervently for his health. What was the young Theodore to do? *I do not know the method,* he said, *of driving out demons.* <note>original: "Modum daemones exigendi ignoro"</note> Then the boy's father handed him a whip: *Strike my son with this,* he said, *and the hostile power of the demon will depart.* Theodore obeyed. But at the first and second strike, the spirit laughed; at the third strike, it fled and departed. George the Priest, a disciple of Theodore, relates these things in the *Life* found in Metaphrastes <note>Symeon Metaphrastes (10th century), the most important Byzantine hagiographer</note>.

<margin>32.</margin> Sometimes Exorcists also place their fingers into the mouths of the possessed [*Energumenorum*] <note>Energumens: those "worked upon" or troubled by an unclean spirit</note>. But they do so following the example of the Elders, who were holy men. Which ones? Abbot Patroclus, a dweller in the desert, as witnessed by Gregory of Tours <note>St. Gregory of Tours (c. 538–594), a bishop and historian who recorded many Gallic miracles</note> in the *Life of the Fathers*, chapter 9. Likewise Columbanus, as witnessed by Jonas in his *Life*, and St. Clair, Abbot of Vienne, in his *Life* found in Volume 1 of Surius.

From what has been said, it is clear that there is no crime in Exorcism; there is no superstition. But perhaps these individual things do not displease [the critics]; what displeases them is that all these things are joined together, and that we employ so many "engines" <note>original: "machinas" — referring to the various ritual tools and physical methods used alongside prayer</note> to rout those who could be cast out by the power of the Word of God. However, even this ought not to displease,

PART III. DISPUTATION.

He was able to cast out demons by a word—not to say a mere nod—yet he employed signs that reflect a certain form of Exorcism. For when he was about to heal a certain demoniac, he first took him aside from the crowd; then he put his fingers into the man’s ears; after spitting, he touched the man’s tongue; finally, looking up to heaven, he sighed and, after he had said *Ephphatha* <note>original: "Ephetethæ" — an Aramaic word meaning "be opened," used by Jesus in Mark 7:34</note>, he conferred health upon him.

## CHAPTER XLVII.

->*The reasons and methods by which Demons are cast out are not always*<-
->*effective; and that this happens for*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
Although the power of Exorcism is great—just as it is for the other methods by which we have said demons are cast out—they do not always achieve the hoped-for results. Nor does this detract anything from the virtue of Exorcism or the efficacy of those methods, since even the methods of casting out demons received and approved in the times of the Apostles were not always able to free the bodies of men from demons.

<margin>2.</margin>
That method which the sons of Sceva the Priest <note>A reference to Acts 19:13-16, where Jewish exorcists tried to use the name of Jesus without true faith and were attacked by the demoniac</note> wished to use was effective, and many obtained a healthy result from it; but in the case of the sons of Sceva, it was so far from having power that the demons even turned upon them, and they brought back the greatest disgrace from the very source where they were hunting for the glory of a name and extraordinary praise.

<margin>3.</margin>
Power was also granted to the Apostles over serpents, scorpions, and demons. However, this power did not have its strength everywhere. A certain man had brought his son to them, whom a Spirit was torturing in a marvelous way, expecting help from them; but he was frustrated in his hope: the son could not be freed from the demon by the Apostles. <note>Refers to the narrative in Matthew 17:14-21 and Mark 9:14-29</note>

<margin>4.</margin>
Origen <note>A prominent early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD)</note> testifies in his 24th Homily on Joshua that the same happened in his own time; and for this reason, he compares the evil Spirits to the Amorites <note>The Amorites were an ancient people mentioned in the Bible as enemies of the Israelites who remained in the land</note>. Just as the latter remained among the children of Israel, so Spirits often remain in possessed men. "Let many prayers be applied," he says, "many fasts, many invocations of Exorcisms; yet against all these the demon remains deaf in the possessed body, bearing the punishments of the Exorcists and the torments applied to him from the invocation of God’s name more tolerably than departing from the man whom he impudently and wickedly occupies."

<margin>5.</margin>
So we read concerning St. Benedict in Hincmar’s <note>Hincmar of Reims (c. 806–882 AD), a powerful Archbishop and historian</note> *Life of St. Remigius*: that he did not rout the demons with the Exorcisms he applied...

<header>
### ON DEMONIACS.
</header>

...from the girl of Toulouse: it <note>the demon</note> nonetheless confessed <note>original: "extorserit" — literally "wrenched out" or "extorted," implying a forced confession during exorcism</note> that it could be cast out by the prayers and efforts of Remigius <note>Saint Remigius (c. 437–533), the Bishop of Reims who baptized Clovis I</note>. Having been asked, the holy man sent letters to her, seeking the health of the girl. See another example of this matter in Bede, book 3 of the *History of the English*, chapter 71.

<margin>6.</margin>
The reason for this matter, unless I am mistaken, can now be attributed to the Exorcisms themselves; now to those who attempt to cast out the demons; now to the wretched ones who are tormented and possessed by the Spirits; and now to other causes.

<margin>7.</margin>
The nature of Exorcisms *is* not the same as that of the Sacraments <note>In Catholic theology, Sacraments are believed to confer grace inherently (ex opere operato), while Exorcisms are "sacramentals" whose effectiveness depends on the faith and piety of the participants</note>. The Sacraments necessarily achieve their effects for this reason: because by divine institution, they are certain and effective signs of heavenly grace; but the Lord did not make this promise to Exorcisms. For this reason, they do not always have as much power as Sacraments to drive away demons.

<margin>8.</margin>
The condition of the Exorcists also sometimes stands in the way. The Apostles testify to this by their own example: if they had first armed themselves with *fasting and prayer*, there is no doubt (as Christ’s prayer teaches) they would have cast out the demon which they were unable to cast out without these defenses.

<margin>9.</margin>
Hence it is what we had warned above, that many conditions are required in Exorcists if they are to perform their duty successfully. But if they omit these, and approach this arduous work unprepared, or if they are negligent in their duty, what wonder is it if they accomplish little or nothing?

<margin>10.</margin>
Add to this that God does not wish this grace to be common to everyone. *To one*, he says, *is given the grace of healing; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another various kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of speech.* <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 12:8-10</note> Wherefore it happens that demons who could not be driven out by many machines <note>referring to the "tools" or rituals of exorcism</note> and Exorcisms, soon yield and leave their seats as soon as they are lightly challenged by others.

<margin>11.</margin>
The sins also of those who are possessed <term>Obsessed</term> <note>The author uses "Obfeffi" (Obsessed), which in this period often referred specifically to the external harassment or internal occupation of the body by a demon</note> sometimes deserve that they are not immediately freed from the demons. For since, as has been said, sins often bring on this torment, it happens by the most just judgment of God: that however effective the Exorcisms and other means employed may be, and though nothing may be lacking in the Exorcists, the demons are nevertheless not cast out, because the sins in those who are possessed have not yet been sufficiently punished. This was also the reason why Saint Eligius, Bishop of Noyon, and Saint Parthenius, though frequently petitioned, were unwilling to free certain people—the latter a certain young man of the Huns, the former fifty men—from the torment of demons. Parthenius said to those pleading for the youth: *Let him be tormented: he is a parricide.* <note>original: "parricida" — one who kills a parent or close relative</note> Eligius said for the others: *Let them experience whom they have chosen to serve by their sin.* Ouen <note>Saint Audoenus, the biographer of Eligius</note> records this of Eligius in chapter 20, book 2 of his *Life*; and Metaphrastes <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a famous 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer</note> records it of Parthenius on February 7th.

<margin>12.</margin>
Sometimes it is also attributed not to the past sins of the possessed—

<sig>R 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: —but that</meta>

### PART III. DISPUTATION.
