...it is said <note>continuing from the previous page</note> that the Spirits delay their departure; but rather because faith is lacking in the sufferers, as well as the hope of attaining freedom. Those praying to God, or expecting His benefits, ought to approach with great confidence; because some of the Possessed <note>Latin: *Obsessorum*; those suffering from demonic preoccupation or possession</note> do not have this, what wonder is it if the remedies applied to them achieve nothing? Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an early Christian bishop and writer</note> and Minucius Felix <note>Marcus Minucius Felix (died c. 250 AD), one of the earliest Latin Christian apologists</note> assign this reason: "The demons," they say, "when adjured <note>commanded under a holy name or oath</note>, will either depart immediately or vanish gradually, according as the faith of the sufferer assists." Tostatus <note>Alonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), a prolific Spanish bishop and theologian</note> strongly emphasizes this same faith or confidence in the Possessed, in question 165 on the 17th chapter of Matthew. In support of this, he also brings forward that saying of the Lord in Matthew: *Amen, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, not only will you do what was done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, "Take yourself up and cast yourself into the sea," it will be done; and all things whatsoever you ask in prayer, believing, they shall be done.* <note>The text cites Matthew 12, but this quote is from Matthew 21:21-22</note> And also that passage from James, chapter 1: *If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all generously... but let him ask in faith, with no doubting.*

<margin>83.</margin>
Add to this that very often, there is no difficulty found in the Possessed, nor in those who apply Exorcisms; yet the demons do not yield when adjured. Just as God permits for many reasons that men be possessed by demons—even without any fault of their own—so He can have just reasons why He allows the demons to retain power over men, even though the victims provide no cause for their own miseries.

# CHAPTER XLVIII.

->*Whether Demons can be cast out from*<-
->*human bodies by sensible and*<-
->*entirely natural things.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
Now that we have examined the means by which demons were cast out from human bodies, whether long ago in the Church of Christ or even today, it would not be out of place if we added one more thing to what has been said, and defined whether it can happen that these same demons may be driven out by certain sensible <note>Latin: *sensibilibus*; things that can be perceived by the senses, i.e., physical or material objects</note> and natural things in which there is nothing divine or supernatural.

<margin>2.</margin>
And indeed, if we inspect the condition of demons and also consider what power sensible and natural things possess, it is not difficult to answer the proposed question. For since demons are entirely spiritual creatures, and since it is the condition of spiritual beings to leave all bodily things far behind them, we might not wrongly say that it is impossible for physical things to act upon them, to exert force on them, or to drive them from their seats.

<margin>3.</margin>
Nor does it weaken the force of this argument that force can be applied to [human] souls by physical things while they are in bodies, or that they can even be separated from bodies by force. The condition of souls in a body is far different from that of demons in a body:

<meta>This page continues the theological investigation into whether physical objects can affect spiritual entities. ->### CONCERNING THE POSSESSED.<-

...condition within the body. Souls are joined to bodies as **forms** <term>form: In the philosophy of the time, the "form" is the essential life-principle that gives a body its nature and functions.</term>; these spirits, however, are like certain movers and governors. For this reason, souls require specific physical dispositions in the body, which these spirits—since they are not the "forms" of the bodies—do not require. Therefore, spirits can exist within bodies regardless of the body's physical state, whereas souls are unable to give life to a body unless it is properly suited to them.

<margin>4.</margin>
Furthermore, although the reality is that bodies *by themselves can do nothing* against Spirits, there are nonetheless *three* examples in the present Disputation that seem to suggest the contrary. Because these are largely drawn from the Holy Scriptures, they neither should nor can be ignored.

<margin>5.</margin>
The first example is provided by the **History of the Kings** <note>original: "Historia Regum"; referring to the biblical books of Samuel/Kings.</note>. There it is read that the psalmist David put to flight an evil spirit from King Saul by the sound of a harp. *For whenever (it is said in 1 Kings 16) the evil spirit of the Lord seized Saul, David took the harp and struck it with his hand, and Saul was refreshed and felt better. For the evil spirit departed from him.* <note>This refers to 1 Samuel 16:23 in modern Bibles. The "Spirit of the Lord" here refers to a spirit sent by God’s permission.</note>

<margin>6.</margin>
The second example is shown by the Angel Raphael to the younger **Tobias**. When Tobias had pulled a fish from the river, he was commanded by the Angel to preserve its heart, gall, and liver. He learned from the same angel that *if a small piece of the heart were placed upon coals, its smoke would drive out every kind of demon, from both man and woman, and indeed in such a way that they would never approach them again.* <note>Reference to the Book of Tobit, chapter 6.</note>

<margin>7.</margin>
The third example is taken from the **Exorcism of Solomon**. As Josephus <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (37–c.100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> testifies, those who put demons to flight by this method (such as Eleazar) would apply a ring to the nostrils of the possessed. Beneath the seal of this ring was a root shown to Solomon, and as the possessed person smelled it, the exorcists would soon draw the demon out through the nostrils.

<margin>8.</margin>
These appear to be the strongest defenses that can be brought forward for this cause. But what of it? Those who, along with Plato, say that demons are corporeal <note>having a physical or quasi-physical body</note> can explain this more easily. However, those who recognize no physical or material density in them face a significant difficulty. Let us discuss each point individually.

<margin>9.</margin>
Regarding the first point, I do not think it should be doubted that Saul was truly **possessed** by a demon. For although he performed many noble deeds during the time he was vexed by the wicked spirit, it should not be inferred from this that he was free from the demon. A person can be possessed by a demon and not always suffer its tyranny, as was shown in Chapter 8 of this Disputation. Moreover, that Saul was truly possessed is taught by Theodoret (Questions 38 and 39 on 1 Kings), Gregory, Abulensis, Lyranus in his book on Kings, and Vallés in chapter 30 of *Sacred Philosophy*. <note>The author cites several famous theologians: Theodoret of Cyrus, Pope Gregory the Great, Alonso Tostado (Abulensis), Nicholas of Lyra, and Francisco Vallés.</note>

<margin>10.</margin>
The doubt remains, however: Whether he was ever liberated from the Demon...

->### CONCERNING THE POSSESSED.<-

...[it happened]: and, if he was freed, whether it was through David's work; and finally, by what kind of work of David he was freed. For not everyone is in agreement on this matter. There are those who deny he was freed. There are those who believe he was freed, yet not by the effect of the harp, but rather by the merit of David’s innocence and uprightness.

<margin>11.</margin>
To state our own opinion: we do not believe Saul was freed from the demon in any way because of David's uprightness or innocence. For Saul’s servants were not looking for a holy man whom the devil could not tolerate, but rather for someone who, by playing the harp <term>harp: The Latin "cithara" refers to a stringed instrument like a lyre or harp.</term>, might mitigate the pain that the demon was inflicting.

<margin>12.</margin>
Nor is it likely that the demon was put to flight by the sound or melody of the harp. It has already been demonstrated elsewhere that the powers of physical and sensible things are not such that they can have any power over a Spirit. Harmony and melody certainly soothe the ears and bring a certain pleasure to the soul, but they lack the power to cast out wicked Spirits from the bodies of men.

<margin>13.</margin>
We do not believe Saul was freed from the demon by any service or aid from David. Sacred History seems to confirm this. As it testifies, a man was sought not to drive away Spirits, but one who, by playing the harp, would cause the King to bear the troubles of the demon more lightly. David is reported to have been found for this purpose; when he played the harp, Saul was refreshed, and he felt the troubles of the demon less.

<margin>14.</margin>
Therefore, the harmony of the harp brought a certain pleasure to the King through David. Just as every pleasure that comes from an external source mitigates a present evil that one is suffering, so the harp considerably broke the pain that Saul was suffering from the demon's tyranny. And in this sense, the demon can be understood to have been "driven out."

<margin>15.</margin>
It can also be said that, by the playing of the harp, the bodily humors <term>humors: In ancient medicine, these were the four fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to control health and temperament.</term> were purged and freed from the affliction of melancholy. Because evil Spirits rejoice in that physical disposition, it happens that when the disposition itself is removed, they are—*by accident* <term>by accident: Or "per accidens." A philosophical term meaning something happens as a side effect or indirectly, rather than as a direct result.</term>—either driven away or prevented from being so troublesome. For no one doubts that music has great power to move men and their humors. Using the example of King Eric of Denmark, *Krantz* <note>Albert Krantz (1448–1517), a German historian known for his chronicles of Northern Europe.</note> shows this in Book 5 of his *History of Denmark*, chapter 3, which we add here word-for-word: *"When Eric,"* he says, *"having now returned to his Kingdom, was holding a formal court and taking delight in the skill of many soldiers and craftsmen, there was present among others a Musician who claimed to possess such skill in the art that he could move men to whatever emotions he wished: making the joyful out of the mournful; the sad out of the lively; the peaceful out of the indignant; and the indignant out of the calm—even boasting that he could make them insane to the point of madness. And as he performed these greater things which he said he could do, he made the King most eager [to experience them]—"* <note>original: "cupidissimum"</note>

If, however, anyone wishes to insist that Saul was entirely liberated from the demon by David's Harp, we will not resist much. Nevertheless, we shall not attribute this effect to the sound excited by the plucked strings, but rather to the power and passion of Christ stretched upon the Cross—of which the Harp was a certain sign. <note>In medieval theology, the wooden frame and stretched strings of the harp were often seen as a "type" or symbolic precursor to Christ on the Cross.</note> Thus it can be said that David's harp routed the demon in the same way that the sign of the Cross has very often cast out the same. <margin>17.</margin>
Likewise, we do not condemn the opinion of those who attribute the ejection of the demon to the sound of the Harp itself, even without regard to Christ's passion. These thinkers believe that the natural power of demons is restricted by divine decree and made subject to natural things; just as theologians teach that these same spirits are subject to and tortured by physical, infernal fire.

<margin>18.</margin>
Furthermore, those who say the evil Spirit was put to flight from Saul by David’s Harp believe it was driven away only for a time, so that he suffered no molestations from the Spirit during that interval. They believe he was truly liberated from the Spirit itself—for a time, I say—since when he again burned with hatred and envy against the triumphant David, he was again seized by the demon. ### PART III. DISPUTATION.

136

<margin>20.</margin> It is said that smoke, produced by the power of fire from a small piece of heart and liver, may drive out demons. There are those who think the weight of this argument is small because the Book of Tobit <note>A book of the Bible recounting the journey of a young man named Tobias, guided by the Angel Raphael; it is considered deuterocanonical by Catholics but apocryphal by many Protestant traditions.</note>, from which the argument is drawn, is not found in the Canon of Holy Scriptures. There are others who admit that the Angel was the author of some superstition for Tobias, while he taught by his own example that demons could be put to flight by smoke; yet they absolve him of blame, arguing he did this so as not to be found out. There is a third group who attribute the expulsion of the demon to the smoke as a sign, just as we spoke previously regarding David’s Harp and the sign of the cross.

<margin>21.</margin> Whatever the case may be regarding this third view (which we do not condemn), it is certain that the Book of Tobit should not be rejected from the Canon of Holy Scriptures. The authority of the Book of Tobit is as great as that of the other books. It is also certain that Raphael was not superstitious, nor was he the source of superstition for Tobias. Angels do not sin, nor do they lead others into sin.

<margin>22.</margin> And although we may deny that this smoke is a sign of a sacred thing <note>In a formal sacramental sense</note>, there is nothing that can compel us to say that demons are expelled by sensible signs <note>Physical things perceived by the senses.</note>. We might say: the Angel does not teach that devils are expelled by the physical force of the smoke, but only asserts that they are to be driven away when the smoke has been raised. Therefore, just as it is not necessary for my washing to be the cause of a lunar eclipse simply because the eclipse happens while I wash, so it is not necessary to say that the smoke is the cause that drives away devils, even though the devils are driven away at the same time the smoke exists. The Angel teaches what will happen; he does not provide the reason *why* it happens.

<margin>23.</margin> This perhaps seems indicated in Tobit, chapter 8. For it is not said that the smoke routed the demon, but rather the Angel Raphael. It is said there: *Tobias took from his bag a piece of the liver and placed it upon live coals. Then (it is added) the Angel Raphael seized the demon and bound it in the desert of upper Egypt.* <note>original Latin: "Tobias de cassidili suo, partim iecoris, posuitq; eam super carbones viuos. Tunc (subiungitur) Raphael Angelus apprehendit dæmonium, & religauit illud in deserto superioris Ægypti."</note>

<margin>24.</margin> What was it, then, that routed the demon? The smoke? No. The Angel Raphael routed it. But how? Was it because of the smoke being raised? Not even that. Nevertheless, when the smoke was raised, the demon was routed. If anything here beyond the work of the Angel routed the demon, it was the merits and prayers of Tobias and Sarah <note>Tobias’s new wife, who had been plagued by the demon Asmodeus.</note>.

<margin>25.</margin> Although we can also say of the smoke what we suggested regarding the sound of David’s Harp: namely, that it happens by divine power, so that the natural strength of demons may be subjected to and constrained even by physical things. For just as by the consecration of a physical thing, which is applied to them, so that Spirit <meta>catchword: Spiritus</meta>

### CHAPTER XLIX.

->*That demons leave with great difficulty the men whom they once possess:*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' set within a square frame featuring a detailed narrative scene with several human figures in a landscape, surrounded by ornamental floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
The fourth part of the Disputation will examine the departure of unclean spirits. And in this part, just as in the others, many things must be discussed: but especially these. It must be shown that demons leave the men they possess with the greatest difficulty. The causes of this must be investigated; and why some are cast out with more difficulty than others, and who those [specific spirits] might be. It must furthermore be explained by what signs especially they betray their departure. Also, what the causes and reasons for these signs are, both in general and in specific detail. By what path they exit when they depart <note>original: "abscindunt," literally meaning to cut away or break off.</note> and leave men. Also, whether they all exit at once when, for example, several of them possess one and the same person. In addition, where those cast out from men go. Why they descend to hell so reluctantly and with such difficulty. Finally, whether it is permissible to satisfy the vow or desire of those who, about to exit, ask for something. These are the main chapters or topics connected with the departure of spirits, and which may present some difficulty. If there are any others, they either do not have any singular difficulty or they are known from the previous parts of this Disputation. But to the first point.

<margin>2.</margin>
No one can rightly doubt, therefore, that demons or unclean spirits leave the men they possess with difficulty. There are many arguments for this fact. And first, indeed, daily *experience* serves here. For how many of the demons are cast out of human bodies who do not cause their Exorcist the greatest labors and troubles? How many Exorcists approach this work who do not believe they are entering upon an arduous task <note>original: "provinciam," referring here to a sphere of duty or a challenging assignment.</note>? And in the administration of which they do not think they have need of the greatest defenses.

<margin>3.</margin>
This experience is confirmed by the *examples of demons expelled by Christ*, who, because they left their seats <note>The physical bodies they inhabited.</note> most unwillingly, [is shown] partly by these words...
<meta>The text cuts off here at the catchword "estati," likely continuing a reference to the demons' "majesty" or "power" (potestati) or perhaps "manifestations" on the following page.</meta>

And the *Demons* likewise *declared the same in many ways.* By what ways, exactly? *First,* because they sometimes denied they could be expelled by men—such as the one who said he cared for neither "little Syrus" nor "little Bernard" <note>original: "Syrulum; neque Bernardulum." The use of the diminutive -ulus suggests the demon was speaking dismissively or mockingly of the exorcists, likely referring to St. Bernard of Clairvaux.</note>, whom we have mentioned several times in this Disputation. *Second,* because they very often could not be expelled, even though the greatest methods <note>original: "machinae"</note> were applied for their ejection. An example is the one whom the Blessed Benedict sent to the Blessed Remigius <note>Remigius (Remi) of Reims and Benedict of Nursia were prominent early medieval saints. This refers to a story where one saint's power was needed to finish the work of another.</note>, discussed in Thesis 14, chapter 23. *Third,* because they let out the greatest cries and shouts as they were being expelled, testifying to the force being applied to them. We shall review more of these later. *Fourth,* because not content with words and shouts, they severely tortured the wretched mortals upon their departure, as is clear from many examples. *Fifth,* because they said they were being tortured if they were ever expelled, just like the "Legion" of demons whom the Lord cast out. Of these, Luke writes in chapter 8: *I beseech you,* the Legion spoke to the Lord, *do not torture me; for He was commanding* (the Evangelist adds) *the unclean spirit to go out from the man.* Sixth and lastly, because they often attacked the exorcists gravely by whatever means they could—sometimes with true charges and sometimes with invented crimes—attempting to turn them away from the duty of exorcism they had undertaken. Not content with this, they were sometimes even blasphemous against God and the heavenly beings. An example here can be the one whom Paul the Simple <note>A 4th-century desert father known for his extreme humility and simplicity, who was a disciple of Anthony the Great.</note>, at the request of St. Anthony, cast out: who indeed attacked Paul and...

<header>PART 4. DISPUTATIONS.</header>

Antoninus <note>Likely referring to a critic of Christianity or a historical figure mentioned in the source material; the text notes he insulted the faithful and Christ.</note> used to call them gluttons <note>original: "Helluones"</note>, lethargic <note>original: "veternosos"</note>, and so on. Moreover, he would lash out at Christ with blasphemies. See Palladius <note>Palladius of Galatia, author of the *Lausiac History*, a 5th-century collection of lives of the desert fathers.</note>, Section 25, *History of the Holy Fathers*.

<margin>8.</margin> By the words "expelling" and "casting out," it is also sufficiently suggested that the envious, wicked spirits depart from human bodies [unwillingly]. These terms are used most frequently in those places of Holy Scripture where they are said to be banished. *In my name they shall cast out demons*, says the Lord in Matthew 10. *Why could we not cast it out?* say the Apostles in Matthew 17. *By Beelzebub, the prince of demons, he casts out demons*, say the Pharisees in Luke 11. Thus we read that the Lord cast out demons in Matthew 9; the Apostles in Mark 6; the sons of the Pharisees in Luke 11; and a certain other man, who did not follow Christ, in Luke 9.

<margin>9.</margin> Indeed, it is read that a certain demon asked Theodore the Archimandrite <note>An "Archimandrite" is a superior of a monastery or a group of monasteries in the Eastern Christian tradition.</note> for permission to leave the man he was possessing. However, he did not so much desire to leave the man as to be freed from the distress that Theodore’s presence brought upon him. George the priest, a disciple of Theodore, describes the whole matter in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a German monk known for his massive collection of lives of the saints.</note>, Volume 2, page 754.

<margin>10.</margin> Similarly, it is recorded that some spirits took flight before they even reached the Saints by whom they were to be cast out: such as the one who was tormenting the daughter of Emperor Gordian, who anticipated the arrival of Blessed Trypho (by whom he knew he would be expelled), according to Metaphrastes <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a prominent 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer.</note> in the *Life of Trypho*, February 1st. Some disappeared at the mere sight of the Saints; like a whole Legion that had invaded a young man, who tore everyone he met with his teeth, but who soon departed upon seeing Arnulph, Bishop of Soissons, as Lisiard, Bishop of that same church, testifies in the *Life of Arnulph*, chapter twenty-four. Some were put to flight at the mere sight of the Cross; like those who were brought to St. Gregory, Bishop of Langres, of whom Gregory of Tours writes in chapter 7 of his *Life*. Some were cast out by a word, as mentioned in Gospel history. Yet even these would not have left their homes if they had not been forced by the most powerful spiritual methods <term>machinis</term> <note>The author uses "machinis" (machines or engines of war) as a metaphor for the spiritual "artillery" of the Church, such as prayer, fasting, and the sacraments.</note>; and those they did leave, they left very unwillingly and with great reluctance. And so it has been demonstrated that demons leave their seats with difficulty.

### CHAPTER L.

*What is the cause why demons desert the humans they possess with such great difficulty?*

<margin>11.</margin> <image-desc>Ornamental initial 'D' depicting a figure seated in a landscape with a building in the distance.</image-desc> One might not incorrectly gather the cause of the demons' difficult migration from human bodies from the desire that demons have for possessing humans. They seem to depart reluctantly for the same reasons they desire to enter: because things that are possessed with pleasure are relinquished only with difficulty.

<page-num>141</page-num>
<header>CONCERNING THE POSSESSED.</header>

<margin>2.</margin>
From this it is clear that they especially retain the desire and the will to do harm within humans. For just as when entering humans it is not their purpose to obtain a remission of their own punishments, but rather to do harm; so in this difficult withdrawal of theirs, they seem to seek entirely to do harm.

<margin>3.</margin>
There are, nevertheless, some who assign *various other* causes for this difficult departure. Whether they do so correctly must be discussed. Some claim that they delay their departure because once they are expelled from humans, they cannot enter and torment those same people a second time. Others say that as soon as they are driven out, they are thrust down to Hell <note>original: "Infernum"</note>, which they violently loathe. The former group seems to rely on the foundation that once conquered by a person, they are never said to approach that same person for a second trial. The latter take their conjecture from the fact that the demons, when they were to be expelled by Christ, asked that he not command their *departure into the abyss* <note>original: "abyssum discessum"; a reference to Luke 8:31, where the demons beg Jesus not to send them into the bottomless pit.</note>.

<margin>4.</margin>
Just as the foundation of the former group is weak, their assertion is also not firm enough. Granted, the demon might not immediately return to tempt the same person by whom it was defeated; nevertheless, we gather that it does return from the fact that, although defeated by Christ, it attacked him again: unless perhaps we wish to say that it was said in vain by Luke the Evangelist (chapter 4) that *when every temptation was finished, the demon departed from the Lord for a time*.

<margin>5.</margin>
But even if a return to the same person is not granted, there may still be the ability to enter another. This is proven by the one who once tormented Artemia, the daughter of the Emperor Diocletian <note>Diocletian was a Roman Emperor (reigned 284–305 AD) known for his persecutions of Christians, though legends often involved his family members in hagiographies.</note>. For when Saint Cyriacus <note>St. Cyriacus was a 4th-century martyr; tradition holds he was a deacon who performed many exorcisms.</note>, having invoked the name of Christ, cast this spirit out, and did not assign it any other convenient home (as it had requested), the spirit, having been cast out, said: *I will compel you with trouble to come into Persia.* What happened next? Soon, the daughter of *Sapor* <note>Likely Shapur II, King of the Sasanian Empire.</note>, the Emperor of the Persians, was possessed by that same spirit. Since her father was anxious for her well-being, he learned that his daughter could be helped by the work of Cyriacus and summoned him. When Cyriacus arrived, Satan mocked him: *Did I not say,* he said, *that it would happen that you would undergo a difficult journey into Persia?* Found in Surius <margin>Volume 4.</margin> <note>Laurentius Surius was a 16th-century German monk famous for his multi-volume collection of the lives of the saints.</note>

<margin>6.</margin>
What of the fact that a demon, once cast out, sometimes returns even to the same person? The teaching of the Lord teaches this. *For when the unclean spirit,* he says, *has departed from a man, it wanders through waterless places, seeking rest; and finding none, it says: I will return to my house from which I came. And when it comes, it finds it swept clean and decorated. Then it goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and live there.* The Lord signifies the same thing in Mark 9 when he commanded the demon, just as it was about to leave, not to enter the man again. For if it could not enter again, why did he command it not to enter?

<header>PART IV. DISPUTATION.</header>
<meta>catchword: With</meta>

<margin>7.</margin>
What the Lord teaches is confirmed by examples, especially that of the person whom Saint Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a prominent mystic and abbot.</note> once cast out. The matter is as follows: while the holy man was staying in Pavia, a possessed woman was brought to him in the hope that she would be freed through Bernard’s merits and protection. But the demon soon began to insult the holy man, saying: "*You will not drive me out from my little friend, you eater of piglets and devourer of cabbages.*" <note>original: "Non me de amicula mea pelles, porculos edens, & brassicas deuorans." The demon mocks Bernard’s ascetic diet or perhaps accuses him of hypocrisy.</note> Then Bernard ordered the possessed woman to be led to the relics of Saint Syrus <note>The first Bishop of Pavia.</note>. But the spirit, becoming even more insolent, cried out: "*Syrus will not cast me out; little Bernard will not cast me out.*" When she was brought back to him, Bernard said: "*Neither Syrus nor Bernard will cast you out, but our Lord Jesus Christ.*" And turning to prayer, he cast out the impudent spirit. However, when her husband returned home, the woman was again invaded by the spirit. Therefore, the husband went back to Bernard. Once again, Bernard expelled the spirit; and lest the demon enter the woman a third time after his departure, he hung this written exorcism around the neck of the possessed woman: *In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, I command you, demon, that you do not enter this woman.* This account is found in book 2, chapter 4 of the *Life of St. Bernard*, recorded by Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a German monk famous for his multi-volume collection of the lives of the saints.</note> in Volume 4, folio 802.

<margin>8.</margin>
The example of Saul, the first King of the Jews, also serves us here. It was shown earlier that he was truly possessed at times; that the spirit actually left him for intervals is very probable, because of what is said at the end of chapter 16 <note>1 Samuel 16:23</note>: *The spirit departed from him.* And yet, it is manifest from chapter 18 that the demon returned to him, where it is said: *But after another day, an evil spirit of God invaded Saul.* Let this be sufficient evidence against the first group <note>The group mentioned on the previous page who argued that demons never return to a person once defeated.</note>.

<margin>9.</margin>
As for the second group <note>Those who argue that demons are cast directly into Hell upon exorcism.</note>, although they seem to speak with some reason, their assertion cannot be established with certainty. From where, I ask, will it be proved? Neither the judgment of the senses, nor the sacred scriptures, nor the confession of the demons themselves supports this opinion.

<margin>10.</margin>
In fact, do not the sacred scriptures clearly suggest the opposite? We know that the angel Raphael drove away a demon; however, he did not banish it into Hell, but relegated it to Egypt. <note>A reference to the Book of Tobit 8:3, where Raphael binds the demon Asmodeus in "the farthest parts of Egypt."</note> Nor do we think it matters much here whether the demon was cast out of a person or a house. In every case, a place must be assigned to the one whom Raphael cast out, just as a place is sought by those spirits who are expelled from human bodies.

<margin>11.</margin>
This is further confirmed by those demons who, when being cast out by the Lord, pleaded that they not be sent into the abyss. For if it were certain that they were to be sent into Hell <note>original: "infernum"</note> immediately after being cast out, why would they ask not to be sent? But because those who are expelled are not necessarily sent to the Underworld <note>original: "Inferos"</note>, and because they observed Christ’s supreme ease and power in the act of exorcism, they feared that He who drove them from the bodies might also drive them into Hell; they prayed specifically that He would not do this.

It refutes contemporary theories by distinguishing between being cast out of a body and being cast into the "abyss."</summary>

### CHAPTER 51.
***That certain spirits of demons are more difficult to cast out; and who they are, and from what cause this arises.***

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap "Q" featuring floral motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
Although all spirits leave human dwellings with great reluctance, there are some among them who are cast out with more difficulty than others, while some are cast out more easily. And just as it is certain that this happens, it is not as certain *who they are* who are more difficult to cast out, or for what reasons this occurs. All three of these points are to be shown in the present chapter.

<margin>2.</margin>
And first, to set aside many other examples, this is clear from the example of that demon which could not be cast out by the Apostles, even though they possessed full and supreme power over demons. For those who had already cast out many in various places labored in vain over one particular spirit, mentioned by three Evangelists (Matthew 17, Luke 9, and Mark 9).

<margin>3.</margin>
Nor is there any reason for anyone to attribute the entire cause of this difficult departure to the Apostles, as if they lacked the faith to complete the work—a faith which did not fail them when they cast other spirits out of men. For although the Lord attributes it to their unbelief that they did not cast out that demon, he nevertheless indicates that a cause also resided in the demon itself. *"This kind of demon,"* he says, *"is not cast out except by prayer and fasting."* <note>original: "Hoc genus dæmoniorum... non eijcitur nisi ieiunio & oratione."</note> In this, the Lord implies that in driving away other spirits, the Apostles had no need of fasting and prayer—the invocation of Christ’s name was enough—but in this case, they needed other aids because this kind is more difficult to drive away than others.

### PART IV. DISCUSSION.

<margin>4.</margin> Likewise, the wonder and amazement of the Jewish people confirms this. For they were not always in a state of stupor or wonder when their own sons, the Apostles, or even the Lord cast out demons. Yet, at the expulsion of certain ones, they cried out: *“Nothing like this has been seen in Israel”* (Matthew 9). <note>original: "Nihil simile visum in Israel"</note> Indeed, they even began to regard Christ as the Messiah: *“Could this,” they said, “be the son of David? The Messiah?”* (Matthew 12). <note>original: "Nunquid, inquiunt, hic est filius Dauid? Messias?"</note> This was clearly because they saw those things being cast out by the Lord which they believed could not be driven away by others.

<margin>5.</margin> But *who are those spirits?* It is difficult to define generally which among them all are those who are cast out with *greater difficulty* than the rest. Is it those of the higher <term>Orders</term> <note>In demonology, spirits were believed to be organized into hierarchies or "orders" mirroring the nine choirs of angels.</note> or the lower? Is it those who cause greater distress to others, or those who cause less? Is it those who have held their seats within humans for a long time, or those who have not been there as long? Is it those to whom a cause was given for their entry into a person, or those who torment the <term>possessed</term> <note>original: "Obsessorum," referring to those whose bodies are occupied by a demon.</note> voluntarily, without any fault on the part of the victim? Although some conjecture might seem possible to be drawn from these points, a certain rule that suffers no exception ought not to be sought from them.

<margin>6.</margin> It is likely that there are some even in the lower Orders—and not only in the higher—whose expulsion requires more labor from the <term>exorcists</term>; and that they are also sometimes those who bring less distress, and those who have not held their seats in human bodies for such a long time, and moreover, such ones to whom no cause for their tyranny was given by the possessed person.

<margin>7.</margin> For those who would say these are only of the higher Orders because they possess greater strength, do not consider that even those of the lower Orders, although unequal to the higher in strength, are still superior to all humans by whom they would be cast out. *“For there is no power,”* as Job says in chapter 41, *“of any man that can be compared with the power of any [spirit], even the smallest.”* <note>original: "Neque enim est potestas... hominis vllius...". This refers to the description of Leviathan, often interpreted as the devil.</note> But this matter is not to be measured by the strength of the spirits, because they are not permitted to rage against wretched mortals as much as they are able; a limit has been imposed upon them. Wherefore it can happen that more is sometimes permitted to some spirit of a lower Order than to another of a higher Order, and the former may be driven out with more difficulty than the latter.

<margin>8.</margin> Those who believe that only those spirits yield with difficulty who leave no rest, neither by day nor by night, to those whom they possess, are refuted by the example of that boy whom the Lord taught was difficult to expel in Matthew 17. That spirit yielded with great difficulty, yet it was not continuously troublesome to the one it possessed; sometimes it even left him, as the parent of the possessed boy testifies in the <term>Evangelists</term> <note>original: "Euangelistas," the authors of the Gospels.</note> (Mark 9 and Luke 9).

In the meantime, however, although a certain judgment does not seem possible to be sought from what has already been said; nevertheless, from one specific thing and about one kind of demon, the answer to our question can be established. From what source indeed? From the revelation of Christ. And from which kind? That one by which the <term>Lunatics</term> <note>In this period, "lunacy" (from *luna*, the moon) often referred to epilepsy or intermittent fits of madness believed to be influenced by lunar cycles.</note>, or the deaf and mute, are said to be <term>Possessed</term> <note>original: "Obsessi," the state of being physically occupied by a demonic force.</note>. This one does not yield unless pressed by prayer and fasting." Thus says <term>Tostatus</term> <note>Alonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), a prolific Spanish bishop and biblical commentator.</note> in question 127 on Matthew 17.

<margin>12.</margin>
And this certain kind of demon is designated by the Lord. The pronoun, *“This,”* provides a great argument for this. All the circumstances by which the event is described demonstrate it. For that demon had miserably twisted the boy; the father had asked the Apostles to expel it; the Apostles had tried to cast it out, but in vain; before its banishment, the Lord required the father's faith; he inquired about the duration of the torture; and he stated it could only be routed by fasting and prayer.

now [he is described as] deaf and mute. Matthew 17 speaks thus: *my son is a Lunatic.* <note>Matthew 17:15. In the original Greek and Latin, "lunatic" literally means "moon-struck."</note> But in Mark 9: *I have brought my son, who has a mute Spirit.* That he was also deaf, Christ’s exorcism confirms: *You deaf and mute Spirit,* he said, *I command you, come out of the man.* Therefore, whether you call it a "Lunatic" spirit or a "deaf and mute" Spirit, it is the same: it is certain that this kind of demon is driven out with difficulty.

<margin>15.</margin> And they are more difficult for a good reason. For what logic can you follow in driving them out? They do not wish to understand what you are saying, since they are called deaf; nor do they ever respond to questions, since they are mute. <note>Exorcists traditionally relied on command and dialogue; a demon that "could not hear" the command or "could not speak" to reveal its name was considered a tactical challenge.</note>

<margin>16.</margin> One must remember here, however, that they are called mute and deaf not because they themselves lack the ability to speak or hear, but because they deprive those whom they <term>possess</term> <note>Latin: *obsident*, literally "to besiege."</note> of these faculties. And they are called "Lunatics" because they torture more severely during certain phases and wanings of the Moon. By the former (deafness and muteness), they show the hatred with which they burn toward wretched mortals, whom they rob of their primary senses; by the latter (the moon cycles), they show their envy toward the Lord of all, God the Greatest and Best. Through this "lunatic" harassment, they desire to shift the blame for the evil they themselves cause onto God’s creations <note>The demon uses the moon's cycle as a mask, hoping the victim will blame nature or the Creator instead of the spirit.</note>, and thus either draw God into hatred among mortals or certainly make Him appear contemptible.

<margin>17.</margin> Therefore, we say that mute and deaf demons are those who are expelled with more difficulty. But is it only these? Or are there others besides them? We leave the definition of this to others. We move now to the Third point proposed for this Chapter, and we investigate the reasons for this difficult departure.

<margin>18.</margin> <term>Nicholas of Lyra</term> <note>A Franciscan teacher (c. 1270–1349) whose "Postilla" or biblical commentaries were standard reference works in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>, commenting on Mark chapter 9, attributes this to the strength and power of the Spirit: that these are cast out more difficultly than others. *For since Spirits are unequal in strength,* he says, *those equipped with greater power are more difficultly driven out of men; those with less power are driven out more easily.* However, these things do not seem to be so well said.

<margin>19.</margin> Firstly, because the strength of <term>unclean Spirits</term> <note>A common biblical term for demons.</note> is immense, surpassing all human power in many ways. And we do not wish this to be said only of those who belong to the higher <term>Orders</term> <note>Theologians classified spirits into a hierarchy or "Orders," such as Seraphim or Thrones.</note>, who surpass in strength those of the lower Orders; we wish it to be said of all of them. The least of the Spirits (of whatever Order or condition he may be) [surpasses] any mortal, even in might and strength

...and overcomes the one strong in power, [as seen in] Job 14. Therefore, if the ratio of strength must be taken into account here, the smallest demon would be ejected by any mortal with no less difficulty than the greatest.

<margin>20.</margin>
Secondly, demons are not permitted to rage against possessed mortals according to the full measure of their own strength. This is taught even by that [demon] who was driven out with difficulty by the Lord in Matthew 17. How, I ask, would he not have killed the wretched boy—whom he was then throwing into the water and fire and *prostrating on the ground*—if he had been permitted to rage as much as he wished by his own strength?

<margin>21.</margin>
Thirdly, because the <term>means</term> <note>Latin: *machinae*, literally "machines" or "engines," here referring to the ritual methods or spiritual "tools" used in exorcism.</note> used for the ejection of demons do not possess the inherent power to break the strength of demons (in the way that heat breaks the force of cold). Rather, they have power over demons only through the will of God. By that same will, the highest Spirits, outstanding in strength, are as easily conquered and ejected from humans as the weak ones whose power and authority are lesser—if God so wills it.

<margin>22.</margin>
What, then, is the cause of such a difficult departure? It is because, evidently, these *Lunatic, or deaf and mute Spirits have received greater power from God over the bodies of the possessed.* And the greater the power granted to them over bodies, the more difficult it is for them to be ejected from those bodies. According to the amount of power they receive over humans, a greater or lesser force seems necessary to drive them out. So says <term>Tostatus Abulensis</term> <note>Alonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), a famous Spanish theologian and bishop of Avila known for his massive biblical commentaries.</note> in question 172 on Matthew 17.

<margin>23.</margin>
Hence it is that the Jews wondered at and proclaimed the power of Christ more in expelling these Lunatic or mute and deaf Spirits than in any others—even more than in the restoration of the dead to life. For after he had cast out a mute demon and the mute man had spoken, the Evangelist Matthew says in chapter 9: *the crowds wondered, saying: "Never has anything like this appeared in Israel."* And in chapter 12, when he had again cast out a mute demon, they came to the opinion that they should believe he is the Messiah. *Is this not,* they say, *the son of David?* Similarly, Luke testifies in chapter 9 that *all were stunned by the majesty of God* after he cured the Lunatic mentioned in Matthew 17. And yet this amazement did not seize them when he raised the dead; they never broke out into similar exclamations. And this is the brief argument for this point.

...it can be established that [the spirits] have already left the possessed; for others, [it can be seen] that they are in the process of departing.

<margin>2.</margin> The former point is clear from one or two arguments; the latter can become known through several. There is this one argument for regained liberty: if none of those signs—which we discussed in chapters 22, 23, 24, etc.—betray a hidden Spirit, and if mortals feel or experience no further trouble or torment. The second argument is if those who were possessed signal that they have been restored to freedom.

<margin>3.</margin> For although Spirits can sometimes hide within humans and not be troublesome, as was taught in the first part of this Disputation; nevertheless, that they should produce no distress at all, or reveal themselves by no sign, either does not happen or happens very rarely. That one whom we have mentioned several times, whom the <term>Blessed Germanus</term> <note>St. Germain (c. 496–576 AD), the Bishop of Paris famous for his miracles and for whom the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés is named.</note>, Bishop of Paris, expelled, was not so troublesome to the girl he possessed; yet he revealed himself by this very fact: he would deprive the possessed girl of the use of her limbs whenever she hurried to church. Thus, if those who have been possessed indicate they are freed after the application of Exorcisms and other weapons of the Christian religion used to fight against <term>Demons</term> <note>Latin: *Dæmones*. In this context, it refers to malevolent spirits or fallen angels.</note>, their freedom is not rashly presumed.

<margin>4.</margin> *But let us examine the signs by which Demons betray their departure.* These are twofold. Some signs the Spirits give because they are forced by the Exorcists; others they give voluntarily, without being forced. Indeed, sometimes they are ordered by the adjurations of Christians to betray their departure by producing signs; sometimes, departing of their own accord, they leave signs of their departure behind. In the first category are the extinguishing of a light <note>Usually referring to a candle being blown out by a sudden spiritual wind.</note>, the breaking of some glassware, or something similar; in the second category are various other things.

<margin>5.</margin> There is truly a great deal of difference between these two types of signs. Those given under compulsion are produced according to the command of those in authority; those given voluntarily are according to the will of the Spirits themselves. Again, in the former, there is usually nothing to criticize; in the latter, there is always something that might deservedly cause displeasure. Likewise, the former are often performed by the work of the Demon alone, outside the possessed persons themselves; the latter, although they are the work of Demons, often occur in or through the possessed themselves. We are primarily concerned here with the latter.

<margin>6.</margin> And what are they? They are many and quite varied. Nor is this surprising. They proceed from a free will, which can be the cause of various and many effects. Nevertheless, from among the many, we must recount several which we have collected from historical accounts of actual events.

<margin>7.</margin> *The first is the confession of the Spirits themselves.* By this, those mentioned by the Holy Evangelist Mark in chapter 1 indicate their departure. For when...

<header>PART 4. DISPUTATION.</header>

<margin>18.</margin> ...that it was [perceived] <note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's description of a miraculous event.</note> that the unclean spirit <note>original: "immundum Spiritum"; a common term for a demon.</note> was present, *who, upon leaving, destroyed the entire wall of the palace from its foundation.*

These are the signs. However, two or three points must be added to them. First, it should not be believed that, just as we have distinguished these signs and sorted them into specific classes, they are always found so distinctly. For although some signs are found on their own, nothing prevents many (or even all) from being observed at once, testifying to the departure of a single Spirit. This is confirmed both by the many examples we have brought forward and by daily experience.

<margin>19.</margin> The second point is that a completely certain and infallible argument for the departure of demons cannot be taken from these signs alone. Just as the Spirits leave these signs behind according to their own will, they are also capable of producing them and yet retaining their seats within the humans they have possessed for some time. Regarding this, there is no doubt among the learned.

<margin>20.</margin> The third point is that these signs are not necessarily joined to the departure of Spirits; it is not as if no spirit is able to migrate from human bodies without simultaneously testifying to its departure with produced signs. Quite often they are joined to the demon's exit, but nevertheless it happens—and not rarely—that they depart with no signs of their departure left behind.

<margin>21.</margin> Nor should these things seem marvelous to anyone, because most of the signs mentioned depend upon the free will of the Spirits themselves; not only in the sense that they are able to produce other signs just as they produce these, but also that they can omit them entirely. In producing these signs, they have full liberty—as we say in the schools <note>Referring to the Scholastic tradition of university theology and philosophy.</note>—*both regarding specification and regarding the exercise of the act.* <term>Specification and exercise</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "liberty of specification" is the freedom to choose between different types of actions, while "liberty of exercise" is the freedom to choose whether to act at all.</note>

<margin>22.</margin> Hence it is that we read of Spirits being cast out many times where it could not be established by signs at their exit that they had indeed left the human bodies. Such were those cast out by <term>Tryphon of Phrygia</term> <note>A 3rd-century saint and martyr.</note>, <term>Berthulph, Abbot of Bobbio</term> <note>A 7th-century Frankish abbot.</note>, <term>Bernard of Clairvaux</term> <note>A famous 12th-century Cistercian abbot and mystic.</note>, and also <term>Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre</term> <note>A 5th-century Gaulish bishop known for fighting heresy and performing miracles.</note>, and many others of whom frequent mention has been made in this Disputation.

...there are reasons why they act, and others why they act in this or that way: so too there can be different causes and reasons; some for why unclean spirits <note>original: "Spiritus immundi"</note> give signs at their departure; others for why they give these particular signs and not others.

<margin>2.</margin>
Both types of reasons and causes must be explained by us; both so that the Disputation <term>Disputatio: a formal academic argument or treatise</term> may be more complete, and because in both cases there are matters that warrant a useful investigation. We shall begin with the former.

<margin>3.</margin>
Why then do *demons reveal their departure with certain signs?* I respond very briefly: partly because they are compelled to reveal it, and partly because they wish to reveal it of their own accord. This is clear from the distinction of signs given in the preceding Chapter. For some signs are commanded of them by Exorcists; others they give voluntarily, neither asked nor forced. In the former case, they are compelled; in the latter, their will is entirely free, and that will is the cause of the signs.

<margin>4.</margin>
But, are they so compelled in the former case that it is absolutely necessary to produce those signs? If not always, they are certainly for the most part compelled. For just as by the power of Exorcisms, and the command of Holy men, and even the use of consecrated things, a necessity is imposed upon them to leave their dwellings <note>The human body they possess</note> against their will, so too they are forced to give signs and evidence of their departure. Again, are the latter signs so free that they could omit them if they wished? They can. For they would not proceed freely from their own will unless it were in their power to stop them. What they give freely, they can freely choose not to give, or freely cease.

<margin>5.</margin>
*Furthermore, let us investigate the second matter: the causes and reasons* why they give these symbols of their departure rather than those. And here the previous distinction of signs ought to serve us. For some reasons apply to the former [commanded] signs, and others to the latter [voluntary] ones. Is this surprising? For the former are produced according to the command and will of men; the latter according to the good pleasure of the Demons. Now, different reasons and causes can move men to demand these or those signs, just as different reasons move demons to leave these or those behind.

<margin>6.</margin>
And what are the causes of the signs that are requested by men? Almost always one and the same: specifically, the desire for proof of the departure of the Spirits. For no other purpose is intended in all the signs—whatever they may be and of whatever kind men ask—than that they may be certain concerning the exit of the Spirits. Therefore, the cause of the signs, and of such-and-such specific signs, is the same.

<margin>7.</margin>
But what are the reasons for the Signs which the demons leave behind of their own will, or at least not compelled by men? I answer that they always give what is most characteristic of themselves, whatever they may ultimately give. Just as "from a bad crow comes a bad egg" <note>original: "mali corvi, malum ovum"; a proverb meaning a corrupt nature produces corrupt results</note>: although various and different reasons...

# PART IV. DISPUTATION.
<page-num>154</page-num>
<header>PART IV. DISPUTATION.</header>
<meta>Catchword: [the] word</meta>
<sig>V</sig>

...and their reasons for choosing some signs over others. This is somewhat obscure; therefore, it must be explained.

<margin>9.</margin>
We have taught above that there are various signs by which departing demons <note>original: "dæmones"</note> testify to their exit. Nevertheless, almost all of them can be reduced to four categories. Some may be called *cruel*, others *foul*, others *barbarous*, and others *slight*. The *cruel* signs are the tearing of limbs, internal pain in the bowels, the casting of bodies to the ground, and many images of death. The *foul* signs <note>original: "sordida"</note> consist of vomiting, both through the mouth and through the nose, the expulsion of filth, a sulfurous stench, and heavy odors. The *barbarous* signs are roaring, bellowing <note>original: "boatus"</note>, incoherent shouts, and other voices of beasts. The *slight* signs are the forms of certain lowly animals.

<margin>10.</margin>
And all of these, as we have said, suit the demons perfectly. The *cruel* signs suit them insofar as they are murderers, a name the Lord calls them by in John, chapter 8. The *foul* signs suit them as unclean spirits <note>original: "Spiritibus immundis"</note>, a name the same Lord gives to them in Luke 11. The *barbarous* signs suit them as lions, to which St. Peter compares them in chapter 4 <note>The author likely refers to 1 Peter 5:8, where the devil is described as a roaring lion.</note>. The *slight* signs suit them as the abject enemies of God, whose condition is most miserable by reason of their sins.

<margin>11.</margin>
Yet, in almost every individual case, the Spirits seem to have a different purpose in mind. They establish *cruel* signs out of the hatred with which they burn toward wretched mortals, and from a lust for doing harm that never leaves them. For just as they are the cause of all the miseries and troubles they bring upon possessed people <note>original: "obsessis"</note>, so they ensure that, as they depart from men, they exercise as much cruelty as they are able and permitted.

<margin>12.</margin>
They leave *foul* signs either to torment those present, or to show their detestation for the sacred things used in their casting out. For they do not only wish to be burdensome to those in whom they have their dwellings; they wish to be so to anyone among mortals who finds their banishment pleasing. Therefore, since they are sometimes unable to harm those present in any other way, they trouble them by stirring up a stench. Thus, because Holy Water <note>original: "Aqua benedicta"</note> is sometimes presented to them, they declare how much they loathe it by their own foul discharge.

<margin>13.</margin>
The *barbarous* signs are proofs of a ferocious and beastly mind toward mortals; at the same time, they wish to testify by these signs how reluctantly they leave them. For just as similar noises are sometimes made by people who are not of sound mind (even if not possessed) for similar reasons, so it is very likely they are given by demons for the same ends.

<margin>14.</margin>
The *slight* signs, unless we are mistaken, for the most part do not have their causes within the demons themselves; nor do the Spirits seem to give them so much of their own accord as they are compelled from elsewhere to give them. A significant proof of this is that to the form...

# CHAPTER 54.

->*By which way demons exit when they leave human bodies.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial Q with a floral pattern inside a square border.</image-desc>
The things which were said in Chapter 9 concerning the Way <note>original: "Via"</note> which Spirits hold in their entry into wretched mortals, serve us in this place as well, so that we may teach what path they maintain in their exit. It is probable that they either always or for the most part maintain the same route both when they enter and when they exit.

<margin>2.</margin>
Therefore, let this first be established: that there is no certain or determined path for them, nor are they so bound to any one route that they cannot desert it and hold any other whatsoever during their exit. Just as every passage <note>original: "meatus"</note> and pore of a human is a most open gate for them to enter, so it is for their exit. What of the fact that they need no passages or pores at all? They are able to penetrate the bodies themselves.

<margin>3.</margin>
If the Spirits were provided with bodies, they would require pores or passages—if not large ones, at least some through which they might insinuate themselves into bodies. But because they are devoid of bodies, they pervade places filled even with the most solid bodies as easily as those which are empty of bodies.

<margin>4.</margin>
They are able, therefore, to exit through a person’s mouth; they can exit through the nostrils, through the ears, and the other passages and pores. They can exit through any part of the human being whatsoever. Regarding those former routes, there is no difficulty; for the latter, Theodore the Archimandrite <note>An "Archimandrite" is a superior of a monastery or group of monasteries in the Eastern Christian tradition.</note> serves us as an example. When he observed a demon hiding in the arm of his doorkeeper Eutychius, he did not compel it toward the mouth or any other passage. On the contrary, lest it should reach the head or another part where the exit seems easier, he blocked its way by placing the sign of the Cross <note>original: "Crucis signo"</note> upon the shoulders. He compelled the demon to seek a way for itself to exit through the arm, just as it both sought and found. Likewise, Gregory of Tours reports concerning the *Miracles of Saint Martin* that when it was observed that a demon had descended into the thumbnail of a certain <term>energumen</term> <gloss>a person possessed by a demon</gloss>, oil taken from the tomb of Martin was poured onto the finger, and the skin having been broken, the demon departed along with the blood. Thus says Gregory of Tours in chapter 9 of *The Glory of the Confessors*.

<margin>5.</margin>
Nevertheless, while they are able to have and hold many ways in their exit from human bodies, they seem to observe two primary ones; although one of these is more suitable to them as unclean Spirits <note>original: "Spiritibus immundis"</note>, the other is nonetheless more common.

<margin>6.</margin>
The former seems to have belonged to those Spirits who, having left a heavy stench behind them—

<header>PART IV. DISPUTATION.</header>

...and thus they deserted their dwellings, many of which we reviewed in Chapter 52. Gregory of Tours <note>A 6th-century bishop and historian known for his writings on miracles.</note> expressly testifies to this in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 9: that after the head of a certain possessed person <note>original: "Energumeni," a term derived from Greek meaning someone "worked upon" by an external spirit.</note> was anointed with oil taken from the tomb of Saint Martin, the demon suddenly exited through a purging of the bowels <note>original: "per fluxum ventris"</note>. This latter type of exit was common to many others, but especially to three specific types: First, to those who gave signs of their departure in the mouth of the possessed by manifesting small creatures, such as ants, flies, or spiders. Second, to those whose departure was betrayed by a swelling of the throat or neck of the possessed person themselves. Third, to those who departed with foul and filthy vomiting. Examples of these were given in that same Chapter 52.

<margin>7.</margin> These things we have said are probable; nevertheless, they are not so certain that it would be reckless to assert the contrary. For these latter spirits can also give signs of their departure in or around the mouth of the possessed and yet exit by another way. And the former spirits can leave a stench behind them and fly out through the mouth. But as we have said, the points we bring forward have the appearance of probability, not the necessity of absolute truth.

### CHAPTER LV.

#### *Whether all exit at the same time, if ever there were many who*
#### *possessed a single human being, and are forced to depart.*

<margin>1.</margin> The question of the previous chapter was perhaps more a matter of curiosity; this one seems more useful. For since it is established that many spirits are sometimes within one person, if they do not all depart at once when commanded <note>original: "adiurati," meaning under oath or solemn command in an exorcism.</note>, exorcists <note>Priests or practitioners trained to drive out evil spirits.</note> may easily understand that they have not yet obtained a full victory over the enemy. This is the case even when they have great and manifest signs of the departure of some; they must progress further and not cease until they have cast out the last one, if they wish perfect health and safety to be restored to the afflicted mortals.

<margin>2.</margin> Unless, perhaps, we wish to say that such is the power and virtue of the spiritual engines <note>original: "machinarum," referring to the rites, prayers, and sacred tools of exorcism.</note> by which the Spirits are cast out of their dwellings; that although they might be able and willing of their own accord to depart sometimes all together, and sometimes some without the others, nevertheless a necessity is then incumbent upon them to depart all at once when they are attacked by these engines. But who would assert this?

<margin>3.</margin> What, then, is the answer to the proposed question? It is this: *The spirits do not always exit at the same time when they exit of their own accord, without being forced or when only lightly tested; nor do they always exit together when they are urged on by even more grievous torments.*

<margin>4.</margin> The first point is clear from the condition of the Spirits themselves. This condition is entirely free. One does not depend on another, either in how things happen or how they ought to happen. Each is able to exist by himself. Each is able to act by himself. Therefore, one can leave the human he possesses by his own will, even though another is unwilling to cease from his vexation of the same person.

<margin>5.</margin>
Furthermore, regarding the departure of spirits from humans, the logic is no different than that of their entry. It is not necessary for all to enter *at the same time*. One can invite another into fellowship, or receive another into the dwelling, as the Lord clearly suggests in Matthew 12 <note>Original: Matth. 12. This refers to the parable where an unclean spirit returns to a "swept and put in order" house bringing seven other spirits more wicked than itself.</note>. Therefore, some of these can depart from mortals while others persist within them, continuing to cause distress.

<margin>6.</margin>
If we consider the varying strengths of spirits, it will also be quite consistent with reason to say what we are saying. Their powers are not all equal; some are more robust than others. Therefore, these higher spirits can drive the lower ones from their seats even against their will—and although they may not always do so (as seen in Luke 11 <note>Original: Lucæ 11. A reference to the "strong man armed" who keeps his palace until a "stronger than he" arrives.</note>), they certainly have the power to do it.

<margin>7.</margin>
It is also certain that one spirit may yield to the command and will of another. We brought forward many arguments for this in the sixteenth chapter. If they indeed yield to the will and command of one who is outside the <term>possessed person</term> <note>original: "Obsessum," a person whose body is occupied by a demonic presence.</note>, who is to say one would not yield to the will of others who possess the same human being at the same time?

<margin>8.</margin>
Otherwise, *one might perhaps doubt whether all depart at once when they are tested by <term>exorcisms</term> <note>Ritual prayers and commands used by the Church to expel evil spirits.</note> or other weapons with which Christians fight against them. This is because we sometimes read (unless we are mistaken) that they were cast out by Holy men; and we read of them all being cast out together.* Yet, even here, it is not necessary to admit that all are forced to depart at the same time.

<margin>9.</margin>
*The first reason for this is taken from the unequal power of demons over men. For while many can be in one and the same person, their power over the possessed is not equal; thus, those who have lesser power could be cast out, while those who have greater power might retain their seats.*

<margin>10.</margin>
*The second reason is taken from the "engines" <note>original: "machinis," used here metaphorically to mean the methods or spiritual tools used for expulsion.</note> by which those to be expelled are defeated. For not all spirits are subject to all things. Even in the age of Christ and the Apostles, the invoked name of Jesus served to drive out certain spirits; for others, that name alone did not have the power, as is shown by the case of the "Lunatic" <note>original: "Lunaticus," referring to the boy in Matthew 17 and Mark 9 whom the disciples could not heal; Jesus told them that "this kind" only comes out through prayer and fasting.</note> whom we have mentioned several times. What if, therefore, the name of Jesus is applied to some, but those things which the Lord teaches are required—fasting and prayer—are not? Some of both kinds of spirits may lie hidden in a person. Will not the former then change their seats (depart), while the latter retain them?*

<margin>11.</margin>
*The third reason is supplied by the condition of the exorcists.* We said in chapter thirty-eight that many things are necessary for them if they wish to perform their office well. But some of these qualities may be lacking in them; some, although present, could be made more perfect; and some, even if perfect, must be repeated if the desired effects are to be obtained. It can therefore happen,

<header>PART 4. DISPUTATION.</header>

It can happen that some flee when exorcisms are attempted even lightly, or attempted only once; others do not depart unless those same rites are repeated over and over.

<margin>§2.</margin>
Experience observed in our own age confirms all these things. For it has been noted not rarely that certain spirits have departed, leaving behind specific signs; others have kept their seats in the same men; and these very spirits later, when tested by more powerful means <note>original: "gravioribus machinis," literally "heavier engines," a metaphor for more intensive or frequent spiritual rituals used by the exorcist.</note>, went out once the signs were given. I pass over the confession of demons, who have occasionally provided evidence for this matter.

<margin>§3.</margin>
Since these things are so, exorcists do no wrong when, about to engage with demons, they first inquire how many of them there are who afflict the wretched person, and seek out the names of each individual, or at least the principal leaders; they do not finish the exorcising before victory has been won over every single one. For in this way, full liberty is restored to mortals. In this way, all harassment from demons ceases. In this way, it is understood that their labor and exhaustion were not in vain.

<margin>§4.</margin>
However, although it is not always necessary for all to depart at the same time when they are pressed by the weapons of the Christian religion, which are contrary to them; nevertheless, we seem to gather from three points that they usually depart together. *First*, from the fact that we read that holy men—about whose <term>Spirit-Battles</term> <note>original: "Daemonomachia," a Greek-derived term used in ecclesiastical history to describe the struggle between saints and demons.</note> annals exist—used either a single exorcism or some other method in the healing of any <term>possessed persons</term> <note>original: "Daemoniacorum," refers to people whose bodies are occupied by demons.</note>. The *second* point is that we read either never or very rarely that one or another demon was cast out from a person while in the meantime others remained stuck in the same person. The *third* is that the "engines" <note>original: "machinae," referring here to the prayers and rituals of the Church.</note> with which the demons are tested are all loathsome to them; and because of that, if they put one to flight, it is likely that all are put to flight.

### *To what place spirits of demons tend when they are cast out from men.*

<margin>1.</margin>

In the second place are beasts and cattle that serve human needs. An example of this is provided by the herd of swine, into which an entire legion of expelled spirits was permitted to enter; these spirits then, having made a great charge, drove the herd headlong into the sea to the great loss of their owners. This is found in Matthew 8. <note>In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus casts out demons who then beg to enter a herd of pigs.</note>

Third are cultivated places, suitable for human use and inhabited by them. For just as there is no doubt that some demons take pleasure in the company of mortals and even enter some of them, so it may be believed that some who have gone out from humans seek human society again. This same legion of demons serves as an example here, which begged *that it not be sent away from the region in which it was staying*. <note>original: "ne extra regionem, in qua versabatur, mitteretur." Refers to Mark 5:10.</note> Furthermore, the Disputation on Infested Places <note>The author is likely referencing his own previous or upcoming section on "haunted" locations.</note> provides many more examples here.

The fourth place is the upper air, which God the Best and Greatest has assigned to some until the day of final judgment for the purpose of testing humanity. Just as many spirits, by God’s permission, enter humans from this air, so too, when ejected from humans, they return to this place as if to their own assigned and proper domain.

The fifth place is *solitude or the wilderness*: Here the demon had its seat which brought death to the men who sought to sleep with Sarah, as described in Tobit, Chapter 8. <note>Reference to the demon Asmodeus in the Book of Tobit, who killed the husbands of Sarah on their wedding nights until he was driven away by Tobias.</note> And there is more concerning this place in that Disputation on Infested Places.

Finally, the sixth place is *Hell* <note>original: "infernus"</note>, which the Lord said was *prepared for the devil and his angels*. Matthew 25. Those who pleaded against the *Abyss* <note>original: "Abyssus"</note> begged that they not be sent here. Matthew 8. For although, as <term>Jansenius</term> <note>Cornelius Jansen (1510–1576), a Dutch theologian known for his "Harmony of the Gospels" (Concordia Evangelica).</note> well notes in chapter 31 of his *Gospel Harmony*, *Abyss* properly signifies a depth of waters, it is nevertheless sometimes used (especially in the New Testament) for Hell; this is because it is beneath the earth, swallowing up the damned dead in such a way that they cannot emerge from there. It is understood in this sense in Romans 10, and Revelation 9, 11, 17, and 20.

There is a great and manifold difference between these places: but what must be considered here is the pleasure and difficulty which the spirits ejected from humans find in them, which we must now discuss.

Regarding those *first* places, therefore, the <term>shape-shifters</term> <note>original: "versipelles," literally "skin-turners," a term for demons or deceptive people who can change their appearance or character.</note> turn to them most willingly. Nowhere do they perceive greater pleasure than in these. And it is no wonder, because they easily achieve their wicked intent here—namely, the harming of humans—which they bring partly to bodies and partly to souls when they have their seats within men.

Indeed, in this kind of dwelling, they seem to have more experience with the impious or evil men than with the good. Unless, perhaps, the condition of the impious is such that their salvation is entirely despaired of. For although they harm men...

<margin>11.</margin> After human bodies, they prefer *beasts and cattle* that serve human needs in the remaining places. They do this not so much to bring trouble to the beasts, but to bring loss to the humans who own them. Wherever they can more greatly inconvenience mortals, their residence is more pleasing to them, because their primary thoughts are to inconvenience mortals. Hence, those whom the Lord cast out of a man in Matthew 8, because they had no hope of being sent back into men once ejected, begged that they might be allowed to enter the pigs—and they obtained it.

<margin>12.</margin> But if habitation in the aforementioned places is denied, they ask that they may at least be permitted to be and dwell *among men*. The same ones cast out by the Lord, mentioned above, teach this. For what other reason did they ask to be sent into that region? <note>original: "ob regionem mitterentur rogarunt"</note> And the wicked ones dwell more willingly in those places where they once gave evidence of their wickedness, and where hope shines for what they might be able to achieve—such as places inhabited by humans.

<margin>13.</margin> What if no place is given to them even among men? They will choose *vast solitudes* <note>original: "vastas solitudines"</note> above the rest. For they do not shrink from these as they do from the air or from hell, places destined for them by the will of God, whom they hate. Both the air and hell are a kind of cross and torment to them, although hell is the greater.

<margin>14.</margin> And just as the demons either desire these places or choose them above others, so above all things they detest, flee, and dread the *Abyss, or Hell*. This fact is clear from their own confession in Matthew 8. But why? Is it because, being shut up in hell, they cannot inconvenience the living? Is it because they endure no punishments outside of hell, but must undergo them as soon as they are bound in hell? Is it because their punishments are greater and heavier in hell than outside it? Is it because once sent into hell, they never have the opportunity of returning from there? We shall discuss these causes in the following chapter.
