<meta>catchword: abundantly</meta>

Whether one or more of these reasons hold weight is a matter of curious, yet perhaps fruitful, debate. To some, it appears that demons are deprived of some good: for instance, they flee Hell because they would be unable to satisfy their lust <note>original: "libidini"; here referring to a malicious drive or craving to do harm</note> for harming humanity, or because they are deprived of their freedom to wander by the necessity of an infernal prison. To others, they seem to be afflicted by an active evil, such as the punishments they must undergo, or the increase of those punishments added to their previous ones.

<margin>3.</margin>
There are those who wish all the stated causes to be valid for these Spirits. Others accept not all, but several; some fewer, some more. We shall define the matter as it stands with a few Assertions. <term>Assertion: A formal statement or proposition put forward for academic or theological defense.</term>

<margin>4.</margin>
Those who believe that demons dread and shudder at Hell *because they cannot satisfy their lust for vexing human beings* think correctly. This is the first Assertion. The reason for this is manifest: Hell was destined for them not so they might do harm there, but so they might pay the penalties they have earned. Therefore, since they take no small pleasure in the torment of men, and are deprived of it when they are shut up in Hell, they cannot help but hate Hell as much as they possess a desire and pleasure for harming humanity.

<margin>5.</margin>
However, not all power to torture mortals is taken away once they are confined to Hell. Only that power which they hold over the living is removed. Meanwhile, regarding the power by which they can rage against the damned, it is so far from being taken away that it is believed they then begin to rage even more atrociously against those miserable souls. For demons are not thrust back into Hell only to suffer, but also to be ministers of divine justice and the torturers of damned men; they occupy these places for that purpose now.

<margin>6.</margin>
Secondly, we believe those think correctly who believe demons shudder at Hell because of the loss of a certain benefit when they are confined to the infernal prison. And what is that? *That the freedom of wandering is taken away from them.* There is no doubt that all created things enjoy the liberty for which they were naturally suited; and even more so those which obtained more excellent natural endowments than the rest. This matter is very clear by an examination of all things. But Spirits excel all others in natural dignity. Therefore, they will be, above all, the greatest lovers of liberty. Now, the Spirits of Demons are deprived of this when they are shut up in the prisons of Hell. They cannot, therefore, help but hate and detest them.

<margin>7.</margin>
Let this be the third Assertion. They err who say that Hell is a horror to demons *because they must sustain the punishments there which they long ago deserved*, from which they are free while situated outside of Hell. Wherever these miserable beings are—whether in the air, in the wilderness, in cattle, in men, or even in heaven itself if they were permitted to return there—they are most miserable. They always carry their own tormenting fire with them. Because this...

<page-num>162</page-num>
<header>PART IV. DISPUTATION.</header>

Since the disputation on Haunted Places <term>Haunted Places: Locations believed to be inhabited or disturbed by spirits, often discussed in demonology as 'loca infesta'.</term> teaches this more abundantly, it is not necessary to pursue it further here.

<margin>8.</margin>
From this it is clear that those who wish the punishments of demons to be suspended until the final day of the general judgment are in grave error. Although there were once men of no small learning who held this opinion, in our times that opinion is not defended without a serious risk of heresy. It is now the sense and consensus of all who think rightly that immediately after the sin committed by the wicked Spirits, their various punishments were decreed by God and endured by those wretched beings.

<margin>9.</margin>
Nevertheless (which is the fourth Assertion), although the demons have always suffered and do suffer the punishment they once earned, in whatever place they may be, there is no doubt that *their torment is increased by the prison of Hell*; and because of this addition to their pains, Hell is hateful to them.

<margin>10.</margin>
Theologians call this an *accidental punishment*: *just as the former, which is owed to their sins, is called essential*. For this is not properly owed to their sins as that *essential* one is, but follows from the condition of those wretched beings; it arises from the fact that, being shut up in Hell, they are deprived of the ability to wander and are unable to satisfy their lust <note>original: "libidini"; here referring to a malicious drive or craving to do harm</note> with which they desire to harm humanity (which is grievous to them). And thus far concerning places.

---

## CHAPTER LVIII.

->*Is it permissible to comply with the wish and desire of demons when, as they are about to depart from human bodies, they ask for something?*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
Demons departing [a body] sometimes have something to ask. To omit everyday occurrences, this is clear from the example of the several thousand who are read to have requested of the Lord, when they were just about to be cast out, that they not be sent outside the region of the Gerasenes <note>original: "Gerasenorum"; referring to the biblical account in Mark 5 and Luke 8 where a legion of demons is cast into a herd of swine.</note>, and that they be allowed to enter into the pigs.

<margin>2.</margin>
Hence the question arises: *Whether their desire can be satisfied if they ask for something upon departing.* Christ’s example seems to suggest that sometimes it can; yet their supreme and tireless zeal for doing harm suggests the contrary.

<margin>3.</margin>
The matter, if we are not mistaken, stands thus: *If what they ask is not unjust, the petition can be satisfied; if otherwise, it cannot.* The former occurs in three ways. For they either ask that no evil be brought upon them, or that they not be deprived of some good they possess, or that they might obtain some new good. The latter contains two kinds of things: those which wound the honor of God, and others [which we shall begin].

<margin>4</margin>
The petition of the Demons should never be satisfied if they ask for anything that wounds the honor or glory of God. Nothing is to be preferred to the honor of God, even if the wicked Spirits are not thought likely to depart from the person,

<meta>catchword: unless</meta>

<summary>This page argues that demons suffer immediate "essential" punishment for their fall, but face "accidental" torment when confined to Hell because it restricts their ability to harm humans. It also begins a discussion on whether an exorcist can grant a demon's request during its departure, citing the biblical precedent of the Gerasene swine.</summary>

<keywords>demonic punishment, essential vs accidental pain, Hell as prison, Gerasene demoniac, exorcism ethics, divine honor, Haunted Places</keywords>

--- Page 206 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the treatment of demons during the rite of exorcism, specifically whether an exorcist should ever grant the requests or petitions made by the spirits they are attempting to cast out.</meta>

<page-num>163</page-num>
<header>->ON THE POSSESSED.<-</header>

<margin>5.</margin>
Unless their petition is satisfied in this matter, the petition must not be granted. Thus, if they should ask for anything that would hinder the salvation of one's neighbors, they are not to be heard. After the honor of God, we can hold nothing more prior than the friendship of God and our own salvation. Therefore, if the loss of even one person’s salvation must occur—even if the safety and peace of the entire world were expected through the works of demons—one must not acquiesce to the demons.

<margin>6.</margin>
When they request not to be burdened with new evils—specifically, that they, wretched as they are, should not be thrust down into hell—one may acquiesce to the petition. Exorcists <term>Exorcists: Clerics or individuals authorized by the Church to perform the rite of driving out demons.</term>, that is, are able to choose not to banish them into hell, whom they would have the power to banish by the authority divinely given to them, if they so willed. Why is this a wonder? If exorcists are without sin when they do not cast demons out of possessed men, they will not be guilty of a crime if, when they do cast them out, they do not send them back to the lower regions.

<margin>7.</margin>
If they should ask not to be deprived of a "good" which they possess, they may sometimes be heard. The example of Christ supports us here. Certain spirits asked Him <note>original: "Rogabāt eum quidam"; referring to the 'Legion' of demons</note> that they not be driven out of the region of the Gerasenes <note>A region mentioned in the Gospels where Jesus cast out demons into a herd of swine.</note>, which they held as if in possession. Nor were they driven out by the Lord. Perhaps there was no good for them in that region? Why then do they ask not to be driven out? Just as different demons delight in different vices, so too are different spirits attached to different regions: especially those in which they have a perspective on the habits of men through long custom, and where they have a greater hope and opportunity for doing harm.

<margin>8.
Job 1.
1 Cor. 5.
1 Tim. 1.
</margin>
What of the fact that if they should ask for some "good," they might sometimes obtain it? A certain "good" for them is the vexation and torture of men; this can sometimes be granted to them when they ask. Was it not granted to one who asked God <note>Satan in the Book of Job</note> that he might afflict Job? Add to this that the Apostle Paul handed over a certain Corinthian to a demon; he also handed over Alexander and Hymenaeus <note>Biblical figures mentioned in 1 Timothy 1:20 whom Paul "delivered to Satan" so they might learn not to blaspheme.</note>. Can an Apostle command a demon to enter men, and yet, when a demon asks to enter a man as it is being expelled, can the Apostle not grant the permission?

<margin>9.</margin>
Nevertheless, great caution is needed here. Many things must be observed by Exorcists in this granting of permission. One must not easily acquiesce to the petition of demons here. It is necessary that, if the power to enter anyone is to be conferred, they must deserve it by their own works; and it must be someone upon whom, due to their demerits, heavy punishments should be taken, just as the Apostle taught by his own example regarding Alexander, Hymenaeus, and the Corinthian.

<margin>10.</margin>
Nor is this enough. It is also necessary that those who perform the office of Exorcists have command and legal right over those whom they hand over to the demon, so that by reason of their office they have both the power and the strength to inflict punishment. Such was the case with Eloquius, Bishop of Noyon <note>Commonly known as Saint Eligius or Saint Eloi (c. 588–660), a goldsmith and bishop.</note>, who granted fifty of his subjects the power to be raged against by demons because they would not abstain from impious and sacrilegious rites, as Ouen <note>Saint Audoenus, who wrote the "Life of St. Eligius."</note> testifies in his *Life*, chapter 20.

<meta>catchword: Must</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the ethics of exorcism, arguing that while demons' requests should generally be denied, exorcists may occasionally grant them permission to remain in a region or afflict certain individuals if those individuals are being divinely punished for their sins.</summary>

<page-num>164</page-num>
<header>PART IV. ON THE DISPOSITION OF DEMONS</header>

<margin>11.</margin> There must also be proposed here the hope of a greater good: namely, that those who did not seem able to be helped by other means may be believed to be helped through this; and that the spirit may be saved while the demons rage against the body. This same hope was proposed in the <term>Eulogy: Likely referring to a specific hagiographic account or saintly life previously mentioned in the text.</term> of which we spoke. Hence, when he was asked, he did not immediately relax this punishment:
> Let them learn first, he said, whom they have chosen to serve, before they are released from the tyranny of the demon. <note>original: "Discant, inquit, prius, cui seruire elegerunt, antequam à tyrannide Daemonis absoluantur."</note>
The same hope was proposed by Saint Paul, as his own words show:
> Whom (understand here Hymenaeus and Alexander) he handed over to Satan, he said, so that they may learn not to blaspheme. <note>original: "Quos... tradidit Satanae... vt discant non blasphemare." Referring to 1 Timothy 1:20.</note> Likewise (in 1 Corinthians 5) he delivered the Corinthian to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

<margin>12.</margin> There must also be an absence of any desire to please the demons. One must not gratify them here as if they were friends; rather, they are to be used as <term>lictors: Civil officers in ancient Rome who carried out the sentences of magistrates, often acting as executioners.</term> and executioners. Although it is pleasing to them to cause harm, it is troublesome for them to cause harm according to the command and will of men. Therefore, one does not serve the malice of demons here; rather, their malice and their eagerness to do harm serves us.

<margin>13.</margin> I would add to this that this power is not to be given to demons except by those who hold the highest right over them and can drive them out of human bodies whenever they please. The Sacred Scriptures teach that Saint Paul possessed such power, and the very facts of the "Eulogy," which we have now mentioned for a second time, show the same. Indeed, after the just punishment was taken from his own people, he offered them holy water; once they had taken it, the spirits soon departed. Because this right is granted to few in this time, I would think that the petition of demons in this matter ought to be satisfied most sparingly.

<margin>14.</margin> Furthermore, although we are able to satisfy their desires in certain cases, as has been said, we are in no way bound to do so, even if they ask for things that are for the benefit of the person. A certain noblewoman once brought a possessed servant to Theodore the <term>Archimandrite: A title in Eastern Christianity for the superior of a monastery or group of monasteries.</term> and asked him to drive out the demon. Theodore immediately commanded that the demon not move from its place. What did the demon do? With loud cries, it shouted that it was being tortured and begged for the opportunity to depart. Did it obtain its wish? It did not obtain it until it seemed right to Theodore. So says George the Priest in the *Life of Theodore* found in <term>Surius: Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a German monk and hagiographer famous for his multi-volume collection of the lives of the saints.</term>, Volume 2.

# THE FIRST PART OF THE DISPUTATION ON HAUNTED PLACES.
<note>original: "DE LOCIS INFESTIS"</note>

## IN WHICH THE TYPES, MANNERS, PURPOSES, CAUSES, AND SIMILAR MATTERS OF THE PLACES THEMSELVES, THE SPIRITS, AND THE DISTURBANCES BROUGHT UPON HAUNTED PLACES ARE INVESTIGATED, EXAMINED, AND EXPLAINED.

### <term>INTRODUCTION: From the Greek word *eisagoge*, meaning an introductory manual or primer.</term> TO THE FIRST PART OF THE DISPUTATION, CONCERNING HAUNTED PLACES.

<image-desc>A large woodcut ornamental initial 'A' featuring intricate floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>

The subject of the present Disputation requires the definition of three points. First, it must be demonstrated that there are certain places haunted by <term>Spirits and Ghosts: The author distinguishes between 'Spiritibus' (spirits/demons) and 'Spectris' (apparitions or ghosts of the deceased).</term>. <note>original: "Spiritibus & Spectris infesta"</note> Second, the reasons by which the status and condition of such spirits become known must be assigned. Third, a method must be prescribed that can be followed in driving out spirits of this kind and in cleansing those places of them. Most of these matters could be understood by the more learned from what has been said elsewhere concerning spirits and the <term>Possessed: Those suffering from 'Demoniacis,' or direct demonic control of the body.</term>; however, because not everyone possesses the same sharpness of intellect, and some matters here present a singular difficulty, I will gladly—

<margin>2.</margin> Furthermore, the first Chapter requires the explanation of three things that are mentioned in the title: the **places** that are haunted; the **Spirits** who do the haunting; and the **troubles and difficulties** which are brought upon people in Haunted Places by those haunting Spirits.

# CHAPTER 1.

## *It is taught through various examples, from nearly all times and places, that certain locations are haunted by Specters and Spirits.*

<margin>1.</margin>
There is no doubt that certain places are haunted by Specters and Spirits. The history of past deeds declares and confirms this fact with excellent examples. We omit recent and everyday accounts and put forward some from former times, which for that reason ought to have greater weight here: because they are very numerous, they have approved authors, they occurred in various and widely separated places and times, and they are confirmed by the opinions of both Pagans and Christians.

<margin>2.</margin>
Blessed Augustine relates that the house of a certain Hesperius, a man of Tribunitian rank <note>A "vir tribunitius" was a high-ranking Roman official or veteran officer.</note>, was greatly troubled by Spirits. We include his own words. "A man of Tribunitian rank," says Augustine, "named Hesperius, who is among us, has an estate in the territory of Fussala <note>Fussala was a town in North Africa near Hippo, where Augustine was Bishop.</note> called Cubedi; where, when he discovered through the suffering of his animals and servants that his house was enduring the harmful violence of malignant Spirits, he asked our priests, while I was away, if one of them would go there, so that the spirits might yield to his prayers. One went; he offered there the sacrifice of the Body of Christ <note>original: "sacrificium Corporis Christi" — referring to the celebration of the Mass.</note>, praying as much as he could that the affliction might cease: and by God's immediate mercy, it did cease. He had, moreover, received from a friend some holy earth brought from Jerusalem, where Christ, having been buried, rose on the third day; and he had hung it in his bedroom, lest he himself should suffer any evil." Blessed Augustine writes this in Book 22 of *The City of God*, chapter 8.

<margin>3.</margin>
In the Baths of Angulus <note>original: "Thermis Angularibus" — likely referring to the ancient baths at Angulus in Italy.</note>, Blessed Gregory recounts that the Spirit of a certain Paschasius was seen and encountered by Germanus, the Bishop of Capua. Having entered the Baths, he found the Deacon Paschasius serving in the heat. The man of the Lord, Germanus, did what he was asked; and returning after a few days,

# ON HAUNTED PLACES

...he did not find the aforementioned Paschasius <note>original: "Paschasium." Paschasius was a deacon who, according to Gregory's *Dialogues*, was seen performing penance after death by serving in the baths at Angulus.</note> in that same place. Thus writes **St. Gregory** <note>Pope Gregory I (c. 540–604), known as Gregory the Great.</note> in book 4 of his *Dialogues*, chapter 39. Gregory provides another example similar to this, which he claims to have received from Felix, the Bishop of Porto. In his *Life* <note>Referring to the biography of St. Gregory the Great written by John the Deacon.</note>, one also reads that a certain Spirit made its home behind the apse of the oratory where Gregory was accustomed to celebrate praises to God. This same spirit frequently disturbed the holy man while he was intent on prayer with untimely attacks: it led horses out of the stable and drove two of them headlong <note>Presumably over a cliff or into a pit.</note>; and it attempted to scratch religious men of the same profession as St. Gregory, appearing sometimes in the form of a cat, and at other times attacking them with a spear under the guise of an Ethiopian <note>In the religious literature of this era, demons were frequently depicted as "Ethiopians" or dark-skinned men to symbolize the "darkness" of sin and the underworld.</note>. So says John the Deacon in his *Life of Gregory*, book 4, chapter 89.

<margin>4.</margin>
Another Gregory, known as Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century theologian and Bishop of Nyssa.</note>, mentions haunted baths in his *Life of Gregory of Neocaesarea* <note>Gregory of Neocaesarea (c. 213–270 AD), also known as "The Miracle-Worker."</note>. He teaches that the Specters present there brought many evils; and no one who entered those baths at night ever came out alive in the morning, except for the Deacon of Gregory of Neocaesarea, who was protected by the sign of the cross and suffered no harm. We record the event in Gregory’s own words. "When the Deacon," he says, "had entered the city in the evening, he was weary from the journey and deemed it necessary to refresh his body with a bath. In that place, however, a certain homicidal Demon held dominion, dwelling in the bathhouse; its deadly power operated after dark against those who approached. For that reason, there was no access to it after sunset, nor was it used then. When he [the Deacon] approached it, he asked the man in charge to open it for him and not to begrudge him the use of the bath to refresh himself. But the keeper testified that none of those who dared to enter at that hour had returned on their own feet, but that the Demon had overcome everyone in the evening; many, through ignorance, had suffered the most grievous things, receiving lamentations, wailing, and graves instead of the hoped-for recreation. When he reported these things and others of this kind, the Deacon did not diminish his desire in the least, but insisted entirely, forcing him to let him in. The keeper, thinking it enough of a gain if he did not share in the danger alongside his guest's ignorance, gave him the key and withdrew far from the bath. Once he was undressed inside, manifold terrors and various ways of causing stupefaction were prepared by the Demon: namely, visions of every kind, showing a nature mixed with fire and smoke, which rushed before his eyes and rang in his ears in the forms of men and wild beasts, drawing near to his breath and pouring around his body in a circle. But he, fortifying himself with the sign of the Cross and invoking the name of Christ, passed through the chambers unharmed. Having progressed further inside, he fell upon even more terrible sights, the Demon having transformed into a more hideous appearance. For at the same time, with an earthquake appearing—"

Therefore, when the man of God, Parthenius, learned of this and was asked by them, he came to the workshop with a ready and cheerful heart. Having summoned the unclean demon at work and invoked the terrible and holy name of Christ, he made him vanish from all the boundaries. The demon cried out in everyone’s hearing: "I am driven out by fire into the Gehenna <note>A term for hell or a place of fiery torment.</note> of fire!" When the Saint gave the order, the dyers filled the cauldrons and, in his presence, put in the wool. From that time forward, it received the proper dye without any hindrance. Thus, both the public officials and all the dyers were freed from the danger of the Emperor <note>Failure to fulfill an imperial contract for purple dye could result in severe punishment or execution by the state.</note>. So says Metaphrastes.

<margin>7.</margin> In the time of the Emperor Anastasius, Glycas <note>Michael Glykas was a 12th-century Byzantine historian and theologian.</note> writes as follows in Part 4. In those times there was Coades, King of the Persians; when he had learned of gems of great value in a certain castle, and was prevented from obtaining them by the **spirits** <note>original: *Genijs* — local guardian spirits or demons</note> inhabiting the place, he employed every kind of sorcery. For he summoned and used both Jews and various others; yet none of them were able to achieve anything. At last, the **Bishop** <note>original: *Antistes* — a term for a high-ranking priest or bishop</note> of that place drove out the Demon with the sign of the Cross alone. Thus says Glycas.

<margin>8.</margin> In the time of the Emperor Romanos Argyropolos, in the province of Thrace, at the foot of Mount Cuzena, *a voice with miserable wailing and lamentations, heard from the month of March*, first indicated the presence of Spirits; later it even portended the slaughter of the Romans in Coele-Syria. Cedrenus <note>George Kedrenos, a 11th-century chronicler who compiled a "Synopsis of Histories."</note> records this, and after him John Kyriotes <note>The text refers to John Skylitzes, known by the title *Curopalates*, a high-ranking official and historian.</note>, in the *History of the Greek Emperors*.

<margin>9.</margin> Pliny writes in Book 7, Epistle 27, that there was a house in Athens in which *a huge and emaciated shadow, with the clanking of chains with which it seemed to be bound, filled the house itself.* Because of this, since no one dared to inhabit the house, the rent was reduced to a tiny price. But Athenodorus <note>Athenodorus Cananites, a Stoic philosopher and friend of Augustus.</note>, having set out for Athens, rented the house. Having observed the shadow, he boldly followed it: when he saw the place where it ceased to appear, he dug up the ground, and there found a body in chains, similar to the shadow that had appeared; once the corpse was removed, it freed the house from the horror. Fulgosus <note>Battista Fregoso, author of "Factorum et dictorum memorabilium."</note> mentions this in Book 1, chapter 6. We relate this example at length in Pliny's own words in Chapter 86 of the present Disputation.

<margin>10.</margin> A certain Pythagorean named Arignotus reports in Lucian's *The Lover of Lies* <note>original: *Philopseude* — a satirical dialogue by Lucian of Samosata mocking superstitious beliefs.</note> that something similar happened in Corinth, in the house of Eubatides. It was uninhabitable because of terrors: so much so that if anyone lived there, they would suddenly flee in fright. Thus it had already fallen into decay, and the roof was breaking. There was no one who dared to enter. Arignotus, hearing these things and armed with incantations and chants, entered the house to drive out the Shadow, should it appear. While he sat silently in the vast atrium reading by lamplight, a squalid, hairy Demon appeared, blacker than darkness: it tried by any means to terrify and overcome him: and it turned itself now into a dog, now into a bull, and now into a lion. Arignotus was not moved by any of these things: but taking up a chant, he drove the Spirit into a certain dark corner of the dwelling, where it soon vanished. In the morning, taking up shovels, he ordered the place to be dug up where he had observed the Spirit hiding itself during the night; the corpse of a deceased man was found, which, once exhumed and given proper burial, all infestation left the house. Thus says Arignotus in Lucian.

The story goes, he says, that a Byzantine maiden of noble parentage named Cleonice—whom Pausanias <note>Pausanias was a 5th-century BC Spartan regent and general who was later accused of conspiring with the Persians.</note> had summoned for the purpose of lust—was sent by her parents, who were compelled by necessity and fear. She requested that the light be removed before entering the bedchamber; but while she was moving through the darkness in silence toward the bed of the already sleeping Pausanias, she accidentally stumbled into the lamp and overturned it. He, startled by the noise, drew the dagger that lay nearby and, as if being attacked by some enemy, struck and laid low the girl. After she died from the wound, she allowed Pausanias no rest; instead, a Specter <note>original: *Spectrum*</note> presented itself at night, and in his sleep, it uttered this verse to him with great indignation:

Because of this deed, his allies and Cimon, being ill-disposed toward him, closely besieged him at Byzantium. He escaped, however, and terrified by that vision, he fled to Heraclea to the oracle of the dead <note>original: *manium oraculum* — a place where souls were summoned to provide answers</note>, where the soul of Cleonice was called up and he prayed for her to set aside her anger. She appeared before Pausanias and showed that he would soon be released from those evils when he came to Sparta—obscurely signaling, as I gather, the fates hanging over him. Thus writes Plutarch in the *Life of Cimon*.

<margin>12.</margin> At one time, the house of Dion <note>Dion of Syracuse (4th century BC), a disciple of Plato who attempted to liberate Syracuse from tyranny.</note> was not without Specters. Plutarch is also a witness to this in his *Life of Dion*. While the conspiracy was being formed, he says, a huge and monstrous Specter appeared to Dion. He happened to be sitting at home late in the day, lost in thought in the portico; suddenly a noise was made there, and looking back while the light was still clear, he saw at the other end of the portico a tall woman, whose clothing and face were not at all different from a tragic Fury; she was sweeping the house with a broom. He was violently struck with fear and trembling, called his friends, told them what he had seen, and begged them to stay and spend the night with him because he was completely paralyzed with dread, fearing that if they left him alone, the monster would appear to him again. However, it did not return, but his son, who was nearly an adult, in a fit of grief and anger arising from some small and childish occasion, threw himself headlong from the roof of the house and died. And this is from Plutarch.

<margin>13.</margin> Before the body of Gaius Caesar Caligula was buried, the guards of the Lamian gardens <note>The *Horti Lamiani* was a set of private gardens on the Esquiline Hill in Rome.</note> were disturbed by shadows. Indeed, in the house where he died, they affirmed that no night passed without some terror until the house was finally consumed by fire. Suetonius records this in his *Life of Caligula* and in nearly these very words.

They possess a citadel in which there is a hall; in that hall, beneath the chimney-hearth, an old woman is accustomed to be seen, appearing now for a hundred years whenever someone from the family is about to die.

<margin>18.</margin> The Diocese of Hildesheim in Saxony also suffered an *infesting Spirit* which they called "Hudekin" in the Saxon tongue—that is, the "hooded one" or "capped one"—from the cap with which its head was covered. Marvelous things are reported of it. It seemed to take great delight in the company of men, to whom it exhibited itself sometimes under a human appearance in peasant's clothing, and sometimes mocked them invisibly. It advised princes on great matters and did not refuse its services to others. It was frequently found in the kitchen of the Prelate, assisting the cooks. At first, the spirit warned the Master of the Kitchen to restrain the boy’s insolence. Not content with this revenge, he harassed both the Master of the Kitchen and many other courtiers in various ways, as **Johannes Trithemius** <note>A famous German Benedictine abbot (1462–1516) known for his chronicles and studies on the occult.</note> describes at length in his *History of the Monastery of Hirsau*, around the year of our Lord 1132. Finally, he was compelled to leave that province by the Bishop of that place, Bernard, through **Ecclesiastical Censures** <term>Ecclesiastical Censures: formal spiritual punishments or exorcisms used by the Church to command spirits</term>.

**William of Paris** <note>Also known as William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), a philosopher and Bishop of Paris who wrote extensively on the soul and spiritual beings.</note> testifies that in Poitiers, in the parish of St. Paul, in the year 1447, there was a Spirit that broke cups and glassware by throwing stones; yet, it injured none of the mortals present. **Bodin** <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist whose work "On the Demonomania of Sorcerers" was a standard text on witchcraft and spirits.</note> mentions this in Book 3, Chapter 6 of *On the Demonomania of Sorcerers*.

Not far from the town of Bingen, where the little river **Nahe** <note>original: "Naas"</note> joins the Rhine, there is a village commonly called **Kempten** <note>original: "Camon," which the author notes means "Head of the Mountains" (Caput Montium).</note>. Here, in the year 858, there was a Spirit that brought many troubles upon the inhabitants. At first seen by no one, it began to throw stones at people and knock on doors. Soon, taking on a human appearance, it gave answers; it revealed thefts; it splashed anyone it could with a mark of infamy; and it stirred up discords and rivalries. Gradually, it set fire to and burned down the barns and all the houses. It was more troublesome to one man in particular than to the others, sticking to his side constantly wherever he turned, and burning his house down. Not content with this harassment, in order to incite the entire neighborhood to kill the innocent man, the spirit lied, claiming that the place was infamous because of that man's crimes and therefore subject to these infestations. The torment only came to an end when priests sent by the **Archbishop of Mainz** <note>original: "Moguntino"</note> drove out the pestilential Spirit with **lustral water** <term>lustral water: holy water used for purification or blessing</term> and communal prayers. These things are recorded by Sigebert, Martin, and the *Chronicle of Hirsau*.

<margin>21.</margin>

Finally, that holy man <note>St. Gregory the Great</note> drove it out with the protection of Litanies and holy water.

# ON INFESTED PLACES
<note>original: "DE LOCIS IN FESTIS" – This is likely a printer's error for "INFESTIS," meaning haunted or troubled locations.</note>
<meta>catchword: V. per-</meta>

...in the County of Horn <note>A historical territory in what is now the Netherlands and Belgium.</note>. Indeed, in the place where they were accustomed to sleep, the walking of a groaning **Specter** was heard; a voice was also heard which urged the Maidens to rise and go with him to the fire to attend to a sick person. Several times their feet were dragged from the bed for several paces by the Specter; sometimes they were tickled under the soles of their feet so much that, from excessive laughter, they nearly died; pieces of flesh were torn from some; for most, their legs, arms, and faces were twisted completely in the opposite direction. I pass over the remaining troubles they endured for three years, which may be seen in **Wier**, Book 3, Chapter 9, on the *Deceptions of Demons* <note>Johannes Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who argued against the persecution of witches and provided medical explanations for many "supernatural" phenomena.</note>.

<margin>23.</margin> Around the year of our Lord 1098, not far from **Worms** <note>A city in Germany famous for its imperial diets and religious history.</note>, for many days and nights, a very great multitude of armed knights and foot soldiers appeared, as if they were proceeding to a scheduled parley or to war. Running back and forth, now here, now there, as if in troops, around the ninth hour of the night they would return to a nearby mountain from which they were accustomed to emerge. Finally, one night, a Monk of the **Limburg Monastery** <note>A Benedictine abbey in Rhineland-Palatinate.</note>, located not far from the mountain from which they used to exit, took several others with him and approached the haunted place. Fortifying himself with the sign of the holy Cross, he adjured those coming out of the mountain to say, by the power of the holy and indivisible Trinity, *who they were*. One from the troop replied to him:

> We are a phantom, he said, and not a crowd of living soldiers; but rather the souls of men killed in this place not many years ago, who served as soldiers in this world for a Prince of earthly rulers. The armor, clothing, and horses, which were our instruments of sin while we lived, are even now, after death, certain signs of our torment. Everything that you now see around us is entirely ablaze for us, although you do not see our fire at all.

And when the Monk inquired whether they could be helped by men, the Spirit replied:

> We can be helped by fasts, and prayers, and especially by the offering of the body and blood of Christ <note>The Eucharist or Mass.</note>, and we beg for this.

After these things were said, that entire multitude of Spirits cried out as if with one voice three times:

> Pray for us; pray for us; pray for us.

Soon they all appeared to dissolve into fire. Moreover, the mountain itself, as if it were burning, emitted fire and a very great crashing of trees and noise. So says the **Hirsau Chronicle** <note>Written by Johannes Trithemius, recording the history of the Benedictine abbey of Hirsau.</note>, around the year of our Lord 1098. There are similar Specters which once made the **Plain of Marathon** <note>A famous ancient Greek battlefield.</note> a place of horror; also those which **Calcerandus Rochensis** of Spain beheld, which were like omens of the great upheavals in Sicily, during which the raging commoners drove the Viceroy **Hugo de Moncada** from the city of Palermo, at that time when the Kingdom of Sicily passed to **Charles V** <note>The Holy Roman Emperor (1500–1558).</note>.

### PART ONE

<sig>B 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Mountain</meta>

...reached the mountain: concerning which **Thomas Fazello** <note>Tommaso Fazello (1498–1570) was a Dominican friar and is considered the father of Sicilian history. His work *De Rebus Siculis* is a foundational text on the island's past.</note> writes thus: *“A few days before (namely, before the riot was stirred up, while King Ferdinand <note>Likely Ferdinand II of Aragon, known as Ferdinand the Catholic (1452–1516).</note> was still living), when Calcerandus was lying awake in his small bed at first light, he heard a great multitude of men making a noise in the courtyard. He ran quickly to the window and saw at first a crowd of men and the appearance of foot soldiers; soon, he saw men with spears and shields follow, and then cavalry divided into troops. Through the empty shadows, he seemed to see with his own eyes the battle-lines of armed men rushing together as if in a spectacle of war, attacking the royal house which Hugo was using. Moreover, many others at that same time confessed that they had seen soldiers equipped with arms rushing together at night at the summit and the base of **Mount Pellegrino** <note>original: "Peregrini montis" — A mountain overlooking the city of Palermo, Sicily.</note>.”* These things are from Fazello, Book 10 and the last of his *History of Sicily*.

<margin>24.</margin> Among the Northern peoples, many places are haunted. **Olaus Magnus** <note>Olaus Magnus (1490–1557) was a Swedish archbishop and writer whose work "History of the Northern Peoples" introduced much of Scandinavian folklore to the rest of Europe.</note> reports that among them, night travelers and those intent on guarding flocks and herds are accustomed to be surrounded by portents of various kinds, with a marvelous harmony. The inhabitants call this nightly play of monsters the **Dance of Elves** <note>original: "Choream Eluarum"</note>; they hold the opinion that the souls of those men who give themselves over to bodily pleasures, having slipped from their bodies, roll about the earth. Sometimes the footprints of these ghosts are found in the morning in the dewy grass; at other times, they are seen as if burnt out by fire. Olaus, Book 3, Chapter 11, *On the Northern Nations*.

<margin>25.</margin> On the island of **Iceland**, beneath the Arctic Pole, there is a headland which, like Mount Etna, seethes with perpetual fires. There, the **Specters** of those who have been drowned or killed by some other violent accident present themselves to the meetings of people known to them, so clearly that they are accepted as living by those unaware of their deaths. Nor is the error discovered until the **Shadows** have disappeared. The same Olaus, Book 2, Chapter 3.

<margin>26.</margin> There is a fortress in the farthest lands of subpolar **Finland**, subject to the Kingdom of Sweden. A very vast river of unfathomable depth flows past it. Near this place, Specters appear from time to time; and when the death of the Governor of the fortress or of some soldier is imminent, a **Harper** <note>original: "Cytharædus" — A player of the lyre or kithara.</note> is seen and heard playing throughout the night in the middle of the waters. Olaus also mentions this, Book 2, chapters 19 and 20. Among the **Lapps** <note>original: "Philappas" — Referring to the Sami people of Lapland.</note> there is also a huge number of Specters; these associate with them, talk with them, and banquet with them; it is said they cannot be kept away or driven off by any means. And since they are especially terrified by the spirits of their kinsmen, to prevent this from happening, they keep the corpses dug up and buried under the hearth. **Peucer** <note>Caspar Peucer (1525–1602), a German reformer and physician who wrote on divination and the supernatural.</note>, book on *Divination*, folio 283.

# ON HAUNTED LOCATIONS

The "Mountain of Sorrows" should be mentioned, just as Hector Boece writes in Book 4 of his *History of the Scots*. <note>Hector Boece (1465–1536) was a Scottish historian; the "Mountain of Sorrows" or *Mons Dolorosus* is often associated with the site of Stirling Castle in early chronicles.</note>

<margin>28.</margin>
In the region around the Syrtes of Libya, <note>The Syrtes are two gulfs off the coast of Libya, famous in antiquity for dangerous shallows and sandbanks.</note> occasionally—and especially when the weather is calm and the winds are still—the forms of various living creatures appear in the air. Some of these remain still, while others move. Sometimes they flee, and at other times they pursue those who are running away. Those whom they overtake are enveloped in a cold touch. Diodorus Siculus reports this in Book 3, Chapter 4.

<margin>29.</margin>
Citing Aristotle’s *On Marvelous Things Heard*, <note>original: "de Admirandis auditionibus" — a collection of wonders attributed to the school of Aristotle.</note> Thomas Fazello <note>Tommaso Fazello (1498–1570), a Dominican friar and historian of Sicily.</note> records in Book 1 of *On Sicilian Affairs* that there was once a mound on the Island of Lipari to which no one dared approach at night. For there, the sound of cymbals and castanets, as well as immense noises, shouting, and wild laughter, could be heard. Terrified by these things, the inhabitants of Lipari dreaded going there lest some evil should befall them. However, a certain man, emboldened by unmixed wine, recklessly made his way there. He fell asleep near the cave of the mound, and when his servants searched for him, he was found breathless three days later. He was carried away as if dead; but just as the funeral rites were prepared and he was being carried out in the funeral procession, he suddenly woke up to the amazement of everyone and recounted what he had seen and endured. This is according to Fazello.

<margin>30.</margin>
Certain metal mines are also infested by spirits. Hence the "Anneberg Spirit," <note>Anneberg (Annaberg) was a major silver mining town in Saxony.</note> which killed more than twelve workers with its breath in the cave called the "Rose Crown." The cave was abandoned for that reason, even though it was rich in silver. This spirit would emit a blast from its gaping mouth and appeared in the form of a horse with a long neck and fierce eyes. There is also the "Schneberg Spirit," <note>Schneeberg, another famous mining town in Saxony.</note> dressed in a black hood, who once lifted a worker off the ground in the St. George mine and deposited him in a high part of a cavern—which was once fertile with silver—not without bruising his body. These accounts are from Georgius Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "Father of Mineralogy," who wrote extensively on mining and the folklore of "kobolds" or mine spirits.</note> and Sebastian Münster in Book 1 of his *Cosmography*, Chapter 15.

<margin>31.</margin>
In that part of the Province of Peru belonging to the Ititani people, a girl named Catarina, eleven years of age, became the cause of many disturbances and riots after her death due to her frequent violation of the Sacrament of Confession through sacrilege and her unhappy passing. As soon as her soul departed, a foul corpse remained, of such a terrible stench that it had to be placed out in the open air to keep it from infecting the house. At the same time, a horse that was otherwise tame and gentle began to rage so violently that it struck the wall with its hooves and ran here and there, breaking its restraints. The barking of dogs and restless running about were heard. A certain youth was dragged out of his bed by his arm, and one of the maidservants was struck on the shoulder by a heel, the marks of which remained for many days. These things happened while Catarina’s body was not yet buried. After the burial, as a servant girl wished to enter the bedroom where the girl had been...

This also comes from Isselt in the same passage.

## CHAPTER II.

### *That there are many kinds of places infested by spirits: and that all can be reduced to two categories, and what the difference is between them.*

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial P with floral or vine patterns.</image-desc>
In the preceding chapter, it was demonstrated that certain places are infested by *specters and spirits*; however, it was also suggested that these are not all of a single kind. Infested houses were mentioned, such as the one inhabited by Alexander ab Alexandro <note>Alexander ab Alexandro (1461–1523) was a Neapolitan jurist who recorded his own encounter with a ghost in his house in Rome.</note>. Estates were mentioned, such as those of Hesperius which Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo, the influential early Christian theologian.</note> recalls. Fortresses and palaces were mentioned, such as the one in Scotland called the "Mountain of Sorrow" <note>original: "Mons dolorosus"</note> because of the groans of spirits. Cities were mentioned, such as Mainz <note>original: "Moguntia"</note>. Islands and provinces were mentioned among the Northern peoples, as well as the Bishopric of Hildesheim in Saxony. Furthermore, subterranean places in metal mines were mentioned. Private places were noted, such as the house which Theodore, the Archimandrite of Sykeon <note>A 6th-century Byzantine saint known for performing exorcisms and healings.</note>, purified. Public places were noted, such as the "Corner Baths," etc. But all these may be reduced to a smaller number of categories.

<margin>2.</margin>
Indeed, if we reason correctly, two categories can be established. For we can say some places are *infested because of people* and others are *infested in themselves*. We call those *infested because of people* which are only dread-filled because of certain individuals whom the spirits themselves are pursuing. Those *infested in themselves* are those where the reason for the infestation is found in the spirits themselves, and not in the people who live in those places.

<margin>3.</margin>
Thus, *infested because of people* include: any house that received Pausanias, King of the Spartans <note>Pausanias was said to be haunted by the ghost of a girl he had accidentally killed.</note>; the house Nero inhabited after the murder of his mother; and the place where Otho, the Roman Emperor, was found after the slaughter of Galba, etc. For spirits seeking vengeance for the crimes committed followed these men wherever they turned.

<margin>4.</margin>
Those *infested in themselves* would be: the estate of Hesperius mentioned by Saint Augustine; the Corner Baths mentioned by Saint Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great, whose "Dialogues" contain many stories of the supernatural.</note>; the house that Theodore the Archimandrite of Sykeon liberated; the house in Rome inhabited by Alexander; the Northern provinces and fortresses of Olaus Magnus <note>A Swedish writer and archbishop whose "History of the Northern Peoples" (1555) is a primary source for folklore.</note>; the fields of Worms <note>original: "campi Wormarienses"</note>; and the metal mines, etc.

<margin>5.</margin>
Truly, the difference between these two types of places is manifold. The first difference is taken from the time when the spirits begin to cause trouble. For...

<meta>This page continues the classification of "infested places" (haunted locations). ...in those places that are infested because of the people, the people themselves are found in the locations before the locations become dreadfully haunted by **specters**. Because Nero, Pausanias, and Otho <note>Marcus Salvius Otho (32–69 AD), Roman Emperor who succeeded Galba.</note> were found in certain places, they suffered from troublesome spirits which they previously lacked. In the latter case, the locations themselves are infested before any trouble is brought to the people by the spirits, just as the examples cited in the first chapter prove.

<margin>6.</margin> A second difference is derived from *duration*. Those places remain infested as long as the people whom the harassing spirits follow stay in those places and do not remove the causes of the trouble. But once the people are removed or the causes of the trouble cease, the harassing spirits stop. Yet these latter places remain infested even if they are completely deserted by people.

<margin>7.</margin> A third difference is supplied by the *purposes assigned to the spirits in these places*. Those found in the former places are usually the avengers of crimes committed; just like the spirit of the maiden killed by Pausanias <note>Pausanias was a Spartan general who accidentally killed a girl named Cleonice; her ghost supposedly haunted him until his death.</note>, the shades <note>original: "manes"</note> of Nero's mother <note>Agrippina the Younger, whom Nero famously had assassinated.</note>, and the Emperor Galba. But those in the latter places are not the same. And although they sometimes afflict mortals, it is not always so; it is not their primary purpose to do so.

<margin>8.</margin> The fourth difference concerns the *forms* in which the spirits show themselves in said places. The spirits of the former places *mostly* present themselves under the appearance (and thus human) of those who suffered injury and seem to seek vengeance through these terrors. Hence Nero knew he was being persecuted by his mother's spirit; Pausanias by the Byzantine maiden; and Otho by the spirit of Galba. But the spirits of the latter places are seen sometimes in their own forms, sometimes in foreign forms, as the examples of the first chapter demonstrate.

<margin>9.</margin> Fifthly, the spirits of these places differ in that *in the first kind, fewer are generally found* who cause trouble; in the latter kind, more. We more rarely hear of certain spirits following and bothering their victims everywhere; more often we hear of various spirits being troublesome in certain and defined places.

<margin>10.</margin> Finally, they differ in this: that in these places, a different method of *expiation* <note>original: "expiandi," referring to the ritual cleansing or purification of a site.</note> must be observed than in those. In those infested because of people, the primary concern (if full security is to be obtained) is with the people because of whom the places are infested; in the others, consideration must be given not so much to the people living in the infested places as to the places themselves, as will be taught in its proper place in the preface of the third part of this Disputation.

<margin>11.</margin> Furthermore, although these places are distinguished by the reasons already mentioned, they nevertheless have many things in common, especially the fact that in both...

# CHAPTER III.

->That there are three kinds of spirits that infest places, which is the subject of the present discussion.<-

<margin>1.</margin> <image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' with floral motifs.</image-desc> In the argument prefixed to this chapter, one thing is held as certain, while another is called into question. The certain point is this: there are several kinds of spirits by whom places can be infested. The question is: which specific spirits are they? Nor is this a question of their power <note>their inherent ability to do so</note>; rather, it is a question of the fact—for we do not ask which ones *are able* to make places infested, but which ones *actually* infest them in reality.

<margin>2.</margin> *First of all, it is manifest by common admission.* And not without reason. Since there are good spirits and evil ones: and among both groups (to say nothing of God, the author of spirits) some are human; such as, among the evil, the souls of the damned; and among the good, the blessed minds and those still to be purged. Some are angelic, such as, among the evil, the Devils; and among the good, the heavenly spirits, distinguished into nine orders or choirs <note>The traditional celestial hierarchy, ranging from Seraphim and Cherubim down to Archangels and Angels</note>.

<margin>3.</margin> *In truth, there is no question regarding power,* namely, which spirits are capable of infesting places. For since all spirits possess great power over corporeal things, and since places—and the things within those places—are considered corporeal things, there is no doubt that any spirit, provided they so wish and are not prohibited by a higher authority, is able to infest a place.

<margin>4.</margin> *Those, therefore, who actually infest.* There are three primary kinds of spirits. One is entirely incorporeal; two are human. That is: first, the Devils; second, the souls of men damned to the punishments of the lower world; and third, those who are being expiated by the pains of purgatory and are troublesome to the living.

<margin>5.</margin> *Meanwhile, we do not deny that good angels* have been seen in certain specific places in the past, and are occasionally seen even now. We have brought forward many examples for this argument in that *Discussion* <note>original: "Disputatione"</note> which we gave concerning the *Apparitions of Spirits*. Nor do we so confine the good spirits of men to the heavens as if we were casting them into chains; it is not forbidden for them to appear outside of heaven, since it was demonstrated in the aforementioned *Discussion* that these, too, have often been seen in other places. But it is one thing for spirits to *appear* in certain places; it is quite another for them to be, as it were, attached to places and troublesome.

<margin>6.</margin> But if anyone should wish to argue decisively that by their very presence or works, locations were or are infested, we shall not resist much; which yet

# PART ONE.

...nonetheless, in *this discussion*, when we speak of **Haunted Places** <note>original: "Loca Infesta," referring to locations troubled by supernatural presence</note>, we want it to be understood that they are infested by those three types of Spirits mentioned earlier.

<margin>7.</margin>
Indeed, we believe that no one is so foolish as to think that all the troubles perceived, or the disturbances heard in haunted places, are caused *only by good Angels*, or perhaps by those *happy human spirits* <note>the souls of the blessed in Heaven</note>. Many things happen here that can only be done by wicked and perverse spirits, or certainly by the wretched spirits of men, as will be demonstrated elsewhere.

<margin>8.</margin>
Likewise, there will be no one who thinks all troubles and disturbances are stirred up by those *evil spirits* of the angelic kind. Just as not everything that happens can be attributed to those blessed heavenly ones, so too not everything belongs to Demons. Certain things have only Demons as their authors; others only humans. Thus, some signs reveal only humans, and others reveal only Demons.

<margin>9.</margin>
Furthermore, the things that are certainly done here by human spirits are not all of the *same condition*, although some reveal wretched spirits; however, they are not always damned. For not all wretched spirits are damned spirits, although all who are damned are wretched. Those who are purified by **purgatorial punishments** <note>referring to the doctrine of Purgatory, where souls undergo temporary cleansing</note> are wretched; but those who have been sentenced to the **punishments of hell** <note>original: "infernalibus supplicijs"</note> are both wretched and damned.

<margin>10.</margin>
Moreover, although it is not difficult to show by certain reasoning that places are infested by the aforementioned *three* kinds of spirits, it will suffice for those who prefer brevity to illustrate the matter with *examples*.

<margin>11.</margin>

Also, the foul and dreadful specter that appeared to **Cassius Parmensis** around the time he was killed by order of Augustus. # ON HAUNTED PLACES

...[we saw], a great crowd of both cavalry and infantry that was seen in the fields of **Worms** <note>original: "Wormatiensi," referring to the city of Worms in Germany</note> for many days and nights; concerning these, see Chapter 1.

The mother of **Saint Elizabeth, Queen of the Hungarians**, also appeared to her daughter after her death. She explained the punishments she was enduring because of a life lived somewhat negligently, and she asked to be helped by her daughter’s intercessions. Finally, having obtained her wish, she gave thanks for her timely liberation when she appeared to her daughter a second time after prayers had been poured out to God. This is testified by **Jacobus Montanus of Speyer** in Chapter 23 of her *Life*.

<margin>13.</margin> Finally, for those who are consigned to the torments of hell, there is the Shadow that troubled the house in **Athens** which **Athenodorus** <note>Athenodorus Cananites, a Stoic philosopher who famously exorcised a haunted house in Athens by following a ghost to its unburied remains</note> later inhabited. There are the spirits of **Nero’s** mother, of **Cleonice the Byzantine Virgin**, and of the Emperor **Galba**. Also, the **Ethiopian** <note>original: "Aethiops." In early modern and medieval spiritual texts, "Ethiopian" figures were frequently used as symbolic representations of demons or the damned</note> who appeared to the monk **Isidore** (concerning which, see Thesis 8, Chapter 8). Lastly, there are the numerous apparitions encountered in the **Northern Regions** <note>original: "Regiones Aquilonares," likely referring to Scandinavia or the Baltic lands</note>.

For although the nature of the appearance and the haunting of these Spirits does not necessarily prove they should be considered among the damned, it is clear from other evidence that they will never have a share with the blessed. From what evidence? Because they departed this life destitute of true faith (to say nothing of other crimes). No matter how uprightly a life was led, it cannot benefit a person for salvation if they exchange this present life for the next without true faith. On this point—to say no more—the opinion of the **Blessed Augustine** in his book *On Faith, to Peter* is clear:

> Hold most firmly, he says, and doubt not in any way, that not only all Pagans, but also Jews, Heretics, and Schismatics who end this present life outside the Catholic Church, will go into the eternal fire which is prepared for the devil and his angels.

In the same way, those who departed with Christian faith but without charity <note>in this theological context, "charity" (caritas) refers to the state of grace or divine love, as opposed to mere intellectual belief</note> will be numbered among the damned Spirits; as the same **Augustine** testifies in the same passage with these words:

> Hold most firmly, and doubt not in any way, that not all who are baptized within the Catholic Church will receive eternal life; but only those who, having received baptism, live rightly—that is, those who have abstained from the vices and lusts of the flesh. For just as Infidels, Heretics, and Schismatics shall not have the Kingdom of Heaven, so too criminal Catholics will not be able to possess it.

...and the disturbances and terrors they stir up in various places.

<margin>15.</margin>
Another point is that *infernal punishments are not endured in only one place.* Granted, there is one specific place that claims this right above others and which, after the final Day of Judgment, will be the sole seat and dwelling of the damned; yet for now, besides this place, God the Best and Greatest has several others in which He exacts due punishment from the damned according to their deserts. Are not the Demons damned? Do they not endure the fire of hell? And yet the Apostle Paul calls them *the world-rulers of this darkness, and spiritual wickedness in high places* <note>original: "mundi Rectores tenebrarum harum, & Spiritualia nequitia in cœlestibus," a reference to Ephesians 6:12</note>. Moreover, it is a common and by no means empty opinion among mortals that the sublunary air <note>The region of the atmosphere below the moon, which in ancient science was thought to be subject to change and decay</note> is full of Demons.

<margin>16.</margin>
The third point is: *The souls who departed from this world not fully purified are not contained in a single place.* Their primary place, which we call Purgatory, is established not far from Hell, in the bowels of the earth. The greatest part of these souls migrates there upon death. Besides this, by the singular providence and mercy of God, they have certain other places in which they are purified. But these matters belong to another discussion.

---

## CHAPTER IV.

->*That there are various spirits, both of Demons and of wretched men, who are accustomed to be troublesome to mortals and to make places haunted.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
We have established three kinds of Spirits that are known to make places haunted: Demons, the souls of damned men, and those souls being purified. We must now determine whether there are ranks and orders within each category, or whether, on the contrary, everyone in each category is of one and the same condition.

<margin>2.</margin>
Regarding Demons, then (let us begin with them), **Psellus** <note>Michael Psellus (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine polymath whose work on demonology was highly influential in the Renaissance</note>, a certain philosopher and Christian (though he seems unrefined in Christian doctrine), distinguishes six kinds according to the variety of their locations. The first is called **Fiery**; it wanders in the higher air. The second is named **Aerial**, roaming in this air closest to us. The third is called **Terrestrial**, because it stays mostly around the earth and opposes man in earthly matters and machines. The fourth is called **Aquatic and Marine**; it is immersed in moisture, living by choice near lakes and rivers, stirring up waves and storms at sea, and sinking ships laden with men. The fifth is **Subterranean**, living under the earth and harassing those who dig wells and mines; it creates cracks in the earth, shakes foundations, and stirs up fire-breathing winds. The sixth and...

# ON INFESTED PLACES

The last type is the Light-shunning <note>original: *Lucifugum*</note>, which is inscrutable and entirely dark; it is filled with cold passions and violently destroys many things. So says Psellus in his book *On Demons* <note>Michael Psellus was an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher whose work on demonology was highly influential in the Renaissance.</note>.

3. Others better distinguish troubling Demons into two types: the *Mild* <note>original: *Mites*</note>, and the *Grim* or *Fierce* <note>original: *Tetricos* or *Truculentos*</note>. They wish the *Mild* ones to be called *Household Spirits* <note>original: *Lares*, the Roman term for protective domestic deities</note>, who dwell in houses in the dead of night and indicate they are doing something by various noises, yet they actually do nothing. The Germans (says *Georgius Agricola* in his book *On Subterranean Creatures*) call them *Guteolos* <note>A Latinization of the German "Gütchen," meaning "little good ones."</note> because of their goodness; others call them *mountain dwarfs* <note>original: *vrunculos montanos*</note>, because they mostly appear as Dwarfs, three-quarters of a foot <note>original: *dodrantes*, about nine inches</note> in height. They deem the *Fierce* ones worthy of the name *Specters* <note>original: *Laruarium*</note>: these terrify, molest, and disturb the family. Cassian mentions both in *Conference 7, chapter 32*. Of the former, he speaks in these words: 

> It is clear that some of the unclean Spirits (whom the common folk also call *Fauns* <note>Nature spirits from Roman mythology often associated with prankish behavior.</note>) are so seductive and such jokers that, constantly haunting certain places or roads, they are by no means delighted by the torments of those passers-by they can deceive; but content with only laughter and mockery, they strive to weary them rather than harm them. 

Of the latter, however, he says: 

> Others are clearly so given to fury and ferocity that they are not content to merely vex the bodies of the humans they possess with cruel tearing, but even rush upon those passing at a distance and hasten to afflict them with the most savage slaughter. 

Many of this latter type are found. Of the former type was the one mentioned by *William of Paris* <note>William of Auvergne (c. 1180–1249), Bishop of Paris and a noted theologian.</note> (in chapter 8 of the second part of the second principal part), who used to play with a jester whom *William* testifies he saw; nor would he allow the man to rest. This spirit disturbed the quiet of the night now by throwing stones at the wall, now by the tumult and noise of furniture, and now by dragging the bed away.

4. But this distinction is not between separate types of Spirits, but rather concerns the different duties of a single type of Demon. I would believe there are no Demons who are *only* Mild, nor any who are *only* Fierce. Those who are now mild are later fierce; those who are now fierce are later mild. For even the mild ones do not lack the power or the will to cause harm or to please. And those who rage against us out of hatred (because they know a thousand arts) even transform themselves into Angels of light and sometimes simulate the greatest mildness.

5. Others distinguish these troubling Spirits according to the nature of the Orders in which they were created by God. In this, they do not err when they distinguish nine Orders of bad Angels just as they do the good ones; nor in the fact that they think that any spirits, from whatever Orders they may be, can make places infested. For although Spirits of the higher Or-

### PART ONE.

Blessed spirits <note>referring to angels or the souls of the saved</note> do not undergo the lowest duties; these belong to the higher Orders. Wicked spirits have no regard for the reason of their own condition: and often, they do not attend to what they ought to do according to the nature of their state, but they carry out whatever their lust draws them to. On this subject, see elsewhere in the *Disputation on Demoniacs*.

<margin>6.</margin>
*The spirits of damned humans are of two kinds.* Some are wretched solely because of original sin <note>The Christian doctrine that all humans are born with a "stain" of sin inherited from Adam, which is removed by baptism.</note>, with which they departed from this life; others are wretched because of the actual sins they also committed. That these latter ones can be troublesome in certain places seems clear from many examples brought forward in the first chapter of this Disputation. Regarding the former, there is a greater difficulty, *especially* if those who departed with the stain of original sin were infants, or of a still tender and immature age.

<margin>7.</margin>
For since this manner of haunting by these spirits is also a kind of punishment—one which God, the Best and Greatest, exacts from them for their own crimes—those who did not offend God by their own will seem entirely free from this; nor had they committed anything for which they should be more severely punished, as these latter ones have.

<margin>8.</margin>
*Universally, however, I would not easily deny that these spirits can be troublesome.* Why is that? Because the fact that the ghosts <note>original: *manes*</note> of the deceased are troublesome to the living occurs not only because of the sins the deceased committed, but sometimes also because of the ill-merit of the living, which deserves to be avenged by the haunting of the spirits of the dead.

<margin>9.</margin>
Cleonice, the Byzantine maiden, did not deserve to appear several times after death to the living Pausanias; rather, the sin and cruelty of Pausanias demanded this <note>Pausanias was a Spartan general who accidentally killed the maiden Cleonice; her ghost was said to have pursued him until his death.</note>. It was not her own fault, but the guilt of her son, that compelled the deceased mother of Nero to often intervene in the affairs of the living <note>The Roman Emperor Nero murdered his mother, Agrippina the Younger, and was reportedly haunted by her spirit and the Furies.</note>. And that Galba was more troublesome after death was deserved by the impiety of the living Otho <note>Otho orchestrated the assassination of Emperor Galba to seize the throne; Galba's ghost allegedly appeared to Otho in visions before his own downfall.</note>. On these matters, see Chapter 1.

<margin>10.</margin>
Suppose a certain father loved his son more than was right, and in that love seriously offended God; or another, who fathered a son through unspeakable lust. What shall prevent us from saying that living parents can be terrified, afflicted, and troubled by the ghosts of their deceased children?

<margin>11.</margin>
It will be proven, in Chapter Seventeen, that it happens by the just judgment of God that cruel murderers are infested by the spirits of the innocents they killed. But indeed, one can be deprived of life innocently—not only an adult who has seriously offended God, but even an infant who is burdened only by original sin. Why, then, should this one not be as troublesome to the author of the slaughter after death as the other? We think this can be said with probability.

Souls that must be purged <note>referring to souls in Purgatory</note> are also of two ranks. Some are paying the full penalties they contracted in this life for more serious sins; others are setting aside even lighter faults through the fire of purgatory. Both can take part in the affairs of the living and, by raising a clamor <note>original: *strepitu*, referring to poltergeist-like noises</note>, demand help from those still alive. However, this is especially true for those who are weighed down by the heavy burden of the penalties they must pay. The faults of the former group <note>those with lighter faults</note> seem to be more easily expiated, so that because of this, it is not necessary for them to implore the help of the living through this kind of haunting. The punishments of the latter <note>the more serious sinners in Purgatory</note>, because they are to be avenged more severely and for a longer time, can for this very reason either be expiated or obtain the assistance of the living.

# CHAPTER V.

## Which of the aforementioned Spirits, above all others, most frequently interfere in human affairs and make places infested.

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial O with floral scrolling motifs.</image-desc> It has been demonstrated that all Spirits can be troublesome, and indeed are. Let us now inquire whether they are all equally troublesome. However, there are two senses to this question. One is whether they all cause equal amounts of trouble; the other is whether they all haunt and are present to mortals with equal frequency, or rather if some are present more often than others. The latter point is what must be defined here; the former has its place elsewhere.

<margin>2.</margin>
However, the definition of this matter is quite difficult. For no certain argument can be sought here from the effects, since the spirits of both humans and Demons often perform the same actions. Nor is it clear from the confession of the Spirits themselves, because such testimony is suspect and is very rarely obtained. Nor is it discerned from the condition and attributes of the Spirits, since it is extremely difficult to understand which properties belong to which group.

<margin>3.</margin>
Yet this matter is not entirely impossible for the intellect to grasp. For since the things that happen here occur through reason and design, if we follow reason as our guide, we can certainly look upon the truth itself from afar, even if we do not attain it perfectly.

<margin>4.</margin>
Reason indeed strongly suggests we believe that the spirits of damned men very rarely interfere in the affairs of the living and stir up troubles; the spirits of those who must be purged <note>souls in Purgatory</note> do so more frequently; and above both of these, the Spirits of Demons.

# PART ONE.

...the presence and interest of the spirits of damned men? Is it perhaps because they themselves seek it out? Or because it so pleases God, the Best and Greatest? <note>original: *Deo Opt. Maximo*, a common Latin honorific for God adapted from the Roman title for Jupiter.</note> Or can the Demons, under whose power they are damned, wish for this?

<margin>6.</margin>
The spirits of these mortals cannot desire this themselves, for they have no reason to seek it; indeed, they have every reason to wish to remain hidden and never return to the living. The former is clear because they can hope for no good; the latter is clear from the evil they incur by their return to us.

<margin>7.</margin>
If some good purpose were available to these miserable ones which they could achieve through the company of the living, they might perhaps strive to return. But there is absolutely no such purpose. It is not for the sake of wealth or the body, as they are no longer capable of these things. Nor is it for the sake of the soul, for such is the condition of these spirits that, according to the state of their soul, they must be perpetually miserable and unhappy.

<margin>8.</margin>
Furthermore, the evil they incur by returning to us prevents them from desiring it. That evil is the loss of their honor, which they wish to keep intact among us, but which is brought into the most immediate danger by this return. Or do these "sons of pride" perhaps take no account of honor? Of whom the divine word says, *Their pride ascends always?* <note>original: *Superbia ascendit semper*, a reference to Psalm 73:23 (Vulgate 72:23), describing the ever-increasing arrogance of the wicked.</note> Or is their honor not called into question when they are understood to be the companions of Demons, the enemies of God, and—for all eternity—the most miserable of creatures?

<margin>9.</margin>
Is it perhaps by the will and command of God that the spirits of the damned frequently take part in the affairs of the living? But how is this established? That they might return to us by God’s will is certain; but that they should return *very frequently* is neither certain nor likely—in fact, it is improbable.

<margin>10.</margin>
It is characteristic of God, the Best and Greatest, to be a most diligent observer of the laws He has ordained. Now, He has already decreed concerning those who have lost their salvation that as soon as they depart from this life, their punishments should immediately await them in their fixed places, which they must endure forever. Will He rashly violate this decree? Will He wish for them to linger in places other than those ordained since the constitution of the world?

<margin>11.</margin>
What, then, is doubtful here? Is it whether their punishments await the lost immediately after death? Or that these wretches endure them in specific places? Or that God is a diligent observer of His own laws?

<margin>12.</margin>
The first point is clear, if only by the example of the rich man, Epulo <note>A traditional name for the "Rich Man" (Dives) from the parable of Dives and Lazarus.</note>, who bears witness to the torments he endured immediately after death in that miserable and lamentable plea: *I am tormented in this flame.* (Luke 16) <note>original: *Crucior in hac flamma*.</note> I know that some mock this argument and teach that because the verb is in the present tense...

<margin>15.</margin>

Perhaps they would believe those rising from the underworld: *If they do not believe Moses, the Prophets, and the Word of God, neither will they believe those rising from the dead.* Or perhaps He wishes them to return so that through them He may exact just punishments upon sinners and avenge sins by inflicted evils? In this, the Angelic minds serve Him, called *Ministering Spirits* <note>original: *Administratorij Spiritus*</note> because of this and other duties (by which they serve God).

<margin>16.</margin>

Although prison is a just punishment for them, God, the Best and Greatest, who disciplines them with this just penalty of imprisonment, can turn other punishments toward them; which they may endure with their greatest torment even while positioned outside of Hell. We only wish to establish this: *that those who belong to the lower orders and choirs frequently make places haunted <note>original: *infesta*, meaning disturbed or hostile</note> and are troublesome to the living.* See Chapter 12, regarding those possessed by demons.

# CHAPTER VII.

<margin>1.</margin>
<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' showing a seated scholar at a desk.</note> An answer to the proposed question seems difficult, specifically because the return of spirits from the places of Purgatory to the living happens according to the will and judgment of God; which is called a *great deep* <note>original: *abyssus multa*</note> in Psalm 35, and cannot be grasped by human wit.

# CONCERNING HAUNTED PLACES
