...future punishments are signified, which after the day of judgment the Rich Man <note>original: *Epulo*, a name frequently used in Latin theology to refer to the wealthy man in the parable of Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16).</note>, along with other damned souls, will have in common. <margin>13.</margin> It is also in certain specific places that the miserable sustain their punishments: in Hell <note>original: *Infernus*</note>, the perpetual prison of the Damned. <margin>14.</margin> Indeed, it is far from God to violate the laws He himself has established. He is faithful in all His words. *God is not like man, that He should lie; nor like the son of man, that He should be changed (Numbers 23).* With Him there is no change, says Blessed James in chapter 1. *For I am God (He says) and I change not (Malachi 3).* What follows from this? Namely this: that the spirits of damned men do not easily return to our world.

<margin>15.</margin> But we must also ask: for what reason would God wish for the miserable to be present in the affairs of the living? Is it so they may serve as witnesses of the punishments of Hell among the living? The living already have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them. They have the Word of God; let them believe it. Perhaps they would believe those rising from the underworld? *If they do not believe Moses, the Prophets, and the word of God, neither will they believe those rising from the dead.* Or perhaps God would want them to return so that He might exact just punishments from sinners through them, avenging sins with inflicted evils? For this task, the angelic minds serve Him; for this and other duties (in which they serve God) they are called Ministering Spirits <note>original: *Administratorij Spiritus*, referring to angels who carry out God's will on earth.</note>.

<margin>16.</margin> From these things it is easily gathered either that the spirits of damned men never take part in the affairs of the living—which is a claim that should not be made—or that they take part very rarely, which is what we have proposed to prove in this chapter. For although God is a most diligent observer of His own laws: yet in those cases...

# CHAPTER V.

## *Which of the said Spirits, above all others, most frequently involve themselves in human affairs and render places infested.*

<margin>1.</margin> <image-desc>Large decorative ornamental initial letter 'O' with floral scrollwork within a square border.</image-desc> **I**t has been demonstrated that all Spirits can be troublesome, and indeed are so. Let us now inquire whether all are equally troublesome. Now, there are two senses to what is being asked. One is whether all cause equal trouble; the other is whether all haunt and are present to mortals with equal frequency, or whether some are present more often than others. The latter must be defined here; the former has its place elsewhere.

<margin>2.</margin> Now, the definition of this matter is quite difficult. For a certain argument cannot be sought here from the effects produced, since the spirits of men and of <term>Demons</term> <note>The author distinguishes between the "ghosts" of deceased humans and "demons," which are fallen angels.</note> often perform the same actions. Nor is it clear from the confession of the Spirits themselves, because such testimony is suspect and is obtained only very rarely. Nor is it discerned from the *condition and attributes* of the Spirits, since it is extremely difficult to understand which properties belong to which beings.

<margin>3.</margin> Yet, this matter is by no means impossible for the intellect. For since the things that happen here are done with reason and purpose, if we follow reason as our guide, we can—if not perfectly attain the truth—at least perceive it from afar.

<margin>4.</margin> Indeed, reason entirely persuades us to believe that the Spirits of damned men very rarely take part in the affairs of the living or stir up trouble; the Spirits of those to be cleansed <note>those in Purgatory</note> do so more frequently; and above both of these, the Spirits of <term>Demons</term> do so most of all.

The first point is clear from this: they can hope for no **good**. The second is clear from the **evil** they incur by their return to us.

<margin>3.</margin> Nor should we attempt to guess based on the sins which are purged by the fire of Purgatory—as if those who committed lighter sins, or those more easily deserving of pardon, might return more easily, while those who perpetrated graver sins return either never or only with great difficulty. This is because it is quite difficult for us to judge the gravity of sins committed by others; furthermore, among those who have returned to us from the places of Purgatory, some seem to have sinned lightly, and others more gravely.

<margin>4.</margin> Likewise, the status of the person matters little here; whether the one who returns to us was a member of the clergy <note>original: *sacris initiatus*—someone initiated into sacred orders</note> or a layperson <note>original: *homo profanus*—a "profane" or secular man, not meaning "foul-mouthed" but simply not a member of the priesthood</note>, as if the latter would be present to the living more easily than the former, or vice versa. It is not only the clergy who return, nor only the laity. They return from both groups, and with equal frequency. A secular status does not cause them to return, nor does a sacred status prevent it, or the other way around.

<margin>5.</margin> Truly, although no certain guess can be taken from these and similar matters, it should not be said that there is *absolutely no* way to tell. It is said with a great deal of probability that those return to the living more easily *who, while they lived, earned as it were the right to return*; that is, those who exercised themselves in the study of those virtues which are most accustomed to win over the divine mercy and goodness. Nor is this surprising. Since these spirits return by the singular mercy of God, can it not be believed that this privilege is granted more easily to those who, while they lived their common life with us, won that same mercy of God for themselves through more numerous and greater reasons?

<margin>6.</margin> But what are these reasons? What are these virtues? There are two primary ones. A burning and singular love toward God; and an ardent zeal for helping one's neighbor, especially those who have died piously in Christ. It cannot be otherwise than that *God loves those who love Him* <note>original: *Deus diligentes se diligere*</note> and, because of this, He does good for them. And it is entirely fitting that *by the same measure a man has measured to others, it shall be measured back to him* <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 7:2; the author suggests that those who helped the dead will be helped in return.</note>. Because of this, a dead man may be able to experience or even seek the prayers <term>suffragia: intercessory prayers or good works performed by the living to shorten a soul's time in Purgatory</term> of the living if, while he was alive, he took up the patronage of the dead and helped them by whatever means he could.

<margin>7.</margin> There is also another class of the piously departed that is accustomed to return quite often and implore the help of the living: those, I say, who were weighed down by debt <note>original: *ære alieno*—literally "another's copper," a standard Roman and Scholastic term for debt</note> and did not make full and perfect restitution <term>restitution: the act of returning property or money to its rightful owner to resolve a sin or injustice</term> when they departed from this life. Regarding the return of these souls, very many examples are reported in our own times. Who would dare to condemn them all as false?

<margin>8.</margin> We know that such things do not burden the souls themselves, but rather their heirs, if the heirs do not restore the goods which the deceased seriously commanded to be restored. Nevertheless, the restitution—

It is a gift of grace to the Spirits that they may return; it is no injustice if that return is denied.

# CHAPTER VIII.

->*Which of the spirits of damned men return more easily or more frequently to the living, causing distress by stirring up disturbances.*<-

<note>The woodcut initial 'E' depicts a serene landscape, contrasting with the dark subject matter of the damned souls discussed in this chapter.</note>

This is a worthy inquiry, because the troubles stirred up by these spirits are attributed either to the sins of the Spirits themselves or to the sins of the living.

There is a great argument for this: you will not easily find that these spirits have brought troubles without observing either some crime <note>original: *delictum*—a legal or moral offense</note> on the part of the spirits, or some fault on the part of the people who endure the troubles. But this is even more significant: although it is a heavy thing for these spirits to be shut up in the prison of hell, and they would rather wander about, they nevertheless return to the living against their will—so that they may be recognized by them—and whenever they return, they return to their own punishment (if not that of others), which is at the very least the penalty owed for sin.

3. Indeed, there does not seem to be any other cause for their return to the living. Those who return do not seek good for themselves, nor do they seek it for others, no matter to whom they show themselves. Those to whom they appear take no delight in their presence; in fact, they endure these troubles most reluctantly. Therefore, is there any cause other than their own fault, or the fault of the living, for why they harass the living?

4. And while it might sometimes happen that the living endure troubles through no fault of their own, who would believe that the deceased endure some evil they do not deserve? It turns to the benefit of the living if they suffer adversity while undeserving; but these spirits of the dead hope for no such benefit <note>original: *emolumentum*—profit, gain, or spiritual benefit</note>. Therefore, if we do not attribute it to the fault of the living, let us at least attribute it to the crime of the deceased that they return unwillingly.

5. However, not all the sins of the spirits who return, nor all the sins of the living to whom they return, are the cause of this homecoming. Why? Would it not be necessary for absolutely all the spirits of damned men to return to the living, since there is none among them whom his own sins did not thrust down to the underworld? And among the race of the living, how many are there who have involved themselves in even grave sins, and yet never experience the harassment of these spirits?

6. There are certain specific sins to which this return, joined with harassment, seems to be assigned. And not without reason, both because it happens rather rarely, and because, since it is a singular and unusual kind of vengeance <note>original: *vindictae genus*</note>, it ought to be considered decreed for certain singular crimes, and not indiscriminately for just any. And Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the soul and demons.</note> seems perhaps to have hinted at this in Book 2 of *On Abstinence from Animal Food*. For when he had spoken about depraved and deceitful demons, he soon adds these things concerning souls: "Such," he says, "are also the souls of the dead who have departed from the body filled with various [passions]: for even then they are tormented by the disturbances of anger and lust; and having turned into the nature of demons, they are rendered similar to them: harmful and turbulent, they turn themselves into various forms; and now they present themselves conspicuously to the eyes, now they hide themselves: and thus they elude the keenness of those who are looking, and even those who are thinking." Thus says Porphyry.

7. But what are these sins? I think some of these arise from the very spirits who are bothering—

<margin>17.</margin>
Therefore, the *spirits* of damned men are present to the living neither by their own will, nor frequently by God's permission. Or perhaps this is what the *Demons* want, under whose power they live? First of all, this matter does not depend on the will of *Demons*. Those things which are subject to God's laws (as we have shown to be the case, that the spirits of the damned are in Hell) are not violated or broken by the will of *Demons*, nor of any creature, unless God permits it. For this reason, no greater necessity for why these spirits can return to us frequently is sought from any source other than the will of God itself. Then, even if it were mostly subject to the will of *Demons*; still, the *Demons* have no cause why they would want these spirits to return to us. For what? Does this return serve them? Is it so that the borders of their kingdom are expanded in the way they seek? Do they need the labor of these spirits to harm mortals? No service is performed for them here. Their kingdom often suffers great desertions <note>original: *defectiones*—referring to souls turning toward God after witnessing a spirit, thereby leaving the Devil's influence</note> by this return. In themselves, they are most ready and most powerful to do harm.

<margin>18.</margin>
Since things are so, if any spirits are rarely present in the affairs of mortals, they are surely the *spirits* of damned men. I would add this too: not only do the *spirits* of damned men return to us *very rarely*; but the living are also often deceived; so that they think they see the spirits of damned men, who are nevertheless nothing but Demons, under the form and image of damned men. How and for what reasons the Demons accomplish this belongs to another place <note>The author likely refers to a later chapter in this work or a different volume.</note>.

For although they have their own determined place; and are punished there, according to God's will: nevertheless they themselves can desire to be present in the affairs of the living; and God can more easily satisfy their desire and expectation.

<margin>20.</margin>
**The spirits of the damned do not strive to return:** because they hope for no good from the living. **They desire not to return:** because they fear the loss of honor <note>The damned may feel shame for their fallen state and prefer to remain hidden.</note>. ## CHAPTER VI.

->*Who among the spirits of Demons, more than others, are most accustomed to involve themselves in the affairs of the living: to make places haunted, and to afflict mortals with distress.*<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' depicting a landscape or figure, beginning the word 'In'.</image-desc>
That Demons exist in vast numbers is beyond controversy. Both secular authors and the writers of the Sacred Scriptures know this. But even if we were deprived of these supports, the example of a single wretched man could serve as a great argument for us, from whom the Lord once expelled a *legion* <note>Referring to the Gerasene demoniac in the Gospels</note> by His word—that is, 6,666 (or more correctly, 12,250, according to Jansen <note>Cornelius Jansen (1510–1576), author of the *Gospel Concordance*</note> in his *Gospel Concordance*, 12250) at one time.

<margin>2.</margin>
However, this multitude is not a confused muddle. The same Order that the spirits held before they were cast out of heaven for their sins, they still hold, and shall hold for all eternity. And this is no wonder. Order follows nature; and spirits always retain that same nature. Therefore, it should not seem a new idea that those spirits are said to have a Kingdom (Matthew 12) and also *Principalities* and *Powers* (Ephesians 6).

### PART ONE. 27

...Orders are distinguished; and in each Order, three Choirs. Likewise, among the spirits of Demons, one may distinguish three primary kinds, and in each kind, three Choirs; which we could (although usage does not so permit) address by the same names that we usually use for the blessed Spirits <note>The author refers to the traditional celestial hierarchy of angels—such as Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones—suggesting that the fallen angels maintain a mirrored, dark version of that structure.</note>.

<margin>4.</margin>
Since things are thus, it is asked: do all these spirits of Demons make places haunted <note>original: *loca reddant infesta*—literally "render places dangerous" or "infested," the root of the concept of a "haunted" location</note>, and do they trouble mortals indiscriminately, or rather, are there certain specific ones from the whole number? And who are they? From which Orders? From which Choirs? This is perhaps a curious question, but it is certainly difficult to explain; and it is one which, if not a great deal, can at least bring some light to the present *Disputation*.

<margin>5.</margin>
The solution to this, however, is not to be sought from the will of the Demons, but rather from the divine decree and the reasons for that decree. If only the will of the Demons were taken into account, you could justly exclude none of them. But if we consider the divine decree, you would rightly doubt the presence of many of them.

<margin>6.</margin>
What do these shapeshifters <term>versipelles</term> <note>original: *versipelles*—literally "skin-turners," a classical term for beings that change their appearance, used here to describe the deceptive and transformative nature of demons</note> seek more; what do they so desire, than first, that they might not be shut up in infernal prisons? Second, that they might harm the human race by whatever means they are able? This is indeed the desire of all of them; but it is more burning in those who surpass the others in the excellence of their nature. What follows from this? That all of them, and especially those of the higher Choirs, desire to haunt the places of the living and leave them no peace.

<margin>7.</margin>
Everyone understands that what we infer here is correctly inferred. But perhaps someone doubts the truth of these propositions. Yet all that we put forward are no less certain. It is certain that all Spirits dread the prisons of hell. It is certain that all desire to harm mortals. It is certain that the dread of prison and the zeal for doing harm is greater among the Spirits of the higher Orders.

<margin>8.</margin>
That they all dread the prisons of Hell, and prefer to be in any other place rather than the places of the underworld, is proved by the fact that they were established there as a punishment for sins, which they detest most greatly. But it is especially shown by their prayer made to Christ when He was driving them out of a certain man; by which they signify that they fear lest they *be tormented before the time* (Luke 8). Then also by their plea, in which they ask to be sent into the pigs and *not into the abyss* (Matthew 8). Indeed, they desire to be sent into pigs rather than into the abyss of Hell, because their punishment in Hell is more severe than it is in the pigs. And they thought they were being tormented *before the time* if, before the Day of Judgment, they were thrust down to the underworld; they held this as a more severe punishment than if, while remaining outside the physical location of hell, they nonetheless carried their own hell within themselves.

<margin>8</margin>
If we speak of these matters generally, all can be reduced to a single category: those where the laws of charity toward one's neighbor are most gravely violated. If we descend to specific types, some involve the duty owed to parents being turned into grave insult; others involve the "bowels of mercy" <note>A biblical idiom (Latin: *viscera misericordiae*) referring to deep, heartfelt compassion or the seat of pity.</note> being closed to those suffering in extreme or heavy poverty; and others involve the oppression of those same people. Thus, for such a return <note>The "return" refers to the spirit appearing as a ghost or haunting a location.</note>, three types of sins should be properly established: *impiety toward parents, a hardened heart toward a neighbor in need, and grave tyranny over subjects.*

<margin>9</margin>
Indeed, the examples of those recorded as having returned lend great weight to our assertion. Yet reason demonstrates even more clearly how fitting this is. First, by the highest right, this punishment is owed to these damned souls. Furthermore, many reasons prove that mortals should recognize that God most justly punishes sins committed against one's neighbor (as He punishes here).

<margin>10</margin>
Everyone knows how much piety toward parents ought to be commended to children. They know how great a punishment is rightfully established for the impious. Since, therefore, it is a heavy punishment for deceased Spirits to return to the living, who can doubt that God most justly wills to avenge the sins of those who were impious toward their parents with this kind of punishment?

<margin>11</margin>
Likewise, those who deny mercy to the wretched are unworthy of mercy themselves; those who, in whatever ways they are most conveniently able, do not help the poor in their need. They prefer—while offending God—to spend their substance on packs of shameless dogs or obscure pimps <note>original: *lenones*—pimps or procurers; the author is criticizing the wealthy who spend money on vice and hunting animals rather than charity.</note>, rather than contributing to the needy members of Christ <note>A theological term for the poor, based on the doctrine that the poor represent the physical presence of Christ's body on earth.</note> with the greatest gain for their own souls. This sentiment is confirmed by the authority of Holy Scripture: *Judgment is without mercy to him who has shown no mercy.* <note>original: "Iudicium illi sine misericordia, qui non præstitit misericordiam." — James 2:13.</note> Therefore, these people are also worthy of this vengeance.

<margin>12</margin>
Nor are those of the third kind to be held in any better regard. Rather, their condition is worse, because they not only fail to help the wretched according to their means, but they actually make the wretched more wretched, adding wounds to wounds and evils to evils. Since their guilt is equal—or even heavier—should their penalty and punishment be any lighter?

...[is punished], so that this type of punishment may be avenged among others; thus it is fitting that the living understand (and they understand by this wretched return) that these are their just penalties. Thus they recognize in reality that God is a strict observer of His own laws: that the laws of charity are pressing, that the laws of humanity toward neighbors must not be violated, that the poor must not be oppressed, and that mercy must be shown to the wretched.

**14** The things we have mentioned—the troubles caused by the Spirits who return—are sins. Sometimes the Spirits themselves are not the cause; rather, the sins of the living deserve that they should have to endure the hauntings of these Spirits. *And some things have been established as the cause of the faults and punishments they [the spirits] endure—either on the part of those living or from the damned Spirits themselves; or at other times, these hauntings serve as evidence of the extreme cruelty inflicted upon those now damned.*

**15** Is the vengeance of the *former* group <note>The "former" refers to those spirits returning due to their own specific sins, as categorized in the previous section (the impious, the unmerciful, and the oppressors).</note> unjust? It is most just. For since they were companions in the faults of these wretched souls <note>original: *miseris*</note> and were, in a way, the authors of the most grievous punishments they suffer, is it not fitting that these wretched ones should take revenge and cause trouble—through stirred-up disturbances and other means, so to speak—against those for whose sake they must endure perpetual misery in hell?

**16** Likewise, the vengeance against the *latter* group <note>The "latter" refers to those who were victims (the seduced and the murdered) whose return is a judgment upon the living who harmed them.</note> is not unjust. Even if the offenses of the deceased do not deserve this return, the established proofs of the extreme cruelty of the living toward them do deserve it. God is accustomed to take notice of such things for these reasons: so that the more He desires charity and mutual love to be recommended to mortals, the more types of vengeance (and especially this return) might make all understand that He is offended if that love is violated.

**17** It would not be difficult to provide examples of both. But what is the need? Many have been cited by us in the first Chapter of our present Disputation <note>The author uses "Disputation" (Latin: *Disputatio*) to refer to this formal theological or philosophical treatise.</note>. Not a few are also observed in the remainder of the Disputation. Nor are the curious lacking daily examples, which we prefer to be noted by others rather than presented by us in this place.

**18** Therefore, to summarize what has been said at length, *there are roughly five types of damned human Spirits who return to the living more frequently and easily, and who cause disturbances:* they are those impious toward parents; the unmerciful; the oppressors of the poor; those wretchedly seduced; and those cruelly murdered.

**19** The first three return because of their own crimes; the last two because of the crimes of people still living. It follows that the former cease their haunting if those they have returned to trouble depart from this life; the latter are not bound to specific people, and can be troublesome now to some, now to others...

## CHAPTER IX.

*Whether Spirits are always present to the living in their own persons while they cause disturbances; and it is shown that some from every kind are sometimes present.*

<margin>1</margin>There are two ways to understand how a Spirit is present to the living through the troubles they bring: namely, either <term>autoprosopos<note>original: "autoprosopos" (Greek: αὐτοπρόσωπος). A technical term meaning "in one's own person" or "personally."</note></term>, that is, in their own person, or <term>heteroprosopos<note>original: "hetroprosopos" (Greek: ἑτεροπρόσωπος). Meaning "in the person of another" or "by proxy."</note></term>, in the person of another. Just as someone can maintain a dual persona—their own or someone else's—so they can be said to be present, manifest themselves, and be troublesome either in their own or another's persona.

<margin>2</margin>Therefore, regarding the Spirits believed to bring troubles to mortals, the question is: Whenever they intervene in mortal affairs and cause trouble, are they always present in their **own person**—performing what is observed while they themselves are present—or is it not they, but others who perform whatever is done in their name, and who for this reason can be said to take on and bear their persona?

<margin>3</margin>The primary question concerns *human Spirits. Regarding Demons, the matter is so certain to some that they have fallen into the suspicion that all troubles are brought about by these [demons] alone, and none by human Spirits. [They believe] human Spirits are so confined to their own places that they are never permitted to depart from there. Consequently, whenever Spirits are seen or cause trouble to the senses of the living under a human form that is recognized, they believe it is always that [a demon acting in their stead].*

And this opinion has notable authors, according to the testimony of Maldonado <note>Juan de Maldonado (1533–1583), a highly influential Spanish Jesuit theologian and biblical commentator.</note>, on Luke 16. For Chrysostom in the final *Homily on Lazarus* and several other places; Tertullian in his book *On the Soul*; and Athanasius, or whoever is the author of the *Questions to Antiochus*, questions 11 and 12; and Isidore in Book 8 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 9; and Theophylact on Matthew 8, all utterly deny that the souls of the dead ever return to the living.

Furthermore, they provide many reasons why such a thing would not be appropriate. First, that it is not useful to the living; for if they do not believe the living, they will not even believe the dead, as Abraham responds to the rich man <note>A reference to the Parable of Dives and Lazarus in Luke 16:31: "If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead."</note>. Secondly, because even if men were to see the punishments of the damned with their own eyes, they would not abstain from their sins any more than before.

### ON HAUNTED PLACES
<meta>catchword: were,</meta>

...[stayed there]. <note>original: "remanerunt" - This completes the sentence from the previous page's final thought.</note>

"Every day," says **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father known for his powerful preaching and skepticism regarding the literal return of ghosts.</note>, "they see thieves and other criminals led to their executions; yet they involve themselves in the very same sins for which those men are being punished." Furthermore, if [the return of spirits] were to happen regularly, over the course of time the matter would fall into contempt; and the dead would no more remind us [of our mortality] than the living do, as **Chrysostom** says in the same place. Finally, such a thing could be the cause of many errors; while a **Demon**, pretending to be the soul of some deceased person, might deceive people and persuade them of whatever he wished, as **Tertullian**, **Chrysostom**, and **Athanasius** argue. FOR even though we know, says **Chrysostom**, that the souls of the dead do not return, the **Demon** often takes on the persona of deceased souls through quiet and dreams—the only way he can. What would he do if he knew that souls actually did return? So say the Fathers. What say we?

4 We freely grant to these [Fathers] that *the spirits of Demons return to the upper world in their own person* <term>autoprosopos<note>original: "autoprosopos" (Greek: αὐτοπρόσωπος). Meaning "in one's own person" or "personally."</note></term>, and are troublesome to those who live there. Reason teaches that this is possible. Daily examples prove it. The common consensus of everyone agrees on this point. Nor is there any reason to demonstrate the contrary.

5 We also grant them this: *That human spirits are not always present*, even at those times when they seem entirely to be so. In how many ways can Demons deceive human senses? How often do they present now these people, now those, when in fact neither are present in their own person <note>original: "autoprosopos"</note>? How often do they stir up disturbances and tragedies which are caused by the demons themselves as the authors, and yet are attributed to human spirits?

6 Now these **Wicked Ones** transform themselves into Angels of light; now they simulate the person of God; now that of holy men, as has been said elsewhere. And if they can fashion and disguise themselves in the persona of these, will they not also be able to do so with the spirits of men—whether of those needing purification <note>original: "purgandorum," referring to souls in Purgatory.</note> or those who are damned?

7 The power of Demons is no less than that of the good Angels (if we consider what they possess by the benefit of their nature). But it is as certain as anything can be that Angels have taken on the persona of men, of Christ, and of God. Why, then, should Demons not sometimes represent the persona of spirits to be purified or of damned men?

8 The most blessed **Augustine**, in his book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 13, proves exactly what we are proving, and concludes from it: *that it has been proven by certain experience that the same spirit has sometimes appeared at the same time in different and greatly distant places; yet in those places, one could not easily say that the spirit itself was truly there in person.* And who would say that those spirits are present or involved in the affairs of the living in their own person <note>original: "autoprosopos"</note>, whom **Necromancers** <note>Practitioners of magic who claim to summon the dead.</note> believe they recall to the living? Reference is to his *Summa Theologica*.</note> [Summa Theologica] Part 1, Question 89, Article 8, reply to the second objection.

<margin>9</margin>
However, even though these things are so, it still must not be said that *human spirits—whether those to be purged or the damned—never, or in person <note>original: "prosopos" — from the Greek, meaning "personally" or "in their own likeness."</note>, return to the upper world and trouble the living with raised commotions and noise.* Or perhaps they are not permitted to leave the places to which they were destined based on their merits? Or are they permitted to leave, but hindered by the weakness of their strength, so that they cannot leave? Or if both this is possible and that is allowed, would they return to the living in vain, because they could have no communion, neither pleasant nor adverse, with them?

<margin>10</margin>
First, it should not be said [that they are forbidden]. The entire capacity for leaving these places has not been taken from them. The proper place of the Celestial Spirits, or the good Angels, is Heaven; no less than Purgatory is for those being purged, and Hell <note>original: "Infernus"</note> for the damned. Nevertheless, these [Angels] care for us on earth. The same Heaven is the proper place for happy souls; and yet **St. Jerome** <note>Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a Church Father best known for translating the Bible into Latin.</note> considers it unworthy to shut them up in heaven. *Do you,* he says against Vigilantius <note>Vigilantius was a priest who opposed the veneration of martyrs; Jerome wrote a famous polemic against him.</note>, *cast chains upon the Apostle, so that they are forced to be held in custody until the day of judgment? And again: Since the Devil and Demons wander everywhere through the whole world, why should the Martyrs be held enclosed after the shedding of their blood?*

<margin>11</margin>
Perhaps this power is granted to them because they are happy, but denied to those being purged and the damned because they are unhappy. But the Demons are no less unhappy, whose proper place is Hell; who yet, as **St. Jerome** says, wander through the whole world. Furthermore, just as the happiness of the former is not situated in the fact that they can be anywhere, so neither is the unhappiness of the latter in this: that they are confined to only one place. The former are happy in the vision of God <note>original: "visione Dei" — The "Beatific Vision," the direct perception of God enjoyed by those in Heaven.</note>, wherever they may act; the latter are unhappy in the punishments of the infernal fire, which they carry around with them wherever they go.

<margin>12</margin>
I know that by the law and sentence of Christ, Purgatory is destined for those to be purged, and Hell for the damned spirits: but that sentence admits exceptions, just as every law and every sentence of Princes does. The public good is always intended by the legislator. If this can be obtained by setting aside the law, the reason for the law is not held to be great.

<margin>13</margin> Second, it must not be said that *Human spirits are not hindered by the weakness of their powers, such that they are less able to leave their own places.* Granted, let the punishment they endure be most heavy; yet it does not break or weaken the strength of these wretched ones. They are burned by fire, but not consumed; they are tortured, but they do not die. Therefore, since the *faculty of movement* <note>original: "se mouendi facultas" — The inherent ability of a soul to move itself, a key concept in Aristotelian and Scholastic physics.</note>, which exists in all spirits, is not lacking in them, they will not be prohibited by any lack of strength from returning to us.

<margin>14</margin> And we do not wish this to be said only of those spirits who are to be transferred eventually to the heavenly dwellings <note>The author refers here to souls in Purgatory who will eventually enter Heaven.</note>. Our discourse encompasses all the spirits of damned men as well; even those who departed from this life at a tender age <note>i.e., infants or young children.</note>. Though they did not have the ability here to carry about their own bodies, in which they were, so to speak, clothed; once they are freed from their bodies, they are easily able to move themselves here and there.

<margin>15</margin> Furthermore, even if all or some spirits were destitute of strength, they could nonetheless be present in the affairs of the living <term>autoprofopos</term> <note>original: "autoprofopos" — A Latinization of the Greek "autoproprosopos," meaning "in one's own person" or "personally," rather than through a demonic proxy.</note>. Could they not be moved by the work of others? If the damned, immediately upon departing their bodies, are snatched by demons to the underworld; if those to be purged are led by good angels to the places of purgatory; what is to stop either group from being brought back to the places of the living by those same beings?

<margin>16</margin> Perhaps these spirits can have no communion with the living, and for that reason, one should not believe they return, as they would come in vain. This third impediment was suggested above, but it too is nothing. *They can have communion with the living, and indeed, no small amount.* Why so? They can show themselves to the living in the bodies they carry about; they can excite commotions; they can inflict distress; they can perform many similar things, which we will follow up more fully in Chapter 13.

<margin>17</margin> And even if they themselves had no communion, there could still be great and weighty reasons why *God, the Best and Greatest* <note>original: "Deus Opt. Max." — Short for "Deus Optimus Maximus," a common epithet for God borrowed from the Roman title for Jupiter.</note>, would wish them to return to the living *in person*. These reasons would have no place if every specter that is seen were a demon; if every commotion that is stirred up were excited by demons; or if every distress inflicted had demons as its authors. It is not necessary to repeat these causes here, as we have pursued them elsewhere.

<margin>18</margin> There is nothing, therefore, that prevents *these spirits from being present in person in the affairs of mortals or the living.* What of the fact that many things show they have been present quite often? For this matter, I omit the common voice of the people and the most grave opinion of learned men...

## CHAPTER X.

->*Which of the troublesome Spirits are present in the affairs of the living in their own person more frequently, and which more rarely.*<-

<margin>21</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' with floral and foliate motifs.</image-desc>
That which we can attain through conjecture and reason regarding the proposed question, we conclude in three parts: the spirits of Demons are present in the affairs of the living <term>autoprosopos</term> most frequently; the spirits of those to be purged <note>Those undergoing purification in Purgatory.</note> more rarely; and the spirits of damned men most rarely. In proving these points, the same reasons serve us here as those we used above in Chapter Five to teach that these last spirits are most rarely troublesome, the second more frequently, and the first most frequently of all.

<margin>22</margin>
Regarding the spirits of Demons, the matter is clear through many arguments. First, because even when many human spirits are present, the demons themselves are not absent; and very often they cause trouble both in their own private name and in the name of human spirits, when it is entirely necessary for them to be present in their own person.

3 **Next**, whenever Spirits are seen in the form of brute animals, or whenever monsters are displayed, there is no doubt that the Spirits of Demons are present <term>autoprosopos</term> <note>original: "autoprosopo" — appearing in their own person or distinct identity, from the Greek "auto-" (self) and "prosopon" (face/mask).</note>. These forms are not suitable for human spirits; however, for many and just reasons, they are suitable for the Spirits of Demons. Indeed, how often are <term>Specters</term> <note>original: "Spectra" — visible apparitions or ghosts.</note> seen in these forms?

4 **Thirdly**, very often the living endure such great and such specific troubles during infestations by spirits that it seems impossible for them to be inflicted by the power of human spirits. Here, if human spirits are sometimes present <term>in their own person</term>, certainly the Spirits of Demons are not far away.

5 If we now consider the nature of Demons, what we assert will be understood more clearly. They themselves desire to be troublesome to the living; therefore, they wish to be present to them. Of deceased men, some (that is, the damned) prefer to remain unknown to people; others, though they do not flee from being known, would nonetheless prefer not to be troublesome if they could explain their needs by other means. Therefore, those who are troublesome, and who desire to make their condition known, will for the most part be Demons.

6 God can also will that these same beings very often involve themselves in the affairs of mortals, partly because of the grave sins that must be punished in the wicked, and partly for the spiritual progress of the righteous, whose virtue He is accustomed to exercise through the agency of Demons. For He accomplishes both—though for different reasons—through infesting Demons, on account of many causes.

7 For in the punishment of the sins of the wicked, mortals understand the gravity of their sins: that their defects and errors are not hidden from God in heaven; the extreme misery of the life to come; and their own most unhappy condition unless they repent. Finally, they learn that the things recorded in the <term>Sacred Pages</term> <note>The Holy Scriptures or the Bible.</note> concerning the most severe torments to be inflicted by Demons in the future life are not to be regarded as mere fables, since they observe and experience evidence for them—however slight—even in this life.

8 They can understand these same things in the testing of the righteous. But beyond that, they may understand what was most truly said by the Apostle: *“The Devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.”* <note>A reference to the New Testament, 1 Peter 5:8.</note> This, I say, they can understand when he attacks us not only through ambushes and in secret, but also openly assaults and agitates us with infestations, troubles, and terrors.

9 Hence, so many examples of demonic infestations have been recorded in writing and handed down to posterity, not only by Church writers but also by secular authors. Hence in our own times—if not among the righteous, whose number is smaller—certainly among the wicked, there are now the mockeries and now the infestations of Demons.

# PART ONE

Furthermore, just as Demonic Spirits are very frequent, so the Spirits of damned humans are very rarely present <term>autoprosopos</term> <note>original: "autoprosopos" — appearing in their own person or distinct identity, rather than through a disguise or a demonic proxy.</note>. For they have no reasons why they should strive to return to the living; nor are there just reasons found why God, Most High and Great, would want them to return repeatedly; nor are they forced to return more frequently by the Demons, under whose power they reside. Since we have taught these things above, there is no need to repeat them here.

<margin>11.</margin>
But *Spirits to be purged* <note>original: "Spiritus purgandi" — souls in Purgatory undergoing purification before entering Heaven.</note> involve themselves in the affairs of the living not so rarely <term>in their own person</term>. For the same causes that prevent the Spirits of the damned from returning, provoke these ones to return. Pride keeps the damned away; but these Spirits are the pupils of humility; and they do not suffer a loss of honor through this return; or if they do, they do not value it as much as the good which they rejoice in the hope of attaining.

<margin>12.</margin>
A great *good* of their own is set before them: namely, freedom from the heaviest punishments; the damned cannot hope for this. Wherefore these, not the others, acknowledge the singular mercy of God in this return of theirs. There is also a *good* for others set before them to whom they show themselves; they partly instruct these people about the punishments of the future life; and partly they invite them to spiritual works of mercy, to their own great benefit. Neither purpose applies to the damned, though the former sometimes happens.

<margin>13.</margin>
*God, Most High and Great,* will also want them to return to us more often, not only for the causes already mentioned, but also because He holds them in the place of children, and deems them worthy that He might eventually exhibit more abundant proofs of His mercy toward them. But these things are not suitable for the Spirits of damned men.

<margin>14.</margin>
Nor are these Spirits bound to purgatorial places by the same necessity as those are bound to hell. A not-insignificant argument for this is that the damned have no hope of eventually leaving Hell; while these are most certain that they cannot be confined to purgatorial places forever.

<margin>15.</margin>
The *confession* of the Spirits themselves, who for the most part cause trouble, confirms these things. For many, adjured by exorcisms to reveal who they are or for what reasons they have returned to the living, have explained their misery and confessed that they are present for the sake of obtaining <term>suffrages</term> <note>original: "suffragia" — intercessory prayers, masses, or pious acts offered by the living to shorten a soul's time in Purgatory.</note>; and they have given credit to their words, because

### CHAPTER XI.

->*Whether, and by what means, it may be established that human spirits are personally present in the affairs of the living.*<-

<margin>1.</margin> It is not our intention in this place to explain what signs reveal the presence of human spirits; that belongs to the second part of this Disputation, and is taught there in many chapters. Instead, we must investigate by what signs it can be detected that a spirit is <term>personally present</term> <note>original: "autoprosopos" — appearing in one's own person or distinct identity, rather than through a proxy or representation.</note> in the affairs of the living. There is a great difference between human spirits being *present* and being *personally present*. They can be present, and yet not be present in their own person.

<margin>2.</margin> Nor should this seem strange to anyone, because even the spirits of blessed men who dwell with Christ in heaven are often read to be involved in the affairs of mortals; yet even then, they are not to be said to have been <term>personally present</term>. Regarding this, St. Augustine, in his book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 13, considers it no small argument that the same spirit has been proven by certain experience to have appeared sometimes at the same time in different and greatly distant places; in which places no one would easily say that the spirit was there <term>personally</term>.

<margin>3.</margin> And certain apparitions of Christ support our view here. He is often read to have been present to some, yet he was not <term>personally present</term>. Francisco Suárez, the most learned theologian of our Society <note>The Society of Jesus, or Jesuits.</note>, in Volume 2 of his commentary on the third part of St. Thomas Aquinas's *Disputation* 51, Section 4, thinks this happened in roughly two ways. Namely, either through a purely imaginary vision—*the kind*, he says, *of apparition believed to have been made to St. Martin; and similar ones which are recorded as happening in dreams, as Eusebius mentions regarding Constantine in Book 1 of his "Life," chapter 23, and as Socrates mentions in Book 1 of his "History," chapter 2, and as Epiphanius relates concerning a certain Joseph in "Against Heresies," 30.* Or through an external and visible representation in some body made of air, in the same manner that the Divine Word <note>The Logos, or Christ before the Incarnation.</note> used to appear in human form long ago before the Incarnation. *And in this way, the apparitions made to St. Carpus and St. Anthony can be explained, and much more so others which are read to have been made to St. Bridget, Catherine of Siena, and others of that kind.* Thus says Suárez.

<margin>4.</margin> Therefore, our spirits—that is, the spirits of the damned and of those to be purged—can also be said to have been involved in the affairs of the living, and yet not be <term>personally present</term> but <term>present through another</term> <note>original: "hetroprosopos" (a variation of heteroprosopos) — appearing through a representation, a proxy, or in a form other than one's own.</note>. For this reason, it must be concluded from one set of arguments that human spirits were involved in the affairs of the living and that disturbances and commotions are to be attributed to them; and from another set of arguments that human spirits are <term>personally present</term> and are themselves the authors of those commotions and disturbances.

<header>PART ONE.</header>

<margin>5.</margin> Furthermore, as is common in many matters, it is easier to demonstrate what things are *not* than what they *are*, and what does *not* happen rather than what *does*. This principle applies here above all. It is not difficult to show when spirits are not <term>personally present</term> <note>original: "autoprosopos" — appearing in one's own person or identity.</note> in the affairs of the living; it is more difficult to teach when they *are* personally present.

<margin>6.</margin> Here, the *form* in which spirits are seen is deceptive; because in whatever way they appear, that appearance can be attributed to spirits other than human ones. The *disturbance* is deceptive; because all disturbances, of whatever kind they may be, can have angelic spirits as their authors. The *times* and *places* where and by whom the troubles are perceived are deceptive; because there are almost no places forbidden to those same angelic spirits. Why say more? Whatever might seem unique to human spirits can almost always be matched by angelic ones.

<margin>7.</margin> Nor can a spirit’s own *confession*, by which they might testify that they are human, give us certain faith. What if they are not human, but a lie of the demons who claim this? And even if they were human, how will it be certain whether they are <term>souls to be purified</term> <note>original: "purgandine" — referring to souls in Purgatory who require purification before entering heaven.</note> or are damned? For although the former can neither wish to lie nor be able to, lies are not foreign to the latter, who act as the companions of demons.

<margin>8.</margin> Therefore, it must be firmly established that it cannot be *certainly* known by the living which of the troubling spirits are <term>personally present</term> and which are <term>acting through another</term> <note>original: "heteroprosopos" — acting through a proxy, mask, or different persona.</note> when they are troublesome and involve themselves in human affairs.

<margin>9.</margin> Nevertheless, it is *more easily* believed of some that they are personally present; namely, those who return from places of purgation and ask for the <term>suffrages</term> <note>original: "suffragia" — prayers, masses, or charitable acts offered by the living to lessen the temporal punishment of souls in Purgatory.</note> of the living. Just as it has been shown that it is *easier* for these to return to the living and to return *personally* than it is for the spirits of damned men; so it is more easily believed that they are present to us in person if their presence is ever detected by certain evidence.

<margin>10.</margin> And what is to prevent them from being present in their *own person* and explaining their needs? They are not forbidden by the command of demons, for demons have no power over these spirits. They are not deprived of the ministry of angels in this work, for angels are most ready to offer their service to the beloved friends of God. Nor would God wish them to set forth their needs in another's person rather than their own; for He who wishes them to be helped by the protection of others must be judged not to forbid them from pleading for that protection in their own person.

<margin>11.</margin> Perhaps they are forbidden from leaving the place to which they are assigned. But neither the damned, nor those who reign in heaven with Christ, are so enclosed in their places that they cannot leave at times...

...sometimes they are not permitted, as has been demonstrated elsewhere.

<margin>12.</margin> Let it be established, then, that it is very likely that the spirits of humans still being purified <note>original: "purgandorum" — referring to souls in Purgatory who require cleansing before heaven</note> are present in their own person, if they ever happen to return to the living and take part in human affairs.

### CHAPTER XII.

->*Whether human spirits know what is being done, either by themselves or in their place by Angels (both good and bad), when they are said to be involved in the affairs of the living.*<-

<margin>1.</margin> <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting two scholars seated in a study.</image-desc>Certain passages of Scripture cause difficulty in the proposed question; these seem to strip away all knowledge entirely from the spirits of the deceased. For in Psalm 145 <note>original: "Pfal. 145" — in the Vulgate numbering used here; in modern Bibles, this is Psalm 146:4</note> it is said: *On that day* (namely, when their spirits have departed from the person and returned to their earth) *all their thoughts shall perish*. And Solomon, in Ecclesiastes chapter 9, teaches that *among the dead there will be neither wisdom nor knowledge. Even a living dog is better than a dead lion; because the living know they will die, but the dead know nothing more.*

<margin>2.</margin> The most blessed Augustine increases this difficulty; in his book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead, chapter 13*, he asserts that the souls of the deceased—even those of the saints—do not know what is happening among the living. He believes he is supported first by what is said in Isaiah 63: *Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not recognize us.* Then, he cites the second book of Kings <note>original: "4. Reg. 2" — following the older naming convention where 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings were called 1, 2, 3, and 4 Kings. This citation refers to 2 Kings 22:20</note> regarding the promise the Lord made to King Josiah: *I will gather you to your fathers, and you shall be gathered to your tomb in peace; so that your eyes may not see all the evils that I am about to bring upon this place.*

<margin>3.</margin> These points apply to all spirits of the dead, however they may return to us; yet they are most relevant to those who take part in human affairs <term>through another’s form</term> <note>original: "heteroprosopos" — from Greek, meaning acting through a different face or persona, such as an angel representing a soul</note>. For if the blessed spirits are ignorant of what happens among the living, how will the wretched ones know? Even if they are involved in human affairs <term>in their own person</term> <note>original: "autoprosopos" — from Greek, meaning appearing in one's own proper person or identity</note>, how will they know if they are acting <term>through another's form</term>?

<margin>4.</margin> We could extend this debate to every kind of human spirit, even those who are happy and reign with God in heaven; but we do not wish to step beyond the boundaries we have set for ourselves: we do—

# PART ONE.
<sig>F 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: Et quid; pencil number: 185</meta>

faith <note>original: "di:", likely completing the word "fidei" from the previous page</note>: we are content with our own arguments. Concerning our own—that is, the spirits to be purified <note>original: "purgandis" — souls in Purgatory</note> and those who are damned—it must be determined: Whether they know what is happening, either by themselves or in their name by Angelic Spirits, while they are involved in the affairs of the living.

<margin>5.</margin>
Because it happens that they are involved in our affairs in two ways; both through another’s persona <term>heteroprosopos: appearing in the form or identity of another, such as an angel or demon masking as the deceased</term> and in their own persona <term>autoprosopos: appearing in their own actual person</term>; first it must be determined whether they know what is happening when they are present through another’s persona; then, whether they know the same when they are present in their own persona.

<margin>6.</margin>
At the beginning, it must be established here that those who wish these Spirits to be devoid of all knowledge as soon as they have laid down their bodies are involved in a grave error. What? Do they perhaps think that souls perish at the same time as the body? But if they do not perish, do they exercise no vital operation? If indeed they do exercise such operations, what else can they do but use the intellect, which is the primary operation and without which others cannot exist?

<margin>7.</margin>
The power of understanding remains in the soul; and it is such a faculty that it does not depend on the body in its operation. Faith teaches this, and Aristotle, the Master of nature, does not oppose it. Why, then, should we call it perpetually idle and sluggish?

<margin>8.</margin>
"I could never be persuaded," says the famous Cyrus as he was dying, in Xenophon's account <note>referring to Xenophon's *Cyropaedia*</note>, "that the soul is foolish when it escapes from a foolish body." We cannot perceive the incorporeal and eternal soul as motionless and sluggish in the manner of dormice <note>original: "glirium" — referring to the belief that dormice hibernate in a state near death</note>. This is the opinion of St. Jerome, in his *Letter to Pammachius against the errors of John of Jerusalem*, concerning the soul situated outside the body.

<margin>9.</margin>
There are also examples here of the Spirits themselves on our behalf. It is said to one of them by Abraham in Luke 16: 
> *Son, remember that you received good things in your life.*
That same man also remembers his brothers and discusses many things with the same Abraham.

There are others who are introduced by Solomon (Wisdom 4) reasoning about their poorly spent lives.
> *They shall be groaning,* he says, *and their memory shall perish. Fearful, they shall come to the thought of their sins, and their iniquities shall confront them.*
These things in brief; whoever wishes for more should read Tostatus <note>Alonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), also known as Abulensis, a famously prolific Spanish theologian</note>: Abulensis on Matthew chapter 25, question 570 and following.

<margin>10.</margin>
What is it, then, someone might say, that on that day when Spirits have departed from their bodies, all their thoughts are said to perish? I respond that they are not said to perish as if there will be none in the future, but because they will not be fruitful in the future. Their thoughts are said to perish because, at the arrival of death, whatever those miserable ones thought and resolved to do will perish, nor do their plans achieve their desired ends.

<summary>This page argues against the idea that the soul becomes unconscious or "sleeps" after death, citing Aristotle, Xenophon, and St. Jerome to prove the intellect functions independently of the body. It explains that biblical references to "thoughts perishing" at death refer to the cessation of earthly plans, not the loss of awareness or memory.</summary>

### CONCERNING HAUNTED PLACES

<margin>11.</margin>
And what is to be said of the claim that among those in the underworld <note>original: "apud inferos," referring to the state of the dead or those in hell/purgatory</note>, there is said to be neither science nor wisdom? This is stated because such things bring no benefit or profit to those wretched souls, and for that reason, it will be as if these things do not exist at all. For this very reason, Solomon—the same one who denies that science and wisdom will exist in the underworld—rightly exhorts the living to work while life remains here, if they hope for fruit in the future life; let them sow here, if they wish to reap there.

<margin>12.</margin>
But the dead are said to "know nothing more" (Wisdom 9) <note>While the margin cites Wisdom 9, this sentiment is famously found in Ecclesiastes 9:5. The author argues this reflects a specific perspective.</note>. This is the voice of the impious, not that of the most wise King Solomon himself. He often speaks in the persona of the wicked, just as he does here when he *asserts that the dead know nothing after this life.*

<margin>13.</margin>
Furthermore, St. Augustine in no way allows that the spirits of deceased men have a full knowledge of the things that are done among us. Beyond the many things they know naturally, he teaches that they know certain things occurring here, not through their own power, but by the Spirit of God revealing them. He says in the same book (chapter 15): *The spirits of the dead can, by the revealing Spirit of God, know some things that happen here—those things which it is necessary for them to know; and those things which are not necessary for them to know, they do not know.*

<margin>14.</margin>
Let it therefore be established that the spirits of deceased men are not entirely devoid of cognition. But do they know our affairs, and the things done through them, while they are said to be involved in our business? We answer that they do not know our affairs—not even those things done among the living in their own names—nor do they know them because they are present in the affairs of the living by their own power, or even that they *can* know them; if they know anything, they know it only because a revelation has been made to them from elsewhere. And we wish this to be said of them while they are <term>heteroprosopoi</term> <note>original: "heteroprosopoi" — appearing under the mask or persona of another, such as an angel or demon masquerading as the deceased</note> involved in the affairs of the living; for the things that occur are performed not by the souls themselves, but through Angelic Spirits.

<margin>15.</margin>
We do not deny that those spirits know many things; indeed, they know by their own power and naturally. They know the spirits of other men; they also know the celestial spirits <note>i.e., angels</note>, although they know the former perfectly and the latter imperfectly. This follows St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, as cited by Gregory of Valencia (in Question 89 of St. Thomas, Article 2, First Part). They know natural things, though in a confused and general way, as St. Thomas notes in the same article. They also know things distinctly from the natural world to which they had a specific habituation while they were in their bodies, whether through knowledge, affection, or some bond of necessity. On this, one should read St. Thomas (Article 4) and Tostatus of Avila <note>Alfonso Tostado, a prolific 15th-century Spanish bishop and scholar</note> on Matthew 15, Questions 185, 186, 187, etc.

<margin>16.</margin>
We also do not deny that through the revelation of Angelic Spirits, they are able to know both our affairs and the things done in their names among the living. For can spirits not speak to one another? And human...

<meta>This page continues the scholastic investigation into how the souls of the deceased perceive the world. While the previous page established that the dead do not naturally know everything happening on Earth, this page explores the mechanism of their knowledge—specifically whether they rely on "mental images" from their past life or messages delivered by angels.</meta>

# PART ONE
<meta>handwritten number 126 in upper right corner; catchword: And who-</meta>

Are angelic matters known to human spirits? Or are most of the things that occur among us unknown to spirits—whether they be demons or good angels?

<margin>17.</margin>
Whether angelic spirits reveal our affairs to the dead, and whether the dead later understand the things angels do in their name among the living, will be discussed later. For now, we consider this certain: unless angels reveal it to them, human spirits—whether they are damned or in purgatory <note>original: "purgandi," those who must be purified</note>—cannot know these things.

<margin>18.</margin>
This is easily understood from the way spirits separated from the body perceive things. St. Thomas Aquinas (Part 1, Question 84, Article 1, Response 1) says this knowledge is twofold: they understand either through <term>species</term> <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "species" are the mental representations or concepts that allow the mind to recognize an object.</note> which they acquired for themselves during this life, or through others which God infuses into them once they have left their bodies. However, they do not bring with them from this life the mental images of our current affairs, including those performed by angels in their name. Nor does God infuse the images of these same things into them once they are separated from the body. How then do they understand either our affairs or what the angels perform in their name?

<margin>19.</margin>
Perhaps they carry the mental images of these things with them from this life? They do not. The images they carry with them are abstracted from things already past and represent those past events; for that reason, they can serve to recall the past, but not future or present events, which are what we are discussing here.

<margin>20.</margin>
Furthermore, who would believe that God infuses new mental images into spirits as soon as they leave their bodies—especially concerning these matters for which there is little or no use? This is particularly true since it is not necessary for spirits to know our affairs or what is done in their name among the living, or because these things can easily become known through the revelation of angels.

<margin>21.</margin>
Therefore, spirits do not know these things through their own power. We believe St. Thomas spoke to this opinion in Part 1, Question 89, Article 8, Response 2. His words are these:

> Apparitions of this kind occur through the works of good or even evil angels, even while the dead are ignorant of them; just as the living, without knowing it, appear to others in their dreams, as Augustine teaches in his book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 10. Thus says Thomas.

<margin>22.</margin>
But do they have through the revelation of angels (who perform their ministries here) that which they do not have from themselves? We believe they do, for the most part. For there would be no punishment for the damned spirits, nor any solace for those in purgatory—things which should not be said—if they were unaware that they were participating in the affairs of the living, even if through the persona of another. And so much for the first point.

<margin>23.</margin>
It remains for us to teach whether, when they are present <term>in their own person</term> <note>original Greek: "autoprosopos"</note> in the affairs of the living, they both know our circumstances and realize they are participating in them, and whether they recognize the things done by angelic spirits in their name or for their sake.

<summary>This page argues that deceased souls cannot naturally perceive the living world because their mental concepts are rooted in the past; instead, any knowledge they have of current events must be revealed to them by angels.</summary>

<margin>24.</margin> And indeed, there is no doubt that they can know all these things through the revelation of others. For their condition is no worse when they are present to the living <term>in their own person</term> <note>original: "autoprosopos," a Greek-derived term meaning appearing as themselves</note> than when they are present <term>through another person</term> <note>original: "heteroprosopos," appearing in the guise of another, or through a medium</note>. Therefore, if they can know these things in the latter state, they can also know them in the former through the revelation of other spirits.

<margin>25.</margin> But do they know things by their own natural power? A single answer cannot satisfy the question posed, because it is not one thing being asked, but many.

<margin>26.</margin> First, therefore, if they ever return to the living in their own person, *they cannot be unaware that they are returning.* Can they be ignorant that they are passing from place to place? Or that they are where they actually exist? Where they act? Where they suffer? Where they stir up commotions? Where they are troublesome?

<margin>27.</margin> But yet (as should be said in the second place) *they do not understand by themselves all the affairs of the living to which they return. While they are present through another, they do not understand our affairs; this is because they lack the "species" <note>mental representations or images of objects</note> and likenesses of things; they are likewise deprived of these even when they are present in their own person: and furthermore, many of their own affairs can be hidden from them.*

<margin>28.</margin> Thus (as we wish to be said in the third place) *they do not always understand whatever the angelic spirits perform in their name*. These matters are varied, just as will be explained by us in the twenty-fifth chapter. And some things indeed they know by their own power, others not at all; however, for the most part, they have knowledge through the revelation of the angels who, as it were, serve them. But these matters belong more to the <term>Schools</term> <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the medieval method of theological and philosophical instruction practiced in universities.</note>.

# CHAPTER XIII.

## Concerning the causes and goals which are proposed for God, as well as for Spirits and Specters, in haunted places.

<margin>1.</margin> The causes and goals for which places are haunted by spirits must be sought either from the will of God or from the will of the spirits. In this chapter, we inquire into what is intended either by Him or by them. But because there are three kinds of haunting spirits, it must be explained whether they all seek the same thing, or something else.

<margin>2.</margin> And although this matter does not entirely surpass human intelligence, it nevertheless holds some difficulty; because we are here examining the reasons and causes of the will of God, of men, and of demons; since we cannot perceive these things in themselves, it is necessary that we pursue them by conjecture from other things. We shall make a beginning, however, with human spirits.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into why spirits return to the world of the living. While the previous page discussed whether spirits possess natural knowledge of human affairs, this page categorizes the types of spirits that "haunt" or disturb the living and explains their differing motivations—either seeking spiritual aid or intending pure malice.</meta>

# PART ONE. 49

<margin>4.</margin> **There are two types of these spirits. One consists of those to be cleansed <note>original: "purgandorum," referring to souls in Purgatory</note>; the other, of the damned.** Just as the condition of each group is different, so too are their goals, wherever they are found testing and troubling mortals.

<margin>5.</margin> For **those being cleansed**, one purpose seems intended in all their actions and the disturbances they cause: that they might be helped by the deeds of the living <note>Such as prayers, alms, or the Sacrifice of the Mass</note>. For the commotions they stir up are not in themselves any relief for their own punishments—this fact is clear enough. Nor do they desire to inconvenience or be a nuisance to the living, for they are good spirits. Neither is it their primary aim to deter the living from vice or rouse them to the study of virtue by these means; for in this regard, Moses, the Prophets, and other methods serve the living. They are, therefore, only acting for their own sake. And just as by a singular privilege of God a different place of punishment has been granted to them, apart from the common one, so also has the power been given so that, if they can, they may help themselves through the assistance of the living.

<margin>6.</margin> For the others—I mean the **spirits of damned men**—this is not the goal. There is no hope of pardon for them, nor can they be helped by any assistance from the living. These most unhappy ones know both of these facts well. Do they, then, seek to bring any benefit to others by these means? They do not. They do nothing good; they desire nothing good; they wish no one well, not even those who were once their best comrades or friends in the world. *Every will of the damned is unjust,* says Blessed Gregory in the 8th book of his *Moralia*, chapter 7. What, then, do they seek through their hauntings? Almost the very same thing as their companions, the Demons. Just as both share the same society and condition, so they share nearly the same pursuits: the most unhappy goals of the most unhappy beings.

<margin>7.</margin> And what of the **Demons?** They seek the same thing they always have, in all times, in all places, with all efforts and all pursuits which they undertake regarding humans—whether of their own accord or by God’s command. Just as they are always enemies of human salvation and safety, so through these terrors which they stir up in various places, they earnestly seek the trouble and destruction of mankind, and beyond this, hardly anything else. They are always the most wicked of villains.

<margin>8.</margin> These terrors bring them no relief in the punishments they endure, which are very great. What is more, they do not even take joy or pleasure from them, though they may seem to "smile" upon wicked spirits. Just as happy minds <note>the blessed in Heaven</note> perceive no trouble or pain even from the most adverse events, so these miserable spirits perceive no pleasure from prosperous ones. The sorrow of the unhappy is pure, unmixed with any joy. The joy of the happy is pure, unmixed with any sorrow. See the double cause of this in the writings of Luis de Molina <note>A Spanish Jesuit theologian (1535–1600)</note>, question 46, dispute 3, on the first part of Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the motivations of spirits who haunt the living. While the previous page established that the damned act out of malice and the souls in purgatory act out of a need for assistance, this page shifts focus to God's ultimate purpose in allowing or commanding such disturbances.</meta>

-># ON INFESTED PLACES<-
# PAGE 50

<margin>9.</margin> Thus, these wretched souls <note>The damned</note> desire no good for the mortals they haunt. Even if they appear to act kindly in some way, or if they seem to be helpful in certain matters, they do it entirely so that they may cause harm later. Whatever they do, or however they do it, all of it is corrupted by the evil goals they have set for themselves. This is as was said regarding Saint Gregory <note>original: "B. Gregorio," referring to Pope Gregory the Great</note> in Thesis 6 of this Chapter. What they are actually plotting in all these things will be demonstrated more fully in Chapter 15.

<margin>10.</margin> Furthermore, regarding **God**, as in all things, so too in these hauntings; His purpose is only for good: whether He merely permits it without commanding it, or whether He even commands it—regardless of which spirits are haunting the places. we teach this concerning *each individual* spirit.

<margin>11.</margin> In the case of **those being cleansed** <note>original: "purgandis," referring to souls in Purgatory</note>, He gives evidence especially of His mercy and goodness; which not only the spirits of the dead themselves experience, but even those still living. For the spirits, they are able, in this way, to beg—so to speak—for the aid of the living, and to redeem the punishments due for their sins through the pious works of others. For the living, they understand from these encounters that they must avoid sin, undertake worthy works of penance with a great heart, and not wait for the most severe punishments of the future life; finally, they are provided with the opportunity to do good and help their neighbor through pious works of mercy.

<margin>12.</margin> In the case of the **damned** spirits of perverse men, besides mercy, He also provides an example of justice. Why is this? Because through these most severe remedies and mechanisms, He urges undeserving mortals toward repentance for their sins and badly spent lives. This is of the highest mercy. And while He brings these same punishments, in a way, before the senses of men—demanding them in those very places where they were earned by the merits of sins—He proves Himself to be a most just Judge: as one who both punishes crimes and punishes them right there, with the greatest grief to the wretched, where they were usually committed with pleasure.

<margin>13.</margin> In **Demonic** hauntings, God acts in two ways. Sometimes He uses the work of demons, and by His command, places are made horrific by phantoms; other times He permits them to exercise their wickedness according to their own lust, and to display specters. Yet in both cases, it is for the benefit of men, if only they are willing. He permitted power to the Demons over Job: over his sons, his daughters, and the entire substance of that most holy man; but with how much benefit to Job? He commanded them (as is perhaps not wrongly believed) to overthrow Sodom and the neighboring peoples: and if not to them, how much fear was struck into others by their example? How many, struck by their punishment, were called back from the foul lust of sinning and followed saner counsels?

<summary>This page explains God's role in spiritual hauntings, arguing that whether He permits or commands them, His intent is always for the benefit of the living. Hauntings by souls in purgatory encourage mercy and penance, while those by the damned or demons serve as warnings of divine justice and calls to repentance.</summary>
