<margin>14.</margin>
Whatever infestations of places are carried out by the work of Demons—if we reason correctly—it is not hidden that God (by whose permission or command they occurred) looked toward human benefit. This is easily perceived both in *general* cases and in *specific* ones.

<margin>15.</margin>
In *general* cases, it is shown that beyond our physical nature, there exists a certain Spiritual nature: that this nature is most hostile to human salvation and safety; that its power over bodies and physical things is very great; and that its company and fellowship is to be avoided more than a plague or a snake.

<margin>16.</margin>
In *specific* cases, we can grasp other benefits. In those hauntings which occur in mineral mines, we may learn that those who seek riches fall into the snares of the Devil; in the story of the field of Hesperia, we learn that the power and virtue of Relics is great; in another case, regarding a haunted house liberated by Theodore, the Archimandrite <note>A title for an abbot or high-ranking monk in the Eastern tradition</note> of the Sykeotes <note>Theodore of Sykeon, a 6th-century Byzantine saint</note>, we learn that consecrated objects are most powerful against Diabolical insults. Likewise, the hauntings stirred up because of Pausanias, Nero, and Otto <note>Historical figures associated with legendary hauntings following their crimes or violent deaths</note> teach us that God is the avenger of crimes by which the laws of brotherly charity, justice, and honesty are violated. Other cases have other advantages. Consult Chapter 1 regarding all these matters.

# CHAPTER XIV.

->*That among places, some are more infested than others: and this happens not from the nature and condition of the places, but according to the will of God and the Spirits.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
Although there are almost no places that do not admit haunting Spirits, there are nevertheless many things that prove there are certain places where they are found more frequently. Once we have indicated where these are, we must then explain why this occurs.

<margin>2.</margin>

The Prophet Isaiah seems to suggest this in chapter 24 <note>Isaiah 34:14 in modern Bibles is the more likely reference</note> when he teaches that the deserted cities of the Idumeans <note>Edomites</note> will become the dwellings of Lamiae <note>original: "Lamiarum," referring here to screech owls or nocturnal monsters</note>, Demons, onocentaurs <note>mythical creatures half-man and half-donkey</note>, and the hairy ones <note>original: "pilosorum," often interpreted as satyrs or wild men</note>. The most holy John says the same in his Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, chapter 18, when he calls the deserted Babylon a habitation of Demons, as Ribera <note>Francisco de Ribera, a Jesuit theologian and commentator</note> explains in that same place. Likewise the Evangelist Matthew, in chapter 4, asserts that Christ endured the insults of the Demon in the desert. But also the inhabitants of the Wilderness <note>the Desert Fathers or early Christian hermits</note> in former times were able to observe this by their own example; in...

First among these is the aged Anthony <note>Saint Anthony the Great (c. 251–356), a central figure among the Desert Fathers</note>: concerning the specters which he *endured in the desert*, Saint Athanasius writes thus. Demons (he says, *in the Life of Anthony*) taking on the forms of beasts and serpents, immediately filled everything where the holy man was staying with phantasms of lions, bulls, wolves, asps, serpents, scorpions, as well as leopards and bears. And each of these roared according to its own nature. The Lion roared, wishing to kill; the Bull threatened with lowing and horns; the Serpents hissed aloud; the Wolves' attack was open-mouthed; the spotted Leopard indicated the various trickeries of its author <note>original: "authoris sui," referring to the Devil</note>. The faces of all were fierce, their voices horrible, and the sound dreadful. Thus far Athanasius. Concerning Anthony also, *making his way through the wilderness to Paul* <note>Saint Paul the Hermit</note>, Saint Jerome records this: He beheld a man mixed with a horse, to whom the opinion of the Poets has given the name Hippocentaur, and a little later: Amidst a rocky valley, he saw a small man-like creature with hooked nostrils and a forehead roughened with horns; the lower part of whose body ended in goat’s feet. This being answered Anthony: *I am a mortal, and one of the inhabitants of the desert, whom the heathens—deluded by various errors—worship, calling us Fauns, Satyrs, and incubi.*

For this reason, the same Jerome calls the desert *fruitful in monstrous animals*: and Cyril, in chapter 34 of *Isaiah*, says: *Evil spirits are said to dwell gladly in deserted places.* And Procopius, on chapter 13 of the same, says: *Demons themselves rejoice in deserted and uncultivated places.* Hence certain of them, when they were about to be cast out of men, requested of Saint Germanus, the Bishop of Paris, that they at least be allowed to wander through the desert solitude if they were not permitted to dwell among men. So says Fortunatus, Bishop of Poitiers, in the *Life of Saint Germanus*, chapter 30.

The example of Gordianus, a man of proven faith, whom Alexander ab Alexandro mentions in book 2, chapter 9 of *Genial Days* <note>Alexander ab Alexandro (1461–1523) was a Neapolitan humanist lawyer</note>, serves this point. When he was traveling toward Arezzo with a companion, and they had wandered far from their path through *difficult and out-of-the-way places, where they saw nothing cultivated, but only woods*; as the sun was setting and they sat down, weary from labor, they finally seemed to hear a human voice in the distance. Following it, they caught sight of the images of three men, immense and formidable beyond human measure; in black and hanging tunics, in mournful and deadly dress, with long beards and hair, and horrible faces. So says Alexander.

The example of the Admiral Adrianus Patritius <note>A Byzantine naval commander</note> also serves, whom Ioannes Curopalates <note>John Skylitzes, a 11th-century Byzantine historian</note> mentions in his *Compendium of Histories*, page 43. So says Fortunatus, Bishop of Poitiers, in the *Life of Saint Germain*, chapter 30.

Following it, they caught sight of the images of three men, immense and formidable beyond human measure; in black and low-hanging tunics, in mournful and funereal dress, with long beards and hair, and horrible faces. So says Alexander.

Finally, it provides them with the opportunity to do good and help their neighbors through pious works of mercy.

Because through these most serious remedies and "engines" <note>original: "machinis," here meaning instruments or devices of divine providence</note>, He urges undeserving mortals toward repentance for their sins and poorly spent lives. This is an act of supreme mercy. By placing these same punishments before the senses of men and demanding them in the very locations where the sins were committed, He proves Himself to be a most fair Judge—one who punishes crimes and does so with the greatest sorrow for the wretched in the very place where those crimes were usually committed with pleasure.

13. In the infestations of demons, God acts in two ways. Sometimes He uses the work of demons, and by His command, places are made terrifying by **specters** <note>original: "spectris," referring to ghosts or frightening apparitions</note>. At other times, He permits these same demons to exercise their wickedness according to their own desires and display their apparitions. Yet, in both cases, it results in the benefit of humanity, provided they are willing. He permitted the demons power over Job, his sons, his daughters, and the entire estate of that most holy man; but how great was the benefit to Job? He commanded those same spirits (as is perhaps not wrongly believed) the overthrow of Sodom and the neighboring peoples. And if there was no benefit for those destroyed, how much fear was struck into others by their example? How many, struck by their punishment and called back from the foul desire for sinning, followed more wholesome counsel?

**9.** Furthermore, there are, above all others, infested places where those who are involved in grave sins have their seats; especially those places where the laws of piety, justice, mutual charity, and honesty are enormously violated. To these places belong those where either the superstitions of the Gentiles flourish, or where true religion is exiled. How troublesome were the Demons to the worshippers of Idols? And in **Livonia**, what did the apostates from the faith not suffer?

**10.** Finally, there are those places in which men of remarkable holiness and piety dwell. Although this is more difficult to teach with recent examples, the histories of past centuries demonstrate so many examples that it would be almost a waste of time and effort to linger over recounting them. **Cassian** <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435), a monk and theologian whose "Conferences" (Collationes) were foundational for Western monasticism.</note> reports in *Conference 7, Chapter 23*, that in the very monasteries where monks once lived, in groups of eight or ten, the Demons so raged and were so frequent that they did not all dare to sleep at the same time during the nights; but by turns, while some tasted sleep, others performed vigils...

### PART ONE.

...celebrating [the rites], they were devoted to psalms, prayers, and readings. The **Deacon** <note>Referring to John the Deacon (c. 825–880), the biographer of Pope Gregory the Great.</note> teaches in the *Life* of **Blessed Gregory**, chapter 89, that the Monks also endured the greatest troubles from **Demons** where Gregory had his Oratory <note>A small chapel or private room for prayer.</note>. Similarly, at **Montserrat** <note>A mountain near Barcelona, famous for its monastery.</note>, the *Annals of Spain* report that a man who was otherwise holy and a lover of solitude, **John Garlinus**, was tempted and overcome by the snares of a Demon (who was pretending to be a hermit), and thus entangled himself in the gravest crimes of fornication and murder. This was also printed by a certain **Patricius of Augsburg** in the German language at Munich in the year 1588. One should also read **Palladius** <note>Palladius of Galatia (c. 363–420), author of the *Lausiac History*, which details the lives of early desert monks and their spiritual struggles.</note>, who provides many examples for this argument.

<margin>11.</margin> And thus far, let the first part of this chapter be explained. But how does it happen that spirits are more troublesome in these places rather than those? This must be investigated in this second section. Indeed, I believe the reason for this must be sought either from the **nature of the places** or from the **will of God and the spirits**. I do not see a third possibility to which we should attribute the cause.

<margin>12.</margin> Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "nature" of any place that would drag or demand these harassing spirits to itself. Anyone who has clearly perceived the condition of spirits and the character of places will easily understand what we say. The condition of spirits is that they are devoid of all corporeal solidness <note>In other words, they have no physical bodies.</note>; the character of places requires that they be the boundaries of physical bodies, and they are affected by the qualities of the bodies they contain. Since, therefore, there is a maximum distance <note>In a philosophical sense, a total difference in kind.</note> between a Spirit and a body, there is no reason to believe that a place, by its own power, drags any spirits to itself.

<margin>13.</margin> There is a great difference between spirits and bodies if we consider the conditions of places. Certain bodies are produced not everywhere, but only in certain, defined locations; and some are preserved and sustained only in specific places. For spirits, however, it is the same to be produced in any place; they can exist in all and be preserved in all. This is not wrongly said, because physical bodies depend on the influence and motion of the celestial spheres <note>The old astronomical belief that the movement of planets and stars physically influenced objects on Earth.</note> and the properties of the bodies surrounding them. Spirits receive no such support from these things.

<margin>14.</margin> The condition of time among spirits is the same as the condition of place. Time has power over bodies because, as the saying goes, *time makes all things grow old*; and as the poet witnesses: *we grow old with the passing of silent years* <note>original: "tacitisque senescimus annis"; a quote from the Roman poet Ovid.</note>. But time has no power over spirits. They neither grow old with time, nor do they weaken with time. They are as vigorous today, after several thousands of years have passed, as they were on the first day they were created. It is no wonder, therefore, if places likewise have no power over them.

Does the haunting <note>original: "infestatio"</note> therefore depend on the will of God, or of the Spirits of the places? It depends on both entirely. Because Spirits wish to be troublesome in certain places, and because God wills that certain places be dreadful and troubled by Spirits, they are therefore haunted and made fearful.

## CHAPTER XV.

->*For what cause and for what reasons do Spirits, especially Demonic ones, haunt these places more than others.*<-

<margin>1</margin>
In this Chapter, we do not inquire *why* places are haunted, but why *specific* places—that is, *these* rather than *those*—are haunted by Specters. The former question was explained earlier in Chapter Six; this latter point, we believe, must be demonstrated, as it is not without benefit.

<margin>2</margin>
And although one might inquire what the goal is for each individual haunting Spirit, a limit must be placed on this discourse; we shall only assign the reasons why *these Demons rather than those haunt certain places*. Indeed, what the human Spirits <note>The author distinguishes between "demons" and the "spirits of the dead" (human spirits).</note> intend, and for what causes God permits or commands these hauntings, was more than sufficiently demonstrated by what was said in Chapter Six.

<margin>3</margin>
>*What, then, is the goal of the Demons in each of these places? I answer that in all of them, they certainly aim to strike terror into men; in some places, they additionally desire to bring harm to them (whatever sort that may be, whether to the body, the soul, or to worldly goods). In other places, they strive for none of these things, but seem only to serve their own whims <note>original: "libidini." In this context, it refers to a demon's irrational desire to cause mischief or satisfy a malicious impulse.</note>.* But let us survey the individual locations mentioned in the previous chapter.

<margin>4</margin>
In deserts and places removed from human society (of which we spoke in the second thesis of the previous chapter), they serve their own whims while they haunt and stir up commotions. Lest they seem to be doing nothing while they dwell in these places, they give several signs of their craft and power through these frightful displays. Perhaps also (as we believe is probable) they cause trouble for the brute animals living in these places—acting as enemies of God and of the goods belonging to men. **Blessed Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420), a Church Father known for his translation of the Bible and biographies of early monks.</note> teaches this in the *Life of St. Hilarion* <note>St. Hilarion (291–371) was an anchorite who spent much of his life in the desert of Gaza.</note>.

What of the fact that they also strive to oppose men in these places, and either provoke them toward evil or call them away from good? In the past, when all places were full of unbelievers, they appeared in deserted locations for this reason: so that they might persuade...

<margin>9</margin>

Literally "skin-turners," a term often used for werewolves or deceptive, shape-shifting spirits.</note> seek to cast them into the pit of despair and drive them to lay cruel hands upon themselves <note>i.e., to commit suicide.</note>.

Serious crimes are deeply pleasing to them: they are often perpetrated by these demons as the authors, and they are avenged by them as the torturers. Therefore, they produce disturbances in those same places as a kind of sign of joy. They triumph over the miserable condition of mortals because of the crimes committed in those spots, and they intrusively make themselves known as if those places (where they have been vigorously served through sin) were their own by right.

<margin>11</margin>
And just as God is present in a unique way to those who serve Him and carry out His will as best they can, so too do demons freely find themselves present and testify to their presence in those places where they are served. For this reason, in Thesis 9 of Chapter 14, we placed among the **places infested by specters** those **where those who involve themselves in serious sins have their seats; but especially those in which the laws of piety, justice, brotherly charity, and honesty are more openly violated.** Thus, the Barbilian estate was infested by demons on account of the crimes of its inhabitants, as John the Deacon <note>A 9th-century monk known for writing the life of Pope Gregory the Great.</note> testifies in the *Life of St. Gregory*, Book 4, Chapter 93.

<margin>12</margin>
Why **places inhabited by holy men** are more frequently exposed to the infestation of demons (as we asserted in Thesis 10 of Chapter 14) is clear in itself. For the same reasons they persecute holy men, they also excite disturbances and infestations in whatever places they are...

## CHAPTER XVI.

### *That not all men suffer troubles from Spirits equally in all*
### *places; but some suffer more and greater troubles than*
### *others, and in what this inequality*
### *consists.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'L' featuring floral patterns and architectural elements.</image-desc>

<margin>1</margin>
It has been demonstrated that places can be infested; it has also been shown that they are infested in such a way that these hauntings and troubles reach human beings. It is now asked whether these reach everyone equally, or if some are troubled more often or more severely than others. Once we have first explained in what this inequality might consist, we will respond to the proposed question as the matter seems to stand.

<margin>2</margin>
These troubles, therefore, can differ in the manner in which they occur, or in the evils <note>Or "harms."</note> which they bring, or in the number and frequency of the acts. In the *manner*, the various methods of troubling must be considered; *In the evils*, the damages that occur to the affairs of mortals by the work of Spirits; *In the number*, the multitude and plurality of the troubles.

<margin>3</margin>
The different methods of troubling consist of these things: either only disturbances and noises are stirred up by the Spirits; or only, without noise, they present themselves to the very sight of the living; or first, they indicate their presence with some noise, and then shortly after reveal themselves to be seen. Again, all these things may happen without speech or discourse, or in such a way that the Spirits even speak. Furthermore, they may occur without any other trouble to the living than what is perceived by these acts, or with some other physical disturbance—such as if they pull the blankets off those sleeping, throw them out of bed, extinguish candles, or overturn the furniture (whatever kind it may be), and so forth.

<margin>4</margin>
The evils which they can bring are chiefly seen in two kinds of goods: those of the body and those of "fortune" <note>Historical term for one's external possessions, wealth, or status.</note>. For the Spirits cannot harm the goods of the soul against our will. Regarding the evils of the body...

<margin>5</margin> Regarding number, we have said that the plurality of troubles is considered, as well as the frequency of the acts by which they are troublesome. Therefore, Spirits must be said to be more troublesome to those who endure more of their assaults; conversely, they are less so to those who experience them either once or not so frequently. Nevertheless, it can happen that one single trouble that occurs might be judged more serious—either because of the manner in which it happens or because of the evil it brings—than many other instances where less harm is inflicted or where the Spirits are less troublesome. From these points, we measure the equality and inequality of these afflictions. Now, let us define whether **all troubles are equal for all people in all cases.**
<margin>6</margin> For this definition, the distinction we established earlier (in Chapter 2) serves us quite well; there, we stated that some places are infested *in themselves* <note>original: "per se"</note>, while others are infested *because of the people* <note>original: "propter homines"</note>. Indeed, in those places infested *because of the people*, the matter presents little or no difficulty. It is absolutely certain that in these cases, specific individuals endure more and more severe troubles. Since these places are not infested *in themselves*, but rather the infestation follows and pursues the person, who would doubt that those for whose sake the places are troubled either endure the afflictions alone or endure more and heavier ones than others?
<margin>7</margin> But in places infested *in themselves*, there seems to be one single rule and condition for all who live and spend time there: that just as the place is shared, so too the trouble should be shared by everyone inhabiting that place. For these places are not infested *because of a person*, but *in themselves*. Therefore, it follows that whoever and whatever kind of people approach these places must endure the specific troubles of those locations.
<margin>8</margin> And indeed, one might not judge this poorly. However, anyone who wishes to take account of historical examples will detect **an inequality of troubles even in these places**; he will observe that some individuals are less infested than the rest, while others have endured more severe troubles than their companions. The former point is confirmed by Spirits lurking within Idols <note>A reference to the common belief that pagan statues were inhabited by demons who would go silent in the presence of holiness.</note>, of whom we read that some immediately fell silent and refused to give answers once Christians were either seen in those same places or had protected themselves with the sign of the cross. This is made clear by Potterius <note>Likely a reference to an author or theologian of the period.</note> regarding every kind of Spirit. In the category of Demons, this is proven by the phantoms <note>original: "spectra"</note> that afflicted Anthony, Paul, Hilarion, and other inhabitants of the Desert <note>original: "Eremi". Referring to the Desert Fathers of early Christianity.</note> more than others; and also by that instance where the phantom of Bingen <note>original: "imago Bingensi"</note> refused to depart from the side of a peasant. <margin>9.</margin>
If we correctly examine the nature of spirits and look more closely at the conditions of men, we see that it allows for an inequality of troubles. Not all spirits possess the same nature, nor is the same purpose for infestation shared by all. Likewise, there are certain men whom spirits might desire to trouble and tempt more justly than others, even in the same locations. If, therefore, a judgment can be drawn from this, it is believable that souls to be purified, the spirits of the damned, and malignant spirits <note>The author is categorizing ghosts into three types: those in Purgatory, those in Hell, and demons.</note> all trouble certain people more than others—or at least desire to do so.

<margin>10.</margin>
*Souls to be purified* <note>original: "purgandæ animæ," referring to souls in Purgatory</note> will be troublesome to two types of people above all others: first, to Catholics; and second, to those joined to them by affinity, kinship, or any other close connection. The reason for this is found in the goal set for these spirits. They seek the assistance of the living. Therefore, they will try to reach those from whom they can hope for such help more than others. From infidels and non-Catholics—who do not believe any souls are being purified—they expect nothing. They know that such people mock the suffrages <note><term>suffrages</term>: prayers, masses, or alms offered by the living to shorten the suffering of souls in Purgatory.</note> of the living performed for the dead. Among Catholics, however (who believe the spirits of the deceased are helped by the merits of the living), they will hope most from those to whom they are more closely joined. For this reason, they will seek out Catholics for aid, and especially those Catholics most closely related to them.

<margin>11.</margin>
Regarding these spirits, I would believe that what is commonly said is true: that heretics <note>In this 17th-century context, "heretics" typically refers to Protestants who rejected the doctrine of Purgatory.</note> are more rarely infested by specters than Catholics, and that the locations of Catholics are more haunted by specters than those of heretics. This is because spirits who have hope of attaining eternal life will not care to return to heretics.

<margin>12.</margin>
*The souls of the damned*, although they wish well to no one and ill to everyone, are nevertheless of a more hostile mind toward those who were the authors of their pains and infernal punishments <note>i.e., those who led them into sin or caused their downfall.</note>. This matter is not in doubt. Since hatred is followed by a lust for vexing, persecuting, and troubling, they will pursue these people above all others.

<margin>13.</margin>
In the infestation of *demons*, one must consider either the crimes for which the spirits justly pursue mortals, or the lust and perverse will by which they desire to do harm. By reason of the former, those who are entangled in more numerous and more serious crimes will suffer greater troubles...

<margin>15.</margin>
Nor were these *Spirits* troublesome only to the Hermits; they also infested others of the same purpose, even of the other sex. They once threw the holy virgin *Euphrasia* from a third-story balcony; sometimes they shoved her into a well; and sometimes they wounded her most severely. As for *Saint Catherine, daughter of the holy mother Bridget* <note>Saint Catherine of Sweden (c. 1332–1381), daughter of Saint Bridget of Sweden.</note>, they sometimes shook her out of her bed, and at other times they even beat her wretchedly. Likewise, they were troublesome to the most holy *Marina*, partly through the terrible forms they fashioned, and partly through the cursed hissings and heavy odors they scattered into the air—as their deeds, described by notable *Authors*, demonstrate. See *Surius in the Volumes* <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a German monk famous for his massive collection of hagiographies (lives of the saints) titled "De probatis sanctorum historiis."</note> he published concerning the *Saints*.

<margin>16.</margin>
*Fulbert* beautifully shows the cause of this in the *Life of Saint Achard, Abbot of Jumièges*, found in *Surius, Volume 5*:
> "The Devil," he says, "does not cease to infest more sublime pursuits with subtler snares. For he flattery-blonds the carnal and the lovers of this world, whom he finds walking in the pleasurable breadth of the present life, as if sparing them—because he is, of course, secure in his possession of them. He turns himself toward the Spiritual and pursues them more fiercely, in the manner of robbers hurrying toward their prey. While these robbers follow a fleeing, innocent crowd, they leap past and leave behind anyone they overtake in the race; but toward those whom they see fleeing far off before their eyes, into them—I say—with the zeal of pursuing, they pour out all their strength and follow with greater force. Nevertheless, if one person escapes from the whole crowd while the rest are captured, there is more often a louder, complaining recital among the robbers about this one who got away than there is exultation over all the captives together."

->So says Fulbert.<-

# Who, above all others, are exposed to the disturbances and assaults of Spirits, and for what reasons Spirits—especially Diabolical ones—persecute certain individuals more hostiley.

<margin>1.</margin> From what was said in the preceding chapter, it is clear who endures assaults and disturbances in places that are inherently infested. It is also certain that in those places which are haunted because of the people residing in them, those very people are infested either alone, or more frequently and severely, for whose sake the locations are troubled. Now it must be explained what kind of people they are for whose sake these places are rendered haunted and horrific with specters; or to put it more clearly, which people the Spirits singularly persecute and disturb.

<margin>2.</margin> The question concerns two types of people—namely, the good and the bad—and one type of Spirit that brings these troubles: **Demons**. Regarding other spirits, the matter holds no great difficulty. Therefore, what is called into dispute is this: whether all those who endure the persecutions of malignant Spirits do so because their own merits <note>In this historical and theological context, "merits" refers to the idea of "just deserts"—the belief that one's actions, good or bad, earn a corresponding reaction from the spiritual world.</note> always demand it; or whether some suffer these things without any such merit on their part.

<margin>3.</margin> And this is what we must define in the present chapter. However, not only this; we must also specifically explain the crimes of those who, because of their own deserts, endure the assaults and disturbances of **Demons**. Thus, it may be understood not only that certain people endure disturbing **Demons** because of their sins, but also which specific sins those are (for there is not just one kind of sin) for which they suffer.

<margin>4.</margin> Regarding the former point, I hold this view: that these victims are not of a single kind, but that the wicked as well as the good endure the assaults of Spirits. That is to say, some suffer because of their merits, others without any merits of their own; and among the former, some endure them for grave excesses, others for slight failings. Thus, speaking generally, there are *three* types of people who endure the persecutions of **Demons**: the *innocent*, the *wicked*, and those in the *middle*.

<margin>5.</margin> For what is said about every kind of persecution <note>original: "persecutionum genere"</note> applies to the disturbances of Spirits. Not all persecutions happen because of sins, nor do all target innocent men. Some are punishments for sins—sometimes enormous, sometimes lighter—while others are brought upon people so that the patience and integrity of the innocent may become known. In exactly the same way, some people for that reason...

# ON HAUNTED PLACES

proves that malignant Spirits will molest some because they have earned it through their sins; others without any fault of their own, but through a great arrangement of divine providence.

<margin>6.</margin> In places that are haunted by their very nature, there is no doubt that the matter stands thus. In ancient times, many Gentiles <note>A term used here for non-Christians or pagans of the classical world.</note> suffered persecution by Spirits on account of their grave crimes. On the other hand, because of slight failings—if not for no reason at all—certainly many dwellers of the wilderness in the region of Bingen <note>original: "agro Bingensi"; likely referring to the monastic and eremitic traditions in the Rhineland, Germany.</note> suffered without any merit of their own. Therefore, if in places that are inherently haunted there is more than one reason for such molestation, is it any wonder if, in places haunted on account of men, different types of trouble are brought about for different reasons?

<margin>7.</margin> For this reason, the judgment of those who immediately condemn as criminals those whom Demons pursue is wicked and perverse. Just as not everyone who is free from the infestations of Spirits lives an upright and blameless life, so too not everyone who endures their assaults does so because their own actions demanded it.

<margin>8.</margin> But there is no need for many words in a clear matter: *Let us investigate the crimes—and indeed those greater ones—which are punished by Spirits through this sort of "executioner's work." These, unless I am mistaken, are of two kinds.* Some are those by which the laws of Christian Charity are most openly violated. Others are those by which a more serious disgrace is inflicted upon God. In the first category are unjust killings, the oppression of the poor, and impiety toward parents. In the latter are blasphemy, violated religion, heresy, and the surrender of oneself <note>original: "traditio sui ipsius," referring to a diabolical pact.</note> to Demons.

<margin>9.</margin> I would not deny that others suffer the pursuit of Demons on account of other faults; nevertheless, I believe these to be the principal ones which are either punished by these troubles or, in order to be punished, most deserve them. Let us demonstrate what we assert in each category.

<margin>10.</margin> *Killings and deaths unjustly inflicted have been punished by these infestations*, as seen in the Emperors Nero, Pausanias, and Otho, about whom we wrote in Chapter 1. To these we add a man whom Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a famous French jurist and author on demonology.</note> writes that he saw in chains (Book 2, Chapter 3 of *On Demon-Mania*), who, overcome by rage, had killed his wife; afterwards, he complained that he was wretchedly beaten every night by his wife's Spirit.

We add another account of Aristodemus, a noble man of the Aepiradae family among the Messenians. When he understood from the oracle of the Delphic Demon <note>The author identifies the classical Oracle of Delphi as a demonic entity.</note> that victory in the long war the Messenians were waging with the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedaemonis"</note> would be theirs if they sacrificed a pure virgin to God: wishing to please his fatherland, he first destined his only daughter for sacrifice. Then, when he learned she had been seduced by someone (who, to save the wretched girl, feigned she was pregnant by him), he burned with such wrath that he cut open his killed daughter. After death, his daughter appeared to him in a foul form and struck him with such terror that he was driven to the same turmoil...

# CHAPTER XVIII.
### *At what times Spirits and Phantoms harass, and why at night rather than during the day.*

<margin>1.</margin>
There are various ways to distinguish time; but one in particular serves our argument: the division into night and day. The question here is whether Spirits choose this time rather than that—that is, night rather than day—to involve themselves in the affairs of the living and to tempt or harass them.

<margin>2.</margin>
It is certain that Phantoms are not so bound to either time that they are under a necessity to stir up disturbances, if they wish, during one and not the other. They are spirits; and for that reason, just as they do not depend on place, so they do not depend on time. Place does not help a Spirit in stirring up trouble, nor does time. Just as they are able to act in every place, so they can act at every time: by night, by day, or in the period between the two.

<margin>3.</margin>
It depends entirely on the will that they harass during this time rather than that. But whose will? Then, is it the will of the Spirits themselves? It is both God's and the Spirits'. It happens by the will of God and the Spirits that they interfere in the affairs of the living; it happens by the will of God and the Spirits that they interfere at these or those times.

<margin>4.</margin>
Nevertheless, I would say it arises chiefly from the Spirits' own will, as they choose the time they know to be most convenient for inciting these harassments. The arguments for this are that they have these infestations in their own power: they do not always stir them up at the same times; they do not always prolong them to the same end; and whenever they wish, they are able to cease from them.

<margin>5.</margin>
And many things prove that places are more frequently infested and men more often vexed at night. For even the Spirits who are accustomed to being troublesome during the day also disturb the quiet of the night; and very many are troublesome at night who are not even noticed during the day. Examples of these should be sought from the first Chapter.

But in many ways, this is proven by the Spirit who [haunted] the house of Alexander of...

This is proven by the phantom <note>original: "Idolum," here used to mean a ghost or apparition.</note> of an old man, wasted away by thinness and filth, who assaulted the philosopher Athenodorus during the silence of the night, as recorded by Pliny in Book 7 of his *Epistles*. Censorinus, in *On the Birthday*, chapter 9, interprets "silence" as *the dead of night* <note>original: "intempestam noctem," literally the "unseasonable" or deepest part of the night when no work is done.</note>.

It is proven by what Plutarch called the deep and nearly *midnight* hour in his life of Brutus, where he speaks of that monstrous and horrifying image <note>The "Evil Genius" of Brutus, which famously warned him "I shall see thee again at Philippi."</note> that appeared to Marcus Brutus as he was wishing to lead his army across from Asia.

From this, Eusebius of Caesarea reports that the *dead of night*, which immediately precedes the cock-crow, is more suitable for an evil demon. And regarding several witches, Nicolaus Remigius reports in Book 1 of *Demonolatry*, chapter 14, that they affirmed that time—the hour or two preceding *midnight*—is exceptionally fit, not only for those gatherings <note>Referring to the Witches' Sabbath.</note>, but for any other demonic terrors, mockeries, encounters, and noises.

<margin>7.</margin> Evil spirits, because they do evil, seek out the night and the darkness. *He who acts wickedly*, says the Lord in John, chapter 3, *hates the light*. The Apostle calls them the *Rulers of this darkness* in Ephesians 6. Finally, their habitation is in the *outer darkness* (Matthew 8). But night and darkness also serve their purpose. Since they desire to terrify by stirring up disturbances and displaying specters, they choose that time which of itself brings terror; namely, so that the disturbances and specters, joined with the night, might increase the dread and strike mortals more forcefully.

<margin>8.</margin> Spirits to be purged look to the quiet and solitude of the night. Both of these serve them. The solitude of external things removes the company of men...

<margin>9.</margin>
Beyond these reasons, both good and evil Spirits may have some common motivations for choosing the night. For instance, they generally flee the sight of men, and here the shadows of night serve them best, since vision—as the Philosophers say in the Schools <note>A reference to Scholastic philosophy, which followed Aristotle’s view that light is the necessary medium for the eye to perceive an object.</note>—is only directed toward its object when it is illuminated.

<margin>10.</margin>

But the light of day does not assist these disturbances; and although night does not assist them by its own nature, it nevertheless ensures that they are more easily heard due to its absolute silence.

<margin>11.</margin>

What if, therefore, they wish to avoid these efforts and move toward their intended goals with fewer resources?

<margin>12.</margin>
Finally, they usually show themselves as blackened figures, which is why they are called *Shadows* <note>original: "Umbrae," a term used since antiquity for the ghosts of the dead or dark apparitions.</note>, and here the night is useful; for it causes almost everything to appear black. These matters are not difficult. Let us proceed to other things.

# CHAPTER XIX.
### *Concerning the various ways in which Spirits infest places: all of which are perceived by hearing, sight, or touch.*

<margin>1.</margin>
That places are infested in various ways is as certain as the fact that they are infested at all. Since there is much to be said about these, all infestations should first be reduced to a few primary categories.

<margin>2.</margin>
We can, therefore, distinguish infestations in their primary division by saying some are *Open* and others are *Hidden*. In the former, the Spirits attack us as if in open warfare; in the latter, they test us as if by ambush. Those of the *former* kind are generally those that happen during the day and in clear light, occurring sometimes with greater force from the Spirits, sometimes with more annoyance, or with greater manifestation. Those of the *latter* kind are those that occur at night: in which either the Spirits do not reveal themselves as clearly, or they do not attack us with such force, or they do not bring such heavy afflictions.

3. Among ***open*** hauntings, I would include those on the island of Iceland; where the ghosts <note>original: "spectra"</note> of the slain are so manifest that they are accepted as living people by those ignorant of their deaths. Also that haunting mentioned in the Life of Theodore of Sykeon <note>A 6th-century Byzantine saint and healer known for his asceticism and power over spirits.</note>, in which the business was carried out by throwing stones; and that which the Clergy of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinus"</note> drove away from the fields of Bingen with litanies and holy water, where they burned down entire houses and barns, etc., which are discussed in the first Chapter under Theses 5, 20, etc. Finally, those mentioned in Chapter 16, Thesis 14 and 15.

4. In the number of ***Hidden*** hauntings, I would hold that which Hesperius, a man of Tribunician rank, suffered in his home; and in his own home, that which Alexander ab Alexandro <note>Alessandro Alessandri (1461–1523), a Neapolitan jurist who wrote about his personal experiences with a haunted house in Rome.</note> inhabited in Rome. Furthermore, that which rendered the house in which the Emperor Caligula died a place of horror; and finally those which followed Nero, Otho, and Pausanias <note>Likely referring to the Spartan general Pausanias, whose spirit was said to haunt the Temple of Athena after he was starved to death there.</note>, and which often troubled the workers in metal mines. These are also discussed in the first chapter under several Theses.

5. ***Another distinction*** of hauntings can be established according to the types of senses by which they are perceived. Sometimes they are perceived by ***hearing***, sometimes by ***sight***, sometimes by ***touch***. Other senses are also used occasionally in hauntings, though this is more rare.

6. The first, perceived by ***hearing***, is the lightest; that by ***sight*** is more serious; and that by ***touch*** is the most severe. But just as the latter is the most severe, so it is the rarest; the former types are not so unusual, and the first is the most frequent.

7. Not just one method of troubling through ***hearing*** is discovered, but rather quite varied ones. Sometimes the Spirits only suggest their presence by a stirring of the air and a light breeze; sometimes they stir up loud noises; sometimes they imitate footsteps; sometimes they break into laughter and giggles; sometimes they let forth sighs and groans; sometimes they cry out and fill the places with shouts; sometimes they speak more sweetly; sometimes they hum or sing, and so on.

8. We do not lack examples for these: the household spirits <term>Lares domestici</term> <note>Ancient Roman protective spirits of the hearth; here used to describe poltergeist-like activity that occurs within a home.</note>, who we have said roam the houses in the middle of the night, terrify almost solely by the noise through which they pretend to be doing something—though they also sometimes break into laughter.
In metal mines, some have revealed themselves ***by their breath*** <note>original: "se flatu," implying a gust of air or the sound of breathing.</note>. In the house which Alexander inhabited, nocturnal ***commotions*** were heard, along with ***horrendous growls and wailing*** and a shrill sound of the voice; just as in the castle of Stirling in Scotland. The Spirit that was once observed in Athens filled the house with the rattling of chains with which it appeared to be bound. The one that troubled the Monastery of Werden <note>original: "Verretense," likely referring to the Benedictine Abbey of Werden.</note> formed words and invited the Virgins to join it. Among the Northern peoples, they [recreate/delight] with harmony...

->### FIRST PART.<-

...refresh travelers, and the keepers of flocks and herds. These, in the year 1444, before that battle which a few Swiss fought against the vast forces of Louis the Dauphin of France near the walls of the city of Basel, were heard for several nights in that area, giving out the cries of soldiers, *the sound of arms, and the din of fighters*. This is according to the witness of Lavater <note>Ludwig Lavater (1527–1586), a Swiss Reformed theologian who wrote a famous treatise on ghosts and spirits.</note>, in the first part of *On Specters*, chapter 17. Concerning these and the rest, see Chapter 1, and Thesis 3, Chapter 67.

Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrrhus (c. 393–457), an influential theologian and historian of the early Church.</note> also mentions a certain spirit in the *Life of Saint James*, section 21, which was stirred up by the Marcionites <note>Followers of Marcion of Sinope, a 2nd-century dualist belief system often considered heretical by the early Church.</note> in the dead of night; using the Syrian language, it troubled Theodoret (who was an opponent of the Marcionites) with these words: "Why do you wage war with Marcion? Why do you take up this fight against him? What trouble did he ever cause you? Cease your warmongering, stop your ill-will: or learn by experience how great a good is peace." *These voices were heard, but no one was seen.*

Cardanus <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an Italian polymath known for his work on mathematics and the occult.</note> also mentions another in book 9 of *On Subtlety*, which in a German town called Schiltach (about eight great German miles from Freiburg) *terrified the master of a house with a whistling sound*. When the master, suspecting a thief, pursued it and found no one, and had been mocked several times by the repeated whistling, he eventually learned through an exorcism performed by holy men that it was a Demon, who afterwards caused heavy damage to the whole town. Cardanus took this from Erasmus, who follows the whole matter at greater length, just as he had learned it from Heinrich Glarean <note>original: "Henrico Clariano," a Swiss scholar and polymath.</note>.

Finally, one we mentioned in Chapter 1, Thesis 7, was perceived by hearing, not sight; about this, John Curopalates <note>A title for a high Byzantine official, often referring here to the historian John Skylitzes.</note> says the following in his *History of Basil and Constantine*, page 79: *At this time*, he says, *an incredible prodigy occurred in the region of the Thracians, at the foot of Mount Cura, where there is a spring of very beautiful and clear water. A certain miserable voice was heard, with lamentation, and "alas," and weeping, like the wailing of a woman; and this happened not just once or twice, but from the month of March until June, day and night; and when some went to explore the place where the voice was coming from, the wailing moved elsewhere.* So says Curopalates.

<margin>9.</margin>
Apparitions and Spirits present themselves to the sight and eyes in various forms. For, to pass over other forms that present no singular difficulty, they are seen now in human form, now in the form of brute animals, now as horrific monsters. Nor are these all of one kind and manner; within each kind, there are variations.

<margin>10.</margin>
How varied are the Spirits seen in human form, yet appearing in one way or another? Sometimes they appeared exactly as they looked when they were living men: such as the Spirit of Paschasius <note>Saint Paschasius (d. 512), a Roman deacon; the story of his ghost being seen in the baths is recorded by Gregory the Great.</note>, whom Germanus, the Bishop of Capua, immediately recognized upon seeing; also the spirit of Metris...

->### ON INFESTED PLACES<-

...of Nero; and those who were observed on the *Island of Iceland*, concerning which we spoke in the first *Chapter*.

*Sometimes* they appear as a sad image, nearly consumed by thinness; like the *Spirit* mentioned by *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Younger (61–c. 113 AD) famously described a haunted house in Athens inhabited by a skeletal, chain-rattling ghost.</note>. Sometimes they appear in the form of a black man; like the one who was troublesome to the *Virgins of Verretensibus*. A personal genius <note>In Roman belief, a 'genius' was a guardian spirit or a supernatural double; here it acts as an omen of doom.</note> appeared to *Marcus Brutus*, described as a dire and prodigious *Specter* with a massive and horrific body: according to the testimony of *Plutarch* in his life of *Brutus*. Those who were seen around the year of our Lord 1098 in the territory of *Worms* <note>A historic city in Germany.</note> resembled infantry well-equipped with arms, as well as cavalry. The one seen in the *Georgian mine* was dressed in a black hood <note>original: "cucullum" - likely a reference to a 'kobold' or mining spirit often depicted in monkish or hooded garb.</note>. The one that infested the house of *Alexander* resembled a man with a squalid face, a threatening look, a black body, and a formidable appearance. Regarding all of these, see Chapter 1.

The same *Alexander* (he is a witness in *book 2 of "Genial Days," chapter 9*) relates the account of *Gordianus*, a man of proven loyalty. While Gordianus was traveling to *Aretia* with a companion, they wandered far from the path through difficult and out-of-the-way places. As the sun was setting and they sat down, weary from labor, they seemed to hear a human voice from afar. Following it, they saw the images of three men, massive and terrifying beyond human measure, in black and flowing tunics, dressed in mourning attire, with funeral beards and hanging hair, and horrible faces.

It is wonderful what *Krantzius* <note>Albert Krantz (1448–1517), a German historian known for his chronicles of Northern Europe.</note> records in *book 8 of "Vandalia," chapter 29*. *In the year 1351*, he says, a great plague raged everywhere through *Germany*. At *Lübeck*, in the assembly of the *Preachers* <note>The Dominicans, formally known as the Order of Preachers.</note>, a lay brother who was in charge of the kitchen more than the others heard a noise beneath him one night while in bed in the hospital house. Meanwhile, he heard a voice speaking at the kitchen window: *"Cook, prepare food for the brothers who are about to depart."* And he from within asked: *"How many are going to pass?"* Then the other replied: *"Thirty-six from the Convent, and two strangers setting out with them."* Marvelling at the untimely summons, he rose from his bed and looked through a hole into the hospital house. He saw sitting at the table the number of brothers he had heard; they were in white, with veiled foreheads, as is the custom for those about to be buried. Shuddering, he returned to bed and did not dare reveal the matter. But when the outcome proved everything—thirty-six brothers from the Convent having been buried, along with two who had come from *Hamburg*—he then openly told what he had seen before. So says *Krantzius*.

<margin>u.</margin>
In the same way, there was not just one form of brute animals under which Spirits were seen. Now they appeared as dogs, now cats, now wolves, now bears, now mice and serpents, etc. Nor do we lack examples here. We said above, concerning that region around the Syrtes of Libya <note>The Gulf of Sidra, notoriously dangerous in antiquity and associated with strange atmospheric phenomena.</note>, that forms of various animals appear in the air, some of which remain still, while others move: and these sometimes flee, and at other times pursue those who flee.

The **Spirit of Annaberg** <note>original: "Spiritus Annebergicus" - referring to mining spirits (kobolds) common in the folklore of Annaberg, a famous silver-mining town in Saxony.</note>, which we mentioned in the first chapter, was seen in the cavern named the **Rose Crown** <note>original: "Corona Rosacea"</note> in the form of a **horse** with a long neck and fierce eyes. In this way, either the specters themselves are reported, or spirits take the form of **males and serpents** <note>original: "mares atque serpentes" - 'mares' may be a typo for 'mures' (mice), as the text immediately compares them to the mice in the next clause.</note>; these were troublesome in a house that was eventually liberated by **Theodore**, the Archimandrite of the Sykeans <note>Theodore of Sykeon (d. 613 AD) was a Byzantine saint known for his power over demons.</note>. Just so were the **mice** <note>original: "mures"</note>, which a certain Prince could not escape even in the middle of the Rhine <note>A reference to the legend of Bishop Hatto of Mainz, who was allegedly pursued and eaten by mice in the "Mouse Tower" on the Rhine as divine punishment.</note>; and the **birds of Diomedes**, which Pliny records were hostile to barbarians <note>In mythology, these birds were said to be the transformed companions of Diomedes; they were friendly to Greeks but attacked foreigners.</note>.

<margin>11.</margin>
The Blessed **Athanasius**, in his *Life of St. Anthony*, also mentions **lions, bulls, wolves, asps, serpents, scorpions, leopards, and bears**. **William of Ramel**, an Englishman, testifies in **Surius** <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578) was a German monk and hagiographer who compiled a multi-volume "Lives of the Saints."</note>, Volume 2, that spirits were troublesome to **Guthlac**, the hermit and confessor, under these same forms. **Theobald** records the same regarding **William, Count of Poitou and Hermit**, in his *Life*; and it is seen in **Symeon Metaphrastes**' account of **Abbot Sabas**, within the writings of **Cyril** <note>Cyril of Scythopolis, a 6th-century monk who wrote the biographies of Palestinian monks.</note>, who described his deeds.

Thus, one of these spirits was troublesome, in the form of a **bull**, to ox-herds on the Barbilian estate, as witnessed by **John the Deacon** in the *Life of St. Gregory*, Book 4, Chapter 93. Another appeared in the form of a **butting ox** to **St. Catherine**, the daughter of **Bridget** <note>St. Catherine of Sweden (c. 1332–1381), daughter of St. Bridget of Sweden.</note>, according to Surius, Volume 2. Another appeared in the form of a **serpent** to a youth who was approaching **St. Nicetas** to ask for counsel, according to **Theoosterictus** in his *Oration on St. Nicetas*, also found in Surius, Volume 2.

Another appeared in the form of a **blackbird** <note>original: "merulæ auis"</note> to **Benedict**, as the Blessed **Gregory** relates in Chapter 2 of his *Life*. Another in the form of a **flying raven** to **Macarius of Alexandria**, according to **Palladius**, Bishop of Cappadocia, in his *Life of the two great Macarii*. Another appeared to **St. Dominic** now in the form of a **sparrow**, now as an **ape** <note>original: "fimiæ" - likely a misspelling of "simiae" (ape/monkey).</note>, as **Theodore of Apoldia** teaches in Book 3, Chapter 7 of his *Life*. Another in the form of a **cat** to a certain monk, as witnessed by **John the Deacon** in the *Life of the Blessed Gregory*, Book 4, Chapter 89. So too, another spirit brought much trouble to a certain **Palestinian Duke** who desired to visit the Tomb of the Lord, appearing in the form of a **ram**; it frequently blocked him from accessing the tomb, as **Caesar Baronius** <note>A 16th-century cardinal and historian known for his "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note> relates at length from Chapter 49 of the *Spiritual Meadow* <note>original: "Prati Spiritualis" - a 7th-century collection of stories about monks by John Moschus.</note>, Volume 6, in the year of our Lord 13 <note>Likely an error in the date or a specific volume reference.</note>.

<margin>12.</margin>
Spirits have also been seen in the form of **monsters**. According to the testimony of the Blessed **Jerome**, the previously named Blessed **Anthony** beheld **a man mixed with a horse**, to which the poets have given the name **Centaur** <note>original: "Hypocentauro"</note>. He also saw a **little man with hooked nostrils and a forehead roughened with horns, whose lower body ended in goat's feet** <note>A description of a Satyr or Faun.</note>. According to Athanasius in his *Life*, the Spirit appeared to the same man in **that form by which the Devil is described in the Blessed Job, Chapter 41: *His eyes,* he says, *were like the rays of the morning star; from his mouth proceeded burning lamps; his hair was scattered with fire; from his nostrils...*** <note>This quote from the Book of Job describes Leviathan, traditionally interpreted as the Devil.</note>

To this category belongs the form of the Devil which he showed to **Blessed Dominic** <note>St. Dominic (1170–1221), founder of the Dominican Order.</note> in the appearance of a deformed and abominable lizard, carrying two large heads; as one reads in his *Life*, Book 3, Chapter 7. Again, there is the form by which he terrified the **Virgin Mary** <note>Likely referring to a specific hagiographic legend or perhaps a saint of the same name, as the description is quite specific.</note>, to whom he appeared in the manner of a ***multicolored dragon***, ***girded over its whole body with serpents***, and ***emitting a foul odor***, as his brother **Gregory of Nyssa** <note>A 4th-century theologian and Church Father.</note> testifies. Also, that form by which a hundred-handed and hundred-footed creature attacked **Bridget** <note>St. Bridget of Sweden (1303–1373), known for her mystical visions.</note>, while she was still a tender girl, as **Surius** <note>Laurentius Surius, the hagiographer mentioned on the previous page.</note> records in Volume 4. <margin>31.</margin>
The third method of harassment is perceived by **touch**. This happens in many ways. First, without any injury to the body or sensation of pain. In this way, those who are sleeping often feel harassing spirits, who now pull away the bedding, now tug at the ears, and so on. To this belongs the example which **Alexander** <note>Alexander ab Alexandro (1461–1523), a Neapolitan jurist who wrote "Genialium dierum" (Days of Leisure).</note> relates in Book 2, Chapter 9 of his *Days of Leisure* concerning a close friend of his. This man had overseen the funeral of a friend. When he was returning to Rome, as night approached, he turned aside to an inn near the road and gave himself over to rest. While he lay alone in bed and was still awake, the **Image of the deceased** <note>original: "Imago defuncti"</note> approached the bed of the sleeper, consumed by extreme paleness and thinness; it placed itself in the same bed and did not leave the man lying there until it was driven away by force. This is the first mode.

To this mode I also think belongs what **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Younger (61–113 AD), a Roman author and administrator famous for his letters.</note> relates in Book 7 of his *Letters*, Letter 27, in these words: "I have a freedman," he says, "named Marcus, a man of some learning, with whom a younger brother was resting in the same bed. It seemed to this brother that he saw someone sitting on the couch, bringing a pair of shears to his head, and even cutting off the hair from the very crown of his head. When it grew light, he was found to be shorn around the crown; the hairs were found lying there. A short time intervened, and again a similar event gave credit to the first. A boy was sleeping in the schoolroom among several others. Two figures in white tunics came through the windows (so he tells it) and sheared the boy as he lay there, and then retreated the way they had come. Daylight showed this boy also shorn, and his hair scattered around." Thus says Pliny.

<margin>34.</margin>
The second mode is when the spirits, not content with this contact, sometimes also push and shove the living, and drive them headlong. **Blessed Augustine** indicates in Book 22 of *The City of God*, Chapter 8, that spirits were troublesome in this way to the servants of **Hesperius**. The **Emperor Otto** <note>Likely Otto I or Otto III, Holy Roman Emperors, both subjects of various medieval legends.</note> also felt these disturbances, as he was sometimes driven out of his own bed by spirits. He felt them at work, but...

The holy man, **Nicholas of Tolentino** <note>St. Nicholas of Tolentino (c. 1245–1305), an Augustinian friar and mystic known for his visions.</note>, also felt this; the wicked Spirit now threw him prostrate on the ground, now beat him severely with clubs, and now dashed him violently against certain corners, as is written in his *Life* in the works of **Surius**, Volume 5 <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578) was a Carthusian monk and hagiographer who compiled lives of the saints.</note>. <margin>15.</margin>Thirdly, they harass by **burning** and by **inflicting blows**. The Emperor **Nero** confessed that he was not only troubled by the presence of his deceased mother, but was also tortured by the lashes of the Furies and by burning torches. For the **Verretensian** virgins <note>Nuns from the convent at Verretis, often cited in period accounts of demonic possession.</note>, small pieces of flesh were often torn from their bodies; while in the opposite direction, now their shins, now their arms were twisted; and **Euphrasia**, whom we mentioned in the preceding thesis, was at times wretchedly wounded by a Spirit, and at other times drenched in boiling oil.

These things confirm the example which **Blessed Augustine** records in *Sermon 177* of those recently printed at **Louvain**. He relates in that same place that a certain **citizen of Hippo**, because he had extracted an oath from a man he knew would commit perjury, was snatched away to the tribunal of God and most severely beaten; and the next day, the traces of the lashes appeared on his back.

<margin>16.</margin>Fourthly, they harass by **bringing death** to the living. Regarding the Ghost in the baths mentioned by **Blessed Gregory of Nyssa**, it is well known; it was so hostile to men that it brought death to nearly everyone. The **Annaberg Spirit** <note>A famous mining spirit or "kobold" from the silver mines of Annaberg, Germany.</note> in the metal mines killed more than twelve men with a single blast of breath. **Hudekin** <note>Also known as Hödekin, a legendary house spirit or kobold from German folklore, known for his "hood" and a temper that could turn lethal if provoked.</note> in **Saxony** most miserably strangled a boy who was insulting him; he cut him into pieces and cooked him.

A horrendous example can serve here, which **Michael Isselt** <note>A 16th-century historian and chronicler of contemporary events.</note> reports to have happened in the year 1584, in the village of **Apeldoorn** in **Veluwe**. Two German nobles, he says (on page 1191), serving in the military ranks, had agreed between themselves to gorge themselves on brandy until one of them expired. If anyone rose first, the Devil would have power over him. It happened while they were drinking most vigorously under this law, that a merchant by chance passed by, whom they forced to join them as a third. He was led into this against his will and out of fear of death. A little later, a malignant Spirit entered the place where they were sitting and broke the necks of both [nobles]. This is according to **Isselt**.

The history which **Siegfried, Priest of Meissen** <note>Sifridus Presbyter (c. 1300), a medieval chronicler.</note> brings forward in Book 2 of his *Epitome* regarding the year 1260, can also serve. A certain student was desperately in love with a girl; when he could not obtain her by any other means, [he sought] the opportunity for himself...

# ON HAUNTED PLACES

This man encloses himself and the youth within a circle, strictly commanding him not to step outside it. Soon, as he turns to his conjurations, many forms of phantasms present themselves, and finally the very image of the girl who was sought appears. Here the youth, overcome by lust and forgetful of the instruction, extends his hand to seize his beloved; but to his great misfortune: for he is dashed against the wall by a **wicked spirit** <note>original: "spiritu Nequam"</note> and breathes out his wretched soul.

<margin>17.</margin>
I add a fifth point to what has been said: that **specters** <note>original: "Spectra"</note> **also damage material goods**. The Spirit that haunted the house of Hesperius was not only troublesome to people but also afflicted the animals. The spirit driven out by **Theodore, Abbot of Sykeon** <note>Theodore of Sykeon (d. 613), a Byzantine saint and bishop known for his power over demons. "Archimandrita" is a title for a high-ranking abbot.</note>, used to break women's looms, among other things. The one that raged in the territory of **Bingen** burned down both granaries and the huts of peasants, reducing the poor wretches to extreme poverty; regarding these, see the Chapter. The one that was troublesome with its whistling in the town of **Schiltach** <note>A town in the Black Forest, Germany. In 1533, a massive fire destroyed the town; it was legally blamed on a woman acting as an "agent" for a whistling demon.</note>, of which we spoke in Thesis 8 of the preceding Chapter, was the cause of the burning of the entire town, with an unfortunate woman as its accomplice.

Along with material goods, I include **infants**, especially those who have not yet been initiated into the sacrament of baptism. In their case, the parents are frequently harmed; for in place of their own children, others are **substituted** <note>This refers to the "changeling" folk belief, where demons swap a human infant for a sickly or malicious spirit.</note> by Spirits; these substitutes usually suffer from serious illness for most of their lives, or when they grow up, they cause great difficulties for their parents through their corrupt behavior.

<margin>18.</margin>
The sixth mode can be that they sometimes solicit people to **sexual immorality** <note>original: "stuprum"</note> and unspeakable encounters: occasionally they even attempt to use force against the unwilling. An example of this was observed in the town of **Bourbourg** in Flanders, not far from Gravelines, in the year of our Lord 1587. There, after four years of trouble endured by a learned and pious man, **Joannes à Porca**, the local priest, along with his most chaste sister, the Spirit finally took on the appearance of a well-dressed young man. Finding the sister alone at home, he first solicited her to immorality with gifts, then with threats. Finally, when he gained nothing by these means, he began to use force against the virgin’s modesty; and he would have succeeded had her brother not arrived and snatched his sister from the Demon’s hands. This is clear in more detail from the Appendix to the history of the year 1587 by **Michael Isselt** <note>Michael von Isselt (c. 1530–1597), a priest and historian who documented the religious and supernatural events of his time.</note>.

**Caesarius** <note>Caesarius of Heisterbach (c. 1180–1240), a Cistercian monk whose writings are a primary source for medieval ghost stories and demonology.</note> records two similar cases, one of which happened at **Bonn**, near Cologne, and the other at **Prüm** in the **Eifel** region. In **Bonn**, when a certain man, fearing for his daughter’s modesty, locked her in the **upper room** <note>original: "solario"; a sun-room or attic chamber.</note> of his house whenever he went out, a Spirit entered to the virgin in the form of a young man and had relations with her. She took it very badly that she had been deceived by a Spirit, and was nearly driven to madness. The father, pitying his daughter’s misfortune, sent her elsewhere so that she might be free from the Spirit's harassment in the future.

### CHAPTER XX.

#### *Concerning the nature and condition of the Voices, Sounds, and Tumults which are perceived by the ears of the living, and are stirred up by Specters, or Spirits, in haunted places.*

<margin>1.</margin>
**I**t is not only how *Voices, Shouts, Groans, Laughter, Songs, or Clamor, Tumult, and whatever falls under the sense of hearing*, are stirred up by spirits in haunted places that we must explain in this Chapter: but also, *we must define whether these are truly stirred up, and are truly such things as they are thought to be in common opinion.* Indeed, this must be established first, so that we may be able to teach the other more easily.

<meta>catchword: Voices</meta>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of sounds produced by spirits. The previous page ended with an account of the hermit Apelles and a demonic apparition that shrieked and groaned; this page provides a philosophical and physiological analysis of why such "sounds" are not true biological voices, drawing heavily on Aristotelian definitions.</meta>

->## ON HAUNTED PLACES<-

<margin>2.</margin> Therefore, the voices that are heard, if we speak accurately, are not actually voices. **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose works on the soul and nature formed the basis of medieval and Renaissance science.</note> says that **Voice** *is the striking of air drawn in by breathing: which is indeed produced by the soul residing in those parts, against that part which is called the windpipe.* <note>original: "Vox est ictus aeris respiratione attracti... ad eam partem, quæ gurgulio appellatur."</note> According to **Aristotle**, only animals possess voices—and not even all of them, but only those that breathe. Furthermore, not every sound made by these animals is a **Voice**; it belongs only to those whose sound is produced by drawing in air and signifies some feeling or concept of the living creature. Now, in truth, **Spirits** are not animals. There is no breathing in them; no soul <note>In the Aristotelian sense of an "anima" or biological life-force that animates a physical body.</note>; no physical part to receive the soul's movement; and no windpipe.

Since the sounds that **Spirits** fashion are not true voices, the *Shouts* they provoke cannot be real either. Why is this? Because the definition of a **Shout** is such that it can in no way exist without a voice. For a **Shout** is nothing other than an intense voice, and no one would attribute **Shouts** to anything other than living beings.

<margin>3.</margin> *Groans* are signs of the feelings of those by whom they are uttered, just as *Sighs* are. Therefore, those who lack feelings cannot utter *Groans*. Yet, it is not the case that wherever feelings can exist, *Groans* can also exist. They also require those physical parts which the voice needs for its formation; since **Spirits** lack these, they may indeed appear to utter *Groans*, but in reality, they do not.

<margin>4.</margin> The same logic applies to *Laughter*. All laughter produced by **Spirits** is simulated; it deceives by its outward appearance. Furthermore, *Laughter* follows the capacity for laughing, which **Philosophers** contend is a feeling belonging to a rational animal. <note>In traditional logic, "man is a rational animal" was the standard definition; laughter was considered a unique property of humanity.</note> Truly, who would call **Spirits** "rational animals"?

<margin>5.</margin> *Song*, *Harmony*, and *Melody*, with which *Northern* **Spirits** <note>original: "Aquilonares Spiritus." These are spirits associated with the North Wind or Northern regions, often appearing in folklore as entities that mislead or entertain travelers in the wilderness.</note> refresh night-travelers and the guardians of herds and flocks, do not differ from the sound produced by pipes, organs, and other musical instruments. Just as you would not properly call this sound a *Song*, neither should you call that which **Spirits** produce *Melody* or *Harmony*. It is merely sound, and nothing besides sound. Furthermore, is not **Song** a certain modulation of the voice? How, then, is it fitting for **Spirits** to *sing* when they are denied a voice?

<margin>6.</margin> Hence it follows that **Spirits**, in fashioning voice, shouting, groaning, laughter, and song, have *no need for organs* as do humans and animals that produce voices. They do not require a mouth, nor a tongue, nor a palate, nor lips, nor teeth—which are required more for articulate speech. Nor do they need lungs, the windpipe or throat, the heart, or the <term>larynx</term> <note>original: "gurgulione." Refers to the structures of the throat used in vocalization.</note> with its twenty muscles; these are necessary for other sounds that are not so articulate.

Consequently, any auditory phenomena they produce are merely simulated sounds rather than true vocalizations or expressions of emotion.</summary>

->### PART ONE ###<-

<margin>8.</margin>
But even when they imitate voices, spirits *possess none of these organs*: this is especially true of those who craft voices privately and in secret. Why would they take on physical parts that serve them no purpose? They are able to simulate voices without any help from the aforementioned instruments <note>The "instruments" refers to the physical organs like the throat and tongue discussed on the previous page.</note>, just as they most often do.

<margin>9.</margin>
However, when spirits appear and present themselves to the eyes of the living, they are sometimes (*though not always*) equipped with these instruments—a mouth, a tongue, a throat, and teeth. This is not because they have any need for them to form voices, but because they cannot as easily achieve their intended goals without them <note>The author suggests that spirits take on human features to be more convincing or relatable to the people they are haunting.</note>.

<margin>10.</margin>
Furthermore, *although all the things just mentioned* exist only in appearance as they are commonly judged, the *sounds* can nevertheless be real. Is it not true that the ears of listeners are sometimes struck? Do they not sometimes suffer distress from hearing them? And could this perhaps happen without a true *sound*?

<margin>11.</margin>
Wherefore, even these same infesting and troublesome spirits—though they cannot utter true *voices*, as has been demonstrated—can and do produce true *sounds*. Not as many conditions are required for a *sound* as are for a *voice*. A *sound* requires far fewer. Indeed, true *sounds* can be and are stirred up by non-living things, even though they are not true *voices*.

<margin>12.</margin>
Hence, it follows that the meaning of the words attributed to spirits is not metaphorical if those words include nothing within them beyond sound; but the meaning is metaphorical if they are attributed to spirits as types of voices. Of the first kind are *clatter, uproar*, and similar things; of the second kind are *shouting, laughter, groaning, weeping, etc.* <note>The author argues that when a ghost "clatters," it is a literal description of a physical sound, but when a ghost "laughs," it is a metaphor, because laughter requires a biological soul.</note>

<margin>13.</margin>
Yet while spirits stir up *sounds*, they are not themselves any of those elements which are necessary to form sounds. There are *three* such elements: the body that strikes, the body being struck, and the medium <note>Usually the air.</note> in which the sound is received. Spirits are none of these. Nevertheless, because they can move striking bodies toward those being struck—between which the intercepted air is broken and fractured to form sounds—they themselves are said to "utter" *sounds*.

<margin>14.</margin>
Spirits therefore produce true sounds when they speak, shout, groan, weep, laugh, create an uproar, or stir up a clatter. But is this *always* the case? Or only *sometimes*? Or is it *mostly*, or rather rarely? Three questions are asked, and each is answered in turn.

<margin>15.</margin>
They do not *always* produce them. The proof of this is that it often happens in the presence of many people that some believe and constantly assert that they hear the uproars and clatters of spirits, while in the meantime the others present perceive nothing at all.
