<margin>16.</margin> I know that here, too, *sounds are sometimes real*—heard by some, but not by others. Just as demons can hinder the organs of sight and touch, or taste and smell, from performing their duties, so too can they hinder the hearing. While they block the senses in some people, they may allow those same functions to operate in others. However, just as this is possible, so is the other: that the hearing is completely deceived, and no true sound reaches it, even though the person remains persuaded that they are hearing real noises. If they can deceive a person into believing they see something when in reality they see nothing outside themselves, can they not also deceive someone into believing they hear sounds that they do not actually hear? Therefore, they do not *always* produce real sounds.

<margin>17.</margin> **Sometimes, however, they do produce them.** The common perception and consensus of all people could serve us here: those who hear *real sounds*, uproars, and noises are entirely convinced of it, and they cannot be persuaded to believe the contrary. But beyond this, a two-fold reason supports the same point. The first is that sometimes the organ of hearing is quite seriously damaged by the perception of these sounds <note>The author implies that if a sound is loud enough to cause physical pain or ear damage, it must have been a real physical vibration in the air, not just a mental trick.</note>. The second is that these sounds are perceived by everyone within a shared location, even if there is only one specific person among them whom the spirits are actually pursuing.

<margin>18.</margin> But I would say that, *for the most part*, real sounds are stirred up. This is partly because spirits do not find much difficulty in this task, and partly because the uproars that are heard are perceived by everyone, *as a rule*; this is shown by the examples provided in the first chapter and is confirmed by daily experience.

<margin>19.</margin> Meanwhile, although real sounds are heard and excited, one must not believe that they are always produced by *those objects* by which they seem to be produced. Often, furniture is thought to have been thrown about, when it has actually remained completely unmoved. Often, the sound of a hammer is stirred up when there is no hammer in the house. Often, a commotion is judged to be caused by the clashing of weapons when there are no weapons present, but only the empty forms of weapons.

<margin>20.</margin> In this matter, the *air* serves the spirits most of all. They agitate the air, and through its various collisions, constrictions, disruptions, and impacts—and, so to speak, its "overflowing"—they simulate at one moment the roar of lions, then the lowing of bulls, the hissing of serpents, the grunting of pigs, and so on.

<margin>21.</margin> Therefore, the air here is not merely the *medium* through which sound is carried to the ears, but it also takes on the role of the *striking* body at one moment, and the *struck* body at another <note>In traditional physics, sound requires a striker (like a drumstick) and something to be struck (the drum). The author argues spirits use the air itself as both the tool and the target to create noise.</note>. It acts as the *striker* when something else is struck by the air as it is driven by the spirits...

<margin>22.</margin>
And in this way, spirits indeed form sound when they are stirred up by colliding bodies, and they are truly heard as *real* sounds. Nevertheless, (as we have said) it is not always a *true* and real sound that is perceived. Just as with sight, so it happens with hearing. Do not those who suffer from **phrensy** <note>original: "phrenesi." In the 17th century, this referred to a state of delirium or mental disturbance accompanied by hallucinations.</note> believe themselves not only to see wonders, but also to hear wonders? And yet there is nothing there, neither outside their sight nor outside their hearing. And we, when we are seized by sleep and dreaming—how often do we respond to those whom we imagine in our dreams are questioning us or speaking to us? Yet here, no voice or sound reaches our ears.

<margin>23.</margin>
Therefore, the hearing of spirits happens in various ways, and not just one. There is *one* way in which the living are not deceived; because the sound that is carried to the ears is real, and it is truly stirred up by those bodies from which it is believed to be stirred. There are *others* by which the living are deceived, which are themselves diverse.

<margin>24.</margin>
First, it happens that the living are deceived—not indeed by the object of hearing (the sound, I mean) as if it were not actually carried to the ears—but by the *author* and *cause* of the sound. This occurs when a sound is judged to be stirred up by hammers, or swords, or furniture, when in fact it was produced only by the shaking of the air. Secondly, a deception occurs when a sound is judged to have been made *outside* the person, when it was actually stirred up within the person or in the **eardrum** <term>miringa: a historical term for the tympanic membrane or eardrum</term>. For just as spirits can produce sounds in the external air which are carried to human ears, so they can produce them within the ear itself; yet the one hearing it would believe it was made outside the ear. In both of these ways, just as in the first, a *true and real* sound is always perceived.

<margin>25.</margin>
Sometimes there is no *real* sound that is perceived, yet it is still judged to be perceived, as we said happens in those with delirium and those sleeping. And this happens in *two ways*: by the derivation of the **sensory impressions** <note>original: "specierum." In scholastic philosophy, "species" were the mental forms or images through which the senses perceive the world.</note> of sound to the organ of sense, and by the **imagination**. In the latter case, it is solely the operation of the imagination; in the former, there is some involvement of the hearing. But these matters belong to another place. Let us proceed with our own.

# CONCERNING HAUNTED PLACES. #

The same rule must be observed regarding things seen. First, we must deal with the condition of the things seen; then, subsequently, we must discuss the manner in which Spirits and Specters are perceived.

<margin>2.</margin>
In that first part, *three* things are asked. First, whether these Specters are truly what they appear to be. Second, if they are not truly so, whether, when they are so seen, *they are at least living things*. Third, whether, if they are not living, *they are at least truly physical bodies*.

<margin>3.</margin>
Because Specters present themselves to the sight of the living primarily in *three* distinct forms—namely, *human, animal, and monstrous*—the first of those three questions requires explanation. These are: 1. Whether they are real humans who are seen in human form. 2. Whether they are real *animals*, which are seen in the likeness of beasts. 3. Whether they are real *monsters* when monstrous forms are encountered.

<margin>4.</margin>
*They are not humans, those spirits who are seen in human form,* no matter what shape they may simulate—mournful, joyful, friendly, or terrifying; heavy or light. This is certain regarding human Spirits, because they represent the deceased, who cannot be recalled to life except by a most profound miracle (which is not present here). Regarding Devils, it is even more obvious, since it is their nature to mock humans, and their powers are not so great that they can produce a new human or call back the dead from death to life.

<margin>5.</margin>
*The animals that are seen often deceive by their appearance, but sometimes they actually are what they seem to be.* In those cases, they are either newly produced by the works of Spirits, or they are brought in from elsewhere. Most often, those that are seen in the dead of night—or those that do not last long and quickly vanish at other times—are deceptive, whatever they may be, whether they represent the forms of "perfect" or "imperfect" <note>In the biology of this period, "perfect" animals referred to complex creatures like mammals, while "imperfect" or "incised" (insecta) animals referred to insects or worms.</note> animals. *Works of Spirits* are sometimes produced when they are called "imperfect" or "segmented" animals. *When perfect animals* are seen and are real, they are not made by Spirits, but brought in from elsewhere.

Regarding this last category (for the others are well-known), Saint Jerome <note>original: "B. Hieronymus." Jerome was a 4th-century scholar and theologian.</note> provides one example in his *Life of Hilarion*. *To Hilarion,* he says, *animals were also brought every day; among which was a Bactrian Camel of enormous size, which had already crushed many people. More than thirty men brought it, tied with very strong ropes, shouting as they came. Its eyes were bloodshot; its mouth was foaming; its rolling tongue was swollen; and above every terror, a monstrous roar resounded. The old man [Hilarion] therefore ordered it to be released. Immediately, however, both those who had brought it and those who were with the old man fled, every single one of them. But he alone went forward to meet it and spoke in the Syrian language:* <note>original: "sermone Syro." This likely refers to Aramaic or Syriac, the common tongue of the region where Hilarion lived.</note> *“You do not terrify me, Devil, with such a great mass of bo—*

*If monsters are ever seen, they are almost always the works of Spirits.* In the animal kingdom, we know of no such thing as Blessed Jerome reports—a man mixed with a horse <note>a centaur</note>; and another with a forehead rough with horns, whose lower body ended in goat feet <note>a satyr</note>. If some, along with Pliny (Book 7, chapter 2), have admitted the existence of Satyrs in the eastern mountains of India—some four-legged, others running upright, with human likeness—they do not contradict our argument. This is because these creatures themselves reveal a Demon; it is through them that the Demon fakes human speech and sense, and displays human, or even superhuman, power and wisdom.

<margin>7.</margin>
Therefore, if the things that are seen are truly neither humans, nor beasts, nor monsters, then they are certainly in error who believe that these apparitions contain the *spirits' own functions*, whatever those may be; or that they are the *sources and organs* of those functions; or anything else that such a condition would naturally require.

<margin>8.</margin>
*Are they at least living and animated things?* They are not this either. And this was to be explained in the second place. For how shall we call them living things when they belong neither to the human race nor to any kind of brute animal?

<margin>9.</margin>
There is only one kind of form used by Spirits to terrify and harass people that has been placed in the category of living things: namely, those "imperfect animals" <note>Early modern science often classified insects or creatures thought to arise from spontaneous generation as "imperfect."</note> which can be produced by the works of Demons; besides this, hardly any other.

<margin>10.</margin>
Meanwhile, however—as must be said in the third place—*the Specters that are seen are physical bodies in themselves*, under whatever shapes they may appear. The humans who are observed are real bodies. The beasts are real bodies. The monsters are real bodies.

<margin>11.</margin>
*These bodies, however, are of three kinds.* Sometimes they are indeed *true and living* versions of what they appear to be; such as the "imperfect animals" we mentioned, or perfect animals brought from elsewhere. Sometimes they are *true but not living*, as if the spirits were to carry around the body of a dead man from a gallows <term>patibulo: the cross-beam of a gallows used for executions</term>. Sometimes they are *neither living nor true*; as if they were to fashion something out of the air that simulates the external form of a person or some other living creature.

<margin>12.</margin> We have very often said that these are bodies which are seen. However, they are not always so. It happens not infrequently that things which are presented to the eyes are judged to be bodies, when in truth they are not bodies at all. Just as spirits deceive the hearing, they can and do deceive the sense of sight.

<margin>13.</margin> From what has been said, we infer that *there are four ways in which specters are presented to the eyes of the living.* The first is in real, living animals. The second is in the bodies of animals alone <note>meaning the physical remains or corpses of creatures</note>. The third is in only the external forms of animals, but not in the actual bodies of those animals, though they are still in real physical matter <note>such as shapes formed out of air or mist</note>. The fourth is in the forms of animals alone, without any other bodies or animal bodies being present <note>purely optical illusions or mental projections</note>.

<margin>14.</margin> *In what ways do spirits accomplish all this?* Because this is not difficult to gather from what has already been said, it should now be briefly pointed out rather than explained at length. *Real animals, therefore*, if spirits take them from elsewhere for their own use, require no external matter; the spirits themselves excel in this power, so that they can transport bodies from place to place. If they "produce" them, they require the help of external things—specifically those things in which the power by which animals are produced lies hidden <note>The author refers to the "seminal reasons" or latent natural forces that spirits were thought to be able to manipulate to "grow" creatures quickly</note>.

<margin>15.</margin> When they *display the bodies* of humans and animals <note>referring to corpses or inanimate remains</note>, they have no more trouble than when they transport living bodies from place to place. In fact, they have less; for in this case they transport the bodies of the dead, which cannot resist, whereas in the other case they move living animals, which are able to resist in some way.

<margin>16.</margin> *When they display the forms of animals in a foreign body*; there is nothing of the animal there except the external shape, to which they adapt the air—which is the medium they most commonly use. Just as this body of air is easily dissolved, so the external form fashioned in the air vanishes very easily.

<margin>17.</margin> *The fourth way, by which sight is most greatly deluded*, is varied, just as the things that converge to create sight are varied: the object, the medium, and the power <note>The "object" is the thing seen; the "medium" is the air or light through which it is seen; the "power" is the eye or the faculty of vision itself</note>. Sometimes they affect the object in one way or another; sometimes the medium; sometimes the power. To this I would add that way by which the sight is not affected at all, but the entire occupation is in the imagination, and is completed by the imagination—even though the living person thinks their sight is being affected. These things are stated very briefly. More on these matters, and with great precision, can be found in our colleague *Luis de Molina* <note>A famous Spanish Jesuit theologian (1535–1600)</note> in his commentary on the first part of *Saint Thomas* <note>Thomas Aquinas’s Summa Theologica</note>.

# CHAPTER XXII. #

## On the reason and manner in which Specters touch: how they bring burning and beatings to the living, and exist as a cause of death. ##

<meta>catchword: Because</meta>

<summary>This page classifies the four ways spirits create visual apparitions—ranging from possessing living animals to manipulating air or the viewer's imagination—and notes that moving the dead is easier for spirits than moving the living. It concludes by introducing the next topic: the physical harm and even death that these specters can cause.</summary>

<keywords>specters, visual deception, Luis de Molina, Thomas Aquinas, demonic manipulation of air, imagination vs. sight, transport of bodies, physical apparitions</keywords>

--- Page 313 ---
<meta>This page continues the investigation into how spirits interact with the physical world. While the previous page focused on the visual projections and illusions spirits create to deceive human sight, this page transitions into the physical and tactile effects of these encounters, specifically addressing how spirits can be felt and how they cause physical harm or coldness.</meta>

-># PART ONE #<-

<margin>1.</margin>
That living beings sometimes perceive spirits through touch is certain. This was proven by many examples above in Chapter 19, regarding the distress brought upon humans by spirits; although they occasionally perceived this through other senses, they felt it primarily through the sense of touch. However, within the modes reviewed above, there are five difficulties which must be explained in this chapter. The first is whether spirits themselves possess the power of touching and can truly be said to touch. The second is why the bodies of spirits that are touched are almost always perceived as cold, or certainly not warm. The third is by what means they cause the burning sensations <note>original: "vstionis"</note> that they sometimes inflict. The fourth is how they deal blows and wounds when they seem to be destitute of all weapons. The fifth is how they bring about death and slaughter.

<margin>2.</margin>
If the question concerns the kind of touch that Aristotle calls "mathematical," it is entirely clear that specters <term>Spectra: a general term for apparitions or ghostly forms</term> can be said to touch. Indeed, it can happen that (as is the core definition of this kind of touch) there is no medium between the specter and another body, and the extremities of both exist at the same time. But if we speak of that touch which is within the power of living things—which is primarily capable of feeling "primary qualities" <note>In Aristotelian physics, primary qualities are hot, cold, wet, and dry</note>—then specters should neither be said to touch, nor to be equipped with the power of touching. This is because they lack the principle of such touch: namely, a soul providing life and form to the body.

<margin>3.</margin>
Furthermore, although they do not truly touch <note>in the biological or sensory sense</note>, they are truly touched by the living. For living beings are equipped with the power of touching, and they feel the impression of tactile qualities whenever they either touch specters or are touched by specters.

<margin>4.</margin>
Indeed, the bodies of spirits that are touched are, for the most part, perceived as quite cold. This is observed both by those who endure nocturnal distress from spirits and by those who engage in unholy unions <note>original: "nefarios congressus"; likely referring to folkloric or demonological accounts of sexual contact with spirits</note> with them. This is not surprising. For the most part, they use the service of either the bodies of the dead or bodies compacted out of air. These are cold by nature and are not capable of heat—at least, certainly not that natural heat belonging to living things.

<margin>5.</margin>
Sometimes people are burned by the touch of one of these spirits. But how? Is it perhaps by that infernal fire by which the damned are tortured? Or by some other heat innate to the assumed bodies? Or by a heat which they, by their own power, *produce by themselves*? Or by assumed "sublunary" <note>meaning fire from the physical world beneath the moon, as opposed to celestial or hellish fire</note> fire? Or some other kind? It is not infernal fire. This is not because they are unable to bring it from hell to the living, but because no necessity compels them to bring it. For the bodies they carry around are not tortured by it; and spirits existing outside of hell are indeed truly tortured by that infernal fire, even though that fire remains circumscribed within the boundaries of hell. Nor is it a heat innate to the assumed bodies. None [is granted] to them...

# ON TROUBLESOME PLACES #

[the fire] is not innate to them; rather, they seem to reject it all by their very nature. *Not by a sublunary fire <note>original: "sublunari" — fire found below the moon, in the earthly realm of the four elements</note>, for it can hardly be believed that they would drag it from its own natural place and make it serve them here among us. By what kind, then? By something produced by themselves. And in what manner? By the aid of other bodies which are able both to kindle and to nourish fire.*

<margin>6.</margin> But besides this, they know and perhaps employ two other modes of burning <note>original: "vstionis"</note>. One is by means of glowing coals, firebrands, and other things that catch fire and can sustain it. The other is by means of nettles and things that are not hot in form, but hot in virtue <note>In medieval science, something "hot in virtue" produces the effect of heat, like a chemical burn or a sting, without being physically on fire</note>; since they know the powers of these things, they cause burning in wondrous and hidden, yet true, ways.

Nor will anyone doubt that these things happen in true, though hidden, ways if they remember the marvelous things mentioned by Pliny in Book 2, chapters 103 and 107: specifically, the flame that issues from a rock in Nymphaeum <note>An ancient site in Illyria famous for its natural gas vents</note> and is ignited by rain; also the spring of Jupiter in Dodona, which, although it is cold, ignites torches held near it, just as it extinguishes lighted ones thrown into it; furthermore, a cold spring in the land of the Illyrians, over which spread-out clothes are set on fire.

<margin>7.</margin> They inflict *blows and wounds* in three ways. Sometimes through assumed bodies <term>Assumed bodies: physical forms or "shells" taken on by spirits to interact with the world</term>; sometimes by the aid of stirred-up air; and sometimes by neither of these, but by their own naked force and power. The *first mode* presents no difficulty. Just as we use a club, a spear, a sword, or similar instruments to inflict wounds, so the Spirit uses the limbs of its assumed bodies. The second, which is done by the action of stirred-up air, is clear. For no one is ignorant of the great power of agitated air; the proof of this is found in houses blown apart by its force, stirred-up seas, shattered trees, and so on. The *third* is confirmed by the powers of Demons, which are so great against physical bodies that they are able to break and pull them apart with the slightest effort.

<margin>8.</margin> By the same means through which they inflict wounds and blows, they also bring about *death*; this is because the wounds and blows they deal are a certain path toward death, and when the progress along this path is furthered, death is eventually reached and life is lost. To these I would add poison, which they can breathe upon living things to deprive them of life.

# CHAPTER XXIII.

->*Who the true and proper authors are of those things perceived during the infestations and troubles caused by spirits, whether by sight, hearing, touch, or any other way; and it is shown which of these should be attributed to human spirits, and which not at all.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
We have reduced the troubles by which spirits are usually hostile to the living to three categories: we have taught that some are perceived by sight, some by hearing, and some by touch. We have explained the logic behind each. Following this, the true and genuine author of these things must be investigated, and we must discuss whether the individual spirits who are troublesome are themselves the authors of all the troubles attributed to them, or whether they are instead sometimes brought about through others, yet attributed to these spirits because they are stirred up either in their name or in their presence.

<margin>2.</margin>
The primary question concerns human spirits <note>The souls of the deceased</note>, not demons. For since demons are so strong in intellect, knowledge, and power, they are able to stir up all the troubles we have reviewed through themselves and their own strength. <margin>3.</margin>
First, the spirits of demons far surpass human spirits in the sharpness and clarity of their intellect. <margin>4.</margin>

## CHAPTER XXIII.

> *Who are the true and proper authors of those things which are perceived in the infestations and troubles caused by spirits, whether through sight, hearing, touch, or any other way; and it is shown what things ought to be attributed to human spirits, and what least of all.*

FIRST PART.

## CHAPTER XXIII.

->*Who are the true and proper authors of those things perceived*<-
->*during the infestations and troubles of spirits, whether by*<-
->*sight, sound, touch, or any other way; and it is shown*<-
->*which should be attributed to human spirits,*<-
->*and which not at all.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
We have reduced the troubles with which spirits are usually hostile to the living to **three** headings: we have taught that some are perceived by sight, others by sound, and others by touch. We have explained the reasons for each of these. After this, their true and genuine author must be sought, and it must be discussed whether the individual spirits who are troublesome are themselves the authors of all the troubles attributed to them; or whether they are rather brought about sometimes through others, yet attributed to these or those spirits because they are stirred up in their name, or while they are present.

<margin>2.</margin>
The primary question concerns human spirits, not **demons**. For since these demons excel so much in intellect, knowledge, and power, they are able to stir up by themselves and through their own strength all the troubles we have listed. However, there is doubt, for many great reasons, whether these same things can be brought about by human spirits <note>The author is questioning if a "ghost" of a deceased person actually has the raw power to cause physical hauntings, or if they need a demon to act as their agent</note>.

<margin>3.</margin>
For first, in sharpness of intellect and clarity, the spirits of demons far surpass human ones. For although some mortals excel in this, and some "monsters of nature" <note>original: "naturæ monstra"; here meaning intellectual prodigies or people with unnaturally sharp minds</note> have existed among men, yet demons seem to exceed all men as much in the excellence of their intellect as they do in their very nature. And by how much do they exceed them in nature? So much that no human perfection can reach theirs.

<margin>4.</margin>
Secondly, the knowledge of human spirits is much inferior to theirs. Demons have a varied experience of things and have observed much in the vast world since the creation of the world. And what is most important: they received from God Most High (when they were first created) the "species" and "images" <note>original: "species atque simulachra"; in Scholastic philosophy, these are the mental forms or patterns through which an intellect understands reality without needing physical senses</note> of all things, which are like a nursery of the sciences. Because of this, they can see the natures and properties of things in these images as clearly as in a mirror whenever they wish. What of these things is found in human spirits? How little have they experienced while in their bodies? How few things have they observed in the world? Of which...

# ON HAUNTED PLACES
<meta>catchword: That (original: Quod)</meta>

<margin>12.</margin> We have very often said that the things which are seen are bodies. Yet they are not always so. It happens not infrequently that things presented to the eyes are judged to be bodies, when in truth they are not bodies at all. Just as spirits deceive the hearing, so they can and do deceive the sight.

<margin>13.</margin> From what has been said, we infer that *ghosts* <term>Spectra: From the Latin 'spectrum', referring to an apparition or phantom.</term> *present themselves to the eyes of the living in four ways.* The first is in true animals. The second is only in the bodies of animals. The third is only in the external forms of animals, rather than the actual bodies of animals, though they utilize real matter. The fourth is only in the forms of animals, without any other bodies or animal bodies whatsoever.

<margin>14.</margin> *In what ways do spirits actually accomplish all this?* Since this is not difficult to guess from what has been said, it should now be briefly indicated rather than explained. If spirits take up *true animals* from elsewhere for their use, they do not need external help; they themselves possess the power to transport bodies from place to place. If they "produce" them, they require the aid of external things—specifically those materials in which the natural power to produce animals lies hidden.

<margin>15.</margin> When they display the *bodies* of men and animals, they have no more trouble than when they move living bodies from place to place; indeed, they have less trouble, because they are moving the bodies of the deceased, which cannot resist, whereas living animals can resist in some way.

<margin>16.</margin> When they display the *forms of animals in a foreign body*, there is nothing of the animal there except the external form, to which they adapt the air—which is the substance they mostly use. However, just as this airy body is easily dissolved, so the external form shaped in the air vanishes very easily.

<margin>17.</margin> The *fourth way, by which the sight is most greatly deceived*, is varied, just as the things that contribute to sight are varied: the object, the medium <note>In Aristotelian physics, the 'medium' is the substance (like air or water) through which a sense-perception travels.</note>, and the power of vision itself. Sometimes they affect the object in one way or another; sometimes the medium; sometimes the power of sight itself. To this I would add the way in which the sight is not affected at all, but the entire activity is in the imagination, and is completed by the imagination—even though the living think their sight is being affected. I state these things very briefly. More exact details on these matters can be found in our author Luis de Molina <note>original: "Ludouicus Molina", a prominent 16th-century Jesuit theologian.</note> in his commentary on the first part of Saint Thomas <note>original: "D. Thomæ", referring to St. Thomas Aquinas.</note>.

## CHAPTER XXII.

### *On the reasoning and the manner by which ghosts touch: how they bring burning and blows to the living, and exist as a cause of death.*

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the physical manifestations of spirits. Having previously categorized the four ways spirits appear to the eye, the author now transitions from the sense of sight to the sense of touch, examining the mechanics of physical contact between the living and the spiritual.</meta>

# FIRST PART

<margin>1.</margin>
That living beings sometimes perceive Spirits by touch is certain. This was proven by many examples earlier in Chapter 19, based on the distress brought upon men by Spirits; for although they perceived this distress through other senses at times, they felt it most especially through the sense of touch. However, within the modes reviewed above, there are five difficulties which must be explained in this Chapter. First: whether Spirits themselves possess the power of touching and can truly be said to touch. Second: why the bodies of Spirits that are touched are almost always perceived as cold, or certainly not warm. Third: by what means they cause the burning sensations <note>original: "ustionis"</note> they sometimes inflict. Fourth: how they deal blows and wounds when they seem to be destitute of all weapons. Fifth: how they bring about death and slaughter.

<margin>2.</margin>
*Whether Phantoms* <term>Spectra: Apparitions or ghostly sightings.</term> *can be said to touch is entirely clear if the question concerns what Aristotle calls "mathematical touch."* <note>Aristotle defines "mathematical touch" as two objects being in contact such that their boundaries are together, with nothing in between, but without the biological sensation of feeling.</note> *Indeed, it can happen (which is the definition of this kind of touch) that nothing exists as a medium between the Phantom and another body, and the extremities of both exist at the same time. But if we speak of that touch which is a power of living beings—and is especially capable of perceiving the primary qualities <note>The "primary qualities" in Aristotelian physics are hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>—then Phantoms should neither be said to touch, nor to be equipped with the power of touching. This is because, fundamentally, they lack such touch, as they are not formed by a soul.*

<margin>3.</margin>
However, although they do not truly "touch" [in a sensory way], they are truly touched by the living: for living beings are equipped with the power of touching, and they feel the impression of tangible qualities whenever they either touch Phantoms or are touched by Phantoms.

<margin>4.</margin>
The bodies of Spirits that are touched are, for the most part, perceived as quite cold; this is observed both by those who endure nocturnal harassments from Spirits and by those who engage in wicked meetings <note>original: "nefarios congressus." This likely refers to accounts of witchcraft or demonic pacts common in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note> with them. This is not surprising. For the most part, they use the service of bodies that are either deceased or compacted out of air: which are both cold by nature and are not capable of heat—or at least not that natural heat belonging to the living.

<margin>5.</margin>
The living are sometimes burned by the touch of Spirits. But how? Is it perhaps by that fire with which the damned are tortured in hell? Or by some other fire innate to the bodies they have assumed? Or one which they *produce by themselves* through their own power? Or from fire taken from the sublunary <term>Sublunary: The region below the moon (the Earth), which in ancient science was the realm of changing elements like fire and air.</term> realm? Or some other source? It is not infernal fire. This is not because they lack the power to bring it with them from hell to the living, but because no necessity compels them to bring it. For the bodies they carry about are not tortured by it; and Spirits existing outside of hell are indeed truly tortured by that infernal fire, even though that fire remains confined within the boundaries of hell. *It is not fire innate to the assumed bodies.* No...

# PART ONE

## CHAPTER XXIII.

*Who the true and proper authors are of those things perceived during the infestations and troubles caused by Spirits, whether by sight, hearing, touch, or any other way; and it is shown what should be attributed to human Spirits, and what should not.*

<margin>1.</margin>
We have reduced the troubles by which Spirits are usually hostile to the living into **three** categories: we have shown that some are perceived by sight, others by hearing, and others by touch. We have explained the reasons for each of these. Following this, their true and genuine author must be sought, and we must discuss: Are the individual Spirits who cause trouble the actual authors of all the distress attributed to them by their own power; or rather, are these things sometimes done through others, yet attributed to certain spirits because they are stirred up in their name, or while they are present?

<margin>2.</margin>
The principal question concerns *human* Spirits <note>By "human spirits," the author refers to the souls of the deceased.</note>, not **Demons**. For since Demons excel so greatly in intelligence, knowledge, and power, they are certainly able to stir up all the troubles we have reviewed by themselves and through their own natural strengths. However, whether such things can be brought about by human Spirits is a matter of doubt, supported by many significant arguments.

<margin>3.</margin>
First, in the *sharpness and clarity of their intelligence*, the Spirits of Demons far surpass human ones. For although some mortals excel in this regard, and there have been some among men who were like "prodigies of nature" <note>original: "naturæ monstra," referring here to intellectual giants or those with preternatural talent.</note>, nevertheless Demons seem to exceed any human being in the excellence of their intelligence just as much as they exceed them in their very nature. And by how much do they exceed them in nature? To such a degree that no human perfection can reach their level.

<margin>4.</margin>
Second, the *knowledge* of human Spirits is much lower than that of Demons. The latter have a varied experience of things; they have observed much in this vast world since the moment it was created. Furthermore—and this is the most important point—they received the "species and images" <term>Species atque simulachra: In Scholastic philosophy, these are the mental representations or forms through which an intellect understands reality.</term> of all things from God, the Best and Greatest, when they were first created. These forms serve as a kind of "nursery" for the sciences. Because of this, whenever they wish, they can see the natures and properties of things as clearly as if looking in a mirror. What of these qualities are found in human Spirits? How little have they experienced while confined in bodies? How few things have they observed in the world? Of which...

Man is compared to *grass, which is here today, and tomorrow is cast into the oven.* He is compared to *the flower of the grass which quickly falls away.* (Isaiah 40). But of the Demons it is said, that *there is no power upon the earth that ought to be compared or likened to their power.* (Job 2). <note>The author references Job 41:33 (numbered as Job 2 in some older commentaries), describing the power of Leviathan or the devil.</note>

6. And indeed, these reasons sought from the condition of the Spirits themselves rightly render the mind doubtful. But those matters which are joined with such troubles increase the difficulty greatly. For how varied are they? How great? How many-sided? How astonishing? Almost surpassing human belief? First, a variety of movement is observed: then diverse forms of things are produced and placed before the eyes of the living: bodies are formed, and indeed very diverse ones, according to the condition of age and sex; and these same things are moved from place to place: Various sounds are made; now deep, now light; disturbances are stirred up; voices are heard: force is brought against the living: they are pushed forward, they are pulled back. Sometimes death is brought upon them: sometimes wounds are inflicted. Finally, six hundred <note>A Latin idiom meaning "countless" or "innumerable."</note> things similar to these are noted. Is it to be believed that human Spirits are the authors of all these things?

7. The Spirits themselves who are said to appear claim to possess this power, and to effect these and similar things. Yet the magnitude of the things that are done, and the weakness of the Spirits, persuades us that they do not. In this difficult, arduous, and doubtful matter, we shall teach as much as we can attain by reason and conjecture (deferring to the judgment of those who think better of it), if first we establish one or two things about which there is no doubt.

8. The first is, that all these things are not wrongly attributed to human Spirits when, while these Spirits are present, Angels (whether good or bad I do not labor over now; this later point will be explained in the following chapter) perform these things in the person <note>original: *in persona*; acting as the legal representative or wearing the "mask" of another.</note> of the human Spirits. Because of this, we do not speak wrongly when we say we have seen human Spirits, even though whatever we saw was the work of Angels; or that we have heard human Spirits and suffered trouble from them, even though the authors of the troubles were Angels. Does not a person rightly say he has seen the Emperor, who saw the cloak that covered the Emperor? Is he not said to be punished by the King, who suffered punishment from the King's ministers, who sustained the person of the King? He was not lying who said to the people of the Jews in Deuteronomy 6, *Hear, O Israel: I am the Lord your God* <note>original: "Audi Israel: Ego sum Dominus Deus tuus"</note>; and yet it was not God speaking [Himself...]

# FIRST PART

...but an Angel: who was able to say that he was the *Lord God*, because he was representing the person of the Lord God. <note>The author refers to a common theological argument that when "the Lord" speaks in the Old Testament, it is often an angel acting as a divine representative.</note>

<margin>9.</margin>
The second point is that all those works which we have reviewed can rightly be attributed to human Spirits, even when they themselves are not present *in person* <note>original: "autoprosopos," a Greek term meaning "in one's own person" or "face-to-face"</note>; but nevertheless, they are performed by Angels in their [the spirits'] stead. It is the custom of Scripture that images of things are marked with the same names by which the things themselves are usually called. The images of heavenly powers, which were formed from metal and placed over the Ark of the Covenant, retain the name *Cherubim* (Exodus 25). King Pharaoh, who while sleeping had seen images of ears of grain and oxen announcing a future famine, testified that he had seen nothing but *ears of grain and oxen* (Genesis 41). And Pharaoh's Cup-bearer, while in prison with Joseph, said he had seen a vine in his dreams in which there were three branches; and yet he saw neither a vine nor branches, but images of those things (Ibidem). And we too, when we see a painted panel, address it by the names of those whose forms the appearance represents.

<margin>10.</margin>
Nevertheless, although these things are so, the human Spirits are not entirely without a role here. Although they themselves are sometimes not present, they are not always absent. Although they do not do everything by themselves, it should not be said that they do nothing at all. Sometimes they are present in their own person. Sometimes they bring certain things about. And sometimes they are even capable of things which they nevertheless do not do.

<margin>11.</margin>
When, therefore, are human Spirits present during these disturbances? What are they capable of in these matters? What do they do and strive for by themselves?

When they are present *in person* is not always clear. See what was said above in chapters 10 and 11.

It is not always certainly established what they do here by themselves.

What they either can or cannot do, we teach in the following Assertions.

<margin>12.</margin>
The first is this: *The Spirits of deceased men are able by their own power to move to various places; nor do they have need of any carrier for this.* So teaches Tostatus <note>Alfonso Tostado de Madrigal (c. 1400–1455), a prolific Spanish bishop and biblical commentator known for his exhaustive scholarship.</note>, in his commentary on Matthew 25, question 772. For why should they not be able? Is all power of moving themselves taken away from them after they have laid aside their bodies? Who would believe it? Do they always remain in those places where their bodies perish? What could be said that is more absurd?

<margin>13.</margin>
Human Spirits are natures existing *by themselves* <note>In scholastic philosophy, "subsisting by themselves" (subsistentes per se) means the soul is a distinct substance that does not depend on the body for its existence after death.</note> when they have left their bodies; and they are strong in the perfected power of both understanding and desiring. What if, therefore, they then perceive some place suitable for themselves, and desire to be and to dwell there; will they not be able to move themselves to that same place by their own strengths, unless they are prohibited by the authority of a superior (which nevertheless leaves their natural right to them)? So if they understand the present [place] in which they live to be...

<meta>Catchword: tas</meta>

...troublesome and ruinous, and they wish to depart from there; will they not be able to?

<margin>14.</margin> To Aristotle, those are the most imperfect animals which are so fixed to their places that they cannot move from there <note>Aristotle refers here to "sessile" organisms like sponges or shellfish that appear rooted like plants</note>; and yet among these very things, there are none that cannot move forward to some extent or in some degree. And shall the spirits of men, who hold the primary place among created natures after the heavenly spirits, be destitute of all power of movement?

<margin>15.</margin> Those heavenly minds <note>referring to angels</note> possess the power of moving themselves, and indeed a very great power. So the Philosophers teach consistently with the school of the Theologians. But human spirits, once separated from the body, approach very closely to the condition of these; therefore, they themselves will also excel by that same power of movement as the others.

<margin>16.</margin> Hence it is that a twofold power of movement has been bestowed upon souls, or human spirits: one, by which they give life to the body; the other, by which they move themselves. They exercise the former when they are enclosed within bodies; the latter, while they are freed from bodies. They have the former in common with brute animals; the latter with the heavenly spirits, who are devoid of all entanglement with matter.

<margin>17.</margin> But if they can move themselves, why is it said in *Luke 16* that the soul of Lazarus, that man of the Gospel, was *carried away by angels into the bosom of Abraham*? Why is a carrier needed for a spirit that is firm and robust? The opinion of certain people is far too absurd, concluding from this that souls stripped of their bodies cannot move themselves from a place, because they are said to be *carried away* by angels like a dead and lazy weight. The word *to carry* <note>original Latin: "portandi"</note> does not have that force here, nor does it signify bearing a burden; rather, it is used for *to lead forth* <note>original Latin: "producere"</note>; as in that passage of *Psalm 90: In their hands they shall bear thee up, lest haply thou dash thy foot against a stone.* For the Prophet does not mean that the Angels would literally carry Christ in their hands, but that they would so guide Him wherever He walked, and so look after Him, that He could no more strike against a stone than if He were being carried by hand. In the same way, it is signified that the soul of Lazarus was carried by angels. Therefore, it can no more be proven from this passage that souls cannot move than it can be proven from that Psalm that Christ could not move. Lazarus's soul did not stand in need of the angels' service out of weakness; rather, the angels were performing the duty of honor which was owed to him.

<margin>18.</margin> These same angels perform the same benefit for *blessed souls* when they depart from this world; otherwise, these souls could soon fly across to the heavenly kingdoms by themselves without any help or companionship from the heavenly spirits. For these souls cannot be ignorant of the place, or where and by what way they are heading; for they are blessed, and they perfectly know the things which pertain to their condition. Nor do they lack the power of movement; this has now been demonstrated. And since an ardent desire...

<header>PART ONE</header>

...firmness <note>The text continues from the previous page's word "robustas," meaning firmness or strength</note> might hold them; so that they may be present with Christ; and with the highest obedience, so that they may carry out the sentence that was passed for them when they left their bodies, they will immediately transfer themselves to the heavens. See Tostado <note>Alfonso Tostado (1400–1455), a prolific Spanish bishop and theologian</note>, on Matthew 25, question 777.

<margin>19.</margin> And although the *spirits of those to be purified* <note>original: *purgandorum Spiritus*; those destined for Purgatory</note> descend to the place of punishment not without a guardian Angel, yet that angel is not a "carrier" but a "leader." Those spirits know, after they have departed from the body, what place is destined for them. And although they dread the punishments, they offer themselves to them most promptly; they even hasten to the places of punishment because they know these are owed to their sins; and once these are paid, the entrance to the eternal and immense heavenly joys lies open to them. Yet they have an Angel as a leader and companion, partly so that he may show the way (which they might be ignorant of) and partly so that they may receive some consolation from them. See Tostado on Matthew 25, question 778.

<margin>20.</margin> Similarly, for *damned spirits*, if indeed they wanted to carry out the divine sentence by their own will, there would be no need for carriers. Yet they have carriers (not just leaders), and indeed <term>Demons</term> (although Jerome on Daniel chapter 7 and Ambrose in book 5, epistle 21 seem to assert that good Angels do this). This is both because they are ignorant of the place of punishment destined for them, and because they dread and resist the punishments and the place of punishment they must enter. Just as they detest and blaspheme God Himself, whose sentence they loathe, so it is that unless force were applied to them by Demons—acting as ministers of divine justice—and they were snatched away to the underworld, they would by no means seek the place of hell by themselves. On these matters, see <term>Domingo de Soto</term> <note>A Spanish Dominican priest and influential Scholastic philosopher</note> at the end of his Commentary on the 4th Book of Sentences, and Theodore Peltanus <note>A 16th-century Jesuit theologian</note> in his work *On Purgatory and the Dwellings of Souls*, and Tostado on Matthew 25, question 779. *Therefore, the spirits of the dead are capable of the power of movement.* And this is the first of our assertions.

<margin>21.</margin> The second assertion is: *The same spirits of the dead can return to the living by their own natural power; although it is not always permitted for them to return.* For since they are endowed with the power of moving themselves and are able to change locations, why would they be any less able to return to the world above <note>original: *superos*; the world of the living</note> than to penetrate any other places? And since a good purpose invites them to seek certain places, can this purpose not be found among those in the world above just as well as in any other locations?

<margin>22.</margin> Nevertheless, while they are able by the <term>natural power</term> <note>original: *virtute naturali*; the inherent capability of a spirit as a non-physical being</note> innate to them, this is not always permitted to them—especially not to those of whom we are speaking, the *troublesome spirits*. These are assigned to certain places according to the measure of their deserts: from which it is not permitted to depart except by the will of Him who decreed the punishments. But it is one thing to ask...

<header>ON INFESTED PLACES</header>
<note>original: *De Locis Infestis*; referring to places believed to be haunted or troubled by spirits</note>

...one thing is what they owe by the merit of their faults; another is what they are capable of by the powers of nature.

<margin>23.</margin> **The Third Assertion.** *The spirits of deceased men cannot, by their own power, produce the appearances of things through which they are seen by the eyes of the living, if real bodies are not actually present.* I shall explain this, as it is stated rather obscurely. There are two ways it happens that the spirits of the dead come before the sense of sight: sometimes only in bare appearances, which are made of forms, and sometimes in real bodies, which transmit their own forms to the eyes. We are speaking here of the former. But this is twofold: sometimes the forms themselves are not outside the human eyes (just as the things that seem to be seen are not actually there); other times they are formed in the air and then transmitted to the eyes. In neither way are they the work of human spirits.

<margin>24.</margin> To what, then, should they be attributed? Since they have no existence outside the organ of sight, they must be produced with great skill and sharp industry. Sometimes they are created by a varied and complex composition of the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed to govern health and perception</note>; at other times by the stirring of <term>phantasms</term> <note>Mental images or impressions stored in the imagination</note>. But what can human spirits do in this regard, since they are given no power over these humors or phantasms? Nor do they know how both ought to be composed and mixed to exhibit whatever forms they might wish.

<margin>25.</margin> Likewise, when forms are shaped in thickened and arranged air, they do not have human spirits as their authors. Here, too, great knowledge and excellent power are necessary—qualities which are lacking in most, if not all, of the spirits who are troublesome. Not to mention that it can perhaps be believed that these spirits, once free from their bodies, are no more capable of this than they were when they were joined to their bodies.

<margin>26.</margin> **Let this be the Fourth Assertion.** *Neither can a person’s imagination be directly disturbed or affected by these spirits of the dead.* Every impression made upon a human imagination is achieved through the forms and likenesses of things, which act as instruments. Therefore, those who lack the power to produce these forms can do nothing to a person's imagination. The spirits of the dead lack this power. This is not surprising, because even while they were alive, they could do nothing to another's imagination directly; whatever they could do was achieved through the service of the external senses.

<margin>27.</margin> **From this we now descend to the Fifth Assertion;** *by which we say that the troubles some people suffer in sleep—due to the likenesses, idols, and various forms that occupy the imagination—cannot have human spirits as their authors.* If they cannot bring these things to those who are awake, would they be able to do so to those who are sleeping and weighed down by slumber? Does sleep perhaps grant these spirits greater knowledge or more robust strength than they otherwise have?

<margin>28.</margin> **These troubling spirits also cannot assume bodies by their own virtue and strength...**

# PART ONE #

...of the human spirit. Let this be the sixth point of those we are presenting. Furthermore, by the name <term>assumption</term> <note>original: *assumptionis*; the act of a spirit taking on a physical form or "clothing" itself in a body</note> in this context, we do not mean that union by which spirits are joined to a body as a moving force, in which they strive to appear and show themselves; rather, we mean a composition and an assembly of air of such a kind that it mirrors a human form or figure. We are not difficult in admitting the former type of union, but we suspect the latter is impossible for human spirits for two reasons. The first is that even among excellently learned philosophers, there is no agreement on the method by which that assumption is achieved; the second is that the powers of human spirits, while they sustain their own bodies, are unequal to this task.

<margin>29.</margin>
Are the powers of separated spirits perhaps greater than those joined to bodies? Powers follow natures: the more perfect a thing’s <term>Being</term> <note>original: *Esse*; a philosophical term for the fundamental existence or "is-ness" of a creature</note> is, the more complete and vigorous its powers are. But the Being of spirits that give form to bodies is more perfect than that of those separated from bodies; just as <note>Alfonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), also known as Tostatus Abulensis, was a celebrated Spanish theologian and Bishop of Avila known for his massive commentaries</note> Tostatus of Avila teaches in his commentary on Matthew, chapter 25, question 85.

<margin>30.</margin>
Perhaps they will then know what they were ignorant of while situated in bodies regarding this assembly of bodies and air. But from where can those spirits about whom we are disputing—the damned, or those not yet blessed—know this? They do not understand it of themselves. From where then? Does some teacher perhaps immediately offer himself to them to teach them?

<margin>31.</margin>
And even if they were to understand the theory, and especially the method of composition; and even if they possessed powers no less as souls abstracted from bodies than as those enclosed in bodies: yet it is still not believed that they are able to form these bodies. This is because much greater powers, not merely equal ones, seem necessary here than those communicated to human spirits by <note>original: *Deo Opt. Max.* (Deo Optimo Maximo); a common formula meaning "To God, the Best and Greatest"</note> God, the Best and Greatest.

<margin>32.</margin>
Furthermore, just as human spirits cannot by themselves assemble and condense these bodies, so too they are not the ones who create the forms and figures under which they are seen by the living. This is the seventh of our Assertions. These figures and forms have the same authors as the condensed bodies themselves; this is because the boundaries of condensed bodies are the figures, and they do not differ in reality from the condensed bodies themselves.

<margin>33.</margin>
Therefore, a sad and emaciated face, or a more cheerful countenance, is not the work of human spirits; nor is a male or female form, nor the appearance of an older or younger person; nor an unshaven and longer beard; nor fierce eyes; nor whatever else can pertain to the form. Just as a garment has as its author not the one who wears it, but the tailor; so these forms [do not have as their author] the spirit who wraps <note>original: *circum-* (catchword for *circumdat*)</note>

### ON INFESTED PLACES ###

...carry them about; but rather that One, who is the assembler and maker of bodies in which the <term>forms</term> <note>original: *formae*; in Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the organizing principle or soul that makes a thing what it is</note> exist.

<margin>34.</margin> **By the same reasoning, the colors that are seen in these bodies should not be attributed to these Spirits as their authors.** Let this be our eighth assertion. Are they able to induce color into bodies that are already formed? Not even Angels—who are far more excellent than these spirits—can do this by their own power. Whenever they add color to things, they do so not through themselves, but with the aid of other physical substances. Therefore, since colors follow the nature of bodies, they must have the same authors as the bodies themselves.

<margin>35.</margin> **In the meantime, however, although human Spirits cannot assume bodies by their own power, they can nonetheless move and carry around bodies already formed and, as it were, lent to them.** And this becomes a new point among our Assertions. For what is there to prevent them from doing this? If they were able to move their own bodies, which they once cherished and animated, why should they not be able to move similar bodies which they do not animate? These Spirits are the "forms" of bodies, and they are the movers of bodies. In this case, although they are not the animating forms, they are nonetheless the movers; wherefore they will be able to move these objects as well. <note>Alfonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), also known as Tostatus Abulensis, was a celebrated Spanish theologian and Bishop of Avila</note> Tostatus teaches this in many places in his commentary on Matthew 25, question 773, although <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher</note> St. Thomas teaches the opposite in the first part of his *Summa*, question 117, article 4.

<margin>36.</margin> **However, they cannot move just anything that is lent or handed over to them. What if these objects exceed huge mountains in mass? What if they surpass anything human in enormous magnitude, yet nonetheless retain a human form?** The power of human spirits in these "assumed" bodies is no greater than the power they possessed in their own physical bodies. Therefore, if any bodies exceed human proportions by a <term>disdiapason</term> <note>original: *disdiapason*; a musical term for a double octave, used here to describe a vast or "two-fold" scale of difference</note>, they will not be moved by the power of human Spirits alone, but rather by some higher power. Let this be the tenth of our Assertions, following the opinion of Tostatus of Avila on Matthew 25, question 774.

<margin>37.</margin> **But if the assumed bodies are smaller than the size of human bodies, the spirits will move them much more easily.** This is because motion is easier where the power of the <term>agent</term> <note>the one performing the action</note> is greater and the resistance of the <term>patient</term> <note>the object being acted upon</note> is lesser. If the bodies reach the proper stature of humans, the spirits will move them; although they will not do so as easily as they moved their own bodies, which they once "informed" <note>gave life and structure to</note>. This is because the power of Spirits that both inform and move a body is greater than the power of those that only move a body without informing it. Let this be the eleventh point.

<margin>38.</margin> **Furthermore, in this movement of bodies by Spirits, the same method of moving used in one's own body is not preserved.** In a living person, the Spirits move the body in such a way that when one part is moved, that part impels and moves another; but in the case of these assumed bodies, the spirits move them by pushing and advancing the whole mass at once. This is the twelfth point.

We wish this to be our fourteenth Assertion. Nor is this surprising. Spirits use these bodies as instruments; just as, therefore, whatever is done through instruments is attributed to the primary agent, so whatever is done through the motion of these bodies must be attributed to the Spirits themselves who move the bodies.

<margin>42.</margin>
But what are these actions? They are all reduced to *three* primary classes. Some are perceived by sight; some by hearing; and some by touch. By *sight* are perceived the bodies themselves, their size, colors, shapes, and motion. By *hearing*, noises, tumults, shouts, groans, and similar things. By *touch*, impulses, dragging, blows, and things of that kind.

<margin>43.</margin>
Therefore, human Spirits are able to move the *sight*. <note>That is, they can cause themselves to be seen by others.</note> For although they do not form the color and shape themselves (which are the objects of sight), they nevertheless bring these things along with them and thrust them before the eyes of the living. And because these <term>species</term> <note>original: *species*; in early modern science, "species" were the images or likenesses that objects were thought to emit so they could be perceived by the eyes</note> leave their mark on the senses, for this reason it can most rightly be said that Spirits are seen, and that they move the sight.

<margin>44.</margin>
They are able to *excite tumults and noises*. Because they can strike the bodies they carry about against other bodies, so that the air intercepted between them is broken and pressed, yielding a noise. By seizing tools, they can strike other bodies no less than blacksmiths do. They can also produce a disturbance of the air within the very bodies they carry about, creating whistles, sounds, and other things that affect the hearing.

<margin>45.</margin>
And they can do these things to bodies devoid of sense <note>inanimate objects</note>, as well as to those endowed with sense. Thus, it can be truly said here that these Spirits affect the senses: now producing pain, now bringing pleasure, no less than the bodies of the living still produce these effects in other living beings.

For those things that fall under sight can always be attributed to the Spirits themselves; those of hearing and touch, not always. ## CHAPTER 24.

### *Which of those things perceived by the living during disturbances and infestations by spirits should be attributed to Angelic spirits and not human ones: even though human spirits may seem to be their authors.*

<margin>1.</margin> We have inquired into what can be attributed to human Spirits regarding the disturbances brought upon the living by Spirits. Because that contribution is small, it would not be out of place if we show who the authors of the remaining disturbances are. For it is of little value to know who are not their authors; it is of great value to know who they are. <note>The Latin text repeats "who are not" (qui non sint), but the logical flow of the argument—moving from the negative to the positive identification of the agents—suggests the author is now focusing on identifying the actual authors.</note>

<margin>2.</margin> And indeed, if what was said in the previous Chapter is consistent with reason and not far from the truth, the answer here is straightforward. For it must be granted that for all things not performed by human Spirits, *Angels* (*whether good or bad will be discussed later*) *are the authors*. Why so? Because this entire *Dispute* <term>Dispute</term> <note>original: *Disputatio*; a formal academic inquiry or debate common in Scholastic philosophy</note> concerns the disturbances that Spirits bring, and there are only two kinds of these Spirits: some are *Angelic*, and others are *human*. (*Nothing is said of God here*) Therefore, those things not done by human spirits must necessarily be done by *Angelic* ones.

<margin>3.</margin> However, because certain matters here present a difficulty, and the subject is worthy of more diligent discussion, it will be worth our effort if we revisit all the modes of disturbance that we ran through in the previous chapter; and in each case, we shall explain not just what they *can* do, but what *Angelic Spirits* actually perform.

<margin>8.</margin> These things are within the power of Spirits, and they can perform them in the *ways we have just recounted*: as the learned well know; and as Benedict Pereyra <note>original: "Benedictus Perierius" (1535–1610), a prominent Jesuit theologian and author of *De Magia*</note> confirms with examples in the first book of his work *On Magic*, chapter six. Theologians teach how effectively and quickly these things are performed by Angels; they say that physical matter is subject to their command <note>The author uses the phrase "ad nutum," meaning at their beck and call or a simple nod.</note>, so that they are able to suddenly form whatever bodies they wish, and are able to lay those same bodies aside as soon as they please.

*And just as these Angelic Spirits form bodies, so too they are the ones who prevent those bodies from losing their shape; they preserve them; and it is to them that the eventual dissolution of those bodies must be attributed.* They accomplish the former through a specific action distinct from the matter itself. Dissolution is attributed to them for this reason: they simply cease to preserve the forms, allowing them to return into the original air from which they were compacted. This is the **fifth work** of the Angels in these disturbances.

<margin>15.</margin>
*Likewise, the figure and form under which human spirits are seen must be attributed to them.* Just as they are the authors of the physical bodies, so too are they the authors of the outward appearances that accompany those bodies. Although it should not be denied that human spirits <note>i.e., the souls of the dead</note> are able to change these forms to some extent by contracting or expanding the "body" they carry about, let this be the **sixth work**.

<margin>16.</margin>
*Colors, through which spirits strike the eyes of the living, must also be attributed to the Angels.* Is it any wonder? These are not the effects of human spirits; therefore, they must belong to these Angelic ones. Colors follow the composition of bodies; depending on the varying compression of the matter from which they arise, and the quality of light they receive, they appear as one color or another. But it is the Angels who compose the bodies. The Angels compress the matter in various ways. Therefore, colors are a certain work of the Angels.

<margin>17.</margin>
*Eighthly, it must be believed that the Angelic Spirits are the authors when huge, vast bodies are presented and moved about—bodies which, by their sheer mass, rightly terrify the living, even if they bear a human shape.* The reasoning for this is the same as what has already been said: human strength <note>Even in spirit form</note> is not sufficient to move such massive bodies. However, this is also easily demonstrated by the reason why spirits return. Human spirits return so that they may be recognized; therefore, it is fitting that they should be seen not in some strange form that exceeds the human scale, but in an ordinary form familiar to people, such as they once possessed in life.

<margin>18.</margin>
*Sometimes, too, immense commotions are heard. Great noises are heard,* which occasionally seem to shake entire houses; and these are heard even in places where it is certain that "troublesome" human spirits are the ones present. Yet, these are not the works of human spirits. Just as with those massive bodies mentioned before, it is the Angels who stir up these tumults and noises. These things do not exceed the powers of Angels, but they do exceed the powers of humans.

<margin>22.</margin>

However, it is not the case that whenever Angels cause trouble, the work of human spirits is necessarily added.

## CONCERNING HAUNTED PLACES
<meta>catchword: These:</meta>

disturb the humors <note>In pre-modern medicine, "humors" were the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—thought to determine a person's health and temperament.</note>, or the spirits that exist within the human body; they can likewise pull apart the joints and connections of the limbs, causing the greatest pain to men.

They are able (13.) to move and shape the **animal spirits** <term>animal spirits<gloss>In early science, these were subtle vapors or fluids in the nerves believed to transmit sensory information to the brain and commands to the muscles.</gloss></term> which serve the functions of the internal senses; in this way, they can represent certain things—whether past, present, or future. Once these same spirits have been shaped by the images of external things, the [angelic] spirits can direct them back toward the external senses. Thus, they mock men in wonderful ways, so that people seem to see before their very eyes things that are not actually there.

They are able (14.) to move the **phantasms** <note>original: "phantasmata"; refers to mental images or fragments of memory stored in the mind.</note> of those who sleep, and represent various things to them, even those yet to come, just as they do with diviners. They are able (15.) to deceive the external senses, either by stirring the animal spirits from within and (as we said) directing them toward the external senses, or by offering false objects and mere **simulacra** <gloss>images or likenesses that have no substance</gloss> of things from the outside, rather than the things themselves.

They are able (16.) to excite all kinds of **affections** <gloss>emotions or passions</gloss> in a human being: joy, pain, love, hatred, fear, hope, and so on. They do this either by presenting the images and forms of things that cause these emotions, or by internally stirring the imagination to represent such things, or by agitating the humors which are the physical "material" of these emotions. The aforementioned Spirits can accomplish all these things through **local motion** <note>The physical movement of matter from one place to another.</note>. A desire for brevity does not permit me to provide individual examples for each case.

<margin>17.</margin>
They can also perform wonders by utilizing natural causes—those which we call *secondary* causes. For the powers and forces of these causes are many, great, noble, admirable, and stupendous, as taught through numerous examples by:
*   **Pliny**, in book two of the *Natural History*, chapter ninety-six.
*   **Proclus**, in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*.
*   **St. Augustine**, in book twenty-one of *The City of God*, chapters four and five.
*   **Albertus Magnus**, in book two of *Minerals*, Treatise 2, chapters 1, 11, and 17.
*   **Fracastoro**, in his book *On Sympathy*.
*   **Ficino**, in book four of *Platonic Theology*, chapter one.
*   **Cardano**, in *On Subtlety and the Variety of Things*.

And the Spirits in question know which virtues reside in which things. They know the places where things lie hidden. They know which things ought to be combined, mixed, and in what way they should be tempered. They know the seasonable and opportune time when they ought to be applied for work. They know all these things. And since they are able to transport things to wherever they please with the greatest ease and speed, the things they can achieve with this assistance are marvelous; they are all the more marvelous to mortals because men do not understand how these things happen, even though they occur naturally.

# PART ONE.

<margin>8.</margin> These things Spirits are capable of, and they are capable in the ways we have recounted, as the learned well know; Benedict Pererius <note>Benedictus Pererius (1535–1610) was a prominent Jesuit theologian; his work *De Magia* (On Magic) was a standard reference for understanding the supernatural in the Renaissance.</note> confirms this with examples in the first book of *On Magic*, chapter six. Why, then, could they not be responsible for everything observed in haunted places? However, since the question is not about their *power* <note>original: "potentia"</note>, but about the *fact* <note>original: "facto"</note> of what they do; let us discuss what the Spirits themselves actually provide in these disturbances, and which functions and duties are so uniquely theirs that they ought not be attributed to human spirits.

<margin>9.</margin> Therefore, let this answer be given to the question: *In these troubles and infestations, there are two kinds of things that have as their authors not human, but Angelic Spirits.* <note>In the language of the time, "Angelic Spirits" could refer to both good angels and fallen angels (demons), as they share the same metaphysical nature.</note> Some are things that cannot be accomplished by humans; others, although they could be done by human effort, it is nevertheless not likely that they were. Regarding the former, there can be no doubt that they have Angels as their authors, since they can have no others. Regarding the latter, the very condition of both Angels and human Spirits seems to persuade us that they are responsible. Both types are varied. We shall demonstrate this in each category.

<margin>10.</margin> In the first category are, primarily, **tricks and illusions of the senses**, by which the living are deceived so that they believe they perceive things which they do not truly perceive; rather, these things exist either only in the external senses, or are merely **simulacra** <gloss>images or likenesses with no physical substance</gloss> formed in the air. We said above that these things cannot be done by human Spirits; thus, it follows that whatever trouble is brought about in this manner is brought by Angels.

<margin>11.</margin> Next are **impressions produced upon the human imagination**: yet, such impressions are made without the aid of an external body (which would first affect the external senses and then transmit its likeness to the **phantasy** <term>phantasia<gloss>The mental faculty that receives and stores sensory images, similar to what we call the "imagination."</gloss></term>). For those things which are excited from external objects with the help of the outer senses can be done by human Spirits while they move bodies around. But those things which lack this help of physical bodies, and happen through the stirring of the humors, spirits, and images that have their seat in the phantasy—because these exceed human strength—acknowledge Angels as their authors.

<margin>12.</margin> Thirdly, there are **nocturnal illusions, which happen to those who are sleeping and weighed down by slumber.** These too must be attributed to Angels. They are able to insinuate themselves into a person’s phantasy. They can present various idols to those sleeping just as easily as to those awake. And since human Spirits are likewise unequal to these tasks, they nonetheless require an author; they will have as their authors the Angelic Spirits by whom they are produced.

<margin>13.</margin> Fourthly, those **works of Angels are the bodies which are formed and carried about** <unclear>bodies</unclear>. The reasoning for this is the same as for the previous points: but yet
