# PART ONE.

<margin>19.</margin>
Tenthly, those physical disturbances <note>original: "molestiæ tactiles," literally "tactile troubles," referring to events involving physical touch or impact.</note> which are judged impossible to be performed by men must be attributed to Angels. Just as we establish human strength as the certain rule for human disturbances in all other matters, so we intend that same rule to apply to those disturbances which exceed such strength, attributing them not to human spirits, but to Angelic Spirits. In this category are almost always fires, the overturning of buildings, burnings, incisions, wounds inflicted without weapons, and similar things; while these may appear to be done by human Spirits, in reality they are mostly performed by Angels.

<margin>20.</margin>
To what has been said, I add an eleventh point: that whenever human Spirits are rendered visible to some in assumed bodies <note>In Renaissance theology, an "assumed body" was a temporary physical form made of condensed air or other elements, used by a spirit to interact with the material world.</note> while remaining invisible to others, one must recognize the work of Angels. There is no doubt that this happens at times, because people existing in the same location see them, while others do not. That this is the work of Angels is as certain as the fact that it cannot be the work of human Spirits alone.

<margin>21.</margin>
And the things we have discussed so far belong to the category of those that are attributed to Angelic Spirits for this reason: because they cannot be done by human ones. There are other things which, although they could be done by human spirits and do not exceed human strength, nevertheless seem more rightly attributed to Angels rather than the spirits of men, for just reasons.

<margin>22.</margin>
In this category are the grave harms that are sometimes brought upon the living by Spirits, such as death, the breaking of limbs, and similar things. Although these could be done with human Spirits as the authors, we nevertheless believe they are brought about by Angels and not human Spirits, for the reasons we provide in Chapter 29 in the second part of our *Disputation* <note>original: "Disputationis," referring to the formal theological debate or treatise the author is composing.</note>.

<margin>23.</margin>
From what has been said, it is clear what the difference is between the troubles that Angels bring upon the living and those brought by human Spirits, if we look at the authors of the disturbances. Angels can be troublesome without the work of human Spirits; human Spirits cannot be so without the work of Angels.

# ON HAUNTED PLACES. CHAPTER XXV.

### ->To which type of Angels—the good or the evil—must we attribute those acts that are joined with the disturbances brought by human Spirits upon the living?<-

<margin>1.</margin> It is certain and manifest from the two preceding chapters that many aspects of the infestations and disturbances brought about by human Spirits <note>The author uses "human Spirits" to refer to what we would call ghosts—the souls of the dead.</note> are not actually caused by them, but by Angels. However, since Angels are of two kinds—the evil, who fell from God’s grace because of their sins and were sentenced to the punishments of hell; and the good, who persevered in grace and earned for themselves that most happy eternal life they now lead—it is rightly asked: *Which of them should we recognize as the true authors and effectors of these disturbances?* Should we look to the good (the blessed spirits) or the evil (the Demons)? This question must be answered in the present chapter.

<margin>2.</margin> Indeed, no one is ignorant of the fact that all disturbances, of whatever kind they may be, and everything that contributes to such disturbances, can be managed by both groups. For three things are necessary for such actions: the will (that they desire it), knowledge (that they know how), and power (that they are able). Since each and every one of these traits is found in both good and evil Angels, what is to prevent these disturbances from *potentially* having either as their author?

<margin>3.</margin> Regarding their **will**—that they are capable of such desire—there is no doubt. This duty can be imposed upon them by God, and who shall resist His will? They can also take up these tasks of their own accord, for such actions are not foreign to their nature. Finally, both groups not infrequently perform these and similar services among the living.

<margin>4.</margin> Likewise, the matter of their **knowledge** is beyond controversy. Both excel in the greatest knowledge because of the innate forms <note>original: "congenitas species." In Scholastic philosophy, this refers to "impressed species"—knowledge directly infused into the angelic mind by God at creation, rather than learned through the senses.</note> of all things granted to them at the beginning of the world. In these forms, as if in a mirror, they can most perfectly behold whatever things they wish, in whatever number, and at whatever time. When the observation and experience of many events are added to this innate knowledge, it cannot have failed to increase greatly as time progressed.

<margin>5.</margin> Nor is there any doubt regarding the **power** of both. "Material nature," say the Philosophers <note>Likely a typo for *Philosophi* in the original text.</note>, "is subject to the Angels for every local motion." Does this apply only to the good? No, to the evil as well. Now indeed, these disturbances, and whatever...

<margin>6.</margin>
Perhaps there is an objection to what has been said: that some of these angels fell from the more perfect state in which they were created? This is no obstacle. Their powers, which are required for these tasks, were not undermined or diminished because of this fall. Their nature remained as whole and perfect in them as it did in the others who did not fall from their state, though the latter were also showered with greater supernatural gifts. <note>The author is following the scholastic view that "demons" retain their high angelic intelligence and physical capabilities even after their fall; they only lost their moral goodness and divine grace.</note>

<margin>7.</margin>
*Likewise, these duties are not foreign to the condition of the good Angels. For although they are entirely occupied in the contemplation of the Divine Majesty, they do not set aside the care of human affairs and the concerns which the Greatest and Best God has entrusted to them; indeed, they carry out the duties imposed upon them all the more diligently and ardently as they perceive and observe clearer and greater proofs of the divine benevolence toward themselves.*

<margin>8.</margin>
And good Angels can even be the authors of those troubles *which are attributed to the Spirits of damned men. Likewise, evil Angels can be the authors of those things attributed to Spirits being purified <note>original: "purgandis Spiritibus," referring to souls in Purgatory.</note>.* For why should they not be able? Does the condition of human Spirits prevent them from performing what they are capable of by their own natural powers? It does not.

<margin>9.</margin>
*Therefore, both types of Angels are able to be the authors of all these troubles and the things joined with them, whether they are brought about by good spirits in need of purification, or by the evil spirits of damned men. But are they actually the authors?* This presents a greater difficulty.

<margin>10.</margin>
Indeed, we believe this question is correctly answered if we say: *Of all those things attributed to the evil spirits of damned men, which cannot be done by those spirits themselves, the evil Angels—not the good—are the authors and architects. Furthermore, all things thought to be done by Spirits being purified, which nonetheless cannot be done by their own power, are to be attributed to the good Angels as the efficient causes.* To put it briefly: Demons are the assistants of Damned Spirits in their disturbances; but blessed Angels are the assistants of those being Purified in theirs. See Thomas Aquinas, Part 1, Question 89, Article 8, Reply to Objection 2. <note>This citation refers to the "Summa Theologica," where Aquinas discusses how the souls of the dead can interact with the living.</note>

<margin>11.</margin>
What we are saying seems to be required by the condition of both groups. *For what partnership has justice with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols?* So says St. Paul in 2 Corinthians 6. And these words can teach us that good Angels do not serve the Spirits of those who have lost their salvation; but the same words, inverted, will prove that evil Angels do not intrude themselves into the affairs and business of Spirits being purified. *For what partnership has iniquity with justice? What fellowship has darkness with light? What accord has Belial with Christ? What agreement have idols with the temple of God?*

# ON INFESTED PLACES

<margin>12.</margin> However, to get down to the specifics of each type of Spirit, it should not be said that good Angels are the attendants of damned men in these hauntings. As soon as these souls leave this common and mortal life, they are immediately abandoned by all good Angels; they are handed over to the torturers of hell to be tormented forever. Because of this, they must look to the service of those hellish beings, not the good Angels, if they have need of assistance in any matter.

<margin>13.</margin> But the hatred and cruelty of the Demons proves this point even more clearly. Since they burn with an incredible hatred toward the wretched, who would believe that they would allow those forced into their power and completely subjected to them to depart for even the shortest time or by a hair's breadth? Therefore, they do not only stay with the unhappy souls in hell, but—if these souls are ever compelled to return to the living by God's command—the demons follow them as they go; they promote the souls' evil attempts in whatever ways they can.

<margin>14.</margin> And although the Spirits of damned men may be involved in the affairs of the living against their will, they are never present without wishing ill upon the living, desiring that their returns bring them harm. *The entire will of the damned is unjust*, says Blessed Gregory in the *Moralia*, Book 18, Chapter 1. <note>original: "B. Greg. 18. Moral. cap. 1." Referencing Pope Gregory the Great's influential commentary on the Book of Job.</note> Truly, who would believe that good Angels would lend their efforts to these matters? And who could be convinced that evil ones would refuse them?

<margin>15.</margin> This return to the world is believed to be a kind of punishment for the damned Spirits. For although they greatly desire to be outside of hell to satisfy their lust for wandering, they nevertheless flee from appearing to the living, lest their own miserable condition become known to the living. *Their pride always rises.* <note>original: "Superbia eorum ascendit semper." A biblical allusion to Psalm 73:23, suggesting that the damned remain trapped in their arrogance even in suffering.</note> Now, it is not good Angels but Demons who attend to the punishments of the damned. Therefore, the disturbances observed in this kind of haunting are attributed to these demons, not to the blessed Angels.

<margin>16.</margin> Immediately after their death, as the sentence of the Just Judge is passed upon these Spirits, the wretched souls fall into the power of the Demons. They are snatched away by Demons to places of torment. They are held in those same places by Demons. They are tortured by Demons. They are led out of hell by Demons (whenever they are permitted to go out). And shall the good Angels, and not the Demons, be the authors of the mere troubles they bring to mortals outside of hell, and the things connected to those troubles? *So much for the Spirits of damned men.*

<margin>17.</margin> Furthermore, just as good Angels are not the attendants of damned Spirits, so too the evil spirits (or Demons) do nothing regarding the troubles connected with <term>Spirits being purified</term> <note>These are souls in Purgatory who, according to Catholic doctrine, undergo temporary suffering to be cleansed of sin before entering Heaven.</note>. ...that human spirits suffer nothing from evil angels. <margin>18.</margin> Indeed, the Devils follow the living; they cause trouble for the living. But they completely abandon those who have died piously in Christ, even if they are still being purified by the pains of purgatory. They pursue the former because they hope to bring about their ruin; they abandon the latter because they know that all labor undertaken against souls who are entirely secure in their salvation is in vain.

<margin>19.</margin> The Demons are not ignorant of the condition of these Spirits. They are not ignorant of the reasons why these souls are permitted to return to the living. They know they are enrolled in the number of the heavenly citizens. They know that their return is granted to them by a singular favor of God, so that, being more quickly released from their punishments, they may enjoy the presence of God. <margin>20.</margin> Would the Wicked Spirits lend their efforts to such a task? Not at all.

Thus, the spirits being purified are exempt from the power of Demons: they are not accompanied to the places of purgatory by them, nor do the demons cause them any trouble in those places; indeed, they are not even present while the souls undergo their purifying punishments. This is the better opinion. <note>original: "Aliij aliud. Vide fol. 1945. Bel. Tom. 1." The author notes that others hold different views and directs the reader to the works of Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a highly influential Jesuit theologian and Cardinal.</note> And if they ever return to the world above by the kindness of God, they have good Angels as their companions, not these evil ones. <margin>21.</margin> How then can it be said that their [temporary] bodies are formed or other things performed by the work of demons, which are necessary for this manner of haunting?

It is by God's singular benevolence and favor that these Spirits return to the living. It also cannot be denied that this return is a certain rare work of God. <margin>22.</margin> However, to say that the work of Demons is either necessary in this matter or that God requires it is something that should not be believed.

It is unworthy for those who have triumphed over the Devil, who are heirs to the kingdom of Heaven, who are fellow citizens of the good Angels, and who are all but the possessors of heavenly blessings, to depend on the help of malignant Spirits—especially in a matter from which so much benefit comes to both the good Spirits and to living men. <margin>23.</margin>

While these men lived, they neither could nor should have used the works of Demons unless they wished to incur God's grave offense. This point is clear in everyone's opinion. Now that they are deceased, will they be both able and obliged to do so? They shall not be obliged, and they shall not be able.

Since they burn with an unbelievable hatred toward these wretched souls, who would believe that the demons would let them out of their power or yield even a finger's breadth—even for the shortest time—once the souls are reduced to their power and made entirely subject to them? Therefore, they are not only present with these unhappy souls in hell, but whenever the souls are forced to return to the living by God's command, the demons follow them as they set out; they promote the souls' wicked attempts in whatever ways they can. <note>The author suggests that if a ghost is malevolent or "damned," it is being actively "managed" by a demon to cause further harm to the living.</note>

<margin>14.</margin> And although the spirits of damned men may be involved in the affairs of the living against their will, they are never present without wishing ill upon the living, desiring that their returns bring them harm. **The entire will of the damned is unjust,** says **Blessed Gregory** <note>St. Gregory the Great, a 6th-century Pope and influential theologian.</note> **in Book 18 of the *Moralia*, chapter 1.** Indeed, who would believe that good angels would lend their efforts to such tasks? Or who could be persuaded that evil ones would refuse them?

<margin>15.</margin> This return to earth is believed to be a certain punishment for these damned spirits. For although they greatly desire to be outside of hell because of their lust for wandering, they nevertheless shrink from appearing to the living, lest their miserable condition become known to the living. **Their pride always ascends.** <note>original: "Superbia eorum ascendit semper," a reference to Psalm 74:23, implying that the damned remain arrogant even in their suffering.</note> Now, it is not good angels who flock to the punishments of damned men, but demons. Therefore, these troubles are attributed to these spirits, and not to the blessed angels.

<margin>16.</margin> Immediately after their death, as the sentence of the **just Judge** <note>A common title for God in his role as the final arbiter of souls.</note> is passed upon these spirits, the wretches come into the power of demons. By demons they are snatched away to places of torment. By demons they are held in those same places. By demons they are tortured. By demons they are led out (when it is granted to go out) from hell. Could it be that only the troubles they bring to mortals outside of hell—which are themselves linked to their punishments—have good angels, and not demons, as their authors? **So much for the spirits of damned men.**

<margin>17.</margin> Furthermore, just as good angels are not the servants of damned spirits, so the evil spirits—the demons—accomplish none of those things associated with the troubles of spirits who are to be purified. # PART ONE

How can it be believed that human spirits suffer nothing from evil angels? If [demons] are clinging to their sides while they are involved in the affairs of the living, and provide or perform almost everything that is necessary here, how can it be believed that the spirits suffer no distress or are affected by no trouble from them?

<margin>18.</margin> The Devils certainly follow the living; they produce trouble for the living. But they completely abandon those who have died piously in Christ, even if they are still being expiated by the punishments of Purgatory <term>purgatorijs pœnis; the purifying sufferings believed to cleanse a soul of venial sins before entering Heaven</term>. They persecute the living because they hope to bring about their ruin; they abandon the dead here because they know all labor is undertaken in vain against souls who are entirely secure in their salvation.

<margin>19.</margin> The demons are not ignorant of the condition of these spirits. They are not ignorant of the reasons why they are permitted to return to the living. They know these spirits are enrolled in the number of the citizens of heaven. They know their return is granted to them by a singular favor of God, so that, being more quickly released from their punishments, they may enjoy God. Would the Wicked Spirits contribute their efforts to this matter? Not at all.

<margin>20.</margin> Thus, the spirits who are to be purified are exempt from the power of demons: they do not accompany the deceased body to the places of Purgatory, nor do they bring any trouble to them in those purgatorial places; indeed, they are not even present with those undergoing purgatorial punishments. This is the better opinion. <note>original: "Hæc melior opinio." The author is weighing different theological schools of thought.</note> (Others say otherwise. See page 1945 of Bellarmine, Volume 1.) <note>St. Robert Bellarmine was a highly influential Jesuit theologian whose works on Purgatory were standard for the era.</note> And if ever they return to the world above by the kindness of God, they have not these [demons] as companions, but good angels. How then can it be said that bodies are formed by the work of demons, or that other things are performed which are necessary in this method of haunting?

<margin>21.</margin> It is by the singular benevolence and favor of God that these spirits return to the living. It also cannot be denied that this return is a rare work of God. In this matter, to say that the work of demons is either necessary or that God demands it should not be believed.

<margin>22.</margin> It is unworthy for those who have triumphed over the Devil; who are heirs to the kingdom of Heaven; who are fellow citizens of the good angels; and who are all but possessors of celestial goods, to depend on the help of malignant spirits—especially in a matter from which such great benefit comes to both good spirits and living men.

<margin>23.</margin> While these men lived, they neither could nor should have used the works of demons, unless they wished to incur the heavy offense of God. This matter is clear in everyone’s opinion. Now that they are deceased, shall they be both able and obliged to use them? They shall not be obliged, and they shall not be able.

<header>CONCERNING HAUNTED PLACES.</header>

## CHAPTER XXV.

->*To which angels, as their authors, should those things be attributed that are connected to the troubles brought upon the living by human spirits: to the good or to the evil ones?*<-

---

<margin>1.</margin>
It is certain and manifest from the two preceding chapters that there are many things in the <term>infestations<gloss>disturbances or hauntings</gloss></term> and troubles brought about by human spirits which are not caused by those spirits themselves, but have angels as their authors. However, since angels are of two kinds—some evil, who fell from God’s grace because of their sins and were sentenced to infernal punishments; and some good, who persevered in grace and earned for themselves eternal life, which they now lead in greatest happiness—it is rightly asked: *which ones should we recognize as the true authors and executors of these troubles?* Is it the good, that is, the <note>original: "beatos Spiritus"</note> blessed spirits, or the evil, that is, the demons? This question must be answered in the present chapter.

<margin>2.</margin>
Indeed, no one is ignorant of the fact that all troubles, of whatever kind they may be, and everything that contributes to those troubles, can be managed by both. For since three things are necessary here—the will, so that they desire it; knowledge, so that they know how; and power, so that they are able—and since each and every one of these is found in both good and evil angels, what prevents these troubles from having both as authors?

<margin>3.</margin>
And concerning the will—that they are able to desire this—there is no doubt. This duty can be imposed upon them by God; and who shall resist His will? They can also take up these duties of their own accord, for they are not foreign to their condition. Finally, both types of angels frequently perform these and similar things among the living.

<margin>4.</margin>
So too, the matter of their knowledge is beyond controversy. Both excel in the greatest knowledge because of the <term>congenital species<gloss>innate intellectual forms or categories of all things imprinted on the angelic mind at creation</gloss></term> of all things born with them at the beginning of the world. In these, as if in a mirror, they can most perfectly behold what things they wish, how many, and when. When the observation and experience of many things is added to this, their knowledge could not help but receive great increases through the passage of time.

<margin>5.</margin>
Nor is there any doubt regarding the power of both. *Corporal nature*, the philosophers say, *is subject to the angels in regard to every local motion.* <note>This refers to the Scholastic belief that angels move physical objects by applying their will and power to move them from one place to another.</note> Is it subject only to the good? No, to the evil ones as well. Now indeed, these troubles, and whatever...

<header>PART ONE.</header>

<margin>6.</margin> Since these effects are joined with them, all things are brought about and perfected through the movement of physical nature.
Perhaps it stands in the way of these statements that some of these angels fell from the state of perfection in which they were created? It does not. The powers of these angels, which are required here, were not weakened for this reason; they have not been diminished. Nature remained as whole and perfect in them as it did in the others who did not fall from their state, though the latter were enriched with greater and <term>supernatural<gloss>gifts that go beyond the limitations of created nature</gloss></term> gifts.

<margin>7.</margin> *Thus, these duties are not foreign to the condition of the good angels either.* For although these angels are entirely occupied in the contemplation of the Divine Majesty, they do not set aside the care and concern for human affairs which the Best and Greatest God has entrusted to them; indeed, they execute the duties imposed upon them all the more diligently and ardently as they perceive and observe clearer and greater proofs of the divine benevolence toward themselves.

<margin>8.</margin> *And good angels can also be the authors of the troubles that are attributed to the spirits of damned men. And evil angels can be the authors of those troubles attributed to spirits who must be purged <note>original: "purgandis Spiritibus," referring to souls in Purgatory</note>.* For why should they not be able? Does the condition of human spirits prevent them from performing what they are able to do by their own powers? It does not.

<margin>9.</margin> *Therefore, both can be the authors of all troubles and the things connected to them, whether they are brought about by good spirits and those needing purgation, or by the evil spirits of damned men. But are they actually the authors?* This poses a greater difficulty.

<margin>10.</margin> We believe this question is correctly answered if we say: *For all those things which are attributed to the evil spirits of damned men, but which cannot be done by the spirits themselves, not the good angels, but the evil angels are the authors and architects.* Furthermore: *Everything thought to be done by spirits in purgatory, which nevertheless cannot be done by their own power, must be ascribed to the good angels as the efficient causes.* To put it briefly: Demons are the assistants to the damned spirits in their troubles; but the blessed angels are the assistants to those in Purgatory in theirs. See <note>Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, Part 1, Question 89, Article 8, Reply to Objection 2.</note>

<margin>11.</margin> What we say seems to be required by the condition of both. <note>The following quotes St. Paul in 2 Corinthians 6:14-16.</note> *For what participation has justice with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols?* <note>original: "Quæ enim participatio iuſtitiæ cum iniquitate? quæ ſocietas luci ad tenebras? quæ conuētio Chriſti ad Belial? qui conſenſus templo Dei cum idolis?"</note> So says Saint Paul in 2 Corinthians 6. And these words can teach us that good angels do not serve the spirits of lost salvation here; but these same words, when reversed, will prove that evil angels do not thrust themselves into the matters and business of spirits in purgatory. For what participation has iniquity with justice? What fellowship has darkness with light? What agreement has Belial with Christ? Or what agreement have idols with the temple of God?

# THE SECOND PART OF THE DISPUTATION <note>original: "Disputatio"</note> ON HAUNTED PLACES:
## *IN WHICH THE ARGUMENTS AND JUDGMENTS, by which the condition of troubling spirits is recognized, are revealed and discussed.*

### INTRODUCTION <note>original: "Isagoge" — a Greek term commonly used in academic Latin to denote a formal introduction to a subject.</note> TO THE SECOND PART of the Disputation concerning Haunted Places.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'A' decorated with foliate scrolls and a central figure.</image-desc>

<margin>1.</margin>The second part of the Disputation is devoted to investigating the distinction between those spirits who cause trouble. Since it is our purpose to prescribe the methods by which places may be cleansed of <term>infesting spirits<gloss>spirits that "haunt" or occupy a specific location to the distress of the living</gloss></term>, and since not all spirits are driven away by the same means (just as the condition of all spirits is not the same), <margin>2.</margin>the spirits themselves must be entirely recognized and distinguished before the methods for cleansing the places can be provided. The second part of the Disputation serves this specific purpose.

We do not, however, investigate here the distinctions of all spirits that appear; we desire to know only those who cause trouble, <margin>3.</margin> because our Disputation concerns these alone, and not all spirits in general. The classification of other types of spirits has been treated elsewhere, albeit briefly.

Since, however, the spirits who cause trouble are of two kinds

# ON THE SIGNS WHICH DISTINGUISH DEMONIC SPIRITS 
# from human ones.

## CHAPTER XXVI.

### *Whether, and which form, distinguishes human spirits*
### *from demonic ones or from demons appearing*
### *to the sight.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Many feel that the nature of the form <note>original: "Forma rationem" — the outward appearance or shape assumed by the entity</note> must be highly valued in discerning and distinguishing spirits. While their judgment is not reckless, it would be the mark of a flighty mind to admit it without any hesitation. We believe the truth is concluded in three Assertions.

*The first is* that certain forms are common to all spirits; therefore, no certain distinction between spirits can be sought from these.

*The second* is that demons reveal certain specific forms.

*The third* is to make certain probable conjectures concerning human spirits <note>i.e., identifying specific shapes that likely indicate a human soul rather than a demon</note>.

<margin>2.</margin> *A human form is common to all Spirits.* They offer themselves to the sight of the living—not just the spirits of deceased humans, but also Demonic ones. How many examples did we produce in the chapter above concerning harassing spirits appearing in *human form*; yet some of these were human, while others were Demonic?

<margin>3.</margin> One might perhaps easily allow oneself to be persuaded that spirits seen in human form are human; but it is not so easy to accept that Demons lurk beneath a *human* guise. Yet it is just as easy for Demons to fashion and assume a *human form* as it is any other. In this, no greater power is required, nor is greater diligence or knowledge needed than in other transformations.

<margin>4.</margin> Many have been seen under a *human form*. First, there was that one whom the people of Hildesheim called *Hutgen* <note>original: "Hutgen" — likely a variation of "Hütchen" (little hat), a Germanic household spirit or kobold known for wearing a distinctive cap</note>, after his hat; whom we mentioned above in Chapter 1. Then there were two others mentioned by *Alexander ab Alexandro* <note>Alessandro Alessandri (1461–1523), a Neapolitan lawyer and scholar famous for his work "Genialium dierum" (Genial Days)</note> in Book 4 of *Genial Days*, chapter 19. One of these offered himself as a companion to a man who was traveling to Rome intending to commit a terrible crime against his father; the other was ready to carry a certain religious man named *Thomas* across a river. These are discussed in Chapter 30 on the Demonic—and perhaps even the one who approached *Christ* in the desert to tempt Him took such a form.

But even under *human form*, they have very often attacked Holy men and tried to cast them down from the fortress of holiness. A certain demon, in the likeness of a father, approached *William*, Count of the Poitevins <note>original: "Vvilhelmum Pictauorum Comitem" — refers to William X of Aquitaine (1099–1137), who was said to have become a holy hermit</note> and a most holy inhabitant of the wilderness; as *Theobald* relates in his life, chapter 19, found in *Surius* <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a German monk and hagiographer who compiled lives of the saints</note>, Volume 1. Another, in the likeness of a wretched *husband*, approached Saint *Melania*: found in the same *Surius*, in the same volume. A third, in the likeness of a *Monk*, approached Saint *Dominic*: in his Life, Book 3, chapter 12. A fourth, in the likeness of a *woman*, approached Saint *Justina*, for whom *Cyprian* once wasted away with love: just as *Metaphrastes* <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine author known for his "Menologion" or collection of saintly lives</note> writes in the Lives of both.

And the one who was troublesome to the Blessed *Vincent* <note>Saint Vincent Ferrer (1350–1419), a famous Dominican preacher</note> appeared now as a vast *Ethiopian* <note>original: "Aethiopem" — in medieval and early modern hagiography, demons were frequently depicted as "Ethiopians" or black figures to symbolize darkness or the absence of divine light</note>; and now as a certain venerable *hermit* of great age, according to *Petrus Rauzanius* <note>Pietro Ranzano (1428–1492), a Sicilian bishop and historian who wrote about Vincent Ferrer</note> in Book 1, chapter 9 of his Life. And a little black boy was seen, who was troublesome to Saint *Clare*: as is found in chapter 13 of her life. <margin>7.</margin>
Nor is it a wonder that demons fashion *human forms* and faces. Their purpose is not only to strike terror and horror into the living; they also seek the destruction of mortals and the ruin of the soul. Since they can procure this through a *feigned human* form, they seek it with a *human face* in order to kill, just as they use strange forms to terrify. This is the first point. The second follows.

<margin>8.</margin>
*Yet a certain form and face* betrays the demons. Which ones? All those of the second and third order, which we mentioned in Theses 11 and 12 of Chapter 19: those of *beasts and monstrous animals*. These, I say, betray the demons because they suit demons perfectly; moreover, no necessity compels—nor does any reason prove—that the spirits of deceased humans should appear under such forms.

<margin>9.</margin>
And indeed, those forms suit demons perfectly, whether we consider the goals the demons set for themselves under these masks, or the reasons of divine providence, which is not lacking even in this matter. The demons' purpose is to strike terror and to harass; and does not the horrifying appearance of wild beasts and brutes serve this better than the human form, which is naturally friendly? The reason of divine providence demands that these spirits understand their own condition, which is most miserable due to sin and differs little from that of beasts and monsters. It also ensures that men may know how much they must guard themselves against demons, whose outward and simulated form offers proof of the highest cruelty.

<margin>10.</margin>
*No reason compels* the spirits of humans to come forth under these forms. For those spirits are either involved in the affairs of the living so that they may be helped by their prayers <note>original: "subsidijs," meaning spiritual aid like masses or alms</note>—which is the purpose for spirits being purified in Purgatory—or to offer testimony of divine justice within themselves and to pay the penalties they contracted by living badly, even to their own shame; this is the end seen in the damned <note>original: "damnatis"</note>...

St. Basil <note>Basil of Caesarea (c. 330–379), an influential Greek theologian</note>, in his commentary on Isaiah chapter 2, records that they often insolently insult men in the shape of a *cat, a weasel, or a dog tearing itself apart*. These are from Remy. But to the third point.

### ON INFESTED PLACES

...in the lightness of its character, nor in its size or smallness, it should not deviate from the human form.

<margin>14.</margin> No one doubts that this form is the sign of a human spirit. What can represent a human spirit as well as the human form? And indeed, such a form as the spirit used to produce when it lived in and nourished the body. Because this form does not easily represent any spirit other than a human one, a conjecture is made: that demons are hardly ever seen under a human form unless they also provide some sign of themselves through a certain deformity of the human form; from which you may easily detect them, just as one knows *the lion by its claw* <note>original: "ex ungue Leonem" — a proverb meaning that a whole thing can be judged by a small part</note>.

<margin>15.</margin> Hence it is that those who have been terrified by ghosts <note>original: "Spectris"</note> or tempted by spirits in any way, if they noticed nothing beyond the human appearance, believed they were seeing the spirits of men, not demons. On the contrary, they considered them demons if the human appearance reflected some flaw, either in one of its parts, or in its color, or in its attire, or in the excessive bulk or smallness of the body. The Emperor Nero did not doubt that it was the spirit of a man <note>referring to the ghost of his mother, Agrippina, whom he had murdered</note> who reflected his mother, as discussed in chapter 1. But Thomas the Monk—according to the witness of Alexander ab Alexandro <note>Alexander ab Alexandro (1461–1523) was a Neapolitan scholar known for his work on ancient laws and folklore</note> in Book 4, Chapter 19 of his *Genial Days*—believed he had a man as a traveling companion; finally, he discovered it was a true demon, and not before he noticed that his feet, as he was about to cross a ford, were *the feet of a beast, not of a man*.

<margin>16.</margin> From what has been said, it follows that *the external form betrays demonic spirits in two ways*. One is if the ghosts are seen in the shape of beasts or monsters. The other is if they are seen in human form, but of such a kind that *it has a certain flaw* and, in some way, deviates from the usual appearance of men.

<margin>17.</margin> Furthermore, a flaw in the form can happen in many ways. Either by **the addition of some part**, such as if a spirit appears in human form with a tail; or by **the removal of a part**, such as if it appears without a head, arms, or another notable part; or by **its shape**, such as if it reflects a lion in its feet or a donkey in its ears; or by **excess of size**, such as if it is seen with a monstrous magnitude; or by **lack of size**, such as if it appears smaller than any human size; or by **attire**, such as if it is seen in a completely foreign dress that is not in use among men; or by **the motion of the body**, such as if it gestures too much, and being inflamed, is more unrestrained and not at all appropriate for a human, etc.

He gives this reason: that this form suits their habits and character.

> *The goat, he says, is distinguished among other cattle for its heavy stench; the demon testifies to his presence by nothing so surely as an intolerable foulness of odor. The lustful obscenity of goats has even given rise to a proverb: the demon busies himself with this one thing above all—to keep his followers as devoted to sexual matters as possible. Lest an opportunity be lacking, whenever he meets them, he assumes that form which is most suited for this use. The petulance of goats toward anyone they meet is often profuse: the demon traverses and wanders through every place on earth until he finds someone to rush upon and attack. A goat’s saliva is poison to fruit, as Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar and writer on agriculture</note> testifies in Book 1, Chapter 2 of "On Agriculture," and its teeth are a most present cause of death and plague: Satan’s bite is viper-like, his breath lethal and deadly. The goat’s gaze is grim and fierce, its brow rough with horns, its beard long and unkempt, its hair hanging wildly, its legs thin—the entire habit of its body is designed for foulness. And these things suit the demon. See more, if you wish, in Rémy.*

# ON HAUNTED PLACES

<margin>1.</margin> Another method by which spirits are detected is through noise and the sounds that work their way into our ears. Since the criteria for distinguishing the truth are often the same as those for gaining knowledge, we must explain in this chapter whether one can distinguish between the spirits of demons and those of humans by the sounds they raise and their feigned cries.

<margin>2.</margin> We have stated above that the sounds stirred up by spirits are varied; however, they all seem to fall into two categories. Some have the appearance of sounds only produced by living beings, such as the voice, shouting, laughter, or groaning. Others are "naked" sounds <note>meaning simple, mechanical noises like thumping or crashing that lack vocal quality</note>, which can also be associated with inanimate things. Might the former reveal human spirits while the latter reveal demons? *A perfect distinction of spirits cannot be drawn from this.* Demons are able to perfectly stir up the sounds of living beings just as easily as they do naked sounds or those of the non-living.

<margin>3.</margin> Furthermore, the sounds of living beings are of two types. Some are articulate, others are confused—or *inarticulate*. The former are proper to humans, while the latter belong even to brute animals. *Could it be that a human spirit is detected from articulate sounds, and a diabolical one from the inarticulate? Whatever the case may be regarding the latter, the former—articulate sounds—should not be attributed to humans alone; therefore, they do not reveal only humans.* Let it be granted that a true, articulate voice belongs to a human; yet a *false* voice, however articulate it may be—as is the case here—can certainly belong to demons.

<margin>4.</margin> Perhaps an articulate sound of such a nature that it *serves as an index of the mind's thoughts* <note>rational speech that communicates complex ideas</note> would, if heard, come only from a human spirit and thus prove its presence? *Even this cannot be maintained.* Diabolical spirits, being capable of producing sounds, are also capable of articulate sounds and of forming those sounds that serve as indices of thoughts and concepts.

<margin>5.</margin> There is another difference in sound, whereby some are called *high-pitched* and others *low-pitched*. Both are raised by spirits; both are taken in by the ears of the living. But just as we have already said, these do not reveal the type of spirit. High and low sounds can be raised by human spirits, and they can be raised by demons.

<margin>6.</margin> Moreover, there are some sounds that *strike the ears of the listeners harshly*, while others *affect them pleasantly*. Is it possible that the former reveal cruel and grim demons, while the latter are specific—if not to all, then at least to some—to the spirits of deceased humans? *Not even this is certain.* Could not the wicked spirits, who transform themselves into angels of light <note>A reference to the biblical warning in 2 Corinthians 11:14 that the Devil can appear as something holy or beautiful to deceive</note>, also speak with the tongues of angels and soothe the ears?

<margin>7.</margin> Nicolas Rémy <note>A prominent French judge and author of "Daemonolatreiae libri tres" (1595), who claimed to have judged hundreds of witches</note>, in Book 1, Chapter 8 of his *Demonolatry*, seems to teach that demons are revealed by a twofold voice: one that is *muffled and thin, or weak.*

### SECOND PART. 117

The author first supports this with examples of several witches who confessed that their demons—their "Martinelli" <note>A term used for familiar spirits or personal demons</note>—possessed voices like those produced by people speaking into a large jar or a cracked clay pot. He adds the testimony of Hermolaus Barbarus, who (as recorded by Petrus Crinitus in his seventh book, *On Honest Discipline*, chapter 2) testifies that he heard the voice of a whistling demon. This occurred when, having been asked about Aristotle's "Entelechy" <note>original: *Entelechia*; a complex philosophical term for the soul or the "actualization" of a thing</note>, the demon replied to both him and George of Piacenza. To these accounts, we may add what Psellus teaches in his book *On Demons*: that demons deliberately produce thin and faint voices so that their lies are less likely to be detected behind a blurry obscurity. Furthermore, Gennadius, the Patriarch of Constantinople, heard the confused voice of a specter standing at the altar at night; when he crossly rebuked it, the event was recorded in the writings of Cedrenus, Calistes, and Theodoret in the addition to Zonaras (Volume 3, Book 1 of the *Collected Church Histories*). The "lekanomancy" <note>original: *λεκανομάντεια*; a form of divination using a basin or bowl of water</note> of the Assyrians and Chaldeans was also used for this purpose, where demons would utter words from a basin with a shrill voice and a thin whistle. Nicolaus Remigius records these and similar points in the cited passage.

However, these points were not made by Remigius to suggest that the spirits of demons *must* always be distinguished from other spirits by these specific vocal differences. Such voices could potentially be used by any spirit, and while they are common to demons, demons are also capable of producing the exact opposite sounds. Remigius is simply teaching that demons have produced these specific voices while inhabiting assumed bodies.

<margin>8.</margin>
**Nevertheless**, although human spirits cannot be distinguished from demons based solely on what has been said so far, there are certain sounds and noises that seem to belong to demons alone; likewise, there are others that provide a probable sign of human spirits. From these, a certain discernment and differentiation of spirits can be sought.

<margin>9.</margin>
*There are two types of sounds that have demons as their authors. First, those that resemble nothing but brute animals or horrifying monsters; and second, those that occur with a massive uproar and a great shaking and movement of objects.*

<margin>10.</margin>
It is unlikely that anyone other than demons could be the authors of either type. Indeed, these sounds are most fittingly attributed to demons alone. Regarding the first type, there is no other reason for these uproars and sounds stirred up by spirits than to reflect their *strange and monstrous forms*. Therefore, just as they present themselves to the sight in such forms, they also make themselves heard through the manufactured voices of brute animals and monsters. Regarding the second type, they are caused partly to inflict distress—which is the primary goal of infernal spirits in haunted places—and partly because such feats often cannot be accomplished by human strength.

## ON HAUNTED PLACES

<margin>11.</margin> In addition, there are many reasons that compel us to attribute these disturbances and the disorganized cries of brute animals to human spirits. To whom else should we attribute them? To those being purified? <note>original: *Purgandis*; referring to souls in Purgatory</note> But the purpose they have in returning to us does not require such cries. To the damned? Though they may desire to be troublesome, the nature of divine providence requires them to reveal themselves rather than do actual harm; thus, they are said to excite human-like disturbances and sounds, so to speak, rather than those of beasts.

<margin>12.</margin> And for this reason, holy men have detected the presence of demons from their trumpeting, whistling, roaring, howling, grunting, and similar voices of brute animals. See chapter 19 of the present Disputation.

In this same way, an Evil Spirit <note>original: *Spiritus Nequam*</note> revealed itself in a certain house among the Corinthians where Dacius, the Bishop of Milan, once stayed. We include the whole account here using the words of the Blessed Gregory from the third book of his *Dialogues*, chapter 4, as it may serve several points in this Disputation. During the time of Justinian, when Dacius, the Bishop of the city of Milan, was driven out for the sake of the faith and was traveling to Constantinople, he arrived at Corinth. Seeking a large house for his lodging that could accommodate his entire retinue, and finding one with difficulty, he saw from a distance a house of suitable size and ordered it to be prepared for his stay. When the locals of that place said he could not stay there because the Devil had inhabited it for many years, the <margin>b. r.</margin> venerable Dacius replied, saying: "On the contrary, we ought to stay in that very house precisely because the evil spirit has invaded it and driven away human habitation." He therefore ordered it to be prepared for himself and, feeling secure, entered it to endure the struggles of the ancient enemy.

And so, in the silence of the dead of night, while the man of God was resting, the ancient enemy began to imitate the roaring of lions, the bleating of sheep, the braying of donkeys, the hissing of serpents, the grunting of pigs, and the screeching of mice with immense voices and great shouts. Then suddenly Dacius, awakened by so many voices, arose; he was vehemently angry and began to cry out with a loud voice against the ancient enemy, saying: "It has turned out well for you, you miserable wretch. You are the one who said, 'I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High.' <note>A reference to Isaiah 14:13–14, traditionally interpreted as the boast of Lucifer before his fall.</note> Behold, through your pride you have been made like pigs and mice; and you who unworthily wished to imitate God, behold, as you deserve, you now imitate beasts." At his voice, the demon was put to shame; the house became a dwelling for the faithful, and the lying and unfaithful spirit departed. So says Gregory, and after him Baronius <note>Caesar Baronius, a prominent 16th-century Cardinal and church historian</note> in Volume 7, for the year 540.

<margin>13.</margin> Meanwhile, between the two modes already mentioned, I would say that a more certain argument can be drawn from the former than from the latter: although perhaps not even from the former...

...or so certain that it admits no exception. The most wretched condition of the damned perhaps sometimes expresses these cries. Their supreme wickedness also causes it, so that when they desire to harm mortals, they produce even these disturbances, which are better suited for causing harm.

<margin>14.</margin> But let us discuss *how human spirits are detected here*. I would consider one sound in particular to provide a significant argument for their presence: namely, that which *is a certain sign of a sorrowful soul*, such as sighs, groans, weeping, and lamentations. For although these sounds can also be produced by demons, they nevertheless seem proper to humans: they are more fitting for humans, and they serve the purposes of human spirits more than those of demons.

<margin>15.</margin> They seem to be proper to humans because groaning, weeping, and lamenting are characteristic of mankind; for this reason, just as one recognizes a person by their physical form, a strong (or at least significant) argument for a human spirit can be drawn from these sounds.

<margin>16.</margin> These sounds are more fitting for humans because they are testimony of a crushing grief. God seems to require human spirits to express this grief above all others when they return to us; clearly, this is so that the living may understand the miseries of the deceased <note>The author refers here to the "poor souls" in Purgatory who suffer while awaiting entry to Heaven.</note> and, being taught by their example, may be on their guard and pursue a better life. Such a lesson could not be so effectively provided by the wailing and shrieking of diabolical spirits, who are of an entirely different nature and condition than humans.

<margin>17.</margin> Thus, these sighs and groans do not serve the purposes of demons so much as those of human spirits—if not all human spirits, then certainly the good who are in need of purification <note>original: *purgandis*; souls in Purgatory.</note>. For these sounds are perfectly suited to stirring up compassion in the listener. Why, then, should they not be attributed to those to whom mercy can be shown? The spirits of demons are both unworthy of mercy and hope for none; however, the spirits needing purification both hope for mercy and are worthy of it.

# CHAPTER XXVIII.

## Whether, and by what manner of speech, human and diabolical spirits may be distinguished from one another.

<margin>1.</margin> It is not only noises, disturbances, and disordered sounds that are heard being stirred up by spirits: speeches are also heard, which they hold with living men. Because of this, the present Disputation <note>The term for a formal academic or theological argument.</note> requires that...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the types of manifestations found in haunted locations. While the previous page focused on non-verbal sounds like groans and weeping, this page shifts to the analysis of verbal communication—speech—as a method for distinguishing between different types of spirits.</meta>

<page-num>120</page-num>
->ON INFESTED PLACES<-

Let us investigate not only noises, but also **speeches** <note>original: "orationes". While this often means "prayers," the author uses it here in the broader sense of spoken discourse or verbal communication from spirits.</note>; so that we may understand whether they too provide some means of distinction.

<margin>2.</margin> Indeed, if all speeches were of one kind, this labor would be undertaken in vain (for in one and the same speech, which is always similar to itself, what distinction could you establish?). But since there are many kinds of speeches, this discussion cannot be useless; perhaps it is even more difficult because there are so many kinds.

<margin>3.</margin> Some speeches are *declarative*; in which there is either **truth** or **falsehood**. Others are *non-declarative*; although they contain a complete meaning, they do not signify truth or falsehood. Furthermore, the former group looks toward either past time, the present, or the future. The latter group, however, are sometimes prayerful <note>original: "deprecativæ"</note>, sometimes commanding, sometimes questioning, sometimes wishing, and sometimes calling out. Moreover, it can happen to all of them that they are either good or bad, etc.

<margin>4.</margin> And *all these speeches are held by Spirits*: and, what is more, all of them can be held by all spirits. For this reason, an examination of all of them could be established. However, since the matter would involve almost infinite work, we must discuss those that are more common to Spirits and seem to reveal the distinction between them more certainly.

<margin>5.</margin> These are: *openly evil; encouraging toward the good; requesting what is good; revealing hidden things; and vain*—that is, those things spoken only for the sake of showing off or which are trivial.

<margin>6.</margin> These are the categories. Within each category, there are several types. Those that are *openly evil* are those that either result in an insult to God, or cause harm to neighbors, or invite such things. In the first category are blasphemies; in the second are dire curses, insults, outrages, slanders, lies, foul language, and the like. In the third are those that lead to what has been mentioned in any way.

<margin>7.</margin> Those *encouraging toward the good* are as varied as the types of good things themselves; but they belong properly to those good things that are freely chosen and performed by us in some way, such as almsgiving, prayer to God, fasting, and the duties of any virtues, etc.

<margin>8.</margin> Those *requesting what is good* look to the benefit of the one praying. These too are distributed according to the kind of good things; and, among Spirits, they are seen most of all in those works by which they can be helped: such as pilgrimages, Sacrifices <note>The "Sacrifice" here refers to the celebration of the Mass offered for the souls of the dead.</note>, prayers, corporal works of mercy <note>Traditional charitable acts such as feeding the hungry, visiting the sick, or burying the dead.</note>, etc.

<margin>9.</margin> Those *revealing hidden things* look toward either the past, the present, or the future. For although some of these things might not be hidden by their nature, they can be hidden relative to those who would know them. To these, I shall add the secrets of the hearts of any person.

<margin>10.</margin>
We call **"vain speeches"** <note>original: "Vanas orationes"</note> those in which nothing of importance is proposed in what is said; rather, they are undertaken for the sake of a joke or levity, and show almost nothing else than the actions of the speakers. These are the specific types of this category. **Are these human spirits distinguished from demons by such speech?**

<margin>11.</margin>
**If they are distinguished by any kind of speech, they are distinguished only by speech that is "petitionary" <note>original: "petitoria" – speech that asks for something, like a prayer or a request for help.</note> (among the good spirits) and speech that "reveals hidden things."** The former is naturally characteristic of human spirits; the latter is, by its nature, proper to demons. **The other three types are common to both demons and human spirits** (though not to all of them).

<margin>12.</margin>
Therefore, so that the truth of this assertion may stand, three things must be demonstrated. First, that there are three types of speech common to both demons and certain human spirits, which therefore do not universally distinguish the spirits of demons from human ones. Second, that one type belongs to demons alone. Third, that one type is proper to human spirits, and therefore from these two, a distinction can be sought between human and demonic spirits. Let us teach each point individually.

<margin>13.</margin>
**Regarding those that are "openly evil," it is certain that they are familiar to demons.** Why would they not adopt openly evil things, since their aim is to corrupt even those things that are indifferent or even good by nature? Indeed, there is no kind of evil in the entire universe that they flee from, none that they do not occasionally employ. That the **first and second types** <note>referring back to the classifications on the previous page regarding declarative and non-declarative speech used for ill intent.</note> are not foreign to their nature is proven in the cases of the possessed, through whom they sometimes vomit out wagon-loads of blasphemies, insults, slanders, and lies.

## CHAPTER XXIX.

### *Whether, and how, in the troubles that are brought and the evils that are inflicted by the agency of spirits, human spirits can be distinguished from the spirits of demons.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Someone might easily agree with the opinion that from the evils and troubles brought by spirits, no distinction can be found by which human spirits are distinguished from those of demons. This is not only because both human and demonic spirits can be troublesome, but also because both have, at various times, brought great evils and harm.

<margin>2.</margin>
*Demonic spirits* are troublesome even without any physical injury. The matter is clear from daily examples; and, if ancient ones are required, they are proven among others by the spirits who, in Scotland, made the castle of Stirling echo with horrid groans (concerning which see Chapter 1). There are also *human spirits* who are troublesome without any physical injury, as proven by the spirit of Cleonice, a Byzantine virgin; who by her presence alone was a heavy burden to Pausanias, King of the Spartans <note>Pausanias accidentally killed Cleonice and was said to be haunted by her ghost until his death</note>. This was likewise mentioned in that same first Chapter.

<margin>3.</margin>
*Demonic spirits* have indeed inflicted wounds. The virgins of the Monastery of Verret experienced this and prove it by their own misfortune; as does the worker who was carried away from the George mine <note>original: "fodina Georgiana"</note> (concerning whom see Chapter [number unclear]). And that *human spirits* can and do inflict such things is proven by the spirit of Nero’s mother <note>Agrippina the Younger, whom Nero had murdered</note>; who, as Suetonius writes, at times *raged against him with the lashes of the Furies* <note>original: "verberibus furiarum in ipsum sæuijt"</note>.

# CHAPTER XXX.

## *Whether—and from which duties and services sometimes performed for the living by spirits—it can be known which are human spirits and which are Diabolical.*

<margin>1.</margin>
In this context, we use the word "duties" <note>original: "officia"</note> to refer to certain works of spirits that they display in assumed bodies. Although these are varied, they seem to be reducible to four main types: some we call *idle*; others *troublesome*; others *destructive*; and others *serviceable*. The first kind has no regard for humans; the latter three are undertaken with humans in mind and for their sake.

<margin>2.</margin>
They are called *idle* <note>original: "otiosa"</note> not because the spirits have no purpose in them—for spirits do nothing without a goal and reason—but either because they are undertaken for their own sake alone, or certainly not for the sake of humans. In this category, we place the nighttime games of Northern specters, which Olaus Magnus <note>A 16th-century Swedish archbishop and historian famous for his descriptions of Nordic folklore and geography.</note> mentions in book 3, chapter 11, of his *History of the Northern Peoples* <note>original: "Gent. Septent."</note>.

*Troublesome* <note>original: "molesta"</note> are those undertaken by spirits so that the peace of men may be disturbed, or so that they may suffer some adversity; or, if they are not undertaken for that reason, they are nonetheless received with annoyance. Such are the raising of noises, the twitching of ears, and so forth.

I call them *destructive* <note>original: "pernitiosa"</note> when, beyond the annoyance they bring, they also cause harm, whether to one’s worldly goods or to the health of the body.

*Serviceable* <note>original: "obsequiosa"</note> are those by which some good is brought to mortals, or human services are performed.

<margin>3.</margin>
We have discussed the *troublesome* and the *destructive*; and in this chapter, we have noted whether and what distinction they create between human spirits and the spirits of demons. We shall now examine whether any distinction can be drawn from the *services* <note>original: "obsequijs"</note> that spirits bestow upon mortals.

<margin>4.</margin>
For there is *no doubt* that spirits perform certain *services* for mortals. Many Sorcerers <note>original: "Magi"; in this context, practitioners of magic who enter into contracts with spirits.</note> experience this—those between whom and spirits there are pacts...

## CHAPTER XXXI.

->*Can it be discerned from the idle duties of Spirits which are human and which are the Spirits of Demons?*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
Among the fourfold duties of spirits, we have discussed the *troublesome, the harmful, and the subservient* <note>original: "molesta, perniciosa, & obsequiosa"</note>; and we have demonstrated how they contribute to distinguishing between the spirits. One category remains: the *Idle Duties* <term>Idle duties: "Otiosa Officia," referring to supernatural activities that seem to have no practical purpose or result, like play or dancing</term>; these must be examined in this chapter so that they do not seem overlooked. We shall do so briefly, as a judgment concerning them can be easily made from what has already been said.

<margin>2.</margin>
The nature of these duties is clear. They are not undertaken by spirits properly for the sake of men, but for their own sake and for their own reasons. In this category, we specifically place dances and games, certain playful gestures, and those things which have a similarity and affinity with them.

<margin>3.</margin>
There is no doubt that these things are sometimes done by spirits. For to say nothing of those things which spirits have in nightly gatherings with men of lost salvation <note>A reference to the "Witches' Sabbath" or gatherings of the damned</note>, Olaus Magnus <note>Olaus Magnus (1490–1557) was a Swedish archbishop and historian famous for his descriptions of Nordic customs and folklore.</note> reports that among Northern peoples, night travelers and herdsmen often observe a wonderful harmony and game of spirits. The inhabitants call this the "dance of the Elves" <note>original: "choreas Eluarum"</note>. We discussed these in Chapter 1.

<margin>4.</margin> But do these duties distinguish human spirits from demons? Certainly, anyone who compares the natures of these duties and the conditions of the spirits themselves would think so. Since these duties are signs of joy, one would attribute them only to those spirits who can share in joy—such as human spirits needing purification <note>original: "purgandi," referring to souls in Purgatory who are being "cleansed" before entering Heaven</note>. One would exclude them from those who can feel no joy or pleasure, which primarily includes the demons themselves.

<margin>5.</margin> For what is doubtful here? Is it whether these duties are signs of joy? Or whether spirits being purified share in joy? Or whether joy does not reach the wicked, especially demons? All these points are certain and clear.

<margin>6.</margin> That they are *signs and evidence of joy* is held by the common sense and consensus of everyone. From these acts, everyone infers the joy in the souls of others. Everyone believes that if they perform these acts, they have given proof of their own inner joy.

<margin>7.</margin> That *spirits being purified share in joy* is gathered from this: the end of the troubles they endure is the infinite pleasure of eternal life. Moreover, the expectation of that very pleasure, which is a certainty for them, brings them present joy. And it must be believed entirely that they are refreshed by the prayers and intercessions <note>term: "suffrages," or formal prayers and good works offered by the living to benefit the souls of the deceased</note> of the living which are offered for them.

<margin>8.</margin> And just as these human spirits can and do receive pleasure, so too are the *demonic spirits devoid of all pleasure and joy*. The Blessed <note>original: "Beati," those who reign in Heaven</note> who reign with Christ in heaven cannot be affected by any sadness. The damned, who are excluded from heaven and tortured by infernal punishments, can receive no joy. So great is the pain and sadness of the damned that if any pleasure could exist in them, it would soon be swallowed up. So great is the justice of God avenging the sin of the ungodly in hell that He does not wish to cooperate with them in any act by which they might share in pleasure, as our Ludovico Molina <note>Luis de Molina (1535–1600) was a prominent Spanish Jesuit theologian</note> beautifully philosophizes in the first part of his commentary on Saint Thomas. But if Saint Augustine sometimes teaches that *they rejoice in their unhappy power*, he is not to be understood as granting them any actual pleasure, but only suggesting that this power is pleasing to them.

<margin>9.</margin> However, these "idle duties" <note>term: "otiosa officia," referring to supernatural activities that serve no practical or "servile" purpose, like making music or playing</note> which we have mentioned are not characteristic of good spirits. What if they should not even be attributed to them? What if they belong to evil spirits alone? Let us briefly teach these *three* points, according to the plan of our work.

<margin>10.</margin> First, experience teaches this regarding those spirits which we said above are called *Good Fellows* <note>original: "Guteolos," a Latinized version of German folklore terms like "Gütel," referring to house-spirits, kobolds, or brownies</note> by the Germans. It has often been observed that these spirits are lightly mischievous and perform what might be called miming actions. Who, indeed, would doubt...

## SECOND PART.

<margin>7.</margin> These points make the answer to the proposed question difficult. In the meantime, however, I would say those are not mistaken who believe a distinction can be drawn from *sacred places*. For the most part, Demons are excluded from Temples; but human Spirits (whether all or only some will be discussed later) are admitted to them. Because of this, those who are observed troubling or infesting the living in sacred places are considered, for the most part, not to be Devils or Demons, but the spirits and souls of deceased humans.

<margin>8.</margin> There is an established custom among Catholics—and not without reason—that if any places are infested by Demons, they are to be liberated and purified by the exorcisms and prayers of the Church. Why then do we look for infesting Demons in *sacred* places, temples, and oratories, which have been both purified and consecrated to God through exorcisms and prayers? Before places are consecrated for divine use, Demons are banished from them by the authority left to the Church by God; once they are consecrated, shall they then become the dwellings of Demons? Shall they be able to infest them at their whim? Can they be troublesome to mortals in those places, bringing destruction and harm?

<margin>9.</margin> How *many* things are there in temples and consecrated places which the Wicked Spirit hates "worse than a dog or a snake" <note>original: "cane peius et angue," a classical Latin idiom used to describe intense loathing or avoidance</note>? The Images of Saints? Relics of Saints? Sacred vessels? Holy objects used in the administration of the Sacraments? Exercises of piety? The most holy body of Christ under the appearance of bread <note>The Eucharist, which Catholics believe is the real presence of Jesus</note>?

<margin>10.</margin> Nor do the arguments brought forward above in *Thesis 6* contradict this assertion. For they either show that the Spirits of Demons are forced to *sacred places* by power and as if against their will; or that they do not truly make the places "infested"; or that they are not troublesome by stirring up disturbances, but only distract the mind so that it is not joined to God in prayer as is fitting.

<margin>11.</margin> There is perhaps one point that seemed to have some strength: that people who suffer persecution by Demons can be found in sacred places; from this, it might be believed that sacred places are rendered "infested" by Demons. But this is so far from weakening our assertion that it actually confirms it even more. For we have learned from certain witnesses, taught by their own experience, that those who suffered the troubles of such Spirits were safe in sacred places when they were safe in no other locations.

<margin>12.</margin> And so we think the matter stands, for the most part: that they are *human Spirits, and not demons, who are observed in sacred places*. Nevertheless, it can happen, though more rarely, that Demons are troublesome even in these spots. Caesar Baronius <note>A prominent 16th-century Cardinal and historian</note> provides us two examples of this in Volumes 5 and 6 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. He records one event occurring around the year of our Lord 415...

# CONCERNING HAUNTED PLACES

It is said that in a certain church in Alexandria—which was once a most famous shrine to an Idol—even though it had been consecrated to Christ by Theophilus of Alexandria <note>Theophilus was the Patriarch of Alexandria (385–412 AD) known for his efforts to convert pagan temples into churches</note>, it nevertheless endured the infestations of Demons. This continued until the Relics of Saint Mark the Evangelist, Saint Cyrus, and Saint John were brought into it. This is taught by the acts of these same Martyrs, recognized in the later Council of Nicaea and confirmed by Saint John Damascene. (Volume 5).

A second instance occurred around the year of our Lord 471, involving Gennadius, the Bishop of Constantinople, shortly before his death. While he stood praying at the altar of Sacrifice by night, pouring out his prayers to God, a Demonic specter appeared to him. He immediately put it to flight with the sign of the cross, as if using a thrown weapon. As it withdrew, it spoke with a human voice: *“I am going away, and I will be quiet while you are alive; but I will return after your death, and I will overturn the Church in every possible way.”* <note>original: "Abeo, & te viuente quiescam; reuersurus post obitum tuum, & modis omnibus euersurus Ecclesiam."</note> This is recorded in Volume 6, from Theodore the Reader (Collection, Book 1) and Nicephorus (Book 15, Chapter 23).

To these two instances, we *add a third*, taken from the *Life of Saint Dominic* (Book 3, Chapter 12). The holy man had commanded his followers that they should not linger in the Temple after the final bell had been rung. On one occasion, the Devil remained behind, having disguised himself in the form of a monk. He did this so that, by appearing to transgress the holy man's command, he might be rebuked by him as a disobedient brother. His goal was to trick Dominic into violating the laws of silence <note>Monastic silence was a strict rule; the demon hoped to provoke Dominic into speaking unnecessarily</note>, which the holy man observed with the greatest devotion. The Wicked Spirit's hope did not fail: for when he was rebuked, he immediately smirked and taunted Dominic for having broken the laws of silence.

<margin>13.</margin> And so much for *sacred places*. Are human and Demonic spirits also distinguished by their presence in desert and wild places? This is very probable. *It is entirely likely that those who cause disturbances and turmoils in desert places, removed from human use, are Demons and not human spirits.*

<margin>14.</margin> The arguments for this are as follows: first, because whoever has infested such places has historically been regarded as a Demon; second, because they have insinuated they are Demons through many signs; and furthermore, there is no reason why human spirits should be believed to wander or dwell in such places.

<margin>15.</margin> *They have been regarded as Demons*, such as whoever was troublesome in the vast wilderness to Antony and Paul, the first inhabitants of the desert <note>St. Antony the Great and St. Paul the Hermit were 3rd-4th century monks who famously battled demons in the Egyptian desert</note>, whom Saint Jerome mentions. Also, whoever disturbed the nightly quiet of the monks in that same wilderness, whose zeal and piety Cassian <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435 AD) wrote extensively about the spiritual struggles and "noonday demons" faced by desert monks</note> commends. Also, whoever has been found in metal mines, and so forth, which we discussed above.

<margin>16.</margin> Moreover, they *prove themselves to be Demonic spirits by certain signs*, having been observed in the aforementioned places in various strange forms; such as those who [appeared] to Antony...

Is it to give testimony to divine justice by those very torments they endure? But this should be shown to humans, who can be helped by them, not to stones and trees, nor to wild beasts and brute animals found in desert places. Is it to obtain the aid and patronage of the living and be helped by their works? But this should be expected in inhabited places, where people are found.

<margin>19.</margin>
It seems entirely for the sake of the living that the Spirits of the deceased return to the living; whether the reasons are sought from the perspective of the Spirits, or from the perspective of God, by whose will and dispensation their return occurs. It is therefore absolutely necessary that they frequent the places where the living dwell: in cultivated places that serve human needs, and not in uncultivated places alien to human society.
