Among **unbelievers** <note>original: "Infidelium"; in this context, it refers to anyone outside the Catholic Church.</note>, or non-Catholics, not all locations are of a single kind. This is not surprising, as not all unbelievers are of one kind. There are Pagans; there are Jews; there are Heretics <note>The author likely refers to the various Protestant sects emerging during the Reformation era.</note>. Therefore, some places belong to Pagans, where Pagans dwell; others to Jews, where Jews dwell; and others to Heretics, where Heretics reside.

<margin>3.</margin>
We could run through all these places in our discussion. Why do we not? Because it is not necessary. We are content with our own: the Heretics and the Catholics. Let the Pagans examine their own affairs, and the Jews theirs. *What business is it of ours to judge those who are outside?* <note>original: "Quid nobis de his, quæ foris ſunt iudicare?"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 5:12.</note>

<margin>4.</margin>
It might perhaps seem that this inquiry is undertaken in vain, because the places of Heretics are said to be entirely free from all harassment by spirits, and for that reason, spirits cannot be distinguished in those locations; however, because the places of Catholics *are* infested, this study ought not be omitted on their account. But what if *the places of Heretics are not sufficiently free* either? We could prove this with examples; truly, because these cannot be brought forward without both revealing the places infested by spirits and accusing men of heresy, let us set aside examples and proceed by reason.

<margin>5.</margin>
We ask: what exactly would prohibit spirits from the places of Heretics? Do spirits flee from Heretics? And do any spirits at all—even <term>demons</term>—flee from such men? Who would believe this? Who would say it? Who would profess it? How great is the familiarity of the teachers of Heretics with a certain kind of spirit, whose primary occupation is the infestation of places? See the twenty-first chapter of the *Disputation on those Possessed by Demons*.

<margin>6.</margin>
It is manifest that Pagans and Jews suffer the infestations of spirits; why should Heretics be exempted, who are in the same class and state of damnation as those other unbelievers?

<margin>7.</margin>
Either the holiness of the doctrine which the Heretics profess deserves that they should not be attacked by spirits (as some say), or the uprightness of the life they lead, or some singular privilege by which God wishes them to be exempt from these things. Which of these is it? Or what else? It is not the holiness of their doctrine. That is most impious, being contrary to the doctrine of Christ, the Apostles, and all of antiquity. It is not the uprightness of their life; true uprightness of life never coexists with impious doctrine. It is not a privilege, because it cannot be shown when, why, in whose presence, where, or by whose authority this was granted. What else could it be?

<margin>8.</margin>
It is certain, therefore, that *the places of Catholics endure the harassment of spirits*. Let it also be established that *those of Heretics are not immune*. Let us ask, then, whether spirits may be distinguished by these locations.

**First, not all who trouble Catholics are demons.** They are also troubled by human spirits. There were Catholics such as Germanus, the Bishop of Capua, to whom the spirit of Paschasius the Priest appeared several times—an event recorded by Saint Gregory <note>original: "Beatus Gregorius"; referring to Pope Gregory the Great's *Dialogues*, a foundational text for medieval ghost stories.</note>. Does a righteous life protect them? Such a life is often found lacking among Catholics; furthermore, if it is present, it actually provokes the demons' desire to do harm. What of the sacred signs <note>Likely referring to the "character" or mark of baptism on the soul.</note> that are in the souls of Christians? These are not lacking in Heretics, nor are they lacking even in the damned.

<margin>12.</margin>
**Finally, not all who infest Heretics are either spirits of demons or human; but they are sometimes demons, and sometimes human.** We showed at the beginning of this chapter that Heretics are not immune from the infestations of spirits. That they are *now* troubled by the spirits of demons is confirmed by the very reasons we used in that section. That they are *now* troubled by the spirits of damned men is suggested by their shared society and the same desire for harm they share with demons, and similar reasons. 
It is worth adding an example of both from Caesar Baronius <note>A prominent 16th-century Cardinal and Church historian.</note>, Volume 6, around the year of our Lord 513. He shows by the example of Isidore—a follower of Severus, the author of the heresy called the "Acephaloi" <note>A "headless" sect of Monophysites who rejected the Council of Chalcedon.</note>—that the spirit of a damned man terrified and troubled a Heretic. The spirit of the man who struck the Lord in the face before the High Priest Caiaphas appeared to Isidore, indicating that he would be Isidore's companion in punishment just as he had been in crime. (See Chapter 38, Thesis 8.)

That they <note>Referring to the heretics mentioned on the previous page.</note> are also not safe from demons is shown through the story of a certain Palestinian leader, who was himself a Severian <note>A follower of Severus of Antioch, a group considered heretical by the author's church for their views on the nature of Christ.</note>. This man, wishing to enter the Lord’s tomb <note>The Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem.</note> out of a desire for piety, was several times driven back by a ram (this was a demon in the form of a ram). Even after a confession of the sins which he thought were preventing his entry, he was still not permitted to go inside. Only then was he admitted, and the head-butting ram ceased its attack, when he abjured his heresy and testified by Catholic communion that he was a Catholic. This is recorded by Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607), a cardinal and historian known for his multi-volume history of the Church.</note>, citing first from Chapter 36 of the *Spiritual Meadow* <note>original: "Prati Spiritualis"; a famous 7th-century collection of stories about monks and miracles by John Moschus.</note> and later from Chapter 79 of the same work.

<margin>13.</margin>
Let it be settled, therefore, that both groups—Catholics and Heretics alike—are exposed to the disturbances of spirits. Let it be settled that both suffer disturbances from the spirits of men and of demons. From both these points we may conclude that *heretical and Catholic locations do not distinguish human spirits from demons.*

# CHAPTER XXXV.

## *Whether, and by what times, human spirits and demonic spirits—those who sometimes involve themselves in the affairs of the living—are distinguished.*

There are roughly three aspects of time from which a distinction between human and demonic spirits must be drawn, if any exists: *substance, quantity, and quality.* The "substance" of time is contained in day and night. The "quantity" is seen in duration and brevity. The "quality" is found in sacred and profane <note>In this context, "profane" simply means "ordinary" or "secular," as opposed to holy days.</note> days.

It seems certain that we must take all these differences into account when identifying spirits, because the spirits themselves take account of them. We have spoken elsewhere regarding days and nights. Experience also teaches that some spirits are not troublesome for long, while there are others who, through the long duration of their disturbances, even drive their masters from their own seats and homes. Furthermore, because times among Christians are either sacred or profane, it is clear that spirits are troublesome at these or those specific times, just as it is clear that they are troublesome at all.

But as for Substance, Quantity, and Quality of time: do they distinguish human spirits from demons? Because we have distinguished three differences of time, we shall conclude with three Assertions—as far as can be reached by conjecture—what the reality seems to be.

The first is this: *Nights and days do not distinguish human spirits from demonic spirits.* It is not necessary for us to say that those spirits which are troublesome at night are demons, and those which appear during the day are human. Both the spirits of demons and of men are troublesome at night; and in the daytime, in the clear light, both the spirits of demons and of men are troublesome.

<margin>§. 5.</margin> What we are saying is clear from examples of every kind of spirit. Nor does reason contradict this assertion. Just as spirits are not restricted to a specific place, so they are not bound to a specific time. Both space and time exist outside of them; neither truly affects them. They do not require the light of day to see where they are going, nor are they aided by the gloom of night in order to carry out their operations.

<margin>6.</margin> These things are certain. *Nevertheless, human spirits are more fond of light and are naturally more drawn to it;* if not all of them, then certainly those who are to be purified <note>Referring to souls in Purgatory who are undergoing cleansing before entering Heaven.</note>; *demonic spirits, however, are fond of darkness and the night.* Is this any wonder? For those who do evil hate the light; this is the judgment of the Lord in John 3. Yet one may also argue the opposite: since the spirits to be purified do not do evil, they should not hate the light. Therefore, they will dwell in the light, just as those spirits mentioned by Blessed Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), whose "Dialogues" are a primary source for medieval ghost stories.</note> (and by us in Chapter 1) frequented the public baths.

<margin>7.</margin> There is another argument for this matter: that the Royal Prophet <note>A traditional title for King David, the presumed author of the Psalms.</note> indicates that he *who dwells in the help of the Most High* need not fear even the *Noonday Demon* <note>original: "Dæmonio meridiano"; a reference to Psalm 91:6. In medieval theology, this was often seen as a demon that attacks during the day or through spiritual boredom/sloth.</note>. By this, he suggests that most demons are troublesome at night and, as it were, fear the light of the sun; yet some are so bold that they do not flee the light like the others, and they even attack men during the day. This is how the Talmudic scholars, Rabbi Solomon <note>Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, also known as Rashi (1040–1105), a famous commentator on the Bible and Talmud.</note>, and the Chaldean <note>Referring to the Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible.</note> explain the Prophet’s passage, as Genebrardus <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine scholar and expert in Hebrew.</note> notes in his commentary on the Psalms.

<margin>8.</margin> The Second Assertion: Neither the long duration of the disturbances brought by spirits, nor their brevity, *is a certain and indubitable proof* of specific types of spirits. If it were, I ask you: how long? And which ones? Demonic spirits were troublesome for a very long time in the metal mines we mentioned in the first chapter. And a certain little old woman <note>A ghost.</note> was troublesome for a hundred years or more in the castle of the Tarelli family in Parma. What then? If they could be troublesome for a long time, could they not also be so for a short time? Or shorter still? Or the shortest?

<margin>9.</margin> Nevertheless, if the disturbances are of longer duration and outlast several generations of men, it is very likely that their authors are demons. It is rarer for them to be the spirits of deceased men, especially the damned. I would say the reason for the former <note>The demons.</note> is gathered from the single goal set before them: to always do harm to whatever mortals they can. The reason for the latter <note>The damned souls.</note> is that these damned ones are permitted to return to the living under this law: that they may give testimony to divine justice by their own misery. This is not performed as effectively unless they present themselves to the sight of those by whom they were known; for this reason, it can be believed that they do not cause trouble longer than the lifespan of those people allows.

<margin>10.</margin> The Third Assertion is this: Demonic spirits do not claim either sacred or profane <note>In this context, "profane" simply means "secular" or "non-religious" time.</note> times for themselves as their own property. For they can even be present during sacred—

## CHAPTER XXXVII.

->*Whether it can be gathered from the condition of those who suffer from pursuing Spirits, if those Spirits who are troublesome are human or Demonic.*<-

<margin>1.</margin> Here we assume one thing; a second is to be explained; and a third must be defined. We assume that certain living people suffer from infesting Spirits more than other men. We must explain what we understand by the "condition" of these men. Finally, we must define whether from the condition of the men *who endure the troubles of Spirits*, a conjecture can be made as to whether the Spirits who cause the trouble are human or Demonic.

<margin>2.</margin> We assume that first point, and for that reason, it need not be pursued at length. We have an abundance of examples, and it has been demonstrated elsewhere that this happens for the most most just of causes. See Chapters 15 and 17, etc., of this Disputation.

<margin>3.</margin> By the *condition of the living*, we mean the state of life in which they live and move; yet not just any state, but specifically that which is joined with either a wicked or an honest life. Thus, we can say mortals are of a two-fold condition: some who live a Christian life soberly, piously, and justly; and others who wallow in grave sins and are considered men of lost salvation.

<margin>4.</margin> The question, therefore, is this: if it happens that people from these ranks suffer from infesting Spirits, can it be detected *whether the Spirit who pursues them is human or Diabolical?* And perhaps someone will immediately suspect that the evil are only infested by the evil, and the good only by the good; but nevertheless, to one considering the matter more exactly, another conclusion will seem necessary. And not without reason.

<margin>5.</margin> It is beyond all controversy that *a certain judgment cannot be sought from upright and good men*. Why so? Because not all who pursue upright men are human Spirits, nor are they all Spirits of Demons.

<margin>6.</margin> How perfect in morals was the most holy Job? How great is his commendation in the sacred scriptures? He is called *a man simple, and upright, and fearing God, and turning away from evil* <note>original: "vir simplex, et rectus, et timens Deum, et recedens a malo"; quoting Job 1:1</note>; it is said *there is none like him on the earth*; and yet he sustained the most heavy troubles from Spirits. Was it only by the good and human spirits that this good and most humane man was afflicted? It was the most wicked Satan who afflicted that most holy man.

<margin>7.</margin> Thus, we cannot doubt the integrity of the life of Germanus, Bishop of Capua. Saint Gregory <note>original: "B. Gregorius." <margin>9.</margin> Therefore, the distinction [between types of spirits] ought not to be sought from the character of good men. *Should it be sought from the character of the wicked?* It certainly should: if not absolutely and in every way. There can be little doubt that only evil spirits follow, dog, and persecute those who are themselves evil; it is highly probable that, among the wicked, these spirits are almost always demons, not human souls.

<margin>10.</margin> We deny that the good spirits of those to be purified are troublesome to wicked men or to those who have despaired of salvation. For what reason would they be? Should we believe those who have cast aside all care for their own salvation would care for the salvation of others? Furthermore, such wicked men either do not believe that the spirits of the dead are helped by the assistance of the living, or, if they do believe it, they do not wish to help; and even if they wanted to, their assistance, as enemies of God, would have little power before the Most High God.

<margin>11.</margin> What wonder is it that evil spirits follow, dog, and persecute evil men? They follow them as companions; they dog them as promoters [of sin]; they persecute them as torturers and executioners.

<margin>12.</margin> Evil spirits rejoice in the company of evil men; this is caused by a similarity of character and pursuits. For even "every animal," as a certain author says, "loves its own kind." Truly, since these spirits desire all people to be utterly alienated from God, how could they feel disgust for—rather than seek out—the company of those who, by their own depraved pursuits, turn themselves away from God and flee to the camp of the demons?

<margin>13.</margin> Impious spirits also promote the goals of the impious. It is not enough for them that mortals are miserable; they desire the miserable to be more miserable—the most miserable of all. SECOND PART. 151

## CHAPTER XXXVIII.

### *Whether, and by what form, one distinguishes human Spirits—that is, those to be purged from those who are damned.*

<margin>1.</margin>
We should not discuss all the forms of Spirits under which they are seen in this section, since we are not seeking a distinction among just any Spirits who present themselves to the eyes of the living. We must only look at that form which we called "proper to human Spirits" in the twenty-sixth chapter; and we must inquire whether there is any distinction within that form itself by which human Spirits differ and may be recognized. This is because we are specifically seeking the means by which human souls are distinguished from one another.

<margin>2.</margin>
*We have stated that there is one human form* which reveals human Spirits: namely, that which is so human that it possesses nothing foreign or alien to humanity, and in no way or manner degenerates from the human. For while this form reveals human Spirits, it is common to both: those who are sentenced to the perpetual torments of hell, and those who are being purged <note>original: "purgantur." This refers to souls in Purgatory who are undergoing temporary suffering to be cleansed of sin.</note> somewhere on account of the deserts of their sins.

<margin>3.</margin>
But nevertheless, this form is not so singular that it does not admit many distinctions and differences. For just as there is one form for all living people, yet within this form there are certain things that distinguish a man from a woman, an old man from a youth, a Jew from a Christian, or a sick man from a healthy one; so too, within the single form under which human Spirits hide, there can be distinctions that separate these souls from those.

<margin>4.</margin>
I would consider these distinctions to be fivefold. One is derived from quantity <note>size or scale</note>; another from quality <note>outward appearance or complexion</note>; and the remaining three from the "effect of the mind," of which they seem to be indicators. First, they differ as small and large; second, as white and black; third, as joyful and sad; heavy and light; or fierce and lovable. These differences can happen to one and the same human form. But do all of these actually distinguish the Spirit? Let us define that.

<margin>5.</margin>
*The difference taken from quantity does not distinguish Spirits.* Smallness is not an index only of damned Spirits, nor is greatness an index only of those to be purged. Conversely, greatness does not signify the damned, nor smallness those to be purged. Damned souls and those to be purged can both appear under a small form; likewise, both can appear under a large form.

<margin>6.</margin>
Indeed, we have taught elsewhere <note>a reference to an earlier chapter or a different volume by the author</note> that when there is an excessive surplus or an excessive defect in quantity—such as being a giant or a tiny creature—it is not human Spirits that lie hidden there, but Demons <note>original: "Daemonum." The author suggests that extreme physical distortions in an apparition are a "tell" that the spirit is not human at all.</note>.

Since human Spirits manifest in the affairs of the living for this very purpose—so that they may be recognized—it must be believed that they appear in the same form they possessed while they animated their bodies; for they cannot be recognized except by these features.

<margin>7.</margin>
Those who were of a tall stature while living appear in a large figure when seen after death; those who were small appear in the form of a dwarf. Yet, the tall may die a happy death and thus not be damned; and the small may do the same. Similarly, the tall may incur eternal death at the moment of passing from this life; and these dwarfs may do so as well. Therefore, large size or smallness, even if it sometimes distinguishes human Spirits from Demons <note>Demons were often thought to take on monstrous or distorted proportions.</note>, does not distinguish human spirits from one another.

<margin>8.</margin>
*The difference of qualities in form is of great value in judging human Spirits. For those to be purged <note>original: "purgandis," referring to souls in Purgatory.</note>, unless the night clouds the brightness of the face, a whitish color—or the natural complexion they had when alive—is a strong indicator. For the damned, a black color serves as evidence, especially in clear light. This is not only because common human intuition holds this to be true, but also because just as black is appropriate for damned Demons (and the damned have frequently been seen in this form), so a whitish appearance is appropriate for the good and the blessed; and those who have endured the fires of purgatory have been seen in this form.*

The example of Isidore serves well here, which Caesar Baronius <note>A prominent 16th-century Italian cardinal and church historian.</note> records in Volume 6, page 625, around the year of the Lord 513, citing Eviratus from the *Spiritual Meadow* <note>original: "Prato Spirituali," a famous 7th-century collection of hagiographic stories by John Moschus.</note>, Chapter 39. And I said to him: 'Who are you?' He replied: 'I am he who struck the Lord and Creator of all, Jesus Christ, on the jaw at the time of his Passion.'" Thus it is written there.

Although it would be rash to rush to judgment here—since even the blessed spirits of the heavenly minds have sometimes taken on grim expressions, and Demons have fashioned themselves to look lovely and Angelic—it is easy for me to be persuaded that grimness belongs only to the damned, while loveliness (or at least a lack of grimness) belongs to those in Purgatory. This is because those in Purgatory would have no reason to feign a grim look, and the damned have no reason to simulate a pleasant one.

Nevertheless, the status and condition of spirits in Purgatory demands a certain gravity rather than lightness; and although the damned might be able to display a sense of lightness, no necessity compels them to do so.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.
### Whether, and what kind of, noises and groans reveal the condition and state of human Spirits.

<margin>1.</margin>
In the twenty-seventh chapter, based on the things done by spirits that are perceived by human ears, we distinguished human spirits from demonic ones by this fact alone: that sighs, groans, weeping, and the shedding of tears—if not always, then very often—betray the presence of human Spirits. *But are these sounds common to both those in Purgatory and the damned? Or are they unique to one or the other?*

<margin>2.</margin>
One might perhaps guess that these sounds belong uniquely to those in Purgatory, because they seem to be a form of imploring for help and support—the kind of aid that only spirits in Purgatory are able to receive. However, that they also apply to the damned is suggested first (to omit others) by the words of Christ, who teaches that in hell <note>original: "inferno"</note> there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Secondly, it is proven by the spirit of the Emperor Galba <note>A Roman Emperor whose ghost was said to haunt the city after his assassination</note>—surely a damned man—whose massive groans were observed several times, to his own great distress, by the Emperor Otto <note>Otho, Galba's successor, who was reportedly haunted by Galba's ghost</note>. Thirdly, this is confirmed by those spirits who filled the house where Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A 15th-century scholar who recorded many ghost stories in his work "Genialium Dierum"</note> lived in Rome with wailing and the shrill sound of voices.

<margin>4.</margin> The spirits of the damned may heave sighs, weep, cry, and wail; but there are almost always two things, one or both of which betray them: namely, the quality of impatience <note>In this context, impatience implies a lack of submission to divine will or a restless, angry suffering</note> which the groan and wail themselves bring with them, or some other trait that cannot be attributed to spirits being purified.

In contrast, just as the spirits of the damned endure their punishments with extreme impatience, they frequently give the clearest evidence of this state.

<margin>6.</margin> Truly, what we have said regarding the patience of those being purified should not seem strange. They recognize that the penalties they pay are most just; they know they are inflicted by a most merciful father as if upon most beloved children; they know the pains will soon have an end; and they know that their suffering will ultimately be turned into supreme and eternal joy.

<margin>7.</margin> Furthermore, why would those who are truly patient give signs of impatience? Why would they show it to mortals, whose help they implore with tears and sighs? It is enough for them to explain their misery; in this state, they have no need for outbursts of impatience.

<margin>8.</margin> Nor should they be considered impatient simply because they desire to be freed from their punishments, as some foolishly argue. Shall we also accuse Christ of impatience because he asked for the cup of suffering to be taken from him? <note>A reference to Jesus’s prayer in the Garden of Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39)</note>.

<margin>9.</margin> Thus, the impatience of the damned is a certain reality. They do not wish to acknowledge that the punishments they suffer for their sins are just. Even if they did acknowledge them as just, they nevertheless hold an implacable hatred both for the demons who inflict the punishments and for God, by whose will and command they are inflicted. Even if these factors were absent, this alone would make them impatient: they hope for no fruit from their punishments, nor do they expect any end to them throughout all eternity. Can those who are impatient for so many reasons hide their nature or feign patience?

<margin>10.</margin> Hence it is that whenever spirits in Purgatory <note>original: "Spiritus purgandi," souls undergoing purification</note> have been observed, they have shown no signs of impatience, but rather many signs of patience. This is proven, among others, by those instances mentioned by Blessed Gregory <note>original: "B. ### CHAPTER 40.

#### *Whether, and what kind of prayer distinguishes human spirits among themselves—specifically, those to be purified from the damned.*

<margin>1.</margin>
We stated in Chapter Twenty-Eight that there are many types of prayer, but the one specific to human spirits is a single kind: the petition for good. Now we investigate whether there is anything in this prayer that distinguishes human spirits from one another, revealing whether they are spirits to be purified or the damned.

<margin>2.</margin>
Some might deny that such a thing exists. However, anyone who has closely examined petitionary prayer <note>original: *oratio petitoria*—prayer that asks for a specific favor or help</note> and considered its necessary conditions would not be wrong to say that a form can be found which reveals spirits being purified. It is the kind of prayer that both petitions for one's own good and is not defiled by the stains of sin.

<margin>3.</margin>
That these points are well-argued will become clear if we demonstrate two things. The first is that *the prayer of spirits being purified is a petition for their own good; whereas that of the damned is not.* The second is that *those being purified are unable to sin, while the damned are unable to stop sinning.* Our assertion rests upon these two foundations.

<margin>4.</margin>
The *first* point is confirmed by the condition of the spirits who appear. The goal of those being purified is to obtain the help and support of the living and to be aided by their suffrages <term>Suffrages: From the Latin *suffragium*, referring to intercessory prayers, masses, or good works offered by the living to assist souls in Purgatory</term>. Therefore, if they seek anything, they will seek this especially through their prayer. But the condition of the damned is different. These wretched souls know they can obtain no help from the living; they have no hope for the lessening of the punishments they endure. Why, then, should they be said to seriously implore the assistance of the living?

<margin>5.</margin>
The *second* point is held by the opinion of almost all theologians. They teach that it is impossible for spirits being purified to commit any sin. They also teach that the damned cannot help but sin. Could it be that they are all mistaken?

<margin>6.</margin>
We are aware of Luther's assertion that those dwelling in purgatory sin continuously. But for us, authority carries more weight than that of Luther alone. If those being purified sin continually, what would be the purpose of Purgatory? For there would never be a limit or end to their punishments if there were no limit or end to their transgressions.

How can those who have no capacity [to act] be said to sin? So that anything...

...can they do anything that might profit them toward glory or eternal life? Or is it perhaps possible to *merit* <note>original: *mereri*—in Catholic theology, this refers to performing an action in a state of grace that deserves a supernatural reward from God</note> even in that life? The present life is the time for sowing, not the future. *When night comes, says the Lord, no one will be able to work, John 9. What a man sows (in this life, which is the time for sowing), that he shall reap, Galatians 6. <margin>8.</margin> Blessed Cyprian, the most holy Martyr, in his fourth Sermon, which is *On Mortality*, says that death is beneficial for this very reason: it liberates us from the danger of sinning, to which we are exposed as long as we run the course of this present life. This opinion of the Martyr is not displeasing to the Great Augustine. He relates the same in these words, in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 14: *These and similar opinions, says that Doctor <note>Referring to St. Augustine himself, often called the "Doctor of Grace"</note>, in the clearest light of the Catholic faith, testify sufficiently and openly that the dangers of sinning and fearsome temptations last until the laying down of this body; thereafter, no one shall suffer such things. Even if he did not testify to this, when would any Christian, of whatever sort, doubt this matter?* Thus says Augustine.

<margin>9.</margin> Furthermore, just as those being purified <note>original: *purgandi*—those in Purgatory undergoing cleansing</note> cannot sin, so the damned cannot *not* sin. Although this point does not seem to be beyond all controversy like the former one, it is nonetheless more likely to be true because of the most bitter hatred with which they pursue God, and the distinguished authors who defend this opinion. Among these, not the least is Dominicus Soto <note>A prominent 16th-century Spanish Dominican theologian</note>, in the fourth book of his commentaries, distinction 50, question 1, articles 4 and 5.

<margin>10.</margin> Perhaps the Royal Prophet <note>A traditional title for King David, the presumed author of the Psalms</note> also hints at this when, in Psalm 73, he teaches that *the pride of those who hate God always ascends.* For who has a greater hatred of God than the damned? If indeed *their pride always ascends*, how do they not always sin? Those who are blessed in heaven always do well; those who are damned in hell will always do evil. The former will not want to do anything bad that might offend God, because they love God. The latter do not want to do anything good that might please God in any way, because they are God’s capital and sworn enemies. On this matter, see Volume 2 of Ludovicus Molina <note>A Jesuit theologian famous for his works on free will and grace</note>, on the first part of Saint Thomas Aquinas, regarding article 2, question 64.

### SECOND PART

<meta>handwritten page number 181 at top right; catchword: prodi- (likely "prodidit" or "prodiit", meaning "revealed itself" or "came forth")</meta>

...Spirit, and because the damned cannot help but sin, it is absolutely necessary that if any prayer is uttered by a Spirit—one that both contains a request for something good and is entirely free from the stain of sin—it must be shown to be a Spirit in need of purification <note>original: *purgandos Spiritus*—referring to souls in Purgatory who are being cleansed of minor sins before entering Heaven</note>, rather than one of the damned.

<margin>12.</margin>
In the meantime, however, this judgment based on prayer is extremely difficult. It is very hard to determine the state of a human Spirit from this alone. Why? Because it is incredibly difficult to detect whether a prayer is truly free from the stain of sin, or if it has been tainted by it.

<margin>13.</margin>
How often have mortals been deceived by the fake prayers of Spirits? How many people, misled by the appearance of prayer, believed they were dealing with souls in Purgatory or good Spirits, only to discover at last that they were dealing with <term>shape-shifters: from the Latin *versipilles*, literally 'those who turn their skins', describing deceptive entities or demons who change their appearance</term>, evil-doers, and demons?

<margin>14.</margin>
The reason for this difficulty is that prayer does not possess holiness or piety in and of itself, but receives all its character from the mind of the one who speaks it. The nature of the mind is such that it does not always reveal itself through prayer; at one moment it may desire one thing but signify another through its words; at another it may sound pious while harboring impiety, and so on.

<margin>15.</margin>
Is this judgment based on the prayer of Spirits therefore difficult? Yes. Is it impossible? I would not say so. I believe there are three things which, if found in a prayer, provide a probable sign that the prayer is not faked—that is, that it is free from vice—and is therefore an indicator of a Spirit in need of purification.

<margin>16.</margin>
The first sign is if the prayer is not openly evil by its very nature <note>original: *ex suo genere*</note>. This means it does not insult God, as happens with prayers joined to blasphemy; nor does it harm one's neighbor, as occurs in cases of slander, taunts, insults, evil curses, or foul language.

<margin>17.</margin>
The second sign is if the prayer is not only free from evil by its nature, but is also inherently good. This is the kind of prayer by which either the honor of God is promoted, or our own benefit (or that of our neighbors) is served. It belongs to the first category if the Spirits urge that the <term>Sacrifice: referring to the Sacrifice of the Mass</term> be offered to God. It belongs to the second if they invite the living to distribute alms to the poor or to provide help to the spirits themselves.

<margin>18.</margin>
Nevertheless, this is by no means sufficient, because even good deeds can be done with bad intent. It has been proven by certain examples that there were malignant Spirits who requested prayers from the living. <term>Petrus Marmorius</term> <note>Pierre Marmet, a 15th-century French author known for his writings on the supernatural</note> records that in <term>France</term>, at <term>Confolens</term> on the river <term>Vienne</term> in the year 1478, there was a Spirit that claimed to be the soul of a deceased woman. It filled everything with its groans, shouts, and complaints, and even advised that prayers be said and pilgrimages undertaken. Furthermore, it revealed many true things; but who it eventually...

<header>SECOND PART</header>

## CHAPTER 41

### *Whether it can be known from the evils and troubles brought by human spirits: what the condition of those human spirits is who are troublesome.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Just as it was difficult in Chapter 29 to distinguish human spirits from demons based on the *evils* they bring, so it is no less difficult to distinguish human spirits from one another based on those same evils. However, since it seems that only a certain "modesty" <note>original: *modestiæ*—implying a limitation or restraint in the severity of the disturbance</note> remains to human spirits, while more serious evils occur when devils are the authors, perhaps we may find a difference that distinguishes human spirits from each other (though not necessarily from demons) if we look more deeply into the *troubles* <note>original: *molestias*—referring to the specific annoyances or "infestations" experienced by the living</note> stirred up by spirits. Let us perform both tasks, the latter one first.

<margin>2.</margin>
No one who has a proper understanding of the condition of demons would deny that *there is no trouble of which demons cannot be the authors*. Demons possess free will; and indeed, they possess it in such a way that, alongside their free will, they are endowed with remarkable power and strength. Therefore, with the power they have been granted, they can stir up troubles; and since they possess free will, they can stir up whichever ones they wish—great or small, destructive or harmless.

<margin>3.</margin>
Although we must deal with examples here, we could produce some to show that the greatest turmoils were stirred up by the <term>Architects: from the Latin *Architectis*, here used to mean the masterminds or prime movers of spiritual disturbances—the demons themselves</term>; and others to show that they also cause light and almost playful troubles. What human spirits are capable of doing here, the spirits of demons—who are superior in strength—will certainly also be able to do.

<margin>4.</margin>
Demons, therefore, have this in common with human spirits: both are capable of being mildly troublesome. It is therefore useless to seek a distinction between them based solely on the trouble itself.

<margin>5.</margin>
Nevertheless, if it is already established that the troubles proceed from human spirits, it will be possible to infer from some other source whether the spirits are not those to be purged, but rather damned spirits—and conversely, whether those bringing the troubles are <term>to be purged: from the Latin *purgandos*, referring to souls in Purgatory undergoing purification</term> rather than the damned.

<margin>6.</margin>
And the damned will betray themselves first if, alongside the trouble brought, the living are incited *to some sin*, of whatever kind it may be. For since this is utterly foreign to spirits who are to be purged (as was proven above in Chapter 40, Thesis 67, etc.), it can have no other authors than the damned spirits.

<meta>catchword: Furthermore</meta>

<header>ON INFESTED PLACES</header>

<margin>7.</margin> Next, these same spirits are betrayed by light and scurrilous <note>original: *scurrilis*—implying the behavior of a buffoon or jester, which was considered beneath the dignity of a soul undergoing purification</note> gesturing, combined with annoyance. Who would say this behavior is appropriate for spirits being purged <note>original: *purgandos Spiritus*—souls in Purgatory</note>? Their condition is such that they commit nothing by which they might offend God.

<margin>8.</margin> Thirdly, the damned are betrayed if an annoyance is found to be undertaken for no other cause than to vex the living, and no benefit returns to the one doing the vexing. Such behavior cannot come from spirits being purged; for their purpose is not merely to cause trouble, but to look out for their own state through that trouble and obtain our advocacy <note>original: *patrocinia*—spiritual aid such as prayers, penance, or masses offered on their behalf</note>.

<margin>9.</margin> These behaviors betray the spirits of the damned. But from those being purged comes only that trouble *which has nothing of levity in it: which incites no one to sin: and is undertaken for this reason alone; so that the living may be made attentive, recognize the spirit's condition and misery, and assist them with aid.*

### CHAPTER 42

->*Whether certain services performed by spirits exist, from which a distinction between human spirits might be inferred.*<-

<margin>1.</margin> The answer to what is asked in this chapter is easy. The question is whether there is any distinction between the services <note>original: *obsequia*—helpful or obedient acts, such as tidying a house or guarding property</note> which are performed by spirits for the living, that might distinguish human spirits from one another. The answer is that *there is none*. The reason for this is clear from what was said in Chapter 30; because, as we said there, there are no services so unique to human spirits that they do not also suit demons, or could not be performed by demons. # SECOND PART.

## CHAPTER 41.

### *Whether it can be known from the evils and troubles brought by human spirits, what the condition of those troublesome human spirits is.*

Just as it was difficult in Chapter 29 to distinguish human spirits from demons by the evils they bring, it is no less difficult to distinguish human spirits from one another based on those same actions. However, because it seems that human spirits are only capable of modest troubles, while more serious evils occur when devils are the authors, perhaps we may find a difference that distinguishes human spirits from one another (though not necessarily from demons) if we look more deeply into the troubles stirred up by spirits. Let us address both points, starting with the latter.

No one who has a proper understanding of the nature of demons would deny that there is no trouble for which demons cannot be the authors. Demons possess free will, and with that free will, they are endowed with remarkable power and strength. Therefore, by the power they possess, they can stir up troubles; and by their free will, they can stir up whichever ones they choose—whether they be great or small, destructive or harmless.

<margin>3.</margin>
Although we must deal with examples here, we can produce some cases showing that the greatest disturbances were stirred up by the "Architects" <note>original: *Architectis*; here referring to the primary instigators or masterminds of spiritual unrest, typically high-ranking demons</note> themselves, and other cases involving light and almost playful <note>original: *ludicras*; referring to "poltergeist" style activity that seems more mischievous than malicious</note> troubles. Whatever human spirits are capable of in this regard, the spirits of demons, who are superior in strength, will also be able to do.

<margin>4.</margin>
Therefore, demons have this in common with human spirits: both are capable of being slightly troublesome. It is therefore in vain to seek a distinction between them based solely on the level of trouble caused.

<margin>5.</margin>
Nevertheless, if it is already established that certain troubles proceed from human spirits, it is possible to infer whether those spirits are damned, or whether they are those who must be purified <note>original: *purgandos*; souls currently in Purgatory who require purification before entering Heaven</note> and are not damned.

<margin>6.</margin>
First, it betrays a spirit as being damned if the living are incited to some sin—of whatever kind—alongside the trouble being brought. For since such behavior is entirely foreign to spirits who are to be purified (as was proved above in Chapter 40, Thesis 67, etc.), such actions can have no other authors than damned spirits.

<margin>6.</margin>
*Or perhaps spirits are unable to do these things? Why, I ask? Does a spirit always sin? If so, what then would be the purpose of purgatory?* Perhaps, even if they do not always sin, they are unable to provide these services? Yet they provide even greater things than these. If they can celebrate God with praises (as they do); if they can pay the penalties they have deserved; if they take part in human affairs without sin; why must they necessarily sin if they offer and provide their services to humans? This is especially true since no law prohibits them from doing so, and these acts result in benefit and advantage for human beings.

<margin>7.</margin>
*Moreover, it is clear that these services are not offered through the ministry of demons.* Whatever proceeds from demons is either of such a kind that, by its very nature, it deserves reproach; or, even if the act is good in itself, it is corrupted by the perverse intention and will of the ones performing it. There is nothing that demons can perform well. The Wicked One <note>original: *Nequam*; here used as a title for the Devil or a demonic entity</note> performs no service which, however holy it may appear in outward form, is not worthy of eternal and infernal punishments.

<margin>8.</margin>
*What follows from this? What? Precisely that which is contained in the first part of our assertion: that there are certain services which have none but human spirits as their authors:* namely, those which are inherently honorable and are not defiled by the addition of any small circumstance.

<margin>9.</margin>
*Furthermore, just as these services distinguish the spirits of humans from the spirits of demons, so in the same way they reveal the condition of human spirits: they reveal, I say, spirits needing to be purged—*

<meta>The text cuts off here with the catchword "ritus" (spirits) to be continued on the next page.</meta>

<summary>The author argues that certain honorable and helpful acts performed by spirits must originate from human souls in Purgatory rather than demons, because demons are incapable of truly good intentions or untainted actions.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the argument from the previous section, specifically addressing how the "services" (helpful actions) performed by spirits can be used to distinguish between human souls in Purgatory and demonic entities.</meta>

# ->ON HAUNTED PLACES<-

<margin>10. The manner.</margin> And this is the second part of our Assertion. And why should these services not reveal their source? It is necessary that since they belong to human Spirits, they are either those of spirits who are to be purged <note>original: *purgandorum*; souls undergoing purification in Purgatory</note> or those who are damned. But it should not be said that the condition of the former is the same as that of Demons—namely, that they do nothing well and sin at all times. Therefore, they must be the Spirits of those to be purged.

*However, it is extremely difficult to distinguish these services; for there are many things required for the actions themselves. Although we may perceive and approve of those elements which are obvious to the senses, we cannot see those things that do not fall under the senses—which are nevertheless necessary for the integrity of the action if it is to be considered good—such as the "ends" <note>original: *fines*; the specific goals or intentions that motivate an action</note> which are usually intended by the actors.*

<margin>11.</margin> Great is the power of these ends, and great is their authority. No work is so perfect and absolute in its kind and nature that these added intentions cannot corrupt it. There is nothing that brings so much benefit, whether to the public state or to private individuals, that would lack blame if the spirit of the worker is perverse. *It is the ends that crown the works.* <note>A variation of the Latin proverb *finis coronat opus*, suggesting that the final purpose or result is what gives an action its moral value.</note>

<margin>12.</margin> These ends also insert themselves into the services provided by Spirits. Even services, though honorable in themselves, can be performed wickedly and perversely. How so? Because spirits can be presented and displayed by evil ones; and just as their nature is wicked, so their ends in acting are perverse. For this reason, it was excellently stated by us in the third place that it is very difficult to pass judgment on the nature of these services.

<margin>13.</margin> Although it would be reckless to rush to a judgment here, and a sign of a flighty mind to offer a certain one; *nevertheless, there are some things which sometimes provide probable evidence that these services are right and free from fault.*

<margin>14.</margin> Among others, there are three in particular: humility, constancy, and gravity <note>original: *humilitas, constantia atque grauitas*; in demonology, these were signs of a "good" spirit, as demons were thought to be incapable of maintaining a humble or serious demeanor for long</note>. If services, which are otherwise honorable in themselves, are joined with humility, constancy, and gravity, it is likely they are free from fault.

<margin>15.</margin> By their very nature, evil Spirits are enemies and foes of good works and honorable services. Their pride <note>original: *superbia*</note>, which is always ascending, does not allow them to practice humble things. And even if they perform something humble in appearance once or twice, they can hardly be led to be constant in those same acts. And even if they were constant, it is extremely difficult for them to abstain from showing signs of levity and wickedness.

## CHAPTER XLIII.
### Whether there are certain idle and playful actions that distinguish between human spirits—those who are damned and those still being purged.

<margin>1.</margin>
The response to the question proposed is readily available, provided that what was said in the thirty-first chapter presents no difficulty. It was stated there that *idle* <note>original: *otiosa*; actions that appear frivolous or lack a serious spiritual purpose, such as dancing or games.</note> duties either do not suit human spirits at all, or certainly suit them only very rarely, and only some of them. From this it is clear that *no distinction among human spirits should be sought from these activities.* For what of it? Could these spirits differ by some quality that is neither diverse in both, nor suits either of them in any way?

<margin>2.</margin>
And it shall suffice to have suggested this. Yet, because there are two things that might overturn the foundation of our assertion, these must be resolved in the present chapter before the discourse proceeds further. One is that (as Olaus Magnus <note>A 16th-century Swedish archbishop and historian famous for his descriptions of Nordic folklore and geography.</note> records in Book 3, Chapter 11 of the *History of the Northern Peoples*) the inhabitants in Northern parts believe the games and music of nocturnal *Specters* are stirred up by *souls* that immersed themselves in bodily pleasures while they lived. The other is that the jousts and military gatherings in the district of Worms <note>A city in Germany; the author refers to local legends of "ghostly armies" or spectral tournaments seen in the fields.</note> (mentioned in Chapter 1, Thesis 10) do not seem to have any authors but human spirits—just as first their own confession proves, and then the prayer with which they implored the aid and intercessions of the living.

<margin>3.</margin>
Nevertheless, these things in no way hinder our assertion, since one must either deny that these duties were *idle*, or, if that be granted, one must deny that they were spirits of men by whom they were performed and exhibited.

<margin>4.</margin>
And to speak first of the *Northern Specters*, I would not deny that the duties they performed were playful and *idle*; but I would deny that they are human spirits by whom those things are performed. The places where these duties are carried out, the persons in whose presence they are performed, and finally the acts that are discovered in the scorched grass <note>A reference to "fairy rings"—circles of dark or withered grass—historically attributed to the dancing of spirits or demons.</note> after the dances are finished, provide great arguments in favor of Demons—to say nothing of the *duties* themselves.

<margin>5.</margin>
Nor should the multitude of those holding the opposite opinion persuade us otherwise. How many superstitions are there among the Northern peoples? These same people (as Olaus witnesses in Book 2, Chapter 3) maintain that the souls of those who were drowned or killed by a violent accident wander on a promontory in Iceland—that one which, like Etna, seethes with perpetual fires. Whence this...

<margin>6.</margin>
What is their judgment? Were all those who were killed by a violent death remaining on earth after death? And, to follow our example, from where is it established that those who lead the dances of the *Elves* <note>original: *Eluarum*; referring to the "Elf-dance" or "fairy circles" common in Northern European folklore, often interpreted by theologians as the souls of the frivolous.</note>, as they call them, were devoted to bodily pleasures?
Tournaments <note>original: *hastiludia*; literally "spear-play" or jousting.</note> and military encounters in the territory of Worms <note>original: *VVormatiensi*; a city in Germany. The author refers to local legends of spectral armies or knights seen in the countryside.</note> are either received as idle duties; or if they are indeed idle, they are not exhibited by human spirits. And although both points may be said with probability, I would sooner deny that they are *idle*, lest you seem to rashly condemn their authors, than pronounce a harsh sentence on the spirits and relegate the duties themselves to the class of the *idle*.

<margin>7.</margin>
For not everything that can have the appearance of levity must immediately be considered light and idle. Certain things, though seemingly light, can be done for great and serious reasons; for which they ought to be held as serious, not light. I would say that these military exercises exhibited in the field of Worms are of this kind. Divine providence holds this: that it sometimes punishes sins by those very things through which it was offended by sinners. Therefore, because those soldiers could have offended God by fighting, they could also, through this simulated battle after death, expiate <term>expiate: to atone for or make amends for a sin or a crime through suffering or penance</term> the sin which they committed by fighting.

### CHAPTER XLIV.

->*Whether human spirits, through whom places are rendered haunted,*<-
->*can be distinguished by sacred and profane locations;*<-
->*likewise by cultivated and uncultivated locations.*<-

<margin>8.</margin>
Two things are asked, and by the solution of one, the matter will be clear. It is asked first: whether human spirits are distinguished by sacred and profane places. Second: whether they are distinguished by cultivated and uncultivated places. If the former is explained, there will be nothing remaining here to be explained. But how? Because since it was said in Chapter 32 that *human spirits do not wander in uncultivated places, but in cultivated ones*: if their condition is to be known from the difference of the places, one must find something within those *cultivated places* by which they differ. And in this proposal, there can be nothing except *sacred and profane*. Therefore, we must inquire from this whether human spirits can be discerned.

<margin>9.</margin>
In truth, human spirits can be distinguished in these places in two ways. One is that some are admitted to sacred places, while others are repelled from them:

<margin>3.</margin>

They are not shut out by the prayers of the Church, which (far from begrudging them these places) even wishes for them much more excellent palaces, I say. If they can go about their business anywhere, they can surely do so here: where there is a frequent crowd of people, and where the place itself invites one to pray for the deceased.*

<margin>6.</margin>

<margin>7.</margin>

If we consider the purposes God has in mind for the return of these Spirits to the living, we will judge them to be admitted rather than excluded; since even here, through these Spirits, God can give evidence of His mercy and justice, and they themselves can become participants in the suffrages <term>suffrages: intercessory prayers, masses, or alms offered by the living to alleviate the suffering of souls in Purgatory</term> of the living in these places.

Blessed Malachy <note>St. Malachy (1094–1148), an Irish saint and archbishop known for his visions.</note> observed that [his sister] had by no means entered the church. I respond that the Holy Man also observed, after pouring out prayers to God, that same woman entering the church in a white garment, although she had not yet perfectly satisfied for her sins. But whether she entered the church or was unable to enter, the truth of our assertion remains: for it was shown to Malachy through a vision what his sister's status was; in reality, she neither entered the church nor lingered at the threshold of the church. One should consult St. Bernard in his *Life of Malachy*.

<margin>9.</margin>
Furthermore, as for the *spirits of the damned dwelling in or wandering about churches*, and causing trouble for the living, I would either not believe it, or grant it only very rarely and perhaps in only one specific case. What would they have to do in a church? Are they waiting there for the suffrages <note>Prayers or acts of piety performed by the living to benefit the souls of the dead.</note> of the living? Their affairs are utterly hopeless. Are they refreshed by sacred objects, of which there is a great abundance in churches? Nothing sacred pleases them. Do they rejoice in the exercises of piety that take place in churches? They detest all of these things.

<margin>10.</margin>
Perhaps what we are saying is confirmed by the example of *Valentinus*, a man of loose morals and occupied with refined vanities, as *Gregory* speaks of him (*Dialogues, Book 4, Chapter 53*), whose body was indeed buried in the Church of *the Blessed Martyr Syrus*, but was soon dragged out from there. For at midnight, after the burial, says the same *Gregory*, voices were heard in that same church as if he were being violently expelled from it. When the guards ran to see what was happening, they saw two most foul spirits who were dragging *Valentinus* out by his feet, bound. When morning came and they opened the tomb, they did not find the body. *Gregory* records these things. The same example is cited by the **Council of Tribur** <note>A local church council held in 895 AD in Germany, which dealt with various matters of ecclesiastical discipline.</note> in Chapter 71. If indeed God wishes the bodies of damned men to be banished from churches, would He allow the churches to be haunted by their spirits? For it is from the spirits that the bodies derive all the ignominy <note>shame or disgrace</note> they endure.

<margin>11.</margin>
One case perhaps compels the spirits of the damned to churches, even against their will: when, for instance, their bodies are buried in those churches, and the habits and crimes of their past life demand that they not only be shaken by infernal punishments, but also that their extreme misery be made clear to mortals. Then, perhaps by the most just judgment of God, it happens that the wretched ones wander around their own graves, and in this way provide evidence of their unhappiness to mortals. This concludes the discussion regarding the Church.

<margin>12.</margin>
*It seems that the spirits of the damned cannot be so easily excluded from cemeteries.* Why is that? Because it is a common perception among mortals that the shades <note>original: *manes*; a term used for the spirits of the departed that linger near their burial place.</note> of the dead often frequent their graves, wander about, and are seen. What follows from this? Specifically, that there are also spirits of damned men who are sometimes seen. But how so? Because it is not likely that those being purified are the only ones—

...those to be purified <note>original: "purgandos"; referring to souls in Purgatory who are undergoing cleansing before entering Heaven.</note>, regarding whom this is a common and universally accepted opinion.

<margin>13.</margin>
Nor is there any reason why we should exclude these spirits from cemeteries. For what cause would we? Is it because they do not desire to return to these places? But a judgment should not be made about any place based on their own desires: for if it were up to them, they would never return to the world of the living. No places are pleasing to them, as we have taught above. Are they prohibited from these places by the prayers of the Church? Yet it is doubtful whether the Church can command or order anything to them with such authority. Furthermore, they have not been banished from these places by the Church. The banishment <note>original: "proscriptio"; an ecclesiastical exclusion or exorcism performed during the blessing of a site.</note> which is performed in the consecration of these places touches only upon malignant spirits (I mean demons); as is manifest *from the ritual form* which the Church uses in that banishment.

<margin>14.</margin>
Therefore, to conclude this chapter, a certain distinction by which human spirits are differentiated from one another can be sought from *sacred places*, even if it is not a perfect and absolute distinction. Although they do not differ regarding cemeteries, they do seem to differ regarding churches: so that it is a probable argument that *they are not the damned, but rather spirits to be purified, who are more frequently observed in churches.*

# CHAPTER XLV.

->*Whether, and how, places where the deaths of men occurred, and where grave sins were committed, distinguish human spirits—those of the damned and those to be purified.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
Since in the thirty-third chapter we dealt with places that are haunted <note>original: "infestis"; literally "disturbed" or "dangerous."</note> after someone’s *death*, and likewise places haunted because of grave crimes perpetrated in them, we admitted almost exclusively human spirits to *those* locations. Now, so that we do not break the order we have maintained thus far, we must discuss whether, and how, a distinction of human spirits can be derived from this.

<margin>2.</margin>
Therefore, I believe the condition of the spirits can be detected here chiefly from two things: from their past life, but especially from the end of their life. Since these things relate most significantly to the state of the future life, it seems that a judgment about the state of the deceased can certainly be sought from them.

<margin>3.</margin>
And I shall place in the class of spirits to be purified those who passed their life piously, justly, and soberly, even if they were not without their own blemishes <note>original: "næuis"; literally "moles" or "birthmarks," used here metaphorically for minor sins or spiritual imperfections.</note>; or those who died well and blessedly in the Lord. In the number

# ON HAUNTED PLACES
<note>original: "DE LOCIS INFESTIS"; this refers to locations troubled by spirits or "infested" by hauntings.</note>

...however, are from the ranks of the damned; who have departed from this life unhappily and miserably: whether their life matched its end, or differed from its end.

<margin>4.</margin> Thus, spirits are identified as being from the damned by one factor: namely, an unhappy end. They are identified as being from those to be purified <note>original: "purgandorum"; referring to souls in Purgatory.</note> by two factors: a happy end and a life previously led in piety. A necessary conclusion is drawn from the end; a probable one is drawn from the life, unless the end suggests otherwise.

<margin>5.</margin> In the case of the damned, we establish only one method of recognition: an unhappy end. It does not matter how wickedly a life was conducted, provided the end is happy. In the case of those to be purified, we have distinguished two factors: the end and the life. This is not because we believe that everyone who once lived well will be transferred to the heavenly seats (for many conclude a good life badly), but because a bad death rarely or never follows a good life. Therefore, we ought to hope for the best, both for those who had a happy end and for those in whose lives the evidence of piety and charity shone brightly.

<margin>6.</margin> The things we say are all beyond controversy among the Orthodox <note>In this context, "Orthodox" refers to the established Catholic theological consensus regarding Purgatory and the afterlife.</note>. Therefore, for those who love brevity, it would be a waste of great effort to provide confirmation for these points here. However, there are two matters which, just as they contain some difficulty, are not without their own fruit and utility. The first is, *what sort of life may be called "well-spent"*; the second, *what we should consider a "happy death."*

<margin>7.</margin> It is impossible for a man to define the former in specific detail, unless a revelation has been granted to him from above. If a man does not know whether he himself is worthy of hate or love, how can he know it of another? Yet, in a general sense, it is not only not impossible, but actually easy. That is called a well-spent life in which one has lived piously, soberly, and justly. **Sobriety** <note>original: "Sobrietas"; used here in the classical sense of self-restraint and moral balance.</note> disposes us well toward ourselves; **justice** toward our neighbor; and **Piety** toward God. Therefore, those who in life give to God what is God’s, to their neighbor what is their neighbor’s, and to themselves what is due to themselves, are to be said to have lived well.

<margin>8.</margin> Or, if what has been said is not understood in that way, let those be said to have lived well who, after receiving the **Sacrament of Baptism**, have stained their conscience with no lethal crime <note>original: "scelere lethali"; referring to mortal sin.</note>, nor committed anything that would offend the divine majesty; or if they did commit such a thing, they set it aside again through the preceding and following grace of God, with worthy fruits of **penance**.

<margin>9.</margin> A *happy death* is not that which is full of quiet and tranquility; which lacks a heavy sense of pain; which strikes no horror into those standing by; where many consoling friends are present; where there is a distinguished funeral procession; or any other such things. These things can be common even to the most wicked.

<meta>This page continues the theological exploration of what constitutes a "happy" or "unhappy" death, further categorizing how a person's final state impacts whether their spirit might become a restless one. ->### SECOND PART<-

...all things: but those which are joined with no consciousness of mortal sin, and in which nothing of those things that God and the Church require is omitted.

<margin>10.</margin>
From this (so that what we say may become clear from the contrary), it follows that those first suffer an *unhappy death* who have not laid aside through penance the mortal sins they committed in life. Since these sins bring immediate death to the soul, they do not allow the soul’s own life to be restored as long as they possess the soul itself.

<margin>11.</margin>
Secondly, those pass away unhappily who, although they laid aside the crimes committed in life with worthy fruits of penance, nevertheless in their weakness, or at the very gates of death, gravely offend God and neither seek nor obtain pardon for the offense. This offense happens for many other reasons, but especially through the omission of the Sacraments, which were divinely instituted; such as, after Penance, the Eucharist and Extreme Unction <note>The "last rites" or final anointing of the dying, intended to offer spiritual strength.</note> for some.

<margin>12.</margin>
Thirdly, those *conclude this life unhappily* who, although they omit none of the Sacraments and lay aside the sins of their past life with worthy works of penance, nevertheless do not make restitution of others' goods when they are able. The opinion of **Saint Augustine** is eloquent and true: *Sin is not forgiven unless that which was taken is restored.* <note>original: "Non dimittitur peccatum, nisi restituatur ablatum." This legalistic theological principle holds that repentance is invalid if one keeps stolen or ill-gotten goods.</note>

<margin>13.</margin>
These are said to die unhappily, just as those are said to *live well* who fulfill what is just, pious, and sober. And just as there is good hope for the spirits of the latter when they lay down this mortal body, so there is fear for the salvation of the former when they are heard to cause disturbances <note>original: "tumultuari"; in the context of this book, it refers to the noisy activity or "tumult" of a haunting after the body is buried.</note> after the burden of the body has been laid aside.

<margin>14.</margin>
*We have good hope for them*: because good beginnings usually have good ends. *We fear for the salvation of these others*: because their sins seem to be *unto death*, for which the Apostle denies pardon in 1 John 5 <note>Referencing the biblical distinction between "venial" sins and "deadly" sins that lead to spiritual death.</note>. Nevertheless, we pass no *certain and absolute* judgment on either that admits no exception; because *the servant falls and stands for his own Lord* (Romans 14). *The Lord has been appointed Judge of the living and the dead* (Acts 10). It was said to us: *Do not judge* (Matthew 7). *The Day of the Lord will reveal all things* (1 Corinthians 4).

<margin>15.</margin>
Therefore, as we have said, *judgment taken from life and death is highly probable: it is not entirely certain.* Although it rarely happens, there can nevertheless be an exception. We must take care so that we are beyond danger and have good hope; that we may hasten toward a happy death through a good life, so that we may be found among the good Spirits, with the Father of Spirits, in the glory of the resurrection.

## CHAPTER XLVI.

->*Whether and how human spirits who cause disturbances are distinguished by Catholic and Heretical locations.*<-

---

<margin>1.</margin> Locations distinguished as Catholic or Heretical do not necessarily distinguish human spirits from demonic ones, but they do distinguish human spirits from other human spirits. The former point was shown in Chapter 34. The latter point must be explained in the present chapter, though very briefly.

<margin>2.</margin> When it is established that the spirits who appear and cause trouble are human, we believe it is entirely probable that, if they are found among Heretics <note>In the context of this 16th/17th-century text, "Heretics" refers to Protestants (Lutherans, Calvinists, etc.) who had broken away from the Roman Catholic Church.</note>, they are the souls of damned men, not of those who are being purified by the fires of Purgatory. However, the reverse is not true: not every spirit observed among Catholics is necessarily a soul in Purgatory <note>Meaning, a damned soul could also haunt a Catholic area, but a soul in Purgatory would have no reason to haunt a Protestant one.</note>. Therefore, while the condition of human spirits cannot be determined solely by their presence in Catholic places, it can be identified by their presence in Heretical places.

<margin>3.</margin> To confirm this assertion, many words are not needed. There is no doubt that in Catholic places, both types of spirits are found. Therefore, if we show that *the spirits of those in Purgatory do not trouble Heretics*, we will conclude the chapter, and it will be demonstrated that *it is the spirits of damned men who trouble Heretics.*

<margin>4.</margin> The very purpose of these spirits proves this clearly. Why would the miserable spirits of those in Purgatory seek anything in Heretical places, knowing they would not find what they need? Are they looking for the help of the living? Can they hope for any assistance from those who deny that the deceased are helped by the prayers and deeds of the living?

<margin>5.</margin> Indeed, almost all the Heretics of our times openly profess this denial. This includes the "Rigid Lutherans," such as the *Centuriators* <note>The Magdeburg Centuriators, authors of a famous 16th-century Lutheran history of the church organized by centuries.</note> (Century 1, Book 2, Chapter 4); the "Mild Lutherans," like *Philipp* <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a primary founder of Lutheranism alongside Luther.</note> in his sections on Satisfaction; and *Brentius* in the Württemberg Confession. It includes the *Zwinglians* according to *Cochlaeus* <note>Johannes Cochlaeus (1479–1552), a fierce Catholic opponent of Luther.</note> in his *Acts of Luther* for the year 1562; the *Calvinists* in *Calvin's* Institutes (Book 3, Chapter 5, Section 6); and the *Trinitarians* and *Anabaptists* in the books they published recently in the year 1567. Therefore, these [purgatorial] spirits will not be troublesome to them.

<margin>6.</margin> Furthermore, the spirits of the piously deceased would not even desire to return to those Heretics who might admit to some form of prayer for the dead. This is because whatever works or "satisfactions" <term>satisfactions (satisfactiones)</term><note>In Catholic theology, these are acts of penance or prayer intended to lessen the temporal punishment for sins.</note> these people might undertake on behalf of the deceased would result in either no relief from punishment, or at least very little...

<margin>7.</margin> For this reason, regarding what some teach—that in those places where the Catholic religion once resided and Heresy <note>The author uses "Heresy" to refer to Protestant territories during the Reformation.</note> now has its seat, the disturbances of spirits are no longer observed, though they were once frequent—we believe this is entirely to be understood regarding the disturbances of spirits from Purgatory <note>original: "purgandos Spiritus"</note>. Otherwise, there is no reason to believe that other spirits, whether of damned men or of demons, favor and grant peace to Heretics.

### CHAPTER XLVII.

### *Whether and from what times a distinction can be found*
### *between those human spirits who are*
### *accustomed to haunt places.*

<margin>1.</margin> We said in Chapter 35 that the judgment by which the spirits of demons and humans are distinguished based on the *Times* of their appearance is weak and not sufficiently certain. Also weak and uncertain is the judgment which reveals and distinguishes human spirits here. Yet, however much weight that evidence may have, if it is joined with other signs, it gains strength; even if it is not to be highly valued on its own, it certainly should not have been omitted.

<margin>2.</margin> And unless we are mistaken, we can in some way distinguish *spirits to be purified* <note>meaning souls in Purgatory</note> from the *damned* by three differences of timing: the light of day, the duration of the disturbances, and the sanctity of the season. That is to say, when it is already established that the spirits who appear and cause trouble are *human*, it is probable from these factors that they are *souls to be purified, not damned*: because they are observed during the day; because they are troublesome for a longer period of time; and because they are present with us during sacred times <note>referring to holy days or liturgical seasons like Lent.</note>

<margin>3.</margin> While we assert these things, we do not deny that these same spirits to be purified can also be present at night; similarly, they can be troublesome for a shorter time, and even during profane <note>meaning secular or non-holy</note> times. We teach that these times—the nocturnal, the shorter, and the profane—are more suitable to damned spirits. Conversely, as if by a reason peculiar to themselves, *spirits to be purified* demand the opposite.

<margin>4.</margin> The spirits of damned men flee the day because they desire to lie hidden; they love the nights because they act evilly, and therefore they are enemies of the light. If spirits to be purified seek the nights, they do not seek them to hide, but to more conveniently explain their needs to mortals. But they do not flee the day if they understand it can serve their purpose.
