ON HAUNTED PLACES

<margin>5.</margin> In terms of *duration*, the troubles caused by souls in Purgatory <note>original: "purgandi," those to be purified</note> seem to exceed those of the damned. Why is this? Because when damned spirits associate with the living in a troublesome manner, their purpose is for their own misery to become known to mortals; therefore, that haunting will be permitted only as long as there are people alive who knew the deceased, before whom they can be made infamous. Once these people are gone, there are no significant reasons why they should continue to involve themselves in the affairs of the living. However, for those in Purgatory, the intercessions of the living <note>such as prayers, alms, and masses</note> are available to them; these can be offered and bestowed even upon those who are unknown, and thus can continue many years after their death.

<margin>6.</margin> I know there are some who believe the duration of purgatorial punishments lasts only a few years; among such people, the conjecture we provide here is considered weak. However, the opinion of those who extend that time, and do not believe it must be ended so quickly for everyone, is more appealing to us. If purgatorial punishments were brief, how could the Church justify the *anniversary rites* <note>Special masses held on the annual anniversary of a person's death</note> which are offered for those who died piously in the Lord a hundred or more years ago? See Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine (1542–1621), a Jesuit Cardinal and a major figure in the Counter-Reformation who wrote extensively on Purgatory.</note>, Volume 1, *Controversies*, Book 2, Chapter 9.

<margin>7.</margin> Finally, it is likely that the spirits of damned men flee *holy days* <note>Feast days or Sundays</note> because they are companions of demons, who detest all sacred things and even the mere shadows of sacred things. But would the spirits being purified flee these days? Would they not seek them out above others if a free choice were given between holy and profane days? Are they not holy spirits, desiring sacred things—from which they have a greater hope of attaining their goal <note>release from suffering</note> specifically on *holy* days? These matters regarding *Times* are treated briefly, because a judgment derived from them is less certain.

# CHAPTER XLVIII.

## *Whether, from the condition of those spirits who are accustomed to haunt certain people, it can be discovered if it is the spirit of a damned man, or one to be saved, who is being troublesome.*

<margin>8.</margin> <image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'O' containing a floral motif within a square frame.</image-desc> There is no need for many words here: *From the haunting itself, which distinguishes human spirits from one another, no certain defense or evidence is gathered.* If there is anything here that reveals a difference and betrays the spirit's condition, it is not found in the nature of the haunting itself, but from other factors that are connected to it.

PART TWO.

<warning>Ink blot obscuring text in the second paragraph.</warning>

<margin>2.</margin> The first point is beyond dispute. Just as good spirits seeking purification <note>original: "purgandi," those in Purgatory</note> follow certain living people, so do the evil spirits of the damned. The latter do so to torment and cause trouble; the former do so not so much to cause trouble and torment, but rather to look after their own affairs through the living <note>for example, by seeking the fulfillment of a forgotten vow or the offering of prayers</note>.

<margin>3.</margin> The circumstances connected to being followed and persecuted by spir<unclear>its</unclear> are quite varied; however, the conditions of the spir<unclear>its</unclear> are most effectively identified by the *location, the form of the spirits, the evils they inflict, and their method of harassment.* Since we have discussed these in many other chapters, we shall say nothing more of them for now.

## CHAPTER XLIX

->*Whether it can be determined from the condition of those who suffer from pursuing spirits if those spirits belong to the damned or to those awaiting purification.*<-

<margin>1.</margin> Just as one cannot distinguish between different human spirits simply by observing the specific people they follow and harass, neither can the state of the spirit be known from the condition of the people who endure these harassing spirits.

<margin>2.</margin> We stated in Chapter thirty-seven that the men who suffer from attacking spirits can be divided into *two categories*: some of outstanding integrity, and others of lost salvation <note>referring to the wicked or those who have abandoned their faith</note>. It is not necessarily true that the spirits who harass the *good* are souls in Purgatory, or that those who harass the *evil* are the damned. This is because the evil can, and frequently do, suffer at the hands of demons.

<margin>3.</margin> However, when it is established from other evidence that the spirits are indeed human, then from the condition—if not of the good, then certainly of the *evil*—it is possible to infer that the harassing spirits belong to the *damned*.

<margin>4.</margin> Why is this? Because the *good* are exposed to the troubles caused by both the damned and those awaiting purification. The *evil*, however, are almost never harassed except by the damned. Since both these points were proven in Chapter thirty-seven, they need not be repeated here.

# SYNOPSIS ON HAUNTED PLACES.

### Of certain signs, collected from the preceding chapters, which reveal the nature of individual spirits.

We have previously distinguished human spirits from demonic spirits, and differentiated between the types of human spirits themselves. From these earlier discussions, anyone can gather—though not without some labor and difficulty—which spirits are demons, which are the souls of the damned, and which are the souls of those needing purification <note>original: "purgandorum hominum," a reference to souls in Purgatory seeking help from the living</note>. To relieve the reader of this burden, we have gathered what was previously said in scattered sections into specific chapters, and we have assigned the specific marks and indicators for each individual type of spirit.

## CHAPTER L.

### On the eight indications that serve as powerful arguments for harassing demonic spirits.

<margin>1.</margin>
There are eight arguments for the presence of demonic spirits; while each one alone is significant, when all are joined together they provide firm proof. These are: *form*, *disordered sounds*, *speech*, *inflicted evils*, *acts of service*, *jests*, and the *places and persons* that support the harassing spirits.

<margin>2.</margin>
The *form*, or appearance, which reveals a demon is any shape that deviates from the human, whatever it may be—but especially the forms of brute animals and monsters. See Chapter 26.

<margin>3.</margin>
*Cries and noises* that are disordered and unstructured are the second sign. These are considered a great argument for the presence of demons if they reflect something "barbarous" or strange <note>original: "peregrinum," implying something alien or foreign to human nature</note>. Just as these sounds seem alien to other types of spirits, they are, for profound reasons, characteristic of demons. See Chapter 27.

<margin>4.</margin>
*Speech*, if it is to reveal a demon, must be "divinatory"—that is, it must indicate things that natural human knowledge is unable to perceive, whether those things are in the past, the future, or the present <note>this refers to the belief that demons, having superior intellect and longevity, know secrets hidden from living humans</note>. See Chapter 28.

<header>PART TWO. 179</header>

<margin>5.</margin>
Hardships or evils, if they are great and severe and are brought upon the living by spirits, argue that their authors are demons. For such things can be brought about by demons, but not in the same way by human spirits. Furthermore, it is entirely fitting that these should be attributed to demons rather than human spirits. See Chapter 29.

<margin>6.</margin>
Demons are recognized in more than one way *from the acts of service* <note>original: "Ex Obsequijs," referring to spirits who perform chores or favors for the living</note> they provide. They are demons if they perform services exceeding human strength, or those that are foul and violate the laws of nature, or those performed out of a pact as if they were necessary duties. See Chapter 30.

<margin>7.</margin>
If *jests* <note>original: "Ioci," meaning practical jokes, mockery, or playful disturbances</note> are stirred up, it is very likely they are provoked by demons, not by human spirits. From these signs, therefore, just as one knows a lion by its claw <note>original: "Leonem ex vngue," a Latin proverb meaning the whole can be known by a small part</note>, you will detect the presence of demons. See Chapter 31.

<margin>8.</margin>
*Places* which serve as evidence of demons ought to be deserted and far removed from human company. Other places—even though demons are found in them—do not betray their presence specifically, because those places are not the demons' own property. Even in inhabited areas, demons reveal themselves through those locations that are troublesome only because of the people there who lead a wicked and criminal life. See Chapters 32 and 33.

<margin>9.</margin>
A conjecture regarding demons is also drawn *from certain persons*; specifically, those who live ruined lives. If it happens that such people are infested by spirits, it is highly probable that they are being harassed by demonic spirits. See Chapter 37.

### CHAPTER LI.

->Concerning the five signs that reveal those spirits who are still being purified in the fire of purgatory.<-

<margin>1.</margin>
We recognize demons from eight signs, as has been said. However, we recognize the spirits of humans who must be purified <note>original: "purgandorum," referring to souls in Purgatory</note> by fewer, and perhaps less certain, signs. By which signs, and of what kind? *From their form, their groaning, their prayer, their service, and their locations.*

<margin>2.</margin>
The *Form* (or appearance) that serves as an indicator of spirits being purified is human; it is of such a nature that it contains nothing foreign or strange, and brings no horror in itself to those looking upon it, whether by a fierce expression or a black color. See Chapter 38.

<margin>3.</margin>
The *Groaning and sighs* must be entirely free from any lightness or any sign of an impatient spirit; they should be certain indicators of a sad and humble mind. See Chapter 39.

<margin>4.</margin>
*Prayer* also betrays these spirits; I mean *prayer* that is free from sin and, moreover, is a petition for their own benefit <note>usually asking for masses or prayers from the living to shorten their time in Purgatory</note> expressed with a submissive spirit. See Chapter 40.

# CHAPTER XLII.

## *Concerning the three signs that betray the spirits of damned men.*

<margin>1.</margin> <image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'N' decorated with foliage and scrollwork</image-desc> There are not as many signs <note>original: "Indicia"</note> that betray the spirits of damned men as there are those indicating demons or souls needing purgation; and if we examine everything more carefully, we will find very few or none that are certain, except for one.

<margin>2.</margin> The most certain sign is the *place*—namely, that which first began to be haunted by ghosts <note>original: "Spectris"</note> after the death of men who were either unbelievers or, if they were believers, died miserably and in a non-Christian manner. See Chapter 44.

<margin>3.</margin> After this, there are *form and groaning*. The *form* should be human, but horrifying due to a cruel, savage facial expression and color. The *groaning*, however, and sighs are joined with signs of either levity or impatience. These are weaker arguments than the first, and among them, the last is the weakest. See Chapters 38 and 39.

<margin>4.</margin> These are the signs of damned spirits, such as they are. There are no other signs to betray them. For whatever things can be done by these spirits, whatever can happen to them, or whatever is connected with them in any way, is by no means unique to them; rather, these things can also apply to human spirits needing purgation or to demons.

<margin>5.</margin> They can stir up noises and shouts; they can produce various voices and form speech; they can harm and harass; they can move objects from one place to another. Which of these does not apply, if not to spirits needing purgation, then certainly to the spirits of demons?

<margin>6.</margin> Things that happen to them include the bulk or deformity <note>original: "prauitas"</note> of the body, and the short or long duration of the troubles they bring us; and other such things. Which of these is foreign to other spirits?

## CHAPTER LIII.

->*Concerning the adjuration by which troubling spirits are compelled, through the invocation of the divine name, to reveal themselves and their condition.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
Although quite often we arrive at a recognition of spirits through the arguments already stated, it happens not infrequently that we are either destitute of these signs, or even if we have them in abundance, we do not perfectly and certainly know the condition of the troubling spirits. There is, therefore, another method by which they may be more certainly recognized; however, it requires a greater courage in the person who wishes to employ it.

<margin>2.</margin>
That method can be called *<term>adjuration</term>* <note>original: "Adiuratio." In this context, it refers to a formal command or oath issued in the name of God to compel a spirit to speak or act against its will.</note>; by it, spirits are adjured and compelled by the living God, or by the power of the Crucified One, to reveal who and of what sort they are, and to indicate what they want or for what reasons they are causing trouble.

<margin>3.</margin>
No one doubts that this has great power to compel spirits. For those who are good spirits will not be unwilling to reveal their condition when adjured by God, out of the reverence they hold for Him. As for the wicked, even if they do not revere God, they nevertheless fear Him; and when adjured by Him, they do things that they could hardly be moved to do by any other engines of persuasion.

<margin>4.</margin>
Hence, we read of men being adjured in many places in the Holy Scriptures; understanding the force of the adjuration, they immediately performed what they were asked or commanded, led by their religious devotion toward God. The elder servant of Abraham was adjured <note>Genesis 24</note> not to take a wife for Abraham's son from the daughters of the *Canaanites*, but from the kindred and house of Abraham’s father; he held nothing more important than his master's command. Joseph, adjured by his father <note>Genesis 50</note> to bury him in the tomb he had dug in the land of Canaan, urged Pharaoh—even with the Egyptians interceding—so that the promise and his father’s desire might be satisfied. When Moses led the people out of Egypt, he wished to carry the bones of that same Joseph with him into the promised land <note>Exodus 13</note>, because Joseph, while living, had adjured the children of Israel under this name. The people were adjured by Saul when he was pursuing the Philistines <note>1 Samuel 14 / 1 Kings 14 in some older Latin numbering</note> *that no one should eat bread until evening*, until he had taken vengeance on his enemies; and they did not...

<margin>4.</margin>
...all the people ate bread, as it is said in 1 Samuel 14 <note>original: "1. Reg. 14." In the Latin Vulgate Bible, the books of Samuel are often titled 1 and 2 Kings.</note>. The Prophet Micah was adjured by Ahab; and being adjured regarding what he had previously concealed, he predicted the slaughter in Israel, as seen in 1 Kings 22 <note>original: "3. Reg. 22." <margin>5.</margin>
Nor are the devils ignorant of this power of *adjuration* <note>original: "Adiuratio." A formal command or oath given to a spirit.</note>. Hence, when one of them feared greatly for himself from the Lord, he turned to adjuration: *I adjure you,* he said, *that you do not torment me,* as recorded in Mark 5. Whether he gained anything by this adjuration, he himself knows; but this much is certain: in the region of the Gerasenes, he was not driven out of the place, just as he had requested <note>This refers to the "Legion" of demons asking Jesus not to send them out of the country, but rather into a herd of swine.</note>.

<margin>6.</margin>
But regarding the power and authority of *adjuration* there is no doubt; the doubt is perhaps whether it is lawful to adjure spirits, and by what form of *adjuration* it should be done. Furthermore, to whom is this practice suited, and in what places and times should it be used against spirits? Concerning these things, I will speak briefly as the subject requires, according to the plan of this work.

<margin>7.</margin>
*There is no doubt that it is lawful.* For since spirits (whichever ones are troublesome) are either demons or the souls of men, it is clear from this very fact that it is lawful to attempt to adjure them all, because it is permitted to adjure both demons and men without any sin.

<margin>8.</margin>
Regarding men, the examples brought from Holy Scripture at the beginning of this chapter show this. Regarding demons, the deeds of the Apostles show it; they, by the power communicated to them from God, adjured, routed, and ordered them into exile. And Saint Augustine says well in book 10 of *The City of God*, chapter 22: *By true piety,* he says, *men cast out the hostile aerial power that is contrary to piety by exorcising them.*

<margin>9.</margin>
*The form of adjuring is twofold:* sometimes by commanding and, as it were, imposing a necessity, we compel someone to do something for the sake of the divine power; sometimes we do this only by beseeching <note>original: "deprecando." An appeal or prayerful request rather than a command.</note> and exhorting. The latter is used for superiors, whom it is not fitting for us to command; the former, the commanding form <note>original: "praeceptoria."</note>, is used toward inferiors over whom we have authority.

<margin>10.</margin>
But by what force is it permitted to explore the state and condition of spirits? Both are permitted, though to use the commanding form seems to be safer.

<margin>11.</margin>
*Beseeching is permitted:* because it has its place with superiors in such a way that it is blameless even among inferiors and equals; sometimes it even deserves praise. Therefore, whether the spirits who trouble us are our superiors, equals, or even inferiors, we are without sin if we ask them to prove themselves and their condition.

# THIRD PART.
<page-num>179</page-num>
<sig>Z 2</sig>

<margin>12.</margin>
The commanding style <note>original: "præceptoria." This refers to a form of adjuration where the speaker issues a direct command to the spirit.</note> is also permitted: because the condition of the living is much better than that of the spirits who cause trouble. For this reason, the living ought to be called superior to them in a certain sense, and they can exercise authority over the spirits, especially if they are causing harm.

<margin>13.</margin>
Nevertheless, it is beneficial to use the imperial and commanding form: not only because its power is greater, but also because, for the most part, those who cause trouble are demonic spirits. We are forbidden by our religion to use the entreating form <note>original: "deprecatoriâ." A humble request or prayer rather than a command.</note> with them. *I do not want you,* says the Apostle, *to become partners with demons, 1 Corinthians 11.* <note>The text cites 1 Corinthians 11, though the quote "I do not want you to be participants with demons" is found in 1 Corinthians 10:20.</note>

<margin>14.</margin>
Indeed, I would think that it is permitted for everyone to press spirits with adjurations, though not everyone will have the same success. For although adjuration is an act of religion and pertains to divine worship, it is not an act of "Order" <note>The "Sacrament of Order" refers to the specific authority given to ordained clergy like priests and deacons.</note> or something that belongs solely to persons consecrated to God. Anyone who can call upon God can, through God, adjure a spirit to reveal its condition.

<margin>15.</margin>
However, not everyone performs this act with success. An example of this is found in the history of the *Acts of the Apostles, Chapter 19*. When certain people adjured the demon-possessed by the God whom Paul preached, far from achieving anything, they experienced the cruelty of those they thought they could rule over. <note>This refers to the "Sons of Sceva," Jewish exorcists who were beaten by a demon when they tried to use Jesus's name without true faith.</note> Therefore, those who do not profess the Catholic faith can adjure spirits by God; but they cannot always do so successfully (unless they attempt it for the confirmation of their own doctrine), just as they cannot cast the same spirits out of human bodies, as was demonstrated elsewhere in the *Disputation on the Demon-Possessed.*

<margin>16.</margin>
And just as these people often adjure spirits in vain, those will adjure them quite usefully who, initiated into sacred orders, have power over the Body of Christ—both the true <note>The "true body" refers to the consecrated bread of the Eucharist.</note> and the mystical <note>The "mystical body" refers to the Church and its members.</note>. This is not only because there is great power in the Church of Christ, but also because the highest power over demons and all troublesome spirits has been granted to these men above all others.

<margin>17.</margin>
And although holiness of life is not strictly necessary to complete this work successfully, priests will adjure spirits more safely, more confidently, and with a greater hope of victory if the innocence and integrity of their lives are joined to the power they possess.

<margin>18.</margin>
It will also be beneficial to have first practiced the virtues: namely fasting, prayer, and the giving of alms. Just as these protections have, at all times, been a help to those about to undertake other difficult tasks.

[...continued from previous page] they have acted; so it must by no means be said that it is used here in vain. *Piety*, says the **Apostle**, *is useful for all things*, 1 Timothy 4. <note>The author is quoting 1 Timothy 4:8: "For physical training is of some value, but godliness (pietas) has value for all things."</note>

<margin>19.</margin> That priests may also be clothed in *sacred vestments* as a defense against spirits, in addition to these other solid protections, ought not to be condemned. While the priest fulfills his duty, does he do wrong if he uses garments appropriate to his office?

<margin>20.</margin> Furthermore, *in what places and at what times* should an <term>adjuration|a formal command or exorcism performed in the name of God</term> be performed? In those places where we can be present to the spirits whom we are adjuring. Who, while staying in Würzburg <note>original: "Herbipoli"</note>, will adjure those spirits who are causing trouble in Constantinople? Or who will adjure those whom he does not know are even present?

<margin>21.</margin> Therefore, if the spirits are only troublesome at night, an *adjuration* will be applied in vain during the day—when they are thought to be absent—even in those places where they are otherwise accustomed to be troublesome. And if disturbances are stirred up only in the wine cellar, they will be adjured in the upper room <note>original: "solario," referring to an upper floor or sun-lit room</note> in vain. *Adjuration* does not exist without speech; speech is for those who are present, not those who are absent. For the absent, one uses letters.

<margin>22.</margin> Whether spirits are observed to be present in this or that manner matters little to the matter at hand. It is enough if they are seen to be present, and it is enough if they are believed to be present because of the disturbance they have raised. Just as we happen to speak to those who are present, both those whom we see and those whom we only hear, so we can *adjure* both those whom we see face to face and those whom we know to be present by sound.

## CHAPTER LIV.

### *That there is a method by which troublesome Spirits may be banished, and places may be freed from their infestation.*

<margin>1.</margin>
The reasons why locations cannot be freed from the infestation of Spirits—if any such reasons exist—must be sought from two main headings: either from the condition and power of the Spirits, or from the condition of humans and the weakness of human strength. Regarding the "condition," one might understand it to be a barrier because the nature of humans is one thing and that of Spirits is another; thus, even if humans possessed superior strength, they would be prevented by their natural condition from acting against Spirits, because a physical body can have no effect on a Spirit. Regarding "power," they would be prevented if human strength were not as great as that of Spirits.

<margin>2.</margin>
In both ways, humans appear to be prevented from reclaiming themselves and their dwellings from the harassment of Spirits; yet, in truth, they are prevented by neither. If this is not proven by other arguments, it is certainly shown by those examples in which we have elsewhere demonstrated that the Spirits of Demons are expelled from human bodies by men. <note>The author refers to his previous "Disputation on the Possessed" (Disputatio de Daemoniacis).</note>

<margin>3.</margin>
To those examples, others specifically related to our current subject can be added. St. Augustine <note>A 4th-century North African bishop and influential Christian theologian.</note> records that the house of Hesperius was freed by a certain priest; Metaphrastes <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer known for compiling lives of the saints.</note> records another place freed by Theodore of Sykeon, the Archimandrite; St. Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note> mentions the Angular Baths <note>original: "Thermas Angulares"</note> being freed by Germanus, the Bishop of Capua; Glycas <note>Michael Glycas, a 12th-century Byzantine historian and theologian.</note> mentions the castle of the King of the Persians being freed by a Bishop; Antonius mentions the fields of Bingen <note>A town in Germany.</note> being freed by the clergy of Mainz; and the *Chronicle of Hirsau* <note>A history of the Hirsau Abbey in Germany.</note> records that the territory of Worms was liberated from the annoyance of Spirits by religious men; just as we have followed these accounts at greater length in the first chapter of this Disputation.

<margin>4.</margin>
Nor does the *condition of nature* prevent humans here. A human is not merely a body, such that there is nothing beyond the body. Man is also equipped with a Spirit. Just as he reaches toward sublunary and fleeting things through his body, so he reaches toward the ethereal Spirits through his soul, which is enclosed within the body.

<margin>5.</margin>
Nor are they prevented by the *strength of nature*. Granted, there may be some Spirits whose power surpasses all created power; however, that is not the condition of all of them. Places are also haunted by human spirits <note>The author suggests that some hauntings are caused by the ghosts of deceased humans rather than demons.</note>; are those humans who are currently enclosed in bodies perhaps inferior to these?

<margin>6.</margin>
Even if humans were inferior to all Spirits, the capacity to act against them must not yet be denied, even if the Spirits are mightier in force and vigor.
->Because—<- <note>original: "Quoni-" (Quoniam). This is the catchword for the next page.</note>

PART THREE.

<margin>7.</margin>
Because what they cannot do through the powers of nature, they can do through the gift of His grace; for He has all power over all Spirits and is called the Father of spirits. <note>original: "Pater spirituum"; a biblical title for God from Hebrews 12:9.</note>

The Apostles, who in ancient times commanded Demons—those most powerful Spirits—were mere men: indeed, they were men far inferior to Spirits. If you consider the condition of their nature, they were subject to the same needs as we are; nevertheless, Spirits were safe in no place when in their presence. Why then is there not still the same power over Spirits belonging to certain people?

<margin>8.</margin>
Great power has been left to the Church by Christ, not only over men but also over Spirits. This power will last as long as the Church lasts. Christ’s own words teach this: *These signs will follow those who believe: In my name they will cast out Demons.* <note>original: "signa eos qui crediderint, hæc sequentur. In nomine meo Dæmonia eyicient."</note> From the last chapter of Mark. Therefore, it must not be denied that there is some method by which Spirits are put to flight.

<margin>9.</margin>
But even if this power had not been left to the Church, we would not for that reason lack a means of delivering ourselves from the harassment of Demons. Because what we cannot do by natural strength, nor by the free gifts of divine mercy, we can do by offering prayer to God. Prayer is a most steadfast defense, in which the Savior of the world wishes us to place the most certain hope of obtaining all things. John 19. <note>The original text cites John 19, though the promise that prayer will be answered is more prominently found in John 14:13 or 16:24.</note>

## CHAPTER LV.

->*That there is not just one way to free places from the nuisance of Spirits, but various and multiple ways.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
There is not one single way (if you set aside prayer to God) by which places are freed from the infestation of Spirits. Nor can there be only one way they are freed. The first point—however much it may be clear and manifest from the second—is shown by the various methods which we read have been observed by different people; the second point will have to be demonstrated by logic.

<margin>2.</margin>
A certain priest, whom the Blessed Augustine <note>A 4th-century bishop and highly influential theologian.</note> mentions, cleansed places in some ways; Theodore, the Archimandrite of Sykeon, <note>A 6th-century Byzantine saint known for his miracles and exorcisms.</note> in others; Germanus, the Bishop of Capua, in others; and the Clergy of Mainz <note>original: "Clerus Moguntinus"; Mainz is a historic city in Germany.</note> in still others. Augustine’s priest used the Sacrifice of the body of Christ <note>A reference to the celebration of the Eucharist or Mass.</note>; Theodore used holy water <note>original: "aqua lustrali," water used for ritual purification.</note>; Germanus of Capua used prayer offered to God; the Clergy of Mainz...

3. The fact that a single method does not work for all places is first proven by the observation that we see some spirits are driven out by certain means, while those same means have had no effect on others. It is well known that in the Castle of the King of the Persians, those summoned by the King achieved nothing despite using every possible device; yet the Bishop dispelled every phantom <note>original: "phantasma"; refers here to a ghostly apparition or a demonic illusion.</note> with the sign of the Cross, as Glycas <note>Michael Glycas was a 12th-century Byzantine historian and theologian.</note> relates. There is no doubt that many who entered the baths infested by Spirits (which Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his philosophical and mystical writings.</note> mentions) tried many things; yet most of them were slaughtered by the Spirits. However, the Deacon of Gregory of Neocaesarea <note>Also known as Gregory Thaumaturgus or "the Wonder-worker" (c. 213–270 AD).</note>, armed only with the sign of the cross, emerged unharmed. You have these examples at length in Chapter 1.

4. Then there is Christ’s answer to his Apostles on this matter. For when they had been occupied in vain trying to cast out a certain Spirit and asked the Lord the cause of this, they learned *that there is a certain kind of Spirit that is not driven out by just any means, but only by fasting and prayer.* Matthew 17.

5. Spirits are of the most diverse natures; they are of the most diverse conditions. Some are good; others are evil. By the methods through which the former are helped, the latter are not driven away. What terrifies the latter may affect and refresh the former.

6. Since there are *good* spirits or *evil* spirits who cause trouble, one might think a two-fold method should be established by which places are cleansed. However, this two-fold method is not sufficient, because although all good Spirits are of one kind, the evil ones are not of one kind but of many, being most distinct in their natures.

7. Add to this that we must consider not only the Spirits here, but also the places. We have said that some places are <term>infested</term> <note>In this context, "infestation" refers to a localized supernatural haunting or demonic presence rather than a biological pest.</note> because of human beings—places which are not infested in themselves. In cleansing these, we must consider not so much the Spirits who infest them as the humans because of whom they infest. Other places are infested *in themselves*; here, perhaps, the nature of the places must also be considered.

8. Therefore, to bring the *subject matter of our discussion* back to certain headings, two modes must be distinguished by which places can be purged. One pertains to places *infested because of humans*; the other is the way places *infested in themselves* are freed.

9. This latter mode is again two-fold. For either we are certain about the condition of the Spirits, or it is hidden from us. Again, when it is certain, there is one method that serves for proscribing evil Spirits, and another for driving away and dismissing **good** ones. This latter should not be divided, because one...

One is the condition of all good Spirits, of which our Disputation treats; one end, and the same purpose. The previous category <note>Referring to the classification of spirits discussed on the preceding page.</note>, according to the nature of the Spirits (for of the evil Spirits, some are human ghosts and some are Demons), is again divided.

The fifth is that by which help is given to people who suffer from spirits that follow and pursue them. All these modes must be explained—but only after we have first rejected certain false, empty, and destructive methods.

### REMARKS

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'F' featuring a person in a rural landscape with buildings.</image-desc>
*The false methods, which we said must be rejected before we propose and prove the true and good ones, are of two kinds. Some seem to serve for all Spirits and for removing the hauntings of Spirits; some serve only certain ones, namely human spirits. Those former ones are five in number, and they can be identified as follows: **Hostile speech** <note>original: "Oratio aduersa"; here meaning rebuking or yelling at the spirit rather than a pious prayer.</note>, **external weapons**, **burning fire**, **lit candles**, and **locked doors**. The latter are four, of which only two are said to be an obstacle to the infestations of Demons: namely, the **shedding of innocent blood**, and two types of **fumigations** <note>original: "suffimenta"</note> meant to prevent the return and the troubles caused by human Spirits—specifically, the **burial of those same bodies under the hearth**, and a **certain touching of beans** <note>original: "tactus certus fabarum"; a reference to ancient Roman superstitions, such as the Lemuria festival, where beans were thrown to ward off ghosts.</note>. In total, therefore, there are eight. Let us begin with the first of the former group: I mean, hostile speech.*

# FIVE FALSE METHODS FOLLOW
### by which places are thought to be cleansed from the harassment of any Spirits whatsoever.

## CHAPTER 56.

### *Whether places are freed from the hauntings of Spirits by blasphemies, insults, and dire curses.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Certain people have this custom: if they suffer from haunting Spirits and wish to be freed from their harassment, they resort to *blasphemies* and *curses*, devoting the Spirits to all manner of horrors <note>original: "dirisq; omnibus Spiritus deuoueant" — literally "devoting the spirits to the Furies" or "cursing them with dire things."</note>. And because they are soon freed from the trouble, they believe this to be a most certain and undoubted method: one by which, even if places are not always permanently freed, the Spirits are certainly put to flight and prevented from being troublesome to humans.

Apollonius of Tyana <note>A famous 1st-century Greek philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note> used this method, as Philostratus writes in the *Life of Apollonius*, Book 2, Chapter 2. For as he was crossing the Caucasus with Damis and his companions, he says a *Lamia* <note>original: "Lamia, Phantasma" — a type of female demon or specter in classical mythology.</note>, a specter, encountered them, changing itself now into one shape, now into another, and sometimes suddenly vanishing from sight. Apollonius, however, recognizing what it was, rebuked it with heavy and insulting words, and urged his companions to do the same. For he said that this was the best remedy against such invasions. When his companions obeyed his words, the screeching specter fled quickly like a phantom. Thus he recounts it.

In support of this is what Peter Martyr <note>Pietro Martire d'Anghiera (1457–1526), a historian of the early Spanish explorations of the Americas.</note> reports in Book 9, Decade 1 of *On the New World* <note>original: "de Rebus Oceanicis"</note>: that at night, and very frequently on journeys—especially on public roads—the dead encounter the living. If the traveler stands intrepid against them, the specter dissolves; but if he is terrified, it terrifies him further by approaching, so that many are often weakened and stunned by that fear. Thus says Martyr.

<margin>2.</margin>
Whether these people offend God, or how great a sin they commit, is not for us to define. As this present Disputation requires, we teach that this method is utterly vain and reckless; this is because it is neither proven by the example of Holy men, nor confirmed by the authority of the Sacred Scriptures, nor supported by any reason or cause that can be drawn either from the condition of such hauntings or from the nature of the Spirits themselves.

<margin>3.</margin>
Various modes for freeing places from the infestation of Demons... <note>The text breaks off here at "san-" implying "holy [ways]" or "holy [men]" will follow.</note>

### PART THREE.

There is no doubt that men have employed these methods. We have reviewed some of them above; others we shall relate later. However, that this specific method—which consists of blasphemies and curses—was ever used or approved by anyone reputable, we have neither read nor heard.

<margin>4.</margin>
*The Scriptures mention various kinds of Spirits. They likewise suggest the ways in which they are driven out <note>original: "profligantur"</note>. Yet, no place can be pointed out where the Scriptures mention this particular method. If authority ought to be used in any matter, it is certainly here, in the driving out of Spirits.*

<margin>5.</margin>
The condition of this method, which we condemn, is such that it can have no power over Spirits. What can voices, however harshly uttered, achieve? What can the will of one speaking and uttering dire curses do? Spirits suffer nothing from corporeal things. The dire will of the one cursing is an evil for the person who utters the curse, not for the Spirit at whom the curse is directed.

<margin>6.</margin>
As we have said, there are various kinds of Spirits that haunt places. However, they are all affected in such a way that they are either refreshed by these curses and blasphemies, or they are negatively affected. The evil spirits are refreshed <note>In this context, the author suggests that demons take pleasure or find "refreshment" in hearing God blasphemed.</note>; the good spirits are negatively affected. If, therefore, good spirits are driven away by these means, why are they employed to drive out *absolutely all* Spirits? Even the evil ones, who take pleasure in these things?

<margin>7.</margin>
But this method is not even effective by itself for driving away good Spirits. For although these good spirits might yield to those uttering dire curses, they are not *forced* to yield. There is no power in a blasphemous voice, nor in dire curses, nor in any prayer proceeding from a man (unless some power has been divinely conferred, which is not the case here) that is able to drive out and banish <note>original: "proscribere"</note> any Spirits at all.

<margin>8.</margin>
But it may be argued that experience has proved this method to be very effective: that silence was imposed on the Spirits, and places were rendered free from disturbances. I grant that at the uttering of blasphemies, the Spirits fell silent and the places were freed from trouble. But I deny that it was *because* of the blasphemies and curses that the Spirits fell silent or the places were freed. It is one thing for the Spirits to fall silent while God is being blasphemed and they themselves are being cursed; it is quite another for these things to have happened *because* of the blasphemies, or for there to reside in blasphemies a power to impose silence on Spirits and compel their departure.

<margin>9.</margin>
For even if the Spirits fall silent or cease to be troublesome when met with blasphemies and curses, this does not happen because blasphemies possess a power that Spirits cannot endure. There are far different reasons that move the Spirits here—and indeed, some reasons for the good spirits and others for the evil.

<margin>10.</margin>
*For the good spirits, there are two reasons in particular.* The first is that, just as they themselves do not wish to offend God, so they desire that He not be offended by others. Therefore...

and they take the utmost care that they themselves do not provide to others any cause or occasion for doing evil. The other reason is that they hope for no help from these blasphemers and cursers; and for that reason, they do not wish to be troublesome to no purpose.

<margin>11.</margin> *But these reasons do not move evil Spirits.* They do not cease their haunting simply because they cannot achieve some specific wish. In fact, they seek nothing. They do not stop because they wish to avoid offending God; rather, they desire this offense most of all. Why then do they haunt? Precisely because they seek and long for the offense of God. ->“Set out upon your path, and draw the sword from its sheath; now, Aeneas, is the time for courage; now, for a steadfast heart.”<- <note>original: *Tuâ, inuade viam, vaginâq; eripe ferrum, / Nunc animis opus est Aenea: nunc pectore firmo.* From Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 6, lines 260-261, where the Sibyl instructs Aeneas as they enter the Underworld.</note>

Homer writes in the eleventh book of the *Odyssey* that Ulysses <note>the Latin name for Odysseus</note> likewise sat with a drawn sword, not permitting the Shades <note>the ghosts of the dead</note> to approach the sacred blood until he had heard the prophecy of Tiresias.

<margin>2.</margin>
In our own times, there are those who imitate this Lacedaemonian <note>a Spartan</note>, as well as Ulysses and Aeneas. If they are equipped with swords, spears, and other types of weapons, they believe themselves to be safe from the assaults and attacks of Spirits; they consider this to be the most efficient method for driving a Spirit away. Hortensius <note>Lambertus Hortensius, a 16th-century historian and Virgil commentator</note> writes regarding Virgil in this manner: “Many,” he says, “assert that Demons dread the edge of a blade, and this has been found to be true in practice. I have known people to whom this very thing happened during the night hours, though it resulted in a great struggle with poor health <note>likely meaning the encounter left them physically ill from the spiritual strain</note>.” So says Hortensius.

<margin>3.</margin>
It is difficult to say whether these people realize they are wandering in error; but for a true Christian, there should be no doubt that they are wandering in a most serious one. Why is this? Because it is impossible for Spirits, of whatever kind they may be, to suffer anything from swords or spears, unless they are either entirely physical or at least have bodies naturally united to them. Furthermore, no one holds such a view without falling into the gravest error, regardless of those who taught it in the past. On this matter, see Coelius Rhodiginus <note>Lodovico Ricchieri, an Italian humanist and scholar</note>, Book 1, Chapter 29.

<margin>4.</margin>
Catholic minds have outlawed the opinion of Plato, who—according to the testimony of Blessed Augustine in *The City of God*, Book 8, Chapters 14, 15, and 16—teaches that Demons are animals by kind, “passive in soul, rational in mind, aerial in body, and eternal in time.” <note>original: *animalia, animo passiua, mente rationalia, corpore aërea, tempore æterna*</note> Neither are Tertullian (in his book *On the Flesh of Christ*), Origen (in *First Principles* <note>original Greek: *Peri Archon*</note>, Book 2, Chapters 2 and 3), nor any others who followed them or Plato in attributing a bodily substance to Spirits, to be listened to.

<margin>5.</margin>
The ancient philosophers have also been condemned; Aristotle mentions them in *On the Soul*, Book 1, from text 20 to 5. These include Democritus and Leucippus, who said that souls were fires composed of round atoms; Empedocles, who thought they were forged from the four elements; Diogenes, who said they were air; Hippon, who said water; and Critias, who said blood.

<margin>6.</margin>
Demons are not bodies; they do not have bodies naturally united to them. Souls are not bodies; and once they have laid aside their own bodies, they do not naturally have any others united to them.

<margin>7.</margin>
The Holy Scriptures advocate for this view <note>that spirits are incorporeal</note> here, for they address all Angels (and therefore all Demons) as *Spirits*. Furthermore, is not the Demon in the Gospel called an “unclean *Spirit*”? (Luke 11).

# ABOUT INFESTED PLACES

...firmly [believing, in the decree] concerning the Most Holy Trinity] there is one principle of all things; *the Creator of all things invisible and visible, spiritual and corporeal: who by His own almighty power, at the beginning of time, created both types of creatures out of nothing; the spiritual and the corporeal, namely the angelic and the worldly, and then the human, as if common to both, being composed of spirit and body.* <note>original: *Creator omnium inuisibilium & visibilium...* This is a famous passage from the confession of faith *Firmiter*, issued by the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215.</note> Thus says the Council. By these words, it distinguishes the corporeal nature from the spiritual; and it teaches that Angels are spiritual, not corporeal; and that they are even more spiritual than man himself.

<margin>9.</margin>
Arguments for this position are not lacking. If Angels either have bodies or are bodies, how could it be that—as *St. Luke chapter 11* <note>While the text cites Luke 11, the story of 'Legion' is more commonly found in Luke 8 or Mark 5; 6,666 was a traditional number assigned to a Roman legion in medieval military and theological lore.</note> reports—6,666 demons were in one man? Could one man be capable of holding so many bodies? Furthermore, how do they traverse vast distances in the shortest amount of time? Just as in *Job 1*, where one <note>referring to Satan</note> is said to have gone around and walked through the whole earth? And the Angels who move the heavens <note>In older astronomy, it was believed that spiritual beings or 'intelligences' were responsible for the movement of the planets and stars.</note>—if they are not spirits but bodies, in what caves or places do they keep themselves? Moreover, those who were created in heaven and, after their sins, were cast down from heaven; how did they penetrate to the depths <note>the Underworld or Hell</note> without breaking the sky? And those who have moved the heavens for so long, how are they not eventually exhausted? So much for the Angels.

<margin>10.</margin>
By no less authority is it taught that *human souls* are entirely foreign to physical composition. First, the Scriptures that serve this point are those that call souls "spirits." And how many of those are there? In *Ecclesiastes 12* <note>The Latin text says "Ecclesiastici" (the Book of Sirach), but the quote is actually from Ecclesiastes 12:7.</note> it is said: *The dust returns to its earth from whence it came, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.* And in *Matthew 10: Do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul.* And in *Luke 23: Into your hands I commend my spirit.* And in *Romans 8: The Holy Spirit gives testimony to our spirit.* And in *Galatians 5: The flesh lusts against the spirit.*

<margin>11.</margin>
Nor is the common consensus of the Church lacking here. To omit other things, this is proven by the Lateran Council of 1,285 Fathers under Innocent III, where it is defined that man consists of body and spirit. Here, because the *body* is distinguished against the *spirit*, by this very fact it is proven that the soul is spirit, because it is denied to be a body.

<margin>12.</margin>
If logical reasons for this argument are sought, many can be given. We are content with one or two. Is it possible for two bodies to be in the same place? Yet the soul is in the same place as the body. Therefore, either the body is not a body, or the soul is not a body. Furthermore, if the soul were a body, it would certainly not understand any bodies placed outside itself, whatever they might be; because, as the Philosophers say, *that which exists within prevents that which is outside* <note>original: *intus existens prohibeat extraneum*. A scholastic principle suggesting that if a sensing organ—or here, the mind—already possessed a physical quality or "form" in a physical way, it would be blocked from perceiving that same quality in other objects.</note>. Indeed, to whom has such a thing ever occurred, even in a dream?

<margin>13.</margin>
Since these things are so—since spirits are not physical bodies that can be attacked, nor do they have bodies naturally joined to them—why do we arm ourselves with swords and clubs against them? The spear of the Spartan <note>The "Lacon" or Spartan likely refers to a classical anecdote about a man attempting to strike a ghost with a weapon.</note> did not cause the ghost emerging from the tombs to flee. Nor were the shadows terrified by the iron blades of Ulysses or Aeneas <note>Ulysses (Odysseus) and Aeneas are heroes of Greek and Roman epic who descended into the Underworld and encountered spirits.</note>. The spirits who trouble us today do not flee from swords. If they do flee, they flee because they *choose* to, not because they are forced to. The Sibyl <note>A prophetess and guide to the Underworld in Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note> once taught this same Aeneas; it is believed she spoke ironically about this earlier. For Virgil writes of this matter in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*:

> *Then Aeneas, trembling with sudden fear, seized his sword*
> *and offered its drawn edge to those who approached.*
> *And unless his learned companion had warned him that these*
> *were thin lives without bodies, fluttering under a hollow image of form,*
> *he would have rushed in and struck the shadows with his blade in vain.*
<note>original: *Corripit hic subitâ trepidus formidine ferrum...* Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 290-294.</note>

Therefore, spirits flee the edge of the sword not because they are compelled to, but because they wish to.

<margin>14.</margin>
There are various reasons for their will, just as there are various conditions among spirits. The purpose of the evil spirits is to lead people into error by a feigned flight. The purpose of the good spirits is to avoid error: they do not seek help where there seems to be no hope of obtaining it.

### CHAPTER LVIII.

-> **Whether spirits are driven away if a fire is lit or thrown at them: and whether they are forced to leave the places they infest.** <-

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental initial letter I, depicting a seated figure in a landscape within a decorative rectangular frame.</image-desc>
Although (unless I am mistaken) there may be no one who has explicitly taught that fire is extremely effective for driving away and banishing spirits, one might still be led to believe it for two reasons. One is that all spirits who are troublesome are tortured by fire. The other is that they are terrified not only by things that are hostile to them, but even by the *signs* of hostile things, and they loathe them. Because of this, one might believe that spirits either flee because they are tormented by our earthly fire; or, if they are not tormented, they cannot endure the sight of it because it brings to mind the infernal fire <note>The fires of Hell.</note> as a sort of symbolic sign.

<margin>2.</margin>
These things are confirmed by what is written concerning St. Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> in his *Life* by St. Paulinus. The Empress Justina <note>Justina (c. 340–388) was an Arian Empress who famously clashed with the orthodox St. Ambrose.</note> had sent demons to kill Ambrose. But it was in vain. For the Wicked Spirits reported back that not only were they unable to approach him at all, but they could not even gain access to the doors of the house in which the Bishop stayed, because...

...moreover, an insurmountable fire fortified that entire building, so that even those standing far off were burned. Paulinus relates these things, as witnessed by Caesar Baronius <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607) was a cardinal and historian famous for his *Annales Ecclesiastici*, a massive history of the Church.</note> in the fourth volume of his *Annals*.

<margin>3.</margin>
In addition, Sozomen <note>Salamanes Hermias Sozomenus was a 5th-century historian of the early Christian Church.</note> relates in Book 8, Chapter 28 of the *Tripartite History* that a demon appeared to Apelles—a holy man who was a blacksmith—while he was forging iron at night. The demon took the form of a most beautiful woman to provoke him to lust. But Apelles immediately drew a glowing iron from the furnace and struck it into the demon's face; thus, wailing and groaning, the spirit fled swifter than speech.

This argument might be dismissed if one were to say: either that the fire among the inhabitants of the underworld <note>original: *apud inferos*</note> which tortures spirits is not real; or that those spirits are not truly and properly tortured by that fire; or certainly that they are not tortured by infernal fire when they are outside of hell.

<margin>4.</margin>
However, none of these things should be said by a student of truth and a lover of the more common opinion of the Doctors <note>The "Doctors" refers to the Doctors of the Church, the authoritative theologians of the Catholic tradition.</note>. *The fire is real* by which the spirits are tortured; *they are truly tortured by that fire*. They are even tortured by it while existing *outside the common place* of the damned and conversing among us.

<margin>5.</margin>
That it *is a real fire* (so that I might not be tedious in reviewing the opinions of the Church Fathers) is supported by this significant argument: that frequent mention of it is made in the Scriptures under the specific name of "fire." In Mark 9, the damned are said to be sent into unquenchable fire <note>The Latin OCR says *extinguibilem* (extinguishable), but this is almost certainly a printer's error for *inextinguibilem* (unquenchable), given the citation of Mark 9.</note>. In John 15, the branch that bears no fruit is cast *into the fire, and burns*. In Revelation 14, *those who worshipped the beast are tortured with fire and sulfur*. In the final chapter of Isaiah, the punishment of the transgressors is taught to *be a fire that is not extinguished*. Finally, the Lord, in that terrifying judgment, is going to send those who stand at his left hand into the fire *which is prepared for the Devil and his Angels*. Matthew 25.

<margin>6.</margin>
Furthermore, that it *truly tortures the wretched* can be taught by these very passages already cited. The most holy John teaches that they are *to be tortured by this fire and sulfur*, and the Lord teaches they will *burn* using the metaphor of the branch. If indeed it *is prepared* for the Devil and his angels, could it be said to be "prepared" for them to take pleasure in it? Surely they, who because of the gravest sins are worthy of the gravest punishments, are sent into the fire so that they may be punished. Saint Augustine says in Book 20 of *The City of God*, Chapter 10: *In marvelous, yet true ways, the punishment of bodily fire afflicts spirits.*

<margin>7.</margin>
But are they *only* tortured by this fire in hell? They are indeed tortured there; nevertheless, they do not *only* burn there. These wretched spirits always carry their fire with them because they are always wretched, even while they exist outside of hell—just as those who are blessed are blessed wherever they may be.

### PART THREE
B b

<margin>8.</margin>
Since these things are so, why are spirits not driven away by our fire? Perhaps infernal fire tortures them, but our fire does not? For what reason? Is the infernal fire perhaps of a different nature <note>original: *rationis*, here meaning the fundamental logic or essential nature of the fire</note>, and ours of another? Even if it were of a different nature, it should at least be able to do something to a spirit; if it were not as powerful as the infernal fire, it should still be capable of some effect.

<margin>9.</margin>
Perhaps spirits *are* tortured by our fire, yet they refuse to flee. But it is a wonder that they would not flee, since by not fleeing they suffer heavy torments which they could escape by leaving. Perhaps the harm brought by the fire is not so great that they would choose to avoid it over the delight they take in the molestation of men. But what is this delight, and for what reasons is it so great?

<margin>10.</margin>
These arguments seem to have some probability and fight on behalf of fire against spirits; however, they contain nothing of the truth. *Spirits are not driven away by our fire, no matter how great it may be,* because our fire does nothing to spirits, nor do they dread fire as a sign of infernal punishments.

<margin>11.</margin>
No other defenses are needed for this assertion than those by which it has been demonstrated thus far: that spirits suffer nothing from blasphemous prayers, nor from swords and spears. Just as all these things can do nothing against spirits—because they are much inferior to spirits in power and condition—so also, for the same reason, the element of fire can do nothing against spirits.

<margin>12.</margin>
Nor is the reason for this that the one fire is of one nature and ours of another. Whether it is of another nature or not, it should not be denied that fire itself has some power over spirits, *if infernal fire has great power over spirits by its own nature.*

<margin>13.</margin>
The cause why our fire can do nothing against spirits, while the infernal fire can, is this: God wills the latter to be an instrument of divine justice, but does not will the same for ours. He wills that spirits be afflicted and suffer by that fire, but not by this one. In this, it is similar to what happens in the Sacrament of Baptism, where water is effective for the remission of sins, but wine or another liquor is not. <note>The author uses a "sacramental" analogy: just as water only washes away sins because God specifically designated it for that purpose, fire only burns spirits because God specifically empowered hellfire as a tool of punishment.</note>

<margin>14.</margin>
God, the Best and Greatest, possesses this power: that just as He administers corporeal things through spiritual things according to the natural order; so, beyond the natural order, He may act upon spiritual things through whatever corporeal things He judges expedient.

<margin>15.</margin>
Therefore, spirits do not flee from fire because they are tortured by it. Or are they perhaps terrified by it as a sign? Do they flee or detest it because it calls to memory the infernal fire of which it is a sign? This should not be said either. For not all things representing invisible...

<summary>The author argues that natural fire has no power to torture or repel demons because it lacks the divine mandate given to hellfire. He explains that God uses physical elements as "instruments of justice" only when He wills it, much like how only water is effective for Baptism.</summary>

### CHAPTER 59.
*Whether Spirits are put to flight by a lit lamp, and whether infested places are freed from their harassment.*

<margin>1.</margin> Just as we said above that some people arm themselves with swords and spears against Spirits, so there are others who believe that if they dispel the darkness of the night with light, they have nothing to fear from Spirits; and they consider all places to be safe from their infestation.

<margin>2.</margin> Their opinion arises from the fact that they have observed that Spirits are for the most part troublesome at night, when darkness occupies everything; whereas during the day they are observed either never, or very rarely, and even then for a very short time.

<margin>3.</margin> They persuade themselves that Spirits love darkness and flee light because those who appear are almost always the damned: who, since they always do evil and never good, hate the light. Since, as the Lord says: *Everyone who does evil hates the light.* <note>original: Ioan. 3 (John 3:20)</note>

<margin>4.</margin> Those who philosophize in this way, although they do not attain the truth in all things, nevertheless in many things they do not wander entirely from the truth; once we have judged these points, we will declare the core of the controversy <note>original: *caput controuersiae*, the "head" or essential point of the debate</note>.

<margin>5.</margin> First, they do not err in this: that they believe those *who do evil hate the light.* This is the speech of the Lord. Many things could be said in confirmation of this. But in a clear matter, many words are not needed.

<margin>6.</margin> Second, they do not err in this: that they think *Spirits return to and trouble men more frequently in the nocturnal than in the diurnal hours.* The matter is exactly so, and we have given many reasons for it elsewhere. See Chapter 18 of this Disputation.

<margin>7.</margin> Third, it is not an error that they teach *the Spirits of the damned do nothing well; they do everything wickedly.* And this, because it has been demonstrated elsewhere, should not be repeated here. See Chapter 40.

<margin>8.</margin> But because they make a universal law from these things, and wish it to be concluded...

<margin>9.</margin>
*It should not be accepted as a proven fact that all spirits flee the light and seek the darkness. For not all spirits act wickedly; nor, even if they did act wickedly, would they necessarily flee the light and seek the darkness.*
How many examples have we brought forward of spirits who were troublesome during the day, even in a great crowd of people? Nor were these only from the number of those who were pleasing to God—those who, through the punishments they endure, have laid aside the stains they contracted while in the body <note>The author refers here to "Purgandi," or souls in Purgatory, who undergo temporary suffering to achieve purity</note>; but they were also from the class of the damned, who, if anyone should, ought to have fled the light.

<margin>10.</margin>
Furthermore, not all spirits act wickedly, such that they should be said to flee the light for that reason. For those who are to be purified, who frequently involve themselves in the affairs of the living, are so far from acting wickedly that it seems they are scarcely able to act wickedly or offend God at all. This has been stated quite often.

<margin>11.</margin>
Even if they all did act wickedly, it is still not necessary for them to flee the light. *Are there not those found who rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the most wicked things? Proverbs 2. Those who proclaim their sin like Sodom? Isaiah 3. Those who have the forehead of a prostitute <note>original: "frons meretricis," a biblical idiom for being shameless or unrepentant</note> and do not know how to blush? Jeremiah 6.*

<margin>12.</margin>
Someone might ask, "What then? *Does the Lord not say that those who do evil hate the light?* <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 3:20</note>" I respond that this has little to do with the spirits of whom we speak. The Lord is speaking about men. Moreover, the Lord did not include all men without exception, but only those who have not yet made a pact with sin, or who have not yet cast off all shame and rejected fear. Finally, the Lord was indicating what usually happens in most cases.

# ON HAUNTED PLACES

<margin>2.</margin> And at the beginning it is certainly true that *not all disturbances are removed by this means.* For since there are several types of disturbances, as was said earlier in Chapter 19, and some are perceived by sight, some by hearing, and some by touch; even if barred doors prevent spirits from presenting themselves to the eyes of the living, or from inflicting blows or affecting the sense of touch in some other way, they certainly do not prevent them from being heavy and bringing those disturbances perceived by the ears by stirring up tumults from the outside. Alexander ab Alexandro <note>Alexander ab Alexandro (1461–1523) was a Neapolitan lawyer and humanist scholar. His work *Genialium Dierum* (Genial Days) is a collection of ancient customs and personal anecdotes, including ghost stories.</note> once locked the door of his bedchamber with a firm bolt, as he himself testifies in Book 5, Chapter 2 of his *Genial Days*; but though he did not see them, he heard horrible apparitions <note>original: "Species"</note> rioting outside and pounding on the bedroom door with their hands.

<margin>3.</margin> Let the reasoning for those things perceived by sight be that they transmit their images directly to the eyes, and are prevented from affecting the sense when opaque bodies are placed in between. Let the sense of touch also require this, as it must be joined to those things by which it is moved. But the condition of sounds and tumults that strike the ears is different. They do not spread their forms directly to things, nor do they require such a close conjunction with the sense as those things which fall under the sense of touch.

<margin>4.</margin> **Therefore, the living who shut themselves in and block the spirits' access to them are not secure from all disturbances. But are they secure from most?** The definition of this seems to be sought from the condition of the spirits who cause the trouble: who either attack us in assumed bodies, or mock and trouble us through our senses alone, without the aid of assumed bodies.

<margin>5.</margin> ***If spirits do not carry bodies around with them, what help will it be to fortify oneself with locked doors against them?*** Such is the condition of spirits that they are not fended off by any obstacle of bodies. They are able to penetrate anything, however dense or however hard, without injury to either the bodies or to the spirits themselves.

<margin>6.</margin> **What if they do carry bodies? Either these are assumed from elsewhere and are solid and firm, or they are compacted by the spirits' own industry out of air or other flowing matter, and are not solid.** As for these latter ones, just as they can assemble them suddenly, so they can soon dissolve them and assemble them again whenever they please. Therefore, *even here there is no secure liberty:* neither closed doors nor fortified gates are of any avail; for the spirits can either manifest themselves inside in the same bodies with which they were troublesome outside, or they can fashion other bodies for themselves from the air inside and bring about disturbances.

<margin>7.</margin> That which we are saying was learned by the example of the man we mentioned above, Alexander, in that house which was disturbed almost every night by the constant illusions of shadows <note>original: "Vmbrarum"</note> and foul images.

Bb 3

For after the other troubles he had endured, which have been reviewed, he adds the following:

> *“I shall not omit,” he says, “a great miracle <note>In this context, "miraculum" refers to an extraordinary or supernatural event rather than a religious miracle.</note> which happened to me while I was clearly wide awake, with even greater trembling, not long afterward. For when darkness had fallen, I had locked the doors of my bedchamber with a firm bolt; and while I was lying in my small bed, not yet settled into rest, with a lamp lit, I perceived that horrible Apparition <note>original: "Species"</note> already rioting outside and pounding on the bedroom doors with its hands. Not long after, that Phantom <note>original: "Simulacrum"</note>—even though the doors were shut and fastened (hardly believable to say)—entered the bedroom through the joints and cracks. It lay under my bed, and when Marcus, my student and protégé <note>original: "alumnus & cliens"</note> (since he was sleeping within sight), saw its grim and foul face, he was suddenly struck with terror and filled everything with wailing and groaning, crying out in fear at the thing that had entered. This seemed hardly believable to me since I saw the bedroom door was shut; meanwhile, we saw that dread Phantom, which was lying under my bed, stretch out its hand and arm and extinguish the lamp that stood nearby. Once it was extinguished, the spirit began mixing up my books and whatever else was there with a complaining voice, and did not stop overturning everything. Thus writes Alexander.”*

<margin>8.</margin>
Furthermore, if bodies are assumed from elsewhere <note>The author refers to the common belief that spirits "assume" or "put on" physical bodies made of condensed air or other materials to become visible.</note> and are solid, it is a matter of doubt whether Spirits are then able to penetrate to people who are shut inside, and to cause trouble while in such bodies. Some indeed contend that this can happen by no logic; others admit it, yet not by the power of the Spirits themselves, but by some more divine virtue and power. For our part, we conclude the matter with four Assertions.

<margin>9.</margin>
The first is that *by assuming any bodies whatsoever, Spirits are not prevented from being troublesome. For although bodies sometimes hinder them so that access is not open to everyone, nevertheless, because they can lay those bodies aside at will, if they wish to be troublesome, they will put down the bodies and be troublesome in whatever way they please.*

<margin>10.</margin>
The second is that *it is entirely probable that Spirits who appear and bring trouble to men in assumed bodies never penetrate solid bodies standing in their way in the same manner that they can and do penetrate when they are free of bodies.* This penetration <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "penetration" refers to two physical bodies occupying the same space simultaneously, which was generally considered impossible in nature.</note> is a prodigious thing and requires the almighty hand of God. Why, then, would there be a need for wonders and miracles in this infestation of Spirits?

<margin>11.</margin>
The third is that *not even the powers of any spirits are such that they can penetrate solid objects while in assumed bodies: although they may desire to penetrate, so that two bodies are found in the same place, the physical volume <note>original: "quantitas"</note> of different bodies does not permit it. Therefore, as long as the volume of the two bodies remains distinct, they will also require distinct locations. This is what the laws of nature demand.*

<margin>12.</margin> However, we do not wish to impose any laws upon divine power here. And let this be our fourth Assertion: just as one thing can be in different places, so too we do not doubt that different bodies can be situated in one and the same place; at least, those of us who have been raised and instructed in Christian matters do not doubt it.

<margin>13.</margin> Why could this not happen, since it has happened repeatedly? It happened at the Birth of Christ, when He entered into this world while the Virgin’s enclosures remained intact? <note>A reference to the theological doctrine of *virginitas in partu*, suggesting Christ passed through the womb like light through glass.</note> It happened in His Resurrection, when His body emerged from a sealed tomb? # CHAPTER LXI.

->*Whether it is lawful to redeem the vexations and annoyances of Demons, which they bring to certain places, by the shedding of innocent blood.*<-

In the five preceding Chapters, we discussed those methods by which the living fruitlessly fortify themselves against the infestations of any Spirits whatsoever. Besides these, there are certain other methods by which some people fight against specific Spirits—namely, those of Demons or of men—which themselves have no power. Let us examine these in turn. We begin with those used to combat the annoyances of Demons. There are two principal ones. Tostatus of Avila <note>original: "Tostatus Abulensis"; also known as Alonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), a famously prolific Spanish theologian.</note> mentions one; Michael Isselt <note>Michael von Isselt (d. 1597), a Dutch historian and priest known for his chronicles of the religious wars.</note> mentions the other. Let us speak of the latter first.

<margin>2.</margin> Isselt teaches, as we reported in the first Chapter, that there is a lake in Livonia <note>A historical region on the eastern shores of the Baltic Sea, now part of Estonia and Latvia.</note> which is greatly exposed to the annoyances and infestations of Demons, and which transmits much damage to the neighboring peoples. To free themselves from these miseries, every year the wretched inhabitants pour the blood of innocents into that same lake, and they are then certain of their peace.

<header>PART THREE.</header>

This perhaps confirms what has been passed down in historical accounts: that Tamesia <note>original: "Tamesiam"; likely referring to the ancient city of Temesa in southern Italy</note>, a city in Italy, was once vexed in a marvelous way by a Spirit, so much so that the inhabitants thought of abandoning it several times. However, it was liberated after they sacrificed a Virgin to the Gods, following an oracle of Apollo. This is recorded by Aelian in Book 8 of his *Various History* <note>Claudius Aelianus was a Roman teacher and rhetorician; his "Varia Historia" is a collection of anecdotes and natural history</note>.

Now, at this point, the present argument demands that we define two things. The first is: Whether the shedding of innocent Blood has these powers—namely, to remove the troubles caused by Demons. The second is: Whether, if mortals cannot manage it by any other means, they may lawfully free themselves from these same troubles by this method.

<margin>3.</margin>
One might perhaps believe that first point, persuaded by experience, which has now been observed for many years: that at the *pouring of the blood of innocents into a lake*, all demonic infestations were removed. However, although experience provides a significant argument in matters devoid of reason and intelligence, it cannot provide a firm argument for those who use reason, at least not so that we might form a certain and undoubted judgment about the nature of things based solely upon it.

<margin>4.</margin>
Such is the condition of those who possess reason and intelligence: that although they can be affected in some way by sensible things <note>Meaning "physical things" perceptible by the senses</note>, they always remain superior to those sensible things. Thus, if something is observed to happen to them through physical objects, it should be attributed not so much to the power of those physical things as to the will of those who use reason.

<margin>5.</margin>
It is a common axiom among those who philosophize correctly that *those things of inferior power can do nothing against things superior in power*. How much, indeed, do Spirits surpass all physical things in power? And since their power is superior to every physical thing, could they be forced by physical objects to either stop haunting places or change their dwellings?

<margin>6.</margin>
Therefore, *this power does not reside in the shedding of innocent blood to restrain a Spirit*. Those who are troublesome before the blood is shed can remain troublesome after it is shed. The powers of blood are great for preserving the life-spirits of animals within their bodies; but once shed, what power can blood have to either banish the Spirits of Demons from locations or repress their power?

<margin>7.</margin>
And *the blood of innocents*—why is it said to have these powers here rather than the blood *of the guilty*? Does a blameless life grant some power to the blood? And do the habits of wicked men harm their blood, so that what the former can do, the latter cannot? Again, why would these troubles be removed by the shedding of human blood rather than that of brute animals?

<margin>8.</margin>
This is entirely the wickedness of Demons. Being wicked, they desire to make wretched mortals the authors of the gravest crimes; they choose not to inflict any further troubles once blood is shed—troubles they otherwise could have continued. For this reason... <note>The text continues on the next page, explaining the "cause" of why demons pretend to be defeated by sacrifice</note>
