These most wicked villains demand the blood of men as their cause; they demand the blood of innocent men; and they demand it against all laws.

<margin>9.</margin> Nor is this a new pursuit of theirs. These bloodthirsty beings are greatly refreshed by human blood, having been "murderers from the beginning of the world," as the Lord testifies in John 8 <note>original: "Ioannis 8"; referring to John 8:44, where Jesus describes the devil as a murderer from the beginning</note>. Do not the cruel sacrifices, with which they have driven almost the entire world mad, prove this? And their impious and barbaric rites? Regarding these, Alexander ab Alexandro <note>Alexander ab Alexandro (1461–1523) was a Neapolitan jurist whose work "Genialium Dierum" (Genial Days) was a popular collection of ancient customs and laws</note> writes in the following manner:

*The Tauri of Scythia,* he says in Book 6, Chapter 16 of *Genial Days, used to sacrifice strangers as offerings to Diana. The people of Laodicea sacrificed a virgin to Pallas <note>Pallas Athena</note>; the Arcadians offered a boy to Lycaean Jupiter. Many living near the Borysthenes <note>The ancient name for the Dnieper River</note>, out of a foolish spirit, were accustomed to give human victims and to burn human bones in sacrifices to the Gods. The Blemmyes, Cimbrians, Gauls, Druids, and Germans, on fixed days, make offerings with human victims and burn the blood of captives upon the altars; they believed God was most greatly appeased when they tortured men to death, seeking signs of divinity and omens from the sufferings of men.*

*Among the Phoenicians and Carthaginians, it was a practice observed for far too long that they would sacrifice infants of the highest nobility, chosen by lot and dressed in royal finery, as victims to Saturn. It was not permitted to rescue anyone from death whom the lot had destined for it. Because of this, the deaths were mourned with the profuse weeping of many citizens. When they finally ceased these rites, they were later defeated by Agathocles <note>The tyrant of Syracuse who invaded North Africa in 310 BCE</note>; believing the Gods were angry for that reason, they slaughtered two hundred sons of the nobility at the altars to appease the divine power.*

*We have also found it was practiced by the Rhodians and Cretans, who would sacrifice a man glutted with feasts, as well as prepubescent boys, to Saturn on festival days. In Chios and Salamis, the custom thrived for many centuries that they would slaughter and tear men apart for Diomedes and Dionysus. There was a temple of this same Dionysus in Arcadia in which girls were whipped to death at the altar, just as boys were at the altar of Mercury and Artemis Orthia in Sparta.*

*Furthermore, others believed that the greatest burnt offering was made by filling a huge statue woven of wicker with living men, and setting it on fire, so that the men perished in a foul manner <note>A reference to the "Wicker Man" ritual described by Julius Caesar in his accounts of the Gauls</note>. Among the Boii and the Celts, it was considered most religious to clean the head of a captured enemy, encase the skull in gold, and use it as a cup for libations during solemnities.*

*It is recorded that Aristomenes of Messene slaughtered three hundred men at once—among whom was King Theopompus—in a single sacrifice to the Jupiter they call Ithometes. The Spartans reached such a point of madness that they offered a human victim to Mars. The Galatians and Massagetae believed the Gods were not properly consulted unless a man was slaughtered at the altars of the Gods; from his fall, the tearing of his limbs, and the flow of blood, they would divine the future.*

*The Cimbri <note>An ancient Germanic or Celtic tribe known for their conflict with the Roman Republic</note> took criminals who had been spared, fixed them to stakes, and gave them to the Gods as sacrificial victims. The Gauls, in addition to Hesus and Teutates <note>Primary deities of the ancient Celts</note>, and Mercury, whom they appeased with human blood, would—when afflicted by serious diseases or dangers—either immolate men to appease the altars of the Gods or vow that they would do so. At these altars, they even slaughtered the elderly as victims. Among the Lusitanians <note>An Indo-European people of the western Iberian Peninsula</note>, there was an ancient custom of looking into the intestines of men to see the future and to capture all kinds of divinations from them; they also offered the severed right hands of captives as a gift to the Gods.*

*The Thracians considered that Zamolxis <note>A legendary social and religious reformer, regarded as a god among the Thracian Getae</note>, whom they believe to be the greatest God, would not become favorable unless a man fell by a light blow of spears at the altar; they thought this the best and most pleasing victim to the Gods. The Germans also, in their barbaric rite, considered it most religious to appease Mercury with human blood. The Senones <note>A Gallic tribe</note> did the same: having publicly slaughtered a man, they celebrated unspeakable rites on fixed days of the year, believing that crimes were expiated by these portents.*

*Among the Persians also, to give thanks to the Gods, it was customary to bury young men alive and still breathing under the earth. We have heard that this custom spread to the Greeks, so that in the annual celebration to Bacchus <note>The god of wine and ecstasy, also known as Dionysus</note> they sacrifice living men; whoever was thus immolated received the highest praise for uprightness among his people.*

*It would be a long task to follow the customs of the Tauri <note>An ancient people of the Crimean Peninsula, infamous in Greek myth for sacrificing shipwrecked strangers</note>: how they would place a man at the altar, and after solemn prayers, strike the man's head with an iron nail and fix it to a cross; then they would cast the headless body headlong from a huge cliff. This is said to have been common with the Leucadians <note>Inhabitants of the island of Leucas in Greece</note>, who, in the sacred rite of Apollo, to avert the wrath of the Gods, would throw men down from the mountain's lookout and drive them headlong into the sea.*

*It was practiced among the Albani <note>A tribe in the Caucasus region, distinct from modern Albanians</note> that they would place at the altars a man initiated into the sacred rites, who excelled in holiness, having been kept for a long time and sumptuously fattened; then, having been enchanted by a frenzied song and with certain prayers added, they would immolate him with other victims. And the Romans in the Cattle Market <note>original: "foro boario"; the site of the first gladiatorial contests and occasional ritual burials</note>, to appease the wrath of the Gods, did not fear to bury living people under the earth; and for a long time it was permitted to kill a man in sacred rites and immolate him to the Gods; so much so that they appeased Saturn and Latiar Jupiter <note>Jupiter Latiaris, the god of the Latin League</note> with human victims, whose image they washed with human blood while they were sacrificing. These things Alexander <note>Referring to Alexander ab Alexandro</note> says.*

*Satan entangled the people of God in these same miseries long ago, of which the Royal Prophet writes in Psalm 105:*

> *They were mingled among the nations, and learned their works: and served their idols, and it became a stumbling block to them. And they sacrificed their sons, and their daughters to demons. And they shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons, and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan. And the land was infected with blood, and contaminated with their works. What of the fact that even some Christians...*

...[mented]? In the year of our Lord 1273, there were certain people called Flagellants <note>A medieval religious movement whose members publicly scourged themselves as a form of penance</note>, who believed and taught that God could only be appeased by the shedding of human blood. Thus, this practice is a butchery of the Devil.

<margin>10.</margin> Let it therefore be established that there is no such power in the blood of the innocent that it can either impose silence upon demons or force them to leave a place. But if it were certain that troubles could be removed by this method—and could be removed by no other—would it be lawful to buy one's safety by shedding blood and to redeem oneself from harassment?

<margin>11.</margin> First, it should not be believed that Christian people could ever fall into such dire straits that they could not provide for themselves in any way other than this. One can help oneself through prayer made to God, for whom all things are possible; through the sign of the most holy Cross; through exorcisms; and through other methods that we shall explain in the following chapters.

<margin>12.</margin> And even if no other way were possible, *surely this one must not be used.* Not only must the harassment of demons be endured, but all adversity—even the most imminent death—must be faced rather than redeeming oneself from the harassment of evil spirits by the shedding of innocent blood, and this for many serious reasons.

<margin>13.</margin> *The first reason is* that the faithful neither can nor should pay any friendly service (as this undoubtedly is) to demons, who are the most sworn enemies of God and men. *I do not want you to become partners with demons, says the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 10.* <note>original: "Nolo vos socios fieri Dæmoniorum"</note>

<margin>14.</margin> *The second is* that this cannot be performed without the crime of superstition; and in it there intervenes—if not an express, then certainly a tacit—pact <term>pactum: a formal or informal agreement with a spiritual entity</term> with demons, which is itself most severely forbidden to Christian people by both divine and human laws. *And what agreement has the temple of God with idols? 2 Corinthians 6.* <note>original: "Et quis consensus templo Dei, cum idolis?"</note>

<margin>15.</margin> *The third is* that a most grave murder of the innocent is committed here, which can neither be commanded nor approved by any person's private authority nor by the public authority of any magistrate. *You shall not kill the innocent and the just, it is said in Exodus 23.* <note>original: "Infontem & iustum nō occides"</note>

<page-num>203</page-num>
<header>PART THREE.</header>
<sig>Cc 2</sig>

The most learned theologian, <term>Tostatus Abulensis</term> <note>Alfonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), a prolific Spanish scholar and Bishop of Avila</note>, in his commentary on the second book of Kings, chapter 16, question 43, mentions an opinion held by some who believe that the spirits of demons may be put to flight by certain fumigations <note>The use of smoke or incense for ritual cleansing</note>. Aside from being a common belief, this opinion seems to rely on two foundations, according to Tostatus. The first is that these same spirits are attracted by opposite fumigations and are provoked to settle in specific places. The second is that <term>Tobias</term> <note>The protagonist of the Book of Tobit in the Apocrypha</note> was taught by an Angel that by the smoke of the heart and liver of a certain fish, *every kind of demon is driven out*, as the Scripture says in chapter six.

<margin>2.</margin>
In this assertion, although the evidence brought forward to support it is not entirely false, it is not all certain and beyond doubt; indeed, the assertion itself cannot possibly stand as the truth.

<margin>3.</margin>
*It is certain* that demons were driven away by the smoke raised from the heart and liver. The sacred history of Tobias records this. An Angel, who cannot lie, asserted it. The outcome and result proved it.

<margin>4.</margin>
But while this is certain, *it is equally uncertain*—indeed, false—that spirits are delighted, attracted, or provoked toward men by certain fumigations. For what are those fumigations? From what fragrant substances do they come? How could they affect spirits? Whatever these fumigations are, they must be objects of the sense of smell. But objects of smell only affect the sense of smell, and they only attract those who possess the physical power of smelling. Does such a sense have any place in spirits?

<margin>5.</margin>
If indeed spirits are not refreshed by any fumigations, how can it be true, *as the assertion claims, that they are chased and driven away by the opposite?* Does not the same logic apply to the power of opposites?

<margin>6.</margin>
And these very fumigations by which spirits are said to be expelled, must they not also be objects of smell? How, then, are they perceived by spirits, who neither have nor can have the power of smelling?

<margin>7.</margin>
For the same reason that we reject fumigations and odors, we also reject certain herbs which some believe are intolerable to the spirits of demons. Among these are <term>red mugwort</term> <note>original: "Artemesia rubea"</note>, <term>houseleek</term> <note>original: "Barba Iovis," literally "Jupiter’s Beard"</note>, <term>marigold</term> <note>original: "Solsequium"</note>, <term>lovage</term> <note>original: "Leuisticus"</note>, <term>hyssop</term>, <term>sage</term>, <term>pennyroyal</term> <note>original: "Polegium"</note>, <term>elder leaves</term>, and so on. Any power present in these is physical; any effect they may have is only upon bodies, not upon spirits.

<margin>8.</margin>
And when we say these things, we mean them to apply to those spirits *who haunt specific places*. These are not attracted by any herbs or fumigations, nor are they banished by them. However, regarding those spirits *who possess human bodies*, the reasoning is not the same. Certain herbs and fumigations may be contrary to them; for although these substances do not drive the spirits from their seats by their own power...

### CHAPTER LXIII.
### *Whether the spirits of deceased men are prohibited from returning to the living if their corpses are buried under the hearth.*

<margin>1.</margin>
We have rejected two methods by which some arm themselves against the infestations of Demons; two remain to be examined by which freedom from the harassment of human Spirits <note>the author distinguishes here between 'Demons' (fallen angels) and 'human Spirits' (ghosts of the dead)</note> is expected. <margin>2.</margin>

But if they are certain of their salvation, yet must be purified of certain defects before the entrance to the kingdom of heaven lies open <note>referring to the state of Purgatory</note>, they themselves understand that these things are done in vain. ...established by **Augustine** and **Gregory** regarding the aids by which the spirits of the deceased are helped. <note>Referring to St. Augustine of Hippo and Pope Gregory the Great, whose writings formed the medieval Western understanding of Purgatory and the efficacy of prayers for the dead.</note>

<margin>3.</margin> Thus, the spirits of the deceased do not suffer any harm from this type of burial. For it does not delay those who have died piously in Christ, nor does it hinder them from being rescued from the punishments by which they are purified <note>original: "pœnis, quibus expiantur," referring to the cleansing pains of Purgatory.</note>. Nor does it entangle those in more severe punishments from whom all hope of salvation has been stripped away. The living cannot cause inconvenience to any spirits of the deceased. To some, however, they can be of benefit.

<margin>4.</margin> Furthermore, this burial does not cast shackles on the deceased, *lest they should be able to return to the living*. Are corpses kept buried under the hearth <note>original: "sub foco." The hearth was often the center of folk-magic rituals intended to "bind" a spirit to the house or prevent its wandering.</note> so that they do not break out and terrify the living? Since spirits are free from their bodies, unless a necessity is imposed upon them from some other source to prevent their return, why would they be unable to return?

<margin>5.</margin> What about the fact that *a certain injury seems to be inflicted on the deceased here?* To all of them, certainly, because they are denied an honorable and Christian burial, which everyone can justly demand; but to certain specific individuals—those, I mean, who died piously in Christ—because they are prohibited from receiving the prayers <note>original: "suffragia," referring to intercessory prayers or masses said for the benefit of a soul.</note> of the living.

<margin>6.</margin> Nor are the living *free from the crime of superstition here*, those who hide away the bodies of the deceased under the hearth. What, I ask, do their bodies buried under the hearth do to prevent spirits from eventually returning to the living? Does the hearth perhaps have this power, that if it possesses the bodies of the deceased, a law is immediately imposed on the spirits so that they cannot move from that place? Or does the hearth not possess this, but rather it is the nature of spirits that after they have departed from their bodies, if their corpses are enclosed under the hearth, they themselves must remain fixed in a certain place? Or perhaps, if it is neither this nor that, has God so ordained it, that as soon as the bodies are contained under the hearth, all liberty for the spirit to return to the living is taken away?

<margin>7.</margin> *The hearth does not have this power to take away the spirit's ability to return.* For the place itself does not achieve this by its own nature; nor the fire, which is fostered and contained in that place, nor anything else connected to the hearth. These physical things can be separated from spirits by a very great distance, so for that reason they can have no power over spirits; and even if they were not distant at all, they still cannot affect the spirits themselves because they [the hearth and fire] are physical bodies <note>The author argues that physical matter cannot act directly upon an incorporeal spirit.</note>.

<margin>8.</margin> *Nor is it the condition of spirits that they are unwilling to revisit and trouble the places whose corpses the hearth contains.* For if they do not wish to return, it will happen either by reason of some harm which they fear to incur if they return—but none can be brought upon them—or by reason of some benefit which they fear to lose by their return. But there is nothing of which they can be deprived in any way.

<margin>9.</margin> *Are they perhaps prohibited by the law of God?* But what is that law? To whom was it revealed? At what time?

<margin>11</margin>

<margin>12</margin>
*I would say, therefore, that it happens mostly by the help of demons that these spirits of the dead do not return. It pleases them to mock mortals with vain opinions: and so that they may nourish these, they bring it about that the spirits do not return; or, what is more likely, they themselves do not wish to be troublesome to men in the persona of human spirits. What wonder? The opinion of* **St. Augustine** *is clear in book 2 of "On Christian Doctrine," chapters 22 and 23: Demons seduce men devoted to vanity by means of vain things. These "shifters"* <term>versipelles: literally "skin-turners," a term for shape-shifters or deceivers who change their appearance to trick others</term> *affect a likeness of God even in this: that just as God works the effects of grace through the mediation of sensible Sacraments, not as causes sufficient by their own nature, but as signs of the effects; so they themselves perform certain things when men employ means which in truth contribute nothing to the effects themselves; which they then use as if they were certain signs of those effects.*

<margin>13</margin>
From this it is now manifest both that the Philippians are involved in a grave error when they oppose the infestations of spirits in this way, and that the faithful of Christ must not fight against the troubles of spirits with this kind of battle and weaponry. *I do not want you to become partners with demons,* says the **Apostle in 1 Corinthians 10**. *For what participation has justice with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? What consensus has the temple of God with idols? 2 Corinthians 6.*

# CHAPTER LXIV.

## *Whether the throwing of black beans formerly availed against the troublesome spirits of the dead, and whether it may now be permitted to the Christian people.*

<margin>I.</margin>
Another method, by which some fortified themselves against the spirits of the dead, was once in use, especially among the Romans, and was celebrated under the name of the *Lemuralia* <note>The Lemuralia or Lemuria was a feast in ancient Roman religion where the Romans performed rites to exorcise the malevolent and hungry ghosts of the dead from their houses.</note> sacred rites. Regarding this, Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar known for his work "Genialium dierum" (Genial Days), which explores ancient customs and law.</note> briefly writes in book 3 of *Genial Days*, chapter 12: In the Lemuralia, it was the custom to throw beans at night; shouting for the *Lemures* <note>Shades or restless spirits of the deceased who were thought to haunt homes and wander at night.</note> to cast themselves out of the house. It was agreed that these beans should be black; and the person, having washed their hands and with bare feet, would roll them in their mouth and throw them behind their back, and make a clanging sound with bronze. They would pray nine times that the *Lemures*, having been ransomed by the beans, would leave the house. This was done three times in the month of May, until, their spirits being freed from religious obligation, they considered the *Manes* <note>The deified spirits of deceased ancestors, often seen as benevolent, though here requiring expiation.</note> to be purified. Thus says Alexander. But Ovid <note>The famous Roman poet Publius Ovidius Naso (43 BC – 17 AD).</note> said the same long before him in these verses from Book 5 of the *Fasti*:

> The rite was the ancient nocturnal Lemuria,
> These will give funeral offerings to the silent Spirits.
> The year was shorter, nor did they yet know the pious *Februa* <note>The Roman festival of purification; the author notes that in the older calendar, the month of February and its purifications did not exist.</note>,
> Nor were you, two-faced Janus, the leader of the months.
> Yet already they brought their gifts to the extinguished ash,
> And the grandson offered rites at the tombs of his buried grandfather.
> The month was May, named for the elders,
> Which even now retains a part of the ancient custom.
> When it is now midnight, and sleep provides silence,
> And you, dogs and various birds, have grown quiet.
> He, mindful of the ancient rite and fearful of the Gods,
> Rises, and his twin feet have no bindings <note>Bare feet were often required in Roman rituals to ensure there was no "binding" or obstruction to the spiritual energy.</note>.
> He makes signs with his fingers, the middle joined with the thumb,
> Lest a light Shadow encounter him in the silence.
> And when he has washed his hands in pure spring water,
> He turns and receives black beans in his mouth.
> He throws them while turned away; but while he throws: "These I send."
> "With these beans," he says, "I redeem myself and mine."
> Nine times he says this; nor does he look back: the Shadow is thought
> To collect them, and to follow his back with no one seeing.
> Again he touches the water, and clangs Temesean bronze <note>Copper or bronze from Temesa, an ancient city in Italy famous for its mines; the sound was meant to frighten away the spirits.</note>,

<margin>2.</margin>
The use of beans was varied among the ancients; but that which was joined with superstition was either non-existent or certainly none was joined with greater superstition than that which was observed in driving away spirits.

<margin>3.</margin>
Indeed, they had one use which no one can condemn, received from God the Best and Greatest, which the Holy Scriptures mention twice (2 Kings 17 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Samuel 17:28. Older classifications often labeled the books of Samuel as 1 and 2 Kings.</note> and Ezekiel 4). In these instances, they serve as food for men: regarding which Pliny says in his *Natural History*, book 18, chapter 12: *The bean,* he says, *has multiple uses for every kind of four-legged animal, and especially for man; it is also mixed with grain among most nations, and especially with millet, used whole or more delicately crushed. And because it is thought to dull the senses and cause insomnia, it is condemned by the Pythagorean opinion: hence that saying: "Abstain from the bean." Although different authors desire different reasons for this.* <note>Pythagoras famously forbid his followers from eating beans, though the exact reason—whether for health, their resemblance to human embryos, or their supposed connection to the underworld—remains a subject of historical debate.</note>

<margin>4.</margin>
They had another use derived from human institution. For they served in place of pebbles in voting. Just as the Germans of old, once a council was gathered, would murmur and groan in dissent if a proposal displeased them, rejecting the opinion; but if something was pleasing, they would clash their spears and weapons, and signify their approval with the sound of arms and dances—as Alexander ab Alexandro witnesses in book 4 of *Genial Days*, chapter 11—so among the Greeks and certain other nations, votes were cast with beans. This use is in itself without crime and is free from blame.

<margin>5.</margin>
The third use of them was indeed from human institution, but nonetheless by the suggestion of the Devil, and joined with grave superstition. And this type is varied. For at times they were accustomed to be brought home from the harvest for sacrifice: and they were called, as Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> witnesses, *refrina* <note>refrina or refriva: beans brought back from the field to be offered at home.</note>, and a porridge made from them, which was offered to the Gods, was called *fabacia* by the ancients. At other times they were used in auctions, and through them a hope of greater profit was conceived. Their use also served the Greeks for judgment. For a white bean among them was auspicious in casting lots and a sign of a good outcome; a black one was a sign of a bad outcome, according to the same witness Alexander, book 3, chapter 5.

<margin>6.</margin>
To this third superstitious use must be referred that practice by which they are employed to drive spirits from houses: yet in the magnitude and multitude of its superstitions, this one seems to surpass the others; and yet it pertains to nothing of the matter. For what does a bean thrown behind the back contribute to putting spirits to flight? And a black bean at that? And one turned in the mouth several times before? And thrown by a person whose hands are washed and feet are bare? And with the clanging <meta>catchword: tinnitu (clanging/ringing)</meta>

<margin>9.</margin>
*The Spirits of the dead were not served by the throwing of beans.* Whoever among the Pagans departed from this life arrived at that condition of the other life in which neither the use of beans, nor anything else similar, could bring them any aid. The salvation of all was hopeless.

<margin>10.</margin>
Was force, then, applied to them, and were they compelled to depart? *Neither was force applied, nor were they compelled to depart.* For by what thing was force applied? By the beans themselves? According to the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, who held various mystical beliefs about beans, including that they contained the souls of the dead.</note>, beans generate Spirits; they do not drive them away. The living have no power over the said Spirits. The ceremonies were proofs of superstition. Together, all these things constituted grave idolatry.

Those whom God has decreed to terrify and punish through Specters and the Shadows of dead men because of committed outrages—let them use as many and whatever kind of beans they wish, they shall not escape divine vengeance.

<margin>12.</margin>

## C H A P T E R LXV.

### *That there are various ways by which places are freed from the infestation of Demons: and that there are various differences between these ways.*

<margin>1.</margin>
The ways in which war is waged against Demons are many, yet they can all be reduced to five principal methods. The first consists in prayer; the second relies on the use of the most holy Cross; the third on consecrated objects <note>These are often referred to as "sacramentals," such as holy water or blessed salt.</note>; the fourth on Relics; and the fifth on Exorcism, with which we join the Invocation of the name of Christ. If there are any other methods, they are either brought back to these categories or are used quite rarely. Such is the instance mentioned in the *Life of Abbot Simeon*—who was called the "Fool" <note>original: "Salus." This refers to St. Simeon of Emesa, a 6th-century "Holy Fool" who hid his piety behind eccentric behavior.</note>—where a Devil was driven out of a certain haunted village by the playing of a flute, as witnessed by Leontius, the Bishop of Neapolis on the island of Cyprus. There is also the method by which these same spirits are sometimes put to flight by the mere presence of holy men, as was discussed in Thesis 9, Chapter 27.

<margin>2.</margin>
There is a great and multifaceted difference between these methods. *The first* is that some of these cannot be accomplished without speech; some exist without it; and some are exercises of the mind alone. To the first kind belongs <term>Exorcism</term> <note>A formal rite using specific spoken formulas to command a demon to depart.</note>; to the second, consecrated objects, the Cross, and Relics; to the third, Prayer, although this is sometimes vocal.

<margin>3.</margin>
From this, a *second* difference is perceived. For some methods require the cooperation of a human being—indeed, they do not exist without human cooperation, not to mention that they are a human action—such as Prayer, the sign of the Cross, and Exorcism. Others, although they are sometimes joined with human cooperation, do not strictly require it, such as consecrated objects and Relics; it is enough for these to be hung in certain places to drive away the Spirits.

<margin>4.</margin>
Furthermore, some are effective immediately for putting Spirits to flight, while others are not. Prayer does not directly target the Spirits themselves; rather, it reaches toward God, by whose work we ask to be liberated from the infestation of the Spirits. But Exorcism, the Cross, Relics, and sacred objects attack the Spirits themselves directly.

<margin>5.</margin>
*The fourth difference* is that some methods appear effective *in themselves*; others receive all the efficacy they have from elsewhere. To this latter kind belong consecrated objects: if you remove the consecration, they do not differ at all from natural things. All the others are powerful *of themselves* <note>meaning by the power inherent in the holy name or the virtue of the saint</note> for driving away Spirits.

<margin>6.</margin>To this, *the fifth difference is very close. Some methods are merely "impetratory"* <note>From the Latin "impetratorij," referring to actions that work by requesting or entreating God to intervene.</note> regarding the cleansing of places; they do not cleanse the places through their own power. Others are "operatory," so to speak, and are effective *of themselves*. To the first kind belongs Prayer, by which it is asked of God and the Saints that they either obtain freedom from God or that He Himself grants it. To the second kind belong the remaining methods, which directly confront the Spirits themselves.

<margin>7.</margin>*Furthermore, some have only a single use; others have many.* <term>Exorcism</term> <note>A formal rite using specific spoken formulas to command a demon to depart.</note> serves solely for cleansing places and banishing Spirits. The others, besides this, have other purposes, as has been demonstrated elsewhere.

<margin>8.</margin>*Likewise, some methods must necessarily be applied to the places themselves* that are infested with Spirits if the Spirits are to be routed: others can be applied anywhere, and yet they are still effective for banishing Spirits. It is not necessary for Prayer to be performed in the infested places. But if the Cross is made in other places; if Exorcisms are applied to other places; or if Relics and consecrated objects are hung or placed elsewhere than in the infested sites, you will achieve little progress.

<margin>9.</margin>*In the same way, it is advantageous for some to be employed at the very times* when the Spirits are already troublesome: others can be used at other times. For the former, Exorcism is most useful, in which one enters into a struggle with the Spirits; likewise, the Cross is a most immediate weapon against them. For the latter, prayer, Relics, and sacred objects are used.

<margin>10.</margin>*More differences could be assigned among the said methods; but there is no need* for more. Perhaps those already assigned are even too many. Let us therefore discuss and examine each individual method.

...was being tormented. <margin>9.</margin>
Thus, the Lord is to be understood as speaking of true prayer. First, the word itself, *prayer* <note>original: "oratio"</note>, suggests this, which when taken by itself signifies nothing other than the lifting up of the mind toward God. Furthermore, it is evident from the fact that the Lord was frequent in prayer (Luke 6) and was therefore able to cast out the demon; whereas the Apostles, who were less frequent in prayer (as the Pharisees used to object to the Lord concerning them in Luke 5), were unable to cast it out.

<margin>10.</margin>
But indeed, that in which we place our greatest defense, they <note>likely referring to theological skeptics or opponents</note> perhaps consider to be a slight matter in our case. This is because the Lord speaks not of driving demons out of *places*, but of expelling them from *human bodies*. Secondly, it is because He names a *certain* kind of demon which is driven out by prayer—suggesting that *common prayer* should not be called a universal engine against all spirits. A third point is added: that He places no less defense in *fasting* than in *prayer* (for He joins both together), so that it must either be said that prayer and fasting are equally effective at putting demons to flight from places, or that prayer alone is not effective.

<margin>11.</margin>
Three questions are sought through these three arguments, and once these have been briefly answered, we shall conclude the chapter. The first is: can it be demonstrated by the Lord’s opinion that demons are proscribed by prayer *not only from humans, but also from infested places*? Second: is prayer effective for putting *all spirits* to flight, or only *some*? Third: why do we attribute the exile and proscription of demonic spirits to prayer rather than to fasting, since the Lord joined fasting to prayer and suggests the powers of both are equal?

<margin>12.</margin>
Can it therefore be taught by the Lord’s opinion that demons are proscribed by prayer also from *places*, and not only from *humans*? It certainly can. For although the discourse concerns only a demon inhabiting a human, it does not exclude the others that infest places. This is clear first from the fact that He taught that *all things* can be obtained through *prayer*. Then, it follows from the fact that they do not seem so joined and united to the places they make "infested" as they are to the humans they possess; therefore, it is much more difficult for them to leave humans than places. Finally, it is because they are also in humans as if in certain "places"; so that if it is taught that they are cast out of humans by prayer, it is demonstrated by this very fact that they can be driven from *places* <note>The author uses a logical "greater to the lesser" argument: if you can do the hard task of removing a demon from a body, the easier task of removing it from a room is implied.</note> by prayer.

# PART THREE.

<margin>13.</margin>
*Thus prayer is effective for putting to flight all spirits of demons.* Let it be remembered that the Lord spoke of one specific kind [of demon]; but it is certain that all others are put to flight by prayer if it can be demonstrated that even this most difficult kind is driven out by prayer. How so? Because that which is taught to be routed by prayer is more burdensome and difficult than all others. Everywhere the disciples of Christ were casting out spirits by a word and by invoking the name of the Lord; but for this particular demon, invoking the Lord’s name alone was not enough: other engines were necessary for conquering it—*Prayer and Fasting.* <note>The author is referring to the "epileptic boy" narrative in Matthew 17, where the disciples failed to exorcise a spirit.</note> Now we argue from this point: If a demon that is most difficult to drive out can be driven out by prayer, then any demon whose strength is inferior can also be driven out. But that which is most difficult to drive out *is* driven out by prayer. Therefore, every other kind of demon can be too.

<margin>14.</margin>
*Why indeed do we attribute the routing of spirits to prayer, and not to fasting?* Much could be said on this point. Given our purpose and the space available, we will say much in few words. First, fasting also has great power here. Second, not only fasting, but also almsgiving <note>The practice of giving money or food to the poor as a religious act.</note> and other exercises of Christian piety can do a great deal. Third, these things [fasting and alms] do not have power to route demons by themselves. Fourth, prayer does have power by itself. Fifth, the Lord attributed the casting out of demons primarily to prayer. Sixth, He joined fasting to it because fasting brings it about that the mind comes to God through prayer.

<margin>15.</margin>
First, countless things declare the recommendation of fasting, found partly in the Holy Scriptures and partly in the writings of the Holy Fathers. For they teach that it prevents sins from being committed; it atones for those already committed; it grants a return to paradise (from which we were expelled because fasting was violated <note>A traditional theological view that Adam and Eve's eating of the forbidden fruit was a "violation of a fast."</note>); it lifts the mind to God; it redeems us from deserved punishments; it keeps away impending disasters; it obtains great favors from God; and finally, it contributes greatly to the health of both the inner and outer man <note>Referring to the health of both the soul and the physical body.</note>. St. Jerome summarized all these things in a short sentence in his *Letter to Eustochium*: *"Medicinal fasting,"* he says, *"takes away every weakness and grants every virtue and grace."* <note>original: "Medicinale Ieiunium..."</note> Furthermore, Athanasius clearly expresses its power against demons in his book *On Virginity*: *"Whoever,"* he says, *"is vexed by an unclean spirit should be certain that evil spirits depart when afflicted by fasting, fearing the power of fasting."*

<margin>16.</margin>
Likewise, there is no doubt about the excellence of almsgiving. Anyone even moderately versed in the Holy Scriptures recognizes this. Tobit teaches (chapter 4) that *"Almsgiving delivers from death, purges sins, and does not allow the soul to go into darkness."* The same Royal Prophet <note>A traditional title for King David, the presumed author of the Psalms.</note> says in Psalm 40: *"Blessed is the man who considers the needy and the poor; the Lord will deliver him in the evil day. The Lord will preserve him and give him life, and will not deliver him into the soul of his enemies."* The Savior teaches that for the reward of heavenly glory, through almsgiving...

That passage from Proverbs 28 is well known: *He who gives to the poor shall not lack.*

<margin>17.</margin> Nor are the powers of any exercises of Christian piety small. *Piety,* says the Apostle (1 Timothy 4), *is useful for all things.* And Solomon says (Wisdom 3), *The fruit of good labors is glorious.* King Hezekiah was not ignorant of these, nor was the most holy Paul. Thus, the former, when placed in extreme danger of his life, dared to say: *I beseech you, Lord, remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart* (4 Kings 20). <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 20.</note> The latter, however, said: *I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. For the rest, there is laid up for me a crown of justice, which the Lord, the just judge, will render to me on that day: and not only to me, but also to those who love his coming* (2 Timothy 4).

<margin>18.</margin> Regarding what we said in the third place—that these works were not instituted for the purpose of putting demons to flight, nor do they tend toward that by their own nature—there is no doubt. Fasting serves the affliction of the body and was instituted so that the flesh might be subjected to the Spirit; almsgiving <term>Eleemosyna</term> <note>The practice of giving to the poor as a religious duty.</note> works toward relieving the misery of one's neighbor. The remaining exercises of piety contribute to obtaining the joys of the future life. But **Prayer**, by its very nature, is powerful for putting demons to flight. God, the Best and Greatest, willed it to be a certain general protection for mortals to obtain absolutely all good things and to repel absolutely all evils—including the molestations of unclean spirits. This is excellently demonstrated and explained by the form of prayer which the Lord left behind, and which obtained its name from Him, being called the "Lord's Prayer" <note>original: "Dominica," referring to the Pater Noster.</note>.

<margin>19.</margin> That the Lord attributes the ejection of demons most especially to Prayer is shown in this place by many arguments by the most learned <term>Tostatus Abulensis</term>. <note>Alonso Tostado (c. 1400–1455), a prolific Spanish bishop and theologian known for his massive biblical commentaries.</note> Nor does anyone doubt this who both recognizes the power of Prayer and observes what fasting can achieve when joined to prayer. Finally, who can doubt that Prayer is aided by fasting? Are these not its two wings? One, by which it climbs the heavens and reaches the sight of God; the other, by which it obtains from God what it asks. Fasting helps with the former; Almsgiving helps with the latter. Thus, we should believe that Blessed Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his eloquence.</note> spoke excellently when, in his *71st Homily to the People, he calls the one who prays "light and winged."*

<margin>20.</margin> Nevertheless, the Lord did not mention Almsgiving [in the context of exorcism], nor other works of piety. This is because they are not so closely joined with Prayer, nor is there such a great necessity for them in order to pray well as there is for Fasting. It is absolutely necessary that the soul be lifted up toward God through prayer, which Fasting aids; however, it is not strictly necessary [for the act of prayer itself] to perform works of piety in order to obtain what one seeks.

PART THREE.

## C A P. LXVII.

### *Regarding the Use of Relics in Driving Out Demons, and the Reasons Why Demons Cannot Endure Relics.*

<margin>1.</margin>
There is one opinion shared by almost everyone, both Catholics and Heretics alike: *demons flee the relics of the Saints*. Among the Heretics, following others, the Magdeburg Centuriators <note>A group of 16th-century Protestant scholars who compiled a massive history of the Church by centuries.</note> admit this in Century 4, chapter 13, column 1446. Standing for the Catholics are Jerome and Chrysostom. Jerome, in his book against Vigilantius <note>Vigilantius was an early Christian priest who criticized the veneration of relics, which Jerome defended vigorously.</note>, says: *“You,” he says (addressing the demon who, through the mouth of Vigilantius, had called the relics of the saints ‘vile dust’), “are often tortured by this most vile dust.”* <note>original: "sæpè vilissimo hoc tortus es puluere."</note> Chrysostom teaches that they flee just like thieves who take flight if they ever happen upon the royal furnishings. These are his words from the seventh Homily on the seven Maccabees: *“Just as bold leaders of robbers, or impious diggers of graves, if by chance—while they are gathering prey or seeking spoils to be taken—they should run into any of the Emperor’s weapons or ornaments, though they are greedy for loot, they are nevertheless deterred by recognizing the King's insignia; so that they flee, and do not dare to approach or touch them. Thus indeed do the demons, who are truly the princes and masters of robbers, when they see the bodies of the crowned Martyrs laid out, flee far away at once from the sight of them, trembling and leaping back.”*

<margin>2.</margin>
Nor did either these men or those others come to this opinion lightly. The examples in favor of this matter are so many and so clear that anyone who wishes to deny them must be said to be entirely blind in the midday sun. Nor were these examples only given in the earliest times, but in our own times as well; and they were not recorded by those whose faith is suspect, but by those whose integrity it would be less than honorable to doubt.

<margin>3.</margin>
From the many, we have produced some in the *Disputation on Demoniacs*; let us be content here with the *<term>aprons and handkerchiefs</term>* <note>original: "femicinctijs & sudarijs." These were items of clothing that had touched the body of the Apostle.</note> of Saint Paul, of which Saint Luke writes in chapter 19 of the history of the Apostles [Acts] in this manner: *God did extraordinary miracles by the hand of Paul; so that even handkerchiefs and aprons were carried from his body to the sick; and the diseases left them, and the wicked spirits went out.*

We add the following from Theodoret, in the words of Theodoret himself, which, just as it confirms our argument, can also serve in many places in this Disputation. *“The abominable things,”* he says,

Why do you take up this fight against him? What trouble has he ever caused you? Stop your warring; cease from your ill-will; or you will learn by experience how great a good is peace. Therefore, they teach that Demons do not withstand Relics not because they hate, detest, or are forced to flee from them; but so that by their flight, they might invite men to the cult of Relics and to impious superstition. They flee, they say; they are not forced to flee, nor do they flee against their will.

<margin>6.</margin> For the opposite reason, Catholics are led to a contrary opinion and practice. They believe that demons do not merely pretend to flee, but are forced to flee. They believe that relics possess such power and authority that these shape-shifting spirits <note>original: "versipelles Spiritus," literally "skin-changers," referring to the deceptive nature of demons</note> cannot remain in their presence.

<margin>7.</margin> And indeed, as long as our adversaries cling to that thought and opinion—believing the use of relics to be superstitious—they neither can nor should use relics to put demons to flight. This is true even if it were certain that they could be liberated from the greatest demonic harassments through the use of relics, and could be liberated in no other way. This is because "everything that does not come from faith is sin" <note>A reference to Romans 14:23</note> and "everything that is against conscience builds a path to Gehenna" <note>original: "ædificet ad gehennam." A common theological maxim of the era: to act against one's own moral conviction is spiritually destructive</note>; for a sin may never be permitted, whether to achieve some good or to repel some evil.

<margin>8.</margin> But so that the blind may set aside this error and understand how far Catholics are from the crime of superstition, two things must be demonstrated. First, that relics are truly troublesome to demons and torture them, so that we must believe they do not fake their flight but flee because they are forced. Second, it cannot be said that demons, by their flight, entice men to the worship of relics—even if it were true (which it is not) that they were not being tortured. Once these two points have been demonstrated for the sake of our adversaries, we shall proceed with our own arguments.

<margin>9.</margin> That *demons are tortured by the presence of relics* is, first of all, the opinion of the Fathers, who were most holy men. The authority of Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquent preaching</note> alone is sufficient for us. "The relics of the Saints," he says (in his 66th Homily to the People of Antioch), "stop and torment demons, and release those bound by them from the most cruel chains." And in his book against the Gentiles, concerning the Life of St. Babylas <note>A 3rd-century Bishop of Antioch and martyr</note>, Bishop of Antioch and martyr, he says: "Such is the power of the Saints that while they are alive, demons do not fear even their shadows or clothes; but when they are dead, they even dread their coffins." Again, in his Sermon on the Adoration of the Chains of St. Peter, he says: "The Prince <note>referring to Satan</note> of the powers who defected from God shuddered at these chains, and even now he shudders; and fleeing from them with great fear, he is suppressed. The airy multitude of spirits <note>demons inhabiting the lower atmosphere</note>, fearing and trembling at these chains and struck by the bolts sent forth from them, are driven far away," etc.

<margin>10.</margin> Furthermore, the relics of Saint Babylas the Martyr teach the same thing, to omit other examples. # ON INFESTED PLACES

If the aprons and handkerchiefs <note>original: "semicinctia atque sudaria," a reference to Acts 19:12, where items touched by the Apostle Paul healed the sick and drove out spirits</note> of the living were able to do this—items in which the souls of the living never actually resided—will the bones, in which the Holy Spirit once held His seat, not cause torture? Will they not be hated by the demons?

<margin>13.</margin> It is natural for all people to be unable to bear the sight or the presence of those whom they pursue with envy and hatred; they even detest their images, their habits, and their friends. Everything belonging to such a person is heavy, troublesome, and a source of torture. Do the Demons not pursue holy men with hatred? Do they not envy them? If they truly pursue and envy them, can they look upon their corpses with impartial eyes? Can they endure their Relics? Their garments? Their images?

<margin>14.</margin> It is difficult for mortals—and a task only for the most perfect of men—to love those who are dead and not pursue or detest them, if they suffered heavy injuries from them while they were alive. Most people take revenge on the dead whose power they endured while they were living. But how much have certain Demons suffered from the living Saints? And since even the best of men can hardly forget such injuries, will these most wicked spirits forget? Having forgotten nothing, will they not detest the dead? Will they not pursue them with hatred? Will they not endure their presence only with great distress?

<margin>15.</margin> There is no doubt that the Devils were tortured by the presence of Christ. Their own confession is available. *“Have you come,”* some of them asked, *“to torture us before the time?”* <note>Matthew 8:29</note>. But why do they complain of torture? Because, clearly, they feared they would be driven from their seats <note>original: "sedibus suis," referring to the bodies or locations they occupied</note>. How much more must the Lord have tortured those already cast out, when the mere fear that they were *to be* cast out caused such torment? Furthermore, many of the Saints have cast Demons out of their places and dwellings. Therefore, it is impossible for the Saints not to be heavy and troublesome to them.

<margin>16.</margin> From this it is clear that it is foolishly said that *“Demons only pretend to flee”* and are not forced to flight by any power. If the Relics of the Saints cause torture; if they are troublesome and hated: how can the Spirits merely pretend to flee in their presence? How are they not compelled to flee? Do we not free ourselves as quickly as possible from those who are known to be troublesome to us? Is it not with the greatest difficulty that we are kept near them?

<margin>17.</margin> But let us move to another point. Let us show that it cannot be said that *“Demons, by their flight, invite and entice mortals to the worship of Relics.”* This is certain from the fact that the veneration of Relics belongs to that category of things which are good in themselves: and it is the nature of Demons to invite no one to what is good. For what is doubtful here? What is not certain?

### PART THREE

Since Demons flee, albeit unwillingly, and cannot endure *Relics*, let us inquire into the cause. What, then, is that cause? Is it *God*, who compels them to flee from the presence of *Relics*? Is it the *Saints*, whose *Relics* are held, who turn them to flight? Or is that power inherent in the *Relics* themselves, so that they drive wicked Spirits away from places and people? Is it the humans who, as with other things, proscribe them by applying *Relics*? Or, finally, is it none of these, but rather the *Demons* themselves, who although they suffer no physical force from the *Relics*, nevertheless cannot endure them out of hatred?

<margin>29.</margin>
*Here we suggest five modes by which it can be understood how a Spirit is driven away by Relics: we must investigate which one, or which ones, we approve of before we conclude this Chapter.*

<margin>30.</margin>
***That God can command exile or flight for Demons at the presence of the Relics of the Saints*** **is beyond controversy. What is God not able to do, whose name is almighty?** Exodus 15 <note>The author likely refers to the "Song of Moses" regarding God's power over enemies</note>. Likewise, there is no doubt that He has frequently commanded it when the Wicked Spirits proved to be difficult; and He willed by this means to illustrate the glory of His Saints and make it known to the world. Nevertheless, it is not to be believed that Demons take flight for this reason alone, nor always because of this. God can choose not to command the departure and flight of Demons, and yet it is certain that they are still compelled to flee.

<margin>31.</margin>
*It should not properly be said that the Saints, whose relics are kept, drive away Demons*, because just as they do not perform miracles by their own power, they do not turn Demons to flight by themselves. Great was their power over Demons as long as they lived their common life with us on earth; but now that they are dead and reigning with Christ in heaven, they can do nothing against Demons by their own power. If they can do anything, they do it through prayer; just as they obtain other things, they obtain the flight of Demons <note>This reflects the Catholic doctrine of intercession: saints pray to God to act, rather than acting as independent sources of divine power</note>.

<margin>32.</margin>
*Relics do not possess an inherent power that acts upon Demons to drive them from their seats.* If such a power exists, what kind is it, I ask? Spiritual or corporeal? A spiritual power cannot reside in a corporeal <note>physical</note> object, as Relics are. A corporeal power does nothing to drive away Spirits, which is what Demons are <note>The author argues that physical objects cannot naturally affect non-physical spirits; any effect must therefore be supernatural</note>.

<margin>33.</margin>
Are there then humans who, just as they do with other things, *proscribe Demons by applying Relics?* Certainly, since the discourse <note>original: *oratio*; here referring to the words or teachings</note> of Christ clearly proves that this power would be in the hands of men. Mark, the last chapter, etc. <note>Referencing Mark 16:17: "And these signs will accompany those who believe: In my name they will drive out demons..."</note> Therefore, just as those people turn Demons to flight by the use of the name of Jesus, so they do by the use of *Relics* and the use of other things.

<margin>35.</margin>
Therefore, Relics act to put Demons to flight in two ways: first, **in themselves**; second, **from the use** of those applying them against the Demons. In the first mode, the reason why they flee is simple; in the second, it is twofold or bipartite. In the former, they can be said to flee **in themselves** because of the extreme hatred with which they burn toward Relics; in the latter, they are furthermore compelled by the authority of those performing the exorcisms. In that first case, Relics move the Demons to take flight like certain objects [of revulsion]; in the second, they are like certain instrumental causes which the Exorcists—to whom power over these Spirits has been divinely granted—employ.

### PART THREE

<margin>15.</margin>
If the **Cross** had demonstrated its powers only in the flight of Demons, perhaps the power of the **Cross** could be suspect. But now so many, so varied, and so great are the things performed through the **Cross**, that even from these its power in the ejection of Demons must be entirely affirmed.

<margin>16.</margin>
But let us recognize the power of the **Cross** against Demons from the **Cross** itself. The **Cross** is a sign of things most hated by Demons. Therefore, do the Wicked Spirits rejoice in the signs of those things which they hold as hateful and detestable? Are they affected by them? Are they refreshed? Demons are tormented both by the things themselves and by the signs of those things.

<margin>17.</margin>

But how highly does the **Lord** prize the **Cross**? On that highest and supreme day; in His greatest triumph; when He is to come *with great power and majesty*, He wills the **Cross** to be the chief and most illustrious banner. <note>original: "cum potestate magna & maiestate"</note> **Matthew 24.** Can the Devils, therefore, not help but detest the **Cross**?

<margin>18.</margin>
<margin>ss</margin>

But how much does the **Cross** promote it? The **Cross**, in which the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul.</note> judges that Christians ought to glory? **Galatians 6.**

<margin>19.</margin>
I pass over the fact that mortals take from the **Cross** the occasion for many good things, which they themselves do and which Demons detest; and that they take the occasion for fleeing many evils, which they themselves flee and which Demons desire. Is it therefore by this very thing, by which the Demons lure their own flight toward the **Cross**, that they persuade toward good? Do they dissuade from evil?

<margin>20.</margin>
Finally, let us inspect the **Cross** in itself and investigate what might be superstitious within it. There are two things in it: a certain movement of the hands made in the air, and the expectation of the flight of Demons. Which of these is superstitious? The former, or the latter? The former is a natural thing; the other is an office of piety or charity.

<margin>5.</margin>
<margin>21.</margin>
Perhaps neither this nor that is condemned; but rather that the flight of Demons is expected from such a movement of the hand. Why this? Is it because a spiritual and, as it were, divine effect is hoped for from a bodily thing, which has no affinity with it? Yet we observe something similar in the use of the Sacraments; to call these back to superstition, however, would be the height of madness.

<margin>22.</margin>
Perhaps it will be said that the Sacraments have a divine institution <note>That is, they were specifically commanded by God in the Bible.</note>. But what if we say the **Cross** relies on that same foundation? How will such a claim be refuted? If the Scriptures are demanded as proof; the same will be demanded for the sacraments. Since Scriptural proof is found wanting for certain aspects of the sacraments, either their authority will be diminished, or the **Cross** should not be rejected simply because it does not have explicit testimony in the Scriptures.

<margin>23.</margin>
Furthermore, it is not strictly necessary that everything used to produce spiritual effects—even physical things—must have a specific divine institution in the Bible. Some things may have been approved and practiced by the Apostles and their immediate successors; some were received by the primitive Church. For this reason alone, they should not be condemned, but approved; not despised, but held in honor. What if the **Cross** is exactly this kind of tradition?

<margin>24.</margin>
We shall demonstrate in the following points that this is precisely the case; and we shall do so briefly, as our discourse hurries toward its conclusion.

<margin>25.</margin>
First, we have on our side the most ancient writer Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD).</note>, who, in his book *On the Soldier’s Crown*, lists several **Apostolic Traditions**:
> *At every forward step and movement,* he says, *at every coming in and going out, when we put on our clothes and shoes, at the baths, at the table, when the lamps are lit, in our bedrooms, on our seats, in whatever conversation occupies us, we wear away our foreheads with the sign of the **Cross**.* <note>original: "frontem Crucis signaculo terimus"</note>

<margin>26.</margin>
Second, we are served by the Rule of the most blessed Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note>, who, in the 24th chapter of his 4th book *Against the Donatists*, judges that:
> *Whatever is observed by the universal Church and has been kept in all times past is rightly considered to have Apostolic tradition and institution, even if it is the kind of thing that the Church itself could have established.*
And what of it? Has the use of the **Cross** not been present in the universal Church of Christ throughout all past ages?

<margin>27.</margin>
Third, the Rule used by Irenaeus <note>A 2nd-century bishop known for defending orthodoxy.</note> and Tertullian is valid here. Irenaeus in his 3rd book, chapter 3, and Tertullian in his book *On the Prescription of Heretics*, teach that:
> *Whatever is held as such in those Churches where there is a complete and continued succession from the Apostles, descends from Apostolic Tradition.*
Is that succession not present in our Churches? Is the use of the **Cross** not held by us to be an Apostolic Tradition?

<margin>28.</margin>
To these, we add a fourth argument for our cause: by the common consensus of the Doctors of the Church, the use of the **Cross** is held to be an Apostolic Tradition. Can this consensus err or deceive? If it can, would it not be necessary for the entire Church to err—since the Church cannot help but follow its own Teachers and Masters?

<margin>29.</margin>
Let it be established, therefore, that the **Cross** is effective for putting to flight and banishing Demons. But *which* **Cross**? And in what manner? Let us define this, and bring this chapter to an end.

### PART THREE.

<margin>30.</margin>
First, from what has been said so far, it is clearly understood that we mean that **Cross** which we form with our hand in the air; that which we have called **Transient**. There is, however, another kind, which is established in the category of images, and is called **Permanent** or **Constant**. This is either painted on a flat surface or fashioned from some solid material. While it may not be possible to prove with as many historical examples that this kind is effective for driving away demons, it is nonetheless just as certain by logic that it drives them away as does the one formed by the hand.

<margin>31.</margin>
For since demons detest the Cross, why would they not detest this **Constant** one, which both bears the name of the **Cross** and possesses no less power than that **Transient** one formed in the air?

<margin>32.</margin>
Furthermore, might this not serve even more effectively against demons? For since demons take flight at the sight of the Cross, that Cross which persists serves better here than the one which vanishes almost as soon as it is made by the hand. For this reason, while those driven away by the hand-sign might soon return, they seem to be driven away by the physical Cross in such a way that their return is entirely forbidden.

<margin>33.</margin>
Our ancestors seem to have observed this; for in ancient times, once the profane shrines of idols—which were the dwellings of demons—were destroyed, they immediately erected the banner of the **Cross**. Those who emulate our ancestors today in the Indies <note>original: "Indijs"; here referring to the 16th-century missionary efforts in the Americas and East Asia.</note> do the same. For by erecting the **Cross** of Christ, they did not only intend to bring to mind the torments and passion He endured, or to signify that those places where the Cross was erected now serve Christ; they also intended to block every path of access for the demons themselves by using this sign.

<margin>34.</margin>
Perhaps this is also the origin of the Catholic custom of keeping images of the **Cross** of Christ and the Crucified in their homes. Since they desired their homes to be free from demonic infestation, and they knew that images of the **Cross** and the Crucified were hateful to those spirits, they believed their homes were forbidden to demons by the very fact that they were furnished and adorned with images of the **Cross** and the Crucified.

<margin>35.</margin>
It is to be wished that the same piety our ancestors showed in this matter would flourish in our own times. Instead, with the images and symbols of Christ and the Saints now outlawed from many houses, while everything shines with statues of Venus and Priapus <note>Greco-Roman deities associated with erotic love and fertility, here used as symbols of paganism and immorality.</note> and other filthy and profane things, do we not open a wide entrance for demons into our homes and dwellings?

<margin>36.</margin>
The example of a young girl shows this opening of a path; for when she had immodestly gazed upon an image of Venus in the baths and had positioned her body to mimic it, she was immediately possessed by a demon, as recorded by that most serious author Prosper of Aquitaine <note>A 5th-century Christian writer and disciple of St. Augustine.</note> in the sixth book of *On the Promises*.

## ON INFESTED PLACES
<meta>catchword: as here</meta>

<margin>37.</margin>
Just as it is not fitting to hear licentious talk within a family, so too it is not appropriate to keep shameful pictures. A silent picture is a talkative thing, and it gradually creeps into the souls of men. The tongue speaks to the ears, but a picture speaks to the eyes; and a picture is much more talkative than speech, for:
> Things sent through the ears stir the mind more slowly 
> than those which are placed before the faithful eyes, 
> and which the spectator delivers to himself. 
<note>original: "Segnius irritant animos demissa per aures, / Quàm quæ sunt oculis subiecta fidelibus; & quæ / Ipse sibi tradit Spectator." These famous lines are from Horace’s *Ars Poetica*, reflecting the idea that visual evidence is more persuasive than hearsay.</note>
Aristotle even believes that lewd pictures and statues lead to the corruption of morals; for this reason, he wishes it to be provided by the Magistrate through public laws that no images should exist in the city that might remind one of baseness.

<margin>38.</margin>
For this reason, Canon 100 of the Sixth Council in Trullo <note>Also known as the Quinisext Council (692 AD), which dealt with matters of discipline and iconography.</note> rightly commands: *Let your eyes look straight ahead,* and *keep your heart with all vigilance,* as Wisdom dictates. For the senses of the body easily pour their contents into the soul. Therefore, we command that pictures which dazzle the eyes, corrupt the mind, and incite the fires of shameful pleasures shall in no way be printed henceforth. If anyone attempts to do this, let him be deposed. Clement of Alexandria <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who often wrote about the intersection of Greek culture and Christian morality.</note> also spoke well when he rebuked the Pagans for looking at a naked Venus depicted in paintings while lying in their bedrooms: they also have little Pan-figures, nude girls, and drunken Satyrs, etc. Finally, he concludes: *We announce to you that not only the use, but even the sight and the hearing—indeed the very memory of these things—must be laid aside.*

<margin>39.</margin>
The Greeks understood these things: William Durand, the Bishop of Mende <note>original: "VVilhelmus Durantus, Mimarensis Episcopus." Durand (c. 1230–1296) was a prominent medieval liturgist and author of the *Rationale Divinorum Officiorum*, a manual on the meaning of church rituals.</note>, writes of them in Book 1, Chapter 3 of the *Rationale of the Divine Offices* that they paint images only from the navel upward, and not below, so that every occasion for foolish thought might be removed.

<margin>40.</margin>
But how does the Cross put demons to flight? We answer briefly: the **Transient** Cross <note>The sign of the cross made in the air with the hand.</note> puts them to flight in one way, and the **Permanent** Cross <note>A physical crucifix or painted image.</note> in another. The former acts as both the object and the efficient cause; the latter acts as the object only. This is stated briefly, but obscurely. It must therefore be explained.

<margin>41.</margin>
There is no inherent power within a constant and **Permanent Cross** that acts upon present demons in the same way that heat is inherent in fire, by which it warms the surrounding air. It is said to put them to flight by this very fact: that the demons cannot bear it; they detest it and pursue it with hatred.

<margin>42.</margin>
The same hatred causes them to flee the **Transient Cross**. For it is also the Cross itself. Nevertheless, a greater force is brought against them here: for to the hatred by which the spirits flee the Cross of their own accord, there is added a command—in the virtue and with the power of the Cross—by those who command their departure and compel them to withdraw.

## CHAPTER LXIX.

### *On Consecrated Things: in which it is taught that Catholics may use these without any crime of superstition to purge places of demonic infestation and trouble; it is likewise taught which things hold the primary place here, and how they achieve this is revealed.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Enough has been said regarding Consecrated Things <term>Consecrated Things: Objects such as water, salt, or oil that have been ritually blessed by a priest for spiritual use.</term> in that previous discussion concerning the possessed. In our present business, all these things serve us, some directly and others indirectly. They serve indirectly when it is demonstrated that those objects were effective in driving away diseases, breaking chains, driving off locusts, calming the waves of a swelling sea, and other similar feats. They serve directly, however, when they show that the same power has been applied against demons.

<margin>2.</margin>
And indeed, those things already said regarding the casting out of demons from human bodies perform this task excellently; but especially the examples in which we taught that demons were driven from specific places and turned to flight. I speak of the examples of Theodore, the Archimandrite <note>Archimandrite: A title for a superior abbot in the Eastern Church; this likely refers to St. Theodore of Sykeon (d. 613 AD).</note> of the Sykeons, who by the sprinkling of holy water freed a house from the infestation of demons; and of the priests who, from the territory of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntinensi agro." Mainz was a significant ecclesiastical center in Germany.</note>, put to flight a demon that had already caused great distress for three years, using that same lustral water <note>original: "lustrali aqua." Water used for ceremonial purification, synonymous with Holy Water.</note>.

<margin>3.</margin>
These examples could be sufficient for the present argument. However, because certain matters here also present difficulties, we believe they should not be passed over but rather discussed. Among these, the first is: whether the demons merely feign flight in these instances, or whether they are truly compelled by the Consecrated Things to depart against their will. The second is: which Consecrated Things are most effective for banishing demons from specific locations. The third is: how these objects turn the spirits to flight—whether they all act in one and the same way, and whether it is the same way as the Cross and Relics, which were discussed in the preceding chapters.

<margin>4.</margin>
Regarding the first point, we establish this: *Demons do not here feign flight to invite superstition; rather, by sacred things, they are driven away against their will, and [turned] to flight*...

turned to flight. We teach this by two reasons. The first is taken from those things accomplished through the use of *consecrated objects*; the second from the manner in which things are consecrated.

<margin>5.</margin> *We formulate the first reason thus.* It is no less likely that demons are truly banished from places and turned to flight by *consecrated objects*—and not merely according to the demons' own will—than it is that certain remarkable things exceeding the powers of nature have been accomplished by those same objects, and not by the demons' will. But many other remarkable things have been accomplished by *consecrated objects* which could not have occurred by the will of demons. Therefore, demons do not flee sacred things of their own will, but are turned to flight against their will.

<margin>6.</margin> We establish three points here as certain, and from these, we infer a fourth as our conclusion. We posit that great things are accomplished through the *use of consecrated objects*. We posit that these are accomplished neither by the work of demons nor according to their will. We posit that there is no other explanation for the flight of demons than for the works accomplished by the use of *consecrated objects*. From all this, we conclude that force is applied to demons by *consecrated objects* while they flee and cease their infestation of places. We shall explain each point.

<margin>7.</margin> *The first point is proved by almost countless examples, some of which we have cited elsewhere:* such as how the most holy Hilarion <note>Saint Hilarion (c. 291–371 AD) was a famous desert ascetic known for his power over evil spirits.</note> restored health to many of the sick with *consecrated oil*, as Saint Jerome <note>original: 'B. Hieronymus'</note> records in his *Life*; how Saint Monegundis <note>A 6th-century Frankish hermitess known for her miraculous healings.</note> performed the same with *consecrated salt*, as witnessed by Gregory of Tours in her *Life*; how a certain Aphrates, whose life and deeds Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus was a 5th-century bishop and historian.</note> describes, drove away a multitude of innumerable locusts with *holy water* <note>original: 'lustrali aqua'</note>; how Saint Germanus broke the swelling waves of the sea with the same, as the Venerable Bede testifies in Book 1, Chapter 17 of his *History of the English People*; how Evernoldus, Bishop of Ratzeburg <note>original: 'Rateburgensis'</note>, dissolved the chains by which certain men were held bound, as Krantz <note>Albert Krantz (d. 1517) was a historian who wrote 'Vandalia', a history of the northern Germanic tribes.</note> writes in Book 5 of *Vandalia*; and how the blessed Chrysostom <note>Saint John Chrysostom, the 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> restored a man who was all but dead to his former health, according to Metaphrastes <note>Symeon the Metaphrast, a 10th-century Byzantine author who compiled the lives of the saints.</note> on November 13th, etc.

<margin>8.</margin> *But who would say that these things were done according to the will of demons or by their work?* The nature of miracles is such that they cannot be performed by the powers of demons in any way. Therefore, either these are not the works of demons, or they are not miracles.

<margin>9.</margin> Could miracles perhaps be performed by the work of demons? They cannot. This is the sense and consensus of all theologians. Such things exceed the powers of nature. Therefore, they cannot be performed by natural power, which is the only power with which demons are equipped.
