->### PART THREE<-

<margin>10.</margin> Perhaps the things we have listed are not miracles? Why wouldn't they be? By the opinion of all antiquity and the judgment of the entire Church, they have been considered miracles. And most of them (if not all) could only have been performed by divine power; therefore, those events, if not every single one, must be regarded as miracles.

<margin>11.</margin> Demons might be able to drive away locusts; they might be able to break the swelling waves of the sea; they might be able to shatter chains. But can they restore sight to the blind? Can they call the dead back to life? Can they suddenly restore the sick to their former health? There is no power on earth that can be compared with theirs; yet their power is not so great that they can do all the things that have been accomplished through the use of *consecrated objects* <note>The author uses the term *Res consecratæ* to refer to "sacramentals"—sacred signs and objects like holy water or blessed salt that resemble the sacraments.</note>.

<margin>12.</margin> Since these things have indeed been accomplished by *consecrated objects*, and similar things occur daily, why is it denied that demons are put to flight by the power of those same *objects*? *Are not all these things in the same category of wonders (which is the third point to be proven)? Or is the banishing of demons a "greater" work than the breaking of chains, the curing of miraculous diseases, or the restoration of the dead to life?*

<margin>13.</margin> The routing of demons is not a greater work; those other miracles are much greater. And whether it is greater or lesser, it is certainly in the same category as the others. Just as those works are not performed by the natural forces of things, neither is the banishing of demons.

<margin>14.</margin> Truly, just as a person must be out of their mind if they see these wonders occurring through the use of *consecrated objects* and yet do not acknowledge the power of those objects; so too can a person be considered out of their mind who, while attributing those other wonders to the power of *consecrated objects*, makes an exception for the banishing of demons alone. Such a person believes that *consecrated objects* have no power in this regard, even though these items are blessed and consecrated with singular devotion specifically so that they may be effective for this very purpose. This concludes the first argument.

<margin>15.</margin> We establish the second argument as follows: No one can or should consider it superstitious if something requested from God is obtained and achieves its intended effect. But it is requested from God that He will these *consecrated objects* to be effective for the routing of demons, and this is subsequently obtained. Therefore, it is not to be considered superstitious to believe that demons are banished by *consecrated objects*.

<margin>16.</margin> Here there is no doubt that God is asked that the things He created for the use of the human race be made effective for the routing of demons. What else does the form of prayer contain by which they are blessed? "Let us pray," says the Priest (in the consecration of salt and water), "that your creature <note>In this context, "creature" refers to the natural elements of salt and water as part of God's creation.</note>, serving your mysteries, may take on the effect of divine grace for the driving away of demons and the dispelling of diseases. And, in the consecration of the *Agnus Dei* <note>The *Agnus Dei* were wax medallions blessed by the Pope, often bearing the image of a lamb, used as protective sacramentals.</note>: That being blessed by You, they may receive power against all diabolical temptations, etc."

He further asserts that since the Church specifically prays for this power during consecration rituals, believing in its efficacy is an act of faith rather than superstition.</summary>

->## CONCERNING INFESTED PLACES<-
<meta>catchword: More</meta>

<margin>17.</margin> Likewise, there is no doubt that the effects we seek from God through prayer for *Sacred Things* generally follow from the *use of those very things*. For instance, if ordinary water that has not been consecrated is applied to the sick, health does not necessarily follow; if it is used against demons, they are not moved at all. However, when that same water—blessed by the prayer of a Priest—is applied to those same sick people, health follows. When it is used against demons, they howl, and letting out great cries, they are put to flight.

<margin>18.</margin> Can it truly be superstitious to believe that these things happen through *consecrated objects*? Or to use *consecrated objects* to produce these effects? Who could even dream of such a thought? Since God has been petitioned to grant *consecrated objects* the power to put demons to flight, and since demons are indeed driven out by those already consecrated, one must believe both that God wills them to have this power and that it is no sin to believe they possess it.

<margin>19.</margin> Nor could any suspicion of superstition occur to Catholics while they *consecrate things* for this purpose. They have learned from the authority of the Holy Scriptures that *sensible things* <note>Physical objects that can be perceived by the senses.</note> can be effective even for spiritual and supernatural results. They knew that in the Old Law, *water cursed by the priests* <note>original: "aquam à sacerdotibus maledictam"; this refers to the "Water of Bitterness" ritual in Numbers 5 used to test for adultery.</note> revealed the crime of adultery in a miraculous way. The Jewish people, instructed by God, observed this (Numbers 5). They knew that in the New Law, a pool was found which, when stirred by an Angel, restored health to the first person who entered it (John 5). They knew that a *root shown by Solomon* <note>A reference to a tradition, also mentioned by the historian Josephus, that King Solomon possessed secret knowledge of herbs and roots used to exorcise demons.</note> was effective in expelling demons from possessed bodies. They knew that the *smoke stirred up from a fish's liver* was effective for the same purpose—something Tobias had learned from an Angel (Tobit 6).

<margin>20.</margin> God promised his disciples that if they *asked for anything in His name*, they would obtain their wish (John 16). Let us suppose no such promise had been made to the disciples, and they had asked the Lord that if they sought anything in Christ's name, they might obtain it. If they afterwards sought something in Christ's name and received it, would they have been superstitious? Would they have been superstitious if they believed prayers made in the name of Christ were effective after they had experienced that effectiveness in the events themselves? Is it not the same with what we believe regarding *consecrated objects*?

<margin>21.</margin> Even more similar is what we read concerning Gideon in Judges 6. While he was busy threshing grain, an Angel appeared to him, promising freedom for the Jewish people under his leadership. To be made more certain of the promise, he asked for a sacrifice to be offered to the Angel. The question is: after he obtained what he desired through prayer, did he sin—either when he believed the victory was to be won, or when he actually achieved the victory? Who would say he had sinned?

### PART THREE

<margin>23</margin> What we add next is even more to the point. There was a pool in Jerusalem <note>original: "Piscina fuit Hierosolymis"; this refers to the Pool of Bethesda described in John 5:2–4.</note> which provided health to the first person entering it, at the time the Angel chose to visit it. Let us suppose that the pool obtained this power through the prayers of others (for this is not impossible); we now ask: would those who either believed they would obtain health through this "baptism" or who entered the waters to obtain health have been guilty of a crime? What sin is there in this? And is there a sin in using <term>Consecrated Things</term> <note>original: "Rebus consecratis"; physical objects like water, oil, or salt blessed by the Church for spiritual use.</note>?

<margin>23.</margin> We add a fourth point, which closely relates to <term>Consecrated Things</term>. Solomon is said to have identified a root which, when moved near the nostrils of those possessed, drove away any Demon. Let us suppose the King obtained this power from God, for that power could not naturally reside in the root itself. What follows from that? Were all those who later used the root, or believed the use of the root was lawful, superstitious? Who would believe that? And are we Catholics superstitious while we use <term>Consecrated Things</term> and judge that they ought to be used?

<margin>24.</margin> It is impossible for every sin committed here by Catholics—whether they *believe* Demons are driven out by <term>Consecrated Things</term> or they *actually* drive out Demons with them—not to reflect back upon God. They themselves are entirely without fault. Any fault that exists here belongs to God. Why so? Because before these were <term>Consecrated Things</term>, they refused to use them, knowing well that such power does not reside in natural objects. But after they were consecrated, and after they petitioned God that these objects might be effective for putting Demons to flight, they used them. What else could they conclude but that their prayer found a place with God? That it pleases God for them to use <term>Consecrated Things</term> against Demons? And that it pleases Him that they hold this opinion about <term>Consecrated Things</term>?

<margin>25.</margin> Perhaps it might be said that it is their prayer itself that has a place with God; and that it is God who, through His own power, commands the departure of Demons in response to the prayers, with the <term>Consecrated Things</term> contributing nothing to the result. But this should not be said. For if they absolutely cannot hold their beliefs about <term>Consecrated Things</term> without sin, and if they absolutely cannot do what they do with <term>Consecrated Things</term> without sin, then it would be necessary for God *not* to satisfy their desire. Why? Because since they asked for those things to be granted to them *through* <term>Consecrated Things</term>, they cannot help but persuade themselves that the result happened through the objects rather than by some other means.

<margin>26.</margin> Perhaps it is said here, as elsewhere, that God sometimes satisfies the desires of the wicked and permits bad things for those seeking bad things. But who has ever called what the universal Church requests a "sin"? When has God ever satisfied the depraved desire of an entire community?

# ON INFESTED PLACES

But even when He <note>God</note> has satisfied the wicked desires of certain people, He has not done so in a way that leads them into sin, confirms them in sin, or promotes them toward sin; yet we must confess here that if, by our own evil prayer, He has satisfied the use of <term>Consecrated Objects</term> <note>original: "Rerum consecratarum"; these are physical items like salt, water, or oil blessed by a priest to set them apart for holy use.</note> in the driving out of Demons, it was to our own misfortune. *So much for the first point. Now, let us see how they act to drive out Demons.*

<margin>27.</margin> *The types of consecrated objects are various, but they seem to be reducible to three primary ones.* Some pertain to divine worship and are consecrated for this purpose; some have a use in the administration of the <term>Sacraments</term> <note>original: "Sacramentorum"; the core rituals of the Church, such as Baptism or the Eucharist, believed to impart grace.</note>; and some serve the needs of humanity outside the administration of the Sacraments.

<margin>28.</margin> These latter ones are of two kinds. Some are consecrated for the safety of humanity and to drive away diseases; others serve as weapons and protections against wicked spirits. These, in turn, either keep the Spirits away so they do not approach and cause trouble, or they drive them out from where they are already causing distress.

<margin>29.</margin> *These are the types of consecrated objects, but which ones work to banish Demons?* I respond: *All of them are hated by Demons, yet some more than others; for this reason, one must fight against Demons with some more than others.*

<margin>30.</margin> *Those which pertain to divine worship are hated.* First, by this very name, because they are *consecrated*. Demons are the enemies of sacred things. Secondly, because the use of these things cannot serve them, though they might have been free to use them before consecration. Thirdly, because divine honor is achieved through them; and they are no less adversaries of this honor than they are of God Himself.

<margin>31.</margin> *Those used in the Sacraments are hated* for the same reasons, though not for those alone. They are also displeasing for this reason: they become certain instruments and <term>remedies</term> <note>original: "pharmaca"; used here metaphorically as spiritual medicine.</note> with which the heavenly Samaritan <note>A reference to Jesus Christ, identifying Him with the figure from the biblical parable who heals the wounded traveler.</note> heals the wounds of mortals and promotes the salvation of souls (which the Demons always desire to hinder).

<margin>32.</margin> *Those of the third kind are hated, which we ask God to make profitable for our safety and for driving away diseases.* Because, besides the fact that they are consecrated and withdrawn from the Demons’ influence, they also very often achieve their intended effects. Since the Demons look upon these effects with grief, they rightly detest and curse the causes from which those effects proceed.

<margin>33.</margin> Finally, the last kind <note>The weapons specifically for driving out demons.</note> cannot help but be hated. For since they are consecrated for this purpose—to be weapons against Demons—can they be pleasing to Demons?

<margin>34.</margin> Indeed, because they are consecrated for this purpose, they are used most especially in the struggle...

...against Demons, we believe they should be used, though not in the same manner as other things. These objects seem to have their own proper use here; the others do not, so that more protection should be placed in these than in the others.

<margin>35.</margin>
And among these, we believe certain ones are to be preferred in the present business: namely, those by which God is asked that the Demons depart from the places where they dwell. Among this kind are <term>Holy Water</term> <note>original: "Aqua benedicta"</note> and the <term>Consecrated Candle</term> <note>original: "Cereus"; specifically referring to the candles blessed on the Feast of the Purification, also known as Candlemas.</note>, which is usually consecrated on the feast of the Purified Virgin Mother. The very formulas by which they are consecrated teach that these serve most effectively in this battle against Wicked Spirits. When the Water is consecrated, God is asked:

> *that He would deign to pour the power of His blessing into this element: so that this creature <note>In this context, "creature" refers to a created thing, like water or salt, being called to serve a holy purpose.</note> serving Your mysteries may receive the effect of divine grace to drive away demons; so that whatever this water sprinkles in the houses or places of the faithful may be free from all uncleanness and delivered from harm. Let no pestilential spirit reside there, nor any corrupting air; let all the snares of the lurking enemy depart; and if there is anything that envies the safety or peace of the inhabitants, let it flee by the sprinkling of this water: so that the health sought through the invocation of His name may be defended from all attacks.*

In the blessing of the Candle, however, it is petitioned:

> *that, through the sanctification of the wax, the Lord may crush the Devil and destroy him from all the dwellings of those who worship God: from the churches, from houses, from corners, from dining rooms, from the bed, and from all places in which those serving God live and rest; whether they sleep, wake, walk, or stand. Nor should that wicked spirit dare to disturb them further, or strike fear into those whom He has made protected by the anointing of His Holy Chrism.* <note>Chrism is a consecrated oil used in baptism and confirmation, symbolizing the seal of the Holy Spirit.</note>

So say the Ritual Books.

<margin>36.</margin>
Hence it is that the use of these things is most frequent among Catholics in those places and times when Demons are usually most troublesome: near those close to death, where storms are stirred up, where <term>Specters</term> <note>original: "Spectra"; appearing here as ghosts or haunting apparitions.</note> infest places, and so on.

<margin>37.</margin>
But let us come to the manner in which *Consecrated Things* are thought to have power against Demons. Here it is first asked: Do they have power in the same way as the Cross and Relics, which were discussed in the preceding chapters? Or in some other way? Secondly: Do they all work among themselves by one and the same logic?

<margin>38.</margin>
To the first, we say that these work *directly* and *by themselves* against Demons; the others do not. This is not the primary use of Relics—to put Demons to flight—nor of the Cross. Relics are the pledges of the Saints, whom God honors. The Cross is a sign of the benefit <note>The salvation of humanity.</note> won for us upon it. But *by their very nature*, Consecrated Things were instituted and consecrated for the purpose of putting Demons to flight.

## CHAPTER LXX.
### *Concerning Exorcisms, and the Consecration and Blessing of places against the infestations and troubles of malignant Spirits.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Regarding Exorcism, which is employed to drive away Demons, two things especially can be examined. First, whether it is truly effective for expelling Demons from their locations. Second, whether the things adopted by Catholics in this rite are superstitious or harmful. Much has been said on both points in that *Disputation on the Possessed*; since all of that can apply here, I shall say nothing further here regarding the nature of Exorcism itself. However, since there is another method besides Exorcism—partly for barring Demons from places and partly for banishing them—which is very close to Exorcism, it would be worthwhile to investigate its powers and defend it from the slanders of our Adversaries <note>The "Adversaries" likely refers to Protestant critics who, during the Reformation, often labeled Catholic sacramentals and rituals as superstitious.</note>.

### Let us pray.

> Almighty and eternal God, who has bestowed upon your Priests, above all others, such grace that whatever is worthily and perfectly performed by them in your name is believed to be performed by you: we implore your immense mercy; that what we are now about to visit, you may visit; and whatever we are about to bless, you may ✠ bless; and upon those things which we are about to do, extend the right hand of your power: and may there be, at the entrance and arrival of our humility, through the merits of your Saints, the flight of Demons: and the entry of the Angel of peace, Amen.

<margin>3.</margin>
There is nothing here to be condemned. There is no doubt that *grace has been bestowed upon Priests above other men.* **St. Chrysostom** <note>original: "B. Chrysostomus"</note> <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD) was an Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the most prolific Church Fathers. His work "On the Priesthood" is a standard text regarding the spiritual authority and terrifying responsibility of the clergy.</note> teaches in his *book on the Priesthood* that *Priests are more to be revered than Princes and Kings. That the royal purple is nothing, the diadem is nothing, the golden garments are nothing: all these are shadows and lighter than spring flowers when compared to the dignity of the Priesthood.*

<margin>4.</margin>
There is no doubt that it can be believed that whatever is worthily and perfectly performed by Priests in the name of God is performed by God. These divine words prove it: *It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.* **Matthew 10.** *He who rejects you, rejects me; he who hears you, hears me.* **Luke 10.** *Saul, why do you persecute me?* **Acts 9.** <note>The author uses this to show that Christ identifies himself so closely with his Church and its ministers that an action toward them is an action toward Him.</note> *Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?* **2 Corinthians 13, etc.**

<margin>5.</margin>
Is it perhaps evil that we ask God to deign to visit and bless what we visit and bless? If He does this, what evil is there if we ask Him to do it? Indeed, the words already mentioned teach that He does so.

<margin>6.</margin>
Is it evil that we ask for the flight of Demons? But He gave the power to drive them away, and taught the manner of driving them away. Therefore, there is either no crime here, or God himself is not without crime <note>This is a rhetorical argument: if the practice of exorcism were "evil" or "superstitious," the blame would fall on God who instituted the authority to perform it.</note>.

<margin>7.</margin>
Is it evil that *we seek the entry of Angels?* But we seek this so that they may resist the attempts of Demons. Therefore, either the flight of Demons must not be sought, or it is permissible to ask that the Angels of peace be with us. If, as it is said in **Psalm 33**, *The Lord sends Angels around those who fear him, and rescues them,* what evil is there if we ask for the help of Angels? If *He has commanded his Angels (**Psalm 90**) concerning us, to guard us in all our ways,* to ask that they guard us in certain places we cannot <meta>The catchword "possu-" indicates the text continues with "possumus" (we can / we are able).</meta>

...can we [not]? Good Angels wage a perpetual war against evil Spirits, as **Origen** <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253 AD) was an early Christian scholar and theologian. He wrote extensively on the spiritual struggle between celestial forces.</note> testifies regarding that saying of Christ, *Do you think that I cannot,* etc. <note>original: "An putas, quia non possum," referring to Matthew 26:53, where Jesus mentions that he could call upon twelve legions of angels.</note> and do we sin when we ask that they might undertake this for our sake? Finally, no one is ignorant of how much power Angels have both here and in other matters. The opinion of **St. Augustine** is well known: *Every visible thing in this world,* he says, *has an Angelic power set over it.* <note>original: "Vnaqueque... res visibilis in hoc mundo habet Angelicam potestatem sibi propositam." From Augustine’s *83 Diverse Questions*, Question 79.</note> And in his eighth book on the *Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 24, he says: *To the angels, who enjoy God's presence and serve Him blessedly, every corporeal creature is subject; every irrational life; every will, whether weak or depraved, so that they may do with or among their subjects what nature and order demand in all things, at the command of Him to whom all things are subject.*

**8.** Perhaps it is displeasing to some that these things are sought through the merits of the saints. Truly, this should not be displeasing. How many and how great were the benefits God bestowed upon the Jewish people because of the merits of the Patriarchs, **Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob**? Are the merits of the Saints of the New Testament not to be compared with these?

**9.** Is it displeasing that we form the **Sign of the Cross** while asking for a divine blessing? But the use of the Cross in all blessings was accepted long ago. *By this sign of the Cross,* says **St. Augustine** in his 119th Sermon *On Time*, *the body of the Lord is consecrated, the font of Baptism is sanctified: Priests and the other clerical ranks are also initiated.* He says the same in Tractate 118 at the end of chapter 10 of John: *Unless the sign of the Cross is applied either to the foreheads of the believers, or to the water itself by which they are reborn; or to the oil with which they are anointed with Chrism, or to the sacrifice by which they are nourished; none of these things is rightly performed.* <note>original: "Signum Crucis... nisi adhibeatur... nihil eorum ritè perficitur." Augustine emphasizes that the Cross is the essential "seal" of all Christian sacraments.</note> But more on the sign of the Cross elsewhere.

**10.** Truly, the Verse which is placed before the Prayer, and by which *The help of God, who made heaven and earth* <note>original: "Adiutorium Dei, qui fecit cælum & terram," a common liturgical opening based on Psalm 124:8.</note> is sought, can in no way be displeasing. It is all the more just as it is certain to us that we can do nothing without God’s help, and that God’s aid will not fail all those who implore it in whatever necessity. What of the fact that this verse perfectly suits what **Cassian** <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435 AD) was a monk and theologian whose "Conferences" (Collationes) shaped Western monasticism.</note> says regarding a similar verse (*O God, come to my assistance* <note>original: "Deus in adiutorium meum intende," the opening of the Divine Office from Psalm 70:1.</note>)? In his 10th Conference, chapter 10, he says: *For every state, it is adapted properly and competently for all attacks. For it contains an invocation of God against dangers, it has the humility of a pious confession, it has the vigilance of perpetual concern and fear, it has the consideration of one's own fragility, the confidence of being heard, and the assurance of a protection that is always present and standing by.* These are the words of Cassian. One may read more in his work regarding the many things that recommend this verse.

**11.** However, the fact that this Verse is divided—the Priest saying the first part and the surrounding people saying the latter part—detracts nothing from its value.

Is there anything here that is superstitious or unworthy of a Christian man? *The power of the Psalms is great. A Psalm, says **Basil** <note>St. Basil the Great (c. 330–379 AD), whose "Homilies on the Psalms" describes the spiritual psychological benefits of psalmody.</note> in his commentary on the Psalms, is the tranquility of souls, the arbiter of peace to be entered; at whose nod overflowing and tumultuous thoughts contract and fall silent. And again: A Psalm is a certain amulet for routing and driving away demons, the conciliator of Angelic protection.*

<margin>13.</margin>
And although they seem to be effective only for that which they request, there is no doubt that they are also effective for the routing of demons: either because they were written at the dictation of the Holy Spirit; whom—and whose prayer—the Wicked Spirits cannot but avoid and detest.

<margin>14.</margin>
But why are these (**Gradual Psalms**) <note>The fifteen "Songs of Ascents" (Psalms 120–134) traditionally associated with the steps of the Temple and spiritual progress.</note> chosen, and not others? I ask, why would others be chosen and not these? No doubt, the Church, moved by great and weighty reasons, chose these above the rest in this business: why it took fifteen; why it divided them into three classes; why it took five in each act. But even if the reasons were lacking to us, this matter could not be justly condemned; because, as **Origen** <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD), an early Christian scholar. The quote emphasizes that liturgical tradition often carries hidden spiritual significance.</note> says in his 5th homily on the Book of Numbers: *In ecclesiastical observations, he says, there are some things of this kind, which it is necessary for everyone to do, yet the reason for them is not clear to everyone.*

*The Psalms are followed by a repeated **Lord have mercy, Christ have mercy, Lord have mercy**. But why do we use this formula of praying? Why is it repeated? Why is it repeated a third time? Why in the Greek idiom? Why in this business? Why before the Lord’s Prayer?*

We use it following the example of the institutions of the Blessed **James** and **Mark**: of whom the former was the most holy Apostle of Christ; the latter, His Evangelist. <note>Refers to the ancient Liturgies of St. James and St. Mark, which are among the oldest known Christian prayer structures.</note> For they are read to have used these same things in their Liturgies. ### PART THREE

<margin>16.</margin>
*Let "Lord have mercy" be said with great affection and contrition.* <note>original: "Kyrie eleyson cum grandi affectu ac compunctione dicatur."</note>
This is the repetition of the same prayer by the same people. This is evidence of great affection and contrition, as the Council suggests. For indeed, it is not done in vain, as taught by the Lord’s prayer in the garden, which was repeated several times; and by the Blind Man, whose persistent and repeated prayer the crowd rebuked as he passed by (Luke 8). <note>The author likely refers to the blind man at Jericho in Luke 18:35–43.</note>

<margin>17.</margin>
*St. Thomas (Part 3, Question 83, Article 4) <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential medieval theologian.</note> believes the threefold repetition pertains to the glory of the Mystery of the Trinity, or to pray against a triple evil: ignorance, guilt, and punishment. Amalarius Fortunatus (Book 4, Chapter 1) <note>Amalarius of Metz (c. 775–850), a prominent writer on liturgy.</note> gives this reason: "While we implore divine mercy," he says, "through 'Lord have mercy,' 'Christ have mercy,' and again 'Lord have mercy,' we celebrate in the Church, in some way, three stages of the Divine Majesty and Trinity. The first is before the assumption of humanity, when the Trinity was invoked without the union of human nature. The second is after the assumption of man, when Christ was seen on earth and believed by his followers to be nothing less than God and the Son of God. The third stage is from that time when he willed to glorify that assumed man more than he was while he was mortal." So says Fortunatus.*

<margin>18.</margin>
*In form, we retain the Greek idiom because we received the prayer from them. And not wrongly, since, as Blessed Augustine says in Letter 178 against Pascentius: just as the Greek language has the term "of one substance" <note>original: "Omoušion" (Homoousion), the Greek theological term defining Christ's relationship to the Father.</note>, which is believed or spoken by the faithful as the one substance of the Trinity entirely; so too is the nature of the one God asked by all Latins and foreigners <note>original: "barbaris."</note> to have mercy, so that in the praises of the one God, not even a foreign tongue itself is alien to the Latins.*

<margin>19.</margin>
But why use it in this place, where we have a war with infesting spirits? Why in almost all other places where divine mercy is implored? The Council of Vaison <note>original: "Valense Concilium," referring to the Second Council of Vaison (529 AD) which expanded the use of the Kyrie in the West.</note> did not wrongly decree in Canon 3 that *Lord have mercy* should be said frequently at Matins, at Mass, and at Vespers. Christians do not act wrongly now when they repeat the same thing in the Canonical Hours; sometimes in the Office for the Dead; sometimes in public and private Litanies; and sometimes before and after taking food. The Exorcist <term>Exorcist: a cleric authorized to perform rites to expel evil spirits.</term> does not act wrongly when he is about to expel troublesome spirits from places, saying: *Lord have mercy, Christ have mercy, Lord have mercy.* Just as its power is no small thing elsewhere, so its power is expected to be no small thing in this place.
And its power, among other things, is excellently shown by two examples. It is well known that during the reign of Theodosius the Younger <note>Eastern Roman Emperor, 408–450 AD.</note>, while Patriarch Proclus with the clergy and the greatest part of the city's multitude were supplicating, a boy was lifted up into the air. While the people were stunned and crying out *Lord have mercy* for a long time, the boy was let down again and said he had been commanded that the clause "Who was crucified for us" should not be added to the Thrice-Holy hymn. <note>The "Thrice-Holy" or Trisagion is a standard hymn in Eastern and Western liturgies. This anecdote refers to a miraculous earthquake in Constantinople where the Kyrie and Trisagion were used to seek divine protection.</note>

<summary>This page justifies the use and repetition of the "Kyrie eleyson" (Lord have mercy) within the rite of exorcism for places, citing authorities like St. Thomas Aquinas and St. Augustine. It emphasizes the prayer's power against spiritual "infestation" and its history as a universal plea for divine mercy.</summary>

### ON INFESTED PLACES

...so say Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine historian and theologian.</note>, and the Abbot of Ursperg <note>Burchard of Ursberg (d. 1231), a German chronicler who wrote a history of the world.</note> in his account of Theodosius. Paul the Deacon <note>An 8th-century monk and historian best known for his history of the Lombards.</note> says the same in Book 14 of his *History*.

The same Paul, in Book 16, is the authority for the story that during the reign of Emperor Justinian, when Antioch was shaken by an earthquake, the citizens who remained performed Litanies barefoot, crying out "Lord have mercy" <note>original: *Kyrie eleyson*</note>. Then, a man who worshipped God had a vision of someone who told him that all the remaining people must be informed to write above their thresholds: "Christ be with us, stand." <note>original: *Christus nobiscum, state* — a command for the earthquake or the evil causing it to stop.</note> Once this was done, the wrath of God ceased. So writes the Deacon.

<margin>20.</margin>
It is most fitting that the Lord’s Prayer <note>The "Our Father" or *Pater Noster*.</note> is placed before an Exorcism (as it almost always is in other rites). For in the Lord’s Prayer, the sum of all things to be sought from God is contained, and the humble petition of the lowly has always pleased God. Moreover, the "Lord have mercy" <note>original: *Kyrie eleyson*</note> is a confession of a humble heart. Therefore, by that very act, we bind God's heart to us and piously look forward to the things we hope for the more often we repeat this phrase. For this reason, we use "Lord have mercy" with the utmost justice.

<margin>21.</margin>
Perhaps someone might laugh at the fact that the Lord’s Prayer is recited—asking "Thy will be done," "Thy kingdom come," "give us our daily bread," and so on—when our entire thought is focused on casting out the demon. But the Lord willed that when we are about to pray, we should say the Lord’s Prayer: "When you pray," He says, "say 'Our Father'." Furthermore, it is not only these things that are sought in the Lord’s Prayer; we also ask that we be delivered from evil and that we not be led into temptation.

Next, even if the only goal is the banishment of demons <note>original: *Daemonum proscriptio*</note>, the entire Lord’s Prayer is still rightly recited. First, because the reverence we show toward God makes us wish for nothing in His prayer to be changed, omitted, or added. Then, because all parts of the prayer also contribute in some way to the driving away of spirits. God’s name is "hallowed" better when there are fewer enemies <note>referring to demons</note> to hinder us from doing good. "God’s kingdom comes" more easily if the demons have no kingdom among us. We perform "God’s will" more readily if we are troubled by no snares of God’s enemies. Under the name of "daily bread," is not every good thing contained? And is it not a good thing to be immune from the harassment of demons? The remaining points are clear in themselves.

Most justly, indeed—just as in other needs—so in this one, we say the Lord’s Prayer because we believe it has the greatest power with God. "The Father recognizes the words of the Son," says Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> in Homily 14 on Matthew. And Saint Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430), a pivotal Western theologian.</note> says in Book 50, Homily 42: "We have seven ways to win our case, since such a Legal Expert <note>original: *Iurisperitus* — referring to Christ as the divine lawyer/advocate</note> dictated our prayers to us, He who sits at the right hand of the Father."

<summary>This page justifies the use of the Lord's Prayer and the Kyrie Eleyson during exorcisms, citing historical miracles in Antioch and the theological arguments of Church Fathers like Chrysostom and Augustine. It emphasizes that the Pater Noster is the most powerful prayer because it was authored by Christ Himself.</summary>

### PART THREE

<margin>22.</margin>
Does the *Number* of repetitions displease you: because the prayer is repeated a third time? Yet, in accordance with the division of the Psalms into *three* classes, the Lord’s Prayer <note>The "Our Father" or *Pater Noster*.</note> is said three times. Furthermore, if a prayer said once is good, why is it bad when repeated? Did Christ not turn to prayer three times in the garden? What if the honor of the most Holy Trinity is proposed here?

Moreover, Chrysostom, Euthymius, and Theophylact <note>Three major historical commentators on the Gospels; Chrysostom (4th c.), Euthymius Zigabenus (12th c.), and Theophylact of Ohrid (11th c.).</note>, in their commentaries on the 26th chapter of Matthew, teach that this number is accustomed to declare the truth, perfection, and constancy of a matter. Maldonatus <note>Juan de Maldonado (1533–1583), a highly influential Spanish Jesuit exegete.</note> proves this to be true through the following examples from Holy Scripture in his commentary on Matthew 26. *That vessel,* he says, *full of every kind of animal, which Peter saw, was lowered from heaven three times. Acts 10. St. Paul says he asked the Lord three times to take the spirit of Satan from him, 2 Corinthians 14 <note>The text likely refers to 2 Corinthians 12:8; the citation "14" may be a printer's error or refers to a specific commentary division.</note>. Peter denied Christ three times: Matthew 26. Christ questioned Peter three times: "Do you love me more than these?" John 20 <note>This event occurs in John 21.</note>.*

<margin>23.</margin>
Next, a threefold petition is added following the division of the Psalms. In the first, three things are asked of God: That He might graciously enter the house; that He might establish a perpetual dwelling in the hearts of the faithful; and that He might allow no wickedness of spirits to dominate the house. All these are worthy of God and useful to us in a beautiful order. Worthy of God: *because His delights are to be with the sons of men. Proverbs 8. To those who keep His words, He promised that He and the Father would make their dwelling with them. John 14.* And for this reason, He conquered the enemy, so that the enemy might not rule over us according to his lust. How truly useful all these things are to us! And in such a beautiful order? He cannot make a dwelling within us unless He has first entered into us. And once He has entered and made His habitation, can the wickedness of evil spirits rule over us?

<margin>24.</margin>
In the second petition, almost the same things are asked: but additionally, that in the places which are blessed, a sacrifice may be made to Him, and a devout liberty may exist. This "liberty" ought to call the mind back to God, from whom the place obtained it; hence it is called "devout." It is most worthy that service be exhibited even in secular places, since God's benefits toward the human race exist everywhere. He understood this who said: *In every place of His dominion, bless the Lord, O my soul. Psalm 102 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 103:22.</note>.*

<margin>25.</margin>
The third prayer encompasses almost the same things. It is not wrong for the same things to be asked more often: because what is sought seriously must be sought effectively and by many. To this, it adds a request to God that the blessing of the house remain inviolable, and that the community might merit the good things it asks for. In the former, the exercise of good works is sought; in the latter, perseverance. Because both are good, to ask for both is not evil, but good.

<margin>26.</margin>
There is one thing used in this part that displeases: *Holy Water* <note>original: *Aqua lustralis*, water used for ceremonial purification.</note>. All these things which we have commended thus far, the Adversaries <note>Likely referring to Protestant reformers who rejected many Catholic sacramentals like holy water.</note> corrupt and deprave in such a way—

*This Gospel reading, among others, serves two purposes here. First, by this, Christians are reassured that their prayers—which they direct to God for the protection <note>original: *immunitate*; refers to spiritual safety or exemption from demonic influence.</note> of the house or place—are not improper. Second, it is effective for the driving away of demons. We shall teach both.*

That all these things can be done, and are done well,*

### PART THREE

The Gospel passage concerning Zacchaeus teaches: namely, that by Christ’s entry into the house of Zacchaeus, He signified that He must remain there; that He brought salvation by His presence; that Zacchaeus was transformed into a different man; and furthermore, that the piety of Zacchaeus was effective in these and similar matters.

<margin>30.</margin>
But *for the driving out of Demons, it is effective for three reasons.* First, because by the reading itself, acts of certain virtues are stirred in the souls of the listeners, of which the Demons are the sworn enemies and adversaries. Second, because it inflames the devotion and piety of those praying when they understand, through Christ's arrival in the house of Zacchaeus, that not only are Demons expelled, but also that wonderful transformations of souls occur, to the great benefit of mortals. Third, because what is said in the Gospel are partly the words of the Son of God and partly the oracles of the Holy Spirit. Can the Demons listen with a calm mind to the words of Him who, while living a common life with us, cast them out by His word? Who came into the world *to destroy the works of the Demons?* <note>original: *vt opera Dæmonum diſſoluat*; a reference to 1 John 3:8.</note> At whose sight they once testified with great cries that they were being tormented?

<margin>31.</margin>
That the words of the Gospel are effective for the ejection of Demons is also suggested by the fact that not only the sacred words, but even the physical volumes and papers have performed miracles. Gregory of Tours <note>A 6th-century bishop and historian famous for his history of the Franks and lives of the saints.</note> relates in *The Life of the Fathers*, chapter 6, that when the city of Auvergne was burning in a conflagration, Saint Gallus <note>A 6th-century Bishop of Clermont known for his holiness.</note> entered the Church and prayed most longly to God before the holy altar; rising, he took up the volume of the Gospels, and having opened it, he placed himself in the path of the fire, and suddenly the fire was extinguished, so that not even embers remained.

So too Saint Martianus, when a creeping flame was already approaching the Church of Saint Anastasia, took the holy Gospel in his hands and climbed through the tiles onto the roof; by his prayers and tears, he kept the church unharmed by the fire. So says Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos, a 14th-century Byzantine historian.</note> in Book 5, chapter 22. Again, Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century chronicler and theologian.</note> left written in his history of Basil the Macedonian that the people of Rhodes <note>An island in the Mediterranean.</note> embraced the faith of Christ after a book of the Gospels was rescued from a fire unharmed. What need is there for more examples?

<margin>32.</margin>
Hence the Fathers in the Eighth Council of Constantinople, Canon 3, did not speak wrongly when they said:
> *We have decreed that the sacred image of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of all, should be honored with the same respect as the Book of the Holy Gospels. For just as through the eloquence of the syllables contained in the book, all obtain salvation, so through the operation of images in color, both the wise and the unlearned <note>original: *idiotæ*; meaning the simple or uneducated folk.</note> alike enjoy the benefit of what is at hand. For what the word is in syllables, this the writing <note>meaning the painted representation.</note> also proclaims and commends in colors.*

We do not [need to] prove the righteousness of the blessing of incense in this place. # PART THREE.
Ii 3
<meta>catchword: Here</meta>

...holy Angels? But if neither of these is evil, how can that which we ask to be blessed—whether through our intercession or that of the Angels—be considered evil? Is it an evil thing to ask for what is good?

<margin>35.</margin>Not only is the use of incense free from any fault, but it is also effective for the driving out of demons, and indeed for five specific reasons. First, because God has been asked (and would He be asked in vain?) to will that it be effective for this purpose. Second, because incense is among the class of consecrated things, which are inherently hated by the [evil] spirits. Third, because it has been consecrated through the intercession of Saint Michael and the Angels; for this reason, it must be believed that they take account of it and join with it in the expulsion of demons. Fourth, because the smoke which is stirred up from it is raised in a vaporous quality <note>original: "vafetali," likely referring to the aromatic or medicinal properties of the smoke thought to repel spirits</note> that is effective for the routing of demons, as is proven by the prayer with which the thurible <term>thurible: a metal censer used for burning incense</term> is consecrated. That prayer goes as follows:

> *Lord God, who—while a harsh fire devastated the children of Israel as they murmured in the desert because of their rebellious audacity—deigned to hear Aaron as he prayed, taking the thurible from the altar fire and placing incense before You, and to deliver them from that fire: bless, we beseech You, this thurible. Grant that as often as incense is burned within it, You may make the prayer of Your people a pleasing fragrance, resulting in the flight of demons, the repelling of phantasms <note>phantasms: ghostly apparitions or mental delusions caused by spirits</note>, and the departure of unclean thoughts. Through Christ, etc.*

Fifth and finally, because both the wood <note>referring to the aromatic resins or coals</note> and the vessel are things loathed by demons. Incense represents the prayer of the Saints, which rises like incense in the sight of God (Psalm 140) <note>Modern Bibles: Psalm 141</note>. The thurible, moreover, represents the body of Christ. For Saint Augustine, in his 6th Homily on the Apocalypse, beautifully interprets the "golden thurible" as the holy body of Christ. He says that the Lord Himself *was made into a thurible, from which God received the odor of sweetness and was made merciful to the world, because He offered Himself as a fragrant offering.* See also Pope Innocent III, in Book 2, Chapter 16, of *The Mysteries of the Mass*.

<margin>36.</margin>The prayer used after the incense has been blessed is twofold: both are as just as the things requested in them. Unless, perhaps, it is displeasing that such a rite is held in a [private] house and not in a consecrated place. But the ears of God are attentive to the prayers of the suppliant, in whatever place they are poured out.

The conclusion consists of a brief blessing; concerning this, the Ritual Book states: *Afterward, let him bless the house and all who dwell within it, saying:*

> *And may the blessing of God Almighty, the Father, † and the Son, † and the Holy Spirit, † descend upon this house and all who dwell within it, and remain forever. Response: Amen.*

<margin>37.</margin> Nothing here can be condemned. In this, we imitate Christ and the holy Patriarch of the Old Law, Jacob. When Christ was being carried up to heaven, he blessed his disciples with raised hands, as recorded in the last chapter of Mark <note>original: "Marci vltimo"; see Mark 16:19 or Luke 24:50</note>. Jacob, for the sake of giving a blessing, extended his hand; he placed his right hand upon the head of Ephraim and his left upon the head of Manasseh, as seen in Genesis 48.

Add to this that the Lord sometimes commands His people to be blessed under the Sacrament of a threefold invocation. For in Numbers 6, it is held thus:

> Thus shall you bless the children of Israel, and you shall say to them: May the Lord bless you and keep you. May the Lord show His face to you and have mercy on you. May the Lord turn His countenance toward you and give you peace.

And so much for the blessing.

<margin>38.</margin> Theodore the Archimandrite <term>Archimandrite: a title for a superior abbot in the Eastern Christian tradition</term> seems to have used this form, or certainly one similar to it. When he was asked by Theodore, the royal leader, to free a house from troubling spirits, he is said to have entered it and spent the whole night singing psalms and entreating God; he then sprinkled water which he had blessed, and in this way freed it from the harassment of the spirits. See Metaphrastes <note>Symeon Metaphrastes was a famous 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer</note> in the *Life of Theodore*, found in Surius, Volume 2 <note>Laurentius Surius was a 16th-century Carthusian monk who published a massive collection of the lives of the saints</note>.

->**to act against the attacks and troubles of spirits needing**<-

# CHAPTER LXXI.

## *That there is some reasoning and method by which the living can free themselves from the trouble brought upon them by spirits needing purification.*

<margin>1.</margin> Having explained the reasons by which places are freed from the infestation of demons, the next step is to explain the methods by which we ensure that spirits needing purification <note>original: "Spiritus purgandi," referring to souls in Purgatory who manifest in the physical world</note> do not cause trouble. It can be said very briefly that there is but one way: and it is indeed the same way by which we are freed from the persistence of beggars and the poor who ask for alms and charity quite importunately. What is that way? Let the desire of the spirits be satisfied. And what is their desire? That they might be helped out of their misery by our efforts. What efforts? Those that breathe mercy, rather than those that have nothing of piety and benevolence.

<margin>2.</margin> In these few words, I encompass many things; and because they are many things in few words, they must be explained and proven. All of these points pertain either to the condition of the spirits who are troublesome, or to our duty, or to the works by which we assist their poverty.

The author argues that unlike demons, these spirits are like beggars who cause trouble only because they require the spiritual "alms" of the living to be released from their suffering.</summary>

PART THREE. 255

<margin>3.</margin>
*The miserable condition of those spirits is suggested, which requires the help of others and can be relieved. The reason for our duty; that we should assist them; Works are the means by which they are relieved. We will pursue this first point in this chapter, the rest in the following ones.*

Indeed, it is beyond controversy—and does not need to be proven here—that there are certain spirits who are troublesome for this reason alone: to receive some relief from the miseries they endure. But *who can doubt that they can be assisted by the efforts of others?*

<margin>5.</margin>
If they cannot be helped, why are they troublesome in order to be helped? Should they perhaps be accused of recklessness and imprudence? As if they were attempting what is impossible to achieve? But all recklessness and imprudence is far from the spirits who are being purified <note>original: "purgandis Spiritibus"; a reference to the souls in Purgatory</note>. And even if they *could* act recklessly on their own, God—by whose providence it happens that they return to us, take part in our affairs, and are able to trouble us—does not permit them to act recklessly in any way.

<margin>6.</margin>
If no support can be brought to them, is this because of their own condition, which requires that they only wander and trouble the living? Or is it because of the impotence of the living, to whom the faculty of providing support has been denied? Their condition does not require the former; rather, it requires that they pay the penalties they have earned in certain, defined places. Moreover, this should happen not in assumed bodies <note>temporary physical forms taken by spirits to appear to humans</note>—to which those penalties are in no way owed—but in their very selves, which were the cause of their sins. Truly, if that faculty has been divinely granted to the living so that they may be able to protect themselves from the harassment of *unclean* spirits <note>demons</note>, will the faculty by which they might free themselves from the annoyance of *human* spirits be denied?

<margin>7.</margin>
The Church is one single body, of which Christ is the head. Therefore, there will be a union both of the members among themselves and with their head, Christ, because—as the Apostle beautifully says in 1 Corinthians 12—*the members are concerned for one another: and, if one member suffers, all suffer with it.* The righteous dead who trouble us are certain members of this body, bound to us by the ties of faith, hope, and charity. (*For*, as Blessed Augustine says in Book 20 of *The City of God*, Chapter 9, *the souls of the pious dead are not separated from the Church, which is the kingdom of Christ.*) We are therefore able to suffer with them: we can help them: we can relieve their misery.

<margin>8.</margin>
Saint Ephrem the Syrian, when he was already about to die and was requesting the prayers <term>suffragia: intercessory prayers or pious acts performed by the living to benefit the souls of the deceased</term> of the living for himself, beautifully showed that the dead are helped by the prayers of the living through a double metaphor. *You see*, he said, *an example from the specific creatures of God: as in the fruit of the vine. One grape is bitter in the field, and the wine which is placed in jars; when, therefore, the cluster of grapes thrives on the vine,*

[The author continues quoting a comparison of natural sympathy:] ...then he will be warned by his own condition, which is fixed in the house. *The wine (he adds) is understood to be like me.* Even an onion placed in a field, when it begins to turn green in its season, causes the dry onion in the house to sprout. If, therefore, the offspring of nature <note>original: "rerum foetus"; the text uses botanical metaphors to explain the spiritual connection between the living and the dead</note> agree among themselves in this way, how much more are the dead delighted in the memory of your offerings?

<margin>9.</margin> Since the dead can benefit the dead, as *Elisha* and *Abraham* teach by their example—the latter of whom received *Lazarus* into his bosom (*Luke 16*), while the former raised a dead man (*4 Kings 13* <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Kings 13:21, where a body touching Elisha's bones returns to life</note>). Since the *living help the living*, as the *Apostle* implies when he wishes one to bear the burdens of another (*Galatians 6*). Since the dead help the living—as the deceased *Onias* and *Jeremiah* prove while they pray for the people of Israel (*2 Maccabees 15*)—why then should the living not be able to benefit the dead?

<margin>10.</margin> In *Ephesians chapter 5*, the *Apostle* <note>St. Paul</note> wants us to walk in love <term>dilectione|a specific term for Christian charitable love</term>, just as Christ loved us, who gave himself for us. But Christ demonstrated his love in many ways: *while living on earth, he benefited the living.* For besides restoring physical health to many, he also absolved from sins *Mary Magdalene (Luke 7), the paralytic (Matthew 9), Zacchaeus (Luke 19), Peter (Luke 22), and the thief (Luke 23). The same Christ, when dead, benefited the dead* by his descent into the lower regions <note>The "Harrowing of Hell," where Christ is believed to have liberated the souls of the righteous</note>, where he released many from the pains of hell (*Acts 2*), not to mention those he recalled to life and whose graves he opened (*Matthew, last chapter*). *The same Christ, when dead, benefited the living;* indeed, by his death he earned eternal life for us, and now he does not cease to be our advocate and Patron for us before the heavenly Father in heaven. Finally, *while living, he benefited the dead:* as when he recalled to life the girl in the house (*Matthew 9*), the young man on the road (*Luke 7*), and then *Lazarus* in the tomb. Therefore, we the living—following Christ's example as the *Apostle* requires—can (if we ought not) show signs of love not only to the living, but also to the dead, and assist in the needs they suffer.

<margin>11.</margin> *The Spirits are called our friends.* They desire nothing evil for the living; rather, they desire all good things. Therefore, they are so far from wishing to be troublesome in vain, that they would not even think of bringing trouble upon us unless a certain hope of relief was set before them.

<margin>12.</margin> There is no need for more words to confirm this matter. The examples available here themselves create great faith; I mean the examples of those who returned to the living, revealed their desires in words and deeds, and testified with great signs of gratitude that they had been helped by the work of the living. *Gregory the Great*, the most holy Pontiff of the city and the world, reports (*Dialogues, Book 4, Chapter 40*) that the soul of *Paschasius*, which [was] in

Another source, Gregory of Tours, in his book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 5, teaches that a certain holy Virgin named Vitaliana, already deceased, signaled to Saint Martin that she was being purified by the fire of purgatory for a certain minor sin, from which she was rescued by his prayers.

Regarding Saint Severinus, Peter Damian testifies in his *Letter to Desiderius* that after death he appeared to a certain priest of the same church as Severinus; he indicated that because he had not recited the <term>Canonical Hours|the specific cycle of prayers, such as Matins or Vespers, that clergy are required to pray at set times of the day</term> at their proper times, he had endured the punishments of purgatory, and was finally joined to the company of the blessed.

In the *Life of Saint Malachy*, the most holy Bernard writes that the saint's sister was freed from the pains of purgatory by his prayers; the holy man seemed to be warned several times before this through a vision, so that she might be freed by his intervening prayers. Regarding Bernard himself, William the Abbot writes in chapter 10 of the *Life of Bernard* that a certain man—who had already endured those same purgatorial punishments for an entire year—was helped by Bernard's prayers and joined the society of the Saints in heaven. And a certain priest named Arnulph appeared to Saint Rembert, Archbishop of Bremen; he testified that by a forty-day fast, which Rembert had performed for him at his own request, he was released from the pains of purgatory and granted the happiness of the Saints, as recorded in Surius, Volume 1, *Lives of the Saints*. I omit many others who are mentioned in chapters 75, 76, 78, and so on.

# CHAPTER 72.

### *That it is fitting, for many and great reasons, for the living to help the spirits being purified when they ask for aid by stirring up troubles.*

<margin>1.</margin>
We have explained the condition of the spirits being purified and what they seek by their disturbances <note>original: "molestijs"; the author refers to the hauntings or "troubles" spirits cause to get the attention of the living</note>. Now, although the desire to be free from the troubles they cause might drive us to help them just so we can enjoy peace, that alone should not be our motivation. There are many very serious reasons that compel us to help these spirits in whatever ways we can.

<margin>2.</margin>
Some reasons are drawn from the spirits themselves; others from our own position as the living; others from the evils those spirits suffer; others from divine providence; others from the example of our ancestors; others from the demands of honor; and others from the benefits <note>original: "fructibus"; literally 'fruits' or results</note> that are joined with this devoted practice of piety.

<note>original: "DE LOCIS INFESTIS"; in this context, the author refers to locations where spirits manifest to the living to seek spiritual assistance.</note>

<margin>3.</margin>
*The condition of these spirits is such that they are entirely worthy of mercy, and our efforts should help them in every way. For they are not enemies of God, nor of any living person; rather, they love God above all things, and hold nothing more important than His honor. Toward humans, they both love and desire our safety and well-being, promoting it in whatever ways they can. Therefore, those who are worthy of a benefit would be undeservedly deprived of it* <note>that is, if the living refuse to offer prayers or mass for them</note>.

<margin>4.</margin>
*Their need is of the highest degree. For they are often punished most severely, and they are compelled to pay the decreed penalties—down to the very last penny—unless they are relieved from elsewhere. Hence, it is commonly said that they are oppressed by extreme necessity. And rightly so; for a man is poor who has little. He is poor who has nothing. Even more miserable is he who has nothing and can make no profit from anything at all. But most miserable of all is the one who has no assets, can earn nothing more, and besides owes many debts to a creditor of such severity that he allows no delay and no truce, but most harshly enforces this rule: if he has no money, let him pay with his skin.* <note>original: "si non habet in ære; luat in pelle"; a legal maxim meaning that if a debtor cannot pay a fine, they must suffer physical punishment instead.</note> *Yet this is the condition of these spirits who return to us.*

<margin>5.</margin>
What more? Even for this reason they deserve our intercession and help: that while stationed in their punishments, *they are concerned for our salvation and commend it to God in their own prayers.* Are they not worthy of our prayers, who deem us worthy of theirs? I know there are some who would deny this; but whether they do so rightly, I strongly doubt. Why, I ask, does anything hinder them from praying for us? Is it because they do not yet see God? But in ancient times, Onias and Jeremiah prayed for the Jewish people (2 Maccabees, final chapter), though they did not yet see God themselves. Is it because they are of a far inferior condition than the living? But this is no hindrance, because even the lowliest person, without blame and indeed with praise, prays for the highest heads of the Church. Is it because the severity of the torments they suffer so occupies the mind that it takes away any opportunity for thinking about other things? But <term>Epulo|the traditional Latin name for the "Rich Man" in the biblical parable of Dives and Lazarus</term> in hell sustained greater torments, yet he still prayed for his brothers (Luke 16). And the Martyrs, stationed in the greatest torments, were concerned for the salvation of others, just as Blessed Stephen teaches by his own example (Acts 7). The bitterness of the punishments and penalties that the deceased suffer is not such that it either prevents the use of reason or disturbs the pious affection of the will—as is demonstrated by the very prayer they make for themselves.

<margin>6.</margin>
Let us look deep within ourselves; *from our own nature, we will understand what we owe to them.* We are members of that one body, whose head is

### PART THREE
<note>original: "PARS TERTIA"</note>

-> Kk 2 <-

Is it Christ alone? Not at all. Those who reign in heaven with Christ, and those who are being purified somewhere through the punishments of Purgatory because of the failings they committed, are also members of that same body. Therefore, the duty that the members of our own body perform for one another—as we learn from nature’s teaching—we should also provide to those who are members of the same body under Christ the Head. And what is that duty? The Apostle <note>St. Paul, in 1 Corinthians 12:26</note> says that the members suffer with one another; in turn, they relieve the misery of others by whatever means they can. Why, then, should we not help the spirits being purified?

<margin>7.</margin>
The evils which these spirits suffer should also drive us to perform this duty for them. Indeed, those who have partly seen and partly experienced these things declare them to be so great that human speech cannot capture their magnitude.
> I consider that transitory fire <note>referring to the fire of Purgatory</note> to be more intolerable than any present tribulation. <note>original: "Illum transitorium ignem... omni tribulatione præfenti exiſtimo intolerabiliorem."</note>
— Saint Gregory the Great, in his commentary on the Third Penitential Psalm.

And Saint Augustine, on Psalm 37:
> Although they may be saved through fire, yet that fire will be more severe than anything a man can suffer in this life. <note>original: "Quamvis... ſalui fiant per ignem, grauior tamen ille ignis erit, quàm quidquid poteſt homo pati in hac vita."</note>

And Bede <note>the Venerable Bede, an 8th-century English monk</note>, on the same Psalm:
> He considers that no punishments of martyrs or of thieves are to be compared with the punishments of Purgatory.

Saint Anselm <note>11th-century Archbishop of Canterbury</note> on 1 Corinthians 3 and Saint Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux</note> in his sermon on the death of Humbert teach similar things. Therefore, if in this mortal life we naturally feel pity for criminals—who might otherwise be hostile to us—when public justice punishes them severely, or even for a dog or another beast that is treated unworthily, a great reason urges us to feel compassion for those spirits with a deep affection of the soul, and to faithfully grant them the assistance they so earnestly beg from us.

<margin>8.</margin>
To this is added the fact that by this kind of duty, one should believe that the divine will is satisfied. Since spirits return to the living only by a singular plan of divine providence—and they return for this purpose: to obtain the help of the living and to be snatched away from the most heavy punishments they endure—can it not be believed that he who takes pity on them is satisfying the will of God?

<margin>9.</margin>
The devotion of our ancestors reveals itself here through many great arguments and urges us onward. This matter is clearer than the midday light, and it ought to carry all the more weight with us because there are now so few who follow the examples of our ancestors. For even though the Sects <note>a common 16th/17th-century Catholic term for Protestant denominations</note> are quite divided among themselves, they are all found to have conspired together for the ruin of the deceased; none of them provide any protection to the dead, nor do they allow others to provide it peacefully.

<margin>10.</margin>
The duties of the virtues also (in which the essence of honor consists) meet here in great number. But which ones, I ask? Faith—because against the [errors] of our times...

# ON DISTURBED PLACES
<note>original: "DE LOCIS INFESTIS" — This refers to places troubled by spirits or hauntings, which the author links to souls in Purgatory seeking aid.</note>

...against the Heretics <note>The author is likely referring to Protestants who rejected the doctrine of Purgatory.</note>, we may testify to the punishments of Purgatory by these very facts. We testify to the hope which we conceive here of divine mercy, and to our works which we trust will benefit others. We testify to the charity which we bestow through this kind of duty toward our neighbors, especially those most in need. Finally, we testify to any other virtues whose works we undertake for the sake of the deceased.

<margin>11.</margin> But what great fruit comes to us from these things? Beyond that, a remarkable hope of reward can be stirred up. We can fully promise ourselves that whatever turn we take for the dead while we are living, the living will do the same for us when we are dead, according to that saying: *With the same measure you use, it will be measured back to you.* <note>Luke 6:38</note>. Meanwhile, I will pass over the fact that by this deed we also bind those for whom we offer prayers remarkably to us; and we can hope that they will hold us most highly recommended in heaven, we who were the authors of their rescue from punishments while on earth.

<margin>12.</margin> I could bring forward many more opinions of the Holy Fathers for this argument. But one from **St. Augustine** will suffice for all, who speaks thus in the book *On Care for the Dead*, chapter 4: *Supplications for the spirits of the dead are not to be omitted; the Church has undertaken to make these for all who have died in the Christian and Catholic fellowship, even without mentioning each name, under a general commemoration. Thus, for those who lack parents, children, or any other relatives or friends for these services, they are provided by their one common, pious mother [the Church].* So says Augustine.

<margin>13.</margin> Perhaps it is denied that it is possible for one to take upon himself the burden of another, and freely endure the punishments that another has earned. But a Christian man ought not to deny this. Just as in natural things the foot performs its duty not only for itself, but also for the sake of the eyes; nor again, that the eyes see, is that to be referred to their own benefit, but to the common utility of all the limbs; nor finally, that in a well-ordered family each person produces by his own industry, he does not set that aside as a private stash for his own convenience, but brings it into the common use for all; so, in the Church also, the mystical members serve one another in turn, and perform mutual services for one another.

<margin>14.</margin> The most holy **Paul** recognized this perfectly. Hence in Romans 15, he teaches that the good deeds done by converted Jews profited the Gentiles. *If*, he says, *the Gentiles have been made partakers of their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in carnal things.* <note>Romans 15:27</note>. And he himself, as if the common teacher of all the faithful and Doctor of the Gentiles, teaches that his own sufferings benefit others. *I rejoice*, he says in Colossians 1, *in my sufferings for you, and I fill up those things which are lacking in the sufferings of Christ, in my flesh, for his body, which is the Church.* <note>Colossians 1:24</note>. ...exhorts the Ephesians to similar pursuits, and in the Ephesians, all Christians. 
> "Be," he says in chapter 5, "imitators of God, as most dear children, and walk in love just as Christ loved us, and gave himself up for us." <note>Ephesians 5:1–2</note>

He means to say: Just as the head of the mystical body, Jesus Christ, moved by burning charity, gave himself up for his members; so it is necessary that each member of the same body give themselves up for one another.

<margin>15.</margin>
God is more inclined toward showing mercy and pardoning a deserved punishment than toward condemning or punishing. *His mercy is over all his works.* <note>Psalm 145:9; cited as Psalm 144 in the Latin Vulgate</note>. "Your mercy is magnified even unto the heavens," says the same Prophet in Psalm 56, "and your truth" (and justice) "even unto the clouds" (which are below heaven). But it is well established that he has often involved, and daily involves, many people in calamities, not only on account of their own crimes but also because of the crimes of others. Because of the sin of **David**, he wiped out seventy thousand Jews with a plague (2 Samuel 24). Because of the sacrilege of one man, **Achan**, he turned three thousand of the same people into a shameful flight (Joshua 7). Because of the flight of one man, **Jonah**, he tossed the sailors along with the other passengers in a storm for a long time (Jonah 1). Because of the sin of the Pharisees against Christ, he oppressed the entire Jewish nation with innumerable disasters, and so on. If, therefore, God Most Good and Great <note>original: "Deus Opt. Max." (Deus Optimus Maximus)</note> inflicts these and similar evils upon the innocent because of the crimes of another, why should he not pardon the temporary punishment of a just or even an unjust man because of the voluntary <term>satisfaction</term> <note>In this context, "satisfaction" refers to performing a penance or good work to make up for the temporal punishment due to sin.</note> of another?

<margin>16.</margin>
Because of the remarkable piety of **Abraham**, God spared **Lot** and **Abimelech** (Genesis 19 and 20); and he declares himself ready to spare all the people of Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighbors on account of only ten just men (Genesis 18). Because of the remarkable devotion of **David**, he spared **Solomon** (1 Kings 11). Because of the charity of the Apostle **Paul**, two hundred shipwrecked souls were spared (Acts 27). Because of the intercession of **Moses**, the whole of Israel was spared (Exodus 32). Because of the faith of those presenting him, he provided health to both parts of the man <note>This refers to the healing of both the body and the soul of the paralytic in Matthew 9:2.</note> (Matthew 9). Finally, he says himself in Ezekiel 22: *I sought for a man who might build up a wall and stand in the gap against me on behalf of the land, that I should not destroy it.* Since, therefore, these blessings of God are admitted, why is his benevolence denied in the pardoning of temporary punishments which some take upon themselves for others? Why is it denied that the living can take up burdens on themselves for the piously departed and satisfy for them?

<margin>17.</margin>
How much the <term>merits</term> <note>In Catholic theology, merits are good works performed through grace that God promises to reward.</note> of upright and holy men can achieve is beautifully shown by **Blessed Chrysostom** in Homily 2 on Psalm 50. "Holy David," he says, "not only pleased God when he was in the body, but even after his death he is found to have provided solace to the living. For it happened to Hezekiah..."

### ON TROUBLESOME PLACES
<note>original: DE LOCIS INFESTIS. This heading refers to Purgatory or the places where spirits endure purification.</note>

vi
<meta>catchword: be done [fiant],</meta>

...to King **Hezekiah**, the enemy nations surrounded Jerusalem in the times of the Jews. And since Hezekiah was a righteous man, he prayed to God: prostrated in tears, he pleaded, asking for vengeance against his adversaries. The Prophet **Isaiah** came to him and said: he should not think that he was heard because of his own justice. And certainly, **David** had already passed away and had been resting for many years. What, therefore, does He say to him? *I will protect this city for my own sake, and for the sake of David my servant.* <note>Isaiah 37:35</note> David is dead, yet his merits remain active. So says **Chrysostom** <note>John Chrysostom, a 4th-century Church Father known for his eloquent preaching.</note>. From this, the most holy Pope **Leo** [the Great] excellently states in Sermon 3 on the Fast of the Seventh Month: *We trust that through the merits and prayers of the Apostles, the mercy of our God will be granted to us in all things.*

<margin>18.</margin>
Someone might ask then: what is it that is said by the Apostle in Galatians 6? *Each one will bear his own burden.* I ask in turn: what is it that the same Apostle says in the same place—that he *wants one to bear the burdens of another?* <note>Galatians 6:2–5</note> Is the Apostle perhaps contradicting himself? Or is there with him a "Yes and No"? <note>Meaning, is he being inconsistent?</note> God is faithful (I call God to witness, he says in 2 Corinthians 1): *Our word, which is directed to you, is not "Yes and No" in itself.* There are, therefore, those who say the Apostle is speaking of those who depart from this life without repentance; no one else will take up their burden, but they themselves will pay the eternal punishments they have deserved. **Anselm** <note>Anselm of Canterbury, an 11th-century theologian.</note> says on this passage: *Each will be weighed down by the individual conscience of their sins.*

<margin>19.</margin>
But even those who are purified by the pains of <term>Purgatory</term> <note>The state of final purification for those who die in God's friendship but still require cleansing from the effects of sin.</note> bear *their own burden*; for they receive nothing that they did not earn while in the body. For they earned this by persevering in faith and charity until death: that even after death they might be helped by the works of others. Let the same answer be given to that passage in Romans 2: *He will render to each according to his works.* And to that in Galatians 6: *What a man sows, this he shall also reap.*

<margin>20.</margin>
This is the opinion of **St. Augustine** in his book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead*, Chapter 1, where he speaks thus: *Since these things are so (namely, that the dead are helped by others), you indicate that you do not sufficiently see how this opinion is not contrary to what the Apostle says (2 Corinthians 5): "For we must all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil." By this Apostolic sentence, he warns that what can be beneficial after death should be done before death: not then, when one is already to receive what they did before death. Truly, this question is resolved in this way: because a certain kind of life is acquired while one lives in this body, so that these things might help the deceased; and through this, according to what they did through the body, they are helped by those things which were religiously performed for them after they left the body.
