## CHAPTER 73.

->*That the methods used to free infested places from the trouble of demons*<-
->*do not help in removing those troubles*<-
->*brought about by the good spirits of men.*<-

<margin>1.</margin> It has been demonstrated that there are **spirits to be purified** <note>original: *Spiritus purgandi*; these are souls in Purgatory who are undergoing a process of cleansing before entering heaven.</note>; and that they can be helped; and that it is right for them to be aided by the works of the living. It follows that we should teach *how* they are helped. Generally speaking, there seem to be two ways here, just as there are two ways to be freed from the pestering of the poor and beggars (whose condition we have said these spirits resemble). One way is harsh and inhuman; the other is human and worthy of a Christian. The first happens with the poor sometimes by a simple refusal of **alms** <term>alms: charitable donations or acts of mercy given to those in need</term>, sometimes by harsh words, and sometimes even by the infliction or threat of blows. The second is by the distribution of alms, or by showing a heart that sympathizes and desires to help.

<margin>2.</margin> Both of these methods can be used against the troubles caused by these **spirits undergoing purification**. However, to act by the first method is inhuman; Christian duty demands, as we have said, that we act by the second. Who would approve of treating friends harshly? Friends, I say, to whom we can grant what is asked without any loss to ourselves—indeed, even with great benefit.

<margin>3.</margin> Hence it is that the method by which we free ourselves from the trouble caused by these spirits differs from that former method in this first respect: we must deal with these spirits as friends, and not hostily, as one deals with those others <note>The author refers to demons, who are treated as enemies, whereas souls in Purgatory are considered "friends" or "brothers" in the faith.</note>.

# CHAPTER 74.

### Concerning the various ways in which it happens that one is freed from the nuisance of spirits needing purification: and concerning the multiple differences of these methods.

<margin>1.</margin>
The most holy Doctor of the Church, **Augustine**, in his 34th Sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*, mentions *three* ways by which the living are freed from the nuisance of these spirits, just as the spirits themselves are freed from the pains of Purgatory. He says, "There is no doubt that the dead are aided by the prayers of the Holy Church, by the saving sacrifice <note>original: *salutari sacrificio*; a reference to the celebration of the Eucharist or the Mass.</note>, and by the alms which are distributed for their spirits, so that the Lord may deal more mercifully with them than their sins deserved." For the entire Church observes this as a tradition handed down by the Fathers—that is, the Apostles.

<margin>2.</margin>
To these three, **Blessed Gregory** adds a *fourth*, namely **Fasting**, as the sacred Canons teach (13. q. 2.): *The souls of the deceased,* he says, *are released in four ways: either by the offerings of Priests, or the prayers of the saints, or the alms of loved ones, or the fasting of relatives.* **Ivo, Bishop of Chartres**, repeats these same points word for word in Book 5, Chapter 124. Mention is also made of these in the *Life of Remigius, Bishop of Rheims*, written by Hincmar.

<margin>3.</margin>
To the things already mentioned, **Saint Bridget** adds the **Restitution** of another's property in the 6th book of her *Revelations*. This is perhaps because some of the deceased are said to have returned to the living specifically to warn them to restore to the true owners the things which they possessed while alive but had not returned. It is also perhaps because...

...as one would have learned from Saint Augustine, *sin is not forgiven, unless that which was taken is restored.* <note>original: "non dimitti peccatum, nisi restituatur ablatum." This is a famous maxim from Augustine’s Letter 153, emphasizing that repentance for theft requires returning the stolen items.</note>

<margin>4.</margin> There are those who also demand *Pilgrimages*, because we read that these are requested by certain Spirits. In the Life of Remigius, Bishop of Reims, *Tears* <note>Refers to ritualized penance or mourning for sins.</note> are added. And from Blessed Athanasius, *Oil* and *Wax* <note>Likely referring to donations of oil for sanctuary lamps and wax for candles.</note>, as can be seen in his Discourse on those who have fallen asleep <note>A traditional term for the deceased.</note>.

<margin>5.</margin> Others add different methods, and some add all *duties of piety* in general. Perhaps this is not wrong. Since any works of the living can benefit other living people because of the connection between them—as different members under one Head—why should the works of the living not also benefit the dead? For as **St. Augustine** testifies, *they are living members of the same body.*

<margin>6.</margin> But whether there are three methods, or four, or even more; there is no doubt that the living are freed from the harassment of Spirits by these very means, if relief from their misery can be brought to those Spirits. For whatever is effective in easing the punishments of these Spirits also removes the disturbances caused by those Spirits.

<margin>7.</margin> Whether they actually provide relief must be discussed later when we examine each one individually: it is certain, however, that these acts are exercises of noble virtues. *Prayer* is an act of religion, as are the *Sacrifice of the Mass* and the *use of wax candles*. *Almsgiving* is an act of mercy. *Fasting* along with *weeping* are acts of temperance. The *Restitution of another’s property* is an act of justice, as is the fulfillment of *Pilgrimages*. All of these, insofar as they are undertaken to relieve the misery of the Spirits, are duties of the most excellent Charity.

<margin>8.</margin> Therefore, there is a great distinction between them. For although all of them can be commanded by Charity, *in themselves* they are duties of specific virtues. But besides this, there are other differences between them; once we have briefly judged these, this Chapter shall be concluded.

<margin>9.</margin> Some acts are of such a nature that they cannot be omitted without sin: in this category is the *Restitution of property*, and the *Pilgrimage* which must be undertaken because of a vow. Others, just as they are undertaken with praise, so they are omitted almost without fault. Therefore, these are referred to as works of *Supererogation* <term>Supererogation: In Catholic theology, these are "works of exceeded duty"—good deeds that go beyond what is strictly required by God's commandments.</term>. *Restitution of property* is not such a work, nor is the *fulfillment of a vow of pilgrimage*.

<margin>10.</margin> Furthermore, among those first acts, some tend directly toward God: such as *Prayer, Wax Candles, and the Sacrifice*. Others serve to relieve the misery of one's neighbor; such as *Almsgiving*. Others serve to subject the body to the spirit; such as *Fastings and tears*, which consist of the affliction of the flesh.

<margin>11.</margin>
From this, a fourth distinction is drawn, which teaches the relationship to the three types of human goods. Specifically, **Almsgiving** involves the use of the "light" of external goods <note>Referring to material wealth or possessions.</note>. **Fasting**, accompanied by weeping, involves the body. **Prayer** involves the soul. **Sacrifice** involves almost all of these.

<margin>12.</margin>
Furthermore, some of the aforementioned methods are available to many people, others to fewer. Only those who possess "the goods of fortune" <note>Meaning those who have financial means or material wealth.</note> can provide Alms, just as they are the ones who can afford to light wax tapers. The <term>Sacrifice of the Mass</term> <gloss>The central act of Catholic worship, believed to be an offering of Christ for the sins of the living and the dead.</gloss> can be performed by priests alone. Fasting is difficult for those with failing physical strength. However, prayer with tears is common to everyone.

<margin>13.</margin>
Finally, some of these methods require the moral uprightness of those performing them, while others do not. Almsgiving and Fasting belong to the first category <note>Meaning the spiritual "value" of the act depends on the virtue of the person doing it.</note>; the Sacrifice of the Mass and Prayer belong to the latter, especially the Mass. More will be said on these in their proper places.

### CHAPTER LXXV.

->*That the spirits of the pious deceased, who are sometimes troublesome to the living, are aided by prayer; however, it is one thing when done by the prayer of the righteous, and another by that of the wicked.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative initial R featuring floral motifs inside a square frame.</image-desc> It is the belief and consensus of all Catholics that spirits who must be purified are helped by these means. The "dread mysteries" <note>original: "tremenda mysteria." This is a traditional term for the Eucharist, emphasizing its sacred and solemn nature.</note> are never celebrated in the Church unless a commemoration is also made of the deceased who have gone before us and died in the Lord with the sign of faith. The <term>Canonical Hours</term> <gloss>The official set of daily prayers, such as Matins and Vespers, recited by clergy and monks.</gloss> are never recited or sung by ecclesiastical persons unless God’s peace is also sought for the souls of the faithful departed. One never rises from the table after a meal unless God is also asked to grant eternal rest to the deceased. If one happens to pass by cemeteries, there is a pious memory of the faithful departed. If conversation happens to turn to the dead, we simultaneously wish them divine consolation. If we hear that someone has departed this life, we pray that God may look kindly upon their soul. I omit many other similar examples.

# ON THE PLACES WITHIN

Theodosius the Younger <note>Theodosius II (r. 408–450 AD), Eastern Roman Emperor.</note> lay prostrate at the Relics of St. John Chrysostom and supplicated for the souls of his parents, Arcadius and Eudoxia, already deceased, as witnessed by Theodoret in Book 5 of his *History*, chapter 26. Constantine the Great, as Eusebius records in Book 4 of his *Life of Constantine*, wished to be buried in a celebrated temple so that, even in death, he might share in many prayers. Josaphat, as Damascenus relates in his *Life*, prayed for his father in this manner:

> "Place him in a place of refreshment, in a place of rest: and do not remember his former iniquities."

Palladius writes thus of Macarius: according to his custom, Macarius poured out prayers for the deceased. Of Theodore, Archimandrite of the Sykeotes, Gregory the Presbyter records in his *Life* that he supplicated God for the salvation of his deceased mother; this is found in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578) was a German monk and hagiographer famous for his collection of the lives of saints.</note>, Volume 2.

<margin>3.</margin>
Those who, while living, requested prayers for themselves after death serve as another argument for us. Such include Ephrem the Syrian, who requested prayers to be offered for him after he died, as is clear from his *Testament* in Surius, Volume 1. Edward, King of the English <note>Edward the Confessor (c. 1003–1066).</note>, who, according to Aelred in his *Life*, desired the same to be bestowed upon him when dead. St. Eusebia, who wished for these to be performed for her by the holy virgins of her order, as Metaphrastes records in her *Life*. Euphrasia, the wife of Antigonus—a very wealthy man of Constantinople in the time of Theodosius—wished that she and her deceased husband be commended to the prayers of Euphrasia the Younger, her daughter, as is clear in her *Life* in Surius, Volume 2. St. Kunegunde the Empress, who wrote to the congregation at Kaufungen <note>original: "in confugia," likely referring to the convent she founded.</note> that they should commend the soul of her deceased husband, Emperor Henry, to God and refresh it with the "nourishment of prayer." Surius, Volume 2, in her *Life*. Blessed Paulinus of Nola, in Letter 5 to Bishop Delphinus, commends the soul of his brother to his prayers. He commends the same soul in Letter 6 to Amandus, the bishop of the same name.

<margin>4.</margin>
And these lived in the time of the <term>Law of Grace</term> <gloss>The era of the New Testament and the Christian Church, characterized by the grace of Christ rather than the Old Testament Law.</gloss>. What of those who preceded it? They too performed the same, and provided an example for both our ancestors and us to follow. This is excellently demonstrated by Judas Maccabeus alone, whom Holy Scripture commends for this reason. Following his deed, this statement is added:

> "It is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the deceased, that they may be loosed from their sins." 2 Maccabees 12. <note>original: "Sancta & falubris eft cogitatio pro defunctis exorare..." This is the classic scriptural defense for the doctrine of Purgatory.</note>

<margin>5.</margin>
Catholics are not moved here by the example of their ancestors alone; they also follow their doctrine. Clement, the disciple of the Apostles, says in his first Letter: *"It is necessary to pray diligently for the dead."* If we wish, says Blessed Chrysostom in Homily 2 on the *Acts of the Apostles*, *"to do good for the dead, let us offer continuous prayers for them."* And in Homily 41 on the *First Letter to the Corinthians*...

While she was *sleeping* (as Jacobus Montanus writes in her *Life*, found in Surius, Volume 6), *the ghost of her mother appeared to hover before her, and with a mournful face and on bended knees, she prayed that Elizabeth would have mercy on her as soon as possible. She said that because of a life led somewhat negligently, she was paying the penalty in fire. Soon after this vision, Elizabeth woke up, and after pouring out prayers and tears to God, she fell back into sleep. The ghost appeared again and gave immortal thanks for her timely liberation, saying that Elizabeth’s prayers were held in such high regard by God that she could bring help and relief both to those who have departed this life and to those who still remain.* So says Montanus.

We also add Tetta, a most upright virgin and sister to a King of the English <note>St. Tetta (8th century), Abbess of Wimborne and relative of the Kings of Wessex.</note>; she obtained pardon through prayer for her deceased virgin sister, who was still paying penalties for several small stains of sin. The proof was the earth of her burial mound, which had sunk down and then risen up again, filling the empty gap. Rudolph, the disciple of Rabanus, records this in the book *On Holy Charity*, otherwise known as the *Life of Lioba*.

For that which proceeds from those who are in the grace of Christ is by far the most excellent: because it has the power not only of **obtaining favor** <note>original: *impetrandi*</note>, but truly...

...but also of making satisfaction <term>satisfaciendi: the act of making amends or paying the "debt" of temporal punishment due to sin</term>. Far removed from this is the prayer of sinful men, which only obtains the power of entreaty <term>impetrandi: the act of asking for a favor or mercy without the merit of "paying" for it</term>.

<margin>10.</margin> Hence it is that the prayer of sinners is said to help the deceased in only one way, while the prayer of the just helps in two. The Empress Kunegunde <note>St. Kunigunde of Luxembourg (c. 975–1040), Empress of the Holy Roman Empire</note> seems to have taken this into account when she preferred that the soul of her deceased husband be commended to the prayers of religious men; because, as she said, *the prayers of the just are very powerful with God.* This is recorded in her *Life*, found in Surius, Volume 2.

# CHAPTER LXXVI.

->*That the sacrifice of the Mass helps the spirits of the pious dead who ask for the aid of the living after death, and how it does so.*<-

<margin>1.</margin> Another aid, by which the living are freed from the annoyance of spirits being purified, and the spirits themselves are freed from their torments, is the *most holy Sacrifice of the altar*. Regarding this, following the lead of others, the **Council of Trent, Canon 6, Session 22** states: *If anyone says that the Sacrifice of the Mass is only one of praise and thanksgiving; or a bare commemoration of the Sacrifice performed on the Cross, but not propitiatory <note>original: "propitiatorium"; meaning a sacrifice that actually gains God's favor and covers sin</note>; or that it benefits only the one receiving it; and that it should not be offered for the living and the dead, for sins, punishments, satisfactions, and other necessities, let him be anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church</note>.*

<margin>2.</margin> This doctrine sustains the most serious attacks from the enemies of the old religion <note>A reference to Protestant reformers</note>. But it is held and defended all the more steadfastly by Catholics, the more it is fortified by great protections. None of the qualities that prayer possesses in itself (discussed in the preceding chapter) are lacking here.

<margin>3.</margin> First among these is the consensus of all Catholics now living, confirmed not so much by words as by their very actions. No sacrifice of the Mass is performed in which a commemoration of the dead is not made. There are, furthermore, "Masses for the dead," as we call them—some being anniversaries, others celebrated on the first, seventh, or thirtieth day after burial, and so on.

<margin>4.</margin> This consensus is confirmed by the examples of our ancestors. For the soul of his brother Satyrus, **Blessed Ambrose** offered the *Sacrifice*, as is clear from the funeral oration he delivered at his death. Regarding the mother of **Blessed Augustine** <note>St. Monica</note>, Augustine himself testifies in Book 9 of his *Confessions* that the same *Sacrifice* was offered for her.

It cites the Council of Trent and the practices of Church Fathers like Ambrose and Augustine to validate the efficacy of offering Mass for the deceased.</summary>

### PART THREE.
<meta>Handwritten number "238" in the top right corner; catchword "Nor" at bottom right.</meta>

Thus Saint Bernard, while he was staying in Verdun in France, offered the *Sacrifice of the Altar* <note>original: *Sacrificium altaris*; another term for the Mass</note> for the Bishop of Ostia, who had recently passed away, as is clear from Chapter 4, Book 4 of his *Life*. Saint Gall the Abbot did the same for Columban, according to Chapter 25 of his *Life*. For Saint Gall, John, the Bishop of Constance, offered it, as seen in the *Life of Gall*, Chapter 29. Saint Severus, Bishop of Ravenna, offered it for Prelate Geminianus, as recorded in his *Life* found in Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578) was a famous German monk who compiled a massive multi-volume collection of the lives of the saints</note>, Volume 1. Anselm offered it for the soul of Osbert, who at one time had been quite alienated from him, as recorded in his *Life* written by Eadmer the Englishman, found in Surius, Volume 2.

Furthermore, Hugh, the Bishop of Grenoble, is said to have commemorated the day of his father’s and mother’s deaths with the *dread Sacrifice* <note>original: *tremendo Sacrificio*; a common medieval way to describe the solemnity of the Mass</note>, which he offered for their salvation, as witnessed by Guigo V, the Prior of the first Carthusian monastery, while describing the course of Hugh's life. And Ulrich, the Bishop of Augsburg, when he learned that Adelbert had fallen in battle, first brought the body to Augsburg and committed it to a dignified burial; then, immediately after, he asked God that his spirit be commended to Him *through the sacred host of the immolation* <note>original: *per sacra immolationis hostiam*; referring to the consecrated bread of the Eucharist</note>. Likewise, Bernard of Haguenau, in his *Life*, testifies that Ulrich—at a time when he was staying in Rome and was not yet a bishop—commended the soul of an elder to God among the *sacred offerings of prayers* <note>original: *sacra orationum libamina*</note>.

And the Bishop of Würzburg, Embricho, just as he loved Babo, the Bishop of Bamberg, during his life, so he honored him in death with the outstanding duties of Christian piety. He placed his shoulders beneath the funeral bier; he publicly offered the *Sacrifice of the Mass* <note>original: *Missae Sacrificium*</note> for the soul of the deceased; and, ascending the pulpit to the great number of listeners present, he delivered a magnificent funeral oration. See the *Life of Babo*, in Surius, Volume 4.

The Venerable Bede also relates in Book 3 of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English* regarding the deeds of King Oswald, that the brothers of the Church of Hexham were accustomed to gather every year, on the day before King Oswald was killed, at the place where he had once erected a cross for the purpose of prayer. There, they offered prayers for the salvation of his soul and *offered the victim of the sacred Offering* <note>original: *victimam sacra Oblationis offerre*; meaning the Mass</note>.

<margin>5.</margin>
The desires of the living also have a place here—those who earnestly requested that this same *Sacrifice of the Mass* be offered for themselves after death. Such examples include Ephrem the Syrian in his *Testament*; the Venerable Bede in the preface to the *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, Bishop of Lindisfarne, in Surius, Volume 2; Margaret, Queen of Scotland, in her *Life* in Surius; and many others. And lest we become tedious by listing more, we conclude with a single discourse of the Blessed Augustine, who, in his thirty-fourth sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*, teaches that the entire Church is accustomed to pray for the dead in the Sacrifice of the Mass.

# ON INFESTED PLACES
<page-num>278</page-num>

Nor is there any reason to doubt the testimony of the holy Doctor <note>Referring to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, discussed on the previous page</note>. The Liturgies of James, Clement, and others still exist, which excellently confirm this matter. There exist the Councils of all the Provinces which made mention of the *Sacrifice* <note>The Mass</note> for the deceased. See Chapter 82 of this Disputation.

<margin>6.</margin>
Under the Old Law <note>The religious system of the Old Testament before the coming of Christ</note>, the souls of the departed were not aided by this specific *Sacrifice*. This is not surprising, as the *sacrifice* of the Mass belongs to the New Law, not the old. Nevertheless, souls were not entirely deprived of the power of *sacrifices*. Those very *sacrifices* of the Old Law were of benefit to them, as is proven by the *Sacrifice* offered by the leader Judas Maccabeus for those killed in battle (2 Maccabees 12). From this same source, Blessed Augustine, in his book *On Care to be Had for the Dead*, chapter 1, proves that our sacrifice benefits the deceased.

<margin>7.</margin>
The doctrine of the ancient Church agrees with these examples. Most solemn is the discourse of Blessed Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), a prominent Early Church Father known for his eloquence</note> in his 69th Homily to the People: *“It was not in vain,”* he says, *“that these things were ordained by the Apostles: that a commemoration of the departed should take place during the awesome Mysteries <note>original: tremendis Misterijs; a traditional term for the Consecration of the Eucharist</note>. For they know that much gain and great benefit comes to them from this.”* Blessed Augustine speaks to the same purpose in his 32nd Sermon, *On the Words of the Apostle*: *“The universal Church observes this,”* he says, *“as a tradition from the Fathers: that prayer is offered for those who have died in the communion of the body and blood of Christ when they are commemorated in their proper place at the Sacrifice itself, and it is also noted that the Sacrifice is being offered for them.”*

<margin>8.</margin>
Furthermore, the very dignity of this *Sacrifice* provides a powerful argument here. For it is not merely twelve thousand talents of silver being offered, as was the case with Judas Maccabeus; but an infinite treasury of all graces: namely, the only-begotten Son of God. This is done through the Church, whose charity and devotion are most pleasing to God—or more truly, it is done through the only-begotten Son of God himself. For the one offering and the thing being offered are the same here, and the offering itself is the same. For He who once offered Himself to God for sins never ceases to offer Himself, even though the Church, through her ministers, also offers Him and joins her prayers and vows to this *Sacrifice*.

<margin>9.</margin>
From this it also follows that this *Sacrifice* offered for the dead has possessed great power, even in cases where those for whom it was offered were not actually deceased <note>The author is arguing that the Mass is so powerful it can aid the living who are presumed dead</note>. John the Almoner <note>Saint John the Merciful, a 7th-century Patriarch of Alexandria</note>, Bishop of Alexandria, demonstrates this with a remarkable example, as Leontius, Bishop of Neapolis, records in his *Life*: *“A certain man, taken captive by the Persians, was held in chains in the prison called Lethe <note>A Greek word meaning 'Oblivion' or 'Forgetfulness'</note>. Now, there was a law among the Persians that those cast into that prison were never to be released (and for that reason, it is fitting that it was called...*

...the broad Lethe <note>original: *latam Lethen*; a reference to the river of forgetfulness in Greek mythology, used here metaphorically for oblivion</note>. When certain men fled from that place and arrived in Cyprus, they told the parents of a young man that he had died in custody. Therefore, those parents celebrated religious assemblies <note>original: *Synaxes*; a Greek term used for the gathering of the faithful for the Eucharist</note> three times every year, as if he were dead. Four years had passed, and behold, the son, escaping from that place, returned home. When his parents looked upon him—not as one who had fled from custody, but as one who had risen from the dead—they were filled with great wonder and inexpressible joy. They told him how they had performed the funeral rites <note>original: *Iusta*; literally "the just dues" performed for the deceased</note> for him as if he were dead, noting also the days of the Holy Epiphany, the saving Passover <note>Easter</note>, and Holy Pentecost, on which they performed these things. When the young man heard this and called it to memory, he affirmed to his parents that on those very days he had been released from his chains by the arrival of a certain person who carried a lamp, and he had enjoyed complete freedom; however, on the following days, he was again bound in chains just as before.
So says Leontius.

A similar example can be seen in the 17th Homily on the Gospels by Gregory the Great.

The Venerable Bede also brings forward another no less miraculous story for the same argument in the 20th chapter of the 4th book of his *History of the English*, which we relate in his own words. "In the aforementioned battle," he says, "in which King Elfwine was killed, it is well known that a certain memorable deed occurred, which I think should by no means be passed over in silence; for if it is told, it will be beneficial for the salvation of many. There was killed there, among others of his soldiers, a young man named Imma. When he had lain during that day and the following night among the corpses of the slain, looking like a dead man, he finally recovered his breath and returned to life; sitting up, he bound his own wounds as best he could. While he was doing this, he was found and captured by men of the enemy army and led to their master, a Count of King Æthelred. The Count received him and took care of his wounds. When he began to be healed, the Count ordered him to be bound at night so that he would not escape. Yet he could not be bound. For as soon as those who had bound him departed, those same chains of his were loosed. For he had a biological brother whose name was Tunna, a priest and Abbot; who, when he heard that his brother had been killed in the battle, came to seek if by chance his body could be found. Having found another man similar to him in every way, he thought it was his brother. Carrying him to his monastery, he buried him with honor; and for the absolution of his soul, he frequently saw to it that Masses were celebrated. By the celebration of these, it happened as I said: that no one could bind him, but he was immediately loosed. Meanwhile the Count, who held him, began to wonder and ask why he could not be bound, and whether by chance he had 'loosening letters' <note>original: *literas solutorias*; these were magical charms or amulets mentioned in folklore that were believed to have the power to unlock shackles</note> with him, of which fables tell..."

### DE LOCIS INFESTIS

...which could not be bound. But he <note>the captive soldier mentioned on the previous page</note> replied that he knew nothing of such arts; "but," he said, "I have a brother, a priest in my province; and I know that he, thinking I have been killed, celebrates frequent Masses for me; and if I were now in the other life, there my soul would be released from punishments through his intercessions." Thus, many were kindled in faith and the devotion of piety to pray, or to give alms, and to offer to the Lord the victims of the Holy Oblation <note>original: *Sacræ Oblationis*; the bread and wine offered in the Eucharist, viewed here as a spiritual sacrifice</note> for the rescue of their loved ones who had passed from this world. For they understood that the saving Sacrifice <note>original: *Sacrificium salutare*</note> was powerful for redemption, both of the soul and of the eternal body. So far, Bede.

Thomas Bozius <note>an Italian priest and scholar, c. 1548–1610</note> relates a third example from Peter of Cluny <note>also known as Peter the Venerable, the 12th-century Abbot of Cluny</note> in Book 15, Chapter 2 of *The Marks of the Church*. And we attribute this to the words of Peter of Cluny: In the Diocese of Grenoble <note>original: *Gratianopolitano Episcopatu*; a region in southeastern France</note>, there is a place with underground veins containing a great deal of iron; this is continuously extracted by the great sweat of the inhabitants and peasants, and once smelted and purified in furnaces, it is sold for profit to blacksmiths or whoever else throughout the surrounding lands. From this, the village where these same men live nearby is called Ferraria <note>original: *Ferraria*; likely the village of Allevard or similar, named for its iron (*ferrum*) mines</note>.

Now, these types of men, while they search the hidden depths of the earth by digging, are accustomed to go further in the hope of greater profit, and to persistently scour the underground caverns for larger quantities of iron ore. While a certain tireless peasant was pressing on with this work at a certain time, and was proceeding further by digging into the innermost parts of the earth, suddenly a massive pile of earth collapsed and blocked the entrance through which he had entered. 

Because he had proceeded further by digging, and the excavated earth had left behind a large empty space, he faced death; and just as if he were in a house closed off by strong fortifications and surrounded on all sides, he could not get out, though he remained unharmed. But surrounded by the darkness of such a gloomy prison, with all hope of escape taken away, and buried as if in a spacious tomb, he believed that while still alive, he was already looking upon death itself. 

When he had not appeared for several days, his wife, believing him dead, turned to helping his soul with spiritual benefits. For an entire year, she had a Mass celebrated for him every week by priests; and by offering bread and a candle for him, she busied herself in assisting the soul of her deceased husband through the saving sacrament, <unclear>as is the custom</unclear> of the Church. There was, however, one week of the year in which the woman, occupied with other business, neglected to provide the Mass for her husband as she had planned. 

Behold, when the span of nearly a whole year had passed, the diggers—accustomed to the work of mining—were again restlessly pressing on toward the place where the aforementioned peasant still lay hidden, yet alive...

...they arrived by digging bit by bit. When the trapped peasant <note>original: *Rusticus*</note> heard their voices and the sound of hammers approaching, he began to shout as loudly as he could. Hearing his voice and recognizing—as they were experts in that craft—that it was a man underground, they encouraged one another and finally reached him after much labor in digging. Looking around at him curiously with lanterns lit, they recognized him as the man they knew had been buried there a year before. Astonished and, as was natural, stunned by the novelty of such a thing, they asked most insistently how he had been able to live there. 

But he replied: "When that barrier of earth, which you have just removed, was placed against the opening through which I had entered, and I was held in this prison you see, remaining for several days without food or light; suddenly, when I was almost failing, someone stood by me with Bread and a light. He comforted me, urged me to take food, and most brightly illuminated the foul darkness with that Candle he carried. Nourished by that Bread for a period of seven or eight days (as it seemed to me), and illuminated for as many days by that Candle, I escaped the danger of hunger and avoided the darkness of this pit. After seven or eight days, however, he would arrive again with fresh Bread and a renewed Light, and having left them for me, he would depart. He never ceased doing this for the space of one year (as it seemed to me), at almost equal intervals of time, except for the space of one week, when for some unknown reason he withdrew his presence and his usual gift." 

Upon hearing this from him and recalling what his wife had done for him throughout that whole year, they immediately explained everything to him. Then, leading the man out of those underground caverns, they restored him—wonderful to tell—safe and sound after a year's burial, to his own wife, to all his neighbors, and to the people rushing to see such a sight. Gathering together and examining both what the woman had done for him and what he told of himself, they found that the Bread by which he was nourished and the Candle by which he was lit were offered on the very same days that the woman had been having Mass celebrated for his soul <note>original: *pro eius requie*; literally "for his rest," a common term for prayers for the deceased</note>, offering both Bread and a Candle to the priest celebrating the Mass. This account is from the Cluniac <note>Peter the Venerable, the Abbot of Cluny</note>, and from the Cluniac, Bozius <note>Thomas Bozius, an author who compiled historical and religious signs of the Church</note>.

# ON HAUNTED PLACES. <note>original: *De Locis Infestis*. While the chapter title refers to "infested" or "haunted" locations, the text here focuses on the spiritual remedies—specifically the Mass—that resolve such disturbances by aiding souls in Purgatory.</note>

To this we add what is read in the *Life of Blessed Anselm*, that he himself for an entire
year persisted in daily Sacrifices <note>The Mass</note> for a deceased friend; who fi-
nally appearing, testified that he had been helped by the prayers of the Saint.

A third example from Blessed Gregory, <note>Gregory the Great</note> Book 4 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 54, may be ad-
joined. He commanded that for 30 continuous days the *Sacrifice of the altar* be offered for Justus
the Monk; and this man later appearing to someone of the same profession,
testified that it had profited him toward freedom from punishments.

Saint Bernard provides a fourth example, who himself offered the *Sacrifice of the altar* for one of his own
whom he had known to be being purified in the other life,
and he commanded that others offer it; and after several days he understood that the same man
was absolved from purgatorial punishments. This is recorded in his *Life*, Book 1, chapter 10.

->William the Abbot.<- <note>William of St. Thierry, biographer of St. Bernard.</note>

Malachy, Bishop of Ireland, supplies a fifth; who, when
he had perceived in a dream that his deceased sister had tasted
nothing for forty days, understood the hunger of what food she suffered from: and having diligently di-
scussed the number of days, he recognized that in that space of thirty days he had
not offered the unbloody *host of the altar* for his sister. He therefore resumed the *Sacrifices*;
and afterward the sister was seen by him in a black garment only reaching the threshold
of the Church, but unable to go further. The holy man therefore understood that satisfaction had not yet
been made for the deceased. Again, therefore, he insisted upon his prior exercises of piety,
and after those things the sister appeared again; but now in a white gar-
ment, and entering into the Church. Yet because she was prohibited from approaching
the altar, he judged that he must not yet cease from the *Sacrifice*. What then?
He returned to those same duties for a fourth time; and he finally knew his sister to be liberated
from all punishment, after he saw her associated with the company of the
Saints: Bernard records these things in the *Life of Malachy*. More examples
are not necessary. "Unless the Catholic Church," says Isidore in Book 1 *On Offices*,
chapter 8, "*believed that sins were forgiven for the faithful departed, it would neither give alms for their spirits nor offer Sacrifice to God*."

<margin>11</margin>
From what has been said, it is manifest that this *Sacrifice* is not performed for the *deceased*
in vain. However, we do not wish this to be said only of that Sacrifice
which is performed by Priests of an entire and proven life: but even by
those whose morals are less approved. Here the unworthiness of the Ministers does not hinder:
for this reason, because the principal agent in this *Sacrifice* is God,
or the Church; and the *Sacrifice* itself has its value <term>ex opere operato</term> <note>Latin: "from the work performed." A theological doctrine meaning the sacrament is effective by the power of the rite itself, regardless of the priest's personal holiness.</note>, as we speak in the schools.

<margin>12</margin>
But just as this is certain: so it is certain that the dignity of the Minister is worth
very much here: and it brings it about that what is meritorious and
satisfactory of itself and *by the work performed*, also becomes meritorious and satisfactory by
reason of the person of the one offering and
ministering.

# PART THREE.

## CHAPTER LXXVII.
### How Almsgiving frees from the disturbances that spirits being purified sometimes cause. <note>original: *purgandi Spiritus*. These are souls in Purgatory whose restless presence or "hauntings" are believed to be relieved when the living perform acts of charity on their behalf.</note>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring intricate foliate patterns and scrolls within a square border.</image-desc>

<margin>1</margin>
The same reasoning we held to prove that the spirits of the pious deceased are helped by Prayer and the saving Sacrifice <note>The Mass</note>, we follow now in demonstrating the power of Almsgiving for this same purpose.

<margin>2</margin>
First, there is the consensus of Catholics. We see most often that when people of greater fortune depart this life, large alms are soon given by the friends of the deceased for the salvation of the dead; and these are repeated on the first, third, seventh, and thirtieth day, and on the anniversary of the burial. Moreover, the deceased themselves, before departing this life, believe that the passage from Luke 16 applies to them: *make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings* <note>Luke 16:9. "Mammon of iniquity" refers to worldly wealth; the passage suggests using it for charitable ends to gain spiritual advocates.</note>; and for this reason, they hold no small concern for the poor in their final moments.

<margin>3</margin>
Second, there is the devotion of our Elders: those who preceded us and professed the same Christian law as we do. Although the matter is certain, it would not be out of place to illustrate it with a few examples.

First is Pammachius <note>A Roman senator and friend of St. Jerome</note>, to whom Saint Jerome gives testimony in a letter: that he watered the holy remains and venerable bones of his wife Paulilla with the "balsam of alms"; knowing it is written: *As water quenches fire, so almsgiving quenches sin (Ecclesiasticus 3:30)*.

A second is Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble: who, as long as he lived, held the day of his mother's and father's death as a day for almsgiving. This is found in his *Life* by Guigo V, Prior of the first Charterhouse <note>The Grande Chartreuse monastery</note>.

A third is the wife of Otto II <note>Empress Theophanu</note>, who, while staying in Rome, desired her husband's soul to be commended to God in the temple of the Apostles, both through prayers and the alms she performed. So it is written in the *Life of Saint Adalbert, Martyr and Bishop of Prague*, in the second volume of Surius <note>Laurentius Surius, a 16th-century hagiographer and collector of saints' lives</note>.

A fourth is Emperor Henry <note>likely Henry II, known for his piety</note>: who, although he had been more troublesome to Herbert, Archbishop of Cologne during his life, wished to honor him after death with generous alms and other exercises of Christian piety. Rupert of Deutz records this in his *Life* found in Surius, volume 4.

A fifth is the people of Bamberg: who poured out prayers to God for their prelate Babo and distributed notable alms to the poor; as can be read in the *Acts* of the same Babo, in Surius, volume 4.

# ON HAUNTED PLACES

<margin>4</margin> The third argument in favor of Almsgiving is the example of those who were distinguished under the Old Law <note>The Hebrew Bible/Old Testament</note>. Tobias <note>The book of Tobit</note> is commanded by his father to *place bread and wine upon the burial place of the righteous* (chapter 4). For what reason, I ask? Was it perhaps for the sake of the deceased, so they might have something to refresh themselves? To whom would such a thought occur, even in a dream? Rather, the father wished to instruct his son to prepare a feast and invite the poor, so that after they had received the grace of the Alms, they might commend the souls of the deceased to God and pray for their salvation.

<margin>5</margin> There are also the records and books of the most holy Prelates of the Church regarding this matter. *It is necessary,* says Clement, a disciple of the Apostles, in his first Epistle to James, the brother of the Lord, *to give Alms for the dead.* And the Blessed Chrysostom, in his 20th Homily, says: *If we wish to do good for the deceased, let us give Alms.* And in his 41st Homily on the first Epistle to the Corinthians: *Let the dead be helped, not with tears, but with prayers and Alms.* And in his 3rd Homily on the Epistle to the Philippians: *Let us give Alms to the poor unceasingly on their behalf.* And in his 21st Homily on the Acts: *It is not in vain that Alms are performed for the departed.* Furthermore, the Blessed Ambrose, in the second book of *On the Departure of his brother Satyrus*, exhorts parents to transmit that portion of the inheritance which belonged to their deceased children to their spirits through Alms given to the poor.

<margin>6</margin> The excellence of Almsgiving and the praise it receives in the Scriptures easily demonstrate what we are proving, but two points especially stand out. The first is that the Lord teaches us that we are received into eternal dwellings through those upon whom we bestow Alms (Luke 16 <note>The original text cites Luke 6, but the reference to "eternal dwellings" is famously from Luke 16:9</note>). The second is that Almsgiving is said to extinguish sin *just as water extinguishes fire* (Ecclesiasticus 3). Indeed, these spirits <note>Souls in Purgatory</note> stand in need of both: specifically, that they may be received into eternal dwellings, and that they may be absolved from sin—that is, from the punishments of their sins. Therefore, Theophylact <note>A Byzantine archbishop and biblical commentator</note> says most excellently on Luke 12: *The distributions and offerings made for the departed are of no small benefit even to those who died in more serious sins.*

<margin>7</margin> We offer no specific examples of those who were aided by Almsgiving because the matter is clear. Did Tobias place *bread and wine upon the burial place of the righteous* in vain? Did Pammachius <note>A Roman senator known for his charity after his wife's death</note> moisten the bones of his wife with the balsam of Almsgiving in vain? Did Clement, Ambrose, and Chrysostom exhort us to perform Alms for the salvation of the dead in vain? Did Bishop Hugo of Grenoble, Emperor Henry <note>Likely Henry II, founder of Bamberg</note>, the wife of Otto II, and the City of Bamberg perform them in vain? It is to be believed that Isidore spoke most excellently in the first book of *On Offices*, chapter 18, when he said: *Unless the Catholic Church believed that sins were forgiven to the faithful departed, she would neither perform Alms for their spirits nor offer a sacrifice to God.*

# PART THREE.

<meta>catchword: Nothing-</meta>

...are performed for the deceased; so too is *Almsgiving* not of one single kind. There is one condition for that which is undertaken in a private capacity, without any knowledge or will of the person for whom it is offered; and another for that which is done by the commission <note>original: "commisssione" - referring to a request made in a will or testament</note> of the deceased. This latter case refers to one who, while still among the living, assigned a sum of money for the sake of their own salvation to redeem their purgatorial punishment through the hands of ministers <note>executors or agents of the will</note>. *Almsgiving* undertaken in the first way—unless it is done by someone who is in a state of grace <note>meaning someone who is spiritually right with God and not in a state of "mortal sin"</note>—profits the deceased very little. For that which does not arise from grace and charity is not *absolutely* pleasing to God, even if, out of mere generosity, He occasionally rewards works that are only *morally* good in a wondrous way. But that which is done in the second way loses none of its value, even if the person who distributes the *Alms* according to the will of the deceased is in a state of the gravest sins. For these *Alms* belong not so much to the immediate givers as to the "masters" <note>the deceased person who provided the funds</note> who donated them.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII.

->*Fasting also benefits spirits being purged, and frees the living from their harassment.*<-

<margin>1</margin> <image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'Q' containing a small figure, possibly a saint or monk, amidst foliate scrolls.</image-desc> It has already been proven, by the well-known opinion of Saint Augustine, that the reasons we have followed thus far are effective for helping the spirits of the deceased and for freeing oneself from their harassment <note>In this context, "harassment" (molestia) refers to the disturbances or hauntings caused by restless spirits</note>. To these, *Fasting* and the *Restitution* <note>the returning of stolen or borrowed goods to their rightful owners</note> of others' property—which may be held by the heirs of the deceased—are usually added. How beneficial these are will be explained in the following sections, and this Chapter deals with Fasting.

<margin>2</margin> Regarding *Fasting*, this is *certain: there are great commendations of it in the Holy Scriptures*. For it is not only advised, but even commanded; and there are so many proofs that it is effective for driving away all manner of evils and for meriting the goods of this and the future life, that it would be a waste of time and effort to be occupied in listing them all.

<margin>3</margin> And just as this is certain, it is also not in doubt that *fasting is undertaken for its own sake for the affliction of the body and the restraining of the senses of the flesh*. For this reason, although Paul, Anthony, Hilarion <note>St. Anthony the Great and St. Hilarion were "Desert Fathers," early Christian hermits famous for their extreme self-discipline</note>, and other dwellers of the desert who had declared war on the flesh did not neglect vigils, rough clothing, and extreme physical labor, they nonetheless always placed *Fasting* in the front line as the strongest defense against the assaults of the flesh. They preached that nothing belonged so much to the profession of a Monk as *Fasting*, and they confirmed this by living example. Indeed, they considered those who did not wear themselves down with constant *Fasting* as hardly worthy of the name "Monk."

# ON TROUBLED PLACES
<note>original: "DE LOCIS INFESTIS" – this refers to locations "infested" or haunted by spirits, often believed to be souls from Purgatory seeking help.</note>

<margin>4</margin> Nevertheless, just as it possesses great power for many other things, so too he who denies that *fasting* is effective for redeeming the punishments of *spirits being purified* <note>original: "purgandorum Spirituum" – souls in Purgatory</note> is ignorant of what the opinion and belief of the Forefathers was regarding *Fasting*. Certainly, the testimony of an Angel confirms that the deceased are helped by it, according to **Bede, in book 9 of his History, chapter 13.** He says: "Many are helped by the prayers of the living, and almsgiving, and fasting, and especially the celebration [of the Mass], so that they may be liberated before the day of judgment."

<margin>5</margin> This is confirmed by *Theodore, the Archimandrite* <note>a superior of a monastery or group of monasteries in Eastern Christianity</note> *of the Sykeonians*, who, not content with prayer alone, undertook a one-week *fast* for his deceased mother; as witnessed by *the priest Gregory, in his Life, found in Surius, Volume 2.* It is also confirmed by *Hincmar, in the Life of Saint Remigius, Archbishop of Reims*, who taught that the deceased are liberated from purgatorial punishments by the prayers of the faithful, alms, *fasts*, weeping, and the offerings of the saving host <note>original: "hostiæ salutaris" – the consecrated bread of the Eucharist</note>. I omit others, of whom we shall make mention later.

<margin>6</margin> This is perhaps confirmed by the ancient custom of the *Jews*, of whom it is certain that they not only prayed for the dead, distributed alms, and offered sacrifices, but also observed long *fasts*. In **the last chapter of the First Book of Kings** <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Samuel 31:13</note>, the inhabitants of *Jabesh-Gilead* are read to have weakened themselves with a seven-day *fast* because of the death of *Saul* and his sons. In **the Second Book of Kings, chapter 3** <note>2 Samuel 3:35</note>, *David* did the same, along with his companions, after he was informed of the death of *Abner*.

<margin>7</margin> The *weeping and mourning* of the Ancients, often prolonged for many days, seems to pertain to this same practice. For there is no doubt that they added other afflictions to such mourning, which were appropriate to the present matter. Indeed, Christ the Lord designates formal fasting itself by the name and title of *mourning*. For when the disciples of *John* questioned him, saying: *Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?* **Jesus answered them in Matthew 9**: *Can the children of the bridegroom mourn (that is, fast) as long as the bridegroom is with them?*

<margin>8</margin> Nor is there a lack of examples here of those who were liberated from purgatorial punishments by the *fasts* of the living. A certain priest named *Arnulphus* had requested a forty-day *fast* from *Saint Rembert, Archbishop of Bremen*, to whom he had appeared after death, explaining his needs; and once the forty-day *fast* was completed, he signaled to the same *Rembert* with a sign of gratitude that he had been released from all punishment. **Surius, Volume 1, in the Life of Saint Rembert.**
Likewise, through the *fasting* which the virgin *Saint Lutgardis* performed for the deceased *Simon*,

But when a subordinate fasts, the work belongs to the subordinate, not the master.

# CHAPTER LXXIX.

## Whether, and how, the Restitution of another's property helps the spirits of the pious deceased: and frees the living from their haunting.

<margin>1.</margin>
Among the suffrages <note>Acts of intercession or pious works offered to God on behalf of souls in Purgatory.</note> by which the spirits of the deceased who are being purified are helped, Saint Bridget the Virgin <note>Saint Birgitta of Sweden, a 14th-century mystic famous for her "Revelations."</note> also included the Restitution of another's property. But if we discuss the matter more precisely, we shall find that while it is indeed absolutely necessary for salvation, it should not, properly speaking, be categorized among the types of suffrages.

<margin>2.</margin>
This is clear first from the opinion of Saint Augustine, who states: *Sin cannot be forgiven unless that which was taken is restored.* <note>original Latin: "Peccatum, nisi restituatur ablatum, remitti non posse." A classic principle of Catholic moral theology: if you steal something, you must return it to be forgiven.</note> Furthermore, it is gathered from this that to restore another's property is not an act of satisfying God for the sin committed against Him by the wrongful taking, but rather an act of ceasing from the desire to sin. For as long as I do not restore what I can and ought by right to restore, I am persisting in an offense against God and my neighbor. For which reason, just as it is absolutely necessary for eternal life...

### ON INFESTED PLACES

...it is, that we desist from sin; likewise, that we restore the property of others to their rightful owners.

<margin>3.</margin> However, it is clear from what has already been said that this [restitution] should not be numbered among the *suffrages* <term>suffragia: intercessory works such as prayers, masses, or alms performed by the living to reduce the suffering of souls in Purgatory</term> of the deceased. Who would say that the souls of the dead are snatched from the punishments they most justly endure simply because the living cease from their habit of sinning?

<margin>4.</margin> Other types of suffrages help the dead under this name because they are certain works of piety which are freely undertaken by the living out of a feeling of compassion for the sake of the deceased. But *Restitution* <term>restitutio: the act of making good on a loss or returning stolen goods, often seen as a requirement for divine forgiveness</term> is not undertaken freely; it is entirely necessary. And it is undertaken not out of a feeling of compassion toward the poor, but lest the living themselves suffer an irreparable loss of salvation if they fail in this duty.

<margin>5.</margin> And for what reason should it be said that *this* restitution benefits the deceased? For either they themselves were unable to restore others’ property while they lived—and thus are free from all fault and blame—or they were able but refused to restore it, and thus suffered the loss of their salvation. Or, they commanded their heirs, as far as was in their power, to make restitution after their death; and in this case, if *Restitution* does not follow, it is entirely the fault of the heirs, not the deceased. If, however, they were somewhat negligent in commanding their heirs, yet that negligence was not fatal <note>In a theological sense, meaning it was a venial sin rather than a mortal sin that would lead to Hell.</note>, that negligence will be expiated <note>Atoned for or "paid off."</note> not by the *Restitution* of the property itself as performed by the heirs, but by the fire of purgatory.

<margin>6.</margin> If the *restitution of another’s property* were to free them, as is said, from purgatorial punishments, must it not be said that they are detained in purgatorial punishments for as long as the *Restitution* has not been made? But what if it is never done? Shall the spirits of those who died piously in Christ always be miserable because of the negligence of others? Who would believe such a thing?

<margin>7.</margin> Again, if the *restitution of another’s property* helps, would the deceased not be snatched from their punishments as soon as it is performed? But what if their own negligence deserves a greater punishment? For there is no doubt that purgatorial punishments are required from the deceased in proportion to the scale of their sins and negligence.

<margin>8.</margin> This is the condition of the spirits being purged: that they endure punishments for their own crimes and errors. Now, however, the fact that *property* is *not restored* after their death is not their crime, but the crime and sin of the heirs and of those whose duty it is to execute the final will.

<margin>9.</margin> But it is said that certain spirits have returned to the living and persuaded them to perform the *Restitution of property* which was neglected through their own fault. Let this be so. Nevertheless, they persuaded them not as if it would benefit themselves, but as something for the good of the living <note original="sed tanquam viuentium bonum">The author argues that when ghosts appear asking for debts to be paid, they are trying to save their living relatives from the sin of theft, rather than trying to "buy" their own way out of Purgatory.</note>.

### CHAPTER LXXX.
### *Whether, and in what manner, the spirits to be purged are helped by Pilgrimages which the living perform for their sake.*

<margin>1.</margin>
It follows that we should define what is to be thought regarding Pilgrimages <term>peregrinatio: a journey to a holy site as an act of devotion or penance</term> which the spirits of the dead sometimes request, and to which they bound themselves while they were alive. We must show whether these must be necessarily undertaken by the living for the sake of the deceased, such that unless they are fulfilled, the souls cannot enjoy their desired rest.

<margin>2.</margin>
First, it is certain here that *the practice of Pilgrimages is most ancient.* For they flourished even in the times of the Apostles (to go no further back), and they are confirmed by the example of the Apostles. The most holy Martyr Ignatius, writing to the Blessed John the Evangelist, strongly entreated him that he might be allowed to seek Jerusalem *for the sake of visiting the holy places.* <note>original: "visendorum Sanctorum causâ"</note> Clement of Rome, the third Pope after the Blessed Peter and his eminent disciple, testifies in the first book of his *Recognitions* that he, together with the most holy Peter, *visited the tombs of the Saints.* And the journey of Saint Paul, which he undertook to Jerusalem so that he might celebrate Pentecost there (Acts 20), excellently *commends the practice of Pilgrimages,* if faith is to be placed in Saint Jerome (Letter 7 to Marcella).

Next, it is certain, and most celebrated, that the practice of these [pilgrimages] has long existed. The things already mentioned prove this; but especially the example of Christ, who is said to have gone up to Jerusalem together with his parents, according to the custom, when he was twelve years old: and then the example of those who flourished in every age. For there has been no era that does not provide examples of *Pilgrims*. We shall bring forward one or two from each.

The *First* century provides those whom we have already recounted: Peter, Paul, Clement, and Ignatius.

The *Second* provides Origen; who, according to the testimony of Eusebius (Book 6, Chapter 11), traveled to *Rome*, and St. Alexander, who traveled to *Jerusalem*, as Jerome records in his book *On Illustrious Men* regarding Alexander.

The *Third* provides Constantine and his mother Helena. The latter *visited these holy places*, while the former invited Christians to visit them as well, by constructing a magnificent temple in Jerusalem on Mount Calvary, as witnessed by Nicephorus (Book 8, Chapter 50, and Book 9, Chapter 32).

The *Fourth* provides Eudoxia and Jerome. Both indeed traveled through Palestine for the sake of religion. She, however, not content with this, contributed ten thousand *sextarii* <term>sextarius: a Roman measure of volume, roughly equivalent to a pint or half a liter</term> of oil for the use of the lamps in the Holy Temple, as Zonaras testifies in Volume 3, regarding Theodosius.

The *Fifth* century offers almost the entire Christian world, which the piety of the Emperor Justinian attracted by building many Temples and decorating them with the Relics of the Saints.

The *Sixth* age offers, among others, the most Christian Kings of France, Clovis and Childeric. The latter, together with many others, visited the *tomb of St. Germain* after he learned that a paralytic had been restored to health there; as Gregory of Tours writes (Book 5, Chapter 32). The former [Clovis], about to fight against the Goths, hoped for a more certain victory if he requested the patronage of St. Martin by undertaking a Pilgrimage in his own name to the Saint's Relics. This is recorded by Gregory of Tours (Book 2, Chapter 37).

<margin>4.</margin>
Thirdly, it is certain that *these were not fruitless*. Did not the Emperor Theodosius obtain victory against Eugenius after he had first lain prostrate at the *tombs of the Saints*? Eusebius records this (Book 11, Chapter 33). Did not Sidonius Apollinaris, the Bishop of Auvergne, writing to St. Jerome (Book 1, Letter 5), freely confess that he *set out to the thresholds of the Apostles <note>original: "ad limina Apostolorum" – a traditional term for a pilgrimage to the tombs of St. Peter and St. Paul in Rome</note> in the hope of obtaining health and had his wish granted?* There are infinite examples for this argument in Augustine (Book 22 of *The City of God*, Chapter 8). ...touched with their hands, they were freed from the infirmities from which they labored. We omit domestic and everyday examples.

<margin>5.</margin>
Thus, there is no doubt that pilgrimages are joined with extraordinary virtues. For this reason, our ancestors undertook them; they invited others to undertake them; and they commended those who had undertaken them religiously. For why would they think they possessed less piety and religion, unless they had worshiped Christ in those places where most of all—as Blessed Jerome says—*the Gospel flashed forth from the cross?* <note>original: "Euangelium de patibulo coruscauit." Jerome uses "patibulum" (gallows or cross) to emphasize the site of the Crucifixion.</note>

<margin>6.</margin>
Fifthly, there is no doubt that those are free from fault—indeed, they perform a deed pleasing to God—*who bind themselves to God by a vow to undertake these pilgrimages.* Or is it that we cannot bind ourselves by a vow to perform what is good in itself? Whatever is good, if mortals bind themselves by a vow to perform it, it is rendered even better, and it becomes more pleasing and acceptable to God.

<margin>7.</margin>
Indeed, a vow makes that which was of itself a free choice into something that must necessarily be performed, once it has been promised to God. Therefore, for those *who undertake pilgrimages out of a vow, the greatest necessity lies upon them to fulfill them.* Hence, Blessed Jerome most excellently exhorts Rusticus (Letter 46) to *fulfill the pilgrimage he had vowed to the Holy Places of Palestine. Pay back,* he says, *what you vowed in the presence of the Lord; lest you be snatched away before you fulfill your promise.* <note>original: "Redde... quod praesente Domino vouisti; ne anterapiaris, quàm tuam sponsionem impleas."</note> And this is established here as the sixth point.

<margin>8.</margin>
From this it is now clear that those are not free from crime who do not fulfill the *pilgrimages* they promised to God. *An unfaithful and foolish promise is displeasing to God;* <note>original: "Displicet Deo infidelis & stulta promissio"</note> Ecclesiastes 5. And some are said to have damnation because *they have made void their first faith—that is, they have not performed the vows they made to God,* 1 Timothy 5. All these things are certain.

But what if they should depart from this life while the *pilgrimages* they had vowed were not yet fulfilled? Would they suffer some detriment to their salvation on this account? And if their salvation is not yet despaired of, can the living undertake *pilgrimages* in their name, for the benefit of the deceased, and thus satisfy their vows? Finally, is the fulfillment of these vows so necessary that as long as they have not been paid, the wretched souls are excluded from the kingdom of heaven? These are the principal chapters of the present argument.

<margin>10.</margin>
The first chapter must be distinguished. *For it happens either by some fault of the living that the promised pilgrimage was not fulfilled, or there is no fault of theirs in this.* If no fault of the living is involved, they suffer no loss of salvation when they depart from this life, nor do they undergo any penalty on this account. If a fault is involved: according to the quality of...
<note>catchword at bottom: of it (ipfius)</note>

<meta>catchword: because</meta>

The guilt itself is subject to punishment. For indeed, if the sin is mortal <note>original: "mortifera," literally "death-bearing." ## CHAPTER LXXXI.

### *Whether, and by what means, the Spirits to be purified are helped by Tapers and lit Lights.*

<margin>1.</margin>
One might not without reason suspect that the Spirits to be purified <note>The "spirits to be purified" refers to souls in Purgatory, a state of after-death cleansing in Catholic theology.</note> are helped by lit tapers and lights, based on their common use regarding the dead. For this practice is neither minor nor simple. As soon as they have breathed out their soul, several tapers—sometimes more, sometimes fewer, according to the means of the living—are placed by the corpse. They then adorn the funeral procession. They are placed over their graves. They are used in Sacrifices <note>original: "Sacrificijs." In this context, it refers to the "Sacrifice of the Mass," the central liturgical service of the Catholic Church.</note> and prayers which are performed for them in the Church on the third, seventh, and thirtieth day, as well as on the anniversary. Often, beyond these occasions, they are lit in temples to the honor of God in memory of the deceased, sometimes out of the piety of the living and sometimes from the last will of the deceased.

<margin>2.</margin>
Nor are these things observed only in our own times. They were also observed in ancient times and in the times of our Ancestors: and indeed among men illustrious for their piety, learning, wisdom, and nobility. At the funeral of the Blessed Virgin, it is testified by Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopolus, a 14th-century Byzantine church historian.</note> in Book 2, Chapter 22, that *lit tapers and torches* were carried before her.

Theodoretus <note>A 5th-century bishop and influential theologian.</note> reports in Book 5, Chapter 35, that the Christian people ran through the sea as if through dry land, and they filled everything with *lamps and tapers*, leaving evidence of joy everywhere when the body of the Blessed Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his powerful preaching.</note> was transferred.

Gregory Nazianzenus <note>One of the "Cappadocian Fathers" of the 4th century.</note>, in his Oration on the praises of Caesarius, considers it part of the pious procession in which his brother's body was carried out that their mother bore lit *torches*.

The Centurion whom Saint Peter converted was buried as he was dying—with all the Christians gathered, along with the Priest Eunomius—with *lit tapers*; as Metaphrastes <note>Symeon Metaphrastes, a famous 10th-century compiler of the lives of saints.</note> relates in his Life, found in the works of Laurentius Surius <note>A 16th-century German monk who published a massive collection of the lives of the saints.</note> under the date of September 13th.

Blessed Jerome mentions *lamps* and *tapers* when he describes the illustrious procession of Paula in these words (Volume 1, Epistle 22, chapter 13, to Eustochium): "*Paula*," he says, "*was moved by the hands of Bishops, who placed their necks under the bier, while other High Priests <note>original: "Pontifices," referring here to bishops or high-ranking clergy.</note> carried lamps and tapers before her; others led the choirs of those singing psalms, etc.*"

Regarding the Emperor Constantine, Eusebius <note>The "Father of Church History" and biographer of Constantine the Great.</note> writes these things in his *Life*, Book 4: "*The corpse*," he says, "*placed in a small chest and covered with a purple covering, was brought to Constantinople, and in the basilica under the highest...*"

# CHAPTER LXXXI.

## *Whether, and by what means, the spirits being purified are helped by wax candles and lit lights.*

<margin>1.</margin>
One might reasonably suspect that the spirits being purified <note>original: "purgandos Spiritus" — referring to souls in Purgatory undergoing cleansing before entering Heaven.</note> are helped by lit wax candles and lights, based on the custom observed around the dead. For this practice is neither a small thing, nor is it simple. Soon after they have breathed their last breath, candles are placed by the corpse—sometimes many, sometimes few, according to the means of the living. They then adorn the funeral procession. They are placed atop their graves. They are used in sacrifices <note>original: "Sacrificijs" — in this context, the "Sacrifice of the Mass," specifically Requiem Masses for the dead.</note> and prayers which are performed for them in the Church on the third, seventh, thirtieth, and anniversary day. Often, besides these, they are lit in temples to the honor of God in memory of the deceased, sometimes out of the piety of the living, and sometimes according to the last will of the dead.

<margin>2.</margin>
Nor are these things observed only in our own times. They were also observed by the ancients and in the times of our ancestors; and indeed among men distinguished by piety, learning, wisdom, and nobility. At the funeral of the **Blessed Virgin**, *wax candles and burning torches* were carried before her, as Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus Xanthopoulos (c. 1256–1335), a Greek historian of the Byzantine Church.</note> testifies in Book 2, Chapter 22.

Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458), an influential theologian and church historian.</note> reports in Book 5, Chapter 35, that the Christian people ran through the sea as if through land; they filled everything with *lamps and wax candles*; everywhere they left signs of joy when the body of **Blessed Chrysostom** <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407); his relics were famously translated (moved) to Constantinople in 438 AD.</note> was moved.

**Gregory of Nazianzus**, in his *Oration on the Praises of Caesarius*, believes it belongs to the pious procession by which his brother’s body was carried out, that their mother carried lit *torches*.

The centurion whom **Saint Peter** converted was buried, upon his death, with all the Christians gathered together with the priest Eunomius, with *lit wax candles*; as Metaphrastes <note>Simeon Metaphrastes, a 10th-century Byzantine hagiographer who compiled standard lives of the saints.</note> tells in his *Life*, found in Laurentius Surius <note>A 16th-century Carthusian monk who published a famous collection of the "Lives of the Saints."</note>, on September 13th.

**Blessed Jerome** mentions *lamps and wax candles* while describing the illustrious funeral of Paula with these words, Volume 1, Epistle 22, Chapter 13, to Eustochium: *Paula,* he says, *was moved by the hands of Bishops who placed their necks under the bier, while other prelates carried lamps and wax candles before her; others led the choirs of those singing psalms, etc.*

Concerning the **Emperor Constantine**, Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), the "Father of Church History" and biographer of Constantine the Great.</note> writes these things in his *Life*, Book 4: *The corpse,* he says, *placed in a small coffin and covered with a purple cloth, was brought to Constantinople, and in the basilica under the highest...*

<header>OF INFESTED PLACES</header>

<margin>3.</margin>
Next, it is certain and most famous that the practice of these <note>Referring to "peregrinationes" or pilgrimages mentioned in the preceding arguments.</note> has existed. This is proven by what has already been said, but especially by the example of **Christ**, who is said to have gone up to *Jerusalem* with his parents according to the custom when he was twelve years old; and thereafter by the example of those who flourished in every age. For there has been no era that does not provide examples of *Pilgrims*. Out of each era, we bring forward one or two.

The *First* [age] provides those we have already reviewed: Peter, Paul, Clement, and Ignatius.

The *Second* provides Origen, who, according to the testimony of Eusebius (Book 6, Chapter 11), traveled to *Rome*; and Saint Alexander, who *made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem*, as Jerome records in his book *On Illustrious Men* regarding Alexander.

The *Third* provides Constantine and his mother Helena. Of these, *she visited these holy places*, while he, by building a magnificent temple in Jerusalem on Mount Calvary, invited Christians to visit those same places, as witnessed by Nicephorus (Book 8, Chapter 50; and Book 9, Chapter 32).

The *Fourth* provides Eudoxia and Jerome. Both of them traveled through Palestine for the sake of religion. Indeed, she, not content with this, contributed ten thousand *sextarii* <note>A Roman unit of volume, roughly equivalent to a pint; thus, a very large donation of oil.</note> of oil for the use of the lamps in the Holy Temple, as Zonaras testifies in Volume 3, regarding Theodosius.

The *Fifth* provides almost the entire Christian world, which the piety of the Emperor Justinian attracted by building many temples and adorning them with the relics of the Saints.

The *Sixth* age offers, among others, the most Christian Kings of Gaul, Clovis and Childeric. The latter, along with many others, visited the tomb of *Saint Germain* after he learned that a paralytic had been restored to health there, as Gregory of Tours writes (Book 5, Chapter 32). The former, about to fight against the Goths, hoped for a more certain victory if he requested the Saint's patronage by undertaking a pilgrimage in his own name to the relics of Saint Martin. This is also from Gregory of Tours (Book 2, Chapter 37).

<margin>4.</margin>
Thirdly, it is certain that *these pilgrimages were not fruitless*. Did not the Emperor *Theodosius* obtain victory against Eugenius after he had first *lain prostrate at the tombs of the Saints*? Eusebius records this (Book 11, Chapter 33). Does not Sidonius Apollinaris, the Bishop of Auvergne, writing to Blessed Jerome (Book 1, Epistle 5), ingenuously confess that *he set out to the threshold of the Apostles* <term>Threshold of the Apostles: a traditional term for a pilgrimage to the tombs of St. Peter and St. Paul in Rome</term> *in the hope of obtaining health, and that his wish was granted*? There are infinite examples for this argument in Augustine (Book 22 of *The City of God*, Chapter 8). Regarding those who visited the relics of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, Blessed Ambrose writes thus (Epistle 85): *You have known*, he says, *or rather you yourselves have seen, many cleansed who were vexed by demons; very many also, when the garments of the Saints...*
