->### PART THREE.<-

[They] were touched by his hands and freed from the infirmities from which they suffered. We omit domestic and daily examples.

<margin>5.</margin>
Thus, there is no doubt that [pilgrimages] are joined with excellent virtues. For this reason, our ancestors undertook various journeys; they invited others to undertake them; and they commended those who had undertaken them religiously. Indeed, why would they consider themselves to have less piety and religion unless they had adored **Christ** in those places where (as Saint Jerome speaks) the Gospel most brightly "flashed forth from the cross"? <note>original: "Euangelium de patibulo coruscauit." Jerome uses this vivid imagery to describe how the light of the Gospel radiates from the sites of Christ's suffering.</note>

<margin>6.</margin>
Fifthly, there is no doubt that those who bind themselves to God by a vow to undertake these **Pilgrimages** are free from fault—indeed, they perform a deed pleasing to God. For if a thing is good in itself to perform, can we not bind ourselves by a vow to do it? Whatever is good, if mortals bind themselves by a vow to perform it, it is rendered even better, and becomes more pleasing and acceptable to God.

<margin>7.</margin>
A vow, in truth, ensures that what was previously a matter of free choice must necessarily be performed once it has been promised to God. Therefore, a supreme necessity lies upon those who undertake **Pilgrimages** out of a vow to fulfill them. For this reason, Saint Jerome excellently exhorts Rusticus (in *Epistle 46*) to fulfill the Pilgrimage he had vowed to the holy places of *Palestine*. "Render," he says, "what you vowed in the presence of the Lord, lest you be snatched away <note>i.e., by death</note> before you fulfill your promise." Let this be established as the sixth point.

<margin>8.</margin>
From this it is now clear that those who do not fulfill the **Pilgrimages** they promised to God are not free from sin. An unfaithful and foolish promise displeases God, as seen in *Ecclesiastes 5*; and certain people are said to incur damnation because they "have made void their first faith"—that is, they did not perform the vows they made to God, as noted in *1 Timothy 5*. All these points are certain.

<margin>9.</margin> <note>The marginal number is partially obscured by an ink smudge in the original manuscript.</note>
But what if someone should depart from this life while the **Pilgrimages** they vowed remain unfulfilled? Would they suffer some loss of their salvation because of this? And if their salvation is not yet despaired of, can the living undertake **Pilgrimages** in their name, for the benefit of the deceased, and thus satisfy their vows? Finally, is this fulfillment of vows so necessary that as long as they have not been paid, the wretched souls are excluded from the kingdom of heaven? These are the principal chapters of the present argument.

<margin>10.</margin>
The first chapter must be distinguished by circumstances. For it happens that a promised Pilgrimage remains unfulfilled either through some fault of the living, or through no fault of their own. If no fault of the living intervened, they neither suffer the loss of their salvation when they depart from this life, nor do they suffer any penalty on this account. However, if a fault intervened, [it must be judged] according to the quality...

## CHAPTER 81.

### *Whether, and by what means, the spirits being purified are helped by wax tapers and lit lights.*

<margin>1.</margin>
One might not unfairly suspect that the spirits in need of purification <note>The author refers to the "purgandi Spiritus," or souls in Purgatory, who were believed to undergo a period of cleansing after death.</note> are aided by the use of lit wax tapers and lights in the rituals surrounding the dead. Indeed, this practice is neither insignificant nor simple. For as soon as they have breathed their last, several candles—sometimes more, sometimes fewer, according to the means of the living—are placed by the corpse. They then adorn the funeral procession. They are placed upon their tombs. They are employed in the Sacrifices <note>This refers to the Requiem Mass, or the "Sacrifice of the Altar."</note> and prayers which are performed for them in the Church on the third, seventh, and thirtieth days, as well as on the anniversary of their passing. Often, beyond these occasions, they are lit in the temples to the honor of God in memory of the deceased, sometimes out of the piety of the living and sometimes according to the last will of the dead.

<margin>2.</margin>
These customs are not only observed in our own times. They were also observed in ancient times and in the days of our ancestors, even among men illustrious for their piety, learning, wisdom, and nobility. At the funeral of the Blessed Virgin, Nicephorus <note>Nicephorus Callistus, a 14th-century Byzantine church historian.</note> testifies in Book 2, Chapter 22, that *wax tapers and burning torches* <note>original: "Cereos ardentesque Faces"</note> were carried in the lead.

Theodoret <note>Theodoret of Cyrus, a 5th-century bishop and historian.</note> reports in Book 5, Chapter 35, that the Christian people "ran across the sea as if across land," filling everything with *lamps and wax tapers* <note>original: "Lampadibus & Cereis"</note> and leaving signs of joy everywhere when the body of the Blessed Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom, the "Golden-Mouthed" Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> was translated <note>The "translation" refers to the formal moving of a saint's relics to a new location.</note>.

Gregory Nazianzen, in his *Oration in Praise of Caesarius*, considers it part of the pious procession by which his brother's body was carried out that their mother carried lit *torches*.

The Centurion whom Saint Peter converted, as he was dying and after all the Christians had gathered with the Priest Eunomius, was buried with *lit wax tapers*; as Metaphrastes <note>Symeon the Metaphrast, a famous collector of hagiographies.</note> narrates in his *Life*, found in the works of Laurentius Surius under the date of September 13th.

Blessed Jerome mentions *lamps and wax tapers* while describing the illustrious funeral procession of Paula <note>Saint Paula of Rome, a disciple of St. Jerome.</note> with these words in Volume 1, *Epistle 22, chapter 13, to Eustochium: "Paula," he says, "was moved by the hands of Bishops, who placed their necks beneath the bier, while other prelates carried lamps and wax tapers before her; others led the choirs of those singing psalms," etc.* <note>original: "Paula, inquit, translata Episcoporum manibus... cùm alij Pontifices Lampades Cereosque præferrent..."</note>

Eusebius writes these things concerning the Emperor Constantine in his *Life*, Book 4: *The corpse, he says, placed in a small casket and covered with a purple shroud, was brought to Constantinople, and in the basilica under the highest...*

They are also excellent *monuments* to remind the living of great matters. They are *proofs of piety* by which the living testify to their love toward the deceased. Finally, they are *sometimes welcome aids and reliefs for the spirits being purified*. This last point is our subject here.

<margin>5.</margin>
But when do they benefit them? This must be defined by the purpose of those who set out the *Lights* and light the *Wax Tapers*, not from the Tapers or Lights themselves. Wax tapers, of themselves, serve to drive away darkness. Whatever other purposes they have are obtained according to the will of men—sometimes the living, sometimes the dead—who can give purposes to *Wax Tapers* and *Lights*, just as they can to all *indifferent matters* <term>adiaphora: actions or objects that are religiously neutral, neither commanded nor forbidden by God</term>.

<margin>6.</margin>
And just as they can wish for *Wax Tapers* to serve various ends and light them for various causes, so too can they wish to benefit those spirits being purified who can be helped by the intercessions <term>suffragia: prayers, indulgences, or pious acts offered on behalf of the souls of the deceased</term> of men. Why should they not benefit those who have died piously in Christ through a zeal for piety, if they often serve profane things to the heavy detriment of the living?

...distributed for the deceased, it then benefits the deceased when it is used for the needs of the poor; likewise, let lit **Wax Tapers** benefit the deceased when they are lit for the well-being of the departed to observe and amplify the worship of God.

<margin>8.</margin>
Hence it is that Blessed Athanasius <note>Athanasius of Alexandria (c. 296–373), a Greek Church Father and defender of Orthodoxy.</note> said most excellently in his *Sermon on those who have fallen asleep* (cited by Damascene <note>John of Damascus, an 8th-century monk and polymath.</note> in the sermon *That those who have departed from here in faith are greatly helped by sacred operations and the benefits of the living*) that **Oil and Wax** bring the greatest reward and benefit the deceased when they take on the nature of a burnt offering. For these are acceptable to God, and they bring back with them the greatest reward. For Oil and Wax are a burnt offering <note>original: "holocaustum"</note>; moreover, the unbloody sacrifice is an offering of atonement; but the benefit bestowed upon the poor is proof of every good reward.”*

<margin>9.</margin>
And a Christian man cannot doubt that **Wax Tapers** lit for this purpose benefit the spirits who must be cleansed <note>A reference to the souls in Purgatory who undergo purification before entering heaven.</note>. For if alms distributed to the poor benefit these spirits when they are given by the living for their well-being, why would wax tapers lit for the honor and worship of God Most High not benefit them as well?

<margin>10.</margin>
We have taught elsewhere that prayer primarily benefits these deceased spirits. Yet **Wax Tapers** lit by Christians for the sake of the deceased are either a type of prayer themselves, or they are certainly not without prayer. Therefore, they will benefit them.

<margin>11.</margin>
Entirely in the same way as Fasting—which, since it causes the affliction of the flesh *in itself*, benefits the living rather than the dead—it nevertheless benefits the dead if the living wish for it to benefit them by way of a <term>suffrage: a spiritual work (like prayer or fasting) performed by the living and offered to God to lessen the punishment of souls in Purgatory</term>. Thus, although the **Lights and Wax Tapers** lit by the living do not benefit *in themselves*, they can still result in the benefit and profit of the deceased according to the will and intention of the living.

<margin>12.</margin>
No good deed can be undertaken by Christians that cannot—if they so desire and no sin stands in the way—be bestowed for the profit of their neighbors and the deceased. But it is a certain good to light **Wax Tapers** for the glory of God and the worship of the Divine Name. They can, therefore, confer this as a help and consolation to the deceased, and not in vain.

<margin>13.</margin>
From what has been said, it is gathered that the spirits who must be cleansed receive fruit from lit **Lights and Wax Tapers** in two ways. First: if they themselves, while they were still among the living, provided the funds for this purpose, and [bequeathed] **Oil, Wax, and Lights**...

# CHAPTER LXXXII.

### *That our Ancestors placed the greatest protection for helping the Spirits of the faithfully departed, above all else, in the Sacrifice of the Mass.*

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial M with floral patterns.</image-desc> We have explained the ways by which Spirits to be cleansed <note>Referring to souls in Purgatory.</note> are freed from punishments, and the living are freed from the disturbance caused by them. One thing must be added to what has been said. It must be shown, namely, that *the Sacrifice of the Mass holds the chief place above all others*. For although Catholics easily understand this, because there are some who are so far from believing it that they rather think it is very harmful <note>A reference to Protestant Reformers who rejected the idea of the Mass as a propitiatory sacrifice for the dead.</note>—or at least so that we may stop their mouths—a few things must be added in favor of the **Mass**.

<margin>2.</margin>
Truly, we shall be content with one, *one* argument, which is taken from the *example of our Ancestors*. These men declare the excellence and dignity of the Mass in many ways, *above all other* protections by which the faithfully departed are helped.

<margin>3.</margin>
First, they demonstrate this by the fact that *in the very age of the Apostles they offered the Sacrifice of the Altar for the deceased*. *“We make offerings for the deceased on the anniversary day,”* says Tertullian <note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155–220 AD), an early Christian author from Carthage.</note>, a most ancient writer, in *The Military Crown* <note>original: "De Corona Militis"</note>. He has similar things in his book *On Monogamy*, and in *Exhortation to Chastity*, and in the second book *To His Wife*. But the Liturgies of James the Apostle and Mark the Evangelist prove this even more clearly; they commend the needs of both the living and the dead to God.

<margin>4.</margin>
Second, they demonstrate this because *they taught that the Sacrifice should be offered even for the deceased*. One may indeed gather this from the custom received from our Ancestors; however, the speech of Saint Clement <note>Clement of Rome, traditionally the fourth Pope.</note> is also eloquent here, in Book 6 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, chapter 19. *“For the brothers,”* he says, *“who have died in the Lord, offer [sacrifices] in your Church.”* Added to these is Saint Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan and influential Latin Doctor of the Church.</note>, who in Book 2, Letter 8, to Faustinus, regarding the death of his sister,

> *It was not in vain,* he says, *(Homily 3 on Philippians) sanctioned by the Apostles that in the celebration of the venerable Mysteries, a memory should be made of those who have departed from this world.*

He says these same things in so many words in *Homily 96 to the People of Antioch*. Blessed Augustine seems to agree with Chrysostom. For he says this in *Sermon 32 on the Words of the Apostle*:
> *The entire Church observes this, as handed down by the Fathers: that for those who have died in the communion of the body and blood of Christ, when they are commemorated in their own place at the Sacrifice itself, prayer is offered; and it is commemorated that the Sacrifice is also offered for them.*

<margin>6.</margin>
Fourthly, they thought that this benefit should by no means be delayed, but should be performed immediately for the salvation of the deceased. Indeed, the **Sacrifice of the Mass** was performed for the deceased even before their bodies were committed to the grave, with the bodies present, which urged those praying to pray more intently. Dionysius the Areopagite teaches this, as Durantus <note>Jean-Etienne Durant, a 16th-century liturgical scholar.</note> testifies in *On the Rites of the Church*, Book 1, Chapter 23. Thus Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History."</note> attests in Book 4 of the *Life of Constantine*, Chapter 71, that Constantine was buried with the Liturgy. St. Bernard says of Malachy, while he was not yet buried (*Life of Malachy*, Chapter 18):
> *Meanwhile,* he says, *the funeral rites are prepared, the Sacrifice is offered for him, and all things are completed according to custom with the highest devotion.*

<margin>7.</margin>
Fifthly, this was constantly celebrated by them at **All Times and in All Places**. The testimony of Damascene <note>St. John of Damascus, an 8th-century monk and theologian.</note> is most clear on this. This is his prayer (from the *Oration on those who have migrated from here in the faith*, etc.):
> *Moreover, the divine Apostles,* he says, *disciples of the Savior—who began to preach by the word throughout the entire circle of the world what they had seen with their own eyes—decreed that a memory should be held of those who have fallen asleep in the faith during the awesome, unpolluted, and life-giving Sacraments. The Apostolic Church and the Church of God still observes this firmly and even without contradiction from the ends of the earth to its furthest reaches, and from that time until the present, and even unto the end of the world.*

<summary>This page cites various Church Fathers and historical figures—including Chrysostom, Augustine, and John of Damascus—to argue that the tradition of offering Masses for the dead is an apostolic practice observed universally and immediately upon death.</summary>

<header>CONCERNING TROUBLED PLACES</header>

From the same chapter, Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a prominent scholar and bishop in Visigothic Spain.</note> shows that the custom of **Sacrificing for the deceased** is an **Apostolic Tradition**, using these words (from Book 1 of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 18): *To offer the Sacrifice for the rest of the faithful departed, or to pray for them—because it is observed throughout the whole world—we believe was handed down by the Apostles themselves.* <note>original: "Sacrificium pro fidelium defunctorum requie offerre... ab ipsis Apostolis traditum sit."</note>

But here, too, the **Councils** serve us; they were celebrated in almost every province of the Christian world and make excellent mention of the Sacrifice for the dead as a most accepted and common practice. For Africa, there is the 3rd Council of Carthage (chapter 29) and the 4th (chapter 79). For Spain, the 1st Council of Braga (chapters 34 and 39). For Gaul, the Council of Chalon-sur-Saône, as recorded in the Canon: *It has seemed good* <note>original: "Visum est," a standard opening for conciliar decrees.</note> (from *On Consecration*, distinction 1). For Germany, the Council of Worms (chapter 10). For Italy, the 6th Council under Pope Symmachus. For Greece, chapter 69 of the *Chapters Collected from the Greek Synods* by Martin, Bishop of Braga.

<margin>8.</margin> Sixthly, that every year on the very anniversary of their falling asleep <note>The term "falling asleep" (dormitio) was the common early Christian metaphor for death.</note>, they repeated the **Sacrifice of the Mass** for the deceased. Tertullian mentions this custom in *On the Soldier's Crown*; as does John of Damascus in his *Sermon on the Faithful Departed*. Gregory Nazianzen <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers."</note> says the same in his 10th Oration in praise of Caesarius: *And some honors indeed we have paid,* he says, *but others we shall give, offering annual honors and commemorations.*

<margin>9.</margin> Seventhly, that they offered this host <note>From the Latin "hostia," referring to the bread/body of Christ offered in the Mass.</note> not only on the annual days of their death, but also on the **third, ninth, and fortieth days**, as the previously cited John of Damascus testifies. Furthermore, Ephrem <note>St. Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), a prolific hymnodist and theologian.</note> requested in his will that this Sacrifice be offered for him on the thirtieth day. Regarding the fortieth day, Saint Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan.</note> speaks thus in *On the Death of Theodosius*: *We have recently lamented the death of that Prince, and now we celebrate the Fortieth Day, with Prince Honorius standing by the sacred altars; just as Joseph paid the duties of burial to his father Jacob for forty days, so also does this man pay the funeral rites to his father Theodosius.* Saint Remigius, in his will—which we read recorded in various books (says Durandus <note>Guillaume Durand (c. 1230–1296), a famous liturgical writer.</note> in Book 2 of *On the Rites of the Catholic Church*, chapter 43)—bequeathed a vineyard and certain other things to his grandson Agarimerus, so that an **Offering** might be made by his Fathers at the sacred altars for his commemoration on all feast days and Sundays.

<margin>10.</margin> Eighthly, that they did not think this benefit should be easily denied to the deceased. For although certain other things might be denied to those performing penance, the Sacrifice of the Mass was not denied to them when they died. Concerning these, the 2nd Council of Arles (Canon 12) holds: *Regarding those who have departed this life while performing penance, it has pleased us that no one should be sent away void of communion; but because he honored his penance, his Offering (that is, the Mass for him) shall be received.* The 4th Council of Carthage (chapter 79) decreed: *Penitents, if by chance while on a journey, or*

or at sea, their memory should be commended with prayers and offerings. This same rule was established in the First Council of Vaison (chapter 2) and the Second Council of Vaison (chapter 4). <note>Vaison-la-Romaine is a town in southeastern France where several early church councils were held.</note>

<margin>9.</margin>
Ninthly, that *whenever they wished to punish someone with a heavy penalty, they deprived the deceased of the benefit of this sacrifice.* <note>Deprivation of a funeral Mass was used as a posthumous disciplinary measure.</note> Blessed Cyprian <note>Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an important Early Christian writer and bishop.</note> teaches this in Book 1, Epistle 9, with these words: *Our predecessors as Bishops,* he says, *wholesomely decreed that no brother departing this life should nominate a cleric to a guardianship or trusteeship. And if anyone should do this, no offering should be made for him, nor should the Sacrifice be celebrated for his falling asleep. For he does not deserve to be named at the altar of God in the priest’s prayer, who wished to call away priests and their Levite ministers from the altar.* <note>original: "ne qui frater excedens... non offerretur pro ipso." In this context, "Levites" refers to deacons.</note> Likewise, the Council of Braga (Canon 35) forbade the *Sacrifice to be made for those who had laid violent hands upon themselves; or for Catechumens who had departed from this life.* <note>Catechumens were those receiving instruction in the faith but who had not yet been baptized.</note>

<margin>10.</margin>
Tenthly, that *they testified that this practice is uniquely profitable to the deceased.* Blessed Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), Archbishop of Constantinople, famed for his eloquence.</note> says in Homily 21 on the Acts of the Apostles: *It was not in vain,* he says, *that it was ordained by the Apostles that in the celebration of the venerable Mysteries, a memory be made of those who have departed from here. They knew that much gain and much utility comes to them from this.* He says the same things in as many words in Homily 69 to the People of Antioch. Blessed Augustine speaks to the same effect in the *Enchiridion* (chapter 110): *It is not to be denied,* he says, *that the souls of the deceased are aided by the piety of their living friends, when the Sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them.* <note>original: "Sacrificium Mediatoris." Augustine refers to the Mass as the sacrifice of Christ, the mediator between God and man.</note> Theophylact, commenting on chapter 12 of Luke, says the same: *The offerings and distributions which are made for the deceased,* he says, *are of no small benefit even to those who have died in grave sins.* <note>Theophylact of Ohrid (c. 1055–1107), a prominent Byzantine commentator.</note> Blessed Gregory, in Book 4 of the *Dialogues* (chapter 55), says the same: *The sacred Oblation of the saving host,* he says, *is often accustomed to help souls even after death; so much so that sometimes the souls of the deceased themselves seem to seek it.* <note>original: "hostiæ salutaris." Gregory the Great (c. 540–604 AD) emphasizes the supernatural power of the Mass.</note> Cyril of Jerusalem, in his fifth *Mystagogic Catechesis*, says the same: *We believe it to be the greatest help for the souls for whom the prayer of that holy and most awesome Sacrifice, which is placed upon the altar, is offered.* John the Almoner says the same in the 4th Thesis of this chapter. <note>John the Almoner (d. 619 AD) was the Patriarch of Alexandria, known for his extraordinary charity.</note>

<margin>11.</margin>
Eleventhly, that *they either offered this specifically for those dearest to them or desired it to be offered.* Blessed Ambrose, in his *Oration on the death of his brother Satyrus*, says: *To You now, almighty God, I commend this innocent soul; to You I bring my victim. Receive, graciously and serenely, this brotherly gift, the Sacrifice of a priest.* <note>original: "Sacrificium sacerdotis."</note> This same Ambrose, in his orations on the passing of Theodosius and Valentinian, promises that he will sacrifice for their souls. St. Augustine, in Book 9 of the *Confessions*, writing of his mother Monica, says: *Let as many as read this remember, at Your altar, Your servant Monica, with Patricius, formerly her husband.* The examples cited in Thesis 4 of Chapter 76 serve here as well.

<margin>14.</margin> Twelfthly, that the deceased themselves requested this benefit of the *Sacrifice* <note>original: "Sacrificij"; referring here to the Sacrifice of the Mass or the Eucharist.</note> to be bestowed upon them. Augustine writes the same thing concerning his mother in Book 9 of his *Confessions*: *She did not command us these things,* he says, *but only desired that a memory of her be made at your altar, which she had served without missing a single day.* <note>Augustine’s mother, Saint Monica, famously asked her sons to remember her at the altar rather than worrying about her physical burial place.</note> Ephrem the Syrian <note>A 4th-century deacon and prolific hymn writer from Mesopotamia.</note> asked for the same Sacrifice to be made for himself; as did the Venerable Bede; and likewise Queen Margaret of Scotland, as was demonstrated in Thesis 4, Chapter 76.

<margin>15.</margin> Thirteenthly, that *while they make mention of the intercessory prayers by which the dead are helped, they place this [the Sacrifice] before and above all others,* just as Chrysostom and Augustine do: the former in Homily 3 on the Epistle to the Philippians, the latter in Chapter 110 of the *Enchiridion* <note>A handbook on Christian faith, hope, and love written by St. Augustine.</note>. The Council of Florence follows both of these in the *Union with the Armenians*, so that for this reason Cyril of Jerusalem, in his fifth *Mystagogical Catechesis*, said that the greatest aid to souls is the supplication of that holy and awe-inspiring Sacrifice which is placed upon the altar. <note>The Council of Florence (1431–1449) attempted to reunite the Latin and Greek churches; the "Union with the Armenians" refers to a specific decree from this council.</note>

### THE METHODS FOLLOW BY WHICH
### action must be taken against the disturbances of the spirits of
### damned men.

Having completed and examined the twofold methods—by which we partly fight against the spirits of demons, and partly are freed from the disturbances brought by spirits who are to be purged <note>original: "purgandi Spiritus"; referring to souls in Purgatory who require purification.</note>—it remains for us to discuss how we should counter the infesting spirits of damned men. We examine this in the following few chapters. This is the first in the order of the entire Disputation.

# CHAPTER LXXXIII.

### That the living do not lack a means by which they may free themselves from the disturbance brought by the spirits of damned men.

<margin>1.</margin> There are those who believe there is either no way, or certainly one unknown to mortals, by which the living can free themselves from the ferocity <note>original: "efferationem"; referring to the hostile or wild behavior of malevolent spirits.</note> and disturbance of the spirits of damned men. And perhaps not without reason. For neither among

### PART THREE. 295

These methods seem useful for driving away the Spirits of Demons; however, they are not the same as those used to assist the souls of those being purified <note>original: "purgandorum animæ"; referring to souls in Purgatory who require prayer and sacrifice to reach heaven.</note>. This is because the Ghosts <note>original: "Spectra"</note> of damned men differ greatly from those other types of spirits, just as they differ from demons.

<margin>2.</margin>
Nor do any other reasons seem to remain here. For what are they? Are they the ones we mentioned at the beginning? Curses? Beatings? Drawn swords? Fires? etc. But since these have no power against any spirits, what progress will they make against the Spirits of damned men?

<margin>3.</margin>
Nevertheless, from three points—unless we are mistaken—it can be gathered that the living do not lack their own weapons with which to shield and defend themselves from the harassment of these Spirits. First, from a comparison of these with other Spirits. Second, from the condition of the society that exists among Christians. Third, from those who appear to concur with and contribute their efforts in any way to the troubles brought by the spirits of the damned.

<margin>4.</margin>
The spirits that are the subject of our current dispute occupy a middle ground, in this manner of harassment, between the souls of men being purified and the damned spirits of Demons. Since, therefore, we free ourselves from the harassment of the former through the duties of charity performed on their behalf <note>i.e., through prayers and the Mass for the dead.</note>, and from the latter through the excellent protections of the Christian religion <note>i.e., exorcism and spiritual defenses.</note>, shall we not be able to shake off the harassment of these [spirits of the damned]?

<margin>5.</margin>
Although the desire of these spirits to cause trouble might be much greater than that of the souls being purified, it is still not greater than that of the Demons. And although their powers are great, they are nevertheless far inferior to the powers of the Demons. If, therefore, we have power against the latter, shall we not have it against the former?

<margin>6.</margin>
Such is the condition of the society of Christians that it constitutes a kind of Commonwealth <note>original: "Respublica"; the author uses this term to describe the Church as a structured, legal community with rights and defenses.</note>. This is indicated by many things, but most often by the title "Kingdom of Heaven" in the Holy Scriptures, by which the Lord identifies it. Therefore, since every Commonwealth has the right to shield and defend itself against enemies, shall this be denied to the Commonwealth so excellently established by Christ the Lord? Shall this society alone be unable to defend itself against its enemies or free itself from their harassment? Or perhaps these Spirits are not enemies? Why then are they troublesome? Why do they begrudge us peace? Why do they torture us with terrifying sights <note>original: "terriculamentis"; specific phenomena intended to frighten the living.</note>?

<margin>7.</margin>
Someone might say: "These spirits are not subject to the living; they are outside the Church of Christ." This is true. And for that reason, we do not deal with them as if they were subject to us, but as enemies; who, although

### CONCERNING HAUNTED PLACES

...although they are not subject to us by right <note>The author is using a legal framework here: since spirits are not human citizens, they aren't under human laws, but their "illegal" harassment gives humans a "natural right" to evict them.</note>; nevertheless, they make themselves subject to us by this very fact: that they are bothersome to us. Thus, it is permitted by natural law to cast off from our necks those troubles which they bring upon us without right.

<margin>8.</margin> There seem to be three factors in total *who concur in these disturbances*. First, the souls of the deceased themselves, who exhaust us with the noises and terrors they stir up. Second, the Demons, whose work it is to assemble and form the bodies that serve these Spirits <note>A common Renaissance belief was that ghosts were "clothed" in bodies made of thick air or elemental matter by demonic agency.</note>. And third, God; by whose permission or command everything happens here. By what reasoning, then, shall we be denied the right to vindicate ourselves from this trouble?

<margin>9.</margin> It has already been demonstrated that these Spirits possess neither the strength nor the malice that Demons possess. Therefore, if we are able to free ourselves from the harassment of Demons—as we surely are—we will certainly be able to release ourselves from the infestation and insults of these spirits.

<margin>10.</margin> Or do we perhaps lack the strength against Demons? On the contrary, the most sufficient powers over Demons have been bestowed by the Lord of Demons and of all creatures. *Behold, says the Lord, I have given you the power to tread upon Demons.* <note>original: "Ecce, inquit Dominus, dedi vobis potestatem calcandi super Daemones." A paraphrase of Luke 10:19.</note>

<margin>11.</margin> Nor is God Himself an obstacle to us here. For although these Spirits are troublesome through their disturbances—sometimes by His permission, sometimes by His command—they are troublesome in such a way that just as their occurrence depends on His will, so too their cessation must depend on it. Through our urgent prayers, He can mercifully grant their departure, just as He permitted their presence when His justice demanded it. But let us move to the methods. First, we shall exclude the false methods, then prove the true ones.

### PART THREE

...against those of the spirits to be purified; or against some others. We include the matter in two Assertions. The first must be explained in this chapter.

<margin>2.</margin>
It is this: *The methods we use against the disturbances brought by spirits who are to be purified* <note>original: "purgandis Spiritibus"—referring to souls in Purgatory who supposedly haunt the living to ask for prayers.</note> *must by no means be used against the spirits of damned men.* The reason for this Assertion is that these spirits are not bothersome for the same reason as those being purified; nor, even if they were, would it be permitted to challenge and attack them using these same methods.

<margin>3.</margin>
The reason why the spirits of damned men are bothersome was demonstrated above, in Chapter Thirteen. Indeed, no one should doubt that they do not have the same purpose as those being purified. Those to be purified are persistent so that they may be helped by the works of the living <note>Refers to "suffrages"—prayers, alms, or Masses offered to shorten a soul's time in Purgatory.</note>; but these damned souls have no hope of salvation. For how can those who despair of the possibility of being helped ask to be helped?

<margin>4.</margin>
Furthermore, if after death they were not immediately snatched away to their punishments; or if, being snatched away, these spirits did not perceive the Judge's sentence before the future Universal Judgment of all mortals; or even if, after the sentence was passed at death, they hoped it might be changed at some time, or at least mitigated: then they might perhaps return to the living and, with their commotion and trouble, implore the help of the living, either so they would not be condemned to the punishments they deserved, or so they might be relieved from those they endure. But none of these things have any place among the unhappy damned.

<margin>5.</margin>
Immediately after death, their merited punishments follow them. It is easy in the sight of God, it says in Ecclesiastes 11, *on the day of death to reward everyone according to their ways.* Job says in chapter 21: *They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they go down to the underworld.* The rich man Dives, as soon as he died, was buried in hell, *Luke 16*, and immediately in his torments he uttered this cry: *I am tortured in this flame.* If the Blessed man immediately follows his glory, should the punishments of the wicked be delayed for a long time? *After you have finished your day,* says Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father.</note> in Homily 37 on Matthew, *judgment and punishment follow.* See Francisco Suárez <note>A prominent Spanish Jesuit philosopher and theologian (1548–1617).</note>, Volume 2, on the Third Part of St. Thomas, Dispute 52.

<margin>6.</margin>
Thus, the Judge's sentence is passed immediately after death, and is not delayed until the common Resurrection of the flesh—regardless of what Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325) whose views on the timing of judgment were later considered non-standard.</note> says in Book 7 of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 21. The Apostle Paul says beautifully in Hebrews 9: *It is appointed for all to die once, and after this, the judgment.* Now, says Saint Augustine in Book 2 of *The Origin of the Soul*, chapter 4: *One believes healthily and most correctly that souls are judged when they have left their bodies, before they come to that judgment in which they must be judged once their bodies have been restored.* Men enlightened by God, says Damascene <note>St. John of Damascus (c. 675–749), a Syrian monk and theologian.</note> in his Oration on the Deceased, say...

->### ON HAUNTED PLACES<-

because when we breathe our last <note>original: "exhalamus spiritum"—literally to exhale the spirit, meaning to die.</note>; as if on a scale, human works are tested. And if punishments follow immediately upon death; can the sentence, which precedes the punishments, be delayed?

<margin>7.</margin> Nor can there be hope for the wretched that there will ever be an end to their torments, because the fire that tortures them is eternal; or that the bitterness of the punishments might be mitigated, because just as the sentence is irrevocable, so is the punishment constant and perpetual. Who would boldly say that the punishment of one who has been handed over to it can be mitigated, or that it has any pause at certain intervals? Blessed Augustine, in his commentary on Psalm 105, asks this, seeing as that rich man did not even deserve a single drop of water? <note>A reference to the biblical parable of Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16), where a wealthy man in hell begs for a drop of water from the beggar Lazarus but is denied.</note>

<margin>8.</margin> Perhaps the wretched can doubt the Judge's <note>Referring to God</note> will. They could, if this were made known to them through Angels—whether good or evil—and if those Angels were the judges themselves. But Angels are not judges. The sentence is not brought by Angels; it is brought by Him about whose will they must not doubt, the Judge Himself, or Angels acting in the person of the Judge. It is written (2 Corinthians 5): *For we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, that every one may receive the proper things of the body, according as he hath done, whether it be good or evil.* And again (Romans 14): *We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ. And every one of us shall render account to God for himself.*

<margin>9.</margin> Since things are so, it should not be believed that the spirits of damned men return to the living for the sake of obtaining help, or that they are troublesome for the purpose of being assisted by the works of the living. But let us suppose it were so: that they were bothersome for this end, and even suppose they were ignorant of the condition of their own state. Nevertheless, it is by no means permitted for us to help them using those same methods by which we assist the spirits who are to be purified <note>original: "purgandis Spiritibus"—referring to the souls in Purgatory.</note>. This is because we cannot believe that these spirits of damned men can be helped by our prayers <note>original: "suffragijs"—formal intercessory prayers or works of mercy offered for the dead.</note> without losing our own salvation; far be it from us that we should even try to help them.

<margin>10.</margin> Such is the condition of the damned: they can never be liberated from the punishments to which they were sentenced, nor can they ever expect relief within them. Once it has been proven how certain and beyond doubt this is, and with how firm and constant a faith it must be held and defended, we shall bring an end to this Chapter.

<margin>11.</margin> First, here is the opinion of the Preacher <note>original: "Ecclesiastæ"—referring to the author of the biblical Book of Ecclesiastes.</note> in chapter 11: *If the tree falls,* he says, *to the South or to the North; in whatever place it falls, there it shall lie.* <note>Ecclesiastes 11:3. In medieval theology, the "South" often symbolized the light of Heaven and the "North" the darkness of Hell.</note> Those to be saved fall to the South; those to be damned fall to the North. Each remains in their own place: the former happy forever, the latter wretched forever. There, says Saint Bernard (in Sermon 59 of the *Small Works*), God will judge each person where He finds them; there, I say, one will remain immutably and irrevocably.

<summary>This page argues that the state of the damned is eternal and unchangeable immediately following death, citing St. Augustine and St. Bernard. It concludes that because the damned cannot be helped by prayers or rituals, the living should not attempt to assist haunting spirits identified as damned.</summary>

<margin>12.</margin>
Secondly, the Royal Prophet <note>A traditional title for King David, the presumed author of the Psalms.</note> serves our purpose here, in Psalm 6: *Turn, O Lord,* he says, *and deliver my soul; save me because of your mercy, for in death there is no one who is mindful of you: but in the underworld <note>original: "inferno"—referring to the place of the dead or hell.</note> who will confess to you?* It is as if he were to say: surely no one. By no means can it happen that someone might eventually confess to you, be converted to you, or escape the punishments of that place.

<margin>13.</margin>
Thirdly, the Prophet Isaiah supports these words in his final chapter: *Their worm,* he says (referring to the damned), *does not die, and their fire is not extinguished.* If the worm is *theirs*; if the fire is *theirs*; and if the worm itself does not die and the fire is not extinguished: it is absolutely necessary that those to whom the worm and fire belong must live miserably in the fire forever, tortured by the worm.

<margin>14.</margin>
Let us hear the Lord: *It is better for you,* He says in Mark 9, *to enter into eternal life lame, than having two feet to be sent into the Gehenna <term>Gehenna: a biblical term for the place of fiery punishment after death.</term> of unquenchable fire; where their worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished.* He says the same more clearly in Matthew 25: *Depart from me, you cursed ones, into the eternal fire, which is prepared for the Devil and his Angels.* And lest anyone believe the fire is eternal but the torture in the fire is not eternal, he adds: *And these shall go into eternal punishment; but the just into eternal life.*

<margin>15.</margin>
The disciple beloved by the Lord <note>Referring to the Apostle John, traditional author of the Book of Revelation.</note> agrees with the Lord, having been taught in the revelation divinely made to him in Revelation 20: *The Devil,* he says, *who seduced them, was sent into the lake of fire and sulfur: where the beast and the False Prophet are tormented day and night, forever and ever.*

<margin>16.</margin>
From this comes that common confession of the universal Church, along with Blessed Athanasius <note>Referring to the Athanasian Creed, a statement of Christian doctrine.</note>: *Whoever wishes to be saved, before all things it is necessary that he hold the Catholic faith.* Which faith is that? *Those who have done good works shall go into eternal life; but those who have done evil, into eternal fire.* And Innocent III says beautifully in his book *On the Contempt of the World*, chapter 10: *It is just,* he says, *that what the impious commit against God in their own "eternal" <note>Meaning the duration of their earthly life, which they lived as if it were their all.</note>, God should avenge in His own eternity.*

<margin>17.</margin>
And from this I would say that the prayer which is established for the damned is said to be undertaken in vain. *Those who departed without faith,* says Blessed Augustine (from the opinion of the Master <note>Referring to Peter Lombard, the author of the "Sentences," the standard theological textbook of the time.</note> in Book 4, distinction 45), *working through love; in vain are the duties of piety performed for them by their kin.* Blessed Gregory holds the same in his 24th book of *Morals*.

<margin>18.</margin>

# CHAPTER LXXXV.

## That the spirits of damned men are driven away by the same means; and their infestations and annoyances are removed, just as the spirits of demons and their own annoyances are driven away and removed.

<margin>1.</margin>
It has been demonstrated that the Suffrages <note>original: "Suffragia" — intercessory prayers or works of piety intended to aid souls in Purgatory.</note> which help to purify souls do not benefit the spirits of damned men; nor are the living freed by these from the troubles they bring. Should they then be attacked with those same engines of war <note>original: "machinis" — a metaphor for spiritual weapons or rituals.</note> with which we fight against demons? *We certainly believe so; although we are not led to this conclusion by arguments as firm as those in the previous case. And this is our Second Assertion, which we explain and prove in what follows.*

<margin>2.</margin>
First of all, it is not hidden that we do not have such firm protections here as we do there. There, we had a forest of examples <note>A Latin idiom meaning an abundance of evidence.</note> through which we proved that the use of Relics, the Holy Cross, and consecrated objects put demons to flight. Furthermore, we relied on the authority of the Church; which proves that some of these things prevail against the assaults of demons by the very fact that they are consecrated for this purpose; and once consecrated, they are offered to the Christian people for this end; otherwise, they would be annoying to the demons in themselves. Here, we seem deprived of both. For examples are not easily found. Even the prayers and Exorcisms which the Church uses against the troubles of spirits seem to be instituted only against the spirits of demons.

<margin>3.</margin>
*Nonetheless, we believe that we can successfully fight against the spirits of damned men with these engines—either the very same ones or slightly modified:* and anyone who wishes to carefully weigh within themselves the nature of those engines and the condition of these spirits will believe it along with us.

<margin>4.</margin>
The souls of damned men pursue God, the Best and Greatest, with an unbelievable and Vatinian hate <term>Vatinian hate: a proverbial expression for an exceptionally fierce and inextinguishable hatred, named after the Roman politician Publius Vatinius.</term>. This is their condition. Our engines, with which we taught that demons must be fought, are greatly pleasing to God. This is the logic of the engines. What follows from both? That the spirits of damned men flee and detest them. In what way, then? Because it is so arranged by nature that we cannot bear the presence of those whom we burn with hatred or whom we detest;

<margin>5.</margin>
That which we infer is easily understood as being correctly inferred; but that which we propose is not so easy: namely, that God pursues the spirits of damned men with *Vatinian hatred* <note>original: "Odio Vatiniano" — a proverbial expression for an intense, inextinguishable hatred, named after the Roman politician Publius Vatinius who was famously loathed by Cicero.</note>: likewise, that the *engines* <note>original: "Machinas" — a metaphor for spiritual weapons, rituals, or exorcisms.</note> with which we fight against demons are vehemently pleasing and grateful to God. Yet both points are nonetheless certain.

<margin>6.</margin>
Regarding the hatred of the wicked spirits toward God, the authority of the Sacred Scriptures is most grave, confirmed by the consensus of all the Church Fathers. *The pride* (it says in *Psalm 73*) <note>This refers to Psalm 74:23 in modern Bibles: "Do not forget the voice of your enemies; the pride of those who hate you ascends continually."</note> *of those who hate you always ascends.* For although there is no doubt that this sentence pertains to others, it is the constant sense and consensus of all that it fits most especially the damned spirits of men, and likewise the angelic spirits [demons].

<margin>7.</margin>
But even if we attend to the voices of the damned, what we say will be easily proven. The voices of damned men are full of blasphemies: full of rages: full of reproaches. Do blasphemies proceed from a friendly mind toward the one against whom they are vomited and breathed out? Perhaps the spirits of damned men are not blasphemous against God? They are, most especially. *They will curse*, says Innocent III in Book 3 of *The Contempt of the World*, chapter 10, *the Most High, and will blaspheme the Exalted One: complaining that he who created them for punishment is wicked, and he is never inclined toward mercy.* Hear John in *Apocalypse Chapter 16* <note>Revelation 16:21</note> saying: *Great hail descended from heaven upon men, and men blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail: since it was made exceedingly great.* So says Innocent.

<margin>8.</margin>
Let us examine the causes of this hatred. Many and great causes are found in the damned spirits. *Hatred*, says Gregory of Nyssa in his 8th homily on Ecclesiastes, *is an aversion from that which brings pain.* With how much pain does God affect the miserable spirits of the damned? He deprives them of goods: he burdens them with evils. But with how many and how great?

<margin>9.</margin>
The damned are deprived of all gifts which they were able to enjoy in this life. Even if they retain certain things granted by nature, those very things are the laws and matter of evils and punishments. But this is the greatest (theologians call it the <term>punishment of loss|original: "pœnam damni" — the primary suffering of Hell, defined as the eternal separation from the presence of God</term>) that they are denied the enjoyment of the sight of God the Best and Greatest. Wherefore Saint Augustine, after he had recounted many losses of the damned, says: *The absence of Christ’s presence, as far as the vision of him is concerned, alone surpasses all the aforementioned evils; and it is more intolerable than all other punishments.* So he says in *The Threefold Habitation*, chapter 2.

<margin>10.</margin>
Thus they are overwhelmed by a torrent of all evils, which, since the sacred writings were unable to explain sufficiently, they [the writers] used the most grievous [evils] of this life...

<margin>11.</margin>
Cassian <note>John Cassian (c. 360–435 AD), a Christian monk and theologian famous for his writings on monastic life and mysticism.</note> sketches the same things in a certain way in his *Theological Confession*, part 3: *Who,* he says, *can say what torments are prepared for the impious and those living wickedly? For in that very place of continual death, which is called Hell <note>original: "Infernus"</note>; what else can there be but a constant flame, persisting tribulation, perpetual punishment, and the infinite calamity of every evil? Furthermore, a river of fire and a foul swamp fill everything. There, certainly, atrocious Angels dwell, whose arms are like the heads of dragons; whose eyes send forth fiery arrows from themselves; whose teeth project like those of an elephant; and who sting for torment like the tails of scorpions; whose appearance brings on trembling and pain and death. And would that death could come to their aid in these narrows! But what is more horrible: he who is placed in torments lives for this purpose, that he may be ruled by tortures; he is made whole again for this, so that having been gnawed by serpents, he may be handled by bites repeated again and again. There, wailing and lamentation, groaning and lowing sound continually, and at the same time a confused shouting is raised everywhere, which the harsh force of torments drives out and the burning of the fire extorts. And what follows.*

<margin>12.</margin>
But there are two things which increase this punishment: severity and duration. It is most intense, that which the wretched suffer. Gout in the hands <term>chiragra</term> is nothing; colic in the belly is nothing; gout in the feet <term>podagra</term> is nothing; toothache in the mouth is nothing; stones in the kidneys are nothing; if they are compared with the punishments of hell, whether one of those evils or all of them together. And by these earthly diseases, only one of the limbs is afflicted. What if all the diseases already mentioned should torture a man? What if they should torture him in all his limbs? Would the matter not be almost intolerable? Again, while people suffer here, the conversation of friends, the comfort of a bed, and other solaces of life are not lacking. But there, no part or limb will be free from torture: no consolation ever. Instead of a bed, a glowing layer; instead of cooling air, fire; instead of a sweet scent, a suffocating stench; instead of the solace of friends, the mockery, insults, and curses of Demons.

<margin>13.</margin>
Its *duration* also increases the misery. The punishment of the wretched is perpetual. *A burning hell* <note>original: "gehenna"</note>, says Blessed Cyprian <note>Saint Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an important Early Christian writer and bishop.</note> in his book to Demetrianus, *will always burn those condemned to it, and a voracious punishment with living flames: nor will there be any source from which the torments can ever have rest or an end. Souls will be preserved with their bodies for infinite sufferings of pain.*

# ON HAUNTED PLACES

And Saint Bernard <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic often cited in spiritual manuals.</note> in his *Book of Meditations*, chapter 3, says: *Exiled far from the blessed fatherland, they will be tortured in eternal Gehenna <note>original: "gehenna Perpetua"; Gehenna is a biblical term for a place of fiery torment.</note>. Never to see the light, never to attain relief: but through millions of millions of years in hell, they are to be tortured: nor ever to be freed from there; where neither he who tortures is ever fatigued, nor he who is tortured ever dies. For that fire consumes in such a way that it always preserves; the torments are carried out in such a way that they are always renewed.*

<margin>14.</margin>
Indeed, how much does the thought of this eternity crucify the mind? In this life, whatever is long-lasting is troublesome and heavy. Even if rest is pleasant, yet if a healthy person had to lie continuously in a soft bed for two years, he could not bear the labor of that long-lasting rest. What if, indeed, the heavy labors of kidney stones <note>original: "calculi"; a common early modern reference for the most intense physical pain imaginable.</note> had to be endured for one year? How great would this misery be? But the pains of this life are nothing compared to the punishments of hell; boiling oil is nothing; the breaking of bones, scorpions, and six hundred of the most heavy evils are nothing. What *misery is it, therefore, to endure hellish punishments forever?* That which is eternal is too long. The condition of the wretched would be good if hellish punishments had to be sustained for as many thousands of years as there ever were leaves on trees; as many as there are grains of sand on the seashore; as many as there are drops in the vastest sea. But *to suffer for eternity is not finished by any myriads of years.*

<margin>15.</margin>
Nor does the hatred of the damned spirits toward their Creator grow only from these things, but also from all the benefits bestowed upon them by God, of whatever kind they may be. The *goods of fortune* <note>Material wealth, status, and external comforts.</note>, with which they abounded while they nourished their bodies, provide material for greater hatred toward God, because these serve for their greater punishments. The *goods of body and soul* provide it; they grieve that they received these from God, who now demands an account for things poorly spent. All the benefits provide it, whatever the Son of God conferred upon the whole human race during the thirty and more years he lived with us, because these too increase the bitterness of the punishments.

<margin>16.</margin>
Great, therefore, is the *hatred* of damned men toward God. And will they be able to bear God with a calm mind? Will they be able to approve anything that is dear and pleasing to God? Can that which He approves please them?

<margin>17.</margin>
But perhaps (which is the second point to be investigated) the *weapons* with which one fights against demons are not pleasing to God. Perhaps they do not please Him. They are most pleasing; they please Him most vehemently. We teach about each one: but according to the nature of our plan, very briefly.

In favor of the *Sign of the Cross*, there are infinite things which God, the Best and Greatest, has deigned to work through it in all times whatsoever: how true these are, and how great, the *Disputation on Demoniacs* <note>Likely a reference to a specific contemporary theological treatise or a previous chapter regarding exorcism and demonic possession.</note> teaches. This is to say nothing, meanwhile, of the heap of most beautiful virtues which are joined with prayer and which please God most highly.*

<margin>21.</margin>
Perhaps there is doubt concerning **Consecrated Things**, whether they are approved by God. And for these, just as for Relics and the Cross, there are wonders and portents, performed only by the singular power and providence of God for the use of these things. Added to this is the fact that *these things ought properly to be called God’s*, as things which have been, in a certain way, transferred from their natural use through consecration to a divine use, much superior by nature: and which God has decreed should help human necessities as if they were certain instruments of divine mercy.

<margin>22.</margin>
One thing remains: **Exorcism**. It has been demonstrated elsewhere that in this there is nothing that can be deservedly condemned. That there are many things in it which are approved and pleasing to God is confirmed by everything we have already said, since the use of those very things in **Exorcism** is primary.

<margin>23.</margin>
These things, therefore, are pleasing to God. They are therefore displeasing and a source of hatred to the spirits of damned men <note>The author here characterizes demons as the "spirits of damned men," a specific theological take on the nature of evil spirits.</note>; they will therefore flee from them, they will detest them, they will not endure them. In the presence of these things, they will cease to be infestuous to mortals and will leave them in peace.

### ON INFESTED PLACES
<note>original: "DE LOCIS INFESTIS"; in this context, "infested" refers to what we would now call "haunted" locations where spirits or demons manifest.</note>

<margin>24.</margin>
Beyond the reasoning already explained at length, there is another reason why we should believe that the methods used to defeat demons are also highly effective against the spirits of damned men. Specifically, it is likely that the spirits of the damned are never troublesome to us unless demons are working diligently alongside them—if not directing the entire affair themselves. For this reason, we must believe that these spirits will cease their haunting if the demons themselves are outlawed and driven out from the places they infest.

<margin>25</margin>
First, it can be believed that when the souls of damned men are present among the living **in person** <note>original: "autoprosopos, personaliter"; the author uses the Greek term 'autoprosopos' to emphasize the soul appearing in its own identity rather than through a proxy.</note>, they have been brought to us, or even compelled, by the work of demons. Thus, they always attend upon the demons, never departing from them by even a fingernail's breadth. For how could they leave those into whose power they have already been delivered? This is especially true of those spirits whose constant aim was to cause harm—just as much as each person's **Guardian Angel** <note>original: "Angelus Tutelaris"</note> was concerned for the good of the living—and to drag people toward the "broad paths" of vice.

<margin>29.</margin>
Furthermore, the **bodies** which are used in these instances are entirely the work of demons. They are not only shaped by demons but are also sustained by them so that they do not dissolve. It is not believable that the spirits of the damned possess such power that they could fashion and sustain bodies for themselves out of the air. Greater power is required here: the power of Angels—not good ones, of course, whose service the damned are unworthy of, but evil ones, into whose unhappy fellowship these wretches have been enrolled. These points were demonstrated previously in Chapters 19, 24, and 25.

<margin>27.</margin>
Since this is the case, it is not necessary to seek new methods here by which we may be freed from the disturbances of human spirits. Those same methods we use to fight against demons can serve us. Furthermore, how these methods are said to prevail against these spirits—and whether the power of all such methods is equal, or if one is more excellent than another—would need to be explained, were it not that we believe what was said previously applies here, and we wish to be brief.

In the first of these, regarding the spiritual necessity of the deceased...*

# CHAPTER LXXXVI.

### Whether burial granted to the deceased prevents their spirits from returning to the living and being troublesome to them.

<margin>1.</margin>
It is the opinion of some that the spirits of the unburied lack their rest and their proper dwelling places for as long as their bodies have not been granted burial, and so they wander among the living, causing disturbances and being troublesome. They believe that once burial is performed, the troubles cease for everyone. Hence the Poet <note>referring to Virgil</note> says in the 6th book of the *Aeneid*:

> *One is not allowed to cross the dreadful banks, nor the hoarse streams,*
> *Until the bones rest in their dwellings.*
> <note>original: "Non ripas datur horrendas, nec rauca fluenta / Transportare priùs, quàm sedibus ossa quiêrint." This refers to the mythological belief that Charon would not ferry souls across the River Styx until their bodies were buried.</note>

And **Porphyry** <note>a third-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, as witnessed by **Benedictus Pererius** <note>a 16th-century Jesuit scholar</note> in chapter 9 *On Magic*, says: *The souls of those lacking burial linger around their bodies. Therefore,* he adds, *those who desire the souls of prophetic animals to be channeled into themselves do so by swallowing the principal members of those animals, thereby making the soul present to themselves, prophesying in the manner of a God. For such a soul, along with the complete consumption of its body, inserts itself deeply into the human body.* These are the words of Porphyry.

<margin>2.</margin>
This opinion, although it contains certain destructive errors, is nonetheless not false in every respect; nor can it be entirely condemned by a Christian. After we have distinguished the truths from the falsehoods, we shall respond to the main point proposed in this Chapter.

<margin>3.</margin>
It is true that the spirits of the dead (especially Christians) desire, or at least approve, that the bodies they nourished while they lived should have their proper burial. This is a certain "good" for them; and it is a "good," as the Philosopher <note>usually referring to Aristotle</note> witnesses, which all things seek. **Saint Augustine** says in the book *On the Care to be Had for the Dead*, chapter 13: *Those ancient righteous men, while they lived, gave commands to their sons concerning the burial or the transfer of their bodies; and once dead, shall they not care whether they are buried or unburied?*

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the necessity of burial for the rest of the soul. The previous page established the classical and theological belief that unburied spirits wander and cause disturbances (hauntings). This page examines historical and legal attitudes toward the denial of burial and the crime of tomb violation.</meta>

-> ON TROUBLED PLACES <-
<note>original: "DE LOCIS INFESTIS"</note>

<margin>4.</margin>
Everyone believes it constitutes an injury and an insult to the deceased if burial is denied to their bodies. In the Old Law <note>The laws of the Old Testament</note>, when God wished to punish certain individuals more severely, He added this to their other penalties: that the wretched souls should lack burial, and their bodies should become food for the birds of the air or for wild dogs. Among the Greeks, as witnessed by Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A 15th-century Neapolitan lawyer and author of *Genialium Dierum*</note> (Book 6 of *Genial Days*, chapter 19), there was such great concern for burial that ten Commanders <note>original: "Praetores"</note>, because they had failed to bury those who died in the naval battle at Arginusae <note>A battle in 406 BCE during the Peloponnesian War; the commanders were executed for failing to recover the dead due to a storm</note>—having been driven off by the violence of a storm—were summoned on capital charges by the Athenians and suffered the ultimate punishment. The Spartans <note>original: "Lacedaemonij"</note>, while leading their forces against the Messenians, used tokens <note>original: "tesserae"</note> on their arms with their names inscribed, so that the soldiers who fell in the war would not remain unburied. A custom grew in Athens that individual tribes would collect the corpses and scattered remains of those of their own tribe who had fallen in war into separate chests; these they would seek out, gather, and carry on wagons during the expedition.

<margin>5.</margin>
For this reason, the benefit of burial was not bestowed upon just anyone, but was withheld from the wicked and those notorious for remarkable crimes. Tyrants, says Alexander in the same passage, who had deserved ill of the Republic and were punished, or those who died by the noose, or an undignified death, or an evil end, were cast away unburied. And among the Egyptians, if someone happened to have lived a life of depraved character, they would cast out the corpse and expose it in the vast wilderness. The Persians also used to throw the bodies of the condemned to wild beasts and dogs.

<margin>6.</margin>
For the same reason, **violating the tombs of the deceased** was anciently considered a crime, because violence offered to the **tombs** was regarded as violence offered to the buried. *Those who violate tombs, the homes of the dead (says Constantine in Law 1, Code on the violation of tombs), seem to commit a double crime. For they both despoil the buried by destroying them, and they pollute the living by their building; hence they also commit the crime of Lese-majesty.* <term>Lese-majesty: from the Latin "laesae Maiestatis," meaning an offense against the dignity of the state or the sovereign; treason.</term>

<margin>7.</margin>
Moreover, heavy penalties were established against the violators of tombs. Those guilty of violating tombs, if they had extracted the bodies or dug up the bones—if they were of lower status—were punished with the ultimate penalty <note>death</note>; those of higher status were deported to an island. Otherwise, they were exiled or condemned to the mines. Furthermore, if they despoiled the corpses: if they had done so while armed, they were punished by execution; if without arms, the penalty proceeded as far as condemnation to the mines. (Law on Tombs, Digest on the violation of tombs, etc.)

<margin>8.</margin>
On this account, those people were not undeservedly counted among the barbarians (of whose rituals Bruno <note>possibly referencing Bruno of Querfurt or a similar chronicler of pagan customs</note> mentions in Book 4 *On Ceremonies*) who threw the bodies of the deceased to be torn apart by vultures or dogs, or cast them into the seas, rivers, and marshes. ...those worn out by old age, they first impiously slaughtered, and then cruelly devoured them after they were slain.

<margin>9.</margin>
Furthermore, just as the previous point is true, so it is false—and foreign to the Catholic religion—to believe that the deceased cannot enter their heavenly dwellings or enjoy rest until their bodies have been committed to burial. As Blessed Augustine asks in his book *On the Care to be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 6: "What Christian heart would incline toward these poetic and mythical fictions, namely that:

> *Neither are they allowed to cross the dread shores and hoarse-sounding currents,*
> *Before their bones have found rest in their final dwellings?*"
<note>original: "Nec ripas datur horrendas...". Augustine is quoting Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book VI, which describes the ghost of Palinurus unable to cross the River Styx because he was unburied.</note>

Who, I say, would incline a Christian heart to these poetic and mythical fables, when the Lord encourages Christians not to fear those who kill the body and afterwards have nothing more they can do?

<margin>10.</margin>
Those who depart from this life in a state of offense against God are immediately snatched away to places of punishment. Unburied bodies do not prevent them from being taken to these places of torment, nor do they prevent them from suffering the punishments due to their sins in those places. This was demonstrated in chapter 84.

<margin>11.</margin>
Those who die piously in the Lord and have no stains left that must be washed away fly immediately to the kingdoms of heaven. So far is it from the truth that burial delays their happiness, that sometimes the manner of their death even increases it. This has also been demonstrated elsewhere.

<margin>12.</margin>
There are those who die piously in the Lord but depart this life not yet perfectly purified <note>A reference to the state of Purgatory, where souls are cleansed before entering Heaven</note>. They are indeed barred from the kingdom of heaven for a short time; however, this is not because burial was denied to them. Nor do they press their case by wandering among mortals; instead, they pay the penalties due for their sins in a certain place, so that they may finally be found to be "polished stones," fit for the heavenly buildings.

<margin>13.</margin>
How miserable would be the condition of the holiest men if their spirits were barred from the divine sight and forced to wander among mortals for as long as their bodies lacked burial? Especially since many of them were thrown to dogs; some were drowned in the deepest seas; others were broken on wheels or fixed to crosses and became food for the beasts of the earth and the birds of the sky. What of those who were reduced to ashes and scattered to the winds?

<margin>14.</margin>
Furthermore, there would necessarily be a massive multitude of wandering spirits. For many have been found in the past, and are found in our own times, to whom the benefit of burial was denied—either through their own misfortune, the malice of the living, or some unjust accident. If the spirits of all these people truly wandered among the living and troubled them because of the burial they lacked, would there not be a perpetual war with the dead?

# ON HAUNTED PLACES

<margin>15.</margin> Civil and Ecclesiastical Magistrates <note>government and church officials</note> could even be accused of the highest cruelty when they desire certain individuals to be deprived of *Burial*. Is it not the height of inhumanity—to say nothing more severe—to outlaw their spirits from heaven and deprive them of all rest, following other punishments already inflicted on them while they were living?

<margin>16.</margin> And if there is no hope of rest for the Spirits as long as their bodies lie *unburied*, will these *wanderers* <note>Latin: *errones*, referring to restless ghosts</note> be wretched forever? This misery would have to be endured by some indefinitely, because the condition of certain bodies is such that no *Burial* can be provided for them, even if there were those who wished and were able to provide it.

<margin>17.</margin> Therefore, those are in error who, whenever they perceive the Spirits of the deceased to be troublesome to them, immediately assume those bodies have been denied *Burial*. Many can be bothersome who have had a burial—even a most honorable one. There were those who, knowing certain corpses were *unburied*, thought their Spirits wandered among the living. Yet many are deprived of *Burial* and are never seen among mortals.

<margin>18.</margin> To respond, then, to what is the primary point here: *it should not be believed that granting the benefit of burial to the bodies of the deceased is a shortcut for freeing oneself from every trouble caused by haunting spirits.* Even when it is established that the bodies of those causing the disturbances are *unburied*, freedom from these troubles is not secured simply by burying the bodies, even if they are given the most honorable and expensive *Burial*.

<margin>19.</margin> The troubling Spirits of which we treat in this Discussion are—as we said in Chapter 3—either Demons (would they seek *Burial* for themselves?), or the spirits of damned men (God, a severe judge over them, does not permit these to return to the living to seek *Burial*), or those who must be purified <note>souls in Purgatory</note>. These latter have a care for their souls, not their bodies; they do not return and trouble the living so that it may go well with their bodies, but so that their souls might be snatched from their punishments.

<margin>20.</margin> However, we do not wish to deny universally that the Spirits of the deceased sometimes return to the living for the sake of *Burial*, or a more honorable *Burial*. But these are usually the Spirits of the upright, and of those who already enjoy God; as the highest good has already been bestowed upon their souls, so their bodies deserve to be held in a more honorable place. Examples here are the Prophets Micah and Habakkuk <note>original: *Micheas & Abacuc*</note>, who appeared to Zebennus, the Bishop of Eleutheropolis, and requested a more honorable *Burial* for their bodies. Also Gamaliel <note>A famous Jewish teacher mentioned in the Book of Acts</note>, who sought the same for himself, as well as for the <term>Protomartyr: Saint Stephen, the first Christian martyr</term> Stephen, and Nicodemus, from Lucian the priest,

<margin>21.</margin>
Thus, I would not generally deny that those held in the prison of Purgatory—or even those consigned to the torments of Hell—sometimes demand *Burial*. What is to prevent them from seeking *Burial* any less than other things when they return to the living? This is especially true since both groups can desire it; they might sometimes even ask for other things, even though they do not return to the living for those reasons alone.

<margin>22.</margin>
However, it is not likely that everyone who lacks *Burial* returns to the living for that reason. It is even less likely that they stop bothering the living as soon as they have obtained *Burial*. There are other reasons why Spirits involve themselves in the affairs of the living, as has been explained by us elsewhere. Therefore, if they demand *Burial*, they are performing something beyond their usual duty.

<margin>23.</margin>
And those who are still being purified <note>referring to souls in Purgatory</note> can seek this more justly than those who are damned. For it is not fitting that the condition of their bodies should be better than that of their Spirits. Yet their bodies are to be treated with honor because worthy fruits of repentance were once perfected in them; because they were dwellings of the Holy Spirit; and because one day they are to be adorned with a glory and splendor exceeding the brightness of the sun.

<margin>24.</margin>
Whenever they do ask, the living perform a duty of mercy while they bestow the benefit of burial upon them, regardless of what kind of Spirits they are who seek it—whether they be worthy or unworthy. They are only prohibited from burial when certain individuals, for just reasons, have been deprived of the same by a Magistrate—such as those excommunicated through Ecclesiastical censure, or those who, because of their crimes, are left as food for the birds of the heaven, the fish of the sea, or the wild beasts of the earth.

<margin>25.</margin>
From these points, it is clear how one should respond to the example provided by Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger, whose famous letter to Sura describes a haunted house in Athens where a ghost was appeased by proper burial</note>, who teaches that after a more honorable *Burial* was provided, the spirit did not return to the living, nor did it bring trouble to them as it used to do before. For this is either a private and singular case—which does not prove that everyone denied *Burial* will press the living for it by stirring up disturbances—or, what is more likely, it was not a human Spirit, but a Demonic one. Although this spirit ceased being troublesome after the more honorable *Burial*, it should be believed that it was not seeking the duty of *Burial* from the living, but something else entirely.
