# ON HAUNTED PLACES

It is pleasing to include here the words of Pliny.
> "There was," he says, "in Athens a spacious and roomy house, but infamous and unhealthy. Through the silence of the night, the sound of iron [was heard], and if you listened more closely, the rattling of chains, first from a distance, then very nearby. Soon an apparition <note>original: "Idolum"</note> would appear: an old man wasted by thinness and filth, with a long beard and hair standing on end; he wore shackles on his legs and chains on his hands, and he would shake them. Because of this, the residents spent sad and terrible nights awake in fear. Lack of sleep led to illness, and as fear grew, death followed. For even during the day, although the image had departed, the memory of it lingered before their eyes: the fear itself became a lasting cause for fear. Consequently, the house was deserted and condemned to solitude, left entirely to that monster; yet it was put up for sale or rent, in case someone ignorant of such an evil should want it. The philosopher Athenodorus <note>Athenodorus Cananites (c. 74 BC – 7 AD), a Stoic philosopher</note> came to Athens. He read the notice, and hearing the price, became suspicious of its cheapness. Upon inquiry, he was told everything, but he rented it anyway—in fact, all the more so. When evening began to fall, he ordered a bed to be prepared for him in the front part of the house. He asked for writing tablets <note>original: "pugilares"</note>, a stylus, and a light. He sent all his servants to the inner rooms, while he focused his mind, eyes, and hand on writing, so that an empty mind would not imagine the ghosts he had heard of or create empty fears. At first, there was the usual silence of night; then, the clanking of iron and the movement of chains. He did not look up or put down his pen, but steeled his mind and shut his ears. Then the noise increased, drew closer, and was heard first at the threshold, then inside the threshold. He looked back and saw and recognized the figure described to him. It stood there, beckoning with its finger like someone calling; he, in response, signaled with his hand for it to wait a little, and again bent over his wax tablets and stylus. It rattled its chains over the head of the man as he wrote. He looked back again to see it beckoning as before; without delay, he took up the light and followed. It walked with a slow step, as if heavy with chains. After it turned into the courtyard of the house, it suddenly vanished, leaving its companion behind. He placed a mark on the spot with some plucked grass and leaves. The next day, he went to the magistrates and urged them to order the place to be dug up. Bones were found, entwined and tangled in chains, which the body—rotted by time and the earth—had left bare and corroded by the shackles. They were collected and buried at public expense, and the house was thereafter free from the spirit, once the ghost <note>original: "manes" – the spirits of the dead</note> had been properly laid to rest."

## C H A P T E R  L X X X V I I.

->*Whether, on account of the censure of Ecclesiastical Excommunication,*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
Writing on the Life and Miracles of St. Benedict, Blessed Gregory, in the second book of his *Dialogues*, chapter 23, relates that there were two women of noble birth who had professed a religious life <note>they were nuns</note>. Because of their unrestrained tongues <note>referring to a habit of gossip or verbal abuse</note>, the holy man threatened them with Excommunication. When they did not depart from their former ways, they died shortly thereafter and were buried in the church. Divine vengeance followed, which St. Gregory recounts in these words: *“When the solemnities of the Mass,”* he says, *“were being celebrated in the church, and according to the custom the Deacon cried out: ‘He who does not communicate <note>original: "qui non communicat"; referring to those not permitted to receive the Eucharist, such as the unbaptized or those under penance</note>, let him depart,’ their nurse, who used to offer the oblation <note>a gift or sacrifice</note> to the Lord on their behalf, saw them come forth from their tombs and leave. Since she saw this repeatedly, she remembered what the man of God had commanded them while they were still living. For he had said he would deprive them of communion unless they corrected their ways and words. Then, with heavy sorrow, the matter was reported to the servant of God (Benedict), who immediately gave an offering <note>original: "oblationem"; here referring to the consecrated Host</note> from his own hand, saying: ‘Go and have this offering made to the Lord for them, and they will no longer be excommunicated.’ Once this offering had been sacrificed for them, and when the Deacon cried out according to custom that those not communicating should leave the church, they were seen no more leaving the church. Thus far Gregory.*

<margin>2.</margin>
Something similar is read in the work of Giovanni Pietro Maffei of Bergamo <note>a Jesuit historian, 1533–1603</note>, in the fifth book of his *Histories of the Indies*, which we record in his own words. *“During those same days,”* he says, *“whether from the inclemency of the weather or from the juices of unhealthy food, a terrible disease invaded the naval crew. They would suddenly expire in the midst of play or their daily duties. Among them, one soldier was thrown into the sea <note>given a burial at sea</note>, which caused great terror to everyone. For at night, deep within the bilge <note>original: "sentinam"; the lowest part of a ship where water collects</note>, frequent thumping began to be heard. At this noise, when the guards descended with a lantern, they found the body of the deceased soldier entangled in the keel directly under the rudder; certainly, everyone’s hair stood on end. When they had recovered themselves from their fear, the matter was reported to the Captain, and there was no doubt that the corpse had been moved...”*

<margin>3.</margin> I add another example from *Glycas* <note>Michael Glycas, a 12th-century Byzantine historian</note>, part 4, where it is recorded as follows: *In the Ecclesiastical History of Philo the historian, it is found that during a time of ancient persecutions, a senior clergyman had been banned from the sacred rites by his Bishop. However, when that senior had traveled elsewhere for some necessary reason, it happened that he was captured by the Pagans and sealed the truth with his own witness <note>original: "testimonio suo veritatem obsignaret"; a standard way to describe dying as a martyr for the faith</note>. Consequently, a church was built in that place and memorial services were performed. But whenever the Bishop pronounced these words, "PEACE TO ALL," the coffin <note>original: "sandapila"; specifically a wooden bier used for carrying the dead</note> moved out of the church. This happened not once, but two or three times. Later, the senior appeared to the Bishop in a dream: "Go," he said, "and tell my Bishop to come here and release me from my bonds. For he excluded me from the sacred office, and therefore I cannot participate in the holy rites with you. I have indeed obtained the crown of martyrdom, but I have not yet looked upon the face of God. If he does not come here and release me himself, no one else will be able to release me." When this command was obeyed, the coffin stopped leaving the church. So says Glycas.*

<margin>4.</margin> From these and similar examples, some—it seems not without reason—suspect that those who depart from this life under a sentence of Excommunication have no rest and wander among mortals until they are absolved by a legitimate Magistrate <note>In this context, "Magistrate" refers to a church official with legal authority, such as a Bishop or the Pope</note>. How much probability this opinion holds will be clear from the resolution of four questions. First, it is asked whether a censure of Excommunication brought against the living affects them when they are dead. Second, whether it affects them so much that it is necessary for those against whom it was brought to wander among mortals. Third, whether the benefit of absolution can be granted to them. Fourth, whether as long as it has not been granted, they are unable to enjoy their desired rest. We shall settle each of these very briefly.

<margin>5.</margin> At the beginning, let it be established that the censure of Excommunication is extremely harmful to the living. *Nothing,* says Blessed Augustine in his 27th Tractate on St. John, *ought a Christian to fear so much as being separated from the body of Christ. For if he is separated from the body of Christ, he is not his member. If he is not a mem—* <note>The text breaks here at the end of the page; the word likely continues as "member" on the following page</note>

...member of it, is not ruled by *His Spirit. For whoever*, says the Apostle in Romans 8, *does not have the Spirit of God, does not belong to Him.* <note>original: "Quisquis autem... Spiritum Dei non habet, hic non est eius"</note>

<margin>6.</margin> But does this harm the deceased? This is the first of the questions proposed in our inquiry. It harms them entirely—specifically in body, in honor, and in soul. In body, because the person is deprived of a dignified *Burial* <term>Sepulturâ: the formal rite of Christian burial in consecrated ground, which was denied to the excommunicated</term>. In honor, because their reputation is damaged in no small way. In soul, because the assistance and prayers <term>suffragia: intercessory prayers, masses, and alms offered by the living to aid the souls of the dead</term> of the living, which possess no small power, are withdrawn from them.

<margin>7.</margin> Furthermore, does it harm them such that the deceased are necessarily forced to wander among the living? This must be explained as our second point. The answer is that *this is not a necessity*. Those who depart this life bound by this chain of *Anathema* <term>Anathema: the most severe form of excommunication, involving a formal curse and total exclusion from the Christian community</term> can—if their merits so demand—be admitted soon to the company of the heavenly citizens. Or they can be shut up in the prisons of hell, or in the places of purgatory, and all return to the living be forbidden to them. While *Excommunication* <note>original: "Excommunicatio"</note> has great power even over the dead, it does not have the power to exclude them from the specific places they deserve <note>The author argues that while the church can affect a soul's spiritual standing, it does not automatically turn every excommunicated person into a wandering ghost</note>.

<margin>8.</margin> Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that these same people sometimes appear to the living after death and cause trouble. This is proven first by the examples we have already cited. Secondly, it is proven by the arrangement of divine providence, which can demonstrate through these means (among others) that the sentence of anathema used by the Church against the stubborn and rebellious is not to be despised.

<margin>9.</margin> From this, the answer to the third question is easy: *namely, that the benefit of absolution can be granted to them.* For the power of Ecclesiastical censure is demonstrated in both ways: by the fact that those buried while under it seem to lack rest, and by the fact that once absolved, they enjoy their longed-for rest.

<margin>10.</margin> In the meantime, however, the benefit of absolution *does not, in itself, guarantee that the deceased enjoy rest and cease to wander; rather, its purpose is that they may be aided by the prayers of the living and be more quickly rescued from the punishments which would otherwise have to be paid over a longer period of time.*

# CHAPTER 88.

## What method must be followed in liberating places from the infestations of spirits when the nature of the spirits infesting the place is unknown.

<margin>1.</margin> The methods assigned thus far for freeing places from the infestation of spirits apply when it is known which spirits one must do battle against. However, since it not infrequently happens that the true condition of the disturbing spirits is hidden, we must explain how the living can free themselves from such trouble.

<margin>2.</margin> There are those who wish the previously mentioned methods to apply here as well; for they argue that whoever is causing the disturbance must be either a spirit of a demon, or a spirit of a human—either one of the damned or one needing purification. Nevertheless, these people do not seem to judge correctly. For what if you use those methods by which demons are driven out, yet the spirits causing the trouble are actually the souls of men who are being cleansed in the purgatorial fires? Likewise, it can happen that when you wish to use the methods meant to help the souls of the pious departed, the spirits causing the trouble are actually demons, against whom those methods have no power.

<margin>3.</margin> For this reason, I would not approve of the opinion of those who, as soon as a plan is made to liberate infested places, flee to Exorcisms <term>Exorcismos: formal ecclesiastical rites used to command demons to depart</term>. They think spirits should be banished from places in such a way that no place is left for them except for Hell. Although places are very often cleansed by this method, certain spirits are thereby deprived of the assistance <note>original: "subsidio"</note> that could have been granted to them—at great benefit to the living—if different methods had been used against the spirits.

<margin>4.</margin> I am more pleased by the zeal of those who approach the matter with gentler methods: specifically, those by which the spirits of the pious departed are helped. Even if these methods do not benefit all spirits, they can nonetheless benefit certain deceased souls; furthermore, they assist the living no less—and indeed more—than other benefits of mercy bestowed upon one's neighbors.

<margin>5.</margin> And no one can doubt that these things benefit the living (even if no profit reaches the deceased). Is there not great power in Almsgiving <term>Eleemosynæ: the practice of giving money or food to the poor as a religious act of merit</term>? Undertaken with no evil end, but only with the desire to help the miserable...

<margin>6.</margin>
Thus it is clear that it is possible to benefit the dead. For it may be that some of those who are being purified through <term>purgatorial</term> <note>purgatorijs: relating to Purgatory, a state of cleansing for souls who die in God's grace but still require purification for sins</note> punishments, and are being made fit for the kingdom of heaven, are troublesome to the living. Just as such a soul is troublesome in the hope of obtaining assistance, so he is troublesome not in vain, but to his own great gain, if he is helped by some assistance from the living.

<margin>7.</margin>
Perhaps it is a crime if these protections are performed and applied on behalf of damned spirits, such as might also be troublesome here. It is a crime if those who bestow these aids upon spirits believe that it is the spirits of the damned who are causing the trouble and for whom they are bestowing the aids. But as long as this remains unknown, it is not a crime; rather, whatever service is rendered is a duty of charity.

<margin>8.</margin>
Since these things are so, in order to define what has been proposed in this chapter, I would judge that in this Method of driving away unknown Spirits, one's mind and thoughts should first be turned toward Prayer, the Sacrifice of the Mass, Almsgiving, and other works of piety by which the spirits of the pious departed are helped. And indeed, if after these things the harassment and trouble should cease, we shall congratulate ourselves on the peace; but if not, a plan must be made concerning another kind of weaponry <note>original: "armorum genere"; the author uses military metaphors for spiritual warfare</note>.

<margin>9.</margin>
But this duty must not be set aside immediately, nor should the protections of piety and mercy which we have mentioned be soon abandoned. For what if these efforts are quite slight? What if there is need for more, or for the same to be repeated more often? Experience teaches that harassment is often removed after the third or sixth application of the aids of piety, though it could not be removed after the first or second.

<margin>10.</margin>
The condition of spirits who undergo punishment for their sins is not such that they are helped by just any assistance from the living, even if slight. They endure punishments by reason of the sins they committed; and just as these sins are greater, so they must be expiated by greater punishments, and thus redeemed by greater aids from the living. If the deceased were released by just any <term>intercessions</term> <note>Suffragijs: prayers or works of piety offered by the living to benefit the souls of the dead</note> of the living, then those who die piously in the Lord would ask in vain for intercessions to be made for several years. In vain would the brothers of the Church of Hexham <note>Hagulstaldensis: the Latin name for Hexham in Northumbria, England</note> pour out prayers to God for the soul of <term>Oswald</term>, King of the English, every year on the day before he was killed—as they do, according to the testimony of <term>Bede</term> <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 673–735), an English monk and historian</note>, in book 3 of the *History of the English* <note>original: "Historiae Anglicanae", referring to Bede's *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*</note>, concerning the deeds of Oswald. In vain would the Church celebrate anniversary rites for those for whom they have already been celebrated a hundred or two hundred years before.

<margin>11.</margin>
When the aforementioned pious aids do not help, then one must fight against the spirits with consecrated objects, by raising the Cross and hanging the <term>Relics</term> <note>original: *Reliquijs*; the physical remains or personal effects of saints, believed to hold spiritual power</note> of the Saints. To the evil ones—as those are presumed to be who are not helped by the previous methods—these things are a source of horror and loathing; thus, there is hope that because of these things, they will change their abode.

<margin>12.</margin>
What if they are not driven away even by these? Let the instruments of <term>Exorcism</term> <note>original: *Exorcismorum*; formal religious rites used to expel or ward off demons</note> be applied: <term>Adjurations</term> <note>original: *Adiurationes*; solemn commands or appeals to a spirit in the name of God</note> and <term>Execrations</term> <note>original: *Execrationes*; ritual curses or denunciations</note>, and whatever else has power or authority over spirits by God’s ordinance. Nothing can be applied against these spirits that is considered too inhumane or too cruel.

<margin>13.</margin>
Nor should one’s spirit be immediately cast down if we do not at once obtain what we seek. The spirits must be tested more often; the impression must be made repeatedly. Just as they are not cast out from the bodies of men by one or two exorcisms, so they are not easily driven from places. Some do not leave unless they are worn out by the persistent exorcisms and <term>conjurations</term> <note>original: *coniurationibus*; the act of calling upon a spirit or binding them by oath</note> of the living.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX.

### *On the effectiveness of all the aforementioned Methods, and for what reasons they do not always achieve the hoped-for ends.*

<margin>I.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'M' featuring floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc> It is manifest from what has been said that the power of all the methods used to fight against any spirits, and the troubles they bring, is great. They also frequently achieve the effects that the living hope for. But do they always? Let us inquire into this. Not only this, but let us also explain the reasons why they may not always succeed.

<margin>2.</margin>
In the first matter, a distinction of spirits is necessary. For the nature of good spirits, or those to be <term>purified</term> <note>original: *purgandorum*; souls in Purgatory undergoing cleansing of sins</note>, does not seem to be the same as that of the wicked, and especially of <term>demons</term> <note>original: *Dæmonum*; fallen angels or inherently evil spirits</note>. For the former, pious duties undertaken by the living are not in vain. For the latter, those methods which are otherwise effective in themselves sometimes achieve little.

<margin>3.</margin>
To speak of the first case: the very disturbances brought by these spirits to the living lead us to this conclusion. Since it happens by the singular providence and goodness of God that these spirits return to the living—and they almost always return for this reason, to be helped by the aid of the living—who would doubt that the wretched souls will be helped if the living take upon themselves the punishments which the spirits ought to endure, and fulfill the duties of Christian piety for them, as <term>members of one body</term> <note>Refers to the doctrine of the "Communion of Saints," suggesting a spiritual bond between the living and the dead that allows for the transfer of merit</note>?

Therefore, it can hardly be believed that some of these Spirits are so fixed to certain places that they must be purged there until the final Day of Judgment, or even for several centuries, and cannot be helped by any assistance from the living. For although some have deserved to be tormented for a very long time, nonetheless none have fallen away from the Body of Christ <note>The author is referring to the "Mystical Body of Christ," the theological idea that all Christians, living and dead, remain connected.</note>; wherefore, just as members of a body help one another, so the dead can be helped by the work of the living, especially those who are troublesome to mortals in the places where they are being purged.

<margin>5.</margin>
Among the latter—the spirits of the damned, I mean—the reasons assigned for the places of purging sometimes fail. This is nothing new. Even the Apostles, upon whom full power over Demons was conferred, sometimes gained nothing by their power. One man complained to the Lord about them because his possessed son could not obtain health through them. Mark 9. <note>original: *Marci 9*; a reference to the Gospel of Mark, chapter 9, where the disciples are unable to cast out a spirit until Jesus intervenes.</note>

<margin>6.</margin>
Nor are examples lacking in the present matter. We know of certain places that could not be conquered even after many and most serious "machines" <note>original: *machinas*; here meaning spiritual tools, rituals, or methodical efforts of exorcism.</note>. We know that for certain mortals, there was a perpetual war with haunting Spirits. Perhaps those spirits were of despaired salvation [damned]. Some were; but others were of the most upright character, of proven life, and who were dear to God because of their remarkable virtue.

<margin>7.</margin>
But what is the *cause of this matter?* It is not the same for the spirits of damned men as for the spirits of Demons. Nor is this a surprise, because they do not involve themselves in the affairs of the living or trouble them in the same way. The spirits of damned men are present unwillingly and by compulsion. The spirits of Demons are present willingly and spontaneously. Therefore, the former, if they could, would immediately take flight at the first force or voice of <term>Adjuration</term> <note>original: *Adiurationis*; a formal, solemn command given to a spirit in the name of God.</note>; the latter, if they could, would never depart.

<margin>8.</margin>
Hence it happens that the reasons why the damned do not leave infested places when adjured, nor grant peace to the living, are not to be sought in the will of the damned men themselves, but in the will of Him <note>Referring to God.</note> by whose command they are forced to return to the living. On the other hand, the fact that Demons do not yield when adjured depends on their own will and the will of Him by whose permission they harass.

<margin>9.</margin>
When adjured, the spirits of damned men do not always yield from infested places; they do not grant peace to the living. Why? Because God does not always want them to yield. When adjured, Demons do not always yield, nor do they always cease to infest. Why? Because they refuse to yield, and God does not permit them to yield. Therefore, it is by the will of God alone that the "machines" used to fight against the troubles of haunting spirits do not achieve their effects or their ends in the case of the spirits of damned men: [the will of] God...

*And it happens by the will of Demons that success is not achieved among the spirits of the Demons.*

<margin>10.</margin> And what causes can move **GOD** in this matter? Chiefly two. One is drawn from the fault of the haunting spirits; the other from the sin of the humans who endure their harrassments. For since the sins of the living sometimes deserve these troubles, and the spirits of the deceased are sometimes worthy of being brought in against their own will—to their greater shame—to inflict these things; who does not understand that even after "lawful machines" <note>original: *legitimas machinas*; the author uses "machines" as a technical term for spiritual tools, rituals, and the methodical application of exorcism rites.</note> have been applied, which would otherwise remove them, these same troubles ought not to be removed? This is the case if neither the sins of the living nor the sins of these deceased spirits have yet been satisfied by an equal measure of suffering.

<margin>11.</margin> Furthermore, the fact that *Demons* are not always conquered by these same "machines," nor do they yield, depends partly on their own will, and partly on divine wisdom for just reasons. Just as it happens by their own will and the will of God that they are troublesome to the living and haunt places, so it is by God’s will and their own that, even when commanded under oath, they do not cease their harrassments.

<margin>12.</margin> They themselves yield only with difficulty, because they are greatly "refreshed" <note>The author suggests that demons take a twisted pleasure or find a sense of renewal in human suffering.</note> by the evils and miseries of mortals. Since these miseries increase through such harrassments, they prefer to endure whatever "impressions" <note>original: *impreſſiones*; likely referring to the spiritual "blows" or pressure applied by the exorcist.</note> they can, rather than desert the places they haunt or grant peace to the humans they trouble.

<margin>13.</margin> But divine providence is moved by other reasons. God has in view either the punishment of those who endure the troubles, or the good that both they and others can gather from the harrassment of these haunting spirits. The punishment serves as the avenging of sins; the good serves to increase the crown of immortality and glory.

<margin>14.</margin> God is the avenger of crimes, not only in the world to come—where the proper place of vengeance lies—but also in the present. And here He does not have only one method of vengeance, but many. Among these, that method also has a place by which He exacts the punishment for crimes through the "executioner's work" <note>original: *carnificinam*; a gruesome term comparing the demon's role to that of a state executioner or torturer.</note> of the Demons. If, therefore, He has decreed to avenge crimes through haunting spirits, certain "machines" against the infestations will be applied by the living, but they will by no means enjoy the desired peace, as God is avenging the sins of mortals through this demonic torture.

<margin>15.</margin> And so, these "machines" will be all the less effective the more justly sins are being avenged by these means. Indeed, who can doubt that they are avenged most justly? For although He is able to avenge any sins with any punishments whatsoever, there are nonetheless certain sins which, [if they are to be avenged] through the harrassment of Demons...

# CHAPTER 90.

## *Whether the same methods should be used against spirits who pursue specific people, wherever they may live, as those used against spirits who haunt specific places.*

<margin>1.</margin> There is a brief answer to the proposed question. The question is: To free people from trouble—those who suffer from pursuing spirits everywhere—are the same methods effective and sufficient as those we have shown so far to be most powerful in places haunted *in themselves*? <note>original: *per se*; meaning a location that is inherently haunted regardless of who is there.</note> The answer is: They are *not* sufficient. The reason is obvious, because the condition of those places is far different from these. In places haunted *in themselves*, the spirits have their own homes, as it were; and they are, in a sense, the masters and possessors of the locations. In these places haunted *on account of the people*, the spirits live there like guests; and because of this, they change their seats along with the people they pursue, whereas they keep their seats in those former locations.

<margin>2.</margin> And so it happens that although the spirits might perhaps be banished from this or that place by *those methods* which we said above were effective for putting demons to flight, and although *those living in this or that place* who must endure them might be safe and free from trouble there, they nevertheless fall back into the same troubles as soon as they are found in other places where the spirits have not been banished.

<margin>3.</margin> In these latter cases, the goal must be entirely different: access should be denied to the spirits not so much regarding the *places*, but regarding the *people* whom they pursue. For in this situation, the spirits do not take account of *places* as much as they do of *people*. Therefore, we should not think so much about how we might make the places safe, as about how care may be taken so that no harm is brought to the *people*, in whatever places they may live.

<margin>4.</margin> Furthermore, this is not one single and simple method. And what wonder is that? Since there is not just one kind of person, it seems that different methods must be established. How many types are there, then? Two in total. This is because there are two kinds of people who endure pursuing spirits. One is that of the *wicked*...

# CHAPTER 91.

## *By what means those who endure infestations because of the sins they have committed can be freed from the harassment of Spirits.*

<margin>1.</margin>
The method seems very easy by which those who suffer infestations of Spirits on account of their sins may deliver themselves from that trouble. *Let them extricate themselves from their sins, and they may congratulate themselves on their freedom.* For if it is necessary to endure the troubles of a Spirit solely on this account—because they are entangled in sins—then surely if they extricate themselves from the snares of sin, will they not be released from the troubles of Spirits? And will the effect not cease when the cause upon which it depends ceases to exist? <note>A reference to the legal and philosophical maxim: *Cessante causa, cessat effectus* (When the cause ceases, the effect ceases).</note>

<margin>2.</margin>
In the first place, therefore, these people must be entirely persuaded to stop their habit of sinning and to change their lives for the better. Let those who have wallowed in the filth of vices—through which they fell into the miserable slavery of Spirits—be diligent in the study of virtues.

<margin>3.</margin>
Nevertheless, this is not enough. It is not sufficient to stop the habit of sinning. The *sin* itself (which holds its seat, as it were, in the soul) *must be uprooted fundamentally*. For it is not only the sins themselves, while they are being committed, that subject us to harassing Spirits; it is also the *habits* <note>original: *habitus*; in Scholastic theology, this refers to a lasting disposition or "stain" left on the soul after an act is committed</note> which they leave in the soul after they have been perpetrated. It is just as necessary for the soul to be purged of these habits as it is to stop the habit of sinning.

<margin>4.</margin>
At this point, what is required and effective is *sorrow conceived for the sins committed, and a resolution to change one's life for the better; and after these, sacramental Confession and Absolution*, which alone God willed to be the "second plank" <note>A traditional metaphor in Catholic theology: if Baptism is the first plank that saves a person from the shipwreck of original sin, Confession is the "second plank" (*secunda tabula*) for those who fall into sin afterward.</note> for those who have relapsed. And just as those former things are necessary, so too, if these latter things are lacking, the pardon of sins is expected in vain; in vain...

...our freedom from the infestations of demons. Nothing is to be omitted; all things and each individual thing must be adopted.

<margin>5.</margin>And indeed, all these things are entirely necessary to remove the troubles caused by these Spirits; yet if the reception of the *Body and Blood of the Lord* in the venerable *Sacrament* <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note> is added to them, a greater force is brought against the Spirits. For them, access to men seems to become more difficult the more people are armed with more and greater protections. For are the Sacraments of the Body and Blood of Christ not weapons against Demons? Or are they perhaps only light ones?

<margin>6.</margin>I would suggest a more frequent use of these sacraments to those who have been exposed to the troubles of Spirits because of their sins. This is because the Wicked One <note>original: *Nequam*; a common Latin epithet for the Devil, meaning "the worthless" or "the wicked one"</note> does not easily relinquish the province <note>In the Roman sense, an assigned area of responsibility or command</note> he has once obtained for vexing the living. For this reason, it seems necessary for mortals to be more frequently equipped with those weapons by which one fights against the enemy with a greater hope of victory. With these methods, a certain unhappy woman fought against an infesting Spirit, of whom we shall make mention in the following chapter.

<margin>7.</margin>In addition to this, I would require the pursuit of virtues. This is most worthy, because that saying of the Apostle in Romans 6 also applies to us: *Just as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve justice unto sanctification.* <note>A paraphrase of Romans 6:19</note> Furthermore, the Demons vehemently dread the pursuit of virtues. "Believe me, brothers," said the Blessed Anthony, as witnessed by Athanasius in his *Life*, "Satan greatly fears the vigils of the pious, their prayers, fasts, voluntary poverty, mercy, humility, and above all, their burning love for Christ the Lord." <note>St. Anthony the Great (c. 251–356), a desert father. His biography was written by St. Athanasius of Alexandria.</note>

Is it not the case that this also becomes necessary? *When the unclean spirit has gone out of a man,* says the Lord in Luke 11, *he walks through waterless places, seeking rest. And not finding it, he says: "I will return to my house from which I came." And when he comes, he finds it swept and adorned. Then he goes and takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter and dwell there; and the last state of that man becomes worse than the first.* <note>The Parable of the Returning Spirit (Luke 11:24-26)</note> What does the Lord mean by this parable? He signifies that the Devil finds two reasons to return to the house from which he was expelled: namely, if he finds it either empty or swept clean. The house of those who are content merely to have set aside their sins, but are not concerned with the pursuit of virtue, is "empty." The house of those who only cultivate virtues outwardly, but do not root out sins from the heart, is "swept clean."

<margin>8.</margin>That this method of fighting against Spirits is not adopted in vain could be shown by many examples; we are content with one, that of Catherine...

...the Swedish Virgin and Widow, the daughter of Saint Bridget <note>This likely refers to Saint Catherine of Sweden (1332–1381), who traveled to Rome and Naples with her mother</note>, who, while she was staying in Naples, was asked by a certain woman who was suffering severe nocturnal troubles from a Demon by what means she might free herself from them. Next, she advised a Pilgrimage to the church of the Holy Cross, to be performed with humility for eight consecutive days, barefooted and having laid aside her linen undergarment <note>original: *indusio*; a shift or tunic worn close to the skin, often removed as an act of penance</note>. See Surius <note>Laurentius Surius (1522–1578), a German Carthusian monk and hagiographer who compiled lives of the saints</note>, Volume 2, in her Life, folio 354.

I would also strongly approve of the invocation and protection of *all the Saints*, and especially of *one’s own Angel* <note>The Guardian Angel</note>, to whom everyone is commended from the moment of their birth. For among other duties, this is not the least of his offices: to be a defense for mortals against the powers of the lower regions. Nor does it stand in the way that, if you consider the forces of nature, he might be inferior to certain Demons; because what nature denied, grace supplies. By this grace, it happens that the least among the good is superior to all evil ones, even the most powerful, as Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> teaches in several places following Blessed Augustine.

<margin>16.</margin>
But if the opposing power of the Demons is not broken by these "siege engines" <note>The author uses *machinis*, comparing spiritual practices to military engineering</note>, and they are not prevented from troubling and infesting by these means, they must be tested with other weapons—the same ones by which we trust that *good and upright* men, who endure their assaults, can be usefully equipped. And what are those? The following Chapter will explain these things.

<margin>I.</margin>
Because mortals do not know whether they are worthy of hate or of love <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 9:1</note> as long as they are on a pilgrimage from God in the body; for that reason, even those whom a conscience of crime does not accuse, if they ever suffer from pursuing Demons, I would think they should use, above all, those methods by which we said those who suffer the butchery of Demons on account of their crimes are helped. For it does no harm if we hold ourselves in the number of sinners, since *blessed is the man who is always fearful* <note>Proverbs 28:14</note>; but it harms most of all if, like the Pharisee, we parade ourselves as righteous.

<margin>2.</margin> I add that, even if it were probable that we are in the grace of God and burdened by no weight of mortal sin, these weapons <note>The spiritual practices mentioned previously</note> can still be taken up. For demons sometimes sustain their attacks on the living not only because of grave sins, but also because of light <note>venial</note> sins. The Discussion we provided regarding the Possessed <note>A reference to a previous section of the author's work regarding *Demoniacs*</note> teaches this clearly: so that, just as it is necessary for the wicked to set aside their sins if they wish to be free from the infestations of demons, it is likewise necessary for the righteous to abandon their venial faults and blemishes <note>original: *naeuos*; literally "moles," used here to mean small spiritual imperfections</note>, on account of which they endure the troubles of demons.

<margin>3.</margin> Just as I would recommend it to the former [the wicked], so to the latter [the righteous] I would earnestly recommend: rest from sins; the sacrament of **Confession**; the use of the venerable **Eucharist**; the study of virtues; the invocation of the **Guardian Angel**; and other things similar to these. *What if none of these things help? One must take refuge in other protections. Which ones?*

<margin>4.</margin> The first is the **common Prayer of the Church**, established for this purpose. If a prayer undertaken by any private individual is very powerful, how much more powerful will one be when undertaken by the whole Church? And when it is undertaken out of brotherly charity, which is most pleasing to God? Especially when it is undertaken for a person believed to be righteous, whom the greatest necessity, joined with the deepest humility, compels to implore the common prayers?

<margin>5.</margin> Then there is the use of **Consecrated Things**: primarily that wax image which we call the <term>Agnus Dei: A small disc of wax blessed by the Pope, usually impressed with the figure of a lamb, used as a sacramental protection against evil</term>; that this is effective against the assaults of demons is shown both by the form in which it is consecrated and confirmed by these verses of **Andreas Frusius** <note>André des Freux (d. 1556), a founding member of the Jesuit order known for his Latin poetry</note>:

> He (the Pope) recites prayers filled with wondrous piety,
> Which the fixed formula of the ancient rite holds.
> He asks primarily that the sight of the consecrated Lamb
> May lift the stirred hearts toward the heavenly Lamb.
> And that, mindful of the life and death that bring salvation,
> They may crush the harmful chains of crime and vice.
> So that they may overcome the snares and battles of the Stygian enemy <note>original: *hostis stygij*; the "Stygian enemy" refers to the Devil, alluding to the River Styx in the underworld</note>,
> As well as the worldly teachings and the enticements of the flesh.
> So that they may flee all dangers to eternal salvation,
> And never be destitute of help from above.

<margin>6.</margin> Third are **Relics**. If they can banish demons from certain places, could they not do so from all? Is their force and power less in this place than in any other? If indeed they banish them from all places, do they not set the person free in all places, leaving behind someone who otherwise suffers from pursuing demons everywhere?

It happened to a woman who was most miserably tormented by the Devil, though not without her own fault. The Devil appeared to her in the form of a soldier of very handsome appearance; he deceitfully inclined her heart toward his love through hidden suggestions within and flattering speech without. When he had obtained the woman’s consent, with his arms outstretched, he placed her feet upon one of his hands, covered her head with his other hand, and endowed her with the sign of this covenant. She indeed had a husband who was a vigorous soldier, but he was entirely ignorant of this abominable commerce. That most foul adulterer, therefore, abused her invisibly, even while her husband was sleeping in the same place, and tormented her with incredible lust. 

For six years this evil remained hidden, nor did the lost woman disclose the shame of so great a crime, nor the filth of such continuous baseness, both due to fear of God, whose judgment she feared would intercept and condemn her at any moment. She fled to priests and confessed her sin. She traveled through holy places and implored the prayers of the Saints. But no confession, no prayer, no giving of alms assisted her. Daily, as before and even more importunately, she was infested by the Demon. Finally, so great a crime was made public. Having heard and learned of it, her husband loathed their shared life. 

Meanwhile, the Man of God, Bernard, had come to the aforementioned place with his entourage. When the unhappy woman heard of his arrival, she threw herself trembling at his feet. Bathed in tears, she revealed to her the horrible passion and long-standing mockery <note>original: *ludificationem*; refers to the deceptive and humiliating nature of demonic torment</note>, and that whatever she had done at the command of the priests had been of no use to her. She added that her oppressor had predicted and threateningly forbidden her from coming into his presence, saying it would do her no good, and that once the Abbot <note>St. Bernard of Clairvaux</note> departed, he who had been her lover would become her most cruel persecutor. 

Hearing this, the man of God comforted the woman with soothing words and promised help from heaven, commanding her to return the next day (for it was now nearly at hand) trusting in the Lord. Having returned in the morning, when she had reported to the Man of the Lord the blasphemies and threats she had heard that same night from her incubus <note>original: *incubo*; a demon believed to seek sexual contact with humans</note>, the man of God said, "Do not worry about his threats, but take this staff <note>original: *baculum*; a walking staff or crozier used by the saint</note> of ours, and place it in your bed; and let him do what he can." The woman did what she had been commanded, and lying down in her bed, protected by the sign of the Cross, she placed the staff next to her. He <note>the demon</note> was present immediately, but he did not presume to approach her for his usual work, nor even to approach the bed itself; nevertheless, he threatened most bitterly that, upon the departure of the Man of God, he would return to torment her.

Sunday was approaching, and the Man of God <note>Saint Bernard of Clairvaux</note> wished for the people to be summoned to the Church by an edict of the Bishop. When a great multitude had gathered at the Church on that day, during the solemnities of the Mass <note>original: "inter Missarum solennia"</note>, accompanied by Bishop Geoffrey of Chartres and Bishop Brice of Nantes, Bernard himself ascended the pulpit <term>ambo: a raised platform or lectern used for preaching</term>. He commanded that everyone in the church should hold lit candles in their hands. Doing the same himself, along with the Bishops and Clergy, he publicly exposed the unheard-of boldness of the Devil. With the agreement of all the faithful present, he pronounced an anathema <term>anathema: a formal curse by the church, excommunicating a person or spirit</term> against that fornicating spirit, which had burned with such horrendous filthiness, even against its own nature. By the authority of Christ, he forbade the spirit from approaching that woman or any other woman from that time forward. When those sacramental lights were extinguished, the entire power of the Devil was likewise extinguished. After the woman had made her confession and received communion, the enemy never appeared to her again, but fled, banished never to return. This account is from the *Life of Saint Bernard*.

<margin>8.</margin>
Great is this power of *Exorcism*; but its strength was increased not a little by the holiness of the Man of God. The power of the rite we use is also great, but it is not always as great as his, because our Exorcists fall far short of Saint Bernard in holiness. Thus it happens that our exorcism does not always achieve the desired effect. When this occurs, the persecution of the Spirits must be endured patiently; one must bear what cannot be corrected, and "make a virtue of necessity" <note>original: "ex necessitate facienda virtus," a common Latin idiom meaning to find a way to gain an advantage from a difficult situation</note>.

# CHAPTER XCIII.
## A certain common method by which both the upright and the wicked are delivered from the molestation of persecuting damned spirits.

<margin>1.</margin>
Beyond the two-part method already explained in the two preceding chapters—by which the wickedness of Spirits is avoided both by the evil (who endure it as punishment for sin) and by the pious (who endure it for the exercise of virtue)—there is another method which serves both equally. Although its power is not as great as the former methods, what it can achieve must be explained here.

<margin>2.</margin>
This method seems to consist of *three* modes. *One* is sought from the *place*. *Another* from the company of men. The *third* from *light*. There are certain places (I believe they are temples or churches) in which those who endure persecuting spirits are found to be safe for the most part. They are safe for the most part if they do not act alone, but in

...they enjoy the company of others. Finally, if they flee *darkness* <note>original: "tenebras"</note> and dwell in the *light* <note>original: "luce"</note>.

<margin>3.</margin>
What we say, we have learned from the confessions of those who have suffered from troubling Spirits. These people have testified more than once that they found rest in places consecrated to God, in the company of other people, and in clear light. But even if we lacked their testimony, we would not lack reasons and arguments.

<margin>4.</margin>
These Spirits avoid *Churches* <note>original: "Templa"; while "temple" is the literal translation, in this context it refers to Christian church buildings</note> because they are schools of character and all piety; because they are furnished with Images and Relics; because they contain the venerable body of Christ under the appearances of bread; and finally, because through the consecration performed by a Bishop, all entry to them is closed off to the spirits.

<margin>5.</margin>
They also avoid a *multitude* <note>original: "multitudinem"</note>. They almost always tempt and trouble those who are solitary; there are many examples of this. Two are most famous: Eve, the mother of all living, and Christ the Savior. The spirits attacked the latter in the desert and the former in paradise—and in both cases, while they were alone.

<margin>6.</margin>
They also flee the *light*. What wonder? They are the princes of darkness; they have withdrawn far from God, who dwells in inaccessible light. They rejoice in the works of darkness, being destined for the outer darkness of hell.

<margin>7.</margin>
However, as we have said, the strength of *these mechanisms* <note>original: "harum machinarum"; here referring to the methods of protection or remedies just described</note> is not as great as those we mentioned above. These seem to differ from those in two ways. First, that they grant freedom from trouble only for a time. Second, that they are not as certain as the former ones.

<margin>8.</margin>
In the former methods, the purpose is that access to the Spirits is prohibited, and the living are made free from all trouble. In these latter ones, neither is this the purpose, nor if it were the purpose, could the living hope for or expect it.

<margin>9.</margin>
These latter methods also fail. There are certain Spirits who are troublesome even in the midday light. There are some who do not fear even a great multitude of men. There are some who barely keep away from churches. We have given examples of all these elsewhere.

### A TREATISE
# CONCERNING TERRIFYING
# NIGHTTIME DISTURBANCES,
## WHICH ARE ACCUSTOMED TO PORTEND 
## THE DEATHS OF MEN.

<image-desc>Large ornamental woodcut drop cap 'C' with floral scrollwork and foliage motifs.</image-desc>
*Nighttime noises and terrifying apparitions, which usually precede and indicate the death of certain people, seem to share common ground with the subject of Infested Places. Therefore, it would not be out of place if we were to say a few things regarding their author and their purpose; and if we were to explain the manner in which they occur, as well as the times and places where they happen. For no one can doubt that these noises are raised, and that fear is frequently struck into men by them. Daily experience provides so many examples of these things that they are enough to persuade not only learned and literate men, but even the unrefined common folk of this reality.*

### CHAPTER I.

*In which the Efficient Cause <term>Efficient Cause: The primary source or agent that brings something into being, a concept from Aristotelian philosophy</term> of nighttime terrors that act as signs of death is investigated; and it is shown that they are not produced by God, nor by the souls of those whose deaths they signify.*

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'D' decorated with leaves and vines.</image-desc>
It is a difficult thing to define what the Efficient Cause <note>original: "Causa Efficiens"</note> of these disturbances and terrors might be, or who their author is. But although it is difficult, it is not impossible. Perhaps the true au-

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the "Efficient Cause" (the agent or source) of the terrifying nighttime noises that predict death. It follows from page 330 where the author began exploring who or what might be responsible for these sounds.</meta>

<page-num>338</page-num>
# NIGHTTIME DISTURBANCES.
<sig>Tt 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: stir: &; handwritten page number: 268</meta>

thor <note>original: "authorem"</note> we will find, if we first demonstrate by whom they cannot be made.

<margin>2.</margin>
**First of all, it is certain** that they are made by *someone*. For whatever things are made, since they cannot be the cause of themselves, it is absolutely necessary that they have something beyond themselves—whatever that may be—which is their cause and brings them about. Therefore, these disturbances too will have some cause of their own.

<margin>3.</margin>
**What cause, then, shall we assign to them?** By whom should these disturbances be said to be made? It is necessary that they proceed either from corporeal <note>physical/material</note> things or from incorporeal <note>spiritual/non-material</note> things. For I do not see what third option I ought to admit here.

<margin>4.</margin>
**Furthermore, in the category of incorporeal things, there are several levels.** And to begin with the more imperfect: here are the spirits of men, both the living and those departed from life. There are the spirits of Angels, both good and evil. And He who is the father of all spirits, **God, the Best and Greatest.**

<margin>5.</margin>
**It is not necessary here to distinguish these levels among corporeal things.** For although there are many levels among them, just as there are among the incorporeal, they nevertheless contribute nothing to the raising of these disturbances, no matter which levels they belong to or how they are classified. If there is anything in the category of corporeal things to which we ought to attribute these disturbances and terrors, it would be certain manikins <note>original: "Homunciones"</note> (perhaps you might well call them *household spirits* <note>original: "Lares domesticos"</note>) who are said by some to be a sort of middle-being between man and beast, being neither truly human nor truly animal.

<margin>6.</margin>
**Since there are therefore such varied kinds of things**, from which of them shall we say the disturbances in question are raised? Let us inquire into this. But indeed, we should establish two things here as certain and beyond all controversy; the others, because they may hold difficulty, must be examined more diligently. *It is certain that they are not raised by God, the Best and Greatest; and it is certain they are not raised by the spirits of those whose deaths they signify.*

<margin>7.</margin>
**Regarding God, no one can have a doubtful mind.** It is unworthy to attribute these terrors and mockeries <note>original: "Terrificationes & Ludificationes"</note> to the Divine Majesty; moreover, whatever happens under heaven (if you except two or three things which require purely divine power) He executes either through the proper causes of things or through the work and ministry of Angels.

<margin>8.</margin>
**We are not ignorant that there are some** who think the *human soul*—specifically that of the person whose death these signs precede—departs from the body and they assert it is the author of these disturbances. But these people err most gravely. Can the soul desert the body and in the meantime still vitalize and move it? Or perhaps one and the same soul exists in different places at the same—

## CHAPTER II.

->*It is shown that the Terrifying Events and the aforementioned Disturbances are not caused by certain Little Men: moreover, that such Little Men are not what they are said to be.*<-

<margin>1.</margin> <image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial Q featuring a small figure, possibly a child, seated within a square frame decorated with foliage.</image-desc>Those who argue for the existence of certain <term>Homunciones; literally 'little men,' referring here to nature spirits or elementals like gnomes or kobolds</term>—a species of living creature between beasts and men, yet in human form—who hide in secret places but sometimes reveal themselves to human sight, seem to attribute these Disturbances to them as the authors with some degree of reasoning; just as they also credit them with many services <note>original: "obsequia"</note> they perform for humans.

<margin>2.</margin> But nevertheless, if we wish to reason correctly, we shall find that such Little Men do not exist in the nature of things. Nor, if they did exist, could they foreknow the deaths of men, and therefore they could not signal them; nor if they did foreknow them, would they be the authors of these Disturbances and <term>Terrificationes; terrifying supernatural events or omens</term>.

<margin>3.</margin> For if Little Men exist in the nature of things: where, I ask, do they live and have their dwellings? It is very strange that they are said to dwell among men, and yet no place has ever been found where they have their homes.

<margin>4.</margin> Furthermore, by what means do they preserve and propagate their kind so that it does not perish? (For we must not think that they are immortal and live a perpetual life here, as the Angels do in heaven). Or is their condition perhaps the same as that of humans and brute animals, so that some of them die while others succeed in their place? …nor has a single one of these ever been found who has departed from this life; no one has been found who was substituted to take the place of one who died. <note>The author argues that if these "Little Men" were a real race of beings, we would see evidence of their deaths and the birth or appointment of successors.</note>

<margin>5.</margin>
By what means do they sustain their lives? On what things do they feed? It should not be said that they live on air. To suggest they eat the food of beasts and brute animals is absurd, since they so closely resemble humans and seem to differ in almost nothing except their stature. Should human food, then, be assigned to them? But this is often not available, as many of them are said to dwell in deserted camps and abandoned buildings, which neither men visit nor is human food carried to.

<margin>6.</margin>
We also ask: are they able to become participants in *eternal bliss* and that happiness which we expect in the future life, or does their soul perish along with the body? The latter cannot be said, since they reflect the human form and are said to perform many actions that could not be done without reason. Yet, regarding the former, it ought to be said by no means; for the requirements which are necessary to attain that salvation, and which were instituted by Christ the Lord, are utterly neglected by them.

<margin>7.</margin>
Every reason why these **Little Men** <note>original: "Homunciones"; here referring to elemental spirits or kobolds</note> are asserted to exist is taken from their *Apparitions*; because, namely, they have sometimes been seen among men. But truly, little proof is gathered from this to establish their existence. How many things, I ask you, are there that fall under our sight and yet are nothing but illusions of the senses and conjuring tricks? Or, certainly, are they not the appearances of Spirits in human form?

<margin>8.</margin>
But even if we were to admit these **Little Men** exist, they still should not be called the cause of these **Disturbances** <note>original: "Tumultuũ"; referring to the supernatural uproars or knockings</note>; because they cannot know in advance the deaths of men, of which these Disturbances are the signs. For since they are said to be of a lower condition than humans themselves, and not to possess as much judgment and reason as men, it follows that what men cannot do—namely, to foresee and indicate the deaths of men—they themselves will not be able to do either.

<margin>9.</margin>
Perhaps because they are not distracted by *other occupations*, they attend more diligently to the natures and temperaments of men; and for that reason, they foresee what we, distracted by other business, cannot. Let it be so. But by what logic can they be said to foresee the ends of those who are brought to a violent death? Since, therefore, **Disturbances** precede even the departure of these people from this life, just as they are not the authors of these deaths, so they should not be called the authors of the prior Disturbances.

10. <margin><unclear>p</unclear> [...] <unclear>foreknown</unclear> see 1 Cor 15</margin> Let us even grant this to be the case: that the deaths of men are foreknown; yet, it is immediately clear that these **Disturbances** <note>original: "Tumultus"; referring to the noisy, poltergeist-like phenomena previously discussed</note> cannot be attributed to them. First, because since they are believed to have very small bodies, they ought not be thought to possess great strength. Therefore, these disturbances—which are sometimes massive and require great force—could not be stirred up by them by any means.

11. Furthermore, whoever excites these disturbances must do so through the collision of physical bodies (specifically those that are heard to strike one another). We often hear planks being carried, wood being fitted together, tools being dragged, and nails being driven in; yet, as soon as we rush to the places where the noises are stirred up, we discover by great evidence that there has been no movement among similar physical objects. Thus, these things can be attributed to spirits.

12. Finally, these disturbances are sometimes excited in diverse and greatly distant places. Shall we perhaps establish that these **Little Men** <note>original: "Homunciones"</note> are in diverse places at once? Or shall we say that after they have stirred things up in this place, they migrate to another to stir them up there as well? Whether these things can be said with any reason, I would vehemently doubt.

13. Therefore, from what has been said, we seem able to conclude that these **Terrifying Apparitions** <note>original: "Terrificationes"</note> are the work of spirits. It is spirits who stir up the disturbances; who mimic groans and wailing; who lead funeral processions; who create the tombs in which the bodies of the deceased are hidden. It is spirits who perform all these things and others like them.

## CHAPTER III.

->*It is demonstrated that the said disturbances are not stirred up by the spirits of those men who have departed from this life.*<-

1. It remains for us to inquire by which spirits these disturbances are made: whether by human spirits, who have left this life along with the body they once animated; or by **Angels**, whether they be blessed or delivered over to eternal punishments as their merits required.

2. There is no doubt that human spirits sometimes return to the living. This has been demonstrated by us elsewhere through many arguments. There is also no doubt that they perform many kinds of duties among the living. Nevertheless, whatever they may perform, it is not to be believed that they employ their labors in this specific kind of work.

3. The proper condition of souls after this life is not that they should be ministers of God among men, or perform certain duties <note>original: "munia"</note> in this world by virtue of an office...

...should perform their duties; and be present in human affairs; but only so that they may receive the fruits of their labors; and either fully enjoy God, or pay the due penalties; wherefore in this category <note>referring to the cause of supernatural disturbances</note>, they have nothing to do.

<margin>3.</margin>
It does not happen without the singular providence and dispensation of God that the deceased are present in the affairs of the living: and whatever things require this providence and dispensation of God happen quite rarely. But these **Disturbances** <note>original: "Tumultus"; the author uses this term for the banging and crashing sounds associated with hauntings</note> are not rare; they occur almost daily.

<margin>4.</margin>
It was clear to the **Rich Man** <note>original: "Epulo"; referring to the glutton from the biblical parable of Dives and Lazarus in Luke 16</note> that **Lazarus** should return to the living to warn his brothers of his miserable condition. What does **Abraham** say here? *They have*, he says, *Moses and the Prophets: let them hear them.* The Rich Man urges a second time: he thinks it will come to pass that they will perform penance *if someone from the dead comes to them.* But Abraham rightly says: *If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.* 

<margin>5.</margin>
Could we not say the same? That the living have, I say, Moses and the Prophets? That they have so many examples and proofs of ever-present death? That there is no need for the souls of the deceased to return to the living and remind them of impending death?

<margin>6.</margin>
If we consult the Holy Scriptures, we will find that God has mostly carried out His will through **Angels** (and not through human spirits) whenever He wished something to be done outside the usual order of things. Why then would He use human spirits in this business, and not Angels, if indeed He wished to use the labor of anyone?

<margin>7.</margin>
Since these disturbances and noises are certain **signs of death**, to which human spirits shall we attribute the duty of exciting them? To those who already lead a happy life with God in heaven? Or those who are being purified by the fire of Purgatory? Or those who are companions of demons in hell?

<margin>8.</margin>
**Granting that the first group** <note>the Blessed in heaven</note> could know, through God revealing it, who is about to depart from this life; yet, who would believe that God would reveal this to them (since it does not concern them) and wish them to be, as it were, messengers of men's deaths?

<margin>9.</margin>
Whenever the spirits of the Blessed are involved in our affairs, they are accustomed to **show themselves**, and indeed in such a form that they can be easily recognized, just as the examples of those who have appeared teach us. But where these noises are stirred up, their authors are never seen.

<margin>10.</margin>
Add to this that the Blessed spirits hardly ever take part in our affairs **in person** <note>original: "authoproprosopos"; a Latinized Greek term meaning face-to-face or in one's own person</note>; almost everything that seems to be done by them is carried out by the labor of Angels. And if they do not involve themselves in our affairs even in their own business when they most ought to, would they involve themselves when no reason compels them to take part in the affairs of others?

God does not have only one way by which He avenges sins. He punishes some by this method which we are now explaining, while for others He keeps different methods; yet without any injustice to those who are being punished.

<margin>8.</margin>
These things are said, as it seems, with probability. Whether they are truly so, no one could easily say, unless a revelation has been made to him from elsewhere. However, even this assertion has no small difficulty, as we shall show in the following sections.

<margin>9.</margin>
First of all, *how is it established among men* that these Spirits have any place here? Granting that they might inhabit this world after the final day of judgment; yet that they live now among the living, and take part in our affairs, can be said, but it cannot be proved.

<margin>10.</margin>
Next, suppose some place is made for them among the living; from where can they *know* the deaths of the living—not only those which are natural, but even violent ones? Do they perhaps have human natures fully perceived and understood, so that they are able to know how long they can prolong their lives? And even if this were granted, how will they know violent deaths, which proceed from a free will?

<margin>11.</margin>
Thirdly, God is accustomed to use the work of *Angels* if He wishes anything to be signaled to men. From this, they have acquired the name of *Ministering Spirits*. <note>original: "Administratoriorum Spirituum"; a reference to Hebrews 1:14 describing angels as spirits sent to serve.</note> If, therefore, He wishes to warn men of a present or imminent death, He would use the work of Angels, not of these Spirits.

# CHAPTER V.

*That Good Angels are not the authors of the Disturbances which usually serve as omens of death.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Since (as has been said) these Terrifying Encounters and nocturnal Disturbances <note>original: "Tumultus nocturni"; a term for what we might today call poltergeist activity.</note> under discussion are not the work of human spirits, it is entirely necessary to attribute them to the Angels themselves, whose duties are assigned in this sensible world alongside the human race.

<margin>2.</margin>
However, since these are of *two kinds* <note>Referring to the division between "Good Angels" and "Fallen Angels" (demons).</note> and of almost contrary pursuits, there is a serious debate as to which they should be attributed. It is easier to act as a student here than as a teacher.

<margin>3.</margin>
Anyone who wishes to consider the matter itself might easily be persuaded that since men seem to be warned of *death* and called to give an account to God, these are not the works of wicked spirits who hate the salvation of men, but of *good* ones, who truly love them.

<margin>4.</margin>
But he who weighs everything more carefully will find his mind wavering quite a bit. Indeed, might he not easily admit contrary thoughts? For if the purpose of these Terrifying Encounters is to warn men of death, what need is there, I ask, for so many Disturbances? For such great noise? For even a funeral procession and six hundred <note>The Latin "sexcentis" (six hundred) is often used idiomatically to mean an "innumerable" or "countless" amount.</note> other things? Especially when men could be warned of death by much simpler means?

<margin>5.</margin>
Furthermore, a *certain* proof of following death cannot be sought from this noise. For who can say whether it is an indication of death or if it is stirred up for some other reason? Granted, after death has followed, we might be able to say it was a sign of death; but nevertheless, while it was being stirred up, it could not be said with certainty to be a proof of death.

<margin>6.</margin>
Even if it were the most certain sign of death, one still cannot know *whose* death it portends. Therefore, since every individual living in one family might think it pertains to them, this work would be undertaken by good angels in vain.

<margin>7.</margin>
This noise is also heard in *other places* than where the person who dies is located, and it is heard frequently: in other places these prognostic signs of death are obser-

observed. We know of a man who died at Mainz <note>original: "Moguntiæ"</note>, whose death omens occurred not in Mainz, but in another place where he held his defenses and resources; but how could he, in the absence of those signs, be warned to prepare himself for death?

<margin>8.</margin>
At the very time when many breathe their last, Disturbances <note>original: "Tumultus"; the author's preferred term for what we might call poltergeist activity.</note> are not infrequently stirred up. But who would say they were stirred up for the purpose of helping men prepare for a happy end?

<margin>9.</margin>
These Terrifying Encounters <note>original: "Terriculamenta"</note> precede the deaths of both the worst of men and the most holy men. But just as the latter have no need of them, the former are unworthy of them. For by the just judgment of God it happens, *that those who while living forgot God, while dying forget themselves.*

<margin>10.</margin>
They also precede the deaths of *unbelievers*, and not only those who once embraced the faith of Christ, but also of Jews and Pagans, who impiously rejected it. Since there is no hope of eternal salvation remaining for these, why is it necessary that they be warned of their end and their departure from this life by these signs?

<margin>11.</margin>
Therefore, the purpose of this noise and Disturbance is not for mortals to prepare themselves for a holy departure from this life. Wherefore it should not be concluded from this argument that the Spirits by whom the Disturbances are stirred up are good.

<margin>12.</margin>
Other arguments are also available to confirm this matter. Good Angels are <term>Ministering Spirits</term> <note>original: "Adminiſtratorij"; refers to the biblical concept in Hebrews 1:14 of angels as servants to the faithful.</note>: they most promptly offer their services to God in whatever matters He wishes. If, therefore, they employ their services here, it must be by the command and will of God. But since no reason can be given why God would wish or command these Disturbances to be stirred up, why should we judge they should be attributed to good Angels?

<margin>13.</margin>
It is strange that, while so many and so illustrious duties and offices of the good Angels are described in the sacred scriptures, no mention is made of this so frequent and customary one. It is strange that there is such silence among the most holy <term>Doctors of the Church</term> <note>Referring to early Christian theologians such as Augustine or Jerome.</note>; especially since among them are found those who left behind entire volumes for posterity concerning the functions of good Spirits.

<margin>14.</margin>
Furthermore, not a few nor light arguments of levity are joined with these Disturbances. To say that the authors of these things are Angels, who perpetually contemplate the face of God, is a most unworthy thing.

## CHAPTER VI.

### That the Disturbances which are omens of death are stirred up by evil Spirits.

<meta>catchword: Easily</meta>

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument regarding the origin of supernatural phenomena. Having dismissed the souls of the dead and good angels as the sources of death omens in the preceding pages, he now begins a formal proof that these "Terrifying Encounters" and "Disturbances" are the work of evil spirits (demons).</meta>

<page-num>340</page-num>
<header>ON TERRIFYING ENCOUNTERS</header>

<margin>1.</margin> From what has been said, anyone may easily conclude that Terrifying Encounters <note>original: "Terrificationes"</note> and Disturbances <note>original: "Tumultus"</note>, which are the heralds of death, are stirred up by the work of evil spirits. Since it is necessary that these be produced by spirits; and since neither those who still live in human bodies, nor those who have left their bodies and dwell elsewhere, nor the good Angels are their authors; to whom, I ask, shall we attribute them if not to *evil spirits*?

<margin>2.</margin> And indeed, there is *nothing* in this category of phenomena that is alien to those spirits, or exceeds their powers; there are even *many* things that strongly persuade us to assign these duties to them. We shall demonstrate both points.

<margin>3.</margin> It is necessary that the spirits who are the authors of these Disturbances be *present* in those places where the Disturbances are stirred up. It is necessary that they have the power to stir up Disturbances. It is necessary that they be able to organize a funeral procession <note>This refers to the "phantom funerals" often reported in folklore, where spectral mourners are seen before a real death.</note>. It is necessary that they be able to *know* the future departures of men from this life, which they indicate. Which of these things is lacking in evil spirits?

<margin>4.</margin> No one will deny that spirits can be *present* in those places where Disturbances are stirred up. Their strength is great and their power is vast; they can present themselves in almost any place they wish. Access lies open to them for anyone.

<margin>5.</margin> They are also *capable* of stirring up Disturbances. What are they not capable of doing against physical bodies? Are not almost all things subject to their power? Can they not drive them wherever they wish by their own force? Therefore, since these Disturbances arise from the collision of physical objects, they will be able to stir up these, and even much more serious ones.

<margin>6.</margin> Likewise, it is within their power to assemble a funeral procession. For they cannot only move external bodies; they can also take them up for themselves and adapt them to any use. They can give them whatever forms they like, although they represent the funeral procession not only with physical bodies they have fashioned, but also by the fascination and illusion <note>The author suggests demons can manipulate both physical matter and the human mind to create hallucinations.</note> of the senses—sometimes external, sometimes internal.

<margin>7.</margin> And since they are of the most keen intelligence and excel greatly through experience of events, and furthermore know the natures of things and the temperaments <note>original: "complexiones"; refers to the balance of humors in a person which, in early modern medicine, dictated health and lifespan.</note> of men most exactly, who will doubt that they often foreknow the *deaths* of men?
