## CHAPTER VII.

->*That Disturbances or Terrors that announce death are stirred up by Demons who are of a lower order.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
It has been demonstrated that these Noises <note>original: "Strepitus"</note> are stirred up by the work of Demons and become precursors of death; but whether this is the specific pursuit of all of them without distinction, or only of certain ones, is a question that is not uninteresting. For the condition of all Demons is not one and the same, nor are the occupations of all the same. Some have more serious pursuits than others, just as some excel others in sharpness of mind, power of action, or the will to do harm.

<margin>2.</margin>
For it is beyond controversy that those Spirits fell from absolutely all the orders which they once held in common with the good Angels. <note>In traditional theology, there are nine "choirs" or ranks of angels; the author argues that some spirits fell from every rank, creating a mirroring hierarchy in hell.</note> It is also beyond controversy that their nature was not taken away by sin. Therefore, just as they were not all of equal perfection before sin, so too after sin the condition of nature is not the same for all.

<margin>3.</margin>
Their pursuits and functions follow the condition of their nature. Just as this is certain in all things, so in these Spirits it holds no doubt. Therefore, the functions of the lower spirits are not the same as those of the higher: the latter undergo more weightier duties; the former carry out lighter tasks.

<margin>4.</margin>
What we assert would have been very easy to perceive in the Spirits if they had not fallen from the grace in which they were created. Now, after grace...

The occupations of Demons among the human race are varied. For the purpose of our established method, we can divide them all into two classes: those of greater importance, which we might call *more principal*; and others of lighter weight, which we might call *less principal.*

<margin>7.</margin>
The former (the major works) are defined by three factors: the status of the persons with whom they are undertaken; the scale and difficulty of the tasks themselves; and finally, the severity of the evil intended by the Spirits to disadvantage mankind. Where these things are lacking—that is, where there is neither the dignity of the person nor the difficulty of completing the business, and the intended evils are light—it is appropriate to call these the *lesser occupations* of Demons.

<margin>8.</margin>

<margin>9.</margin>
They carry out the former tasks in order to destroy; the latter, in order to vex and be a nuisance. Just as in this life, while wars are being waged, the goal of the opposing side is not always to destroy the enemies; but sometimes, when the opportunity to destroy is not given, it is satisfying enough to be troublesome, to terrify, and to strike fear. In the same way, the demons—the sworn enemies of the human race—do not always intend to destroy; but sometimes their goal is simply to be a nuisance and to harass.

<margin>10.</margin>

Which others, indeed, than those which the Demons themselves wish to be assigned?* Furthermore, who could doubt that those of the higher Orders claim the major tasks for themselves, while they leave the minor ones to the lower spirits? The distribution of duties is established quite appropriately according to the status of the individuals.

<margin>12.</margin>
Likewise, those spirits of the higher Orders <note>The author uses the term "Orders" (Ordines) to mirror the traditional hierarchy of angels (Seraphim, Cherubim, etc.), applied here to fallen demons.</note> take upon themselves more arduous and difficult burdens. The strength of their nature demands it. Furthermore, they fear less humiliation if a matter does not succeed according to their wishes when the task was difficult.

Among these same high-ranking spirits, there is a more severe hatred toward the human race than among those of the lower Orders; and this hatred is followed by a zeal for doing harm. Thus, it happens that these high spirits are chiefly intent on doing harm and inflicting the greatest possible injuries upon mortals.

Furthermore, even the least Spirit is gifted with enough power of intellect to foreknow the imminent death of men, which is signified by these Disturbances.

<margin>16.</margin>

Therefore, their punishment <term>poena</term> is not as great as that of the superiors. Christians partly agree with these Gentiles <note>In this context, "Gentiles" refers to non-Christian or "pagan" classical philosophers.</note>. Furthermore, Rabbi Moses <note>Referring to Maimonides (Moses Maimonides), a preeminent Sephardic Jewish philosopher and scholar.</note> writes in *The Guide for the Perplexed*, book 3, chapter 25, that this very concept was handed down by an ancient tradition, not only among Christians but also among the Hebrews. See Juan Maldonado’s commentary on Matthew 18.

<margin>7.</margin>
They deny that evil angels are *assigned* by God to individual men in the same way that He assigns good ones to individuals. They believe it does not befit the divine goodness, which so greatly desires the salvation of men, to assign us enemies to infest us, to cast us down from the fortress of virtue, and to separate us from God—the highest and greatest good. They consider the hatred of demons toward the human race to be sufficiently great on its own; they believe the demons are themselves most ready and prepared to trouble us, and they require neither God’s command nor His appointment to do so.

<margin>8.</margin>
While they admit these things, they do not deny the existence of these spirits; rather, they deny that they are delegated and ordained by God for this purpose. They mean that these spirits offer themselves and attach themselves to men of their own accord and will—a point that no one who has thoroughly examined the nature and condition of demons would easily dispute.

### ON TERRORS
<note>original: "DE TERRIFICATIONIBUS"</note>

<margin>9.</margin>
Demons are accustomed to imitating the works of God: they attempt to copy almost everything that God does. This matter is too certain to require proof. For this reason, they are called the *apes of God* <note>original: "simiæ Dei." This was a common medieval and Renaissance concept suggesting that Satan can only mimic or distort God's creations, rather than create anything truly new.</note>. Why then would they not want to imitate God in this regard? Just as God joins good Spirits to men to protect and defend them, so too would the demons want to join evil and perverse ones to them, to harass and destroy.

<margin>10.</margin>
This matter is confirmed by a very ancient opinion, accepted by almost everyone, in which it is believed that at the final moment of life, there is present for every mortal not just a good Angel to lead the soul to heaven (if he departs this life in the grace of God), but also an *evil* one to drag him to the underworld, if such are his deserts. For just as we understand the "good spirit" to be that one granted to each of us by God from birth, it seems not wrong to say that the "evil spirit" is he who was always opposed to a person's pious efforts and urged them to follow worse paths.

<margin>11.</margin>

> *That by Your customary mercy,* &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; *And suppress our ENEMY,*
> *You might be our guard and guide.* &nbsp;&nbsp; *Lest our bodies be defiled.*

# CHAPTER IX.
## *A judgment on the preceding chapters concerning the authors of terrifying apparitions and disturbances.*

<margin>1.</margin> There are two kinds of things that happen. Some occur *for the most part*, and are said to happen *ordinarily*; others occur *more rarely*, and are said to happen *outside the common order of things*. This distinction, just as it holds a place in natural things, should not be rejected here. In nature, it happens ordinarily that a woman carries a child in her womb for nine months; but if this law should fail at any time, and she gives birth to the offspring sooner or later, it is said that something has happened *outside the order of things*. In this category of disturbances <note>original: "Tumultuum," referring to the noisy or chaotic activity of haunting spirits.</note>, those things we have discussed so far are *ordinary*; if any should happen differently, we shall say they occur *extraordinarily*.

<margin>2.</margin> In truth, three things here seem to happen extraordinarily. First, it should not be thought that these disturbances are always stirred up by those spirits who are, as it were, assigned to individuals as their own; sometimes they are stirred up by others. Second, sometimes demons of the *Higher Orders* employ their efforts here. Third, sometimes they are even stirred up by the zeal of *Good Angels*.

<margin>3.</margin> Regarding the first, there is hardly any doubt. It is probable that those who are of the same Order may sometimes handle the same interests and perform the same duties; especially if one does not take the other's work badly, and both are engaged with pleasure in the task undertaken. Since these conditions apply here, there is little doubt that sometimes others besides one's own personal spirit <note>original: "proprij genij." The "Genius" was considered a personal spirit or tutelary deity in Roman thought, here adapted into demonology.</note> are occupied in this.

<margin>4.</margin> Perhaps it is even necessary at times for certain others, besides the assigned ones, to bestow their labor here: specifically when the work of one seems insufficient to complete all those things that are often observed in these terrifying apparitions. For they sometimes occur in various and widely distant places at the same time; and occasionally a grand funeral procession is staged, which requires the labor of many spirits.

<margin>5.</margin> Thus it can be believed that spirits of the *Higher Orders* employ their efforts here. For the lust for vexing the human race and the desire for doing harm—which never leave them—ensure that the higher demons shun no kind of duty, however lowly it may be. Just as sordid and greedy merchants seek profit from anything at all, so do those demons seek to bring harm to men from wherever and whenever they can.

<margin>6.</margin> What we say is drawn from many examples in the histories of the Saints—

[The text begins mid-sentence] can be confirmed by readily available evidence, many of which prove that even the highest-ranking Spirits have undergone menial tasks and lowered themselves to the condition of inferiors; meanwhile, it is not said that this occupation of punishments <note>The author suggests that demons might perform these tasks as a form of "punishment" or "labor," but perhaps one that offers them a perverse distraction or relief from their own suffering.</note>, which they suffer most heavily, is some relief for them (which they seek).

<margin>7.</margin>
We seem to be able to conjecture from two points that these indications of death are sometimes given by the work of *Good Angels*. First, from the fact that God has not infrequently signaled to certain people that the time was at hand in which they were to depart from this life: as this has sometimes been done by a more hidden inspiration, so we might say, not without reason, that it sometimes happens and has happened through these signs, by the work of good Angels, whom God is accustomed to use.

<margin>8.</margin>
To this is added that even with the death of the holiest men, these signs are sometimes joined; and they are observed not only in profane places, but even in *sacred* ones: they are also shown to those who have waged a continuous war with the devil. Moreover, they are not infrequently carried out with spiritual fruit, and as a sign of the holiness of those whose death they preceded. Who indeed would believe that malignant Spirits would employ their efforts here?

<margin>9.</margin>
However, as we have said, *these cases are rarer*. Those defined above <note>Referring to the malevolent disturbances described in earlier chapters.</note> *occur more frequently*. Therefore, just as the privileges of a few do not detract from common laws, so although an exception can be made, it nonetheless should not be denied that these Disturbances <note>original: "Tumultus," used throughout the text to describe the noisy, chaotic activity of a haunting.</note> are stirred up and signs of death are given by the work of *evil Spirits*, and especially of their own <term>genii</term> <note>original: "geniorum." In this context, the author refers to the ancient Roman concept of a personal spirit or guardian assigned to an individual, here interpreted through a Christian demonological lens.</note>.

# CHAPTER X.
## *Concerning the goals which are set before Demons in Disturbances and nocturnal Terrors.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Concerning the Authors and the efficient Cause of nocturnal Disturbances and Terrors, enough has been said: it remains for us to investigate their goals and *effects*. There, it is asked what the Spirits' purpose is in these Disturbances; here, whether these Disturbances are true signs of death and if they actually cause it. The former must be explained in this Chapter, the latter in the following one.

<margin>2.</margin>
*Various goals* seem to be set before the Demons here. First of all, these works are undertaken by them so that they may strike terror into men and bring them some distress. And for this purpose, hardly anything is so... <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

# ON TERRIFICATIONS #

...also if a Disturbance <term>Tumultus<note>In this context, the author uses this term to describe the noisy, chaotic nature of a haunting or poltergeist-like activity.</note></term> is effective: both because they are mostly stirred up at night, which itself brings horror; and because they are joined with death, which is the most terrifying of all terrifying things; and finally, because their causes and reasons are scarcely understood.

<margin>3.</margin>
They then seem to be stirred up to announce a future death. Since they are joined with death, and those things pertaining to a funeral procession are sometimes fashioned with these disturbances, we can hardly doubt that they are undertaken to indicate an imminent death.

<margin>4.</margin>
The third purpose is that, by this means, they may gain credibility for themselves among mortals; and that they might be held as truthful if they ever predict other things, since they do not fail in indicating the deaths of men. Indeed, they labor greatly, and not without cause, to maintain this reputation among Mortals.

<margin>5.</margin>
To these is added a fourth purpose, which is sought from the common ambition of Demons; which, since it is to lead men away from God, to entangle them in errors, and to claim for themselves the worship due to the true God: this is entirely the purpose of Demons here. These Wicked Spirits desire, of course, to lead men into these thoughts, so that they believe there is some divinity <term>numen<note>A Latin term for a spiritual power or localized deity; the author suggests demons impersonate these to steal worship from God.</note></term> by whom these disturbances are stirred up, and finally bestow divine honor upon it.

<margin>6.</margin>
Concerning this fourth purpose, the matter is clear. Sacred Scripture teaches that this is the primary pursuit of Demons. **Like a roaring lion, they go about seeking whom they may devour.** <note>original: "Vt Leo rugiens circumeunt, quærentes quos deuorent." A reference to the First Epistle of Peter 5:8.</note> Nor have they been frustrated among those who considered the *Lares* <note>The Lares were ancient Roman protector-spirits of the household; the author views this historical belief as a successful demonic deception.</note> to be certain household gods, and paid them divine honor, and decreed they should not be abandoned, as Pliny testifies concerning Servius Tullius in Book 37, last chapter.

<margin>7.</margin>
They vehemently desire the third purpose because of the huge profit they hope for from it. Thus, of course, they more easily draw to themselves those who are held by the desire for knowledge of hidden things (of whom there is no small number), and they persuade them to use their counsel and help—with the most immediate danger to their souls.

<margin>8.</margin>
Regarding the first purpose, the same desire to do harm drives them; because this desire is greatest and most burning, they accept whatever means by which they can cause inconvenience; and even if they cannot bring about serious damage, they still please themselves in this regard if they are able to cause trouble and disturb peace.

<margin>9.</margin>
Regarding the second purpose, someone might perhaps doubt it, as it seems it can hardly be possible that they are able to foresee the deaths of men and those things joined with a funeral. But there will be no room for doubt if one wishes to consider how many and how great are the reasons from which those spirits are able to foreknow these things.

<margin>10.</margin>
Human deaths are of two kinds: natural and violent. Demons are able to foreknow both, and to predict and indicate both.

<margin>11.</margin>
They are able to foreknow natural deaths because they are most shrewd, both because of their incredible cleverness and subtlety of mind; and because of their extraordinary experience gained over many thousands of years; and finally, because of their perfect and absolute knowledge of all natural things. By this knowledge, they understand human natures, bodily afflictions, and the habits from which death occurs, just as they understand all other matters.

<margin>12.</margin>
Violent deaths they recognize partly by God’s revelation made through good Angels (for sometimes God uses the labor of Demons to inflict death upon a man); partly they detect them from secret plans, words, writings, and other signs; and partly also from the preparation of those things which are employed to bring about death.

<margin>13.</margin>
The very heavy authority of Blessed <term>Augustine<note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers. His writings on the "Literal Meaning of Genesis" provided the medieval and early modern world with a "scientific" framework for understanding how spirits interact with the physical world.</note></term> confirms this. For he speaks thus in Book 2 of *On the Literal Interpretation of Genesis*, chapter 17:
> *Spirits are permitted to know certain truths regarding temporal affairs: partly because of a more refined sharpness of sense; partly because they are vitalized by more subtle bodies <note>original: "corporibus subtilioribus uigent." This refers to the traditional belief that demons possessed "aerial" bodies that were more refined and faster than human flesh.</note>; partly through a more skillful experience due to the great length of their lives; and partly from the holy Angels, what they themselves learn from Almighty God—even at His command when the Angels reveal things to them—He who distributes human merits with the most hidden justice and sincerity. Sometimes, however, these same wicked spirits even predict, as if by divination, those things which they themselves are about to do. Thus says Augustine.*

# CHAPTER XI.
## On the Effects of Nightly Tumults and Diabolical Terrifications.

<margin>1.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring floral patterns and scrollwork inside a square frame.</image-desc>
Now we must inquire into the power of these Tumults <term>Tumultus<note>A term used by the author to describe the chaotic, noisy phenomena associated with hauntings, such as banging or crashing sounds.</note></term> and Terrifications, and what they themselves achieve. For since signs are of two types—some merely bring something to one's notice, but do not cause what they signify; while others are such that they cause what they signify—it is a question of whether we ought to place these Tumults in the former or the latter category.

<margin>2.</margin>
And indeed, there is no doubt that they belong among the first kind of signs. But since these signs are of two types—some occasionally deceive, while others never fail—what, I ask, are these that are said to be indicators of death? Are they so certain that they never deceive, or do they fail sometimes?

This is asked based on the condition of those who [cause] these Tum... <note>original: "Tumul-". The text cuts off here at the catchword "tuum," indicating the word continues as "tumultuantur" or "tumultus" on the next page.</note>

### ON FRIGHTFUL PORTENTS

...your [spirits] are the authors, it must be defined. Since these are able to foreknow the deaths of men for the most part, it generally happens that, following these signs and the **disturbances** stirred up by them, death follows.

<margin>4.</margin>
Yet it is beyond doubt that they are sometimes mistaken.

<margin>5.</margin>
This is first evident in those to whom a violent death is brought <note>The author distinguishes between "natural death" (aging/disease) and "violent death" (murder, accident, or suicide).</note>. For since this depends on the human will, and because demons do not perfectly perceive the thoughts and wills of men, they cannot give certain signs of the death that will follow from them.

<margin>6.</margin>
But even a death that happens naturally to a man can be hindered—if not by other causes, then certainly by the will of God, by whose command the moments of our life run their course. Can He not give life beyond the order of nature? Can He not recall one from the underworld to life? Why then could He not prolong the same life beyond the laws of nature?

<margin>7.</margin>
Wherefore, although the evidence of death taken from natural causes by demons has great strength because of the powers of nature (which are not small), yet because nature obeys the command of God, such evidence should not be taken as a rule that allows no exception.

<margin>8.</margin>
But let us examine the second part of the proposed question, and let us discuss whether these disturbances are not only signs, but also *efficacious signs* <note>original: "efficacia signa" — in scholastic logic, an efficacious sign is one that actually produces the effect it represents, like a cause.</note> of a future death. For the unlearned common people often judge in such a way that they think whatever are signs of a thing are also its causes and *efficacious signs*.

<margin>9.</margin>
Now, it can be understood in two ways that these signs are the cause of death. First, as they are taken plainly in themselves, with no account taken of the authors by whom they are made; then, as their authors are joined with them, so that those spirits bring about the death which the signs themselves indicate.

<margin>10.</margin>
The first should by no means be said. *These disturbances, and whatever signs are observed, do not cause death, nor are they able to cause it*; because they have no place among the causes that are accustomed to bring about death.

<margin>11.</margin>
Death can happen to a man from without; it can happen from within. Internally, the causes of death are the failure of <term>natural heat<note>In Galenic medicine, "natural heat" was the vital warmth produced by the heart that maintained life and digestion.</note></term>, or of the original moisture which they call <term>radical<note>original: "humor radicalis" — the "radical moisture" was thought to be a finite, oil-like substance in the body that acted as fuel for the natural heat; its exhaustion resulted in natural death.</note></term>; likewise the immoderate force of passion and disturbance of the soul. Furthermore, death is caused by one's own will in those who—through weariness of the present life, or impatience with the evils by which they are pressed, or because they desire to turn away an impending calamity—[inflict] a violent death upon themselves...

<meta>Catchword: [them]selves (tem)</meta>

<summary>The author argues that while demons can often predict death through natural signs, they are not infallible because they cannot read human will and are subject to God's intervention. He also begins to debunk the common superstition that the frightening portents themselves (the "disturbances") are the actual causes of a person's death.</summary>

...they bring upon themselves [death]: likewise excessive food and drink, and a lack of restraint in sexual matters; finally, excessive labor and the exhaustion of the body. <note>The text here concludes a list of internal or self-inflicted causes of death, likely finishing the word "mortem" from the previous page.</note>

<margin>12.</margin>
Death can happen from external causes as well: by a man, by beasts, by demons, or by God through His angels; or from lethal food and drink; or from the lack of either food or drink; or from the harshness of the weather; or by some chance accident. These are the external causes of death. What, then, do these **nocturnal disturbances** <term>Tumultus nocturni: a general term for unexplained noises, bangs, or "poltergeist" activity associated with hauntings</term> have in common with these or the previous causes? They are indeed outside the person; however, they are not of the type that actually bring about death.

<margin>13.</margin>
But they should not be called causes of death just because demons join their efforts with them and thus bring death to men. Firstly, because these signs are not adopted by demons as instruments of death; and secondly, because the demons themselves do not take away our life while they are making these signs; they only announce that the end of life is at hand.

### CHAPTER XII.

->*An inquiry into the manner in which the Disturbances are stirred up and the nocturnal Terrors occur.*<-

<margin>1.</margin>
It can be understood in two ways that these disturbances are stirred up by spirits. One is that the spirits are said to first take on bodies <note>original: "corpora assumere" — the scholastic belief that spirits could condense air into a temporary physical form to interact with the world</note> very similar to human bodies, and thus, like certain men, they might wield hammers and other tools with which the noises are created. The other is that they take on no bodies, yet they stir up these noises nonetheless.

<margin>2.</margin>
Both ways are possible for these beings, just as they are for other spiritual creatures. There is no need for logic to prove this point. Holy Scripture supplies as many examples of the first way as are needed to persuade even the most stubborn. As for the second way, the very rotation of the heavens—which is moved by spirits—proves it is possible for them, even though they assume no body to be able to move it. <note>The author refers to the then-common Aristotelian belief that the celestial spheres were moved by "Intelligences" or spirits.</note>

<margin>3.</margin>
Not only is each way possible for spirits, but each is equally easy. An assumed body does not help a spirit in this task. They are just as unimpeded within a body as they are outside of one. The difference is that in the first way, there seems to be more work involved, since a body must be assumed before the disturbance is stirred up; in the second way, there is less work, as no body is assumed.

<margin>4.</margin>
But *which method do spirits follow in stirring up these disturbances?* There is no doubt that they sometimes stir them up in assumed bodies, because these spirits—the authors of these disturbances—have not only been heard, but have also been seen in human form.

**5.** Meanwhile, however, I would say it most often happens that they assume no physical body at all. By their own innate power and strength alone, without the help of any assumed body <note>original: "assumpti corporis." In demonology, an "assumed body" is a temporary physical form taken by a spirit to interact with the material world.</note>, they bring these things about.

**6.** Since the purpose of the Spirits here is to signal the deaths of men, it is not necessary for this purpose that they show themselves in a visible form. The mere noise that reaches the ears performs this task abundantly; what need, I ask, is there for an assumed body?

**7.** Furthermore, what if the tools that seem to be used in making this noise are not actually being used? And what if the objects judged to be moving are not, in reality, always moving? What we are saying is this: it is not necessary that if we seem to hear boards being carried, a coffin <term>tumba: here referring to a wooden burial chest or tomb</term> being prepared to receive the corpse of the dead, and the same being closed with hammers, that these things are actually happening. That is, it is not necessary for boards to be carried, a coffin to be fitted, or for hammers to be used. Just as spirits do not actually possess human bodies when they present themselves to be seen in human form, so too is a sound not always produced by the things from which it appears to originate; nor are bodies always moved that seem to be moved.

**8.** If there were no other argument for this, it would suffice that immediately after we have perceived the sound with our ears, if we rush to the place where it was stirred up, we find none of the things by which we judged the sound was made. We find nothing out of order; instead, all things are perfectly arranged in their proper places and rows.

**9.** Therefore, all these things happen in the air and through the air. The Spirits strike the air in such a way that it renders now the sound of carried boards, now of a striking hammer, and now various other sounds.

**10.** This is confirmed by the rather dull sound <note>original: "obtusior sonus." A muffled or non-resonant sound.</note> noted in these terrors. For although it may be stirred up in a nearby place, it nonetheless seems to happen from a distance; nor does it strike the ears in the same way as a sound made by the blows of real hammers.

**11.** But truly, even if the sound being stirred up is not actually from hammers and boards, it is nonetheless a *real* sound. This is because whatever is necessary to produce a sound is found here: namely, a striking body, a body being struck, and a medium in which the sound is received and carried to the ears.

**12.** However, these three elements are not always distinct in reality. It is not always the case that the body being struck is one thing, the striker another, and the medium in which the noise from the collision is received is yet another. Sometimes the medium is the same as the striker, sometimes the same as the struck, and often it is the same as both.

**13.** A demon can collide two parts of air together; and then, from the collision of both, a sound arises in the medium, which by the striker and...

<meta>This page concludes the philosophical discussion of how spirits mechanically produce sounds and begins Chapter XIII, which categorizes the specific locations where these death-omens are heard. ...and the percussion <note>The act of striking to produce sound.</note> does not differ from the body, it is excluded. It can also strike the air with some other body; or dash the air against another solid body; and then, because of the medium, the sound differs neither from the striking body nor the body being struck.

<margin>14.</margin> Furthermore, in whatever way the noise is stirred up, it is stirred up by the power of demons. But what kind of power is that? Is it what we call *intellectual*? Or is it the will? Or is it some other power, distinct from both?

<margin>15.</margin> The operation of the *intellect* alone is not sufficient here. Its entire occupation lies in the understanding of things; while it is engaged in this, nothing occurs outside of itself. But these Disturbances are something outside the intellect: they are formed in the air, they exist in the air, they are sustained in the air, and they are carried through the air to the ears of those listening.

<margin>16.</margin> Nor do they occur by the command of the *will* alone. It belongs to Divine Power to produce things by the command of the will alone. It is only in God that the saying holds true: *He spoke and they were made* <note>original: "dixit & facta sunt," a reference to the Creation in Genesis and the Psalms.</note>. This is not the power of Spirits, whether good or evil, such that what they wish and command happens immediately.

<margin>17.</margin> There is, therefore, a third force by which they stir up these Disturbances: that which, I say, we might not inappropriately call *Motive Power* <term>Motiva virtus: the mechanical ability to cause physical movement in the material world</term>. Just as they move themselves by this power, so too do the celestial spheres move, and so too do any bodies they wish. By this power they stir up these Disturbances, and by this they execute almost everything they do among mortals.

<margin>18.</margin> Meanwhile, although this is the only power that stirs up the Disturbances, the work of the other faculties is not rejected here. Just as a human moves or does nothing unless the Will first drove it, and the Will drives nothing unless the Intellect proposed it as something good; so too, with every noise stirred up by the Spirits, the command of the Will is added to the judgment and dictates of Reason.

## CHAPTER XIII.

->In what Places and Times the Disturbances, which are harbingers of death, are stirred up.<-

<margin>1.</margin> We must also observe the Places and Times in which these noises are stirred up, lest we seem to have overlooked any of the things connected to them.

<margin>2.</margin> Six places in particular are noted where they are stirred up. The first is where the person whose death the signs attest is giving up their soul <note>original: "animam agit," meaning to be in the throes of death or dying.</note>. The second is where that person’s friends live, of whatever kind they may be. The third is where they held possessions or estates. The fourth is where they performed certain duties or offices. The fifth is where the things necessary for the funeral are being prepared. The sixth is where the body dies and is buried.

<sig>Yy 2</sig>

<summary>This page explains that spirits use a physical "motive power" (rather than just thought or will) to create sounds in the air. It also lists six specific locations where death-omens typically manifest, including the person's home, their workplace, and their burial site.</summary>

<keywords>motive power, demonic power, intellect and will, death omens, funeral preparations, air as medium, auditory disturbances</keywords>

--- Page 620 ---
<meta>This page concludes Chapter XIII, finalizing the list of six specific locations where death-omens and spiritual "Disturbances" manifest. It transitions from the physical geography of these omens to the specific times (midday and midnight) when spirits are most active, ending the entire treatise with a formal theological disclaimer.</meta>

<page-num>356.</page-num>
<header>ON NOCTURNAL TERRORS.</header>

3. There is no doubt regarding any of the locations mentioned. Daily examples are available here. Nevertheless, in that first location <note>The home of the dying person.</note>, **Disturbances** are heard more frequently, so that it may be believed that demons entirely desire that the news of a coming death reaches the knowledge of those present and the members of the household.

4. By reason of the second location, it happens that noises are observed even in the most remote parts of the world: specifically, where those who are connected to the dying person by some relationship are staying. Therefore, what we said above applies here as well: that the work of a single Demon may not be sufficient, especially if these sounds are stirred up and heard at the same time in diverse locations.

5. And because they also occur in the third location—that is, where the dying person holds property—it follows that they are heard now in the fields, now in the fortresses, which are held in different places; and they occur for the same reason as those discussed in the previous Thesis.

6. But by reason of the fourth location, it happens that they are perceived in the forests, where effort was spent on hunting; they are perceived in workshops, where work was done; and in temples, where divine services were frequented. As we have said elsewhere, in a certain Church of the **Diocese of Mainz** <note>original: "Moguntinæ Diœcesis." Mainz was a powerful Archbishopric in the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, **Disturbances** are stirred up in that very spot where the one who is about to depart this life was accustomed to perform his divine duties.

7. Because (as the fifth location requires) the tomb and the candles pertain specifically to the funeral, it happens that in the houses of craftsmen and **candle-makers** <note>original: "Lychnopeiorum," a term for those who make lamps or candles.</note>, the sounds of everything being prepared and made are very frequently heard alongside this **Disturbance**—whatever is necessary either for constructing the coffin or for fashioning the funeral candles.

8. Finally, by reason of the sixth location, it happens that they are heard in temples and cemeteries, because Christians have their burials in these places. To these we add those places where justice is administered and just punishments are decreed for evildoers according to their merits; in these places, too, sometimes these noises are heard, and sometimes other signs are observed, which serve as certain evidence of the punishments to be inflicted on the guilty. So much for the Locations.

9. There are two primary times when these are stirred up: midday and the dead of night. The latter is appropriate for those Spirits; for, as the Lord says, *those who do evil flee the light* <note>original: "qui malè agunt, Domino dicente, lucem fugiunt." A reference to the Gospel of John 3:20.</note>; just as the night best serves their purpose, since in both [midday and midnight] there is a greater silence, which they more studiously seek for these occupations.

10. Demons especially observe these times; however, other times are not forbidden to them, and they have stirred up these **Disturbances** at other times as well. Just as they freely apply their thoughts to stirring these up, so can they choose whatever times they please for this duty.

*In this Treatise on Haunted Locations and Nocturnal Terrors, we wish nothing to be said that in any way conflicts with the orthodox faith or the judgment of those who think more correctly.*
